en: The first chapter of the Śrāddhakalpa in the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi.
Now begins the section on the praise of the fruits of the rules for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
This wise Hemādri-sūri conquers the swelling of the ocean of milk;
he who desires discipleship here seeks to understand his weightiness and the secret of his policy.
Surely even Bṛhaspati and that sage [Kavi] who vied with him must have been such;
for what man, foremost among the steadfast, did this Hemādri—the crest-jewel of the lords of ministers, whose greatness is honored by his wondrous deeds—not lead to a state of wonder? (27)

By whom— whose conduct was made beautiful by right behavior and reflection, and whose splendor was increased by the intense love of Nandana (the son of Nanda) gratified by his multitude of severe vows—
were the wives of the groups of Brahmins rendered [prosperous] with countless riches bestowed upon them.
In an instant, they uprooted the mountains, displaying the marvelous skill of breaking open the treasury chambers of the earth. || 28 ||

The silken garment of the goddesses of the quarters, the necklace of the Earth resplendent with white luster, the ornament for the hair of the celestial maiden consisting of a mass of freshly blossomed jasmine flowers,
and the beauty of the plaster of nectar applied within the lofty chambers of the cosmic egg— all these belong to Him.
Victorious is that Kīrtti, the minister of Hemādri, the ornament of the world and a bridge of dharma. || 28 ||

By means of which three thousand fierce [brahmins], learned in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, were indeed fed every day with foods consisting of various types such as savory juices, sweets, and linctuses— foods distinguished by diverse qualities, actions, and sequences, and revealed through delicious side-dishes.
And those whose minds were filled with the height of joy by the gold that was repeatedly scattered in great abundance; || 30 ||
Possessing abundant majesty manifested through great devotion to Hari and Hara,
his innate wisdom was fully cultivated; he was beautiful in the sequence of sacrificial rites and radiant with the splendor of a multitude of jewel-like virtues.
How indeed can that illustrious Hemādri, the ornament of the Karaṇas, be described? || 31 ||
And he composed the excellent treatise titled *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, which removes all the sufferings of those in distress without exception.
Thinking, "Some preeminent jewel, ejected by the belching of the milk-ocean as it was agitated by the force of the base of Mount Manthācala,
has gone to the abode of Indra," he churned the ocean of sound with the golden mountain.
The donor of the fourfold assembly is truly a stainless wish-fulfilling gem. || 33 ||
Here, five sections have been composed in succession through elaboration,
concerning vows, gifts, and the company of holy places.
And likewise regarding liberation, the remainder, and the various objects of purpose. || 34 ||
Having fully set forth the propitiation of the consumers of sacrificial offerings (the gods) in the fifth section,
Hemādri now describes that of the consumers of funeral oblations (the ancestors).
By means of the ritual for the ancestral offering (śrāddha), which possesses a most radiant splendor.
Having reflected upon many treatises, this ritual manual for the *śrāddha* is composed with great care;
it must not be introduced here hastily by anyone.
Even a very slight fault [is seen] by one whose intellect is clouded. || 36 ||
And there, in the first chapter, that wise Hemādri, possessing auspicious intentions, speaks of the ritual for the Śrāddha ceremony, joined with a praise of its fruits. (37)

First, the worship of deities such as Śiva, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and others was described in relation to the *liṅga*, images, and other substrates. Next, the worship of deities in the form of Nandā and other wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadhenu*), as well as Hari, Hara, and others, was described in relation to the substrate of the cow. Now, the worship of deities in the form of the ancestors—possessing great majesty and appearing as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Pitṛs, Matsya, Soma, Aṅgiras, Yamakavyavāhana, Agni, Somapa, Ājyapa, Agniṣvātta, and so forth—is being declared in relation to the substrate of the Brāhmaṇa and others. Worship (*ārādhana*) consists of the pleasing of the mind, and the means for that is the ritual characterized as the *śrāddha*. Therefore, that is now being explained.

In this regard, an injunction (*vidhi*), while impelling a person toward its own object of application, requires praise-statement (*praśaṃsā-vacana*) and statements of fruit (*phala-vacana*) that produce interest in the enjoined by creating an excellence in the person’s inclination toward what is to be accomplished. Just as these persons proceed toward the enjoined, so too do the listeners toward the treatise concerning it; therefore, for them as well, the statements regarding the injunction, the fruit, and the praise are the motivators. Thus, those topics pertaining to faith (*śrāddha*) are written first. And since these have attained the status of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) through mutual connection, this constitutes one single section (*prakaraṇa*).
Sumantu said:
No other act has been declared more conducive to supreme welfare than the śrāddha;
therefore, a wise person should perform the śrāddha with every effort.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Therefore, a man should perform a *śrāddha* with devotion, even with vegetables, according to the rules and with faith; in his family, no one shall ever suffer."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa,
there are likewise verses sung by the ancestors; hear them from me,
and having heard them, you should remain there with a disciplined mind.
Blessed indeed would be the wise man born into our family who,

disregarding wealth, shall offer us funeral cakes (piṇḍas); and who, possessing means, shall bestow upon the Brahmins jewels, garments, great vehicles, all enjoyments, and other riches, dedicating them to us.
Or, at this time, a man who possesses only that much wealth, with his mind bowed in devotion, shall feed the foremost of Brahmins according to his ability and according to the occasion.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "In other worlds, they obtain neither water nor food;
those for whom no offerings have been given by their descendants go to a terrible state in vain."
Therefore, O King, one should always satisfy the ancestors who have arisen from hunger and thirst with water and various kinds of food according to one's ability.
Likewise, with foods, garments, and offerings, with flowers, perfumes, and unguents,
and with meritorious rites such as the Pitṛmedha and various kinds of Śrāddha ceremonies.
When satisfied, O Great King, those ancestors grant the desired objects that dwell in the heart, as well as the three aims of life, when they have been gratified by the śrāddha rite.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"He who performs the śrāddha according to this rite with a tranquil mind,
being eternally freed from all taint, goes forth and does not return again."
The twins said: "This most excellent ordinance for the sake of desire has been devised here by the twice-born;
those Brahmins who indeed follow it attain eternal worlds."
[10] Through the worship of the flour-image (piṣṭapūjana), one shall obtain long life, sons, fame, heaven, renown, nourishment, strength, prosperity, cattle, happiness, wealth, and grain.
In the Brahmapurāṇa: "Thus, by the householder, the deities and likewise the ancestors are to be properly worshipped with *havya* and *kavya*, as well as guests and kinsmen with food."
In that regard, a man should observe the conduct based on the Pitṛmedha;
he increases in longevity, wealth, and sons—of this there is no doubt.
In the Devalasmṛti: "One who performs the Śrāddha here shall be free from disease, established in his natural state, long-lived, possessed of sons and grandsons, wealthy, and an enjoyer of riches."
Furthermore, the man who performs the śrāddha rite attains supreme nourishment in the hereafter, vast and auspicious worlds, and extensive renown.
In the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyu Purāṇas*:
"The rite for the ancestors always excels even the rite for the gods;
for the nourishment of the ancestors is auspiciously prior to that of the deities."

Regarding all rites for the gods (*daiva*), because the *śrāddha* that is an auxiliary part of the ritual is performed first, there is the nourishment of the ancestors before the gods; this is the statement of Varāha in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "From this day forward, for those who perform the *śrāddha* in the worlds for the sake of the deceased ancestors, there shall be prosperity."
Likewise, those who perform the offering of funeral cakes with food at the time of the Śrāddha ceremony for the ancestors shall attain nourishment.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three shall be honored, as shall the sacred fires.
The three worlds, the three Vedas, and likewise the three ages;
and the three gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, have been worshipped.
"Even so, I shall be worshipped by them as fourfold in nature:
Vāsudeva is proclaimed as the ancestral offering (piṇḍa) belonging to my father and grandfather,
and the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa is likewise designated as the offering belonging to my grandfather."
The *pitr-piṇḍa* should be known as Pradyumna, and Aparājita;
Ātman and Aniruddha are to be understood by the wise as the *piṇḍa* offerings.
Thus worshipped by him, I, who am fourfold in nature, shall remain present;
I will grant him his desires and whatever he wishes for.
The four Vedas have been honored, as well as the four stages of life;
the four aims of human existence, and likewise the four directions.
And likewise there are four castes, and likewise four ages.
"Paitṛpaitāmaha" means belonging to the father's grandfather; that is to say, reaching back to the great-grandfather. As stated in the *Yama-smṛti*:
"Those who worship the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins who consume the oblations..."
They worship Viṣṇu alone, the inner self of all beings.
In the Brahma Purāṇa:
Having performed the Śrāddha rite in this manner according to the prescribed rules and in accordance with one's own means,
a person gratifies the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Nāsatyas, Sūrya, Agni, the Vasus, and the Maruts;
the Viśvedevas, the hosts of ṛṣis, birds, humans, and animals."
By performing the śrāddha rite with faith, one indeed satisfies the reptiles, the hosts of ancestors, and whatever else is designated as a living being; for it satisfies them all.

The meaning of the statement is that when a *śrāddha* is performed by any person on behalf of his own father and grandfather, there occurs the simultaneous gratification of many others—such as Brahmā, Indra, and so forth—even though they were not specifically intended, as well as the satisfaction of even reptiles and other beings born of different lineages. Furthermore, it is clearly stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya*, *Skanda*, and *Brahma Purāṇas* that for those born in the lineage of the performer of the *śrāddha*, even if they have gone to various wombs and were not specifically intended, there shall be satisfaction for many through the constituent parts of that particular *śrāddha* rite performed in a single performance.
Whatever scattering of food is performed on the ground by humans,
by that those who have fallen into the state of Piśācas attain satisfaction.
O son, by the water that falls upon the ground from the bathing garments,
satisfaction is produced for those who have attained the state of trees.
Those drops of scented water which fall upon the surface of the earth provide nourishment for those who have gone into the wombs of animals.
And those children in the family who are toothless, immature, unfit for ritual acts, and unconsecrated— they perish by eating scattered grains, sweepings, and water.
Furthermore, by the water used for sipping after eating and that which arises from the washing of the feet of the Brahmins,
others likewise indeed attain satisfaction.
Those who have attained the state of Piśācas or even the state of worms and insects—
such is the fate of both the sacrificer and those twice-born ones.
O child, even if there is only a small amount of water,
food, or the remains of an oblation cast into that family, those who have passed into various other wombs attain full nourishment through that food when the śrāddha rites are properly performed.
The śrāddha that is performed by men with wealth acquired through unjust means—
by that, those born in wombs such as the caṇḍālas and pukkasas are satisfied.
In this way, O child, even by relatives performing the śrāddha with food, water, and vegetables, the nourishment of many ancestors is indeed brought about.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "When a *śrāddha* is being performed, nothing whatsoever shall go to waste;
even the remnants [are meritorious], O King of Kings. Therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha*."
O King, whatever water from the feet of Brahmins falls upon the ground,
by that water the ancestors drink as long as any of their kinsmen who died childless continue to do so, using lotus-leaf cups.
O Lord of Men, whatever falls upon the ground while the śrāddha is being performed—
whether it be flowers, scents, food, or even water— [all that belongs to the ancestors].
By that, O lord of men, those who have fallen into the state of worms, or even into the state of insects, animals, or predatory beasts, attain supreme satisfaction.
Whatever remains as leavings on the ground, arising from the washing of the alms-bowl,
by that those who have entered the state of a preta attain supreme satisfaction.
And those of one's own lineage who have met death by an untimely demise—
all of them attain satisfaction through the offering of this scattered oblation.

Thus, it has been stated that the satisfaction of certain ancestors occurs through the constituent parts of the *śrāddha*; however, it has also been stated that the satisfaction of the primary intended recipients—the father, grandfather, and so forth—occurs through the principal rite, namely the feeding of the Brahmins and other such acts. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Whatever *kavya* is given to Brahmins with the ancestors in view..."
For other mortals who possess right faith, that [offering] shall be a source of great satisfaction.
"He is the lord of all the gods of the ancestors"—this is the Vedic revelation.
[This applies] to the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather beyond him.
By giving with devotion to the Brahmins according to their specific requirements,
there shall be supreme satisfaction for all of them until the dissolution of all beings.

Now, one might object: how can there be satisfaction for those who possess an abundance of merit and have gone to the heavenly world—such as human fathers, grandfathers, and so forth—who subsist on nectar (*amṛta*), by means of human food that is perishable through the feeding of Brahmins? Or how can there be satisfaction for those who are more sinful, such as those born as animals who subsist on grass and the like, or those who have entered the state of *preta*s and so forth and subsist on blood and the like? As stated in the *Pādya* and *Mātsya* Purāṇas: "If it is eaten by mortals, or if it is offered into the fire by twice-born men, how can that which is given be consumed by *preta*s whose nature consists of both the auspicious and the inauspicious?"
The resolution of this objection is stated in that very same place.
Regarding this, Devala says:
"If the father has been born as a god due to his engagement in virtuous deeds..."
His food, having become nectar, follows him even into the state of divinity.
In the state of a Gandharva, he becomes an object of enjoyment; in the state of a beast, he becomes grass;
and in the state of a Naga, he follows after the food of a Śrāddha rite in the form of wind.
"In the state of a yakṣa there is drink; likewise, in the state of a rākṣasa there is flesh. In the state of a dānava there is meat; in the state of a preta, blood and water.
In the state of a human, there would be food, drink, and so forth—the essence of various enjoyments. Thus it is said.

Now, an objection is raised: "Just as the transformation of milk into the form of curd, and of curd into the form of buttermilk and so forth, is perceived directly by the senses, such a transformation of food being eaten or an oblation being offered into the fire—into the form of nectar (*amṛta*) or the form of grass and the like—is not observed. Furthermore, it is not possible for that which has been transformed, being devoid of independent power of action, to reach living beings in another location. Nor is it logical for deceased persons, who have fallen under the sway of various *karman*s, to approach the site of a *śrāddha* ceremony. Moreover, it is impossible for this [oblation] to establish a distinct relationship with the ancestors of the performer of the *śrāddha*, whose true forms are obscured by thousands of millions of species, such as Suparṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, Piśācas, Narakins, Kinnaras, beasts, birds, worms, insects, and so forth. These and other such objections are indicated in the Purāṇas.
In the *Padma* and *Matsya* [Purāṇas]:
"How do the *kavya* offerings and the *havya* offerings given here by people reach the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*), and who is said to be the one who conveys them?"
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"If food eaten by another results in the satisfaction of a person, then one should offer food with faith at the śrāddha; those who are traveling abroad would not carry it."
[16] In the Skanda Purāṇa: "If the śrāddha for deceased beings were to provide nourishment,
it would be like adding oil to increase the flame of an extinguished lamp."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"For what purpose is the *śrāddha* performed by the twice-born on the new moon day and other occasions? And do deceased persons, O Brahmin, attain a destination produced by their own karma?"
How can they go and reach the hermitage of that son?
Even the resolutions for this have been indicated in the Purāṇas; therein, in the *Mātsya* and *Padma*, it is said:
"The name and lineage of the ancestors are what convey the *havya* and *kavya* offerings."
Likewise, the mantras for the śrāddha rite should be acquired with devotion.

The meaning is that the names of the ancestors and so forth are to be perceived—that is, they are to be known. Now, one might object: "Since names and so forth are insentient, how can they be the conveyors of the *havya* (offerings to gods) and *kavya* (offerings to ancestors)? Anticipating this doubt, it is said:
"The Agniṣvātta and other deities are established as their presiding lords."

It is stated that the specific ancestors, such as the Agniṣvātta-s and others, are the presiding deities and the conveyors [of the offerings]. Now, one might object: if the name and lineage (*nāma-gotra*) are the conveyors, then a *śrāddha* performed when the name and lineage are unknown would be useless. Furthermore, this would contradict the Āpastamba Sūtra which says: "If one does not know the name, one should offer the first rice-ball with the mantra: 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth, six in number. Anticipating this objection, the fact that even modified words (*ūha-pada*) serve as conveyors is demonstrated in that very same text: "The name-mantras and their substitutes [convey] those who have passed into other births."
These [beings] satisfy living creatures that have become their food.

[17] "Their substitutes" (tadādeśāḥ) means words that have been transformed through methods such as modification (*ūha*) and so forth, which serve as substitutes for names, lineages, mantras, and the like. Furthermore, there is another sense: the meaning is that mantras revealing Agniṣvātta and others, which cannot in any way establish a connection with names such as Devadatta or with mantras that reveal emptiness, as well as the names and mantras themselves, act as their substitutes by performing their function. As it is said: "Authorized by the Brāhmaṇas, he who bears the names of his ancestors worships them correctly, even though they are excluded from the ritual rules and mantras."
This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:

"Even those who have gone to other states of existence" means even those who have entered into various other places, times, wombs (*yoni*), and conditions. By the phrase "having become their food," it is stated that the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) offered undergoes transformation into the form of nectar (*sudhā*) and other appropriate foods for each respective womb, solely due to the extraordinary cause consisting of the mantras and so forth. The mention of "mantras and so forth" is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the entire ritual procedure pertaining to the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, it is said in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"At the proper time, [the gift] acquired by righteous means and presented according to the rule to a worthy recipient..."
These lead the food to that place where the living being resides.
Just as a calf finds its mother when the cows have been lost,
so does the food brought by the Brahmin lead the living being to wherever it resides.
They lead away the name, the lineage, and the mantra, as well as the food that was given;
even when they have reached a hundred wombs, it remains present for them once they are satisfied.
Thus, it has been stated that the mantras and other elements convey the oblation to the ancestors who reside in another world and have not yet arrived at the place of the *śrāddha* offering.
In the same way, after describing the stateless *preta* and the ancestors who do not abide in a fixed location, it is said in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"To those residing in other worlds, by means of their various names and lineages..."
The pindas offered by the sons upon the ground on the darbha grass indeed go to and satisfy the ancestors situated in the realm of the departed.
Those who are foremost on earth in five ways have not reached the places of torment;
they are those born in various forms within the wombs of animals and other such births.
Whatever food these beings have in their various births here,
that very food— consisting of the offerings made with faith— approaches them in each of those states.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, after enumerating the divine groups of ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*), it is said:
"These are always the partakers of the *śrāddha* together with the *viśvedevas*;
having always consumed the *śrāddha*, they indeed satisfy the ancestors."
For those who know the Dharma, wherever they may dwell, abide indeed through the power of yoga.
These [ancestors], being insatiable, bestow excellent nourishment upon the giver of the śrāddha;
likewise, they provide him with satisfaction.
O lord of the earth, [he leads] all the hosts of the ancestors of the donor.
In the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*:
"The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the *śrāddha*;
when satiated by the *śrāddha*, they gratify the ancestors of human beings."

[19] Just as a pregnant woman, while consuming substances offered by a friend to satisfy her pregnancy-longings (*dohada*), is herself satisfied, and by those very substances satisfies the fetus within her own womb, and gratifies the benefactor who provided the longings with reciprocal favors; in the same way, the *agniṣvātta*s and other such deities—possessing inconceivable majesty due to their status as specific gods—having partaken of the *śrāddha*, are themselves satisfied and satisfy the human ancestors presided over by them, and they endow the performer of the *śrāddha* with fruits such as longevity. This is the intended meaning. Regarding this, it has been stated that for those ancestors who lack the power to know supersensuous objects separated by space and time, nor the power to come to the place of the *śrāddha*, satisfaction occurs through the oblation (*havis*) conveyed by means of mantras and so forth, even while they remain in another location. It is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* that for those endowed with supersensuous knowledge and the power of movement, having arrived at the place of the *śrāddha*, satisfaction occurs through a body composed of air (*vāyavīya-śarīra*) while they have entered the bodies of the Brahmins.
Upon hearing that the time for the śrāddha has arrived, the ancestors are satisfied;
reflecting upon one another in their minds, they descend with the speed of thought.
For the ancestors dwelling in the intermediate space eat together with those Brahmins;
having become like the wind, they remain there, and after eating, they go to the supreme goal.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"For the ancestors indeed attend upon those invited twice-born men;
they follow them like the wind and likewise wait upon them as they sit."
Likewise, regarding the position of a single Brāhmaṇa, Baudhāyana says:
"The fathers are on his chest; the grandfathers on his left side;
the great-grandfathers on his right; and those who consume the *piṇḍas* are behind him."
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa* and other texts:
"On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja, under the Maghā asterism,
at the end of the rainy season, Yama [releases] the departed spirits and the ancestors from the abode of Yama."
Having left his own city empty, he departs from the human world.
Afflicted by hunger and confessing their own misdeeds,
they long for milk-rice mixed with honey for the sake of their sons and grandsons;
therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the ritual rule with that very milk-rice.

Since the ancestors, endowed with the power of movement, come to the place of the *śrāddha*, it is for this very reason that when Rāma was performing a *śrāddha* at the Viyogavāpī during the pilgrimage to Puṣkara, Sītā saw Daśaratha and the others within the body of a Brahmin. Thus it is said in the *Padmapurāṇa*: "When the cooked food prepared by Jānakī was offered to Rāma, he bathed in the Viyogavāpī and maintained his state of being well-bathed."
When the sun had moved into the Maghā constellation and it was the Kutapa hour,
all the sages who had been invited by Rāma arrived.
Seeing those sages arrive, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka,
moved away to a distance from where she had been standing in the midst of the brahmins;
concealing herself behind a thicket, she remained there hidden.
Then, perceiving that Sītā had departed, the joy of the Raghus reflected for a very long time: "Why has this virtuous woman gone elsewhere so quickly? I suspect she is overcome with shame. [21]
"Should I first feed the Brahmins, or should I search for Sītā?
I do not know the cause at all now that the time for the Śrāddha has arrived.
Having said this, Rāma fed the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites.
When the foremost of the twice-born had departed, Rāma said this to his beloved:
"O fair-browed one, why did you vanish upon seeing the assembled sages?
O slender-limbed lady, tell me the reason for all of that without delay."
Thus addressed by her husband, she then stood with her face cast down in shame;
shedding a flood of tears, she spoke these words to Rāghava.
Listen, O Lord, to that wonder which you have asked about here:
I beheld your father, O Raghava, within the limbs of a brahmin.
Seeing two others likewise adorned with all ornaments,
I was overcome with shame and withdrew from your presence.
Clad in bark and deerskin, how shall I walk before the king?
O slayer of enemy heroes, this which I have spoken is the truth.
How could this food, which even the servants' servants never consume, be brought by your own hand to the King? Tell me, how can you possibly offer such a thing to him?
"How shall I behold the lord of the earth, whose limbs were once seen by the king adorned with all ornaments, now with his body smeared with sweat and filth? Thus she spoke.
[22] In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, the arrival of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) toward the place of the *śrāddha* is described:
"When the day of the new moon has arrived, the hosts of ancestors, having become like the wind, approach the door of the house of men seeking the *śrāddha*."
Until the setting of the sun, they remained agitated by hunger and thirst; then, when the sun had set, hopeless and filled with sorrow,
they sighed for a long time and departed, reproaching their own lineage.
Ānarta said:
"O Brahmin, deceased men go to the destination produced by their own karma;
how then could they reach the hermitage of that son?"
Bhartṛyajña said:
"O highly fortunate one, this which you have spoken is true:
everywhere, deceased human beings go to a destination corresponding to their own actions."
However, I shall explain to you how they come here to the hermitage of my kinsman, so that no doubt may remain.
O King, O Great-minded One, those who have died and whatever others there may be go [to that state];
they are not born again here among mortals as long as the lineage remains established.
Furthermore, those whose nature is virtuous abide in the abode of the gods;
and even those men who are sinful, having entered another body, enjoy the fruit of their actions in the celestial realm.
O King, even when a meritorious funeral rite (śrāddha) is performed by one’s own descendants for their own sake,
hunger and thirst arise with even greater intensity for those who remain in the world of the ancestors as well as for those residing in heaven.
O King, as many as three generations of fathers and likewise mothers who are uplifted by a *śrāddha* at Gayā enjoy auspiciousness in the worlds of Brahmā;
hunger or thirst never arises for them anywhere.
Nor, O lord of the earth, does one fall from that state;
however, due to the extinction of the lineage, they all eventually fall back down to the great earth.
Having come from there, mortals fall to the surface of the earth;
the sinful incur sin, while those endowed with merit attain the most excellent womb.
Thus, it is established that the ancestors are satisfied by the sacrificial offering given in the śrāddha rite, and that the divine ancestors are the bestowers of the fruit [of those offerings].

Regarding this, some say: the nature of a deity (*devatātva*) consists in being the intended recipient of the oblation (*havis*), but not in being the consumer of the oblation or the bestower of the fruit. This is because we observe that even insentient things possess the status of a deity in such cases as "Svāhā to the pressing-stones" (*grāvabhyaḥ svāhā*); furthermore, it is not accepted that Indra and others possess the status of a deity by virtue of having a physical body and so forth. Since the status of a deity is established through the possibility of being the intended recipient, even for ancestors (*pitṛ*) and others who may possess various forms, the cause of the fruit belongs solely to the ritual action (*karman*). The attribution of the status of a deity to that which is merely a means (*sādhana*) for that action is employed figuratively (*upacāra*) in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of praise. Even the passage concerning satisfaction (*tṛpti*) is intended solely to express excellence (*prāśastya*), as it implies qualities such as sentience only in a figurative sense.

That is not so; for in all the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts, the commencement of the Śrāddha is seen to have the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛtṛpti*) as its primary purpose. Furthermore, the status of being the bestower of the fruit is mentioned many times—in the beginning, middle, and end—of both the injunctions and the mantras. Since the most learned among the refined (*śiṣṭa*), due to the firmness of their understanding, do not perceive anything in the world that would cause doubt, it is impossible to conceive of the falsity of either the satisfaction or the bestowing of the fruit. Just as these scriptural passages concerning the Śrāddha are shown in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas to establish various fruits such as the satisfaction of the ancestors, so too are those passages which establish the sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by not performing it likewise recorded.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"O King, those sinful men who do not daily offer libations to their own ancestors are to be known as mere beasts— two-legged creatures devoid of horns."

Those who, failing to perform the *śrāddha*—which requires little effort yet yields great fruit—accept the misfortune of transgression; whose knowledge is shrouded by the quality of darkness (*tamas*); who do not discern what is beneficial from what is harmful; and who, due to their similarity with cattle, are themselves "cattle" (beasts)—for them it is as follows: "Even he who performs the *śrāddha* with only water or even with vegetables on the new-moon day (*amā*), his ancestors depart after having uttered a curse."
In the Hārītasmṛti: "Neither heroes are born there, nor those free from disease, nor those with a lifespan of a hundred years;
nor do they attain any higher good in that place where the Śrāddha is avoided."
Even with roots, fruits, or likewise with water-offerings, they perform [the rite] when [proper materials] are unavailable; one should never abandon the Śrāddha altogether.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, after enumerating the regular times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the *aṣṭaka* days, it is stated:
"The wise have declared these to be the obligatory times for the *pākaśrāddha*.
However, the occasional (*naimittika*) rite must be performed during lunar and solar eclipses."
This must be done for one's kinsmen; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell.
In the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyu Purāṇas*, after prescribing the *śrāddha* on the *aṣṭakā* days, it is stated:
"The ancestors come to a man at the times of the festivals (*parva-kāla*), and the deities at the times of the lunar days (*tithi-kāla*), just as cows come to a watering place."
If these [ancestors] do not return to him because they have not been honored with the Aṣṭakā offerings, his hopes will become fruitless in every respect, both in this world and in the next.
For those who worship, there is constant prosperity; for the nihilists, there is a downward path.
Those who give to the gods go upward; those who do not give go to the state of animals.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*, there is a variant reading:
"His world shall be in vain, and what he has acquired shall perish.
In the *Viṣṇusmṛti* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, it is stated after enumerating the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such times:
Prajāpati has declared these times for the śrāddha to be obligatory;
one who does not perform the śrāddha on these occasions falls into hell.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "If a man, thinking in his mind that 'the ancestors do not exist,' fails to perform the *śrāddha* out of delusion, they drink his blood."

Thus, the greatness of the *śrāddha* has been described by way of praising the *śrāddha* itself. Now, the majesty of the *śrāddha* is being declared in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* by way of praising the ancestors (*pitṛs*), who are the deities of the *śrāddha*:
"Neither the subtle path of yoga nor the supreme goal of the ancestors can be seen even through asceticism; how much less so with the eye of flesh? (26)
There are four ancestors who possess form, and likewise three who are formless;
having honored their śrāddha rites with care, the gods perform them with great effort.
All the gods, devoted with palms joined in reverence and their minds fixed upon him,
as well as the Viśvedevas, the Vasus, the horned animals,
and the black, white, and hornless goats, likewise worship him according to the prescribed rites.
Prajāpati, Vātasvana, and likewise Divākṛti;
as well as the clouds, the Maruts, and the celestial dwellers beginning with Brahmā.
Atri, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and all the other sages,
as well as the yakṣas, nāgas, suparṇas, and kinnaras together with the rākṣasas—
all of them constantly worshipped those ancestors, seeking the fruits [of their devotion].
Thus, when these great-souled ones are honored and worshipped by the faithful,
they grant all desires by the hundreds and thousands.
Having abandoned the cycle of the three worlds as well as the fear of old age and death,
the ancestors bestow liberation, yoga, sovereignty, the subtle body, bodilessness, complete dispassion, and infinity.
The eternal dharma of liberation is the most excellent among all dharmas;
indeed, it is attained by a great-souled one through the grace of the ancestors.
The ancestors bestow pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, horses, elephants, weapons, and indeed jewels by the millions.
[27] Adorned with swans and peacocks, and possessing pearls and lapis lazuli; draped with networks of tiny bells, and always bearing flowers and fruits.
The ancestors bestow thousands of celestial mansions, frequented by throngs of apsaras and enriched with all objects of desire.

When pleased, the ancestors constantly bestow upon human beings progeny, nourishment, memory, intelligence, sovereignty, and even health. He who gratifies the ancestors with devotion, the ancestors in turn gratify him.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The first group consists of the yogis, who eternally increase yoga;
the second consists of the deities, and the third consists of the enemies of the gods."
The remaining ones are to be known as peacocks; thus all have been proclaimed.
Indeed, the gods worship these [peacocks], who are established within all of them.
The four stages of life worship them in due order,
and likewise, during the rainy season, those four worship them according to the prescribed rule.
Just as those born of mixed castes and even the Mlecchas perform sacrifices,
so indeed should the ancestors be honored, for they are the creators of place and time.
Through constant devotion to his father, he then attains unsurpassed yoga;
through yoga, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, he obtains liberation.
For the sake of sacrifice, having extracted and deluded the world at that time,
the Yoga was placed in a secret cave by the high-souled Kaśyapa.
And a person devoted to their father shall, by means of this yoga in its entirety, obtain everything without effort; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever jewels are upon the earth, as well as vehicles and women—
a man devoted to his father quickly attains all of that.

A king indeed obtains a kingdom, and one who is destitute obtains the highest wealth; a man who is always devoted to his ancestors recovers even when his life-span is exhausted. Whatever desires he may wish for in his mind, his ancestors shall surely grant them to him.
In the *Mātsya*, *Padma*, and other Purāṇas it is said:
"O King, when gratified, the hosts of ancestors bestow longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and even sovereignty."
The power of pleasure is a beloved woman; the power of enjoyment is the capacity for food;
the power of giving is abundant wealth; beauty is the perfection of health.
This is declared to be the flower of the *śrāddha*, and union with Brahman is its fruit.
For it is heard that in ancient times the sons of Kauśika attained liberation;
through five successive births, they reached the supreme state of Brahman.
There was a great sage named Kauśika, a righteous soul in Kurukṣetra;
learn now of his seven sons, both by name and by their deeds.
[29] At that time, the disciples of Garga were as follows: Khasṛma, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi, Vāgduṣṭa, and Pitṛvartin.
When their father had passed away, a terrible famine occurred for them,
along with a great drought that struck fear into all the world.
Then those twice-born ones, guarding the milch-cow in the forest by the command of Garga and others,
said, "Let us kill this one cow, Kapilā, for we are greatly oppressed by hunger."
While they were thus reflecting, the younger brother then spoke briefly:
"Now, she must certainly be killed; let her be employed in the form of a śrāddha offering."
"Employed at a *śrāddha*, she will certainly protect us from evil.
Having been thus authorized by his elder brothers to follow the path of the ancestors, he,
being composed, performed the *śrāddha* after touching Kapilā.
Having assigned two brothers to the rite for the gods (daiva), three others in succession to the father (pitṛ),
and likewise one guest, the giver of the śrāddha himself [participates].
Devoted to his ancestors, he performed the śrāddha ceremony with the recitation of mantras. With that cow, they reported to their teacher without hesitation:
"This cow has been seized by a great tiger; let this calf be accepted."
Thus she became a cow by means of those seven ascetics,
who, relying on Vedic power, were fearless in their cruel deed;
thereafter, drawn away by time, those hunters came to dwell in Dāśapura.

From this it is known that Dāśapura was located in the Daśārṇa country, as seen in the *Harivaṃśa*: "Seven hunters were born among the Daśārṇas, experts in the Dharma. [30] Having attained the recollection of their former births, they experienced the state of being fathers because of that which they had previously performed in the form of a *śrāddha*, even though it was a cruel act.
Born thus in the abode of those hunters of cruel deeds,
they were nevertheless born with the memory of their former lives due to the greatness of their ancestors.
These were the names of those high-souled ones:
Nirvaira, Nirvṛti, Kṣānta, Nirmanyu, Kṛti, Vaidhasa, and Mātṛvartin; they were hunters who were supremely righteous.
Having died after undertaking a fast through the practice of detachment,
those seven deer were reborn on Mount Kālañjara as beings who remembered their former births.
With face turned upward, perpetually terrified, with ears pricked and eyes wide, he is wise yet gluttonous; such are those proclaimed by name as the *nādīs*.
Restraining their senses and subsisting on sparse food, they gave up their lives while practicing the *maru* (desert) penance;
indeed, the stations of those who were thus perfecting the *maru* are located there.
Even today, on the auspicious Kālañjara mountain, those yogis who have attained detachment by leaping from the heights are seen in that very same manner.
Those seven yogins were born as cakravāka birds on Lake Mānasa;
O best of sages, hear from me their names and their deeds.
Sumanas, Kumuda, Śuddha, Chidradarśin,
Sunetraka, Svatantra, and Śakuna— these seven have reached the further shore of yoga.
He saw one named Vibhrāja in a garden, accompanied by women,
sporting with various enjoyments, and possessed of great strength and prowess.

[31] Consequently, they fell away from yoga and became small-minded. Among those water-dwellers, there was one who desired sovereignty; he was a brahmin who followed his father, performed ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and was devoted to his father.
Seeing two other ministers who possessed great strength and many vehicles,
Kaṇḍarīka and Subāla set their minds upon the office of minister.
But Brahmadatta, having been consecrated in Kāmpilya, the best of cities,
became renowned as the king of Pañcāla; he was an expert in all the śāstras,
a knower of yoga, and at that time, he understood the cries of all living beings.
At that time, the king had a wife who was the daughter of Devala;
she was renowned by the name Sannati, who in former times had been Kapilā.
Because she was appointed to the ancestral rites, she became a speaker of the Veda;
thus did that delight of the kingdom rule the realm together with her.
And those four great twice-born ones who did not fall away from yoga were born in that very city; they were then known as the Cakrāhvayas,
the sons of the elder twice-born one, brahmins who remembered their former births.
Endowed with mindfulness, a seer of reality, and eager for the penance of the moon of knowledge—
these shall be your sons, both by name and by their deeds, O Sudaridra.
Then the minds of those twice-born ones turned toward austerity;
"We shall attain supreme perfection," said those best of the twice-born.
Then, having heard those words, Sudaridra, a man of great austerity, spoke with a piteous voice: "O sons, what is this?"
"This is unrighteous," your father said to them;
"having abandoned your aged father, who is poor and dwelling in the forest, what dharma is there for you? Your conduct is indeed unjust."
They said to him, "We have devised a livelihood for you; listen to us.
This event occurred long ago involving a king, and he will give you abundant wealth and thousands of villages in the morning to you as you recite."
Those who were Brahmins in Kurukṣetra became hunters in Dāśapura;
those who were deer in Kālañjara became cakravāka birds in Lake Mānasa.
Having spoken thus to their father, they went again to the forest for asceticism;
the aged king, too, went to the royal palace for his own prosperity.
Then at dawn, as the king was departing from the city surrounded by his army,
accompanied by his ministers and his wife,
he beheld an elderly brahmin approaching and speaking to him.
The elder said: "Those who were born as the foremost of Brahmins in Kurujāṅgala, as well as those born as deer in Dāśapura,"
There were seven cakravāka birds on Kālañjara; we, who were at Mānasa, were unknown to them.

In another Purāṇa, however, it is stated that after the descendants of Kauśika had become cakravāka birds at a certain reservoir of water on the island of Saradvīpa, they were subsequently born as royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*) in Lake Mānasa. Accordingly, there are verses bearing this mark in the Nandikhaṇḍa and other texts:

"Those who, though greatly afflicted by the curse resulting from the murder of their guru and the slaughter of cows, were devoted to their father and possessed beneficial knowledge, were all born for the arising of Śiva."
[33] The seven hunters became deer in Daśārṇa; on Mount Kālañjara they became cakravāka birds;
in the island of Sarat they became cakravākas; and in Lake Mānasa they became swans.
"Having understood this very thing, why do you despair?
Having reflected upon it according to its true nature—that kingship is exceedingly fickle—renounce this human birth and indeed follow our word. Thus [he spoke].

In the *Harivaṃśa* and other texts, however, after beginning with "The seven hunters" and concluding with "They became swans on Lake Mānasa," the remainder of the statement is given: "They too were born at Kurukṣetra as Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas; you have fallen away from them after setting out upon a long journey. Thus it is said in the *Pādma* and *Mātsya* Purāṇas:
"Having heard these words, the king, overcome with grief, fell down."
And both those two chief ministers also attained the recollection of their former births.
"Alas! We have fallen from yoga due to desire and the bondage of karma.
Having lamented thus many times, those three who had reached the further shore of yoga—
Having forgotten [his previous state], he repeatedly rejoiced in the greatness of the *śrāddha*;
then, having given him wealth consisting of many villages, [the king departed].
The king consecrated the one named Viśvaksena upon the throne;
thereafter, all those foremost of yogins assembled at Lake Mānasa.
Brahmadatta and the others, devoted to their father and free from envy,
then all took up the practice of yoga and became forest-dwellers.

[34] By the power of their asceticism, Sanatī and others reached the supreme state through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), having established themselves in the imperishable station by means of supreme yoga.
In the *Harivaṃśa*: "O Acyuta, this indeed happened thus in the past before my very eyes;
bear that in mind, O son of Gaṅgā, and you shall thereby be united with the highest good."
And those others who shall uphold this supreme conduct,
they shall never at any time be born among the animal realms.
O Bhārata, having heard this significant narrative concerning the path of the great ones, the dharma of yoga shall always revolve within your heart.
"By that very persistence, he may at some time attain tranquility;
thereafter, he proceeds toward the state of yoga, which is difficult even for the perfected ones (siddhas) to attain. Thus it is said.

The essential meaning of this narrative of the seven hunters (*saptavyādhopākhyāna*), which consists of an *arthavāda* in the form of a past account (*purākalpa*), is as follows: when even for those who, out of their own hunger, have deceived their teacher—even though she was his property and not permitted—have killed even a cow, and having provided a *śrāddha* meal for their *sapindas*, have performed a *śrāddha* through deception, there occurred in another birth such things as the recollection of previous lives, the attainment of yoga preceded by such knowledge and dispassion, the acquisition of sovereignty, the knowledge of the cries of living beings, and the attainment of liberation; then what need is there to speak of those who perform a *śrāddha* according to the rules, having properly seated the twice-born who are worthy recipients and who know the Vedas and their meaning, after providing them with food consisting of rice, barley, clarified butter, and so forth, prepared from wealth acquired by righteous means and fashioned with exquisite refinement? For them, fruits beginning with long life and health and culminating in the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) come to pass. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: [35] ... (omitted text) ... ... [the results are attained]. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
O protector of the earth, sacrifice brings heaven and liberation, as well as happiness, sovereignty, sons,
excellent women, and various objects of desire.

"The Lord of the Gods ordains [this] for one who performs the *śrāddha*. Likewise, there are other fruits arising from specific types of *śrāddha*: namely, prosperity in the case of the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity-rite); excellence in the performance of a ritual when the *śrāddha* is an ancillary part of that ritual; success in a pilgrimage when it is an ancillary part of a pilgrimage; the non-arising of transgression and the destruction of accumulated sins in the case of independent rites; and the attainment of a distinguished world by the ancestors in the case of *śrāddhas* at sacred sites such as Gayā. However, the satisfaction of the ancestors is the purpose common to all *śrāddhas*. Hārīta has also stated the fruit of reciting the rules for the *śrāddha*.
Whoever performs or even recites this meritorious rite for the ancestors shall be endowed with all desires and indeed attain immortality.
Bṛhaspati, however, has also stated the fruit for those who provide instruction on the knowledge of the *śrāddha* ritual or give their consent:
"The wise man who understands it thus shall obtain the fruit of the *śrāddha*;
both the instructor and the one who consents are recorded in the world as having equal merit."

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Praise of the Fruits of the Śrāddha Rite," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the scholar Śrī Hemādri, the preeminent minister of all affairs under the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva.
[35] Now begins the second chapter:
The Section on the Definition of the Ancestors (Pitṛs).
The Golden Mountain (Meru), whose fame steals away the splendor of the rows of peaks of the Snowy Mountain (Himālaya),
composes this detailed description of the ancestors, rich in many virtues.
This composition brings joy to the assembly of the wise.

In the section just concluded, it was stated that the ancestors (*pitṛs*), when propitiated by those performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), bestow rewards. Now, another section is commenced in order to define them through their origins and other characteristics. Furthermore, the subject matter of this section is introduced by way of a question in the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas*:
"Who, O Lord, are these who are called ancestors? Where do they reside?
Who are remembered as their sons, and how are they remembered as ancestors?"
How did they originate? Whose sons are they, and what is their nature? Indeed, the ancestors (pitṛs) are one thing, while others are the deities even of the gods.
Which ancestors dwell in heaven, and which in hell? For what reason are they not seen there; what is recorded as the cause for this?
Who are the ancestors to be honored, and whom should we worship in turn?
For we have heard that even the gods worship the ancestors in heaven.
[37] We wish to know this in detail, O one of great learning; you ought to speak of its meaning with clear expression.

All of this is now stated. First, regarding their origin: that [origin] is seen to be twofold in the Purāṇas; in some cases they are directly the bodies of Brahmā, and in others by means of an intermediary. Regarding that, it is stated directly in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Then he assumed another body consisting solely of the element of truth (satya-mātra);
as he was thinking of them as his fathers, the Pitṛs were born to him."
Then that Lord also cast off her whom he had created as the Pitṛs.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: Formerly, Prajāpati Brahmā, desiring to create various offspring,
with a one-pointed mind, projected all the subtle elements (tanmātras) outward from his mind.
Having performed the supreme *brahman* and meditating upon it, he indeed went to heaven;
for that Parameṣṭhin had then attained union (*yoga*) within his own self.
From his body emerged the subtle elements (tanmātras), their radiance colored like smoke;
they cried out repeatedly, "Let us drink! and "Let us devour!"
Indeed, those ascetics who desire to ascend upwards have their abode in the sky.
Seeing them, Brahmā, the grandfather of the universe, suddenly said:
"May you all become the ancestors (pitṛs) of all householders."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"That which is called Agni is indeed declared to be the year (saṃvatsara).
From him the seasons (ṛtu) were born, and likewise from the seasons came the seasonal periods (ārtava)."
[38] For the Pitṛs are called the seasonal (ārtava), and they have sons following them;
the months are the Grandfathers (pitāmaha), and the seasonal periods are their sons.
The Great-Grandfathers (prapitāmaha) are indeed the gods, the five-year periods who are the sons of Brahmā.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "In the past, when the three worlds were enveloped in darkness, the waters were produced;
thereafter, during the Svāyambhuva interval, the renowned sons of Brahmā appeared."
Being honored like a father, they indeed became his fathers;
he who is remembered as Prajāpati is considered to be the year.
For the year is remembered as Agni and is called *ṛta* by the wise;
from *ṛta*, however, the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*) were born as gods, and they are indeed those seasons.
The months therein are to be known as the seasonal periods (ṛtu); these became his sons. From them, however, the Pitṛs arose, and the seasons became the Grandfathers (pitāmaha).
Since all progeny are produced from him alone without exception,
he is therefore remembered as the sole great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) of all beings.

In this context, the deities presiding over the year and other periods of time are denoted by the word "Pitṛs," and not time alone, because the quality of being a bestower of fruit—which is an attribute of a conscious being—is impossible in that [mere time]. Furthermore, words such as "year" and so forth are used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) for the deities presiding over the year and so forth; this too has been stated in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"The year itself is one, yet these are the names of those who occupy the stations. For these inhabitants of the stations are proclaimed to have the nature of their respective stations."
Holding to what is possible and what is impossible, those gods are remembered as being of that very nature;
yet in this *manvantara*, others who are presiding deities of time remain here.
They are described as the cause and effect, established in sovereign power and lordship.

And here, by the word "place" (sthāna), time itself is meant; for this very reason, after stating "those who identify with time," it was said: "For these, identifying with place, remain here incidentally.
Thus, these are the Pitṛs, the Devas, and those Pitṛs who belong to the seasons (ārtava).
The state of being the season, the state of being the father, and the state of being the progenitor have been proclaimed.
In that regard, there are five [categories] mentioned in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"The seasons are to be known as the ancestors; from the seasons, five sons were born:
of humans, of animals, of birds, and of reptiles."
And for the five classes of stationary beings, the flowering season and the seasons are prescribed as their [periods].

Thus it is stated. In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, however, six ancestors known as the seasons (*ṛtu*) are mentioned: Madhu, Mādhava, Śuci, Śukra, Nabhas, and Nabhasya. Regarding them, there is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "The ancestors are the seasons; they are the gods. Madhu and Mādhava are the spring (*vasanta*). Śuci and Śukra are the two [months] of the summer heat (*śuṣmin*). Nabhas and Nabhasya are the rainy season (*vārṣika*). Iṣa and Ūrja are the autumn season (*śarad*). Sahas and Sahasya are the winter season (*hemanta*). Tapas and Tapasya are the two [months] of the cool season (*śaiśira*). The seasons are the sons of Brahmā; by means of these six, the year is formed. That year is Prajāpati; the year is called Agni and Ṛta. From Ṛta the seasons were born, and from them came all things stationary and moving. The season is time (*kāla*); from that everything arises, and therefore they are called the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Thus, the direct birth of the ancestors from the body of Brahmā is described.
From him Brahmā was born, and he too created seven sages;
they were then told by that Supreme Lord: "Worship me with this."
"The Śruti declares that they first worship the Self by means of the Self;
and for those who are thus worshipping, Brahmā is the one possessed of the nature of Mahāvaikārika."
"Since this great transgression has been committed by me, you shall all fall away from your knowledge; of this there is no doubt."
Thus, those seven [mind-born sons], produced from himself by that Brahmā,
having immediately fathered sons who were the founders of lineages, departed for the third heaven.
"And all those inhabitants of celestial chariots (vaimānikas) are the seven mind-born sons of Brahmā;
they remain there beholding that offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍadāna) as it is described in the mantras.
And as for those ancestors, O Brahmin, listen to me as I describe them. Thus [it is said].
In this context, "those" refers to Marīci and the others, as well as their sons.
They existed in a former kalpa as the increasers of the gods' soma.
Those seven, beginning with Marīci, who reside in heaven, are remembered as the Pitṛs.
The reason for applying the term "Pitṛ" (Ancestor/Father) to Marīci and the other sons is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas*. For it is said:
"The Lord Brahmā created the gods, thinking, 'They shall worship me.
But they, seeking rewards, abandoned him and worshipped their own selves."
Cursed by Brahmā, those fools were told: "You shall become deprived of consciousness;
do not remain ignorant of anything, lest you then be utterly deluded in this world."
They all bowed down again and addressed the Grandfather;
out of favor toward the worlds, he spoke these words to them once more.
An expiation must be performed, for an infidelity has been committed against you;
ask your own sons, and from them you shall obtain knowledge.
Seeking a means of atonement, they indeed questioned their own sons;
those self-restrained sons gave them many answers in response.
The gods of heaven, who were knowers of dharma, having regained their senses and being pleased, spoke to their sons regarding the expiations for sins born of speech, mind, and action.
"You are indeed our fathers, by whom we have been awakened;
what boon shall be granted to you—be it dharma, knowledge, or desire?"
Brahmā spoke to them again: "You are indeed speakers of truth;
therefore, what has been spoken by you is so, and not otherwise."
"You have been called our fathers," [the ancestors replied], "and we are indeed your sons;
they shall become your fathers—let this boon be granted to them."
"You shall become the gods who are the makers of their bodies, while they, being the bestowers of knowledge, are indeed the fathers; of this there is no doubt."
By that very word of the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
the sons previously attained the status of fathers, and the fathers again attained the status of sons;
for these are mutually both the Pitṛs and the Devas.

In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "These indeed are the Pitṛs; these are both the Devas and the Pitṛs. The seasons and the sub-seasons are their own source from one [principle], yet they are remembered as Pitṛs for one another."

In this regard, in the *Vārāha*, *Ādi*, and other Purāṇas, the sons of the sages such as Marīci are seen to be the Pitṛs; however, in the *Brahmavaivarta* and others, it is stated that the gods are the Pitṛs. In that context, since the word "deva" (god) can be derived from the etymology "those who shine" (*divyanti*), it is reasonable to conclude that in the *Brahmavaivarta* and similar texts, the term "deva" refers specifically to Marīci and the others, because of the similarity with the *Vārāha Purāṇa* and the resulting recognition of their identity. Furthermore, in the *Brahmavaivarta* itself, after describing the creation of the worlds, another reason for the application of the term "Pitṛ" to these beings is stated.
The terrible atmosphere, the earth, the stars, and the directions,
as well as the sun and moon, and likewise day and night.
At that time, this world did not become so shrouded in darkness;
there, Brahmā alone performed supreme and difficult ascetic penance.
They say that yoga is the best of all ascetic practices and the supreme;
it was created by Brahmā with his eye of yoga for one who seeks yoga.
The worlds named Santānaka, where the sun-like ones reside,
are renowned as the Vairājas, the deities among the gods in heaven.
Seven groups of them have been described, worshipped throughout the three worlds;
above those, there exist three who possess the nature of the triple form.
From that come the gods, from them the earth; such is the succession of the worlds.
Those who exist in this world have their origin in Parjanya.
"Rain indeed occurs, and from rain the origin of the worlds is traditionally known. Therefore, those best of beings spoke thus to the ancestors regarding the worlds.
Now, the origin of the Pitṛs from the body of Brahmā occurs through an intermediate stage.
As stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Those who are remembered as the sons of the Unmanifest-born, namely Marīci and the others..."
From them were born the principal groups of Pitṛs, and from those, the deities.
Know, O dear child, that the entire world, the three realms with all things moving and unmoving, originates from the gods; the supreme reality is theirs, and the ancestors are the sons of the sages.

In this regard, it should be understood that the direct birth of the Pitṛs from the body of Brahmā seen in the Purāṇas refers to Marīci and others as being the Pitṛs, whereas the birth mediated by the body of Brahmā refers to the sons of Marīci and others as being the Pitṛs. Thus, there is no contradiction. This being the case, it follows that the sons of Marīci and others are the Pitṛs, Marīci and others are the Pitāmahas, and Brahmā is the Prapitāmaha. Furthermore, that Brahmā who is denoted by the term Prajāpati is the year as the Prapitāmaha; Marīci and others, being the seasons (*ṛtu*), are the Pitāmahas; and the months, being seasonal (*ārtava*), are the Pitṛs. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever among the Purāṇas.
The sons of all those sages, beginning with Marīci, who were the offspring of Manu Hairaṇyagarbha, are recorded as the classes of Pitṛs.

Thus, in the *Manu-vākya*, the birth of Marīci and the others is stated as being without any interval from the body of Brahmā; this too is logical because of the difference in creation due to the difference between *kalpas*. Now, regarding the differences in name, form, and so forth among these ancestors (*pitṛs*), it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"There are indeed seven groups of ancestors; learn their names from me:
the Subhāsvaras, the Barhiṣadas, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas."
The Kravyādas, the Upahūtas, the Ājyapas, and the Sukālins—
these three are formless, while four possess forms.
The Subhāsvaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas—
these three classes of ancestors, O King, are remembered as being formless.
The Kravyādas, the Upahūtas, the Ājyapas, and the Sukālins—
these are proclaimed as the four classes of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas) who possess embodied forms.
In the Brahmavaivarta and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"Seven groups of them are proclaimed, worshipped throughout the three worlds;
three of them are formless (amūrta), and four possess form (samūrta)."
And those which exist above them are formless;
those which exist below them are four, possessing subtle forms.
For this very reason, even among the Chandogas, Pitṛkanyā beheld the subtle Pitṛs. This too has been stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa and other texts:
"By that mental transgression, she—assuming any form at will through her mind—having entreated another father, fell away from yoga."
As she fell, descending from heaven, she saw three celestial chariots the size of motes of dust; within them, she beheld her ancestors,
exceedingly subtle yet not departed, like fires enshrined within hearths.
In the *Nigama* it is said: "Those ancestors who were slain there in battle became threefold;
whatever oblation is offered in the ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*), that goes to them."

In that context, those gods who were slain in the battle with Vṛtra became the *pitaraḥ*. "Threefold" refers to autumn, winter, and the cool season (*śiśira*). These very ones are the *somavantah*, the *barhiṣadaḥ*, and the *agniṣvāttāḥ*. And so says the *Śatapatha-śruti*:

By means of the *mahāhavis* (great oblation), the gods indeed slew Vṛtra; by it they won that very victory which is theirs. And those whom they killed in that battle, them they propitiated with the *pitṛyajña*. They were indeed the fathers; therefore it is called the *pitṛyajña*. Spring, summer, and the rainy season—these are those who won the victory. Autumn, winter, and the cool season—these are those whom they propitiated again. Now, those who sacrifice with Soma are the *somavant* fathers. Those who win the world through gifts and cooked food are the *barhiṣad* fathers. And those whom neither of these two reaches, but whom Agni himself consumes and makes savory, they are the *agniṣvātta* fathers. These, then, are the fathers.
In the Brahma Purāṇa: "The ancestors are remembered as being of two kinds: formless and embodied.
The Nāndīmukhas are formless, while those of the Pārvaṇa rite are embodied."
The pretas eat from the ekoddiṣṭa; such is the threefold determination regarding the ancestors.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*, after describing the creation of the ancestors (*pitṛsṛṣṭi*), it is said:
"Having seen them situated horizontally with their faces turned downwards, Brahmā spoke to them:
'May you all become the ancestors for all householders.'"
But those among them whose faces are turned upwards are designated as Nāndīmukhas.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "The ancestors, O child, were created by Brahmā through austerity; they are five classes of divine beings, knowers of the purpose [of existence], and pure in form."
The Agniṣvātta, the Barhiṣad, the Kāvya, the Sukālin,
and the Yāma— these are said to be the five classes of ancestors who perform sacrifices.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"The Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, Ājyapa, and Somapa ancestors are remembered;
likewise, the Rasmipas and Upahūtas—may those others come to us."
Likewise, O King, others known as the Svāduṣadas and the Nāndīmukhas are remembered;
these are the renowned groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas), and they are born from the gods.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and even the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins,
offer satisfaction to these [ancestors], having excluded the Nāndīmukha Pitṛs.
In the Hārītasmṛti: Soma, Yama, Aṅgiras, and likewise the Somapas, Barhiṣads, Agniṣvāttas, and Hutādas— this is the sixfold group of ancestors.
The moon, the seasons, the fire that burns the dead,
those invited by Soma, those who have drunk Soma, and Brahmins who have not performed sacrifices.
Thus have been stated the divisions of the divine ancestors (devapitṛs) by name and form; now the divisions of the human ancestors (manuṣyapitṛs) are being described. In the Vāyupurāṇa:
"Therefore, I shall proclaim the ancestors who partake in the monthly śrāddha."
The ancestors of the gods are divine, while the ancestors of worldly beings are likewise [human].
The gods are gentle and performers of sacrifice; they are both those born of sacrifice and those not born of a womb.
All these ancestors are indeed gods, and they in turn sustain the gods.
Humans and ancestors are indeed [the first group], while others than these are known as worldly;
likewise, the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather.
Those who have performed sacrifices with Soma and those who are remembered as possessing Soma—
those who are recorded as performers of sacrifice are indeed remembered as the Barhiṣads.
Those who are engaged in these ritual acts until the dissolution of the body are known as the Agniṣvāttas; they are the performers of burnt offerings and the sacrificers of clarified butter.
[47] Because of their similarity in nature to those [Vedic duties], that [Smṛti] was remembered by the twice-born who were to apply it;
as well as those duties pertaining to the stages of life established for the various paths.
And they do not despair at the outset through action joined with faith—
namely, through celibacy, austerity, sacrifice, progeny,
faith, wisdom, and giving; thus it is sevenfold.
Those who remain engaged in these rites until the fall of the body,
together with those gods and subtle ancestors who drink the soma and clarified butter,
rejoice in heaven once they have gone there— those who properly worship the ancestors.
This praise is intended for those who possess offspring and maintain pure conduct;
for them, there is the state of Nirvana, along with kinsmen born of their own lineage.
The inhabitants of the world of Soma obtain satisfaction from those who partake in the monthly śrāddha;
these, however, are the human ancestors who partake in the monthly śrāddha.

The human ancestors who have attained equality with the gods and the *pitṛ*s through virtuous deeds have been described. Now, those human ancestors who have reached a downward state due to evil deeds are being discussed. Furthermore, there are others besides them, those of mixed origin born from various wombs, who have fallen away from the duties of their stages of life (*āśrama*) and are deprived of the offerings of *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
With their bodies split apart, these evil-minded ones become ghosts in the abode of Yama;
having arrived at the place of torment, they grieve only for their own deeds.
Long-lived, yet exceedingly emaciated, bearded and naked,
and overcome by hunger and thirst, they fled hither and thither.
Desiring to obtain [wealth], they seek out rivers, lakes, ponds, and reservoirs; driven by desire and pride, they strive for the food of others here and there.
[48] And they are indeed cooked in various places within the hells of torment,
in the Śālmalī forest, in the Vaitaraṇī river, and in those Kumbhīpāka pits.
In the Karambha-vālukā hell and in the Asipatravana forests,
and likewise upon being crushed by rocks due to their own past actions,
there are indeed many places for those who are suffering.
Those dwelling in hell have been described as human ancestors; now, those dwelling on earth:
those who have not reached the places of torment are the superior ones on earth, being fivefold.
But afterwards, among which beings and in which actions are those ending with the stationary (plants and minerals) included?
Those who are born in various forms among the species of animal births and the like are known as the Vāhlīkas, the Uṣmapās, and the Divākīrtis;
for them, the dark fortnight is the day, and the bright fortnight is the night for sleep.
Also in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Now, those mortal ancestors who dwell in the triple heaven are seen to be of two kinds: some are happy, while others are unhappy."
Those born of one's own lineage who offer funeral oblations (śrāddha) in the world of mortals—
all of them are gathered there, remaining joyful like gods.
Those to whom no one at all from their own lineage gives anything,
they are seen to be tormented by hunger and thirst, and they are miserable.
In the *Manusmṛti*: "Those who have been proclaimed as the principal groups of ancestors— of them too, it should be understood here that their sons and grandsons are infinite."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"O great sage, this ancestral creation has been described to you by way of summary;
its end is not seen even in ten million years."
In the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*:
"The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*), the deities of the *śrāddha*.
Now, the secret ancestors (*guhyāḥ pitaraḥ*) are described in the *Nandipurāṇa*. After enumerating the various classes of ancestors beginning with the Agniṣvātta-s, it was stated by Maheśvara:
Now listen, O best of men, to the immortals, the ancestors, and the secret ones:
Viṣṇu is the divine father of this world, and he alone is the sacrifice;
Brahmā is to be known as the grandfather, and I am the great-grandfather.

These—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are also "Fathers" (pitaraḥ) because they are the cause of the creation of the universe. Since they serve as the presiding deities over the Agniṣvātta and other classes of ancestors who are the foundational supports for the Pitṛs and Pitāmahas, they take the form of deities in the Śrāddha rite when meditated upon in that form. Thus, it is established in all Śrāddha manuals (*śrāddhakalpa*) as a secret esoteric teaching (*upaniṣad*) on the Śrāddha that they generate the power of the Śrāddha to produce fruits both in this world and the next, fulfilling all desires. Furthermore, it is shown that even those not commonly known as "Fathers"—such as the Agniṣvātta and others—generate a unique, unprecedented power (*apūrvā śaktiḥ*), and for this reason they are considered "secret" (*guhya*).
By those who have sacrificed for Viṣṇu, the ancestors are indeed gratified;
when Brahmā is worshipped, he pleases all the paternal grandfathers of a man.
Those great-souled ones by whom I have been worshipped for the sake of their great-grandfathers—
indeed, their great-grandfathers do not go to the terrible hell.
O Gaṇeśa, all of them, including their father and grandfather, go by force to the divine and delightful worlds.
And likewise, their great-grandfather as well.
Those who know the Vaiṣṇava wisdom and worship Viṣṇu, having honored him with all their being—
for them, their ancestors attain satisfaction.
And they abandon those of low birth.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa, Varāha’s words to the ancestors:
"Yama is your presiding deity (adhideva), who is said to be gentle and related to the self (svādhyātma);
Agni is your presiding deity of sacrifice (adhiyajña)—such is this conceptualization regarding you."
"Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya shall be your abodes;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra shall be your presiding lords."
"May these Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras become your forms—
yogins with bodies of yoga, the support of yoga, and observers of excellent vows.
You shall wander at will, bestowing fruits upon all living beings."
In the Mahābhārata, after Viṣṇu had raised the earth submerged in water in the form of a boar, he fashioned the lumps of clay clinging to his tusks into the nature of ancestors and,
having worshipped them, said: "I alone am to be known here as the father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather, residing within these three lumps."
There is no one superior to me; who else is to be worshipped by me myself? Who in this world is my father? I alone am the Grandfather (Pitāmaha);
I alone am the cause here, being both the father and the grandfather of the father.
[51] In the Viṣṇudharmottara: "The *piṇḍa* for the father and grandfather is proclaimed to be Vāsudeva;
and the one for the great-grandfather is likewise designated as the Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa."

The ancestral *piṇḍa* is to be known as Pradyumna, and the invincible Aniruddha is to be known as the Self (*ātman*) by the wise during the offering of the *piṇḍas*. How indeed can one perform the *śrāddha* without the splendor of Viṣṇu?
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "The god Aniruddha himself is [the first], while Pradyumna is remembered as his father;
Saṅkarṣaṇa is his father, and Vāsudeva is his father."

The meaning is as follows: the performer of the *śrāddha* himself is the deity Aniruddha; the performer of the *śrāddha*, the father, is Pradyumna; the progenitor of that performer—the progenitor of the father of the *śrāddha*-performer—is Saṅkarṣaṇa; and his father—the father of the progenitor of the father of the *śrāddha*-performer—is remembered as Vāsudeva.
In the *Smṛtis*, the nature of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) is described as being Varuṇa and so forth:
"The first deity is Varuṇa, and the next is Prajāpati."
The third fire is remembered as the *piṇḍa*; this is remembered as the rule for the *piṇḍa*.
Now, in this section, there are various modes of worship by which the world is produced for those previously mentioned—the Subhāsvaras, Barhiṣads, Agniṣvāttas, and so forth.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The Subhāsvaras, sons of Brahmā, cause the moon to swell."
O King, those who dwell in the world of Brahmā are eternally devoid of physical form.
Likewise, O King, the sons of Marīci are remembered as the Barhiṣads;
they cause nourishment and remain honored in the world of the gods.
O lord of men, the Agniṣvāttas dwell in the world of Vibhrāja;
these sons of the seer Pulastya bring prosperity to all beings.
The Kravyādas, the Upahūtas, the Ājyapas, and the Sukālins—
these are proclaimed as the sons of Kavi, Aṅgiras, the Prajāpati Kardama,
and Vasiṣṭha, respectively.
The worlds known as Jyotirbhāsas and those which are the Marīcins are proclaimed in sequence as the Tejasvins and the Mānasas.
In the *Matsya*, *Padma*, and other Purāṇas:
"The formless hosts of Pitṛs belong to the Prajāpati Vairāja;
those whom the hosts of gods worship are renowned as the Vairājas."
There are worlds named Somapatha where the sons of Mārīca dwell;
they are the divine ancestors whom the gods fully honor.
There dwell those known as the Agniṣvāttas, performers of sacrifice;
there, in heaven, reside the highly resplendent ones named Vaibhrājas.
There are the worlds where the ancestors who sit upon the sacrificial grass dwell, observers of noble vows;
there, thousands of celestial chariots yoked with peacocks are found.
Where the intentions regarding the sacrificial grass stand as bestowers of fruit,
and where the givers of *śrāddha* rejoice in halls of prosperity.
And those hosts of gods and asuras, the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases,
