as well as the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, worship the deities in heaven.
The sons of Pulastya, numbering in the hundreds, endowed with the power of asceticism and yoga,
were the formless ancestors (pitṛs) of Vasiṣṭha and Sukāli.
All of them are indeed mind-born by name, and all are embodiments of Dharma;
they dwell in the worlds of radiant light, beyond heaven.
Where those who bestow the ancestral offerings sport,
shining brilliantly in celestial chariots that abound with all desired objects— even the trees themselves are such—
how much more so the Brahmins who give the śrāddha, being devoted and endowed with ritual action?
In the solar orb, there is a world named Marīcigarbhā,
where the Pitṛs known as the Haviṣmants, the sons of Aṅgiras, reside;
it is there that the best of Kṣatriyas go, having offered śrāddha at sacred fords.
For kings, those ancestors indeed bestow the fruits of heaven and liberation;
they are the ancestors named Susvadhās, where those sons abide.
In the worlds, they are known as the Ājyapas, the heirs born of Pulaha from the patriarch Kardama; these Vaiśyas nourish them as well.
There, those who perform the ancestral rites behold simultaneously all their fathers,
mothers, sisters, brothers, friends, kinsmen, and relatives—
even those who have been the recipients of thousands of gifts over ten thousand lifetimes.
The worlds known as Mānasa are situated above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
where the eternal ancestors named Somapās reside.
All the Pitṛs, the sons of Brahmā, are the bearers of his form;
those yogins who, having attained the state of Brahman, were born through the power of *svadhā*.
Having performed all the acts of creation and so forth, they remain established in the mind;
as stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "There exist the eternal worlds, radiant by name, wherein they abide."
The formless hosts of Pitṛs were indeed the sons of Prajāpati;
they were the excellent progeny of Virāj, renowned as the Vairājas.
The worlds are named Somapatha, where the ancestors of Marīci formerly resided; even the gods cherish them.
The ancestors known as the Barhiṣads, who drink the soma juice, are renowned;
shining brilliantly, those worlds of theirs gleam beautifully in heaven.
The ancestors known there as the Agniṣvāttas, who are well-renowned—
them the hosts of Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
as well as Nāgas, Sarpas, and Suparṇas, all of immeasurable power, honor.
O Brahmin, these are remembered as the sons of the patriarch Pulastya;
furthermore, these groups are declared to be the embodiments of Dharma.
Those who were born of their own inherent power as the poetic wisdom of Agni, the Seer—
these are the Pitṛs, the sons of the Sage, who shine like suns within the luminous realms of the gods.
And those twice-born ones, meditating upon them in worlds where all desires are fulfilled,
became filled with light and, having taken refuge in those worlds, remained in heaven.
For these sons of Aṅgiras were nourished by the Sādhyas in ancient times;
they are remembered as the Pitṛs who dwell in the sun in the sky. Seeking rewards, the joyful hosts of Kṣatriyas propitiate them.
The ancestors named Ājyapās are the offspring of Kardama Prajāpati; they were born from Pulaha after he had been produced by Kardama.
There are also radiant birds that move at will;
those seeking rewards offer these to the Vaiśya groups during the Śrāddha ceremony.
The ancestors of the Prajāpati Vasiṣṭha are named Sukālas;
they are the sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Śūdras honor them. Those worlds where they dwell in heaven are known as the Mānasas.
In the Manusmṛti: "The sons of Virāj, known as the Somasads, are remembered as the ancestors of the Sādhyas;
and the Agniṣvāttas, renowned throughout the world, are the ancestors of the gods born of Marīci."
The sons of Atri, known as the Barhiṣads, were born from Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rakṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras.
Among the Brahmins they are named Somapās; among the Kṣatriyas, Havirbhujs; among the Vaiśyas, Ājyapās; and among the Śūdras, Sukālins.
The Somapas were the sons of Kavi; the Haviṣmats were the sons of Aṅgiras;
the Ājyapas were the sons of Pulastya; and the Sukālins were the sons of Vasiṣṭha.
"One should designate the *anagnidagdha*, the *agnidagdha*, the *kāvyas*, the *barhiṣads*,
as well as the *agniṣvāttas* and the *saumyas*, as belonging exclusively to the Brahmins. An explanation of this statement is provided by the author of the *Manubhāṣya*:

The sons of Virāj are the Virājas, known as the Somasads; they are the ancestors (pitṛs) of the Sādhyas—a specific class of gods—and are to be honored by them. By this, it is indicated that this ancestral rite (pitrya-karman) must necessarily be performed, since it is performed even by the gods named Sādhyas who have already achieved their purpose (kṛtakṛtya). The Agniṣvāttas, however, are so called because they enjoy (svadante) the sacrificial pap (caru), the cake (puroḍāśa), and other offerings cooked in the fire of the gods. They are the ancestors of the gods such as Indra and Agni, and are to be honored by them. By this, the necessity of performing the rite is indicated. This should be understood in the same way for the subsequent categories as well.

The Daityas, Dānavas, and Yakṣas have ancestors named Barhiṣads; those born of Atri are the Atrijas. Suparṇas are birds, and Kinnaras are horse-faced; since even the ancestors of these animals are worthy of worship, how much more so those of humans who are entitled to perform ritual acts? Thus, the necessity of performing the Śrāddha is indicated.

"Those named Soma-drinkers," and so forth. "Soma-drinkers" (*somapāḥ*) are those who drink the *soma*; they are the deities of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, such as Indra, Vāyu, and others. "Sacrificial-food-eaters" (*havirbhujaḥ*) are those who consume the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings; they are the deities of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites. "Ghee-drinkers" (*ājyapāḥ*) are the deities of the *āghāra*, *ājyabhāga*, and other such offerings. "Well-timers" (*sukālinaḥ*) are those who "time"—that is, they conclude, bring to completion, or finish the ritual action; they are the deities of the concluding oblations (*apavargahoma*) and so forth, as prescribed in passages such as "O Agni Ayās, protector against reproach. Regarding "the Soma-drinkers of the poet," and so forth: the "Sacrificial-food-eaters" themselves are the "Possessors of Oblation" (*haviṣmantaḥ*).

"Anagnidagdha," and so forth. *Anagnidagdha* (not burnt by fire) refers to Soma, for there is no cooking of him by fire; therefore, the deities who are worshipped with him are also called *anagnidagdha* by virtue of that connection. Similarly, *agnidagdha* (burnt by fire) refers to those connected with sacrificial offerings such as the *puroḍāśa* which are cooked by fire. Here, the connection is made as follows: one should designate those who are called *agnidagdha* as the *agniṣvātta*; and those who are *anagnidagdha*, one should designate them as the *saumya*, the drinkers of Soma. Likewise, "the *kāvyas* and the *barhiṣadas*. The *kāvyas* are the sons of Kavi; thus, the Soma-drinkers are said to be the sons of Kavi. The *barhiṣadas* are said to be the sons of Atri. This particle *eva* (only/just) is not to be understood according to its specific position [in the sentence]. For if it were according to its position, the meaning would be: "These ancestors belong only to Brahmins, not to Kṣatriyas and others. And that would contradict what was stated previously. Furthermore, these have not been mentioned as ancestors according to a distinction of caste, such that their connection to Brahmins would be asserted by severing them from that [general category]. Therefore, the particle *eva* should be drawn out and connected [to both terms]: "the *agniṣvātta* only" and "the *saumya* only. The mention of "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is an *anuvāda* (a restatement for the sake of illustration), intended to indicate the Kṣatriyas and others as well.

In the Veda, ancestors with such names are heard of: "The Agniṣvātta ancestors, those who were cremated by fire and those who were not cremated. It should be understood that he, having become a friend, has explained those mantras in various ways.

Alternatively, one should not suspect a difference in meaning based on the difference in words when it says "one should designate for the *vipras*"; the mention of *vipras* is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *kṣatriyas* and others as well. Among the principal ancestors, those not cremated by fire (*anagnidagdha*), those cremated by fire (*agnidagdha*), those seated on the sacrificial grass (*barhiṣad*), and those belonging to Soma (*saumya*) are distinct from the *somapa* and *agniṣvātta* ancestors. These four types, beginning with the *anagnidagdha* and ending with the *saumya*, are further divided into two groups: the *somapas*, who are the sons of Kavi, and the *agniṣvāttas*, who are the sons of Marīci; thus, there are six types of ancestors in total. Nor should it be argued that because the *saumyas*, *barhiṣadas*, and *agniṣvāttas* are also the ancestors of the *sādhyas* and others, this contradicts the rule that they belong only to the *vipras*. There is no contradiction, because the intention is to specify that among the social classes (*varṇas*), they belong specifically to the *vipras*. Furthermore, there is no conflict with the statement in the *Vārāha Purāṇa* that "a *śūdra*, permitted by the highest class (*varṇottama*), may worship all the ancestors," for in that case all [ancestors] are prescribed for the *śūdra* only through the permission of a *vipra*, and not independently. Here, however, the phrase "only for the *vipras*" intends an independent specification, and thus there is no contradiction. Nor is there tautology, since the connection of the *somapas*—who are the sons of Kavi—with the *vipras* has already been mentioned previously; this is not a fault, because the intention here is to establish the collective relationship that "there are exactly this many [ancestors] for the twice-born (*dvijas*") alone."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa, this statement regarding the established rule for Brahmins has been spoken:
"Those who are there with their faces turned upwards are designated as Nāndīmukhas;
they should always be honored in the Vṛddhi-śrāddhas according to the injunctions of the Śruti."
Those twice-born ones by whom Agni is placed at the forefront are the Agnihotrins;
let them satisfy those [ancestors] with daily, occasional, optional, and ancestral (pārvaṇa) rites.
And the Vaiśyas always honor those who drink the clarified butter here.

Regarding the phrase "those who maintain the sacred fires" (*agnihotrin*): this applies equally to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well. Thus, having described the ancestral portion for the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) who maintain the sacred fires, he speaks also of those who do not maintain them: "And those people of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have not established the sacred fires—let them worship the worlds with well-timed [offerings], being ever devoted to the fires."
Thus honored, you grant the desired objects of one's longing.
Likewise, in the Vārāha Purāṇa itself:
"O best of the twice-born, the ancestors indeed exist in many ways;
those who dwell in the Bhuvarloka are the sacrificial recipients for those residing in the Bhūrloka."
Then, those beginning with Vasu, who dwell in heaven, are the sacrificers for them;
and the sons of Brahmā, beginning with Marīci, who have gone to the great world, are the sacrificers for them.
They are called the Kalpavāsins;
residing among them are Sanaka and the others; and beyond them are the Vairājas, established in austerity.
[59] The groups of their truths have been declared; such is the lineage of these ancestors, consisting of sevenfold activity within the seven worlds during the first Manvantara.
The Vasus, Sādhyas, Rudras, Ādityas, and the two Aśvins,
as well as the Maruts, are established as common to all social classes;
and the sages born from them constitute the sevenfold groups.
Their daughters were born as the lineage of Somapas:
Agniṣvāttās, Mārīcīs, Vairājīs, and those known as Barhiṣads.
The ancestors of Prajāpati Vaśiṣṭha are known as the Sukālas;
they too are to be worshipped by the three [upper] castes, but not by a Śūdra, because of a separate scriptural injunction.
A Śūdra, however, permitted by those of the highest caste, may worship all the ancestors.

The meaning of this is as follows: In such statements of Manu and others as "the *sukālins* belong to the *śūdras*," because we observe them mentioned separately, one should not assume a specific restriction such that "only *śūdras* have *sukālins*" or "only *sukālins* belong to *śūdras*. Rather, even for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, there are ancestors who are *sukālins*. It should be understood that others also [belong] to the *śūdras* by means of the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
However, there are no separate ancestors of the *śūdra* caste for him;
O Brahmin, apart from his own progenitors, they are not seen among the divine [ancestors].
However, the distinction [between them] is seen through the scriptures, as illustrated by the Purāṇas.

The meaning of this is as follows: no distinction such as being a Śūdra and so forth is observed among the divine Pitṛs. Therefore, the sense is: "If a distinction such as being a Śūdra were to exist among the divine Pitṛs who are perceived through the scripture, then it would be seen by the scripture. Thus, having understood through the scriptures praised by the Ṛṣis that they are worthy of sacrifice and capable [of receiving offerings], and having personally witnessed them and obtained the Smṛti—since the Purāṇa is the Brahman—they have attained supreme Nirvāṇa; they too are indeed possessors of knowledge (jñānin).
The Brāhmaṇas and others are to be known as belonging to the classes of Kaśyapa and the rest, beginning with the Vasus;
likewise, the Gandharvas and others are certainly to be understood without distinction.

The *aniṣvātta*s are proclaimed as the ancestors of the Brāhmaṇas; those of the Kṣatriyas are named the *barhiṣad*s; the *kāvyas* are proclaimed as those of the Vaiśyas; and the *sukālina*s are for the Śūdras, while the *vyāmas* are for those born of illicit unions according to one's own will.
Now, regarding their majesty as described in the Brahmavaivarta and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"O Lord, these gods among the gods in heaven are renowned as the Vairājas;
they are always endowed with yoga and austerity, and are the Pitṛs."
Known as the primordial gods (ādidevas), these beings of great essence and great majesty are always to be worshipped with all desired objects by gods, dānavas, and humans alike.
Swift as thought, subsisting on *svadhā*, with all their desires provided for, they are free from greed, delusion, and fear; they are without anxiety and devoid of craving.
Having fallen from yoga, these individuals reach worlds that are beautiful to behold;
they indeed become divine, meritorious, sinless, and great.
Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, those who discourse on Brahman are born;
having regained yoga once more, they, being formless, desire liberation.
Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest by means of the power of great yoga,
they vanish in an instant like a meteor in the sky or like a flash of lightning.
Having cast off their networks of bodies through the power of great yoga,
they attain a state beyond description or designation, just as rivers reach the ocean.
Through ritual action and the worship of the guru, they diligently establish union;
by means of these, the ancestors who increase yoga cause them to be nourished.
Having drunk the Soma at the Śrāddha ceremony, the ancestors, established in yoga,
cause the three worlds by which all live to swell with Soma.
And the ancestors, nourished by the faithful performers of ancestral rites (śrāddha), shall constantly cause the imperishable Soma to swell and increase him with nourishment and other blessings.
Soma, nourished by the performers of ancestral rites (śrāddha), shall cause the entire world—
including its mountains and forests, and filled with all things mobile and immobile— to thrive.
Thus everything was carried out as commanded by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord;
for those ancestors are indeed the bestowers of knowledge, there is no doubt.
For the power of the ancestors is yoga; from yoga, the Soma proceeds. As stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"Free from anger, devoted to purity, and constantly practicing celibacy..."
The highly fortunate ancestors, the deities of old, have laid down their weapons.

Now, regarding the path of the ancestors, the *Vārāha Purāṇa* states: Having spoken thus to them at that time, Brahmā, the Grandfather, assigned their path— the Pitṛyāna, known as the Southern Course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on the Definition of the Ancestors," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the scholar Śrī Hemādri, the preeminent minister of all affairs under the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva.
[62] Now begins the third chapter:
The Section on the Determination of Deities.
He who causes these creeper-like necklaces of jewel-like virtues to put forth supreme beauty at the throat of those on earth who possess the sovereignty of divine poetry—
he, this Hemādri, the illustrious lord of the royal secretariat, now spreads [this work] for the virtuous.
Dispelling various doubts regarding the determination of the deities in the Śrāddha rite.

Now, the deity-status of these [beings] in the *śrāddha* rite is determined. In this regard, the following doubt arises: Are these statements designating the Agniṣvāttas and others merely *arthavādas* (explanatory praises), or are they injunctions (*vidhis*)? Even if they are injunctions, do they constitute specific rules for particular lineages (*gotra*)—such as the Agniṣvāttas and Somapas—within the general lineages already enjoined by injunctions stating that one should perform the *śrāddha* having taken the lineage-name and personal name? Or do they enjoin the visualization of the identity between the Agniṣvāttas and others and the sacrificer’s own ancestors, such as his father and grandfather, who serve as the deities of the *śrāddha*? Or do they enjoin the deity-status of the Agniṣvāttas and others in the *śrāddha* itself? On this point, Medhātithi considers these statements to be *arthavādas*, because their status as injunctions is impossible. For instance, these [terms] like "Somapa" are not injunctions regarding lineages. This is because the mention here is of names, not of lineages, as is heard in the expression "Somapa is the name. If it is argued that even if it were a lineage-name, the word "name" (*nāman*) would still be applicable, then in that case there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) in the designation of the lineage; it would have to be "The lineage of the ancestors is Somapa," rather than the coreferential "The ancestors are Somapas. Furthermore, if it is claimed that the designation of a distinction in descent is seen through the metaphorical treatment of identity with the lineage—as in "the moon is the face"—[that too is insufficient].

To this it is replied: This must be examined here. What indeed is this that is called *gotra*? That first person who, through his association with qualities such as learning, wealth, heroism, or nobility, becomes most renowned and by whom the family is designated—that original progenitor is the *gotra*. For thus, all Brāhmaṇas and others possess internal subdivisions of *gotras*. Therefore, designation by that alone is appropriate. Indeed, those are the primary *gotras*, for the word *gotra* applies to them in its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*). For their status as *gotras* does not depend on this definition—namely, "the first person who establishes a name is the *gotra"—because *gotras* are beginningless, just like the Brāhmaṇa caste. For the designation "Parāśara" did not begin after the sage Parāśara; if it were so, it would follow that the Veda has a beginning. Therefore, because this designation of *gotra* is eternal, that very *gotra* must be proclaimed at the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the libations (*tarpaṇa*), and so forth. For when an eternal [designation] is possible, the adoption of a non-eternal one in a Vedic rite is not proper. Consequently, Brāhmaṇas should perform the *śrāddha* and other rites after making a formal declaration according to their *gotra*, such as: "To the descendant of the Garga *gotra*, named So-and-so Śarman. However, for Kṣatriyas and others, no such usage of *gotra* exists. For Kṣatriyas and the rest do not remember a fixed *gotra* in the same way that Brāhmaṇas do. Therefore, their *gotra* is merely worldly—the most renowned first progenitor who established the name. Thus, they are designated in the *śrāddha* and other rites by that *gotra*, and not by *gotras* such as "Havirbhuj" and so on. Furthermore, even in the case of names, there is no beginning.

Now, if it is thus accepted that a particular person possesses the status of a *gotra*, then, setting aside the non-scriptural usage of *gotra* among Kṣatriyas and others for the time being, let the usage of *gotra* proceed only by means of those [lineages] established in the scriptures, such as Havirbhuj and so forth.

Indeed, this is not so, because there is no evidence for the status of the Havisbhujas and others as *gotras*; they are not well-known as *gotras*—unlike Svāyambhuva, Ikṣvāku, Nahuṣa, Nābhāga, Bharatarṣabha, Bhagīratha, and so forth—and furthermore, they are not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Therefore, it does not concern *gotras*. Nor are these injunctions for viewing the sacrificial fire as non-different from the Pitṛs, Pitāmahas, and others who serve as the deities of the *śrāddha* for the sacrificer; for we do not observe any corresponding *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, or other indicators that would support such a view. Indeed, one does not find an injunction stating that "one should practice the meditation of viewing the ancestors and others as Soma-drinkers (*somapa*) and so forth," in the manner of the text, "One should meditate on the Sun as Brahman. Furthermore, regarding what is found in the *smṛtis* of Manu, Devala, and Śātātapa:
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas as the great-grandfathers; such is the ancient Vedic revelation.
Furthermore, as it is stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"They indeed call the Vasus the fathers (*pitaraḥ*), the Rudras the grandfathers (*pitāmahāḥ*), and the Ādityas the great-grandfathers (*prapitāmahāḥ*); this is the eternal revelation (*śruti*)."
Furthermore, as it is stated in the Nandipurāṇa and other texts:
"Viṣṇu is the divine father of this world and the Lord of Sacrifice;
Brahmā is to be known as the grandfather, and I am the great-grandfather."
Furthermore, it is said in the Āditya Purāṇa:
"The months are to be known as the fathers, the seasons as the grandfathers,
and the year, well-established for all creatures, is the great-grandfather."

Thus, the statement regarding the non-difference of the Vasus, Viṣṇu, the months, and so forth, from the Pitṛs and others, does not intend to enjoin that one should perform the visualization (dṛṣṭi) of them as the Vasus and so on. This is because such an interpretation is also possible as being intended merely for praise (*prāśastya*), like the passage "The sun is a horse. Furthermore, when an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is possible, it is not proper to assume an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, since there is a lack of authoritative evidence, these are not injunctions for the visualization of non-difference. Nor are they injunctions regarding the status of Agniṣvātta and the others as the deities of the *śrāddha* ceremony; for: "He alone is a true son who follows his father while he is still living..."
One should satisfy those who are present with devotion through various kinds of śrāddha offerings.

[65] Thus, these and other rules for *śrāddha* rites serve solely for the satisfaction of deceased humans; they thereby establish that humans alone possess the status of a deity (*devatā*), for it is indeed a deity who is to be gratified by the oblation being offered. And many verses have been shown in the section establishing the possibility of such satisfaction, which demonstrate that deceased humans are the objects to be gratified in *śrāddha* rites. Now, if you think that "deityhood" consists not in being the object of gratification, but rather in being the intended recipient (*uddeśya*) of the oblation being offered—and that this [status] is established by means of the dative case and so forth—then even that exists in the case of humans. This is because we frequently see such statements in the sections on eligibility (*adhikāra*), for example: "One should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the father, to the grandfather, to the mother, and to the maternal grandfather. This is likewise seen in the *Brahmapurāṇa* and other texts.
Likewise, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should perform [the rites] for his maternal grandfather alone;

however, those known as dvaimātura or dvaimātreya (sons of two fathers) should worship both their maternal and paternal grandfathers according to the rule, with śrāddha offerings and occasional rites as well.

In this context, even though there is no fourth state [of existence], the fact that deceased humans are worthy of worship through *śrāddha* rites is not possible without their being deities. As it is said: "Fathers who fear falling into hell desire sons;
therefore, even one who is devoid of caste should perform the ancestral rites for his fathers."

Likewise, Gaṇagāri says that [the offering] should be made for each one of those who among them may have become *preta*s; Taulvali says that one should offer specifically for the *preta* himself. Furthermore, in the *Śatapatha-śruti*, there is seen the recitation of mantras characterized by the fourth-case endings of the names of the father, grandfather, and so forth: "O So-and-so, this is for you," for the sacrificer’s father; "O So-and-so, this is for you," for the grandfather; and "O So-and-so, this is for you," for the great-grandfather. Similarly, in mantras such as "This food is for you and those who follow you," which establish the washing, anointing, and other rites for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so on, there is seen the manifestation of deceased humans. For it is not logical that a mantra should manifest something that is not integrated into the ritual performance (*prayoga*). Nor is integration into the performance possible for deceased humans without their status as deities (*devatātva*). Moreover, a direct injunction for the purpose of deceased humans is seen in the *Śrāddha* rites. Thus, there is the statement of Vārāha in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
From this day forward, for those who perform the śrāddha rite in the worlds for the sake of the deceased ancestors (pretas), there shall be nourishment and prosperity.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, the words of Brahmā addressed to the ancestors:
"Whatever is given with devotion to Brahmins, specifically designating one's father, grandfather, and his father as well; [that gift reaches them]."
May there be supreme satisfaction for all of them until the dissolution of all beings.

Likewise, because all the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* establish the divinity (*devatātva*) of deceased humans through the injunction for proclaiming the lineage and other details—such as the rule that "in all *Śrāddha* manuals and *Purāṇas*, one should duly recite the names along with the lineage and kinship connections, having designated the ancestral oblation (*śrāddhīya-havis*) for the father"—and because it is seen in the *Smṛtis* of Baudhāyana, Nārada, and others that "for one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of *piṇḍas*; and on each *piṇḍa*, the two names [should be mentioned]," and because of the prescription in the *Āpastamba-sūtra* that "if one has two fathers, one should indicate both on each individual *piṇḍa*," and because specific lineages (*gotra*) are taught in the case of wives and others, and because the arrival of deceased humans toward the site of the *Śrāddha* is stated in the section concerning the production of satisfaction (*tṛpti*).
May there be born in our own family one who might give us milk-rice mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day during the rainy season under the Maghā constellation.

This is because we observe such [texts] as those expressing the prayers of the persons performing the *śrāddha*—who are born within the same family lineage—to deceased humans. If you think that the capacity to bestow the fruits mentioned in the section on praise belongs to those who are the forms of the *śrāddha*-deities, and that this is impossible for deceased humans, that is not so; for it is possible when humans have attained the state of gods (*devabhūya*). Thus, since the status of the deceased ancestors, such as fathers and others, as deities in the *śrāddhas* is understood, this makes known the deity-status of the Agniṣvātta and other classes of manes; therefore, the passages establishing the Agniṣvātta and others are not injunctions (*vidhi*) regarding their deity-status. Nor is there an option (*vikalpa*) between the Agniṣvātta and others and the father and others. For, in the originative injunctions (*utpattividhi*) of the *śrāddha*, such as "one should perform the *śrāddha* for the father, grandfather, and others," "one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the father and grandfather," and "from here onwards, the sons should give to three," it is heard that the rite is to be performed by the sons and others; and words such as "son" are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*). Therefore, since the father and others are established by the originative injunction, it is impossible to enjoin the Agniṣvātta and others therein. Indeed, one cannot enjoin another quality that contradicts a quality already established in an action, because if it were a mere restatement of the pure act (*śuddhānuvāda*), there would be no recognition of it, and if it were a restatement of the qualified act (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*), there would be a contradiction with the non-mention of another quality. Nor can it be said that this is simply another injunction of the *śrāddha* qualified by a different deity, because an injunction of what has already been enjoined is impossible, which would result in the undesirable consequence of it being a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).

Furthermore, it is only heard [in scripture] that the ancestors, such as the Agniṣvāttas and others, are to be "honored" (*upacaryā*). Moreover, no distinct meaning for the word *upacāra* (honoring) is perceived, such as [the meanings of] giving or sacrificing. For this term is generally used, like the verb *karoti* (to do), with reference to an action in close proximity; and the Śrāddha is what is proximate. Since the Śrāddha has already been prescribed as the object to be given by the performer, it cannot be prescribed again. And if it were not something to be prescribed, there would be no proximity. And for that which is not proximate, there can be no denotation of honoring. Even in common usage, in the expression "one should honor [him] like a guru," although the meaning understood is service characterized by washing the feet and so forth, that too—being well-known as related to the guru—is intended merely for the sake of proximity through the sense of a comparison (*upamārtha*). If even for one who is not proximate, actions such as washing the feet were understood as "honoring," then it would be impossible to accomplish that toward the invisible ancestors. Therefore, because there is no word denoting a specific action suitable for prescription, a prescription is untenable. Nor is a prescription of a mere accessory possible that does not fall within an action that is inherently to be accomplished. Thus, the Agniṣvāttas and others do not possess the status of deities either as alternatives to or in conjunction with the [ordinary] fathers and others. For this reason also, there is no conjunction: because it would result in the subversion of the restrictive rule regarding number, namely, "one should give to three only"; and because it is impossible for the fathers and others and the Agniṣvāttas and others to be connected in a single performance. Nor should it be argued that there is a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of the prescriptions for deities: that those whose father's name and so forth are known have the fathers and others as deities in the Śrāddha performed by them, while those whose names are unknown have Soma-pā and others as deities in the Śrāddha performed by them. This is because the Kalpa-sūtras prescribe a method for the Śrāddha in cases of ignorance of names, stating: "If he does not know the names, he should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the grandfather," and likewise, "If he does not find the names, he should give the first rice-ball with the formula, 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth, six in number. Since a systematic arrangement contradicts such a rule, it is impossible. For this very reason, even in the case of the obligatory Śrāddha performed by those whose fathers, grandfathers, and so forth are outcasts, there are no prescriptions for Vasu and other deities. Thus, even a systematic arrangement is not possible.

If the Somapās and others were intended as the deities of the *śrāddha* according to their literal names, then the mention of their lineage (*abhijana*) would be useless. However, everything becomes consistent if they are understood as a single entity. This is stated for the purpose of engaging someone who, out of hatred for his ancestors, might be indifferent toward the ancestral rites, thinking: "Do not think thus; what benefit can the ancestors—who are merely deceased human beings—possibly confer when satiated with *śrāddhas*, or what harm can they cause if not satiated? The answer is this: These [deities], such as the Agniṣvāttas and others, are sons of Brahmā and sons of sages like Marīci; they possess great majesty and preside over the ancestors and others who appear in the form of deceased humans. When satiated by *śrāddhas* performed under human names, they will grant the desired benefit to the performer in the form of obtaining the fruits of their expectations. Conversely, if not satiated, they will bring about the fault consisting in the loss of those expected results. Furthermore, there are indeed practitioners who understand the necessity of performing these rites based on such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and not otherwise.

Now, these are indeed *arthavādas* (explanatory passages). For this reason as well, they are *arthavādas*: because they teach what is not [otherwise] taught. For the *Somāsads* are not the ancestors of the *Sādhyas*, nor are the *Agniṣvāttas* those of the gods, nor the *Barhiṣads* those of the Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Uragas, Rākṣasas, Suparṇas, and Kinnaras; thus, by such statements, the *Somāsads* and others are not enjoined as deities (*devatā*) in the *śrāddha*. Indeed, there is no eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the gods such as the Sādhyas, nor for animals such as the Uragas and Suparṇas, in a rite that is of the nature of *dharma*. For if the gods were eligible, the consequence would be that they would become agents (*kartṛ*), which would entail the loss of their status as deities, since there is a distinction between being a deity and being an agent. Furthermore, animals lack both the requisite power (*śakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Alternatively, because the statement "the *Somāsads* are the ancestors of the Sādhyas," etc., forms a single syntactical unit with what is taught by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), such passages as "the *Somapās* are for Brahmins, the *Havirbhujas* for Kṣatriyas," and so forth, are also merely *arthavādas*. To this it is replied: Even if a clear injunction (*vidhi*) regarding the status of the *Agniṣvāttas* and others as deities in the *śrāddha* is not seen in the verses of Manu, nevertheless, their status as deities is indeed understood from the observation of their association with the *śrāddha* in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* through words ending in the dative case. For instance, after mentioning the *Agniṣvāttas* and others in the *Pādya* and *Mātsya Purāṇas*, it is said: [...text continues... For example, after naming
From them all the Manus were produced; indeed, at the time of creation, they ordained that people should always perform *śrāddha* rites, knowing that this alone is dharma.

And it should not be argued that because this is taught in the present tense, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *śrāddha* enjoined by Manu, and not an injunction (*vidhi*) for a *śrāddha* performed by Brahmins and others; for a mere restatement would be purposeless. If it is argued that it is for the sake of praise (*praśaṃsā*), we say no; for praise is appropriate only for that which is itself being enjoined. Therefore, it must be understood that this is indeed for the purpose of enjoining the *śrāddha* performed by Brahmins and others, having Agniṣvātta and other deities as its recipients. Furthermore, the injunction is directly perceived. Thus it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
Then, in accordance with their acceptance [of the dharma], in age after age,
Prajāpati causes the śrāddha rites to proceed when the dharma has perished.
O best of the twice-born, regarding the original creation of all the ancestors,
they indeed say that the śrāddha must be offered according to one's own dharma in this very manner.

In this manner, the *śrāddha* should also be offered by Brāhmaṇas and others, directed toward the Agniṣvātta and other ancestors. The phrase "by one's own duty" (*svadharmeṇa*) means according to each person's respective duty; that is, while Brāhmaṇas and others use cooked food, a Śūdra uses raw food (*āmānna*), and so forth—meaning by such distinctions of method.
This is also stated in the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas*:
"By accepting these [customs], Manu, the lord of the Manvantara..."
At the beginning of the Manvantara, he caused the Śrāddha rites to be performed in every way.
Therefore, for all the ancestors of excellent complexion in their proper sequence,
a śrāddha should always be offered here according to one's own dharma.

In this regard, although the connection of Agniṣvātta and the others with the *śrāddha* is expressed even by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the *Harivaṃśa* and other texts, it ultimately results in their specific nature as deities (*devatātva*). Furthermore, since the use of the genitive is frequently observed even for deceased humans who are intended as deities, it follows from this also that these [ancestors] possess the status of *śrāddha*-deities. For in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and other works, it is stated that these alone are the direct recipients of the *śrāddha*, whereas for humans, there is merely a connection to satisfaction through them.
"These are always the eaters of the *śrāddha* together with the Viśvedevas."
Having always partaken of these at a śrāddha, they indeed gratify the ancestors.

In this manner, they cause the Pitṛs and all their hosts to be satisfied; thus the giver is glorified. And it should not be said that this is merely a figurative praise or simply the state of being associated with satisfaction, rather than the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) characterized by being the intended recipient of the oblation (*havis*). For, by the phrase "together with the Viśvedevas," there is an expression of a shared state of being an enjoyer (*samānabhoktṛtva*) with the Viśvedevas who are the intended recipients of the oblation. Likewise, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, the status of the Pitṛs as enjoyers of the *śrāddha* is stated:
"The Pitṛs are remembered as being of two kinds: those who are formless (*amūrta*) and those who possess form (*mūrtimat*)."
Those who eat at Nāndīmukha rites, at Pārvaṇa rites, and likewise those who eat at Ekoddiṣṭa rites.

The determination of the embodied ancestors (*mūrta-pitṛs*) is indeed threefold according to what has been indicated. Here, the embodied and unembodied ancestors, such as the *agniṣvātta*s and others, have already been shown in the section defining the ancestors. Furthermore, it is understood that the "Nāndīmukhas" are those who partake in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*; the "Pārvaṇas" are those who partake in the *śrāddha* performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rules; and the "Ekoddiṣṭās" are those who partake in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, as indicated by their inclusion in this general enumeration. Likewise, in many Purāṇas such as the *Brahmavaivarta*, it is stated that these ancestors are to be gratified by *śrāddha* offerings:
"And these ancestors, nourished by the *śrāddhas*, [attain] the imperishable Soma."
Being nourished by the white [rays], they will cause him to increase constantly.
Likewise: "Those among them whose faces are turned upwards are known as the Nāndīmukhas;
they should always be honored in rites of prosperity (vṛddhi-śrāddha) according to the injunctions of the Śruti."

In the section defining the ancestors (*pitṛ*) shown in the *Vārāha Purāṇa* within the division on *śrāddha*, the divine nature of the celestial ancestors (*divyapitṛ*) is clearly understood both through their classification and by their very name. Furthermore, in practice, the status of the *nāndīmukha* ancestors as deities is observed in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. And even when such a rule is observed, it is not proper to assume it to be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the absence of a subverting factor; for experts in logic maintain that while a rule (*vidhi*) possesses purposefulness, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would otherwise be redundant. This is because they hold that whether a matter is praised or not praised, its essential meaning remains neither deficient nor excessive.

[72] Furthermore, those words which are uttered in proximity to other words intended to establish the performance of an action—words that express the result (*phala*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—but whose own primary meaning is not that [action], are nonetheless described in the Śāstra as being subordinate to the action through their function as praise (*stāvaka*). This is done in accordance with the requirement that all words must serve the purpose of the action enjoined by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*), and by observing worldly linguistic usage in sentences such as "This cow yields much milk. Even if such passages appear to have no further purpose or are devoid of purpose, there is no one who can be censured for this, because the Veda is eternal. However, the fact that these words are subordinate to the expression of an action, as required by the injunction to study, is established along with the praise; for instance, in the case of the mantras regarding the deities, since the deity is already enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), another injunction of a different deity is impossible. Moreover, we observe that even pure originative injunctions exist, as seen in the case of the *pādya* (water for the feet) and so forth.
Having performed the ancestral sacrifice known as *tarpaṇa*,
one who maintains the sacred fires should always perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha at the waning of the moon.
In the *Manusmṛti* as well, the origin of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] is established as being purely [for the ancestors]:

"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having offered the *anvāhāryaka* [rice], should perform the monthly *śrāddha* on the waning of the moon. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, in numerous *śrāddha*-kalpas, the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is observed precisely as follows: "One should give to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyo dadyāt*), referring to the daily *śrāddha*, the new-moon *śrāddha*, and so forth. Since the Agniṣvāttas and others are also denoted by the word "ancestors" (*pitṛ*), they too are established by the originative injunction; thus, there is no fault of obstructing the deity-status by a quality already established by the originative injunction. However, regarding those *ekoddiṣṭa* rites for the deceased—namely, the *preta-śrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the annual *sāṃvatsarika*—which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite, let there be no deity-status for the Agniṣvāttas and others, because of the conflict with the human deities (the deceased) who are established by the originative injunction. Therefore, let the deity-status of the Agniṣvāttas and others be optional (*vaikalpika*) in certain *śrāddhas* performed at auspicious times such as the new moon or eclipses—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—provided these rites are not already occupied by deities established by the originative injunction. Moreover, there exists an injunction for the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas to serve as deities in the *śrāddha*, as stated in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*: [The text continues with the citation from Yājñavalkyasmṛti.]

"The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas are the sons [of the ancestors]; they are the Pitṛs, the deities of the Śrāddha," so said Paiṭhīnasi. "He who, knowing this, worships the Pitṛs—the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—becomes dear to them. Who indeed are these called 'Pitṛs,' to whom what is given here becomes inexhaustible? The Vasus are the fathers, the Rudras are the grandfathers, and the Ādityas are the great-grandfathers; to them what is given here becomes inexhaustible."
In the Devala-smṛti: "Everywhere the ancestors are to be honored, the deities of the deities;
they are pure, stainless, and clean, residing in the southern direction."

"The Vasus are to be known as the Pitṛs," and so forth. Therefore, there is an option regarding the deities. However, the authors of the *Mahārṇavaprakāśa* and others maintain a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*) of the deities. For instance, the Pitṛs are of three kinds: some are the progenitors (*janaka*) and so on; others are the sons of Marīci and others, such as Somapa and his kin; and others are the Vasus and so on. Among these, the rite for the progenitors and others is the standard (*autsargika*) Śrāddha. Thus says the Śatapatha Śruti: "Saying 'O [Name], this for you,' [he offers] to the father of the sacrificer."

Likewise, the *Manusmṛti* is well known for its statement regarding "rites for the deceased" (*pretakṛtya*). Similarly, it says: "But while the father is still living, one should perform the offerings for the ancestors alone," and "One should not give anything by bypassing a living [relative]," according to the Śruti. By such statements, the ancestral rite (*pitṛkārya*) is prescribed with reference to a deceased father and others. An exception to that rule of reference is recorded in the Smṛti:

"If the father has been killed by a Brāhmaṇa or the like, or is an outcast (*patita*), or devoid of [proper] associations, or has died in violation of the order of succession, the offering should be given to those very ones to whom he himself would have given."
"Water-rites (udakakriyā) shall cease for those who have abandoned themselves," and so forth.

And thus, one whose father has fallen (patita) performs the *śrāddha* for his grandfather and the others; and one whose father or grandfather has fallen performs the *śrāddha* for the three ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather.
For it is said:

In a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, one whose father and grandfather are living should feed the great-grandfather and those who preceded him; these two [living ancestors] should be fed in person, as previously described. If all three [ancestors] are living, the offering should be made to the three preceding ones.

And it is stated in the Mahāpitṛyajña: "He mentions three ancestors beyond [the immediate ones]; the sixth [ancestor] is assigned to the first rice-ball, the fifth to the second, and the fourth to the third; cessation is understood at the seventh."

In this regard, when three or four ancestors beginning with the father are unfit for the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), and when the offering of rice-balls is prohibited for those from the seventh ancestor onwards, and since the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* are obligatory, there arises the question: how are these two to be performed? In response to this expectation, it is stated: "The Brahmins named Somapās," and so forth; as well as, "The Vasus are to be known as the ancestors," and so forth. Therefore, in the case of deceased ancestors such as the father who have fallen [from their status], the Somapās and others, as well as the Vasus and others, serve as the deities (*devatā*) in the *amāvāsyā* and other *śrāddhas*, as well as in the *pitṛyajña*.
Thus say Āpastamba and Gobhila.

If he should not know [the mantras], he should offer the first ball with the words, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth"; the second with, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space"; and the third with, "Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven."

By this, indeed, the divinity of certain [beings] characterized by singularity is indicated; whereas by their fatherhood characterized by plurality, the Somapās and Vasus and others are shown in another scripture. Therefore, it is these very ones who are designated by such terms as *pṛthivīṣaḍa* and so forth—this is the most parsimonious hypothesis. Furthermore, the divinity of the Somapās and others is established through the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should worship the fathers, the grandfathers, and all the great-grandfathers, as well as their respective ancestors, with food in the proper order."
Then, while reciting "uśantas tvā," he should invoke the ancestors.
May the Somavantas, the Barhiṣads, and those others known as the Agniṣvāttas—all the ancestors of meritorious fame—come to us. Thus.

And there is a Vedic mantra: "May the Soma-loving Pitṛs, those consumed by Agni, come to us by the paths traveled by the gods. Likewise: "O Pitṛs consumed by Agni, come here; sit down, each in his proper seat, O excellent leaders. Likewise: "O Pitṛs seated on the sacrificial grass, come hither; we have prepared these offerings for you; enjoy them. Likewise: "The Aṅgirases, our Pitṛs, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of Soma. Likewise: "Our former Pitṛs, the Soma-loving Vaśiṣṭhas, who have followed after the drinking of Soma. Likewise: "The Soma-loving Pitṛs are invited upon the sacrificial grass to these dear treasures. Likewise: "We invoke the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs according to the seasons, they who are swift to the Nārāśaṃsa Soma-drinking."

And in the *Hārītasmṛti*: "Having honored the Brahmins with water in a vessel according to their status, observing the indicative marks (*liṅgadarśanam*"; and this was explained by Jayasvāmin: "The meaning is that one should honor those ancestors without overstepping them—those ancestors of whichever caste have been honored for the sake of the *śrāddha*, that is, for the fulfillment of the purpose of the *śrāddha*. And these are shown by Manu and others to be the Brahmins known as the *Somapās*. Thus Hārīta himself says: "By that [offering] he gratifies the ancestors of whom Soma is the eldest, and by that he gratifies the *Somapa* ancestors. And it is seen in the *agnaukaraṇa* rite: "Svadhā, obeisance to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; svadhā, obeisance to Agni, the carrier of the *kavya*; svadhā, obeisance to Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras, accompanied by the ancestors. And it is seen in the *pitṛyajña* after the preparation of the six-potherd cake (*ṣaṭkapāla*) and other items known as the *mahāhavis*. Thus in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, beginning with "By means of the *mahāhavis*, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra," and continuing with the explanatory passage ("Therefore, he sacrifices with this"), after enjoining the *pitṛyajña*, it is said: "He offers a six-potherd sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to the Soma-accompanied ancestors, or to Soma accompanied by the ancestors," and so forth. Likewise: "Then they prepare parched grains (*dhānāḥ*) on the *anvāhāryapacana* fire for the ancestors seated on the *barhis* grass"; and "Then, from the milk of a cow that has just calved, stirred once with a single stick, there is the *mantha* offering for the ancestors consumed by the fire (*agniṣvātta*)," and so on. This would not be possible in any way if the terms *agniṣvātta* and the rest were merely explanatory (*arthavāda*). And it is seen in the libation (*tarpaṇa*): "One should satisfy Soma accompanied by the ancestors, Yama, the descendants of Aṅgiras, and Agni, the carrier of the *kavya*," and so forth. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the Vasus and others being the actual deities in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, in the section on the *jīvacchrāddha* (the *śrāddha* performed while one is still alive).

"Having first worshipped the Viśvedevas with the rites of invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, one should say to them: 'O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Vasus; then, O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Rudras; and then, O Brahmin, I feed you for the sake of the Sūryas. Thus it is said.

Thus, some maintain that a fixed rule exists because certain divine ancestors (*divyapitṛ*) are seen as deities; they hold that Hara and others are such instances. However, these are merely methods for cultivating the vision of non-difference (*abheda*). This position alone is reasonable to accept as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), for this very view is observed in practice, this alone is approved by all, including Viśvarūpa and others, and this alone is irreproachable. For it has already been stated that the principle is that [passages] which praise [something else] are subordinate to an injunction (*vidhi*). Even in the Vedic statement "The sacrificial post is the sun," if it were indeed so regarding the post, what would be lost to the ritual? It would simply be better that it possesses such qualities.

[77] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the dharma of the emptiness of form, and so on, up to the dharma of the emptiness of the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in all the dharmas of a buddha, does he thereby become a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is not so. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, those dharmas of a buddha are themselves empty of the dharmas of a buddha, and the dharmas of a buddha are empty of themselves. Subhūti, it is because they are empty that those dharmas of a buddha are called ‘dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if those dharmas of a buddha are empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in those dharmas of a buddha, attain the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend those dharmas of a buddha as real entities, nor does he apprehend them as non-entities. He does not apprehend the knowledge of all modes as real, nor does he apprehend it as non-real. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in those dharmas of a buddha, attains the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, is it possible to fully know those dharmas of a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is not possible to fully know those dharmas of a buddha. Why is that? Because those dharmas of a buddha are unproduced and unceasing. Subhūti, it is because they are unproduced and unceasing that those dharmas of a buddha cannot be fully known. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if those dharmas of a buddha are unproduced and unceasing, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in them, attain the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not think, ‘I shall fully know these dharmas of a buddha,’ nor does he think, ‘I have fully known them. He does not think, ‘I shall attain the knowledge of all modes,’ nor does he think, ‘I have attained it. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in those dharmas of a buddha, attains the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend those dharmas of a buddha, nor the knowledge of all modes, how does he turn over the roots of goodness for the sake of the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns over the roots of goodness by means of a mind that is non-apprehending and signless. He turns them over in such a way that he does not conceive of a donor, nor a recipient, nor a gift. He turns them over in such a way that he does not apprehend a thought, nor a turning over, nor a dedication. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns over the roots of goodness for the sake of the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns over the roots of goodness for the sake of the knowledge of all modes, does he thereby become a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is not so. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, that knowledge of all modes is itself empty of the knowledge of all modes, and the knowledge of all modes is empty of itself. Subhūti, it is because it is empty that that knowledge of all modes is called ‘knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if that knowledge of all modes is empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in it, attain the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend that knowledge of all modes as real, nor does he apprehend it as non-real. He does not apprehend the path of a śrāvaka, nor the path of a pratyekabuddha, nor the path of a bodhisattva, nor the path of a buddha. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in that knowledge of all modes, attains the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any of those paths, how does he enter into the certainty of a bodhisattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the certainty of a bodhisattva by means of the non-apprehension of all dharmas. He enters into the certainty of a bodhisattva by means of the non-apprehension of the thought of enlightenment, and by means of the non-apprehension of the knowledge of all modes. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the certainty of a bodhisattva. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the certainty of a bodhisattva, does he thereby become irreversible? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is not so. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, that irreversibility is itself empty of irreversibility, and irreversibility is empty of itself. Subhūti, it is because it is empty that that irreversibility is called ‘irreversibility. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if that irreversibility is empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become irreversible? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes irreversible when he does not apprehend even the name ‘irreversible. He does not apprehend the marks of irreversibility, nor the signs of irreversibility. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes irreversible. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend even the name ‘irreversible,’ how does he teach the Dharma to others? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to others by means of a mind that is non-apprehending and signless. He teaches the Dharma to others in such a way that he does not conceive of a teacher, nor a listener, nor a teaching. He teaches the Dharma to others in such a way that he does not apprehend a word, nor a meaning, nor a teaching. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to others. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva teaches the Dharma to others, does he thereby produce merit? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who teaches the Dharma to others produces a great mass of merit. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, that merit is itself empty of merit, and merit is empty of itself. Subhūti, it is because it is empty that that merit is called ‘merit. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if that merit is empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having produced that merit, dedicate it to the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates that merit to the knowledge of all modes by means of a mind that is non-apprehending and signless. He dedicates it in such a way that he does not conceive of a donor, nor a recipient, nor a gift

Furthermore, the defects of other alternative views will be stated. Moreover, this prescription regarding the [number of] views does not apply to rites such as the *pitṛyajña*, which are accomplished by means of six potsherds (*ṣaṭkapāla*) and so forth; for in those cases, the status of deity is prescribed exclusively for those beginning with *barhiṣad*. However, in the rite called *śrāddha*, where both [sets of ancestors] are involved, there would be a sublation of the number three if Agniṣvātta and the others were the deities, or else there would be a sublation of the father, grandfather, and so on, or a case of option (*vikalpa*). Even in the case of an option, that which is heard as being obligatory would be sublated in one of the alternatives. These and other defects of option would arise. Furthermore, if those [mantras] heard in the context of the *śrāddha* were to be applied to a sacrifice accomplished by six potsherds and so forth, then there would be the defect of their displacement (*utkarṣa*) from that context.

In a *śrāddha* performed by one whose father has fallen from his caste (*patita*), there would be a sublation of the deities prescribed by Āpastamba and others—such as the Earth and the six [classes of ancestors]—in favor of the status of deity belonging to the [deceased] fathers. Furthermore, if this were merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), there would be the undesirable consequence of sublating the deity-status explicitly stated in the scripture (*śruti*). Therefore, since a faultless position is obtained that accords with the deity-status stated in the *śruti*, the teaching of non-difference regarding those [deities] who are heard in scripture as distinct from human fathers is postulated; this non-difference does not contradict the *śruti* nor does it contradict their status as deities. When the deceased human is designated as a deity in the performance of the *śrāddha*, one must effect a superimposition (*āropa*) of non-difference between humans and [the classes of beings] such as the Soma-drinkers (*somapa*), the Vasus, Viṣṇu, Pradyumna, the months, and Varuṇa. To strengthen this superimposition of non-difference, the following words should be employed: "to those in the form of Soma" by the twice-born (*dvija*); "to those in the form of Haviṣmat" by the Kṣatriyas; "to those in the form of Ājyapa" by the Vaiśyas; and "to those in the form of Sukāla" by the Śūdras. Alternatively, all these words may be used together: "to our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, in the forms of Vasu, Rudra, and Āditya," or "in the forms of Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva," or "in the forms of the month, the season, and the year. In the case of offerings to the fathers (*pitṛdāna*), one should also employ: "to our father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, in the forms of Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and Agni. This will be explained in its proper place in various contexts. For in this way, the status of deity for both [the human fathers and the divine classes] is established within a single performance. There is no sublation of anything, and both the teachings of difference and non-difference are reconciled. And here, primarily, the designation is of the deceased humans themselves; the inclusion of the Soma-drinkers, Vasus, and so on occurs through the method of viewing them as non-different within the nature of the object designated, and not conversely.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa* that when a *śrāddha* is performed specifically for the human ancestors (*manuṣyapitṛ*), satisfaction of the divine ancestors (*divyapitṛ*) occurs; however, their primary designation is not shown there. For, after enumerating the various classes of human ancestors, it is said therein: "When the funeral offering (*nirvāpa*) is given to them by their kinsmen belonging to the same lineage, those [ancestors] residing in the world of Soma obtain satisfaction as partakers of the monthly *śrāddha*."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, Brahmā’s speech to the divine ancestors:
"By means of that which is given with great devotion to Brahmins, on behalf of one's father, one's grandfather, and his father as well, [the merit accrues]."
May there be supreme satisfaction for all, as long as the moon and stars endure.
Likewise, there is no doubt that on the side of the maternal grandfathers as well,
they too are satisfied by those three being satisfied through my command.
Having thus described the satisfaction of human ancestors, that which was spoken for the sake of satisfying the divine ancestors is stated:
"O highly fortunate ones, listen now as I speak of whatever means of happiness shall lead to your satisfaction."
With whatever food they satisfy the ancestors by honoring the best of the twice-born, with that very same food they shall offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) upon the earth;
by that very act, eternal satisfaction for you all shall come to pass.
In the Devalasmṛti as well, it is stated specifically with reference to deceased humans:
"Whatever rite is performed here by humans for the sake of the *pretas*, the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are satisfied by that, not the *pretas*; for the *pretas* are remembered as being the ancestors."

One should not think that by the derogatory explanatory statement (arthavāda), "The *pretas* are not the ancestors," the divinity (*devatātva*) of the *pretas*—characterized by being the intended recipients of the oblation—is negated; for that would contradict the opening statement, "having directed [the offering] toward the *pretas*. Rather, in order to dispel the doubt as to how human beings existing in various states of rebirth (*yoni*) can possess superhuman power and bestow specific fruits through satisfaction and contentment, their status as "ancestors" (*pitṛtva*), characterized by being presided over by the Vasus and others, is stated. It was with this very intention that Yājñavalkya said: [79]
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestral deities of the Śrāddha;
when satiated by the Śrāddha, they gratify the ancestors of human beings.

In this context, it should be understood that by means of the *śrāddha* rite performed for the deceased person—which is itself brought into existence—the Vasus and other deities are gratified, and they in turn bring about the satisfaction of the deceased person by acting as its presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). This has been explained in detail in the section concerning the justification of such satisfaction.
Furthermore, regarding what was stated in the *Nandipurāṇa* after enumerating the divine groups of ancestors:
"Those men who have attained various states of existence, whether auspicious or inauspicious, across diverse wombs..."
But the ancestors, being worshipped by those various individuals, satisfy them in turn.
"For those whose ancestors and gods have been well-sacrificed for by their sons and grandsons,
the gods satisfy their fathers and grandfathers.
This too has been explained by the very words of Yājñavalkya.
And as it is stated in the Nandipurāṇa: "Those by whom Viṣṇu is worshipped with intent have thereby gratified their ancestors;
Brahmā, when worshipped, delights all the paternal grandfathers of a man."
"Those great-souled ones by whom I am worshipped, having dedicated [this] at the time of a śrāddha—verily, their great-grandfathers do not go to the terrible hell. Thus it is said.

Even that [text] does not establish Viṣṇu and the others as the primary objects of reference; rather, it establishes their inclusion within the very nature of the object to be addressed by way of the practice of viewing them as non-different [from the ancestors]. One should provide a similar explanation for other such statements as well. Thus, it is established that while deceased humans possess the status of deities (*devatātva*) in the *śrāddha*, they are included within the essential nature of the divine ancestors (*divyapitṛ*) through the application of the view of non-difference. And in this way, the scriptural indications (*liṅga*) are also rendered consistent. Thus, it has been described how the ancestors and others who have gone to another world are to be addressed as the deities in the *śrāddha*.

Now, in response to the inquiry as to who, where, and how many are to be designated [as recipients], it is said: First, in the primary *pārvaṇa* rite, there are three paternal ancestors—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—and three maternal ancestors—maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather. Thus, six [ancestors] are to be designated along with their wives both in the feeding of Brahmin guests and in the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*). Accordingly, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"Facing east and south, one should offer the rice balls; immediately after each rice ball..."

Since the plural number in the word *piṇḍān* (pindas) indicates plurality, and because of the maxim that "when there is no reason to bypass the first [option], one should take the first," it is understood that exactly three are intended—just as in the injunction, "One should sacrifice *kapiñjala* birds for the spring. For this very reason, it is stated in this same Purāṇa:
"The wise man should offer three pindas mixed with honey, ghee, and sesame.
Jātūkarṇa also says:
"Having performed the ritual washing, one should offer three pindas according to the rule.
Thus, these three pindas are to be given to the three [ancestors], namely the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather. And so says the Śatapatha Śruti:
"‘O So-and-so, this is for you’—thus [he offers] to the sacrificer’s father; ‘O So-and-so, this is for you’—thus to the grandfather; ‘O So-and-so, this is for you’—thus to the great-grandfather."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* as well, it is stated that three [ancestors], beginning with the father, are the sharers of the *piṇḍa*:

"The fourth and subsequent [ancestors] are the sharers of the *lepa*; the ancestors beginning with the father are the sharers of the *piṇḍa*; the giver of the *piṇḍa* is the seventh among them; such is *sāpiṇḍya* for seven generations."

[81] Here, the fourth is the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*). Those for whom he is the first are "those beginning with him" (*tadādyāḥ*); this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the type where the qualities of the members are understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), because it is stronger than the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* type. For in the former, there is inclusion of what is heard [in the compound], whereas in the latter, there is no such inclusion. Therefore, three persons—the fourth, fifth, and sixth—are partakers of the *lepa* (the smearings of the rice balls). The father and the others—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are three; these are the partakers of the *piṇḍas* (rice balls). This is appropriately stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather..."
For these three persons are to be understood as being connected by the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).

"Furthermore, the other relatives connected by *lepa* (the smearings) are said to begin from the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*); these three, together with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), constitute the seven.

Thus, in the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), the three beginning with the father are the intended recipients (*uddeśya*). In the feeding of the Brahmins as well, these very same individuals are the intended recipients. And so it is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa* and other texts.
"When a deceased person has attained the status of a *pitṛ* following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite,
one should worship the ancestors who preceded him in all *śrāddha* ceremonies.
This is also seen as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.

"I shall worship the fathers, the grandfathers, and the great-grandfathers, as well as all their ancestors, in due order with food. Thus it is stated; likewise, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen in the sūtras of Śaunaka and others: "When the father has received the *arghya*, when the grandfather has received the *arghya*, and when the great-grandfather has received the *arghya*, the Brāhmaṇa should pour out the *arghya* for them."
In the *Yamasmṛti*, when the placement of the *arghya* vessels is prescribed, their connection to the ancestors and others is understood:
"One should place the vessel for the paternal ancestors first; upon it, one should place that for the grandfathers;
then, having placed that for the great-grandfathers, one should not lift it up nor move it."

In this context, since the vessels for the *arghya* offering are connected with the feeding of the invited Brahmins, and because that connection with the meal exists, the relationship with the deities residing therein is established, and not otherwise; thus, even in the feeding of the Brahmins, there is deity-status for all three.
Now, let it be that only these three have deity-status, since in the *Kalpasūtras* it is stated that in the *Amāvāsyā* Śrāddha, deity-status belongs to only these three.

It is not so; for Viṣṇu has stated: "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers, or the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single collective act (tantra)," and Yājñavalkya, after describing the procedure for offering the rice-balls (piṇḍas), said: "In the same manner, one should offer [the balls] to the maternal grandfathers, and then the water for sipping (ācamana)."

Regarding this, Śaṅkhaśrīdhara says: "This might be so if this statement of Yājñavalkya were prescriptive (*upadeśaka*); however, the learned consider it to be a transference rule (*atideśaka*). Why? Because it is a prescription in the form 'it should be done thus. From this sentence, one understands only that 'it should be done in that same manner,' but not that 'this [specific rite] itself should be performed. For a single sentence cannot both prescribe and transfer, as that would result in the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, the meaning of this sentence is understood as follows: whoever—such as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) or others—is known from another scriptural injunction to be the performer of the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*, when performing that *mātāmaha-śrāddha*, he should perform it in the same manner as the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, and not otherwise.

This is incorrect, because there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means, the connection with all the agents [of the sacrifice] is understood, and by context (*prakaraṇa*) as well, that very same connection is established. Now, one might object: "In this case, only the words 'the same applies to the maternal grandfathers' are heard, but not even the words 'one should perform the *śrāddha*. Therefore, if this sentence were intended merely as an extension (*atideśa*), the injunction would concern the literal meaning [of the extended rule]; whereas if it were intended as a qualified injunction, it would concern the literal meaning [of the primary rule]."

Not so; for in this context, one must necessarily supply either by *anuṣaṅga* (supplying from a previous sentence) or by *adhyāhāra* (mental insertion) the remainder of the sentence, namely "one should perform the *śrāddha*. Indeed, without that, no injunction is possible for anyone.

Now, it might be argued that as soon as another element to be enjoined is introduced, the injunctive force shifts to each of those respective elements—as in the sentence "the cloth becomes red," where one sets aside the meaning "the cloth exists" and instead adopts the meaning "it becomes red."

It is not so; for it is the very nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) that its object is something not already established, and not that its object is another thing to be enjoined. Otherwise, even the status of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) would collapse. As for the principle that the injunctive power has another thing to be enjoined as its object, that applies only when one item is already established and there is a second item as the object; however, when nothing is established, it must be discerned that the object includes even subsequent items. [Objection:
"A son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) must perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather by rule."
If there is a connection of purpose between both, he should perform it for both as well.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Yama-saṃhitā*, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) is prescribed as a mandatory rule specifically for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*). Therefore, it is understood that the entitlement for the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) alone does not exist there by necessity. Consequently, from the word "son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikā-suta*), the exclusion of the son of a non-appointed daughter is precisely understood, because the function of a word is to imply the exclusion of others. Hence, in order to avoid contradiction with this statement, the rule "the same applies to the maternal grandfathers" (*mātāmahānām apy evam*) must be explained as being intended merely as an extended application (*atideśa*).

Not so. For there are two kinds of *putrikā-putra* (the son of an appointed daughter): one who is related only to the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), and another who is related to both the maternal grandfather and his father. Among these, the *putrikā-putra* who is related only to the maternal grandfather must perform the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather as a rule; however, as for the *śrāddha* for his father, he may or may not perform it.
