It is for the purpose of precluding the mandatory performance of the paternal *śrāddha* for such a person that the statement "the son of the appointed daughter [must offer] according to the rule" (*niyamāt putrikāsutaḥ*) is given, and not for the purpose of precluding the mandatory performance of the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha* for other types of *dauhitras*. This will be explained in detail in the section on eligibility (*adhikāra*). The teacher Karka has also said: "In an injunction such as 'the *śrāddha* should be performed,' since no distinction is understood, it is understood that the *śrāddha* for both [sets of ancestors] must be performed. Furthermore, from the words of the author of the Sūtras—"having sprinkled water, he should give three *piṇḍas* each"—this repetition (*vīpsā*) is only appropriate when the ritual application (*prayoga*) includes the *piṇḍas* for the maternal grandfather. Also, from the indicative mark of the mantra: "To the fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers. For these reasons, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is obligatory in the *pārvaṇa* rite. Moreover, because of the instruction regarding the commonality (*tantra*) of the *vaiśvadevika* portion—namely, "for the maternal grandfathers also, the procedure (*tantra*) or the *vaiśvadevika* [is the same]"—if the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather were not performed at the time of the ritual application for the paternal *śrāddha*, with reference to what would the commonality of the *vaiśvadeva* portion exist? Marīci also says: [Text follows...]
Likewise, one endowed with devotion should perform the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva rite, or that [portion] belonging to the Vaiśvadeva. Thus it is said.

Thus, it is established that the primary *pārvaṇa* śrāddha has six deities. Furthermore, that which is performed without the *pārvaṇa* ritual—whether it be the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) śrāddha prescribed for common times such as the *aṣṭakās*, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), or eclipses; or that daily śrāddha characterized as "obligatory" (*nitya*) which is performed every day—that too must have exactly six deities, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the *pārvaṇa* procedure and because of the statement of Dhaumya:
"Wherever the fathers are honored, there the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*s) are also [honored]."
"It must be performed without distinction; otherwise, hell is certain. Thus [it is said].

Regarding this, Śaṅkhaśrīdhara says: "The statement of Dhaumya refers to those cases where a śrāddha for both groups [of ancestors] is prescribed as a rule, such as in the case of a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) or an auspicious śrāddha (vṛddhi-śrāddha); it also refers to the case of those who belong to two lineages (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa), adopted sons (datta), and the sons of appointed daughters (putrikā-putra). This is incorrect, because there is no contradiction with either logic or scriptural authority if it applies to all cases; furthermore, if it were restricted to the thirteenth lunar day and so forth as desired by others, it would result in the fault of being a mere restatement (anuvādaka), since the śrāddha for both groups on the thirteenth lunar day and other such occasions is already specifically enjoined within that context by particular statements.

If it is argued that [the text] is not a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) because it prescribes something without distinction, this is not so; for the status of the preceding portion—“wherein the ancestors are honored,” and so forth—as a restatement remains unrefuted. Furthermore, even in the case of a prescription without distinction, since there is no additional element to be performed, only what is already established is taught; thus, everything would be a mere restatement. This is because respect (*ādara*) is not distinct from the *śrāddha* itself, as it is already established by such injunctions as “one should perform the *śrāddha* endowed with respect.”

But if that were so, since the two groups [of ancestors] would thus be required in every *śrāddha*, those who teach the performance of the *śrāddha* for the two groups on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) and other such occasions would merely be restating what is already established.

This is not the case; for their purpose is to demonstrate the excessive sin incurred by performing the rite otherwise through negligence, and because it will be stated later that these are indeed injunctions (*vidhi*). This is also the case in the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti*:
"From all other [materials] mentioned, [one should offer] rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) mixed with honey and sesame."
One should offer [the oblation] to the paternal ancestors, maternal grandfathers, and others, according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtras.

The meaning of the phrase "of the father, maternal grandfather, and so forth" is as follows: one should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) at the *amāvāsyā* (new moon) *śrāddha* for these three—the father and his two ancestors—and likewise for the three beginning with the maternal grandfather. Kātyāyana also says: "Excepting the *karṣū-samanvita* [śrāddha], the first of the sixteen *śrāddhas*, and the annual (*pratyābdika*) śrāddha, there shall be six rice-balls in the remaining cases; such is the settled rule."

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is accompanied by the *karṣū* (trenches). By this, it is implied that in rites such as those involving the *karṣū*, there is no *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*). In the *Smṛtis* of Devala and others, it is stated:
"One may perform the *ṣaṭpiṇḍa-śrāddha* even with a single Brāhmaṇa;
one should cause the six *arghya* offerings to be given there, and likewise provide food for the six."
The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from the mouth; the great-grandfather is said to eat from the palate; the maternal grandfather from the throat;
the maternal great-grandfather from the heart; and the elder (maternal great-great-grandfather) is situated at the navel.
Even so, O great sage, one should perform the Śrāddha for the six deities;
he who causes it to be performed divided [into separate rites] becomes a slayer of his ancestors.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, regarding the practice of offering the *piṇḍas* and the subsequent meal (*anvāhārya*):
"Therefore, everything should be performed by one who knows the tradition while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).
Thus, having formed six *piṇḍas* from the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-śeṣa*), he should likewise offer water."
One should pour water into the water-vessels with the left hand.
Pulastya also said: "Three maternal grandfathers are traditionally recognized, beginning with the mother’s father;
their daughters' sons should perform the śrāddha for them just as they do for their own fathers."
The phrase "like unto one's father" means that [the care for] the three generations is equal in terms of necessity and respect. Vyāsa also said:
"A twice-born man should satisfy his paternal ancestors and maternal grandfathers with the śrāddha;
thus he becomes free from debt to his ancestors and goes to the world of Brahmā."
Also in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Therefore, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha for the three beginning with the father,
and likewise for the maternal grandfathers, for the sake of discharging one's debts."

Because it is stated that [the rite] is for the sake of discharging a debt (*ānṛṇyakāraṇāt*), it is understood from the implication that if it is not performed, the debt toward the ancestors remains unpaid; thus, its necessity is established. For this very reason, the Brāhmaṇḍa Purāṇa also mentions the fault incurred by its non-performance: "He who performs the *pārvaṇa* solely for the sake of his father, but does not perform it for his maternal grandfather, is born as a slayer of his father."

Now, if the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather is mandatory for every daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) without exception, then how is it established in the *Skanda Purāṇa* that the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather is mandatory only for the daughter’s son who inherits the property? For it says:
"The Śrāddha for the maternal grandfathers must always be performed according to the rules by the daughter’s son who inherits the wealth, for the sake of expiating his debt."
[87] From this, it is understood that for anyone other than a daughter’s son who inherits the wealth, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is not mandatory.

It is not so; for, by considering the supplementary statement beginning with "this [wealth] is sufficient for men," it will be explained in the section on eligibility that the term "heir to the daughter's son's wealth" (*dauhitradhanahārin*) is intended as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any daughter's son in general. Furthermore, even though any daughter's son at all possesses the entitlement to perform the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rites for the maternal grandfather) on occasions such as the new moon, this statement is made for the purpose of granting the right to the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha* and other rites specifically to that daughter's son who is the heir to the wealth. It does not conclude with the exclusion of other daughter's sons from entitlement. As for the verse of Manu:
"For the daughter's son shall indeed take the entire inheritance of a father who has no [other] son;
he alone shall offer two funeral cakes, one to his own father and one to his maternal grandfather. Thus [it is said].

This demonstrates that the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather who is without a son is indeed mandatory; furthermore, this should be explained as having the same meaning as the preceding [text]. Thus, it is established that in a *śrāddha* prescribed for common times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), there are six deities: the three beginning with the father and the three beginning with the maternal grandfather. This status of being a deity belongs to each of them individually, and not to them collectively. Accordingly, the *Śruti* shows the dedication to each one individually: "O so-and-so, this is for your father," "O so-and-so, this is for your grandfather," and "O so-and-so, this is for your great-grandfather. So says Manu.

"Whatever is mixed with honey—cow’s milk, ghee, and milk-rice—is said to be inexhaustible when offered to the ancestors and the deities. Regarding this, Hariharācārya maintains that because the word "devatāḥ" (deities) ends in the plural and because the analytical statement (*vigrahavākya*) is taught as "the deity and the deity" (*devatā ca devatā ca*), the plurality of the deities is understood; thus, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) is apprehended as residing in its entirety within each individual.

[88] And Vaijavāpa says: Having invoked the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the sacrificer by their names with the verse "uśantas tvā," and having murmured "May they come to us," they point toward the vessels. By addressing each one individually—saying "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*"—he indicates that the father and the others are designated individually at the invocation, the offering of *arghya*, and so forth; thus he considers each one to be a separate deity. Āśvalāyana also addresses them individually, saying: "Svadhā to the father, svadhā to the grandfather, svadhā to the great-grandfather."

And Viṣṇu [states]: "With the words 'Salutation to all the Vedas,' one should first offer the food to those facing east"; thus, regarding the offering of food, he indicates each individual ancestor, such as the father, by means of words ending in the dative case.

And Kātyāyana [states]: "He asks, 'I shall cause the *svadhā* to be uttered'; when it is replied, 'Let it be uttered,' he shows that the designation is to be made for each individually, saying, 'Let the *svadhā* be uttered for the fathers, the grandfathers, and the great-grandfathers. Likewise, in the application of the ritual washing (*avanejana*), he shows that the designation is to be made for each individually, saying, 'O so-and-so, wash yourself'—referring to the three ancestors of the sacrificer beginning with the father. Also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should likewise give food to the fathers by means of an invitation, having respectfully taken hold of the thumb of each individual Brahmin."

"O you of such-and-such lineage, this food is for you; *svadhā*! *Namaḥ*! In this regard, the explicit separate designation "O you of such-and-such lineage, this food is for you" is observed. Thus, by such statements from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*, it is understood that the ancestors and others constitute deities individually.

But surely, from Gautama’s statement, "One should give the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon day," and from Vasiṣṭha’s statement, "Having invited the Brāhmaṇas on the preceding day, one should give to the ancestors," it is understood that the ancestors constitute a collective divinity; for in those passages, by the use of the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) in the term "to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), their mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is understood.

Not so. For the dative case does not express deityhood; rather, that must be inferred by it. And it cannot be so inferred, because of the contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti shown previously. Furthermore, mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) is observed in both worldly and Vedic usage in relation to the act of denotation.

Now, one might object: since both types of statements are observed, why may it not be assumed that the status of being a deity belongs either to each [word] individually or to them collectively? To this, someone replies: An option (*vikalpa*) occurs only when two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of equal strength are encountered; however, that is not the case here. For from the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇa*), the status of being a deity is understood for each [word] individually, whereas for the collective group, it is understood through the dative case (*caturthī*). And the dative case is weaker than the wording of the mantra. Indeed, the wording of the mantra is more authoritative than the dative case because it is integrated into the performance (*prayoga-samavāyin*); as it reveals the objects while they are being employed, it denotes the very nature of the deity. The dative case, however, does not directly denote the nature of the deity. Therefore, there is no valid basis for an option between the individual and the collective positions.
That is not so; for the *śruti* is the dative case-ending, while the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is the wording of the mantra, and *śruti* is more powerful.
[Objection: If that is the case, then it follows that the deitieship belongs to them collectively.

Not so. By the reasoning stated previously, the position that each [brāhmaṇa] is a deity individually is established; furthermore, because it is not touched upon by more numerous scriptural statements, the individual position is stronger. Moreover, if the status of being a deity were to belong to them collectively even when combined, then even when there is a plurality of brāhmaṇas, the collective group might occasionally be the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*) with respect to each single brāhmaṇa, rather than necessarily being distinct. Alternatively, the status of being a deity for the collective group would apply only in the case where there is a single brāhmaṇa.

Not so; for there is no scriptural statement that deityhood is based on the plurality or singularity of Brāhmaṇas. If it is argued that this performance (prayoga) having a collective deity is one thing, while the performance having individual deities is another, then—since no distinction would be perceived due to the difference between collective and non-collective deities, and since even a single performance would not be understood as having a common procedure (*tantra*)—the contingency (*prasaṅga*) would be untenable. Consequently, when separate performance is required, it follows that "there should be four Brāhmaṇas," according to the rule:
"Even if he is very wealthy, he should feed two at a rite for the gods, three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each."

Otherwise, the *smṛti* of Manu and others—which establishes that the "three-brāhmaṇa" and "one-brāhmaṇa" options are respectively the primary (*kalpa*) and secondary (*anukalpa*) forms—would be contradicted by such a view. Furthermore, even in the case of the "one-brāhmaṇa" option, Bṛhaspati demonstrates that each individual ancestor (father, etc. is a separate deity by showing the division of the served food and the performance of renunciation (*tyāga*) directed toward each one individually:
"If one should feed a single brāhmaṇa because the prepared food is small, one should divide the food into small portions and assign them to those [ancestors]. (Baudhāyanadharmasūtra 2.5.8.1)
In this regard, a statement has been composed by someone named Pracetas:

"When the object of invitation is one, or when the twice-born [guests] are one, there shall be a single *arghya*, a single *pavitraka*, and a single offering of the *piṇḍas*"; thus it was spoken by Gālava.

In this statement, although there is a plurality of those to be designated (*uddeśya*), since the injunction for offering the *piṇḍas* is made without even conceiving a division when the number of twice-born (*dvija*) is one, it is understood that the deities (*devatā*) act as a collective whole. In this regard, this statement must first be considered as contradicted by the texts that prescribe a division [of the offerings] and by the texts that prescribe the offering of separate *piṇḍas*. Alternatively, it should be explained as referring specifically to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. The meaning is that, provided there is unity in the object to be designated, whether there be a multiplicity or a singularity of Brāhmaṇas, only a single *śrāddha* should be performed; for if there were a difference in the objects to be designated, then even if the number of twice-born were one, the performance would already be established as distinct by the aforementioned texts. Furthermore, if one were to adopt the view of a collective deity in another ritual application involving the invitation of only one Brāhmaṇa, the connection of the invocation verse "uśantas tvā" would not be possible there.

Now, one might object: since the word *pitṛ* in the plural form in the mantra "uśann uśanta āvaha pitṝn" denotes the deitieship of the fathers and others as joined together in mutual association—by virtue of being a *dvandva* compound or a *ekaśeṣa* compound of the same meaning—how can there be a suspicion of non-connection (*ananvaya*) when the application (*viniyoga*) is precisely to that [mantra] on the basis of this indicative mark (*liṅga*)?

It is said: by means of the verse "uśantas tvā," one should invoke the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the sacrificer by their names. This is because the application according to the words of Vaijavāpa is for a ritual performance involving individual deities, following the indicative power (*liṅga*) as in the case of the *aindrī* verse. Therefore, even in the view that there is a single Brāhmaṇa [for all], the status of being a deity belongs to the father and others individually; thus, the renunciations (*tyāgas*) must be prescribed by designating each one individually, and never by designating them collectively through a copulative compound (*dvandva-samāsa*) expressing mutual conjunction. This is established. Now, this is considered: do these have the status of deities together with their wives, or alone? On this point, Hari and Hara maintain that they are alone. Accordingly, in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, the ritual formula is seen to be composed entirely devoid of the qualification "together with their wives."
Then, having respectfully taken hold of the thumb of each brahmin one by one, [he should say]: "O you of such-and-such a lineage, this food is for you; svadhā! obeisance! Thus.

In the first [formula], the words *amuka* (such-and-such) intend to express both the relationship and the personal name; in the second, the lineage (*gotra*) is explicitly stated. Thus, the ritual formula is completed as follows: "O our father, Yajñadatta Śarman, of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, this food is for you; *svadhā*, obeisance, obeisance! Even in the *Kalpasūtras*, the construction of the sentence is seen to be devoid of such specific qualifications. For example, in the *Sāṅkhyāyana-gṛhya*: "Having designated the food with the words 'O [Name], this is for you,' one should feed him. Also in the works of Viṣṇu: "To the father and grandfather, by their names and lineages, for those facing north," and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence here for the status of the father and others as deities when they are qualified by their wives. Nor should it be argued that: "At the Anvaṣṭakās, at the Vṛddhi-śrāddha, and likewise annually, the Śrāddha for the mother is performed separately; elsewhere, she is together with her husband."

Thus, because of the statement in the *Śātātapa-smṛti*, "The Śrāddha for the mother must be performed together with the husband of the mother," one might suppose that the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) belongs to the father and others as qualified by their wives. However, such a supposition would contradict the direct injunctions found in the Purāṇas and other texts previously cited. Furthermore, because of the expression "together with the husband" (*patinā saha*), and according to the grammatical rule *sahayukte ’pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19), the husband is subordinate due to his association with the word "together"; since he is thus not the primary element, it is impossible for him to function as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) which establishes primacy. Consequently, the actual liturgical formula (*prayogavākya*) would have to be "To the mother who has her husband" (*sabhartṛkāyai mātre*). Moreover, just as in the case of the injunction "He takes the *pātnīvata* cup," where it is established that *Patnīvat* alone is the deity, and although the mantra "Drink the Soma together with the god Tvaṣṭṛ" mentions concomitance (*sahatva*), the deity is not *Tvaṣṭṛ* along with [Indra], so too here, because of the independent scriptural statement "One should perform the Śrāddha for the father and the grandfather," the deity is not the father together with his wife. Nor should it be argued that while in the former case [the *pātnīvata*] it is so because of a conflict with the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), here the deity-status must be inferred, and therefore, by the force of hearing the word "together," it must be inferred that the deity is the father specifically accompanied by his wife. For even there, since the root *grah* ("to take") signifies merely the act of taking, the deity-status must indeed be inferred based on what is intended; this is just as in cases such as "He takes the *aindravāyava* cup," where Indra, Vāyu, and others are the deities. For these reasons as well, the father and others do not have the status of deity as qualified by their wives. This is because: [The remainder of the passage follows with further logical arguments.]
One should not give separately to women, except on the anniversary of their death;
for it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction is derived solely from the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered to their husbands.
Sentences such as these demonstrate precisely that women do not possess the status of being the primary object of the injunction (*uddeśyatva*), even when they function as qualifiers.

Nor should it be argued that because the separate giving [of property] is prohibited, the non-separate giving is thereby permitted; for this would imply that the status of being the primary object is authorized even as a qualifier of the husband, which contradicts the fact that the mention of "women" (*yoṣit*) is not intended as a qualifier. This is because, under this view, since men also do not give separately due to their association with their wives (*patnīsāhityāt*), there is no separate giving for them either. Therefore, what is enjoined here is simply this: "one should not give to women."
Since it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction comes from the mere morsels of food provided by their own husbands.

Thus, this explanatory statement (*hetuvannigada*) also illuminates this very same meaning. For here, the term "ball of food" (*piṇḍa*) is designated as "the husband’s ball of food" (*bhartṛpiṇḍa*), and not as "the wife’s ball of food" (*patnīpiṇḍa*). If the wife were also intended as a beneficiary (*uddeśyatva*) in that ball of food by way of being a qualifier of the husband, then that ball of food would be designated by both as "this ball of food belongs to the two," and thus designated for the two. Therefore, it is stated that while the wives are satisfied by the portions of the balls of food offered with reference to the males alone, the wives are not themselves the intended beneficiaries. For this very reason, in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, separate balls of food are prescribed for the wives in the performance of the *Amāvāsyā* Śrāddha performed by one who maintains the sacred fires; however, they are not prescribed as intended beneficiaries by way of being qualifiers of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). As it says: [The text continues with the citation from the Matsyapurāṇa.]
Therefore, having formed six balls from that remainder of the sacrificial oblation,
one should likewise offer water with vessels of water using the left hand.

Having thus described the ritual procedure for offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to the six ancestors beginning with the father—including the drawing of lines, washing, taking up [the water], pouring out, re-washing, salutation, and the worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, at the beginning and end—it is said:
"Then, having performed [the rites] in between, the wise man should offer *kuśa* grass to their wives;
he should perform the respective offerings of the rice-balls and so forth, as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*)."
Thus it is also stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Excluding the single anniversary of death (kṣayāha), there is no separate rite for women;
some great sages, however, desire a separate śrāddha for women."

Thus, even in the *Sāṅkhyāyana Gṛhya Sūtra*, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the wives is prescribed separately; it is not, however, as a qualification of the husband. Therefore, since the ancestors (father and so forth) alone constitute the deities, the injunction regarding the father and others should be performed without the qualification "together with his wife" (*sapatnīka*). To this, it is replied: The status of being a deity belongs only to those [ancestors] together with their wives, because of the statement: "In other cases, together with the husband. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of using the expression "to the mother who has her husband" (*sabhartṛkāyai mātṛ*), because the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the wife, though implied, is not intended here. If both the accompaniment by the husband and predominance were intended, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, if two qualities were enjoined regarding an already established ritual act, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is because many reasons for non-predominance are perceived, and these are stronger than a single reason; according to the maxim: "When there is a collision of contradictory properties, the majority shall possess the common property. Now, those reasons are demonstrated. First of all:
On the Anvaṣṭakā days, at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), and likewise annually;
on these occasions, there is a separate śrāddha for the mother.

Having thus stated, by this collection of words, merely the distinctness of the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, the statement elsewhere regarding its exclusion [from other rites] was made. In that other passage, where it says "together with the husband," although there is also a statement of primacy—which consists in the exclusion of the non-primacy previously mentioned—this is indeed an intended statement. This is because it exceeds the mere exclusion of what was intended to be stated. Regarding the duties of women, their non-primacy has been declared due to their dependence on the husband; that very point is also understood from common worldly experience. Therefore, because of a contradiction with the force of the actual fact (*vastu-bala*), it is inferred that the primacy brought about by the force of the word (*śabda-bala*) is what is intended.

But surely, when the performer of the *śrāddha* is designated as a deity through his own action, primacy is brought forth by the force of the word itself—given that the identity of the deity is established by the single word [denoting him]. Furthermore, from worldly usage and other sources, the wife’s dependence on her husband is understood in relation to her own actions. Since there is no contradiction between these two, how can it be said that primacy is not intended [for the wife] on the strength of those [worldly facts]?

It is said in reply: By reflecting on such statements as "the rite for the deceased is well-known," one understands that this *śrāddha* performance benefits the deceased human being through the medium of feeding. Thus, when the wife is fed along with the husband, she possesses dependence upon him regarding her own purpose. When this [dependence] is established, however, there arises a contradiction with the subordinate status (*aprādhānya*) understood from worldly convention and other sources regarding the activity of the performer of the *śrāddha*. Consequently, in deference to that [conventional understanding], the primary status (*prādhānya*) is understood to be unintended. In an originative injunction for the *śrāddha* such as "one should perform the *śrāddha* for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather," the fathers and others are understood to be the deities (*devatā*). Since their primary status is already established by that prior understanding and is not obstructed, it is proper not to resort to the subordinate status of their wives—which arrives later—as the deity-status of these newcomers is relegated to the end according to the maxim: "The insertion of newcomers occurs at the end. Therefore, there is no conflict even with a quality enjoined in the originative injunction; for it cannot be set aside by what is enjoined in the originative injunction in the same way that the *phalacamasa* (the cup of soma) is set aside by another means. It is all the more impossible when it enters as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*), because everything has a requirement for a qualification. For this very reason, it connects with a qualification prescribed in general, just as Soma is connected with qualifications such as "having three peaks. Nor does this lead to the consequence that Tvaṣṭṛ would also be a qualification, because there is no such injunction. In the present case, however, there is a difference: the rule "the *śrāddha* for the mother should be performed together with the husband" enjoins the status of deity in the *śrāddha* itself. Furthermore, in the *śrāddha* for the father and others, the wives' status as deities is subordinate. This is because Śātātapa has stated that in the husband's *śrāddha*, the wife is entitled to a share.
"When the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has been performed, she attains a single form with her husband's ancestors; therefore, the wife is a sharer in their portions. Thus it is said.

For the word *aṃśa* (portion), by denoting a single part of a great substance (*mahādravya*)—specifically that which is to be consumed by the ancestors and others—indicates that the great substance possesses the nature of being "possessed of portions" (*aṃśitva*), thereby implying that the ancestors and others who consume it are the primary deities (*pradhānadevatā*). In this context, "having a single form" (*ekamūrtitva*) refers to a similarity consisting of proximity and likeness, brought about by the departure from the state of a *preta* and the attainment of the state of a *pitṛ*, which serves as the qualification for being a consumer of the *śrāddha*. It does not, however, mean a primary identity of form (*aikarūpya*), because such is impossible. Indeed, neither the unity of two conscious selves (*kṣetrajña*) nor the unity of their bodies is observed anywhere in the scriptures, nor is it accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), nor is it uncontradicted. For those who maintain the doctrine of multiple selves (*nānātmavādin*) hold that in a single body, differences among conscious selves arise due to discordance in cognition, desire, effort, and activity. Furthermore, even in the *Bṛhaspati Smṛti*, the status of the mother and other relatives as deities is seen in the *śrāddha* for the father and others through their association with him.

"A mother eats the śrāddha food, which is like nectar, together with her own husband; likewise the paternal grandmother with her own [husband], and the great-grandmother with her own. Thus it is stated in the Śaṅkhasmṛti as well.
Except for the Anvaṣṭakā rites, the Śrāddha for the mother, and the Ekoddiṣṭa performed on the anniversary of death,
there shall be no separate rite for women.
Also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Upon the birth or death of a relative, she has attained oneness with her husband in respect to the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and the lineage (*gotra*);
therefore, no separate offering of a rice-ball exists for wives."

Surely, in this case, since that wife has attained oneness with her husband, it is understood from the prohibition against offering a separate *piṇḍa* for the wife that she is not an object of the ritual dedication (*anuddeśyatva*).

Do not say so. From the statement “it does not exist separately” (*pṛthak na vidyate*), the admission is understood that it certainly exists non-separately (*apṛthak*). Nor should it be argued that, because there is no separate offering for the husband either, the mention of the wife (*patnī*) would be unintended; for in this context, when the *śrāddha* is performed for the wife together with the husband, the reference must not be made by way of a rule regarding primacy or non-primacy relative to the husband—either as primary alone or as equal in primacy—but rather solely as a qualification of the husband. Since the mention of the wife is intended to convey such a state of non-primacy, a reference concerning such primary and non-primary subjects is indeed appropriate. For example, the cooking for Caitra’s meal is distinct from the cooking for the feeding of the assembly; yet, it is not the case here that the cooking for Caitra’s meal does not exist, nor has the mention of Caitra become unintended. Rather, even though they are not separate, it indicates his non-primacy. It is the same here for the wife. This very passage must be explained in this manner. Otherwise, if the meaning were merely that “it does not exist,” the sentence would have been simply “it does not exist separately” (*pṛthak na vidyate*); in that case, the word “separately” (*pṛthak*) would be redundant. By this very point, the objection raised against the mention of women (*yoṣit*) in the verse “One should not give separately to women except on the day of their death” is also refuted. As for what was said—that in the passage “Since their satisfaction is declared to come from the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) of their own husband alone,” the *piṇḍa* is designated as the husband’s *piṇḍa* and not the wife’s *piṇḍa*, and therefore women are not the intended recipients there—that too should not be asserted. For the husband’s primacy is expressed. Even though there is no difference in the status of both husband and wife as deities (*devatā*), it is proper to refer to them by the one who is primary. Therefore, it is established that in *śrāddhas* for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) and others performed on the new moon and other occasions, the wives of those ancestors are also to be intended, albeit in a non-primary capacity. Accordingly, the formulaic statement for the ritual application—such as “O our father Yajñadatta Śramaṇa, of the Vāsiṣṭha gotra, together with your wife (*sapalnikai*), this food is for you”—is to be understood in accordance with established custom (*ācāra*).

Regarding those who hold this view: if, in a *pati-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for the husband), the wives are intended as the recipients (*uddeśyatva*), then one must duly proclaim their relationship, names, and *gotras*. This is for the sake of fulfilling injunctions such as, "The name and *gotra* of the ancestors indeed cause [the offering] to reach them during the *havya* and *kavya* rites"; thus, the *gotra* and name of the wives must also be recited. According to their opinion, the formula for the ritual application (*prayoga-vākya*) should be formulated as follows: "O our father, Yajñadatta Śarmā, of the Vāsiṣṭha *gotra*, together with your wife of the Vāsiṣṭha *gotra* named Sāvitrī, this food is for you," and so forth. In this view, when the father has many wives, the ritual formula should be employed in the form: "Together with your wives of the Vāsiṣṭha *gotra* named so-and-so and so-and-so, this food is for you," and so forth. This is because, even for those other than one's own biological mother, there is no distinction regarding their entitlement to a share in the husband’s *śrāddha*, based on statements such as, "She [the wife] has attained oneness with her husband. Now, an objection may be raised: since the mother is designated by the term "mother" (*mātṛ*) in the statement, "The mother eats the *śrāddha* together with her own husband," it is understood that the wives of the father other than the biological mother are not included in the collective invocation. To this, [the proponents of this view] reply: [This is not so]. For it is stated: "By the power of the words, 'She has attained oneness with her husband,' etc., there is no distinction; therefore, in the husband’s *śrāddha*, they all participate in the shares equally. Thus, the wives of the father, including those other than the biological mother, are indeed intended in the invocation.

This is not so; for all [the wives] are mothers. How is this so? If among all the wives of one husband even one should have a son, Manu declares that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.

This is because of the statement of Manu. Now, one might object: since the meaning of the text is understood to be that for other [wives], in the absence of a son born of the same womb, the status of having a son is achieved through the son of a co-wife, this statement does not refer exclusively to the son of a co-wife. How, then, is the formulation of the ritual application (*prayoga-vākya*) justified here in its general form?

It is replied: because in this statement, the intention is merely to convey that even by means of a co-wife’s son, the status of being "one who possesses a son" (*putravatī*) is attained. If the intention were such that "if one is possessed of a son, the other is not," then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to supply additional words to the literal sense of the text.
[Objection: But surely there is no fault of *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipsis), because every word has as its purpose the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*).

[Reply: Not so. It is the very nature of words to primarily convey their own meaning (*svārthasamarpaṇa*), not to primarily exclude others; for if they were primarily intended to exclude others, it would follow that all words would function merely as restrictive enumerations (*parisaṃkhyā*). Moreover, if the phrase "if she has one" were intended to exclude others, then in the case of two women each having a son, third and subsequent women who also have sons would not be eligible [for the rite] by virtue of those sons.

Now, as for the phrase "if she has one," this is not intended to exclude a second [son], but rather to show that a co-wife who already has a son does not become "one who possesses a son" through the son of another co-wife; rather, that status arises only through her own son. Conversely, it is only for a woman who is childless that the status of being "one who possesses a son" occurs through the son of a co-wife. Thus, the word "only" (*eva*) is used specifically for the purpose of excluding those who already have a son.

Not so; for a single word lacks the capacity to exclude the term *putravatī*. A word excludes only that meaning which is the opposite of its own primary meaning (*svārtha*), and not anything else. And it is only the plural number that is the opposite of the singular word-meaning, whereas the term *putravatī* itself is not.

But surely there is the word *eka* (one), which is incapable of excluding those who possess sons; rather, it will be the word *putriṇī* (woman with a son) itself that effects the exclusion. But this is strange: that the word *putriṇī* itself should be the excluder of those who possess sons! For an object other than its own primary meaning is excluded by a word, but not its own primary meaning itself. Indeed, it does not happen that "one should not invite a woman with a son" when there is an exclusion of one who has a son. Furthermore, even in the case of "why should one not not invite a woman with a son," the word is not an excluder.

Do not say so. For in this context, it is not the word *putriṇī* that functions as the differentiator (*vyāvartaka*), but rather the negative particle (*na-kāra*), and that [particle] is not present here. Furthermore, since one who is already a mother by her own son cannot be the object of a doubt regarding the absence of being a mother, and since the fact that others possess sons is established by her being a mother through her own son, it would follow that demonstrating that "one who possesses a son by her own son" is a mother would be unnecessary—being both unrequested and useless—and moreover, vitiated by the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Indeed, no such instruction is ever given: "She who becomes a mother by a certain son is a mother by that very son. For if that were the case, then for a single person, the status of being the qualificand and the subject of restatement, as well as being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the indicated, and being known and unknown, would all occur simultaneously with respect to that same person. Therefore, the word *putriṇī*, when assisted by another co-occurring word, excludes [others from] being a mother; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

It is said in reply: although it is impossible to teach that "she who has a son by a certain son is possessed of a son by that very son," nevertheless, because it is possible to teach that "by one woman’s son, the co-wife—whether she herself be childless or not—becomes possessed of a son," the word *putriṇī* ("possessed of a son"), even when accompanied by other co-occurring words, is not capable of excluding [the status of] being "possessed of a son. Thus, since the statement is intended to mean that "one woman is possessed of a son by virtue of her son, while another who lacks a son becomes possessed of a son [through him]," this statement refers specifically to the son of a co-wife. Consequently, all the wives of the father are to be designated as participants together in the paternal *śrāddha*, which is common to them all.

[99] But if this were the case, then even while one's own son exists, the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika) would have to be performed by the son of a co-wife, since he too possesses the entitlement by virtue of being a son.

Not so. The funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) for him are performed separately by as many [relatives] as have the entitlement; however, it will be stated that they are performed once by a single person with the consent of all. Otherwise, it would follow that even all uterine brothers would have to perform them separately. Furthermore, although the son of a co-wife may be the eldest, the mother’s entitlement to the funeral rites belongs to her own biological son alone, because he is more intimate (*antaraṅga*).
Now, if she were already possessed of a son through her own son, yet were also to be considered "possessed of a son" through the son of a co-wife, then—
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father, even one should have a son,
they all become possessed of sons through that son.

If it is argued that because of this statement, when a *pitṛśrāddha* is performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions, the uncle who has sons must also be designated since he too is a "father" (in relation to his nephew), and thus the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for one with two fathers would follow according to the *smṛti*—then, alas, by what could the designation of an uncle who has no sons be prevented from occurring in a *pitṛśrāddha*? If you hold the view that he is not to be designated because his status as a "father" in relation to the uncle is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), then a son would never perform a *śrāddha* for an uncle who has no sons. If you say that he should perform it because [the uncle] is said to perform the duties of a son, then why, alas, should he not also designate the uncle in a *pitṛśrāddha* performed at times such as the new moon? Furthermore, even the second father who is designated by a *dvaimātura* (son of two fathers) is likewise only figurative, and therefore does not deserve to be designated.

To this it is replied: we do not here maintain that women other than one’s own mother—namely, the wives of one’s father—are intended as recipients of the rite by virtue of being mothers, but rather solely by virtue of being the wives of one’s father. This is because, in the passage, “The mother eats the śrāddha together with her own husband, which is like nectar,” the word *mātṛ* (mother) functions as a designation for the wife of the father in general; furthermore, in many scriptural texts, the rule regarding the status of being an eater at a single śrāddha is seen to be predicated upon the term *patnī* (wife). Moreover, when the grandfather has many wives, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the simultaneous inclusion of all those wives. Since there is no such doubt even in the case of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), the inclusion of all of them is established without further deliberation. However, in the śrāddhas for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) and others, the inclusion of their wives by virtue of their accompanying presence is to be understood from the instruction that these are similar to the paternal śrāddhas, as expressed in the formula, “In the same way for the maternal grandfathers,” and so forth.
One should not give [offerings] to women separately, except on the anniversary of their death;
for it is traditionally taught that their satisfaction comes solely from the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) offered to their own husbands.

This is to be understood from such statements as these. Thus, the following has been established: in the performance of a common *śrāddha* at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) for deities such as a father who has many wives, the ritual must be carried out with formulas characterized by the mention of both male and female ancestors, such as: "O our father Yajñadatta Śarman, belonging to the Vāsiṣṭha *gotra*, together with your wives belonging to the Vāsiṣṭha *gotra* named so-and-so—this food is for you," and so forth.

Here the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated. Regarding that, first of all, in the primary *pārvaṇa* rite, there is no entitlement for the wives of the paternal grandfather other than one's own mother, nor for the wives of the great-grandfather other than the mother of the paternal grandfather. For it will be stated that they have no mandatory entitlement in the *śrāddha* rites when their own uterine sons are present, because of the intervention of sons born of other wombs. However, such entitlement may occur optionally through compassion or affection. Yet this does not deserve to be connected with the obligatory rule, due to the contradiction between the permanent and the non-permanent (*nityānityasaṃyoga*).

Now, it might be argued that this co-participation of those [women] as wives of the father and others follows from the background of obligatory rites (*nityavidhi*) and does not depend on a separate entitlement; or rather, precisely because it follows from the background of obligatory rites, it proceeds by inferring a distinct, constant entitlement.

Not so. Even as a wife, her accompaniment can only occur by depending upon an entitlement that is already established independently. For what is already established (*klpta*) sublates what is merely to be inferred (*kalpya*); what is certain sublates what is uncertain; and what is consistent sublates what is inconsistent. Furthermore, there is no mention of those other than the mother and so forth by way of accompaniment, because of the contradiction between the association of the permanent and the impermanent. Indeed, there is no rule that the wives of fathers and others must necessarily exist apart from the mother and so forth. Thus, their occasional accompaniment is not fit for connection with obligatory rites (*nityakarman*). The mother, however, exists invariably and therefore deserves to be accompanied. For this very reason, even for those who have no sons, there is no accompaniment of these women in obligatory rites, since their very existence is itself non-permanent. As for the view that their accompaniment is intended simply because of their status as mothers—that too is incorrect. For their motherhood is secondary (*gauṇa*), just as a paternal uncle’s fatherhood is secondary. According to the maxim that "between the secondary and the primary, the understanding rests on the primary," the meaning taught by a sentence containing the word "mother" belongs to the biological mother alone. Otherwise, since a paternal uncle also possesses a secondary form of fatherhood, he would be entitled to perform the *Amāvāsyā* Śrāddha like a "double-lineage" (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) performer.
Now, if the understanding were based on the primary sense, then the field-owner would likewise not be included in the designation.

Not so. This is because of such scriptural injunctions as, "One should offer two balls [of rice]; they should mention two [names] for each ball," and because of the rule, "One should give to the fathers and the grandfathers. For this very reason, sentences such as "two balls" are meaningful; otherwise, since that [offering] would already be established by the mere fact of being a father, those statements would be redundant. Furthermore, since the production of sons such as the *kṣetraja* is prescribed specifically for the purpose of offering balls to the *kṣetra* (the field) and others, the designation applies even to a non-primary [son], but not in the case of the mother. Moreover, since the mother is the intended object (*uddeśya*), there is no mention of those other than the biological mother, as they do not possess the status of "motherhood" (*mātṛtva*).
"Manu declared that all those [women] become possessed of sons by means of that son.

By this, what is ordained is that the son of a co-wife performs the duties of a son; it does not establish that the co-wife of one's mother possesses the status of a mother or performs the duties of a mother.
Now, what indeed is this so-called "duty of a mother"?
It is said: [it is] the accomplishment of the mother’s *śrāddha*—which is prescribed as a permanent obligation (*nitya-adhikāra*) and performed by the son—as its deity.
Now, what is meant by "the duty of the son" (*putrakārya*)?
It is said: it is the accomplishment of satisfaction and so forth for the mother who has gone to another world, by means of the *śrāddha* and other rites.
But what is the distinction here? For that very same *śrāddha* which is the duty of a son is performed by the mother as a deity; thus, the function for both is one and the same.

True, this is so; however, what is intended here is a distinction of purpose (*prayojana-bheda*) resulting in a distinction of ritual action (*kārya-bheda*) for a single person who performs the *śrāddha*. Therefore, where a son proceeds with the *śrāddha* having in mind the accomplishment of his own perpetual obligation (*nityānuṣṭhāna*), there the son performs only his own duty; thus, in the *pārvaṇa* rite, there is no mention of the mother’s co-wife as a joint object of intent. By this very principle, those regular (*naiyamika*) *śrāddhas* prescribed for specific times such as the *aṣṭakā*, the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), and eclipses, are explained; for they possess the extension of the rules (*dharmātideśa*) of the *pārvaṇa*. Furthermore, those performed out of a desire for purification, a desire for a fruit, or a desire for the satisfaction of the ancestors (*pitṛ-tṛpti*), these too possess the extension of the *pārvaṇa* rules. Such indeed are the ancestral *śrāddhas* (*pitṛ-śrāddha*). Thus, it is established that in the ancestral *śrāddha* occurring on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such times, the mothers’ co-wives are mentioned as joint objects of intent without exception. However, where a separate *mātṛ-śrāddha* is prescribed, as in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and others, then according to the maxim "the primary [term] conveys the meaning," the mother alone is the object of intent, not the others. But when one should perform a *śrāddha* at a specific time such as the *mahālaya* or at a specific sacred site (*tīrtha*) like Gayā, out of a desire for the satisfaction of various ancestors, then one should perform the *śrāddha* for the mothers’ co-wives whether they have sons or are sonless. Even for those who have sons, because the son of the co-wife may also occasionally possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the *śrāddha* out of compassion or affection. By this same logic, the wives of the paternal grandfather other than the father’s mother, and the wives of the great-grandfather other than the paternal grandfather’s mother, are also explained. By defining the secondary status (*gauṇatva*) of the mothers’ co-wives, it is also established that the fathers of those [co-wives]—the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*)—possess only a secondary status, and thus they do not hold the status of a deity (*devatātva*) in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*. However, when one desires to perform a *śrāddha* at a specific place or time out of a desire for the satisfaction of various ancestors, then one should perform it for them as well by virtue of their occasional entitlement; this is the settled rule. Thus, when the status of the six deities—the performer’s paternal grandfather and others together with their co-wives, and the maternal grandfather and others together with their co-wives—is established for the primary *pārvaṇa* prescribed for times such as the new moon, it is also established that they alone are the deities in the common-time *śrāddhas* (regular, occasional, optional, social, and purificatory) which possess the extension of *pārvaṇa* rules. As for the journey (*yātrā*), when the entitled person himself begins the journey, it is already established that he should perform the *śrāddha* for his own ancestors. But when he is himself incapable and, at the start of the journey, encourages another person through conciliation and so forth and impels him to act, then a doubt arises: should this performer perform the *śrāddha* for his own ancestors, or for the ancestors of the entitled person? In that case, since the instruction for the *śrāddha*—"Whoever should go on a pilgrimage to a sacred site"—establishes the performer as the subject, and since the words "father" and so forth, which prescribe the deities of the *śrāddha*, require a relative, the performer who is in close proximity must be the relative.

Now, even when an action is performed by anyone at all, agency belongs only to the qualified person (adhikārin), because qualification and agency are co-located (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Indeed, no one can conceive themselves as the agent of an action that produces a fruit inhering solely in another; nor does the word cause one to understand what they are not entitled to. Therefore, in actions where scripture is the means of valid knowledge, agency is revealed by the word as belonging only to the qualified person. Hence, the result accrues to him alone. Otherwise, how could an act performed by one person be said to have been performed by the qualified person himself?

This is true; however, it is precisely *śakti* (capacity) that is brought forward here by the word "to be postulated. Therefore, when an action is performed by one agent, the claim of agency on the part of another who is entitled to the fruit of that action is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). For worldly agency is an object of knowledge established through perception and other means of valid cognition. And in the world, people designate as the "agent" in a given case only that person whose effort brings about the completion of that action.

Or rather, when an action is performed by another agent, the discourse regarding agency on the part of the qualified person (*adhikārin*)—by virtue of being the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*)—is indeed primary. However, that direct agency which was understood at the time of comprehending the qualification has already attained a state of grammatical non-coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Therefore, it is the agent himself who should perform the *śrāddha* for his ancestors.

To this it is replied: Even in the state of a secondary option (*anukalpa*), the rites must be performed exactly as they are understood to be in the primary case (*mukhya*). And in the present context, the *śrāddha* is understood to be for the ancestors related to the authorized performer (*adhikārin*). Thus, even when another person performs it, he performs it for those very same ancestors. Although the *śrāddha* remains situated in the state of the performer, it is merely an auxiliary to the journey (*yātrā*) and not an auxiliary to the performer himself; for, while its purpose consists in the fulfillment of an action directed toward no other end, it is grasped by the injunction regarding the qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*). Therefore, the *śrāddha* is for the ancestors who are the objects of the qualification for the journey. However, for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the deities are as in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*).

"The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is called occasional (*naimittika*). Since the occasional rite is thus characterized by this definition, there is no extension of the *pārvaṇa* rules to it; therefore, the status of being a deity does not belong to six [ancestors], but rather to only one. And even though this [rite] occurs at a common time, the wife does not have the status of a deity together with her husband, because that would result in a contradiction with the designation "ekoddiṣṭa. Therefore, the wife is a partaker in the portions of her husband's ancestors.
If it is argued that, by the force of such statements, there should be a sublation of the weaker means of knowledge;

Not so. Since there is no conflict when a sentence finds scope within a domain already established by a designation (*samākhyāna*), it is improper to sublate [the designation] when the coexistence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is attained. However, regarding the annual rites (*sāṃvatsarika*), for some they are dedicated to a single deity due to the tradition of the conduct of their father, grandfather, and others, and by virtue of the support of specific Smṛti texts; for others, they are dedicated to three deities. In that case, the mother and others, as well as the maternal grandfather and others, are not intended [as recipients]. This will be determined in detail in the section on the annual rites. On the other hand, it will be stated in the section on the *preta-śrāddha* that the sixteen *śrāddhas* are dedicated to a single deity. Now, when the performance of the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha* occurs in connection with those *śrāddhas*, if they are performed by being brought forward from their own time along with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—since it is stated that "one should perform them again"—then the monthly rites, which recur and are dedicated to three deities, must be performed. This is because they are performed once the state of being a *preta* has ceased following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Furthermore, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* consists of two ritual acts—the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*—and thus is dedicated to four deities. The *Nārāyaṇabali*, however, is dedicated to five deities: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva with his retinue, Yama, and the *preta*. Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa* and other texts.
One should indeed offer five lumps of food while recollecting the divine form:
first one should give to Viṣṇu, then to Brahmā, and then to Śiva.
One should offer the fourth ball of rice to Yama together with his retinue,
mentally announcing the deceased by name preceded by their *gotra*. Then,
having likewise uttered the name of Viṣṇu, one should cast the fifth ball as before.

By the phrase "having thus uttered the name of Viṣṇu," the vision of non-difference (*abheda-dṛṣṭi*) has indeed been stated. This being so, a formula for such a practice is inferred: "O Yajñadatta, our father, of the Vāsiṣṭha lineage, this is for you," and so forth. Thus, the determination of the deities has been made regarding the primary *pārvaṇa* rites—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—as well as the *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*, the *śuddhi-śrāddha*, the *yātrā-śrāddha*, the *puṣṭi-śrāddha*, the occasional rite known as the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the annual rites that recur every month, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the *nārāyaṇabali*. Now, the determination of the deities for the *ābhyudayika* (prosperity) rites is being made. Regarding the *vṛddhi-ābhyudayika* (rites of increase and prosperity), the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
And here the ancestors known as the *nāndīmukha*s are to be worshipped.
As stated in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*:
"Having thus performed the circumambulation, [one worships] the *nāndīmukha* ancestors on the occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*)."
One should sacrifice; the ritual acts consist of balls made of barley mixed with curd and jujube fruits.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The disciplined householder should worship the host of ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas. Thus it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
At birth, at the initiation ceremony, and at the marriage of a son,
one should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed rule.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"During a continuous flow of festive joy, and on auspicious occasions such as sacrifices and marriages,
the Mothers are to be worshipped first, and the Fathers immediately thereafter."
Then the maternal grandfathers are to be honored, as well as the Viśvedevas in the same manner.

In this context, by the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) used in the plural, three are meant: the mother, the paternal grandmother, and the paternal great-grandmother. For this very reason, the *Śātātapa-smṛti* states: "The three mothers should first be worshipped with great effort.

By the word "father" (*pitṛ*), the father, paternal grandfather, and paternal great-grandfather are meant; and by the word "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*), the maternal grandfather, the maternal great-grandfather, and the maternal great-great-grandfather are meant. For this very reason, Pulastya says:
"Three maternal grandfathers are traditionally recognized, beginning with the mother's father.
Kātyāyana also said:
"Having recited the *āyuṣya* mantras for the sake of peace, one should remain there with a concentrated mind."
"Thereafter, one should commence the offering of the *śrāddha* for the six ancestors.

Regarding the phrase "for the six," this is intended to refer to two groups of male ancestors, because the *śrāddha* for the mothers is prescribed in another *smṛti* as: "The mothers are to be honored first. In that context, the group of *nāndīmukha* ancestors was previously shown:
"Those among them whose faces are turned upward are designated as *nāndīmukha*."

These divine ancestors (*divyapitaraḥ*) and the human ancestors (*manuṣyapitaraḥ*), such as the mother and others, are the primary objects of the rite; furthermore, the *nāndīmukha* ancestors are to be included within the nature of these objects by means of viewing them as non-different from them. This has already been determined through the detailed exposition of the prima facie and final positions (*pūrvottarapakṣa*). In this context, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) for the *nāndīmukha* ancestors should be performed with such statements as: "This is the seat for the *nāndīmukha* ancestors" and "I shall invoke the *nāndīmukha* ancestors. The ritual manual of Kātyāyana is exactly like this.

He asks, "Shall I invite the Nāndīmukha ancestors? [The response is: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. In place of the word *akṣayya*, one says: "The Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers.
These very same ancestors are the deities even in the *abhyudayika* rite that forms part of a ritual action.
At the time of the *niṣeka*, at the *soma* sacrifice, and likewise at the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony—
The Śrāddha performed at the Puṃsavana rite, being an auxiliary part of the ritual, is to be understood as being like that performed on an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi).

Because of this statement, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the rules for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* [from the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*]. Thus, since it is established here that the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother; the father, paternal grandfather, and paternal great-grandfather; and the maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather constitute the deities of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, it is these very individuals who are intended to be designated by the term "Nāndīmukha" in such injunctions as: "In the case of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), one should worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors. As for those mentioned in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Those who may be beyond the paternal grandfather, they indeed are the Nāndīmukhas."
They should have expressions of serene faces; indeed, they are considered to be auspicious.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
these three are indeed proclaimed as the "tear-faced" (aśrumukha) ancestors.
Those three who precede them, however, are the "joyful-faced" (nāndīmukha).

We shall explain in the section on miscellaneous times that these deities are intended for the *śrāddha* specifically on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, and not for the *nāndīmukha* rites performed on occasions such as the birth of a son. For now, this much is established: in rites such as the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and marriage, whoever is the performer should offer the *śrāddha* to the human ancestors characterized as *nāndīmukha*. Furthermore, regarding these primary rites, there are various options for the performer. To illustrate, Śaṅkha and Likhita, having introduced the topic with "on the tenth day, having raised [the child] for the naming ceremony," state:

On that very day, the father—or another elder of the family—should perform the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), which is connected to the family deity (*kuladevatā*) and the *kṣatra* [lineage] and so forth. By this, it is stated that for those sacraments (*saṃskāra*) beginning from the naming ceremony, in the absence of the father, the agency belongs to the members of the family according to their proximity, in order to fulfill the injunction regarding the performer required by the necessary rites. Regarding the initiation (*upanayana*), however, Yājñavalkya says:
"Having initiated the pupil, the teacher [should teach him] preceded by the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*)."
"One should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purity and conduct.

Regarding this, Aparārka and others maintain that because of the mention of the "teacher" (guru), the father himself must perform the initiation (*upanayana*). However, Āpastamba and others point out that in the absence of the father, or when he is unfit to act as the initiator, another person may perform it;

for the *Brāhmaṇa* states: "He who initiates one who is ignorant enters from darkness into darkness, as does he who initiates one who is already wise. Therefore, one should desire to perform the sacramental rite for one who is endowed with noble lineage and learning, and who is composed."

Yājñavalkya states: "But those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their brothers who have already been consecrated. From the forthcoming statements, such as "one should initiate oneself," it is understood that even someone other than the father may act as the officiant for the initiation (*upanayana*). Regarding the marriage of a girl, Kātyāyana says:
"She herself should give away her own biological daughter; in the absence of the father, however, the kinsmen [should do so];
or else the maternal grandfather, or another, or the mother, [should give] the daughter born according to the Dharma. Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.

The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, and likewise the mother— each subsequent person among these, provided they are of sound mind, becomes the giver of the daughter in the absence of the preceding one.

"One who is in his natural state" means one whose intellect is unimpaired. For an act performed by one who is not in his natural state—even if he is otherwise capable of independence—is as good as undone. As Nārada says:
"Even if one is independent, whatever act he performs while having fallen from his natural state, that act shall indeed be considered invalid, because of the cause of his lack of independence. [109]

"Even though he is independent" means that although he is entitled to independence by virtue of being the father and so forth, [the gift] should be understood as not having been performed at all—such as the verbal betrothal (*vāgdāna*) of a daughter—if his mind has become deranged due to wind-disorders (*vāta*) or other causes, and he has thus fallen from his natural state. Likewise:
"The father himself may give the daughter, or the brother with the father’s consent;
likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a kinsman (*sakulya*), or a relative (*bāndhava*)."
"But if the mother exists and remains in her natural state, she [is the giver] for all;
however, if she is not in her natural state, those of her own caste should give the girl.

Thus, since there is an option regarding the agent, when the paternal uncle is the performer of the initiation and other rites, to which ancestors should he perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*? To his own [ancestors], or to those related to the one being initiated and the others?
But surely, why should the sequence not be that a father should first perform [the funeral rites] for his own kin and not for those who are not his own?

It is said in reply: Since the words "mother," "father," "maternal grandfather," and so forth, which enjoin the deities of the *śrāddha*, are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*), when there is a requirement for a correlate, that very relative who is taken as the performer of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is understood. Why, then, is there doubt? For when someone other than the father has attained the eligibility for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), then according to the maxim that "one who is authorized in the principal [act] is necessarily authorized in its subsidiaries," that same person attains eligibility for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Thus, he becomes the specifier of the referent of the terms "father" and so on by virtue of being their relative. Therefore, it is certain that he too should give [the offerings] to his own [ancestors].

Now, one might object: here the father alone is the primary qualified person, while another is qualified only in his absence; furthermore, the injunction regarding the deity is satisfied by the primary person alone and does not accept a secondary person presented only upon the impossibility [of the primary].

Not so. For it is the *adhikārī* (the person entitled to perform the rite) who is the qualifier, not the father. This injunction regarding the deities is connected only with the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* that arises from the rule: "One should not perform a Vedic rite without having first performed the *pitṛ-śrāddha*. And the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* alone is not connected exclusively with the father, because it is prescribed for rites other than the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) of a son as well. Therefore, we conclude that whenever anyone—whether a brother or someone else—attains the entitlement to perform an initiation (*upanayana*) or similar rite, he should at that time perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for his own ancestors. Consequently, when someone other than the father, such as a brother, performs an initiation or the like, he should offer the *śrāddha* specifically for his own ancestors.

But surely, in the case of initiation (*upanayana*) and similar rites, only the one being initiated is the qualified agent (*adhikārī*), while the initiator is merely the performer (*kartṛ*), like a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*). Now, if only one who shares in the fruit of the ritual action is the qualified agent, then it would follow that in the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on the birth of a son), the qualification belongs to the son alone. This is not so; because the father himself desires for his son qualities such as purity (*pūtatva*) and the like, the qualification belongs to the father alone. However, in the present case, there is no possibility of anyone other than the father desiring a fruit inherent in the one being initiated and the others.

Not so. That which is called *upanayana* (initiation) is an operation belonging to someone other than the one being initiated (*upaneya*), for in that case, it is impossible for the one being initiated—who functions as the object (*karman*)—to simultaneously function as the agent (*kartṛ*). However, in the case of a "passive-reflexive" (*karmakartṛ*) agent, agency is indeed intended; yet here, there is no group of words whatsoever that indicates such an intention. In expressions such as "I cause myself to fall" (*tam aham ātmānaṃ pātayāmi*), the identification of the agent and the object is justified by the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as "we" (*asmad*) and "self" (*ātman*). Therefore, those being initiated and the like have no entitlement to their own purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

But surely, the verb *nayati* here does not have the sense of "leading to" (initiation), but rather, due to the proximity of the prefix, it denotes another ritual act such as the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*).

Not so. For when joined with a prefix (*upasarga*), this [root *nī*] signifies only the act of bringing someone into the presence of a teacher (*ācārya-samīpa-prāpaṇa*), and it does not denote any other meaning that is not well-established. Furthermore, since this meaning serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) by establishing the specific proximity between teacher and pupil required for study, the person to be initiated (*upaneya*) cannot be prompted by an injunction toward this activity in the form of initiation (*upanayana*), which has a performer distinct from the one being initiated. This is because of the logical principle that persons are enjoined as agents only toward their own actions. Moreover, if the one to be initiated were the qualified agent (*adhikārī*) on the grounds of sharing in the fruit of the ritual action, then he would likewise be the qualified agent for the *puṃsavana* and other rites—which benefit him—simply because they are his own sacraments (*saṃskāra*), even while in the womb; and the same would apply to a deceased person regarding funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*) and the like.

If it is argued that this is so because he is incapable, the same applies to the initiation as well; for surely the one being initiated is not capable of setting the teacher and others in motion, just as a sacrificial priest does not set himself in motion toward the role of a domestic chaplain, nor do a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya set themselves in motion toward a sacrifice.

But surely, one who has not been prompted by an injunction himself—why would he prompt another? Yet, Kṣatriyas and others, while being prompted by an injunction toward a sacrifice, do indeed prompt the priest and others toward officiating at that sacrifice; and one who is prompted toward study prompts [others] toward teaching. Furthermore, in this context, approaching [the teacher] is not enjoined by the rule "one should approach," such that one, being prompted there by that injunction, would prompt the teacher toward the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). If it is argued that the approaching of the student is enjoined by implication through the injunction for initiation, and the taking in marriage of the girl is enjoined by the injunction for marriage— [The response follows: No, because the injunction is for the sake of the purpose. Just as the injunction for the *agnihotra* is for the sake of the *svarga-kāma* (one desiring heaven), and the injunction for the *soma-yāga* is for the sake of the *svarga-kāma*, so too the injunction for the *upanayana* is for the sake of the *brahmacarya* (Vedic studenthood). And since the *brahmacarya* is for the sake of Vedic study, the injunction for the *upanayana* is ultimately for the sake of Vedic study. Therefore, the approaching [of the teacher] is merely a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of the injunction for Vedic study. Consequently, one who is prompted by the injunction for Vedic study does not prompt the teacher toward the initiation ceremony. For the teacher is already established in his own duty by the injunction for officiating at sacrifices. Thus, the objection is refuted. Not so; for an injunction does not operate with respect to what is already established by the nature of the matter (*arthaprāpta*). Furthermore, when an action enjoined for one eligible person (*adhikārin*) implies another action belonging to a different eligible agent for the sake of its own accomplishment, that implied action is not mandatory for the former. For example, the activity of a priest (*yājaka*) implied by the injunction for sacrifice, or the act of selling implied by the injunction for buying for someone. Nor is there any sin in the non-performance of such an action. Therefore, why should the agent of going—implied by the initiation (*upanayana*)—be prompted to act by that initiation? Rather, it is the initiator (*upanetṛ*) himself who, for the sake of accomplishing his own enjoined rite, should prompt the one to be initiated (*upaneya*).
