It is said: For indeed, in the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and other such rites, there is a connection with misfortune for the one being initiated (*upaneyādi*), who is the object of the action. And he, desiring the warding off of that misfortune, is the primary *adhikārī* (eligible person) regarding the means for it; and the application of those means is precisely initiation and so forth. Just as someone sinking in water or mud, though lacking the power to lift himself out by his own effort, becomes an *adhikārī* regarding the means for warding off his own misfortune upon seeing another strong man on the bank, and having fulfilled his eligibility through the prompting of that other man—saying "Lift me up"—he wards off the misfortune; likewise is this case of the one being initiated and others regarding initiation and so forth. However, one who has died in the womb or a father and the like, who is unable to fulfill their eligibility even through the prompting of another regarding the means for warding off their own misfortune—such as the *puṃsavana* rite or funeral rites (*aurdhvadehika*)—is not an *adhikārī*. Furthermore, whoever is mentioned as the prompter of another in a ritual that benefits oneself is the very one who holds the eligibility therein. And this boy of eight years and so forth, a Brāhmaṇa and the like, is stated to be the prompter of the distinguished teacher (*ācārya*) regarding his own initiation. Thus, the wise one says in the *Smṛtimāhārṇava*: [112] (The verse follows).

"In the eighth year from conception, during the spring, a Brāhmaṇa should have himself initiated; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year, during the summer; and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year, during the rainy season.

However, in another Smṛti, it is observed that even those eligible persons other than the one to be initiated may themselves act as the initiator if they are incapable of doing so. As Yama says: "In the eighth year from conception, one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa; in the eleventh, however, one should initiate Kṣatriyas; and in the twelfth year, one should initiate Vaiśyas."
Manu, Śaṅkha, and Vyāsa [state]:
"One should perform the initiation (upanayana) for a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."

This has been established by Aparārka and others who explain the word *upanayana* as having the causative suffix (*ṇic*) with the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *upa*. Therefore, there is eligibility (*adhikāra*) for those to be initiated (*upaneya*) and others in the rites of initiation and so forth. For this very reason, it is heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "Satyakāma Jābāla, having addressed his mother, came to Gautama to have himself initiated. Furthermore, in the case of a maiden, her own agency as both the performer and the instigator of her own marriage is observed. Consequently, even for them, there is eligibility in their own marriage which wards off their own disadvantage. At that time, the agency and instigation of others [such as parents] exist solely as the fulfillment of that eligibility. However, in the case of fathers, mothers, brothers, and others who are not prompted by another, their status as fulfillers of eligibility arises from the injunction (*vidhi*) itself; for if they do not fulfill it, a scriptural hearing of fault (*doṣaśravaṇa*) is recorded. Since there is no such injunction for others besides them, the statements regarding the father and so on in that context are [understood] as being accompanied by the prompting of the maiden.
"In the absence of givers [of the bride], a maiden may herself choose her husband (*svayaṃvara*).

These and other such rules were stated by Yājñavalkya and others. Therefore, even when the marriage is performed by the mother, maternal uncle, or others, the maiden herself should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for the groups beginning with her father.

Now, one might object: since there are injunctions that the mother, maternal uncle, and others also act as the performers of the marriage, and since faults are declared for their non-performance, they too possess the authority [to perform the rite]; thus, the *śrāddha* must indeed be offered to their fathers as well.

This is not so. For there is no repetition of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) for every individual entitled to the rite (*adhikāra*), because the primary act (*pradhāna*) is one and the same, as in the case of a sacrificial session (*satra*). For in that case, even though there is a difference in the individual entitlements, the primary act is indeed one, since the injunction prescribes the agency of those acting in combination. Nor should it be suspected that here the reverse is true or that there is an option (*vikalpa*), because the girls alone possess the primary entitlement by virtue of being the sharers in the fruit [of the rite]. And this being the case, since the primary act called "marriage" is one, would it not follow that there should be only one *nāndīmukha* śrāddha for both the giver and the receiver of the girl, and not two separate śrāddhas? [The answer is: These two—receiving and giving—are indeed two distinct primary acts; and furthermore, because they are prescribed separately in the rule: "In the marriage of a daughter or a son... Otherwise, it would simply have been said, "in marriage. Therefore, when a certain teacher initiates another's son, he should perform the *nāndīśrāddha* for the father of the boy to be initiated (*upaneyapitṛ*); and a maternal uncle or similar relative, performing the marriage of a girl, should do so for the father of the girl. For this very reason, although it might follow that the śrāddha should be offered to the parents of the person being consecrated (*saṃskārya*), Kātyāyana states that when the father himself is the one performing the consecration, then the śrāddha is to be offered to the father of the performer of the consecration.
"A father should give [the offerings] to his own ancestors during the sacramental rites of his sons;
until the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the marriage, for them, but in his absence, according to their order.
If, however, the performer himself were to give to all his own ancestors, then it would not be necessary to state, "The father [should give] to his own ancestors."

Now, in the case of the *saṃskāra* rites, only this much is prescribed: "one should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) to the ancestors"; everything else is merely restated (*anūdita*). Therefore, the connection "if the father [is present], [he should offer] to his own ancestors" is not what is being prescribed.

Not so. For in the case of an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*), the restatement of the principal element (*pradhānānuvāda*) is useful because it serves that purpose; however, in the case of an injunction of the principal element (*pradhānavidhi*), there is no restatement of subordinate elements. Furthermore, the restatement of subordinate elements must be made of those already established by implication through the injunction of the principal element; yet such a restatement is improper here, as it would result in a failure to achieve syntactic unity with the injunction. Indeed, the acquisition of the subordinate elements occurs only after the operation of the injunction of the principal element has concluded. And that conclusion occurs preceded by the restatement of the elements associated with it. Consequently, if one were to attempt a restatement of subordinate elements within the very sentences that enjoin the origin of the principal action, the following defects would ensue: mutual dependency (*parasparāśraya*), syntactical split (*anekavākyatā*), a disjointed operation (*viramya-vyāpāra*), and the fact that within a single sentence a single element would function as both an injunction and a restatement. Moreover, in a sentence containing both an injunction and a restatement, the restatement comes first and the injunction follows, because in that case the injunction proceeds by taking something as its objective.

Now, it may be argued that words, even without an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), first attain the status of a single sentence by being directed toward a single meaning through the expression of their own individual referents; subsequently, they assume the form of an injunction or a restatement through the discrimination between what has already been obtained and what has not, or through the discrimination between what is obtained from the word and what is obtained from the meaning.

Not so; for without the cognition of whether a passage is an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*), the meaning of the sentence itself cannot be understood. Furthermore, the subsequent discernment of what is enjoined—performed by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not—is intended either to eliminate the possibility that the previously perceived relationship of injunction and restatement is actually reversed, or to remove doubt. For if that [doubt] were not removed, one would interpret the meaning of the sentence by relying on a different kind of relationship between injunction and restatement. In such a state, [the interpretation] would indeed bring about contradiction. For this very reason, when a quality such as *soma* is heard in an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) of a rite, it cannot be a restatement; rather, here there must be an injunction of a quality. However, [if one were to say] "let this quality, 'until the marriage' (*ā udvāhanāt*)," be enjoined: since the father has no authority over the sacraments of his sons after the marriage, he has no entitlement to perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* for them; thus, an injunction to that effect would be purposeless. Moreover, because its object is already established, it would lose its status as an injunction. Therefore, if the father is the agent, this relationship is enjoined for him alone and not for anyone else. For this very reason...
But in his absence, the rule "in that order" is applicable. In the absence of the father,

whoever else might perform the consecration should offer [the oblation] in that order— that is, starting from that father, according to the sequence of the ancestors of the person being consecrated— and not to his own ancestors.
Is it not the case that this is not its meaning, but rather [it means] "following the sequence of those," that is, following the sequence of the subsequent offices?

Not so. For if this were the case, then by considering the understanding of the reversal of what was previously prescribed—introduced by the word *tu* (but)—one would have to conclude that the father’s agency was previously enjoined. And thus there would be a redundancy, because since the son’s sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed by the father, no other person’s status as the performer of the *śrāddha* could obtain; for according to the maxim, "one who is authorized in the principal act is authorized in its subsidiary parts," the father’s authority is already established. Furthermore, if such a meaning were accepted based on the sequence of subsequent entitlements, it would result in a reference to something not present in the context. Moreover, in this view, the sequence understood from another scriptural statement, when being connected here, would become a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Surely this statement prescribes precisely this meaning—that those performing sacraments such as marriage with maternal uncles and others who are distinct from one's paternal uncles must perform the *śrāddha* for their own fathers alone—because of the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the phrase "for their own fathers."

This would indeed be the case if, in the phrase "by that sequence," the sequence of the performers were being stated; however, this has already been explained as meaning "this [sequence] is from the father's side. Furthermore, if all performers were to offer [the śrāddha] to their own fathers, then the expression "to the father of one's own father" would not need to be mentioned. Therefore, teachers, mothers, maternal uncles, and others should offer the śrāddha to the fathers of the person for whom the rite is performed—such as the initiate (*upaneyādi*)—and not to their own fathers.

Now, the ultimate [meaning] regarding the cloth is stated here: when the father performs the marriage, initiation, and other rites for his son and others, he should perform the *nāndīśrāddha* for his own ancestors and give [the gifts] to his own [relatives], according to the scriptural injunction: "He should give to his own. And when others—such as the grandfather, brothers, paternal kinsmen (*sakulya*), or the mother—who have obtained authority by virtue of the scriptural statement, perform the rite, they too should offer it to their own ancestors; for in the rule, "In his absence, however, [one should act] according to his order," the phrase "to his own" is supplied by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). Thus, it is only one who is authorized for the principal rite who is authorized for its subsidiary parts. Furthermore, because words such as "mother," "father," and "maternal grandfather" in the injunction "One should perform the *śrāddha* for the mother, father, and maternal grandfather" are relative terms, the rule finds its completion only by taking the relative who is the actual performer (the *adhikārin*). As for those whose authority is not explicitly stated by a direct scriptural word, they should perform the *śrāddha* for those belonging to him.

Thus end the deities of the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*. Now, that which is performed with reference to the gods is called *daivika*; such is the definition of the *daivika-śrāddha*. Regarding this *daivika-śrāddha*, any deity whatsoever who is intended to be propitiated has been described; thus, these are the deities for all varieties of *śrāddha*. Now follows the determination of the deities as prompted by the specific qualified person (*adhikārin*) in those very same *śrāddhas*. In that regard, first speaking with reference to the *dyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (one belonging to two lineages), the *Nāradasmṛti* states:
"Those who belong to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇakas*) should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*) separately to both [fathers]."
In that case, the seed-owner and the owner of the field should each take half of the inheritance from the produce.

Here, by the use of the word "separately" (*pṛthak*), it is stated that three *piṇḍas* are to be offered for each group of ancestors, thus making six *piṇḍas* in total. For this very reason, the *Devalasmṛti* states: "Those who belong to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇakas*) should offer the *piṇḍas* and water separately to both [sets of ancestors].
Six *piṇḍas* must be given to the six; by acting in this way, one does not go astray."
Baudhāyana and others, however, state that there are only three *piṇḍas* for six deities:
"The offering of *piṇḍas* should be made for two fathers; on each *piṇḍa*, the names [of both] should be mentioned.
Thus, there shall be three *piṇḍas* for six [ancestors]; by acting in this way, one does not err."
Āpastamba also says:
"If one should have two fathers, he should designate both [fathers] for each individual rice-ball."

Thus, there is an option of either six groups of six *piṇḍas* or three [groups], just as it should be understood regarding the house and the state. Here, in the *smṛtis* of Devala, Baudhāyana, and others, the word *piṇḍa* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *śrāddha* rite. For this very reason, the *Pravarādhyāya* states: "One should perform two *śrāddhas*, or one *śrāddha* directed toward the ancestors; in a single *piṇḍa*, one should mention both the adoptive father and the biological progenitor up to the third generation. In this context, it should be understood that one should perform two *śrāddhas* for the two paternal lineages and offer six *piṇḍas*; or else, one may perform only a single *śrāddha* for the two lineages, and at each *brāhmaṇa* seat, one should mention two ancestors—father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—along with their relationships, names, and *gotras*. In the *Hārītasūtra*: "For them, the first *pravara* belongs to the progenitor; they should offer two [portions] in each *nirvāpa*, or in a single [offering] they should mention both; in the second [generation] the son, and in the third the grandson."

The meaning of this is as follows: *Pravara* refers to the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*) and so forth, which is connected to the biological father (*bījī*). This must first be relied upon by the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), and thereafter the one connected to the mother’s husband (*kṣetrasambandhī*). *Nirvāpa* is that in which the offering is prepared; it refers to the *Pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice). In that rite, those who are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* (sons belonging to two lineages) should offer two *piṇḍas* (rice-balls) for each of the two sets of ancestors. The repetition "two for each" (*dvau dvau*) indicates this understanding: two *piṇḍas* for the two fathers, two for the two grandfathers, and two for the two great-grandfathers. This being the case, in the *Amāvāsyā-śrāddha*, six *piṇḍas* are offered to the two groups of paternal ancestors. Alternatively, in the rule "or they may mention both in a single [offering]," the repetition "two for each" (*dvau dvau*) should be understood. Thus, when offered to the two groups, there are only three *piṇḍas*. The son of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* should offer two *piṇḍas* to his second grandfather, or he may mention both grandfathers—specifying their relationship, name, and *gotra*—within a single *piṇḍa*. This is an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, according to the view that distinguishes the *piṇḍas* for the son of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, on the *Amāvāsyā* day, five *piṇḍas* are to be given: one to the father, and two each for the other two (grandfather and great-grandfather). According to the non-differentiation view, however, there are only three. The grandson of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* should, in the case of differentiating *piṇḍas*, offer two *piṇḍas* to his third great-grandfather; in the case of non-differentiation, he should mention the names of both great-grandfathers, and thus four *piṇḍas* are to be given, or only three. Someone else, however, has provided another interpretation of the phrase "or they may mention both in a single [offering]": both [the father and grandfather] are *kṣetrajas*; one is a *kuṇḍa* and the other a *golaka*. Among them, the *kuṇḍa* should, in the first *piṇḍa* related to the father, mention both the biological father (*bījī*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*); in the other two *piṇḍas*, he should mention only the person connected to the field. The *golaka*, having mentioned both fathers in the first [offering], should in the other two *piṇḍas* mention the biological father and grandfather of the biological father respectively. The sons of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, however, in the second *piṇḍa* dedicated to the grandfather, should mention both the biological father and the owner of the field as grandfathers; in the first and third *piṇḍas*, they should mention only one father and one great-grandfather respectively. In that context, the son of the *kuṇḍa* should mention his own father the *kuṇḍa*, both his own grandfather (the owner of the field and the biological father), and his own great-grandfather (the progenitor of the owner of the field)—thus mentioning four. The son of the *golaka* should mention his own father the *golaka*, both his own grandfather (the biological father and the owner of the field), and his own great-grandfather (the progenitor of the biological father)—thus mentioning four. The grandsons of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* should, in the third *piṇḍa* alone, mention both great-grandfathers. This latter interpretation does not accord with other *Smṛtis*; therefore, the previously stated interpretation—taking the repetition (*vīpsā*) in the phrase "or they may mention both in a single [offering]" as primary—is the more reasonable one to adopt. This is made clear by the very statement of Hārīta, wherein the option between six *piṇḍas* and three *piṇḍas* is expressed by the word "or" (*vā*). Regarding the doubt that the number six might refer to the maternal grandfather's *piṇḍas* when considering the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* as the qualified performer in such rules as "six *piṇḍas* are to be given to the six," that doubt is refuted. Thus, the determination of the deities of the *Śrāddha* related to the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* has been made. Now, however, the case of multiple *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* is addressed. In that regard, if one of the two fathers of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* is himself a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, then after offering two *piṇḍas* to the two fathers and two *piṇḍas* to the two grandfathers, he should offer three to the great-grandfathers, totaling eight *piṇḍas*. When, however, one of his fathers and one of his grandfathers are themselves *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, then after offering two *piṇḍas* to the two fathers and three *piṇḍas* to the grandfathers, he should offer four to the great-grandfathers, totaling nine. When both fathers of the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, then after offering two *piṇḍas* to the fathers and four to the grandfathers, he should offer four to the great-grandfathers, totaling ten. When both fathers of the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas* but only one grandfather is a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, then after offering two *piṇḍas* to the fathers and four to the grandfathers, he should offer five to the great-grandfathers, totaling eleven. When both fathers of the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, both grandfathers are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, and he himself is also a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, then after offering two *piṇḍas* to the fathers and four to the grandfathers, he should offer six to the six great-grandfathers, totaling twelve. When, for this same person, all three grandfathers are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, then after offering the aforementioned numbers to the fathers and grandfathers, he should offer seven to the seven great-grandfathers, totaling thirteen. And if all his grandfathers are *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, then after offering as before to the fathers and grandfathers, he should offer eight to the eight great-grandfathers, totaling fourteen. In the case where multiple names are mentioned within a single *piṇḍa*, it is established that there are only three *piṇḍas* for everyone. Furthermore, for that *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* whose grandfather alone is a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, he should offer four *piṇḍas*. For one whose father alone is a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*, he should offer five. For one whose father is

[Objection: "In this case, they should offer two balls for each [deceased] pair; since there are statements such as 'six balls are to be given to the six,' only six balls are prescribed. Therefore, the exclusion of any higher number is understood. [Reply: Not so.
If these statements are intended to prescribe the number six, how could they also be intended to exclude other numbers?
If you argue that just as prescriptions regarding rice (*vrīhi*) and the like implicitly intend the exclusion of *priyaṅgu* and other grains, so too should these [statements] be, [we reply: no.

No; this mode of operation would apply to sentences intended as restrictive (niyamārtha). A sentence is restrictive when it serves to restrict a rule that might otherwise apply only optionally (pakṣe ’prāptau). However, where something not previously established in any respect is being enjoined, there the function is purely prescriptive (prāpakatva) and not the exclusion of other alternatives. In the present case, since the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍadāna) to six, seven, or more ancestors was not previously established, the statements such as "to six" do not have the purpose of excluding the seventh and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, since the general injunction "one should give to the ancestors on the new moon day" establishes that one may give to six, seven, or more according to one's own desire, the statements beginning with "to six" serve to restrict that choice.

It is said: since it has been immediately restricted that "one should give to the three beginning with the father," and because of the principle that words such as "father" and so forth denote the primary sense, there is no inclusion of secondary fathers and so forth; therefore, the status of being the deities of the *śrāddha* for six [ancestors], which was not otherwise established, is what is enjoined, and thus this does not exclude others.

Now, let us grant that the injunctions prescribing the number six do not aim at the exclusion of numbers such as seven; however, from what source is there the attainment of the number [of ancestors] beginning with the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*), which you yourself accept, as well as the number pertaining to the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) offered for their sake? [One might argue: "Six rice-balls are to be given to the six [ancestors]"—from this very injunction alone [the number is established], since the principle is the same. But here there is no restriction to the number three, because the intention is merely to include the secondary (*gauṇa*) ancestors, the father and the rest. Therefore, we consider it logical that this injunction serves as an exception to the rule of taking only the primary meaning or to the statement restricting the number to three; thus, there is the attainment of seven and so forth, and this injunction regarding the number six is rightly seen to be intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the secondary ancestors, the father and the rest.

But surely, according to the maxim that "in an injunction, the literal meaning of the word is not [the only] intended sense," how can there be an intention to indicate by implication (*upalakṣaṇa*)? It is thus: since this [injunction] lacks the character of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), the exclusion of seven is untenable; once it is determined that its purpose is merely to restrict the number to three, and since an injunction would be useless when the number six is already established by itself, it is understood that the expression of the number serves the purpose of indication.

But if this were the case, the performer of the *śrāddha*, having achieved his purpose by means of any number such as four or more according to his own desire, might—contrary to the rule—adopt a number such as six or more; likewise, he might even adopt the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*) and others as deities.

Not so. For by this statement, the restriction regarding the number three—which applies to the primary father and others and is obtainable through words supported by logic—is indeed sublated; however, it is not the restriction of the number three that applies to the general category of fathers and others obtainable through mere words. Thus, there is no room for the two previously mentioned defects. Furthermore, in accordance with other injunctions, it is logical that the phrase "six funeral cakes" (*ṣaṭ piṇḍāḥ*) functions merely as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). As it is said in the *Pāraskara-smṛti*: "Those born from [fathers] of two gotras, and if they have a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-suta*)," and so forth.
One should have the days of death for the three classes of ancestors performed here on the third lunar day.

Those who, by virtue of being *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas*, belong to two lineages (*dvigotra*), have as their progenitor a father connected both to his own ancestors and to the ancestors of the [adoptive] father; thus, if such a son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) belongs to three lineages—two belonging to the lineages of the biological fathers who procreated him and one belonging to the maternal grandfather’s lineage—he, being connected to these three groups, should cause a *śrāddha* to be performed at a common time, such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth, on occasions other than the anniversary of death for these three groups. Therefore, Kārṣṇājini, referring specifically to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, says:
As many paternal groups as there may be, by so many [groups] should those such as the *dattaka* (adopted son) perform the union of the deceased with their own paternal ancestors.

Then, his sons [attain it] together with two [of their own], while their grandsons [attain it] equal to that with one; the lineage ceases in the fourth generation; therefore, this [lineage] extends through three generations.
"In ordinary times, there is no distinction among those belonging to a group;
however, on the anniversary of death, they should perform the śrāddha for a single individual according to the prescribed rule."

The meaning of this is as follows: For *dattaka* (adopted) sons and others who belong to two lineages (*dvaimātura*), all those paternal ancestors belonging to their biological fathers’ lineage—whether they be paternal grandfathers and so forth—who, through that connection, have become uncles and the like in relation to themselves, and those who, through a connection with the primary or secondary father, have become brothers and the like—all these constitute the paternal lineages of the *dattaka* and others. Among them, for those who have passed away, the *dattaka* and others should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (the rite of joining the deceased with the ancestors) together with the ancestors born from the same class as themselves. However, *dvaimātura* sons should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of each deceased person among those various lineages with his own father and the two preceding him. A *dvaimātura* grandson, however, should join [the deceased] with his own father, the *dvaimātura* grandfather, and the single paternal grandfather of that [grandfather], uniting him with the respective members born from those specific lineages. A *dvaimātura* great-grandson, on the other hand, may or may not join the deceased who stands within the secondary paternal lineage; for this secondary paternal succession extends only to three generations. Just as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed by the *dattaka* and others for all those connected to every paternal lineage, so too, at common times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the obligatory *śrāddha* must be performed in connection with all lineages. To express this, it is said: "At common times, there is no distinction among the members of the lineages. But regarding the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), it is said: "One [should offer] for one [deceased] alone"; that is, whatever *śrāddha* is performed on the day someone died, that belongs to him alone and not to another. Thus, it is established that as many paternal grandfathers and great-grandfathers as there may be, the *dvaimātura* descendants, having designated them in the *śrāddhas* of the new moon and so forth, should offer separate funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for each, or else they should recite the names of all of them upon a single funeral cake.
Now, [I shall describe] the deities of the śrāddha who preside over the sons of appointed daughters (putrikāputra).

In this regard, first of all, the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is of four kinds. One is indeed made such by an agreement (*saṃvit*) to the effect that "this very girl is my son. However, another son of hers acquires the designation "son of an appointed daughter" through the power of *yoga* even without such an agreement. There is, however, this distinction: he does not stand in the place of a son, but rather in the place of a grandson or a daughter's son (*dauhitra*). For this reason, in the statement of Śaṅkha and Likhita, he is designated as a daughter's son. As for the son of an appointed daughter, Prācetasa says: "For an appointed daughter is like a son; her offspring is the giver of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to the maternal grandfather and the paternal grandfather; there is no difference between a son’s son and a daughter’s son regarding the favor [of the ancestors]. The third type of son of an appointed daughter is one born of a daughter who has been given away by means of an agreement such as: "Whatever offspring she may have shall be mine for the performance of ancestral rites (*svadhākara*). In this case, he becomes related as a son to both the maternal grandfather and the biological father. Furthermore, under the view that a girl can be an appointed daughter even by mere intention (*cintitā*), there are likewise varieties of sons of an appointed daughter occurring through mere mental conception even without an agreement. These will be clarified in the section on the classification of sons. Such being the case, the traditional law (*smṛti*) states:
"But the maternal grandfather’s [estate] belongs first to the mother and so forth, and the paternal [estate] belongs first to the father;
for, according to the Dharma, there is a right of succession from the mother and from the father.

Nor should it be thought that this statement refers exclusively to the daughter's son (*dauhitra*); for within the *Manusmṛti* itself, the meaning of this statement is understood as pertaining to the relationship with the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).

"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his mother, the second to her father, and the third to his own father. These two statements do not refer to the son of an appointed daughter in a general sense; rather, they apply specifically to the son of an appointed daughter who has been designated as a son.

But surely, because of the general statement "one should offer [the oblation] for the son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāsuta*), how can it have as its sole object the specific case of the son of an appointed daughter?

It is said: For that son who is not designated as the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) is indeed designated; however, since he is directly related to his maternal grandfather by virtue of being a secondary son (*gauṇasuta*), when performing the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather, he should perform it beginning with the maternal grandfather himself. This is because, in the *śrāddha* for a father, the entitlement belongs to the father and those following him. But as for the son of an appointed daughter who has been designated as a "son," he is the son of the maternal grandfather’s son; thus, being in the position of a grandson (*pautra*), when performing the *śrāddha* for his own maternal grandfather—which is equivalent to a *śrāddha* performed for a grandson—he should perform it beginning with the mother, who stands in the place of the father.

[Objection: Surely, according to the maxim that "the statement of non-existence does not bear too heavy a burden," let the status of mother and so forth belong to the maternal grandfather’s *śrāddha* performed solely for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) on the basis of that scriptural statement. [Reply:
Not so; for by the propriety inherent in what is explicitly stated in proximity, the scriptural statement is restricted to a specific case.

Now, one might ask: what is this "propriety" (*aucitya*) regarding matters whose purpose is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as the rule "having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the *śrāddha* prior to that"? Understand that it is simply the following of the nature of the rite as known from other scriptural statements, such as "one should perform the *śrāddha* prior to that," as well as the force of the reason presented within the same sentence. For here, having taught that the sequence begins with the mother and then the father, the reason stated to establish that sequence is the existence of a corresponding qualification, as in: "because there is a qualification [to perform rites] according to dharma, both on the mother's side and the father's side. And since this reason, by virtue of being a reason, requires something already established, it takes as its object only the person entitled to the *śrāddha* who stands in the position of a grandson. If it is argued: "Since such a thing lacks prior establishment, let there be a mere statement of a reason (*hetuvan-nigada*)," [we reply: no.

No; for a statement "like a cause" (*hetuvad-nigada*) occurs when the status of being a cause is impossible, not when it is possible. Furthermore, this injunction regarding the precedence of the mother does not apply to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) who has become a secondary son (*gauṇa-putra*), but rather to one who is specifically of the nature of a daughter's son (*dauhitra*), as indicated by the term *mātāmahyam*. Otherwise, the designation would have been *paitṛkam*. [Objection: But surely, because he occupies the position of a grandson (*pautra*), the designation *paitāmahyam* (belonging to the grandfather) should apply. For the son of a son is a grandson, and in relation to whom someone is a grandson, in relation to that same person he becomes a grandfather. Therefore...

Not so. For indeed, the status of being a son produced by *saṃvit* (contractual agreement) in the case of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) results in the grandson’s status toward his maternal grandfather being a mere conceptual construct; it is neither worldly nor Vedic, and thus incapable of generating subsequent legal transactions.

But if this were the case, then when sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others perform the ancestral *śrāddha* rites for their fathers, they would not designate the *kṣetri* and others as their paternal grandfathers.

It is said in reply: We do not here absolutely deny the existence of a more subtle relationship in the form of father, grandfather, and so forth—which is secondary (*gauṇa*), which is accessible through natural worldly usage (*svarasato laukikavyavahāragamya*), and which is produced by the method taught in the scriptures. Rather, we deny the usage consisting in the employment of words expressive of that [primary relationship]. For this usage, being natural and witnessed by all people, possesses greater force; it is sublated by another usage in the form of employing words such as "mother" and "maternal grandfather," which refers to a relationship that has arisen with greater intensity and does not fall within the scope of the delusion that these words denote the lineage of the progenitor. Therefore, when the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) performs a *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather, he sublates the employment of words such as "father" and "grandfather" by employing words such as "mother" and "maternal grandfather. This is just as the son of a brother—the grandson of one who has attained a secondary status as a father—is the secondary son of his paternal uncle; when he performs a *śrāddha* or any other worldly transaction, he sublates the usage consisting in the employment of words denoting the relationship of "fatherhood" by employing words denoting the relationship of "paternal unclehood," which is the actual relationship witnessed by all people in its natural state.

But if this were the case, then by parity of reasoning, the performance of the *śrāddha* rite for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) should also be carried out using the very same terms—such as "maternal grandfather" and so on—as would apply to others.
Not so; for if that were the case, the specific instruction regarding the son of an appointed daughter would be purposeless.
If it is argued that such an instruction is necessary to establish his eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the obligatory *śrāddha*, [we reply: no.

No; for even without the act of adoption (*putrīkaraṇa*), the daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) necessarily possesses the entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather who has no other son. Nor should it be suspected that this entitlement belongs only to a daughter’s son who inherits the estate, because that will be refuted later. Therefore, for a daughter’s son who has been adopted, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather and others is indeed fit for the application of terms such as "father" and so forth, and [the offerings are made] to the maternal grandfather and others. However, for a daughter’s son who lacks the status of adoption, the *śrāddha* is fit only for the application of terms such as "mother" and "maternal grandfather" to the mother and maternal grandfather respectively. Furthermore, this is supported by the fact that in the injunctions prescribing the procedure for that *śrāddha*—such as "but for the maternal grandfather, [he offers] to the mother and others" and "the first funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is for the mother"—only the terms "mother" and "maternal grandfather" are heard. And it is logical that an injunctive word performs the function of a mantra.

Now, is it not the case that the words "mother," "maternal grandfather," and so forth were employed here with the intention that these very terms should be used even at the time of performing the *śrāddha* rite; rather, they were used as constituent parts of a sentence intended solely to enjoin the status of being a mother and so on?

True. However, wherever an injunctive word (*vidhi-śabda*) is honored at the time of performance as a reminder of what is to be executed—just like a mantra—it is accepted everywhere precisely because it possesses the power to remind one of that which is enjoined, and solely by virtue of the requirement of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); it is not accepted because it was employed with that specific intention. Furthermore, there is no other relationship in the case of the *kṣetraja* son and others. Nor is there any injunctive word distinct from the terms "father," "grandfather," and so forth. Therefore, for them, it is logical that they be commemorated only by the words "father," "grandfather," and so on. As for the statement that the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for the maternal grandfather) of the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) is preceded by the mother, Vyāghrapāt states an exception to this rule regarding the *vṛddhi* (prosperity) rites.

"One who knows the rule, having followed the prescribed procedure, should always perform the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather preceded by that for the mother, especially during the Vṛddhi ceremony. Thus it is said.

Nor should it be suspected here that this statement is intended merely to establish a sequence between two rites—the *mātṛ-śrāddha* and the *mātāmaha-śrāddha*—which might both be required simultaneously at a single time, such as during the *Anvaṣṭakā* or at a specific sacred site (*tīrtha*), where place and time are common to both; rather, it is neither a rule prescribing the mother’s status as a deity for the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* performed by the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), nor an exception to that rule. This is because this statement is found in the context of the sequence for the son of an appointed daughter, and because otherwise there would result a contradiction with the precedence of the *mātṛ-śrāddha* over the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* which will be stated later in the section on *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Furthermore, an option regarding the sequence is not logical, since hundreds of statements in all the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* prescribe the precedence of the *mātṛ-śrāddha* every day.
Thus [are described] the deities of the *śrāddha* performed by the sons of appointed daughters (*putrikā*).

Therefore, it has been stated that in the obligatory *śrāddhas* pertaining to those who belong to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), even the secondary group of ancestors (*pitṛvarga*) possesses the status of a deity.

[127] Now this must be addressed: among these *śrāddhas* performed for secondary ancestors (*gauṇa-pitṛ*), does the group of wives also attain the status of a deity through their co-presence with their husbands—just as the group of wives belonging to the primary ancestors does—or not? In that regard, since the status of deity has already been established for the group of secondary ancestors by another scriptural statement, it is stated that they possess the status of a deity together with their wives; therefore, their status as a deity is not scripturally established when they are devoid of them.

But if this is so, then in the case of a secondary father (*gauṇa-pitṛ*) whose wife is either absent or, though present, deceased, her exclusion would follow from the *Amāvāsyā* and other Śrāddha rites. And that being the case, the scriptural injunction which is mandatory—“Six balls of rice (*piṇḍa*) must be offered to the six”—would be contradicted. Now, should one perform the offering to the father even when he is deceased, out of fear of contradicting that mandatory scripture? If, on the other hand, that mandatory scripture is contingent upon the death of the father and others, then let it likewise be contingent upon the death of the mother; or let there be the principle of the Śrāddha entitlement belonging to one whose father is living. Furthermore, the principle that "the primary sense prevails here" finds no application in this instance, because the primary mother—who has attained the status of the wife of the secondary father—is absent, and thus it is logical for the secondary father to be included. Therefore, since the secondary father and others occupy the position of deities (*devatā*) here, let the secondary mothers also occupy the position of deities by virtue of their association with them.

To this it is replied: Just as in the primary *śrāddha* for the father, the secondary mothers do not possess the status of deities by virtue of being performed together, so too here, this rule of performance together applies only to those [mothers] who would otherwise obtain a separate *śrāddha* through an independent entitlement. This is because the injunction regarding their performance together serves as an exception (*apavāda*) to the injunction for a separate *śrāddha*. Furthermore, there is no permanent, independent entitlement for a *śrāddha* for secondary mothers; for the injunction for a mother’s *śrāddha* is fulfilled by including the primary mother.

[Objection: If that is the case, then who should perform the *śrāddha* rites for the secondary wives of one’s father? [Response: From the perspective of worldly convention (*lokadṛṣṭi*), we say it is he alone, because he occupies the position of a son. Even he performs these rites out of compassion or affection—either to avoid contradicting worldly custom or to wash away the stain of having accepted her as part of his retinue; thus, his entitlement (*adhikāra*) in this matter is not permanent. As for a son who is taken in a secondary capacity by both a woman and a man, just as he performs rites for many men when taken by many, so too does he do so for the woman and the man. However, even though there may be several maternal grandfathers (*mātāmaha*), since the purpose of the rite for the maternal grandfather is fulfilled by the *śrāddha* for the principal maternal grandfather alone, there are not multiple *śrāddhas* for the maternal grandfathers. Nor should the names of all of them be recited in a single *śrāddha*, because there is no scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) to that effect. Alternatively, a secondary son who has been formally provided for by the husband is indeed recognized as the son of the wife as well, because at the time of marriage, the wife makes a vow not to transgress against him in matters of duty (*dharma*) and desire (*kāma*). For this very reason, she possesses inherent ownership (*svatva*) over the wealth and religious merit acquired by him. Indeed, Āpastamba and others have stated: "No division of property exists between husband and wife, because they have joint authority over wealth and religious duties. For they do not teach that theft occurs on the part of the wife when necessary religious acts requiring wealth are performed using the husband's property while he is away on a journey or deceased. Therefore, since the secondary son has a separate entitlement to the *śrāddha* of his secondary mother, it is established that there is an exception stating "with the husband" elsewhere, and thus her status as a deity (*devatātva*) in the *pārvaṇa* rite is through association with him. And this should not be asserted regarding the stepmothers of one’s own mother, because it was previously stated that the purpose is fulfilled by the existence of the principal mother. This being the case, the *śrāddha* for the secondary maternal grandfathers should also be performed just like that for the secondary fathers. Thus have been described the deities in the *śrāddhas* pertaining to the entitlement of the *dvaimātura* (son of two mothers).
Now, the Śrāddhas for which one whose father is still living is the qualified performer are being described. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

While the father is living, one should perform the *śrāddha* for those for whom the father performs it. While both the father and the grandfather are living, one should perform it for those for whom the grandfather performs it. While the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather are all living, one should not perform it at all. He whose father has died should, having placed the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for his father, offer to the two ancestors beyond the great-grandfather. He whose father and grandfather have both died should, having offered two rice-balls to them, offer to the grandfather’s grandfather. He whose grandfather has died should, having placed the rice-ball for him, offer to the two ancestors beyond the great-grandfather. He whose father and great-grandfather have both died should, having offered two rice-balls to them, offer to the grandfather’s grandfather.

A wise man should likewise perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers; he should do so according to the rule by omitting the enumeration, and for the remaining ancestors, he should perform it without mantras. [ViDh 75.1–7]

The meaning of this is as follows: The first position is that one should perform the *śrāddha* for those for whom the father performs it, provided the father is alive while the others are deceased. The second is that [one should perform it] when the father and grandfather are alive while the others are deceased. The third is when all three are alive. The fourth is for one whose father is deceased, but whose grandfather and great-grandfather are alive. The fifth is for one whose father and grandfather are deceased, but whose great-grandfather is alive. [In this context, "grandfather" refers to the father’s father, and "great-grandfather" to the father’s great-grandfather. The sixth is for one whose grandfather is deceased, but whose father and great-grandfather are alive. The seventh is for one whose father and great-grandfather are deceased, but whose grandfather is alive. This is the intended sense here: the *śrāddha* should be performed in sequence for the three ancestors who are either deceased or not yet deceased. Regarding the restatement of what is already established by logic (*nyāyaprāpta*), there is a concern that it might not apply because it is treated as a single performance; thus, it is stated that for the remaining cases, it is "devoid of the [specific] mantras. The meaning is that for those other than the father and maternal grandfather, the mantra containing the word "father" (*pitṛ*) should be used, excluding any modified (*ūhita*) mantras. Furthermore, the mention of the number [of ancestors] here serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*), and does not constitute a prohibition against the *śrāddha* mantras for paternal uncles and others. Because the verb "should perform" (*kuryāt*) is not connected with a relative pronoun (*yat*), there is no sin (*pratyavāya*) for one whose father is living if he does not perform it; rather, for one who does perform it, a specific excellence of fruit (*phalaviśeṣa*) arises.
Now, the deities of the *jīvacchrāddha*.

There are eight [deities]: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Rudra, Indra, Prakṛti, Mudgala-Puruṣa, and Śiva. There are sixteen: Śarva and his wife, Bhava and his wife, Rudra and his wife, Ugra and his wife, Bhīma and his wife, Īśa and his wife, Mahādeva and his wife, Paśupati and his wife. There are ten: Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Samāna, and Udāna; their presiding lords (adhipatis); and the Pṛṣātakas and the Rudras. There are three: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, the deities of the *vyāhṛtis*. There are six: the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and others together with their wives, and the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahas*) and others together with their wives. Furthermore, there are the deities of the *anvāhārya* (or *aukaraṇa*) and the *vaiśvadeva* as taught in the *Pārvaṇa* [rite]. These are understood through injunction (*vidhi*), the wording of the mantras (*mantravarṇa*), and extended application (*atideśa*). We shall demonstrate the injunctions and so forth in their respective contexts. Thus.
The deities of the *jīvacchrāddha*;
now, the deities in the *śrāddhas* that constitute the constituent parts of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

In that regard, for the *deva-śrāddha*, [the deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. For the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*, [the deities are] the *devarṣis*, *brahmarṣis*, and *kṣatrarṣis*; in some texts, they are the *devarṣis*, *kṣatrarṣis*, and *manuṣyarṣis*. For the *divya-śrāddha*, [the deities are] the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. For the *mānuṣa-śrāddha*, [the deities are] Sanaka, Sanandana, and Sanātana. For the *bhūta-śrāddha*, there are three groups: the elements beginning with earth, the organs beginning with sight, and the fourfold collection of living beings (*caturvidhabhūtagrāma*). For the *pitṛ-śrāddha*, [the deities are] the fathers, grandfathers, maternal grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and great-great-grandfathers. For the *mātṛ-śrāddha*, [the deities are] the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother. For the *ātma-śrāddha*, [the deities are] oneself, one’s father, and one’s grandfather. All these are deities qualified by the term *nāndīmukha* (joyful-faced), because it is recited in the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-vidhi*) proclaimed by Śaunaka:

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). On the preceding day, one must indeed perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha. One should perform eight śrāddhas with an even number of Brāhmaṇas through the offering of separate funeral balls (*piṇḍa*) for the sages, gods, humans, spirits, ancestors, mother, the self, and so forth. Since these śrāddhas are subsidiary parts of the rite for the purpose of renunciation, the deities for the śrāddha of the sacrifice are Kratu and Dakṣa; or else the Viśvedevas known as Satya and Vasu, according to the statement: "Satya in the *nāndīmukha*, Vasu [in the śrāddha]. Thus are the deities for the śrāddha that is a limb of renunciation.

Thus, the deities associated with the two primary rites—namely, the feeding of Brahmins and the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*), which are included within the meaning of the term *śrāddha*—have been stated. Now, those associated with the primary rite known as *agnaukaraṇa*, which is part of the *śrāddha*, are being described. First, regarding that, in the section on the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*:

Having taken [the food] out, he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods. Indeed, he who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices turns toward the gods; yet, by performing this ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*), he has acted as if toward the ancestors. Therefore, he makes amends to the gods. Impelled by the gods, he then gives this to the ancestors. For that reason, having taken it out, he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods. He offers them indeed to Agni and to Soma.

Furthermore, in the *Mahābhārata*, the rule regarding the fire in the rite of offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) is seen together with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of an ancient account (*purākalpa*). Thus:
When that sacrifice had commenced, all the great seers performed the ancestral rites according to the procedures prescribed by the rules.
The sages, ever devoted to dharma and firm in their vows, having performed the ritual scatterings of seeds,
indeed offered libations with the waters of the sacred fords.
[132] O Bhārata, though the ancestors and gods were gratified by the offerings of food given by the four castes, they indeed could not digest that food.
Afflicted by indigestion, those gods, together with the Pitṛs,
sought refuge in Soma alone, being oppressed by the offerings of funeral oblations.
Having approached Soma, those ancestors, afflicted by old age, said:
"We are distressed by the food offered as a libation; let that which is beneficial for us be ordained here."
Then Soma replied to them: "O gods, if you desire what is most beneficial, go to the abode of the Self-Existent; He shall provide that benefit."
O Bhārata, at the word of Soma, those gods, together with the Pitṛs,
approached the Grandfather seated upon the peak of Mount Meru.
The ancestors of the gods said:
"O Blessed One, we are greatly afflicted by the food offered as funeral oblations.
Show us favor, O God; let that which is for our welfare be ordained."
Having heard these words of theirs, the Self-Existent One spoke thus:
"This Fire here at my side shall bring about your welfare."
Agni said:
"We shall eat together there when the funeral offering has been presented;
moreover, the food will undoubtedly be digested along with me."
Having heard this, O King, those ancestors then became free from their fever;
for this reason, an offering is first made to Agni.
O bull among men, when the funeral offering has been cast into the fire first,
the Brahmarākṣasas cannot indeed violate that offering.
[133] And the *rakṣas* turn away when the god Vibhāvasu is present.
From the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa* and the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, it is understood that Yama also possesses the status of a deity, as evidenced by the recitation of the *mantra* for the oblation:
"Svadhā to Agni Kavyavāhana; and obeisance to Aṅgiras."
"Oblation to Soma accompanied by the ancestors; reverence to Aṅgiras!
Oblation to Yama Vaivasvata; reverence!"—thus he should say.
In the *Āpastamba-Sūtra*, Yama is mentioned as an optional deity, as it is stated: "Some say one does not offer to Yama. Thus have been described the principal deities of the Śrāddha.
Now, those associated with the subsidiary rite known as the Vaiśvadeva are being set forth. Regarding that, the origin of the Viśvedevas is described in the *Brahmāṇḍa* and *Brahmavaivarta* Purāṇas:
"Dakṣa’s daughter was herself renowned by the name Viśvā."
O knower of dharma, she was given to the wise Dharmasena according to the prescribed rites.
Her sons were the high-souled Viśvedevas, according to the sacred tradition;
they are renowned throughout the three worlds and honored by all people.
Their true nature is described in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"Born from the great-souled Dharma upon Viśvā, the daughter of Dakṣa,
they are known as the Viśvedevas— the best of gods and possessed of great strength."
They are the conquerors of even those warriors who fight alongside Śakra;
indeed, by the mere remembrance of their names, the asuras flee in an instant.
Holding arrows and bows, they have two arms and wear white garments;
they are adorned with armlets, earrings, crowns, and bracelets.
Endowed with fortitude and beauty, adorned with divine garlands and unguents,
all those followers of Indra are the guardians of the celestial realm.
In the *Yama-saṃhitā*:
"The Viśvedevas, however, are all on the right side, holding arrows in their hands;
they have two arms, while those on the left side are intent upon their bows."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "One should meditate upon all the gods as holding bows and arrows in their hands, adorned with various ornaments and fine attire."
Regarding their status as ancestral deities (*śrāddhadevatā*), the account is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa* and *Brahmavaivarta* Purāṇas:
"Great-souled beings, equal [to the gods], performed intense and supreme penance on a delightful peak of the Himavat mountain, frequented by hosts of celestial sages."
In that place frequented by all the Apsarases and constantly served by Gandharvas,
the Pitṛs, being pleased, spoke to them with pure minds.
"Choose a boon; we are pleased. What desire shall we fulfill for you?
Thus spoke Brahmā, the one of great splendor, who had been thoroughly gratified by his ascetic penance.
"I am pleased by this austerity; what desire shall I grant you?
Thus were all addressed then by Brahmā Viśvakarman.
They all spoke together to Brahmā, the purifier of the world:
"In our śrāddha ceremony, that which is to be given should be for us; for this is the boon we desire."
Then Brahmā, who is honored by the thirty gods, replied to them: "It shall be exactly so; whatever boon you desired shall indeed come to pass."
The ancestors replied, "So be it; this is indeed so, there is no doubt.
Whatever is cooked here must be eaten by us together with you, for you shall indeed be the first to eat at the śrāddha prepared for us."
This which has been declared shall come true among men:
they shall indeed honor you with garlands, perfumes, and food.
If he gives to you, he will then give to us;
therefore, our dismissal shall come first, and the dismissal of the deity afterwards.
And also the protection of the one who performs the *śrāddha*, as well as the rule regarding the guest;
[this concerns] the spirits, the deities, and the ancestors in the rite of *śrāddha*.
"In this way, all this shall indeed be accomplished correctly.
Having thus granted them the boon, Brahmā, the god who bestows grace upon all beings, together with the hosts of ancestors, wandered about as he pleased. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Kratusmṛti and the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
"One should always perform the śrāddha in this manner and cause it to proceed preceded by that [preliminary rite];
otherwise, indeed, the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas plunder it."

In this context, the rite performed with reference to the Viśvedevas, which constitutes a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, is called "divine" (*daiva*). Together with that, it is "always divine"; one should proceed—that is, perform it—"preceded by the divine" according to the rule of "always [being] divine. If that is not performed, then the Rākṣasas destroy the fruit of the *śrāddha* or take it for themselves. Here, indeed, because the meaning of the compound is understood as "the rite denoted by the word *śrāddha* exists together with the divine rite," and because the "divine" is designated separately from the *śrāddha* as being subordinate, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is understood. This is because its helpfulness is understood through the statement that it serves to protect the *śrāddha*. This is also stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
For the twice-born, the rite for the ancestors (pitṛkārya) is superior to the rite for the gods (daivakārya);
indeed, the rite for the gods is traditionally held to be the preliminary nourishment for the rite for the ancestors.
[136] One should first employ a deity as their protector;
for the *rakṣasas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection.

The meaning of this is as follows: in the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), the Vaiśvadeva rite is distinguished; that is, it attains preeminence by virtue of its primacy. To the question "How so?", he says: "For the rite for the gods (*daiva*), when performed prior to the rite for the ancestors, serves to sustain and complete the latter by means of warding off the Rākṣasas who cause obstacles. By this, it is understood that the Vaiśvadeva is merely a subsidiary act (*aṅgakarma*). Furthermore, regarding the performance of the New Moon *Śrāddha*, which possesses two primary rites dedicated to the ancestors (the *pitṛs*) and the maternal great-grandfathers (*mātāmaha*), Yājñavalkya states, "Or the Vaiśvadeva may be common (*tantra*)," because he declares it to be initiated by the primary rite. Therefore, it is said that one should perform it first. Consequently, having performed each of the items to be mentioned below in the place of the Vaiśvadeva, one should perform them in the place of the ancestors. And thus says Devala:
Whatever rite pertaining to the ancestors (paitṛka) is performed with respect to Brāhmaṇas,
all of that should be performed there, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
"In the paternal rite," meaning a rite dedicated to the ancestors, that is, a *śrāddha*;
as it is also stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"First, one should honor the Brahmins who have been assigned to the *vaiśvadeva* [portion]."
And after that, one should honor those who have been assigned to the portion for the ancestors.
In the Vṛddha-Śātātapa it is also stated:
"Facing north, one should offer to the gods; facing south, to the ancestors. In the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, one should give according to the rule, beginning with the deities."

By the mention of the *pārvaṇa* [rite], it is specifically prescribed that the *vaiśvadeva* offering must precede the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha alone. The absence of the *vaiśvadevika* portion in the *ekoddiṣṭa*, *ābhyudayika*, and *nitya* śrāddhas will be stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "The Viśvedevas, having been sent away by the command of Brahmā, were performing intense penance; they remain always for the sake of protection at the sacrifice to the ancestors."
Therefore, in the rite for the ancestors, food should first be given to them.

The mention of "food" (*anna*) is intended as an illustration for the fragrances and other items as well. Thus, when it follows that all items related to the *śrāddha* must be offered first to the Viśvedevas, an exception is seen in certain places in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should dismiss the gods afterwards, and the twice-born ancestors first;
for the maternal grandfathers also, this same sequence with the gods is prescribed."
The mention of "the grandfather" (paitāmaha) is intended as an elliptical indication for the father and the great-grandfather as well.
This is according to the *Śātātapa-smṛti* and the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"For those who have been seated for the Viśvedevas, the final washing of the hands [is performed]."
And the dismissal is prescribed for them, since protection resides therein;
O lord of men, everything else should first be given to them.
"Last" means final. "Washing of the hands" refers to the offering of water for the purpose of washing hands that have been smeared with food after eating.

Thus, this status of the Viśvedevas as deities in the Śrāddha rite—as stated in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* and other texts—is set aside in the case of the daily Śrāddha (*nityaśrāddha*) and similar rites. Śātātapa says:
"The daily Śrāddha and likewise the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be without deities."
The Śrāddha for the mother, however, should be performed separately with an even number of Brahmins, without deities, and facing east;
all other Śrāddhas should be diligently joined with the deities first.

In this context, the *mātṛśrāddha* (rite for the mothers) is intended to precede the *abhyudayika* (prosperity rite), as indicated by the signs of employing pairs of Brahmins and seating them facing east. Furthermore, when that [mātṛśrāddha] is performed at a different time, separate from the two other *śrāddhas* for the father and maternal grandfather and so forth, it should be performed without the *daiva* (deities) portion, i.e., devoid of the *vaiśvadeva*. However, when all three *śrāddhas* are performed at one and the same time, then the performance of the *vaiśvadevika* should be done either by the method of *tantra* (single performance) or by *āvṛtti* (repetition); thus, one should perform the three *śrāddhas*, according to the rule: "Or the *vaiśvadevika* may be performed by *tantra*."

This is to be understood from the words of Vasiṣṭha. In that regard, the performance of the three types of Śrāddhas occurs at different times: "On the previous day one should perform the Śrāddha for the mothers; on the day of the rite, likewise the Śrāddha for the fathers; and on the following day, one should perform the Śrāddha for the group of maternal grandfathers."

This will be demonstrated by such statements in the section concerning the *ābhyudayika-śrāddha*. Śrāddhas performed on auspicious occasions (*ābhyudayika-nimitta*), other than those for the Mothers (*mātṛ-śrāddha*) which are performed separately, should be performed optionally without the *vaiśvadeva* rite. Accordingly, regarding the *ābhyudayika*, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Some men desire [the rite] to be devoid of the *viśvedevas*;
here, an even number of twice-born ones should be employed, and they should be honored circumambulating from left to right."
From the mention of "some" here, it is understood that there is an alternative view;
as stated in the Śātātapa-Bhaviṣyat Purāṇas:
"That *śrāddha* which is performed for a single person is called occasional (*naimittika*)."
That too should be performed as a non-divine rite; one should feed an odd number of twice-born brahmins.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:

"The *pārvaṇa* rite should begin with the deities (*daivapūrva*), whereas the *ekoddiṣṭa* is without the gods (*surair vinā*). Likewise, the *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the deities, having a single *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*. Such [details] will be stated in the section on the *ekoddiṣṭa*. Regarding the reason for the absence of the *vaiśvadevika* rite in these *ekoddiṣṭas*, it is declared in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
For the sake of the funeral offerings of the gods who had perished in battle with the asura Vṛtra,
the Lord of the Thirty-three reached Gayākūpa.
In every city there, on the fourteenth day of the month of Mahālaya,
Vṛṣa began to perform the śrāddha rites according to the prescribed rules with great faith.
Then, with the *śrāddha* mantras, he summoned the ancestors (pitṛs) such as the Agniṣvātta-s,
as well as other deceased beings (pretas) belonging to his own class who had been slain by weapons.
He beheld the Viśvedevas entering the bodies of the Brahmins, but he did not see them themselves, and for that reason he delayed.
Then Śakra suddenly beheld Nārada and questioned him;
he explained the reason for the non-arrival of all the gods.
"While the Supreme Brahman was performing a śrāddha at Gayā, the Viśvedevas were seen by me; why then do you delay?"
Having heard these words of Nārada, Vṛddhaśravas then became enraged and performed a śrāddha according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, excluding the Viśvedevas.
Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, also caused those hungry ghosts to attain the supreme state;
and he made this agreement known to those brahmins.
For all the gods are stationed for the purpose of protecting the śrāddha;
without them, the protection of the śrāddha shall indeed be ensured by me alone.
[140] "Let the Śrāddha rite, excluding the Viśvedevas, proceed from now on. As he spoke these words aloud, the Viśvedevas arrived.
O Puruhūta, we were summoned of old by the divine Ordainer;
but now, O Lord, having reflected thus, be gracious to us at last.
O Maghavan, today we are by no means sinners;
why do you, O Lord of Heaven, exclude us from the śrāddha today?
Thus, though washed by the waves of tears from grief for the earth,
he did not soften to their entreaties as they despaired.
Then, from that steam and heat, numerous eggs were produced;
from them were born hundreds of thousands of men who resembled Rākṣasas.
Thus commanded by all the gods, those beings, eager to swallow the world, were told:
"The Śrāddha rite performed in our absence shall become your food."
"Since you were born from the earth by means of heat-born eggs, you shall be known by the name Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Having said, "Dwell [here]," the Viśvedevas vanished.
Then, having beheld the universe crowded with *kūṣmāṇḍas*,
the Creator of the world summoned the Viśvedevas and Indra, and the Ordainer established an arrangement.
Henceforth, let the śrāddhas known as ekoddiṣṭa always be performed without the Viśvedevas; may the slayer of Vṛtra be true to his word.
This other Śrāddha, devoid of the Vaiśvadeva rite, shall be for the satisfaction of the Kūṣmāṇḍas,
wherein the protection of the vessels is not performed with lines of ashes.
"O Kūṣmāṇḍīs,
let this sacrificial food (śrāddha-pāka), which has not yet been sprinkled with water consecrated by mantras, be eaten by you with ease.
Having said this, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) performed the act of propitiating the Kūṣmāṇḍas.
Having divided them, he gave them to Agni, Vāyu, and Arka.
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors, a śrāddha for one killed by a weapon must be performed according to the rules of the ekoddiṣṭa rite, and not for anyone else.
Having spoken thus, Viriñca vanished after dismissing them all;
from that time forth, the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha came to be performed without the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
Now, their names as the Viśvedevas are stated; first, in that regard, [they are mentioned] in the Mahābhārata.
All the gods, who have Agni as their mouth, were already enumerated previously;
I shall now state the names of those high-souled ones who are entitled to shares.
Sahaḥkṛti, Vipāpman, Puṇyakṛt, Pāvana,
Grāṣṇikṣama, Samūha, and likewise Divyabhānu.
By name they were Vivasvān, Vīryavān, Hrīmān, Kīrtimān, Kṛta,
Vidhyartha, Somapūrva, and Sūryaśrī.
Soma, Sūrya, Sāvitra, Dattātman, Puṇḍarīyaka, Uṣṇīṣābha, Nabhodaśa, Viśvāyu, and Dīpti.
The destroyer of hosts, the well-attired, the enemy of Yama, Śaṅkara, Bhava, Īśa, the agent, the one who has accomplished his task, the sustainer, the world, and the performer of divine deeds.
Gaṇita, Pañcavīrya, Prācīna, Rañjita,
Saptakṛt, Somavarcas, Viśvakṛt, and Kavī.
The protector, the good protector, the grandson, and indeed the Lord;
the one who has conquered his self, the hero among sages, the one with bristling hair, and the creator of light.
Atikarman, Pratīta, Pradātā,
Aṃśumant, Śailābha, Paramakrodha, Dhāroṣṇī, and likewise Bhūpati.
Sajīva, Vikarī, and the eternal Viśvedevas—
these illustrious ones have been proclaimed as those who move within the sphere of the course of time.

These Viśvedevas, named Sahakṛt and the others as mentioned in the Mahābhārata, are to be employed collectively in the Śrāddha rite after reciting each name according to its respective form, ending in the vocative case and so forth. Alternatively, for brevity, one may mentally bring all of them to mind at once—from Sahakṛt up to Vikari—and perform the ritual application in such a manner as: "O Viśvedevas, beginning with Sahakṛt and ending with Vikari, this is your water for the feet (*pādya*)," and so on. Furthermore, these [deities] are to be combined only among themselves, and not together with Purūravas, Ārdrava, and others mentioned by Bṛhaspati and others. This is because, by the scriptural injunction—"I shall state the names of those great-souled ones who receive their portions"—which prescribes the connection of the sacrificial oblation denoted by the word *bhāga*, it is understood that these very deities, Sahakṛt and the rest, who are denoted by the single word containing the pronoun *eteṣām* ("of these"), are the effectors of the ritual performance precisely when they are mutually dependent.

Now, one might object: "It should not be said that they depend on Purūravas, Ārdrava, and others prescribed in other scriptures; for since all *śrāddhas* are already encompassed by specific prescriptions such as 'Kratu and Dakṣa' for the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Sahakṛti and the others find no scope anywhere and thus are not fit to be mentioned as deities in the *vaiśvadevika*. To this we reply: According to the maxim, "The relative strength of those [rules] struck down by purposelessness is reversed," even though they are prescribed generally, they set aside Purūravas, Ārdrava, and others who are prescribed specifically, and enter as deities. Regarding the view of one who thinks that these [deities] apply to all *śrāddhas* because there is no specific restriction, a specific restriction is now stated. By the maxim, "Or rather, [they belong] to the archetype (*prakṛti*) because of the lack of repetition," they enter into the *pārvaṇa* alone due to the context, and not into the *karmāṅga-śrāddhas* and others which are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *pārvaṇa*.

[Objection: But surely it will occur by way of extension (*atideśa*). [Reply: No; because it is sublated by the ritual acts (*kratu*) and so forth that pertain to extension. Thus, it is established that in the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, Sahakṛti and the others possess the status of deities as alternatives alongside Purūravas and Ārdrava in the Vaiśvadeva rite. Now, those names by which their inclusion in the ritual is well-known are stated. In the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti*: "Kratu, Dakṣa, Vasu, Satya, Kāma, and likewise Kāla."
Dhuri, Rocana, Purūravas,
and Ārdrava— these ten are proclaimed as the Viśvedevas.
These [deities] are to be assigned and employed in these respective *śrāddhas*.
It has been stated in the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti* itself:
"In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu; in the *nāndīmukha*, Dakṣa; and in the *satya-śrāddha*, Vasu."
"In the *naimittika* [rite], Kāla and Kāma; in the *kāmya*, Dhuri and Rocana; and Purūravas and Ārdrava are declared for the *pārvaṇa*. Thus it is stated.
Also in the *Śaṅkhasmṛti*:
In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa are to be proclaimed; in the *vaiśvadevika*, Satyavasu and Vasu; in the *nāndīmukha*, Dhuri and Rocana; and in the *kāmya*, Dhuri and Rocana.
"Purūravas and Ārdrava are declared for the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], while Kāla and Kāma are proclaimed for the *naimittika*; thus one should recite [the names] in all cases.

Here, by the term "iṣṭi-śrāddha," the śrāddha that is an auxiliary part of a ritual (*karmāṅga*) is intended. Accordingly, the śrāddha that constitutes the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the Soma sacrifice (*somayāga*), and the impregnation rite (*niṣeka*) is also included. Furthermore, the śrāddha that is an auxiliary part of a ritual will be discussed in the section on the various types of śrāddha.

"At the time of the impregnation rite (*niṣeka*), during the *soma* sacrifice, likewise at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and at the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the *śrāddha* should be known as a subsidiary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), performed like an occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*). [144]

In this context, the term *karmāṅga* (auxiliary to a rite) is defined as follows. By the phrase "like the *vṛddhi*" [śrāddha], the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*—such as the employment of the words *daivata*, *tattva*, and *svāhā*, and the offering of rice-balls mixed with curds, jujube fruits, and so forth—are extended [to this rite]. The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed in the *Smṛtis* of Yājñavalkya and others. Thus, through such statements as "having circumambulated clockwise, one should worship the *vṛddha-nāndīmukha* ancestors," the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* has been demonstrated by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha and others; it is cited as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* performed on occasions such as the birth of a son or a marriage. Here, the word *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is defined as a specific type of *abhyudayika-śrāddha*.
