By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of sacramental rites (*saṃskāra-karman*) such as the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) and the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), excluding the three rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the male-impregnation (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). This is because the *abhyudayika* rite that forms an auxiliary to those three sacraments beginning with conception is designated by the term *karmāṅga*. Furthermore, this is distinct from the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* itself, as seen in Pāraskara’s extension (*atideśa*) stating "like the *vṛddhi*. For an extension occurs only when there is a distinction. Moreover, the distinction is stated in the enumeration of the different types of *śrāddhas*; the various distinctions, such as the optional (*kāmya*) and the *pārvaṇa*, will be explained in their respective sections.

But is it not said that "in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*), there is no restriction regarding time or desire"? And the *ekoddiṣṭa* Śrāddha is denoted by the term "occasional," since it has been defined thus: "The Śrāddha which is *ekoddiṣṭa* is called occasional. Furthermore, because the Vaiśvadeva portion is prohibited in the *ekoddiṣṭa*—as in the rule: "The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the gods; it has one *arghya* offering and one purifying blade (*pavitraka*)"—how can there be [an option of] time or desire? Nor can the word "occasional" (*naimittika*)—derived from the etymology "that which arises on account of a cause" (*nimitta*)—be used to denote rites prescribed for causes such as obtaining new grain, etc. For it is logical that a general rule (*yoga*), which stands in the place of a general scripture, should be set aside by a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), which takes the form of a specific scripture.

True, this is so; nevertheless, because there is a contradiction in the present context, it is by relying on the etymological derivation (*yoga*) that the term "occasional" (*naimittika*) refers to a *śrāddha* performed on specific occasions such as the acquisition of new grain. As stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"In all *iṣṭi* sacrifices, Kratu and Dakṣa are proclaimed as the two Viśvedevas; in the *nitya-nāndīmukha-śrāddha*, Vasu and Satya are the deities; and in the *paitṛka-śrāddha*, the Pitṛs."
"Upon obtaining new grain, the two deities Kāla and Kāma are always [to be honored];
even when the sun has entered Virgo (Kanyā), at the Śrāddha, Dhuri and Rocana [are the deities];
and at the Pārvaṇa [Śrāddha], Purūravas and Ārdrava are indeed the Viśvedevas. Thus it is said.

In all *iṣṭi* sacrifices and in all *śrāddhas* that are constituent parts of ritual acts, as well as upon obtaining new grain—that is, when the occasion for obtaining new grain has arisen—the procedure for the *śrāddha* will be explained here in the section on the times for *śrāddha*, beginning with the words "by the ripening of rice and barley," and so forth. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that when a *śrāddha* is performed with new grain out of devotion to the ancestors prior to the commencement of eating new grain after its acquisition, the two deities Kāla and Kāma are to be invoked as the presiding divinities (*devatā*) in the Vaiśvadeva portion of the rite.

And this [mention of the Vaiśvadevas] is for the purpose of indicating those *śrāddhas* performed on the occasion of eclipses and so forth—which are governed by specific causes (*nimitta*) and include the Vaiśvadeva rite—by way of the section on "causes" (*nimittādhikāra*). Furthermore, the phrase "when the sun has entered Virgo" refers to the second fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada; this is for the purpose of indicating optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddhas*. Thus, because of both contradiction [with other texts] and explicit scriptural statement, it is established that the word "occasional" (*naimittika*) refers to a *śrāddha* performed on occasions such as the acquisition of new grain. Alternatively, in the rule "In the occasional (*naimittika*), there is time and desire," the word "occasional" denotes the *ekoddiṣṭa*; thus, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (which is joined with the *ekoddiṣṭa*) is what is meant. For that [rite] consists of two primary forms—the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the *pārvaṇa*—and therefore the Vaiśvadeva rite exists therein; hence, the injunction regarding time and desire is appropriate. Śaṅkhadhara and Harihara, however, have stated this: some desire the *ekoddiṣṭa* every year, while others desire the *pārvaṇa*. Therefore, since the annual *kṣayāha-śrāddha* (performed on the anniversary of death) is performed in place of the *ekoddiṣṭa* denoted by the word "occasional," it too deserves to receive the designation "occasional"; thus, the injunction regarding time and desire applies to it. However, this is merely their speculative view; since the determination of the meaning of the scriptural statements is established by the method previously explained, this should not be accepted without critical examination.

[146] Now this is considered: Are Purūravas and Ārdravayas to be employed in combination in the performance of the *pārvaṇa* rite, or as alternatives? Likewise, in the case of the *iṣṭi* and *śrāddha*, regarding Kratu and Dakṣa; and likewise, in the case of the pairs prescribed for the *nāndīmukha* and other rites, such as Satyavas and the others, they must be treated as alternatives. In that regard, for now, they are taken as alternatives. For when establishing the rule, Kratu and Dakṣa are understood to be connected to the ritual action individually and separately. However, it is not because each one is a separate deity that there would be a difference in the ritual action due to a difference in the relationship between the substance and the deity. What scope is there for an alternative? For an "alternative" (*vikalpa*) is designated when two things connected to a single ritual action have a single point of entry. Let it be granted that there is a difference in the ritual action; yet the designation of an "alternative" occurs merely through the lack of connection to a single performance. But in reality, there is no difference in the ritual action due to a difference in the deities. This is because it is stated that differences in ritual action arise from different words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*).
But surely the deity is also a quality, and thus ought to be a differentiator?

Do not say so. For a quality (*guṇa*) is not a differentiator merely by virtue of being a quality; rather, it becomes one only when it cannot find a connection within a single ritual action. Otherwise, there would never be an option regarding substances, an option regarding deities, or a combination of the two. Yet, in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites, we observe both options and combinations regarding substances and so forth, as well as a combination of deities in the *soma* sacrifice. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the passage "seventeen [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati" (*saptadaśa prājāpatyān*), the number—which resides in distinct entities—implies a difference in the relationship between substance and deity, so too here, because of the difference in deities, there is a difference in the relationship, and thus a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*). For if you think in this way, you should simply remember the *soma* sacrifice itself as being endowed with multiple deities such as Indra-Vāyu and others.

[Objection: But surely this is already recorded [in the Smṛti]; however, in that case, because Indra, Vāyu, and the others are understood to be connected to a single sacrifice, their connection with the substance is also understood, and thus there is no differentiation of the ritual act (*karmabheda*). Here, however, it is not so, and therefore there is differentiation. [Reply: No; for a quality (*guṇa*) heard in an originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) is what differentiates. [Objection: When an injunction proceeds to enjoin a quality once the ritual act has already been established, then—since that [quality] differentiates the ritual act—there would in some cases be either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*).
Since it might be argued that the ritual application belongs to those two [sets of mantras] as they have been differentiated, it is said in response:
Whatever rite is performed there for the ancestors toward the Brahmins,
all of that must be performed there preceded by the Vaiśvadeva rite.

In such passages from the words of Devala and others as "the Vaiśvadeva offering must be performed," once this originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) is understood, and since the Viśvedevas are mentioned by a single compound, they are understood to constitute the deityhood collectively in mutual association; thus, their conjunction, being so understood, cannot be set aside by a separate performance prescribed in a subsidiary statement (*guṇavākya*).

[Objection: Surely, by the employment of the single word [viśve], the association (*sāhitya*) of all the Viśvedevas is understood according to their own natural sense. If that [association] is broken by a restrictive statement (*vyavasthāvacana*) regarding three, four, or more Viśvedevas, then its purpose of conveying that association is indeed destroyed; how then can there be a collective [deification]? [Reply: It is said: The meaning of the statement, as understood in a general sense, remains restricted to that portion which is not sublated by another statement. Thus, the status of being a deity belongs to those [Viśvedevas] who are collectively included.

Let it be so; however, this is doubted: should each individual Vaiśvadeva item be performed by designating each one individually with its own name followed by a separate case-ending, or should they be performed by designating them with two names joined in a *dvandva* compound? To that end, this must be considered: does the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) belong to the two together, or is there a conjunction of the two deities? If there is a conjunction of the two deities, then because each possesses the status of a deity individually, the ritual act should be performed by making a designation for each separately, employing the dative case and so forth, preceded by the word *tatsaṃpūrva*. For it has been said: "In this context, 'designation' (*uddeśa*) is defined as the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) expressed as 'of this [deity]'. But when the status of being a deity belongs to the two together—as in the case of Agni and Soma known by the names Purūravas and Ārdravasa—then because they constitute a single substratum in the form of a single deity, the performance should be enjoined after making the designation using a *dvandva* compound. In that regard, some, considering that the injunction of the deities is established by such statements of Śaṅkha and others as "In the *Dṛṣṭiśrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa are to be proclaimed in the Vaiśvadevika," while the injunction of the ritual action or the order of sequence is established by such statements regarding the deities as "preceded by the Vaiśvadevika," or taking the word *vaiśvadevika* itself to be a name according to the principle of direct perception (*pratyakṣanyāya*), state that the designation of each individual deity should be made with its own name followed by a separate case-ending. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an injunction of the deity, since we do not hear any *taddhita* suffixes, dative endings, or words expressing the sense of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) which would establish it? [The answer is: When the sense of the verbal root is restated by the word *vaiśvadevike*, and Kratu, Dakṣa, and the others are enjoined, they cannot take the form of a sacrificial material (*dravya*). Therefore, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣya*), they must be assigned as deities; thus, *taddhita* suffixes and dative endings are unnecessary. To this prima facie view, the following is stated: Who could find room in their heart for the notion that "where there are *taddhita* suffixes or words expressing the sense of the verbal root, there is no injunction, but elsewhere there is an injunction"? [This distinction is untenable.]

But surely, in a case where all these [factors] are present, its status as being intent upon sequence is understood; for according to the maxim that "to the extent that another thing to be enjoined is introduced, to that same extent the injunctive power shifts from one place to another."

This is indeed true; however, since it is possible to enjoin a ritual action qualified by all its attributes within the injunction of that action, there is no fault in enjoining the deities therein. If the deities are enjoined there, then because they are presented in a single compound, they possess the status of deity as characterized by their association; thus, as in the case of Agni-Soma, the application must be enjoined by addressing Purūravas and Ārdrava through a *dvandva* compound. Furthermore, the possibility of the term being a name (*nāmadheya*) is also refuted by the fact that its status is established through another scriptural passage (*tatprakhya-śāstra*).

But surely, in the case of Purūravas, Ārdrava, and others, the non-compounded mention (*advandva-nirdeśa*) is indeed intended, because the two names are not to be used [together]; so how can there be an occasion for the application of option (*vikalpa*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), or a collective compound (*nyāsa-samāsa*) based on that? If, however, they were to be used [together], then one who was ignorant of those two names would lack knowledge of the deity and thus would have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the *śrāddha* at all. Yet, his entitlement has been shown: "Those twice-born who do not know their birth-names should recite this verse with faith. (MDh 3.210)
May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come;
may those who are appointed to this śrāddha rite remain attentive.

If two names were to be employed by means of this scripture, then the plural number heard in the mantra beginning with "O Viśvedevas, come and hear this invocation" would be contradicted. Therefore, the offering of *arghya* and other items should be performed while reciting the term "Viśvedevas. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of mentioning [the names] at the time of performance if they are not actually uttered? we reply that it is merely a mental visualization, like the meditation on the ocean.

To this it is replied: Even if two names are not employed, because the sentence establishing the ritual order is intended to convey the number of deities, and since in reality there are only two deities, the contradiction with the plural form of the mantra remains exactly as it was. Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction because what is intended is the principal [deity] who is distinct [from the others], or because [the plural] is for the sake of honor (*pūjārtha*), then even when two names are employed, there would be no contradiction since that same [principal deity] is intended; thus, dual compounds such as *kratudakṣau* and so forth should indeed be employed. This being the case, the injunction for recitation—“In the *iṣṭi*-śrāddha, Kratu and Dakṣa are to be proclaimed in the Vaiśvadevika section”—would be properly supported. As for the statement made by Harihara that [the plural] is not intended, that was with reference to duality [of the group], not with reference to the names themselves. Therefore, his intention should be understood as follows: even when two names are employed, only the plural should be used, not the dual. As for the reason given here by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* for using the plural—namely, that one asks, “I shall invoke the Viśvedevas,” because the plural form is seen in many Smṛtis and Purāṇas—that may well be so; however, since the *praiṣa* (directive) standing in the place of a mantra is associated with each individual performance, this was stated with reference to the *praiṣa*-sentence itself, and thus another interpretation is possible. As for what... [text breaks off].

It has been stated that [the plural form] is used because one observes the employment of the plural in such passages as, "Having taken [the vessel] without the thumb, one should invoke the Viśvedevas. However, this is not a proof [for the inclusion of all Viśvedevas], since the plural in the injunctive sentence is justified even by referring to those Viśvedevas who participate in every ritual performance. Furthermore, it is not a proof for this reason:
"In the occasional (naimittika) rite, Kāla and Kāma; and in the optional (kāmya) rite, Dhūr and Rocana."

For we observe such usage even with dual endings; furthermore, there is usage with plural endings as well. Since the word *viśva* generally denotes a plurality of objects, its use in the plural is appropriate; consequently, it is fitting that the words *purūravas*, *urvaśī*, and so forth—which serve as its qualifiers and are used in grammatical apposition with it—should also appear in the plural. This is what is being stated.

[150] Should the food placed in each individual vessel set before each Brāhmaṇa be offered separately, designating each time the Viśvedevas, or should it be offered only once, designating them all at once? In this regard, since the deity is one and the same, the offering should be made once, according to the maxim that "joint offering is preferable due to parsimony. Now, it might be argued that the offering must be separate because the separate preparation of the portions serves a visible purpose.

That is not so; for its purpose as a means of feeding [the Brahmins] separately is also established as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). Just as various kinds of food served in a single vessel can be grasped simultaneously by the mind, so too is such simultaneous grasping possible for foods served in separate vessels; thus, a single simultaneous renunciation (*sakṛttyāga*) is logically consistent. And in this way, there will be no repetition of the primary act (*pradhānāvṛtti*) merely to conform to the requirements of the auxiliary parts (*parikalpanāṅga*). This being the position reached, the following is said: Since Āpastamba and others have stated that the Brahmins occupy the place of the *āhavanīya* fire, the renunciation of the food—just like the renunciation of the scent and other offerings—must be performed until that [Brahmin] has received it. Furthermore, since those [Brahmins] are seated separately, the foods served separately cannot be made to reach [them] all at once, because the individual receptions (*prāpti*) are intended to be distinct. Therefore, the foods must be renounced separately. And since there is no other way, the repetition of the renunciation is not a fault; thus, the renunciation should be enjoined for each individual recipient with such formulas as, "To the Viśvedevas named Purūravas and Ārdrava, this food is [offered], not mine," and so forth. In these deliberations, the intent (*tātparya*) lies only in this much: that the designation (*uddeśa*) of the recipients remains in this state. As for the presentation that "such a ritual formula is also of such a nature," that is intended to show that the formula serves as the purpose for the deliberation, not that the formula itself is the direct object of deliberation. Therefore, the connection for the deliberation regarding the true nature of the deity is within the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Thus concludes the determination of the deities for the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Now, the deities for the scattered food (vikira) and the remnants of the meal (bhuktocchiṣṭa). [Manu and Viṣṇu state:]

The remnants of the food and whatever is scattered upon the *darbha* grass shall be the allotted portion for those who have died without performing the sacraments, for renunciants, and for women of noble family.
[151] Hārīta says: Those who die having emerged from the womb with teeth that have not yet erupted—
And for those who have died without having received the funeral rites, [the offering] is given upon the ground.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Whatever scattering of food is performed by humans upon the earth,
by that those who have fallen into the state of Piśācas attain satisfaction."
And those children in the family who were toothless, immature, unfit for ritual acts, and unrefined— they perished by eating the scattered food, the sweepings, and the water.
Manu says:
That which has fallen on the ground as the leavings of food belongs to the group of servants who are neither crooked nor deceitful;
that, they declare, is their share in the ancestral rite (pitrya).
Vasiṣṭha says: According to the Śruti, for those who have died before their sacraments (saṃskāra) and for those who are still in the womb,
Manu has declared both the leavings of food and the scrapings of the dish to be their share.

One should cast upon those who have not yet departed— the food left over, that which has fallen on the ground, the scattered fragments, and the water used for washing— those who are childless and short-lived.
Thus [are described] the deities of the scattered offerings (*vikira*) and the remnants of the meal (*ucchiṣṭa*).

Thus ends the section on the *Śrāddhakalpa* within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the scholar and chief minister of all affairs under the illustrious Mahādeva, the great king of kings.
The third chapter, titled "The Determination of Deities," is concluded.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
The Section on Describing the Places for Śrāddha:
A person whose affliction of sin has been washed away by immersion in the essence of the glorious tīrthas— tīrthas fashioned from the straight-flowing currents of the river of meritorious conduct;
That mountain of gold, whose merit increases with his horripilation,
resolves to extract [the essence] and then exerts himself to determine the requirements for the *śrāddha* rite.

Thus, having stated this context, the determination of the intended ancestors and others has been made as if it were already established, on the basis that the meaning of the term *śrāddha* consists of the feeding of Brahmins and so forth, performed with faith for the sake of deities in the form of one’s father and the rest. Now, another section is commenced to investigate and ascertain the very meaning of the word *śrāddha*. In that regard, the matter to be investigated is introduced by means of the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of *śrāddha*. As stated in the *Bṛhaspati-smṛti*:
"Food that is prepared, rich in condiments, and accompanied by milk, honey, and ghee..."
Because it is given with faith (śraddhā), it is therefore called śrāddha.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "Since faith is the root of the *śrāddha*, it is therefore proclaimed as *śrāddha*;
when it is performed, nothing therein shall go to waste."

"Root" (*mūla*) means the most excellent limb. Thus it is stated in the *Śrāddhakalpa* composed by Kātyāyana: "One endowed with faith (*śraddhā*) should perform the *śrāddha*. This is prescribed; for here, faith does not arise as a causal condition (*nimitta*), but rather it is said that whoever performs the *śrāddha* should do so while being endowed with faith—thus the status of faith as a limb of the *śrāddha* is expressed. And likewise, according to Bārhaspatya-Pārāśara, by means of the third case ending (*tṛtīyāvibhakti*), faith is presented as a qualification of the *śrāddha*:
"That which [is performed] in the proper place, at the proper time, toward a worthy recipient, according to the rule, and with the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)."
A Śrāddha performed with sesame seeds, Darbha grass, and mantras, when endowed with faith, shall be effective.
For this very reason, the *Manusmṛti* states that excellence arises through the application of faith:
"Whatever one gives according to the rule and correctly, endowed with faith—that becomes infinite and inexhaustible for the ancestors in the hereafter. Thus it is said.
In the Nandipurāṇa as well:
"Faith is proclaimed to be the purifier of all purifiers;
faith alone is always the supreme dharma and the most sanctifying."
The elements that have become faith are indeed always pure;
faith is the mother of all beings, and faith is praised in the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
For this very reason, the *Yama-smṛti* states that there is a defect due to the absence of faith:
"That which is devoid of ritual rules, food that is not purified, that which lacks mantras and sacrificial fees,
and that which is offered or given without faith— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume."
Baudhāyana also said: "By faith the intellect is awakened; by faith the mind is purified;
by faith Brahman is attained; faith is the liberator from evil."
"Therefore, the deities do not eat the oblation of one who lacks faith.
Now, since faith is a constituent element of every virtuous rite (*satkarma*), by what specific distinction is this particular rite designated by the word *śrāddha*?
To this effect, it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Whatever one may perform with a mind endowed with faith,
that very act yields abundant fruit for them in both worlds.
This person consists of faith; whatever word one utters, that indeed one becomes. Humans who have faith in the gods become gods, said to be partakers of the divine.

Those who have faith in the ancestors are the Pitṛs; those who have faith in the Daityas are the sons of Diti. Likewise, those who have faith in evil are the wicked, to be known as those destined for hell.
Therefore, having established faith, a practitioner of dharma should perform dharma;
for that merit which is performed by relying upon faith yields abundant fruit.
Faith is indeed the supreme purifier in the world; faith is said to be the very body of a person.
Having established themselves in faith, men, having performed [their duties]...
Through meritorious deeds, they attain a meritorious destination.
In the *Bṛhatpārāśara*:
"A gift that is purified by faith should be given to a worthy recipient even unasked;
for even when asked, one's own pure wealth should be given with faith."
Thus, since every virtuous deed is endowed with the constituent factor of faith (*śraddhā*), how is it that this [act] alone receives the name *śrāddha*?

It is said: the operation of a word with respect to its meanings is threefold—by convention (*rūḍhi*), by etymology (*yoga*), and by both etymology and convention (*yogarūḍhi*). Among these, that which functions through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) is said to function by convention, because it is, as it were, firmly rooted (*prarūḍha*) there. That which functions through the power of its parts (*avayava-śakti*) as far as the etymological connection permits is said to function by etymology, because it functions due to the connection with the meaning of its parts. However, that which, although functioning through the power of its parts, does not function as far as the etymological connection permits due to restricted usage, is said to function by both etymology and convention. And thus, the word *śrāddha* functions by both etymology and convention; this is precisely its name.

But surely, due to contradiction, neither *yogarūḍhi* (both etymological and conventional) is tenable; for if it functions through the power of its parts (*avayava-śakti*), it cannot then function through the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*)—this is the contradiction. True. However, while functioning solely through the power of its parts, because its application is restricted by convention, its part-powers are contracted and it is not entirely dependent on etymology; thus, it functions by means of convention (*rūḍhi*) itself. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the theory of figurative usage (*gauṇavāda*).

Others, however, say: A word applies to its object solely through the connection with either a direct (*pratyakṣa*) or an indirect (*parokṣa*) mode of operation. Where a word operates with its constituent parts (*avayava*) unchanged—as in the case of the word *nighaṇṭu*—there too it is said to operate by way of an indirect function. In that regard, this word *śrāddha* operates toward a specific ritual action through a direct function by virtue of its connection with faith (*śraddhā*). Nevertheless, due to the restriction of usage and because its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) is narrowed down, it does not apply elsewhere. Just as the word *go*, although etymologically derived from "that which goes" (*gacchati*), does not apply to horses and the like despite being based on that derivation, so too the word *śrāddha* is the name of a ritual action, because it is not established [in common usage] for substances and the like.

But surely, since [the substance] is well-known even as an object of action (*karman*), and since an injunction (*vidhi*) has the purpose of inciting activity, and since, if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), it would serve a purpose by generating a specific inclination toward the person regarding the quality portion, there would be a denotation of a substance. As it has been said: "On account of its established status, on account of its being purposeful, on account of its being additional, and on account of the incitement to activity, that which is of the nature of a quality is enjoined."

Now it is said: First of all, it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) with respect to the ritual action (*karman*), because no specific action is heard in close syntactical connection (*samabhivyāhṛta*). Nor is there an injunction regarding the mere productive urge (*bhāvanā*) in the sentence containing the verb "to do" (*karoti*), because that which has an established form (*siddharūpa*) cannot be directly connected with the productive urge. Nor is it an injunction of a quality with respect to the fruit (*phala*), because that which is not connected to an action serving as its substratum (*āśraya*) cannot be connected to the fruit. For it is only when [the quality], such as the *godohana* vessel, is based upon an action such as "fetching water" (*praṇayana*), that it is enjoined for the sake of the fruit.

That is not so; for even if it were a name, the objection remains the same: one must still inquire whose name it is. Furthermore, a name is not accepted as referring to a mere mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because that would result in every ritual action being a name. Now, [it is said]:
"The sons should diligently offer the *śrāddha* for their deceased father;
those who worship the ancestors, the gods, the Brahmins, and the sacrificial fires."

If you consider this to be the name of the ritual action understood from the passages recited in such contexts, then for me too, the way out is easily found: that this is an injunction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) with respect to either the ritual action or its fruit as already understood. Furthermore, the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely "being joined with faith" (*śraddhāyoga*), is exactly the same.
Moreover, the established position of those who know the Veda is that "the *śrāddha* must be performed.

This is because, in this context, we observe grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a substance, and because, as in the case of "cows and so forth," the understanding arises that "the *śrāddha* is to be given," which implies it is something to be bestowed. For it is not possible for a ritual action such as giving to possess the status of being "to be given" (*deyatva*).

If it is argued that the application [of the term] is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the substance, we say no; for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a figurative sense. Furthermore, when a quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined with respect to an action already understood from another sentence, there is no figurative indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). For that [figurative indication] occurs only in the case of a single-word syntactical unity (*padaikavākyatva*), not in the case of a multi-word syntactical unity (*vākyaikavākyatva*). Moreover, designations such as "obligatory," "occasional," or "optional" are not contradictory even when applied to a substance, as seen in the cases of the *camasa* cup, the *godohana* vessel, and so forth. Therefore, since this is not the name of an action, the following is stated in response: its status as a name is established because of the existence of other scriptural injunctions regarding its purpose, just like the word *agnihotra*. For just as the deities intended to be enjoined are obtained through another scriptural injunction recited in the context—such as "That which one offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati"—so too here, the substances are indeed obtained through other injunctions such as "Beans, barley, sesame, wheat, meat, and so forth should be given with faith to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) etc. And because there is no well-known conventional usage (*prasiddhi*) [of the term as a name], it is not an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Indeed, it is precisely because of well-known usage that [terms like] *somena* [in *somena yajeta*] are injunctions of a quality. As for the occasional co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *śrāddha* with the word *anna* (food) found in certain places, that is due to figurative function (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*). And the fact that the word *śrāddha* is used for the substance by indicating the state of being fit to be given (*deyatva*) is also stated through figurative indication. Furthermore, the designation of "obligatory," "occasional," and so forth, has attained great conventional currency in reference to the ritual action (*karman*); thus, by its natural function (*svarasavṛtti*), it does not abandon its inclination toward the action.

But surely, since the primary object (pradhānakarman) such as sacrifice is a means (karaṇa) in all cases, if it were to be designated by a name, the word *śrāddha* would not appear in the accusative case; for it has been stated: "In both the injunction and the restatement, the sacrifice is intended to be the means."

It is said in reply: Just as an axe, though serving as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act consisting of the raising and falling of the axe which is undertaken for the purpose of the result of splitting wood and so forth, becomes an unintended object (*aniṣṭakarma*) because it participates in the series of actions consisting of the destruction and conjunction-disjunction of that wood; likewise, although the meaning of "sacrifice" (*yajyādi-artha*) serves as the instrument in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) undertaken for the purpose of results such as heaven, it is an "object" (*karman*) because it is that which is brought about by that productive activity. Thus, when the state [of being an object] is intended, terms such as *agnihotram* appropriately take the second case ending. Since sacrifice and the like—which are brought about by the very nature of the productive activity—possess the status of an instrument at the stage where the productive activity has heaven and the like as its fruit, there is no contradiction between their being an object and an instrument with respect to a single thing. Only the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is inherently sequential and has exclusively the nature of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is directly connected to the productive activity in the form of the sense of "doing" (*karoti*). Established substances and the like are connected only indirectly through the meaning of the verbal root; therefore, they are secondary. Consequently, the word *śrāddha* is a name for the ritual action (*karman*). Its status as a name for the action is also understood from the statement of Āpastamba: "Now Manu proclaimed this ritual called *śrāddha* for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny; therein, the ancestors are the deities. This being the case, an inquiry is made: Is this the name of only the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) or the feeding of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇabhojana*), or is it the name of the collection of the ritual acts under discussion, namely the offering of the rice-balls, the feeding of the Brahmins, and the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire)? On this point, the teacher Karka says that it is the name of the offering of the rice-balls alone. For indeed, this is the name of the principal act, since it occurs within the sentence of the injunction (*adhikāra-vākya*). And in this context, the offering of the rice-balls is understood to be the principal act. Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen [in the texts].

"May there be born in our family one who would give us milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), during the rainy season, and under the asterism Maghā.

Here, indeed, because an intense prayer is observed regarding the *piṇḍas* (rice-balls) for the ancestors who are the deities of the *śrāddha*, it is understood that the offering of the *piṇḍas* is the primary element. Furthermore, in the *Mahābhārata*, it is described that when the *piṇḍa* is being offered at Gayā, the hands of the ancestors rise up to receive the *piṇḍa*. Likewise, when the performance of the *śrāddha* is intended to be explained, the *smṛtis* state that the offering of the *piṇḍas* (*piṇḍanirvapaṇa*) is what must be performed.
But when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed for him according to the Dharma,
the sons must perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) by means of this very same procedure.

Because of such statements, and because the mere offering of the *piṇḍas* is prescribed even when the feeding of Brahmins is impossible, it follows that—given that the primacy of the *piṇḍa*-offering is understood through these observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*)—the term *śrāddha* is the name for this [offering] alone.
[Objection: But surely the feeding of Brahmins also possesses primacy, since it is connected to the principal deities in the form of the ancestors (*pitṛ*).

[Reply: Not so. Because of the statement, "If one should feed only one person at a *śrāddha*," and because of the inherent capacity of the act of feeding itself, the feeding is directly connected to the Brahmin; thus, there is no evidence that it is for the sake of the ancestors.
[Objection: But if this were the case, the ritual procedure would be a mere metaphorical designation as "pertaining to the ancestors" (pitr̥ya), just as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
[Reply: No; for that is appropriate because it is intended for the Brahmins who are the recipients of the Śrāddha.

[Objection: If the meaning of the word "Śrāddha" consists merely in the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa), how can there be such usage as "He has eaten the Śrāddha" even when one has eaten at the meal where the balls are consumed?

We say that, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to the purpose of feeding [the Brahmins] which constitutes a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. Thus it is established that this is indeed a designation for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*). And in this way, if in some performance the offering of the rice-balls is not accomplished—meaning if an obstacle arises in the performance—the feeding of the Brahmins must be repeated for the sake of the rice-ball offering, because the subsidiaries exist for the sake of the principal. For the feeding of the Brahmins and so forth is a subsidiary to that offering.

Others, however, say that the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary element, and that the term *śrāddha* is a name for that very act. Thus it is stated in the Āpastamba Sūtra: "Now Manu has declared this rite by the name *śrāddha* for the sake of the ultimate welfare of progeny; therein the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. The phrase "for the purpose of the *āhavanīya*" refers to the function of the *āhavanīya*, characterized by the holding of the oblation being cast into it. Since they cannot perform that function without eating, the meaning is that this statement culminates in the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
"Then they too, being restrained in speech, should eat while speaking as they please.

Thus, because the activity of the instigator—which has as its object the activity of the one being directed, namely the feeding of the Brahmins—extends up until the attainment of the secondary *āhavanīya* fire, and because it denotes the performance of the *homa*, the word *śrāddha* is a name (*nāmadheya*) for that [rite]; such is the opinion of Viśvarūpa, Medhātithi, Vāmadeva, and others. And this specific activity is enjoined in many *smṛtis* within the section on *śrāddhas* as being connected with a specific fruit.
"One should feed even a single learned man at rites for the gods and the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit [thereby]. Therefore, one should feed [such a person] with effort.
Thus it is stated in the *Śaunakagṛhya*.
"One should feed at least nine śrotriyas, or an odd number," as it is also stated in the *Manusmṛti*:
"Two for the rite of the gods, three for the rite of the ancestors, or one for each of the two."
"Even one who is very wealthy should feed [the Brahmins], but should not be attached to abundance.
Thus, the word *śrāddha* is the name for the instigating activity consisting of the feeding of Brahmins, which resides in the patron (*yajamāna*).

As for the view presented by Hariharācārya regarding Viśvarūpa and others: because the activity of the one being prompted (*prayojya*) is inseparable from the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*), even the act of eating—which is the activity of the one being prompted and has the Brahmins as its agent—is denoted by the word *śrāddha*. For this very reason, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *śrāddha* with the verb "to eat" is observed, as in the expression: "The *śrāddha* was eaten by him. Likewise, there are such scriptural indications as: "Whosoever among these should eat the *śrāddha*, having been honored," and so forth. Furthermore, in the case of a *śrāddha* performed when the father is still living, since the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is ruled out, the injunction regarding the act of eating serves to indicate the primacy of both the eating and the activities conducive to it: "Or else, in that *śrāddha*, he should feed his own father like a Brahmin," or "His grandfather may eat that *śrāddha*," and so on.

This view appears to be untenable; for since the activity of the person to be employed (the officiant) does not constitute the activity of the qualified agent (the patron), if that [activity of the officiant] lacks a connection with the fruit, its status as the primary action cannot be established. How, then, could it be denotable by the word *śrāddha*, which expresses a primary action?

[Objection: But if this were so, then in the case of the activities of the officiants—the *āgneya* and other rites—their status as primary actions would be absent, and consequently, they could not be denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

Not so. Even though the Āgneya and other rites, which are enjoined as the activities of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), are accomplished through the activities of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) brought about by the sacrificer according to other scriptural injunctions, they are nonetheless accomplished through the activity consisting of the sacrificer’s own *bhāvanā* (productive urge); therefore, there is no contradiction in their being denoted by the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa*, which designate primary rites. In contrast, eating (*bhojana*), which is accomplished not by the sacrificer’s activity but by that of others, is designated [in this context] as the activity of the sacrificer. Thus, although it is pervaded by the *bhāvanā* accomplished by the sacrificer, it is not denoted by the word *śrāddha*. This is just as, in the injunction for the *bhāvanā* of giving (*dāna*), although accepting (*pratigraha*) is included within that *bhāvanā* because it is its pervaded object, it is not denoted by the word "giving. For here too, the meaning of the word "giving" is the production of another's ownership preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership. And the production of another's ownership cannot be established without bringing about acceptance; for it is through acceptance that another's ownership is realized. Therefore, acceptance is indeed pervaded by the *bhāvanā* of giving. Nevertheless, it is subordinate because there is no injunction regarding it as an activity of the sacrificer. This is because acceptance cannot be subject to the sacrificer’s mandate (*niyoga*), according to the principle that a person is enjoined as an agent only with respect to his own activity. Acceptance is not an activity of the sacrificer.
Now, regarding the places for the *śrāddha* ceremony. On this point, Manu says:
"One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung."
And one should ensure that it slopes toward the south with great care.
In open spaces, in clean places, and indeed on the banks of rivers,
the ancestors are always satisfied by what is offered in secluded spots.
In the *Yamasmṛti*:
"Having quickly examined a pure place that slopes toward the south, is smooth, secluded, and possesses auspicious characteristics, one should smear it with cow dung."
In secluded dwellings, at sacred fords, and by rivers— in these solitary places—
the ancestors are always satisfied with the gift of a tooth-stick.
On the banks of rivers, at sacred fords, and with effort on one's own ground;
likewise on the slopes of hills and mountain ridges,
and in secluded houses smeared with cow dung.
Halfway here, near the mountain;
as stated in the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya* and the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"In a region sloping toward the south, at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or even in one's own home."
"One should diligently perform the śrāddha rite when it is joined with the preparation of the ground and other such requirements. Thus [it is said].
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O twice-born one, wherever the shade of a grove of Tulasī trees may be found,
there a Śrāddha should be offered for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors."
Devala also said: "For one who is faithful, the Gayā region is honored, as are the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes."
The ancestors are satisfied by what is given here on riverbanks, at sacred fords, on mountains, on sandbanks, and in secluded places.
Also in the *Śaṅkhasmṛti*:
"On the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at Payoṣṇī and Amarakaṇṭaka,
on the banks of the Narmadā and Bāhudā, at Bhṛguliṅga and the Himalaya."
What is given at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and likewise at Puṣkara,
as well as at Sannihatyā and Gayā, becomes inexhaustible.
"May there be born in our family some supreme among men who,
with a concentrated mind, shall offer us a śrāddha at the banyan tree of Gayāśīrṣa."
"One should desire many sons, so that even one might go to Gayā, or perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull. Thus [it is said].
Now, the forbidden regions:
In the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*, it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"One should avoid the entire region of Triśaṅku for twelve yojanas,
to the north of the Mahānadī river and to the south of Kīkaṭa."
The region named Traiśaṅkava is excluded from the performance of *śrāddha* rites. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The Kāraskaras, the Kaliṅgas, and also the region north of the Indus."
"And regions where the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) have perished should be avoided with effort. Thus [it is said]. Kāraskara is a specific region; Kīkaṭa is Magadha.
[This is stated] in the Brahmapurāṇa.
If a fool offers libations to his own ancestors in the house of another,
the ancestors forcibly seize them from the owner of that land.
In the *Yama-smṛti*:
"But he who performs the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*) on lands belonging to others has his śrāddha rite obstructed by the ancestors of the owners of that land."
Forests, mountains, sacred rivers, and whatever holy fords there may be—
all these are said to be without an owner, for in them there is no private possession.
In the performance of a śrāddha rite, one should avoid a place that is rough, infested with insects, damp, cluttered, foul-smelling, or characterized by unpleasant sounds.
"Unpleasant sound" means a discordant sound.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrāddhakalpa* of the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the venerable Hemādri, the scholar and chief minister of all affairs for the illustrious Mahādeva, the supreme king of great kings.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Description of the Places for Śrāddha.
Now begins the Fifth Chapter.
The Section on Determining the Times for Śrāddha:
Whether it be the *nameru* or the *meru*, in the matter of seizing the earth, she is measured by the sky;
her nature is as beautiful as that of Hari and Īśa, and she is the very image of Hari and Īśa.
The wise Hemādri, whose conduct is profound with the weight of his virtues,
composes here this section on the beneficially ordained times for the Śrāddha ceremony.
Now, because it serves as the locus for the entire ritual performance and shares a common nature [with the preceding], the time for the *śrāddha* is described immediately after the location.
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Janārdana himself, whose essence is Time, creates, protects, and devours the universe."
For this reason, they know that time alone is the supreme cause here in this world.
For neither in the world nor in the Veda, O lord of the people, do injunctions and prohibitions ever occur without depending upon time.
Therefore, time alone is the means for accomplishing merit and demerit;
consequently, a righteous person should perform actions during auspicious times.
It is a settled conclusion that nothing should be done by a wise man at an improper time.
Regarding "meritorious times," these are the divisions of time prescribed as means for accomplishing merit.

Now, one might object: since time is partless due to its being formless, eternal, and all-pervasive—on account of these reasons—how can there be divisions? The resolution of this doubt is found in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "Time is eternal, all-pervasive, and constant; its states, however, are born of causes."
"Through specific characteristics such as the *nimitta* and others, he bestows the fruit of merit in the world. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: It is true that this [atom] has no inherent parts (*svābhāvikāvayava*), because it is eternal, whereas those [parts] belong only to what is impermanent. For that which is called "composite" (*sāvayava*) is produced from parts. Furthermore, that which is other than destruction itself is necessarily subject to destruction. Now, one might object: "A composite is merely that which inheres in parts, not that which is produced from them."

Not so; for it would follow that even a universal (*sāmānya*) must possess parts. Furthermore, the parts of time must be stated to be either of the same nature as [time] itself or to be smaller in dimension relative to the whole (*avayavin*). In that case, its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) and oneness (*ekatva*) would be lost. Moreover, its oneness and all-pervasiveness are established by specific inferential marks (*liṅga*), are accepted by sages such as Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda, and are well-known from the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources. Therefore, time has no inherent parts whatsoever. Nevertheless, he states that "its states (*avasthās*) are born of causes" (*hetujāḥ*), meaning that although there are no natural parts, states do exist through adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*). The "states" consist of divisions such as forenoon, midday, afternoon, day, night, fortnight, month, season (*ṛtu*), solstice (*ayana*), and year. The "cause" is the distinction between various adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) consisting of the accumulation of the sun's movements. These states are "born of that," meaning they are based upon that [sun] as their delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). And these states are threefold according to the distinction of adventitious conditions: being auxiliary to obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rites. Consequently, this time is designated in three ways as "obligatory," "occasional," and "optional. Thus, when divided in this threefold manner, it bestows meritorious fruits. On this point, the *Śatapatha Śruti* says: "Spring, summer, and the rains—these are the gods (*deva*) seasons. Autumn, winter, and the cool season—these are the ancestors (*pitṛ*). That half-month which waxes is the gods; that which wanes is the ancestors. Day indeed is the gods, night is the ancestors. Again, the forenoon of the day is the gods, the afternoon is the ancestors. Here, the connection of time with the gods and ancestors is stated through the division of the northern and southern solstices, the bright and dark fortnights, day and night, and the forenoon and afternoon.

Hārīta then said: "Prajāpati is the year; his northern course (udagayana) is the bright fortnight and the forenoon, which belong to the gods; his southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is the dark fortnight and the afternoon, which belong to the ancestors. There is no other state, because he exists in his entirety; thus sacrifices are performed in both ways, for they are intermingled day by day. Moreover, regarding this they cite: 'He whose two paths carry the offerings to the gods and the oblations to the ancestors, of whom the gods occupy one half and the ancestors likewise the other half, of whom the moments and the seasons are the root—to him, as he sacrifices, let immortality come.'"

The meaning of this is as follows: That specific deity named Prajāpati who is heard of in scripture is indeed this very time consisting of the year (*saṃvatsara*). This [time] has two parts. Among them, one part consists of the northern course (*udagayana*), the bright fortnight (*śukla*), the day (*ahaḥ*), and the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). The "northern course" is the period of time characterized by the six zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*) as enjoyed by the sun; the "bright fortnight" is the period from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) following the new moon until the full moon; "day" means the daytime; and "forenoon" is the first half of the day divided into two parts. And so it is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The forenoon is indeed until the turning [of the shadow], and the afternoon is after that."

The prefix *āṅ* denotes a limit. That period of time which begins from the turning back of the shadow and extends up to its complete revolution is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). This entire collection of divisions of the year belongs to the gods (*deva*); the meaning is that divine rites (*daivika-karma*) are to be performed during this time. The second part consists of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the dark fortnight (*tāmisra*), and the night. The southern solstice is the period characterized by the Sun’s passage through the six zodiac signs beginning with Cancer. The dark fortnight (*tāmisra*) is the period beginning from the first day (*pratipad*) following the full moon until the new moon. Night is the period delimited by the non-visibility of the Sun due to its being obstructed by Mount Meru. This entire collection of divisions of the year belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛ*); the meaning is that ancestral rites (*pitrya-karma*) are to be performed during this time. Thus, time is twofold—divine and ancestral—and has no other state or other form. Why? He says: "Because of its totality" (*kṛtsnabhāvāt*). Since there is no time apart from the year, all time is only this much. Therefore, because it is permeated by the times consisting of forenoon and afternoon—which are of the nature of divine and ancestral—the gods and the ancestors are worshipped in both ways daily, every day, according to the division of forenoon and afternoon; they pray for the visibility of the sacrificial offering (*havya*) and the ancestral oblation (*kavya*) as it is being presented. Now, to show that this is not the first statement regarding this matter, he provides a corroborative citation: "And here they quote. The meaning is: in this regard, the ancient great seers (*maharṣi*) cite and recite [the following verse]. "He whose two paths carry the offerings to the gods and the ancestors"—that is, of whom, Prajāpati in the form of the year, the offerings to the gods and ancestors proceed toward the gods and ancestors. His two paths are the northern and southern solstices, or the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*). Half of him belong to the gods and half to the ancestors. And "whose root is the moments" (*nimeṣa*): a moment refers to units of time such as *kāṣṭhā* and *kalā*; the meaning is that these are the constituents and the originating factors. Likewise, "whose root is the seasons" (*ṛtu*): the seasons are six, and they are mentioned in the Veda: "Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons (*vāsantika-ṛtu*); Śukra and Śuci are the two summer seasons (*graiṣma-ṛtu*); Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two rainy seasons (*vārṣika-ṛtu*); Iṣa and Ūrja are the two autumn seasons (*śārada-ṛtu*); Sahas and Sahasya are the two winter seasons (*haimantika-ṛtu*); Tapas and Tapasya are the two cool-seasons (*śaiśira-ṛtu*). Madhu and Mādhava refer to the two months Caitra and Vaiśākha; these two months belonging to spring constitute the season called spring. The same applies to the subsequent seasons, summer and so on. That year, whose root these [seasons] are, approaches—that is, comes toward—the person who worships the gods and ancestors according to their respective divisions, "immortal," meaning with a view toward the fruit of liberation and the like.

Thus concludes the determination of time according to the division between rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors. Now follows the specific types of *śrāddha*; regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

The non-existence of this [is known] from the single day and so forth; the dark fortnight is for the sake of the barley-grain [offering]. Substance, the excellence of the Brahmin, the equinox, and the sun’s transit [are the occasions].
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a Śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for Śrāddha.

The times, such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and others, will be explained one by one in their respective contexts. "Desire" (*rucis*) means wish; when that wish concerns the performance of a *śrāddha*, the time characterized by it also becomes an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. Its status as a non-occasion (*animitta*) must be refuted by the very same logic used previously to refute the [opposing] view that it is not an occasion for *śrāddha*. Among those, the new moon is discussed: the new moon is the fifteenth lunar day (*tithi*) of the dark fortnight. Its definition has been stated by Gobhila: "That which is the greatest distance between the sun and the moon is the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*); that which is the closest proximity is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Regarding this, the etymology of the word *amāvāsyā* is found in the *Śatapatha-śruti*.

Those gods said, "Nothing else indeed would satisfy him but Soma; let us collect Soma for him. They collected Soma for him. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon. When he is not seen either in the east or in the west on that night, he comes to this world; he enters right here into the waters and the plants. He is indeed the *vasu* (wealth) of the gods, for he is their food. Because he dwells here as their *amā* (home) on that night, it is therefore called *Amāvāsyā*.

In this regard, regarding the first statement, it is said that after the slaying of Vṛtra, when Indra had returned from his absence, the gods [spoke of] Amāvāsyā because of their dwelling (amā) together with Vasu-Indra. In the second statement, however, there is a twofold etymological derivation: it is called Amāvāsyā because of the dwelling (amā) of Vasu—the Moon—in this world on this night.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Those known as the Agniṣvāttas are performers of sacrifice who are established in ritual."
Their mental daughter is considered to be named Acchāmā.
[169] Then, beholding her father named Amāvasu, she,
seeking a husband, chose him for union because of the torment caused by the flower-armed god of love.
But because of that transgression, that beautiful woman, having fallen from her yoga, did not touch the earth at first; she fell instead onto the surface of the ground below.
Because her father, Amāvasu, did not desire her [for marriage],
she became renowned in the world as Amāvāsyā due to his fortitude;
for she is beloved by the ancestors and causes what is given to them to become inexhaustible.

The purport of this *itihāsa* is as follows: she is called *amāvāsyā* because her greatness is well-known for sustaining the humility (*amā*) and fortitude (*sudhairya*) that prevent the fall of the celibacy (*brahmacarya*) favored by the hosts of the most self-restrained ancestors (*paramasaṃyamipitṛgaṇa*).
This is stated in the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*:
"The digit named *Amā* stands at the head of the thousand [rays]."
And by whose splendor the sun is said to be the illuminator of the three worlds.
When the moon enters that [light] ray, it is therefore known as Amāvāsyā;
it is inexhaustible for the performance of religious duties, and especially so for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The digit named Amā, situated at the head of the thousand [rays],
is declared to be the illuminator of the three worlds, established in the realm of the Moon."
Because Soma enters into her on that Amāvāsyā, it is so called; thus it is stated in the Matsya and Vāyu Purāṇas:
"When the Moon and the Sun dwell together [in the same location] except for [the presence of] Amā..."
This fifteenth night is indeed the new moon (amāvāsyā).
*Amā* means together or in one place.
When, having resorted to that *amāvāsyā*, the moon and the sun are seen joined with one another, that is called *darśa*.
And that [full moon] is of two kinds. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Rākā and Anumati are remembered as the two types of full moon (paurṇamāsī);
likewise, Sinīvālī and Kuhū are the two types of new moon (amāvāsyā)."

The definition of these two is found in the Śruti: "That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati, and that which is the later is Rākā; that which is the earlier new moon is Sinīvālī, and that which is the later is Kuhū. Here, it is stated that Sinīvālī is mixed with the fourteenth day (caturdaśī). Regarding this [Sinīvālī], Vyāsa says, intending that she is generally characterized by the appearance of the moon—based on the statement of astronomers that the moon exists in her when she is mixed with more than three muhūrtas of the fourteenth day:
"Sinīvālī is known as the one in whom the moon is visible; Kuhū is remembered as the one in whom the moon has vanished."
"Sinīvālī is always for rites concerning the ancestors (pitrya), while Kuhū is for rites concerning the gods (daiva).
Now, regarding the etymology of these two, with reference to the junction of the lunar phases (parvasandhi):
"Sinīvālī is the measure [of the moon] when the moon has only its waning remnant remaining."
On the new moon day, the sun enters [the earth]; thus is Sinīvālī remembered.

*Sinī* means white; *avasitā* means ended. *Vālī* means a small hair. That which is both *sinī* (white) and *vālī* (hair-like) is *sinīvālī*. "Of the measure of that" (*tatparimāṇaḥ*) means "of the size of a *sinīvālī*," that is to say, the measure of a single hair-tip.

Regarding *kuhū*: as long as the time taken for a crow’s call (*pikena ukte*) lasts, this new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) measured by that duration is known as *kuhū*. Thus it is said: "The new moon day is called *kuhū* when its duration is equal to the time it takes for a crow's cry to be uttered."
*Kuhū* refers to the day and night characterized by the *saṃdhi* (twilight) occurring at a moment measured by the sound *kuhū* uttered by the cuckoo. And this is a constant time for the *śrāddha*.
Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of kings, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is always the time for the *śrāddha*."
"Likewise, they declare [the observance] for the full moon of Māgha and that of Śrāvaṇa.
Also in the *Manusmṛti*:
"A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) at the waning of the moon..."
One should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.

The waning of the moon is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*); on that day one should perform the *śrāddha*. Even there, it is not at any time whatsoever; rather, the meaning is "having performed the *pitṛyajña*, that is, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. The mention of the *vipra* (Brahmin) is illustrative [of all twice-born]. *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* is a name for the *śrāddha*. "Monthly" (*māsānumāsika*) means that which occurs in the month and the following month; the term *māsānumāsa* expresses the repetition inherent in the month, meaning "to be performed month after month. From this, its obligatory nature (*nityatā*) is established. As stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya*: "The *śrāddha* should be performed on the new moon, month after month, when the moon has waned."
Likewise, regarding the *aṣṭakās* as well, learn from me the desired time.
"The *uḍupa* is the moon; learn from me the desired time"—this is the promise concerning the optional time that is about to be described. [Source:
*Brahmapurāṇa*.
In this world, one should offer the *śrāddha* monthly at the waning of the moon;
and on the full-moon days, the *śrāddha* should be performed when the moon is in its proper asterism.
In the domain of the bears (the month of Mārgaśīrṣa), in conjunction with the lunar mansion [Mṛgaśiras]; here too, by means of repetition, its obligatory nature is indicated. Also in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"O Lord of Men, month after month, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
[172] "Likewise, one should perform [the rites] on the Aṣṭakās; hear from me the times for optional rites.
Here, by stating that the times to be described are "optional," the author implies that those previously mentioned are "obligatory" (nitya). [As stated] in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa:
A wise man should always perform the *śrāddha* ceremony at the waning of the moon;
if he desires heaven as well as progeny, O King, he must do so.
Just as those afflicted by cold desire fire and clothing,
so do the ancestors, emaciated by hunger, desire the waning of the moon.
Just as men afflicted by poverty long for wealth,
so do the ancestors, emaciated [by hunger], long for the waning of the moon.
Just as farmers desire rain for the growth of their crops,
so do those who delight in self-satisfaction long for the waning of the moon.
Just as the ruddy goose and his mate long for the sight of the sun,
so do the ancestors desire the śrāddha offering arising from the new moon.
If one performs a śrāddha with even water or with vegetables, yet fails to do so on the day of the new moon (darśa),
his ancestors depart as bestowers of curses.
Likewise: When the day of the new moon has arrived, the hosts of ancestors stand at the door of men's houses, having become like the wind, and long for the śrāddha offering.
Thus they remained, tormented by hunger and thirst, until the setting of the sun;
then, when the sun had set, hopeless and filled with sorrow, they sighed for a long time and departed, reproaching their own lineage. So it is said.
[173] Regarding the necessity of performing the *śrāddha* on this new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there is the following account in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Then King Purūravas, having attained heaven in his own physical body..."
Honored by Śakra at the proper time, he dwelt there according to his pleasure.
At that time, the king was accompanied by Urvaśī in all the celestial gardens;
he could never be restrained.
O protector of the earth, on every new moon day, the moon and the sun always go to see one another when they have entered the same constellation.
When the moon dwells with the granddaughter of Urvaśī,
then the divine man out of affection pours forth the essence of nectar.
Then the ancestors drink that very nectar-like juice of Soma;
O best of excellent kings, that time is declared to be the proper time for Śrāddha for human beings.
Then, O protector of the earth, whatever śrāddha is offered mixed with the essence of nectar,
that the ancestors consume as if it were water.
O best of kings, perform the śrāddha with great care on every new moon day; you shall obtain all your desires.
And those others, O lord of men, who shall perform that act with faith at that time—
the Great-Grandfathers will grant them long life, fame, and heaven.
One who desires sovereignty, one who desires heaven, and likewise one who desires prosperity,
should satisfy the ancestors with a śrāddha at the conjunction of the moon and the sun.
[174] O King, the ancestors dwell eternally in the lunar orb;
hear from me now the division of day and night for them there, which lasts for one month.
For them, the sun rises during the middle of the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
likewise, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the maker of day sets for them.
O King, for them, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) always occurs at midday;
therefore, śrāddha offerings should be given with great care at that time.
Next, Vyāsa describes the supreme merit of this lunar day (tithi) through its conjunction with specific days of the week: "The new moon (amāvāsyā) on a Monday, the seventh lunar day on a Sunday,
and the fourth lunar day on a Tuesday yield fruit equal to that of the equinoxes (viṣuvat)."
*Amā* means *amāvāsyā*.
Śaṅkha also says:
"But *amāvāsyā* [is associated] with Soma, and the seventh [tithi] with Bhānu."
The fourth [lunar day] is presided over by the son of the Earth (Mars), and the eighth by the son of the Moon (Mercury).
The four lunar days (tithis) are equal to those [auspicious occasions] such as eclipses;
here, all acts such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation are said to be inexhaustible.
Maṅgala is the son of Bhūmi; Budha is the son of Soma. Now, regarding the supreme merit of conjunction with the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa:
"When the Śravaṇa asterism, which is destructive of Rākṣasas and belongs to Viṣṇu, occurs on the new moon day,
then a Śrāddha offered to the ancestors is said to be inexhaustible.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
When the new moon coincides with the conjunction of Maitra (Anurādhā), Viśākhā,
or Svāti, the assembly of ancestors then attains satisfaction for eight years at the śrāddha offering.
The constellation Anurādhā is friendly.
When the new moon occurs under Puṣya, Raudra (Ārdrā), or Punarvasu,
then the ancestors, when honored, attain satisfaction for twelve years.
The constellation Ārdrā is Raudra;
the constellations Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā) and Ajaikapād (Pūrvaphalgunī) are for those desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors;
and the new moon day under the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) is difficult even for the gods to attain.

The constellation Dhaniṣṭhā has Vāsava as its presiding deity; Ajaikapād is the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā; and Śatabhiṣā is the constellation of Varuṇa. Sometimes, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, [the moon] enters into conjunction with Varuṇa.
That supreme time of the ancestors is reached by the constellation Ṛkṣa;
indeed, O King, it is not attained by those of little merit.
O King, if at that time Dhaniṣṭhā should indeed be present,
then water and food offered to the ancestors bestows satisfaction upon them.
For ten thousand years by those humans born of that lineage.
At that time, in the month of Māgha— meaning on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight—
and if at that very time the *pūrvā-bhādrapadā* constellation is present, then whatever is performed for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) is [efficacious].
Having attained supreme satisfaction through the śrāddha,
those ancestors sleep for an entire yuga.
"In that very same [context], on that fifteenth day of Māgha"—this is the meaning.
Now follows the determination regarding the two types of new moon (amāvāsyā).
Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
The Śrāddha consisting of the Anvāhārya rice-ball is recommended when the moon has waned,
during the third part of the day, but not too close to the time of twilight.
In this regard, concerning the third part of the day divided into three portions, he himself states the answer to the inquiry as to when the waning of the moon occurs:
"On the eighth part of the fourteenth [lunar day], the moon becomes exhausted;
on the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā), it indeed becomes minute once again."

In this regard, those who know the movements of the planets describe it thus: through twelve thirty-degree portions of the zodiac signs, there occurs either conjunction or separation of the moon with the sun, and each constitutes a single lunar day (*tithi*). Consequently, the fourteenth day or the new moon day consists of twelve such portions. Therein, at the end of the eighth portion of the fourteenth day, the moon wanes; and at the end of the eighth portion of the new moon day, having become minute, it is born again. The word *kila* here indicates that this is indeed how it has been explained by the astronomers. The *Śatapatha-śruti* states this very point:

This very year is Prajāpati consisting of sixteen parts; its fifteen parts are the nights, while the sixteenth part is its constant element. By means of the nights alone, that [sixteenth] part is filled and does not diminish. On the night of the new moon, Soma enters into all these living beings by means of this sixteenth part; from there he is born again in the morning. Therefore, on this night, one should not deprive any living being of its life-breath, even a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity.

The intention here is as follows: Of this Prajāpati, who is of the nature of the moon consisting of sixteen digits (*kalā*), starting from the first day of the dark fortnight up to the fourteenth day, fourteen digits are gradually diminished by the loss of one digit each. On the third part of the fourteenth day, however, even the fifteenth digit is diminished. Then, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), having come to the world of earth (*bhūrloka*) with the sixteenth digit—which is fixed (*dhruvā*) and imperishable—he enters into all living beings. But on the third part of the new moon day, having ascended to heaven (*divam*) by means of that very sixteenth digit, he manifests once again. Kātyāyana himself states the time of the moon’s waning during the specific occasion of the new moon:
The new moon day of Āgrahāyaṇī, as well as that which occurs in the month of Jyeṣṭha—
those who know the movements of the moon declare that there is a special significance for this one.
In this case, the moon remains during the first watch with one-quarter of a digit remaining;
at the very end of that, it undergoes complete waning.
Thus say those who know the circle of luminaries.

The meaning of this is as follows: when the moon is situated in Taurus at the end of the new moon of Jyeṣṭha, and when it is in Scorpio at the end of the new moon of Agrahāyaṇa, these are the points of the moon’s maximum exaltation and depression; due to the resulting peculiarity of the moon's motion, that form which appears on other new-moon days in the eighth watch occurs on these two new-moon days in the very first watch. Furthermore, in order to refute those who believe that the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and other rites should be performed only when the moon is invisible—even though such invisibility may occur there—he shows that the moon can sometimes be invisible even on the third lunar day.
In that year in which there are thirteen months, the third [lunar day] is not seen after the [full moon];
having thus understood the course of the moon.
When that [day] has ended, one should give [the gift] in the afternoon.

[178] The meaning of this is as follows: In a year in which there is an intercalary month (*mala-māsa*), the moon is not visible on the second third-day following the intercalary month. However, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, which is prescribed based on the non-visibility of the moon, is not performed at that time. Therefore, having understood the movement of the moon, one should perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other rites in the afternoon of the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) when it is mixed with the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), even though the moon has waned. Consequently, the established rule is that the offering for the purpose of the *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* must be made even at the end of the fourteenth day. They introduce the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): This is not so; the offering at the end of the fourteenth day is not prescribed immediately after the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. For the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed for the afternoon of the new moon day, according to the statement of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*: "They perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the new moon day in the afternoon."
As for the view that the word "new moon" (amāvāsyā) is intended as an indicator for the day of fasting (aupavasathya):

That is not so; for there is no evidence for secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here, and such indication is improper in a prescriptive injunction (*vidhi*). As for the scriptural passage: "Therefore, on the previous day he performs [the rite] for the ancestors, and on the following day he sacrifices to the gods; thus the sacrificer ransoms the sacrifice from the ancestors and extends it," as well as the statement of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* concerning the adding of fuel to the fires: "In the afternoon they proceed with the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*"; these refer specifically to that case where the new moon occurs in the afternoon of the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*), and thus cannot serve as evidence for a figurative indication referring merely to the preceding day.

Others, however, raise the following prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Even on an *amāvāsyā* (new moon) day occurring within the period marked by the rising of the moon, the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* (the monthly ancestral rite) should not be performed. This is because it is prescribed to follow immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. And the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed for an *amāvāsyā* during which the moon is not visible. Thus says the Śruti: "When this [moon] is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he gives to these [ancestors]. And there is the statement of the Sūtra-author: "On that day when they do not see the moon, on that day perform the *pitṛyajña*. Here, "non-visibility" does not intend to indicate the waning [of the moon], because the rule "when the night has waned" applies even when there is non-visibility. Furthermore, the sequence is not intended to be significant, as there is no authoritative evidence for it.
