Now, if it is thought: "When both [rites] occur on one day, then this sequence applies, and not otherwise; and when the non-appearance of the moon occurs on the very day of the *aupavasathya*, then both occur on one day; otherwise, one performs the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* with reference to the day of sacrifice (*yajanīyadina*)," that is not correct. Because, by the principle of the postponement of the first, there is also a postponement of the *anvāhāryaka*. As for the statement of Laugākṣi:
"Sinīvālī should be used by twice-born men who maintain the sacred fires in rites for the ancestors;
Kuhū should be used by women, Śūdras, and likewise by twice-born men who do not maintain sacred fires. Thus it is said.

Let that [rule] pertain to the domain of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*, and other ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*). To this it is said: "On the fourteenth day, there is no extinguishing [of the fire].
That is incorrect; for Kātyāyana, having introduced the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, says:
"Even though it is seen as stated [elsewhere], that is with reference to the fourteenth day."

"One should wait for the new moon (amāvāsyā), or one may perform the offering at its very end. As for the statement in the Śruti that "one should perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña even while the moon is visible," that is intended to refer to the fourteenth day (caturdaśī). Therefore, the meaning is: "One should wait for the new moon; one should offer these [oblations] precisely at the end of the fourteenth day. By this, it is demonstrated that on the day the moon is visible, the Pitṛyajña is indeed supported by Śruti. And the same author states that the scriptural mention of "non-visibility" is an indicator of the waning [of the moon]: "On whichever day the moon does not come into view..."

"That should be understood with reference to the waning [of the moon], and also when the king has perished. Furthermore, as for the other point raised in the prima facie argument—that even on an *amāvāsya* occurring within a day marked by the rising of the moon, there is no *piṇḍapitṛyajña* or *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*—that too has already been refuted by the statement of Kātyāyana beginning with "even while it is visible," and it has also been refuted by this statement of Gobhila and by Hārīta.

"In that [lunar day] during which the moon, having reached the twilight, appears like a lotus stalk, its waning occurs in the afternoon; the performance of the *piṇḍas* is certain. This instruction intends not to bypass the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Again, Kātyāyana says:
"When the fourteenth day should fill the fourth watch..."
"The new moon (amāvāsyā) is desired for the śrāddha at the very moment it is waning."

Furthermore: since the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and Śrāddha are prescribed for the day preceding the day of sacrifice (yajanīyadina), it is said, "Therefore, [the rite] is performed for the ancestors on the previous day. And when the new moon (amāvāsyā) concludes in the forenoon or at midday on the first lunar day (pratipad), then the sacrifice takes place on that very day; thus, the Piṇḍapitṛyajña and so forth are performed on the Sinīvālī [tithi], which possesses the rising of the moon. This is because there is no evidence that the rule, "The Pitṛkarma should be performed by twice-born men who maintain the sacred fires on the Sinīvālī," refers to anything other than the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka rite. Thus, it is established that when there is a conflict between the two types of Amāvāsyā, the Śrāddha is performed on the Sinīvālī. An exception to this has been stated by Baudhāyana:
"That [lunar day] upon which the fourteenth day continues after midday is to be known as Sinīvālī; it is fruitless for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
Thus spoke Bṛhaspati.
If the new moon begins after midday, it should be known as being pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta); it would not then be the fifteenth day.
And therefore:
those who perform śrāddha rites on an amāvāsyā that is pierced by a lunar day (bhūta), whether out of delusion or even through ignorance, their lifespan is diminished.

[181] This statement of Kārṣṇājini is to be explained as referring exclusively to the *sinīvālī* that is pierced by the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī-viddhā*) and has entered the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). With this intention, Vṛddha-Manu said:
"The ancestors attend upon that lunar day on which the sun sets;
for the Self-born One himself assigned the afternoon to them."
By this it is stated that if *sinīvālī* extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), then she alone is to be accepted; otherwise, however, *kuhū* alone is to be accepted. Thus says Hārīta:
"The afternoon belongs to the ancestors; therefore, for ancestral rites, that [lunar day] which follows into the afternoon is to be accepted, and not the preceding one which follows into it."

Thus, when it is established that *sinīvālī*— which extends into the afternoon— is to be accepted for ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), and since it is likewise established that the *sinīvālī* extending into the forenoon must necessarily be accepted when it also covers the afternoon, Baudhāyana speaks in order to demonstrate its status as the most meritorious:
"If even a single *ghaṭikā* of the new moon extends into the forenoon,
it should always be treated as being overlapped by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*) for ancestral rites."
Jābāla expresses this same point by way of another formulation:
"Even among the *pratipad* days, if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) extends into the preceding [day],
it must always be observed as being pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*) for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*)."

The meaning is that if [the new moon] begins on the afternoon of the previous day and is completed on the very morning of the following day, then it must be observed as *sinīvālī*. As for the statement of Hārīta:
"In the zodiac signs of Libra, Capricorn, Pisces, Virgo, and Gemini, the new moon that is pierced by the fourteenth day (bhūta) should be diligently honored."

[182] Some consider this to concern the subject of vows, fasts, and the like. Now, since there are passages seen that—by means of abandoning the aforementioned *sinīvālī*—are intent upon the adoption of *kuhū*, certain authors of compendiums have recorded a statement under the name of Hārīta:
"If the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs in the forenoon, and if it should persist into the afternoon..."
"Those who know the śrāddha rites understand that the śrāddha must also be performed on the day following [the new moon]. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, Hariharācārya stated: "The root source of this statement is unknown, and its composition contains mutually contradictory terms. To explain: the phrase "if [it occurs] in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇe cet*) refers to the day of the *pratipad* (the first lunar day). Now, the "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) is either the third part of the day or its first half. This being the case, it is untenable to claim that [the rite] would by no means occur at any point in the afternoon, for on the day of the *pratipad*, the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) necessarily remains connected to the afternoon as well—since there is no decrease in the duration of the lunar day (*tithi*) of more than six *ghaṭikās*. If, on the other hand, it were said that [the rite] must not occur specifically in the afternoon of the *pratipad* day, then the phrase "if in the forenoon" would be redundant. Alternatively, if one accepts the primary meaning of the word "forenoon" and conceives of some non-contradictory sense, then that has already been conceived in the *Smṛtimahārṇava*.

For instance: when there is an increase in the lunar day (*tithi-vṛddhi*), the *śrāddha* on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) conjoined with the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) has been prescribed; and that has been ordained by Manu immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, according to the passage beginning "having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors" (*pitṛyajñaṃ nirvartya*). Furthermore, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is explicitly prescribed by the Śruti for the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) and cannot be performed otherwise. Since that [lunar day] lasts for only one period of time, if the entire afternoon is occupied by that [sacrifice], what would be the status of the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha*? To this it is said: "in the forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇe*), meaning not in the entirety of the afternoon. In that case, the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* must also be performed on the *pratipad*. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* says:

"In that case where, because the moon is not visible on the previous day, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* is postponed, [the rule applies] on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) for the purpose of performing the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. However, this interpretation is rejected as being both obscure in meaning and weak. Now, Hariharā has also cited other passages concerning the occurrence of the new moon (*kuhū*), which were stated by certain authors claiming they were written in the *Mahārṇava* but whose authorship was unknown. He presents them as follows: "When the new moon occurs at the time of dawn..."
That time should be known as supreme; what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.

If the new moon occurs for even one *ghaṭikā* on the first day (*pratipad*), then that [first day] should be observed as the new moon for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, provided it is not pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*).

"Even if the new moon (amāvāsyā) should occur for even a single muhūrta on the first lunar day (pratipad), that should be known as the most excellent; the remainder of the lunar festival (parvaśeṣa) is treated like the festival itself.

Here, the phrase "at the time of dawn" (*aruṇodayavelāyām*), being a general application, is incapable of overriding a specific mention; therefore, it applies to a particular type of *śrāddha*. Let this [rule] apply to rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Similarly, the other rule—"even if the new moon should occur for even a single muhūrta"—pertains to gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others. Or else, [it may be interpreted differently].
The *pūrvā* and *darśā* [new moon] sacrifices, even if lasting only three muhūrtas, should be performed by the Bahvṛcas;
the *kuhū* sacrifice should be performed by the Adhvaryus, and according to their preference by the Sāmagāyins.
Let the established rule follow these words.
Now, [there are others] which concern the selection of either the preceding or following new moon day based on the pervasion of the *kutapa* period. Regarding this, Hārīta says:

"Even if the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is pierced by [the previous lunar day] or mixed with the first day of the next fortnight (*pratipad*), it should be accepted by the learned for rites pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya-karman*) when it occurs during the *kutapa* period. Thus it is said; and also in another *smṛti*:

"Whichever lunar day (tithi) extends through midday—whether it be the preceding or the following one—one should perform the ritual on that day; neither its decrease nor its increase is a cause for concern.
Thus said Pracetas.
Sinīvālī and Kuhū are indeed mentioned in the Śruti regarding the rite of Śrāddha;
if they do not exist at midday, how then could the Śrāddha and other rites be performed?
"Sinīvālī is considered to occur when the lunar day (tithi) diminishes, and Kuhū when it increases;
those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas should understand that Sāmnvati is also Kuhū.
In this context, Kutapa and Aparāhṇa are prescribed as constituent parts of the Śrāddha rite.

In this regard, those who prioritize the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)—for instance, when the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka*, and so forth are specifically prescribed for the afternoon—they should perform the *śrāddha* on either the *sinīvālī* or the *kuhū* lunar day, having given precedence to the pervasion of the afternoon. However, those who prioritize the *kutapa* period, such as those who do not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*), and for whom the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the *āmaśrāddha*, and so forth are specifically prescribed during the *kutapa*—they should perform the *śrāddha* on either the preceding or the following new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), having given precedence to the pervasion of the *kutapa*. In that case, the conjunction of the prescribed times is obtained. And thus says the *Smṛti*:

"The lunar day (*tithi*) that extends through the time appropriate for a particular rite—by means of that [day] one should perform the rites; decrease or increase [of the lunar day] is not a cause [for concern].

Regarding this, whatever other prohibitions of *sinīvālī* exist should be explained—where possible—as referring to cases of the increase of a lunar day, to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagnika*), to cases where there is no pervasion of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), to matters concerning gifts and the like, as exceptions (*apavāda*), as restrictive supplements (*upasaṃhāra*), or according to the divisions of the *Kalpasūtras*. The rules concerning *kuhū* are likewise [to be understood]; however, one should not hastily accept an option (*vikalpa*) based on something being both enjoined and prohibited.
Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts, both are traditionally held to be dharma;
however, when there is a conflict between two Smṛti texts, their respective scopes must be distinguished.
Thus concludes the determination of the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Now, the eightfold offerings (aṣṭakā).

By the word *aṣṭakā*, the eighth days of the dark fortnights (*aparapakṣa*) of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa are meant; for the Smṛti of Śaunaka states: "The *aṣṭakās* are on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. According to the view of some, there are only three *aṣṭakās* and three *anvaṣṭakās*. Thus says Viṣṇu: "The new moon days (*amāvāsyā*), the three *aṣṭakās*, and the three *anvaṣṭakās*. They are called *anvaṣṭakās* because they occur after (*anu*) the *aṣṭakās*; that is, the ninth days following the *aṣṭakās*. As stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa: [text follows].
"The new moon day, the three Aṣṭakās in the months beginning with Pauṣa,
the three Anvaṣṭakās, and likewise the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha— these are meritorious," so it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
"When the month of Agrahāyaṇa has passed, there are likewise three black Aṣṭakās.

Now, although this Aṣṭakā is distinct from the four previously mentioned Aṣṭakās, it occurs during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada; its origin and praise are stated here, preceded by a historical narrative (*itihāsa*). In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Those known as the Agniṣvāttas are performers of sacrifice, established in the sacrificial rites."
Among them, however, the daughter born of their mind is considered to be named Acchodā.
Then, seeing that father named Amāvasu, she,
desiring a boon and tormented by the god of the flowery arrows, chose him as her consort along with his wife.
But then, having fallen from yoga due to that transgression, the beautiful woman no longer touched the earth and fell down upon the surface of the ground.
[186] With her face cast down toward the Acchoda lake, dejected and ashamed due to the depletion of her ascetic power,
she prayed to the ancestors for the restoration of her own prosperity.
While she was lamenting, her ancestors spoke thus to that ascetic woman:
"The illustrious ones spoke these words with gracious voices:
'In the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you shall indeed be born from the womb of a fish.'"
Known by the name Satyavatī, she was the auspicious mother of Vyāsa.
"Due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall obtain a miserable lineage;
therefore, you will inevitably become the daughter of King Vasu."
Furthermore, on the eighth day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, you shall exist in the world of the ancestors,
constantly bestowing long life and health, and granting the fruits of all desires.
In the Brahmavaivarta and Vāyu Purāṇas:
"Now I shall explain Time, which is honored in the rite of Śrāddha by those who perform the rites of optional, occasional, and perpetual Śrāddha."
The three Aṣṭakās, which bestow sons and are the root of dharma, are indeed distinguished;
among them, the first, occurring in the dark fortnight, is declared to belong to Indra.
The second [offering] should be dedicated to Prajāpati, and the third to the Viśvedevas;
the first should always be performed with cakes, while the other should then consist of meat.
The third [lunar day] should be observed with potherbs; this is the rule regarding the materials. Furthermore, the Aṣṭakā rite for the ancestors is indeed ordained as a constant obligation.
Or whatever other fourth [lunar day] there may be, one should perform it especially;
on those days, a wise man should always perform the śrāddha, even at the cost of his entire wealth.
In both the next world and this one, he shall always be happy;
for those who worship, there is constant excellence, while for the nihilists, there is a downward fall.
The ancestors at all times, and the deities at the time of the lunar days—
both come to a man like cows to a watering trough.
If those [ancestors] should depart from one who has not honored them with the Aṣṭakā rites,
his world shall be in vain and what he has acquired shall perish. The gods go to the world of the givers, while those who do not give go to the state of animals.

In this context, the fourth [Aṣṭakā] is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, because of the traditional teaching of Śaunaka: "The Aṣṭakā-Aṣṭamīs are the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. If one adopts the view that there are three Aṣṭakās beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, then the fourth is shown in the Padma Purāṇa—following its historical narrative—as being proximate to the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. Furthermore, in the Brahmapurāṇa, when defining the presiding deities and the materials for the libations to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa) for the four Aṣṭakās in sequence, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is specifically included.
On the first day, dedicated to Indra, one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables;
on the second day, dedicated to Prajāpati, one should satisfy them with pure meats.
"On the third lunar day dedicated to Viśvedevas, one should offer cakes in due order during the rains; and on the fourth day, one should always offer vegetables in the middle [of the rainy season]."

[188] Here, the words *śāka* (vegetables), *māṃsa* (meat), and *apūpa* (cakes) in the context of the *śrāddha* are intended to demonstrate that all food prescribed for the rite has each of those specific substances as its primary component; they do not, however, intend the exclusion of other substances. For it is considered logical to interpret an injunction in such a way that it does not subvert another injunction, much less so when it would subvert many other injunctions and remain consistent with what is observed in experience. Indeed, it is observed that food in which vegetables are the primary component is satiating, whereas vegetables alone are not. Vasiṣṭha says:
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Agrahāyaṇa, as well as during the Aṣṭakā festivals.
Furthermore, the Śrāddha is indeed mandatory even on the Anvaṣṭakā days. As Pitāmaha has said:
"On the new moon day, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day, and on the Aṣṭakā days..."

"A learned man who does not perform the *śrāddha* falls into hell. Furthermore, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, it is stated that for one who does not perform the *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*, there is the attainment of an undesirable state in the form of rebirth as an animal, as expressed by the words: "Those who do not give go to the state of animals. Viṣṇu, having enumerated the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following the months of Māgha and Prauṣṭhapada, and the times of the ripening of rice and barley, has said:
"Prajāpati declares these times of *śrāddha* to be obligatory (*nitya*)."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of kings, the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is always a time for the *śrāddha*;
likewise, O supreme monarch, the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the month of Māgha, and the month of Śrāvaṇa."
When the month of Proṣṭhapada has passed, as well as the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight;
when the month of Āgrahāyaṇa has passed, likewise the three dark Aṣṭakā days.
The first [offering] should be made with vegetables, the next immediately after with meats,
and the third likewise always with cakes by one who possesses knowledge.
"Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for the *śrāddha*.
One who does not perform the *śrāddha* on these occasions falls into hell. Thus says Devala.
"This *Śrāddha-kalpa* of Manu has been proclaimed by Manu as the *Mānava*.
However, the *Aṣṭakā* should consist of many *piṇḍas*, but the *Aṣṭakā* itself does not consist of a single *piṇḍa*.

In this context, the terms "many *piṇḍas*" (*bahupiṇḍa*) and "single *piṇḍa*" (*ekapiṇḍa*) in the *Brahmapurāṇa* refer respectively to the injunction for the *Pārvaṇa* rite and the prohibition of the *Ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
"The Śrāddha must indeed be performed during the eight winter *aṣṭakās*;
it is prescribed that during the subsequent *anvaṣṭakās*, it should be done in sequence, beginning with the mother.
Regarding this, there is a Smṛti:

"On the Anvaṣṭakā days, on the occasion of a Vṛddhi-śrāddha, and likewise annually, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; on other occasions, it is performed together with the husband. Thus says the Śaṅkhasmṛti.
"Likewise, the Anvaṣṭakā rite and the Śrāddha for the mother on the anniversary of her death—apart from these Ekoddiṣṭa rites, there shall be no separate [Śrāddha] for women. Thus it is said.
In this *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the procedure for the sacrificial pits (*karṣū*) is prescribed for the *mātṛśrāddha*.
Likewise, the *śrāddha* for women should be performed on the *anvaṣṭakā* days;
having offered oblations according to the *aṣṭakā* rite, one should perform these five in sequence.
O King, the śrāddha should be performed according to the prescribed rules for one's mother and paternal grandmother;
likewise, it should be performed for the paternal great-grandmother, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
[190] O King, the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be performed for him just as for one's own father;
listen now to me regarding what should be done there once the Brahmins have finished eating.
O King of kings, they should be one span in length and four finger-breadths wide;
they should be raised to that same height, and one should have six furrows made therein.
Having strewn sacrificial grass around the fire at the base of each pit, one should offer oblations.
Having performed the sacrifice to Agni, Soma, and Yama as before,
one should cause three trenches to be made at the base for the persons.
The offering to the ancestors is performed as before, according to the rules for each individual;
there, one should fill three trenches with milk-rice.
The offering for women should take place at the base of the three furrows;
and the filling of those furrows should be done with curd, meat, and milk.
O bull among men, it should be performed with food mixed with water;
one should not omit saying, "May this be inexhaustible for you."
Thus concludes the determination of the *aṣṭakās*. Now, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
"Vṛddhi" (increase) refers to a time characterized by occasions such as the birth of a son. And so says Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
"The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is prescribed for occasions such as the birth of a son and marriages," thus it is said. Jābāli states:
"At sacrifices, weddings, consecrations, and at the binding and unbinding of the girdle..."
[191] "Upon the birth of a son and at the rite of releasing a bull, one should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The entire series of rites for one who has been born, beginning with the *jātakarman*, [should be performed]."
A father should perform for his son a Śrāddha ceremony characterized by prosperity (Abhyudayika).

Kātyāyana says: "In the rites of sacramental purification for his sons, the father should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to his own ancestors until the son's marriage; but in his absence, [the rite should be performed] according to their order."
In this context, the *saṃskāras* are:

conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), birth rites (*jātakarma*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first outing (*niṣkramaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), the observance of vows (*vratacaryā*), study (*adhyayana*), the return home (*samāvartana*), marriage (*vivāha*), sacrifice (*yajña*), giving (*dāna*), and so forth. Among these, regarding the *saṃskāras* pertaining to the son, the father shall give [the offerings] to his own ancestors; regarding the remaining *saṃskāras*, he himself is the one entitled [to perform them]. This has already been explained in detail in the determination of entitlement (*adhikāra-nirūpaṇa*). [As stated] in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
At the marriages of daughters and sons, at the entry into a new house,
at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony and other such rites;
During the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
a self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha group of ancestors.
"Upon seeing the face of a son and so forth" means at the birth of a son; as stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Now, in rites pertaining to prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), and in those that are auspicious and most beautiful..."
At birth, at the initiation ceremony, at marriage, and for a son, [one should perform these rites].
One should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed rule. Vasiṣṭha says:
On the previous day one should perform the Śrāddha for the maternal ancestors, and likewise on the day of the rite, that for the paternal ancestors.
On the following day, however, one should perform the rite for the group of maternal grandfathers.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one is unable [to perform them] on separate days, one should perform the three Śrāddhas and the Tantric Vaiśvadeva on the preceding day."
Śātātapa states that even when performed on a single day, the rites must be carried out according to their respective times:
"The Śrāddha for the mothers is in the forenoon, and that for the paternal ancestors is in the afternoon;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—these three Śrāddhas are prescribed for a Vṛddhi ceremony."
Regarding the impossibility of such a distinction in time, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"In the absence of different times for the three Nāndī-śrāddhas,
a wise man should perform them on the preceding day during the forenoon, beginning with the rite for the Mothers."

In the Baudhāyana-sūtra: "One who is about to perform Vedic rites should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas on the very day before; these are said to be the Nāndīmukhas. They do not perform the ancestral (pitrya) and divine (daiva) rites on the same day. For him who performs the ancestral and divine rites on the same day, his offspring become short-lived. Therefore, he performs [the ancestral rite] for the ancestors on the day before; having thus redeemed the sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer proceeds with it. A Brāhmaṇa passage has also been cited previously regarding this.

Since the word *vṛddhi* in the statement of Yājñavalkya—which serves as a general indicator for all times for *śrāddha*—is intended to imply the entire range of times for *nāndīmukha-śrāddha*, the times for *śrāddha* that are ancillary to ritual acts (*karmāṅga-śrāddha*) are also included.
Therefore, Pāraskara says:
"At the time of conception (*niṣeka*), at the *soma* sacrifice, and likewise at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*)."
The Śrāddha performed during the Puṃsavana rite should be understood as a subsidiary part of that ritual, just like the one performed at birth.

The period of impregnation (*niṣekakāla*) consists of sixteen nights, which is the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*) of the wife. During that time, when conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion (*puṇyanakṣatra*), the *śrāddha* that is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the rite called "impregnation" (*garbhādhāna*) should be performed. Here, the word "Soma" is intended as an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*) for rites such as the *agnihotra*. Thus concludes the definition of the *vṛddhiśrāddha*. Now follows the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

Regarding this, Kātyāyana states in the Vājasaneyi-sūtra: "One should perform the śrāddha in the latter fortnight, either on the day after the fourth [tithi], or on whichever day the necessary means for the śrāddha may be available. This means that in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), from the first day (pratipat) until the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should perform the śrāddha on the day following the fourth tithi, or on whichever day the materials for the śrāddha are obtained. Gautama also says:

One should offer to the ancestors on the new moon day, or from the fifth day onwards of the dark fortnight according to one's faith, or whenever all the necessary materials, a suitable location, and Brahmins are available; the restriction regarding time is according to one's capacity.

One view is that the *śrāddha* is performed on a single day during the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). Another view is that it should be performed every day. A third view is that there is a restriction regarding time according to one's capacity; this means the arrangement of the time depends upon one’s ability. In this context, the *śrāddha* is obligatory (*nitya*). Thus says Kātyāyana: “One should not let the dark fortnight pass by even if one has only vegetables. As for the statements in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and other texts—such as “The first lunar day (*pratipad*) is for the acquisition of wealth, the second for the attainment of cattle,” and so forth—which describe specific rewards associated with each individual lunar day within the dark fortnight, these do not undermine the obligatory nature of the *śrāddha* in the dark fortnight. This is because both obligatory and optional (desirable) aspects can coexist, just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. Even when this [dark-fortnight *śrāddha*] is performed on a single day, it must still be performed separately from the *amāvāsyā* (new-moon) *śrāddha*. This is because in Yājñavalkya’s statement, “The new moon, the *aṣṭakās*, the *vṛddhi* [rites], and the dark fortnight...,” the dark fortnight is mentioned separately from the new moon.

By this, that which has been stated by some here—that the *mahāparapākṣika* śrāddha is optional (*vikalpate*) with the new-moon (*amāvāsyā*) and other śrāddhas—is refuted. As for the traditional legal text (*nigama-smaraṇa*), "On whichever day of the dark fortnight it may fall, [one should perform it], especially on the new moon," the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* maintains that since this is not in conflict with either the view of separate performance or the view of non-separate performance, it is not an authority for an option (*vikalpa*). Some, however, hold that there is indeed an option.

Āpastamba says: "The rite should be performed month by month; the afternoon of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa) is better, as are the later days of that dark fortnight. By "later days," he means the tenth day and those following. This is not intended to declare the earlier days, such as the ninth and so on, to be inferior; rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the subsequent days are superior to the preceding ones. Regarding this, Manu, excluding the fourteenth day, says: "In the dark fortnight, the lunar days beginning with the tenth—excluding the fourteenth—are recommended for the Śrāddha, but other days are not like them."

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states that the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) is not to be avoided absolutely, but rather only in the case of a *śrāddha* intended for deities other than those slain by weapons:
"On the days beginning with the first (pratipad), having avoided one— the fourteenth— on that [fourteenth],
offerings are indeed given for those who were killed by weapons."
It will be stated that the mention of "taking up weapons" is intended as an illustration for certain other causes of death as well.
Now follows the second fortnight of Bhādrapada.

In this regard, although the Bhādrapada dark fortnight is indeed included among the twelve dark fortnights by general statements such as, "One should perform the *śrāddha* during the dark fortnight; one should not let the dark fortnight pass even if it be only with vegetables," nevertheless, it is specifically mentioned in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts for the purpose of establishing its status as most meritorious and for establishing the sin incurred by its neglect. As it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O King, the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is superior to the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*)."
During the four months of the sun's southern course, while Keśava is asleep there, [one should avoid meat].

O King, the dark fortnight following the full moon of Prauṣṭhapadī is especially auspicious; within that, the period after the fifth day is better, and even after the tenth it is superior. Furthermore, the thirteenth day joined with the Maghā constellation is highly recommended.

The southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is superior to the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*) for the performance of *śrāddha*. Even among all the days of the southern transit, the four months beginning from the full moon of Āṣāḍha—the period during which Upendra sleeps—are superior. Superior even to all of those is the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) of the month of Proṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada). Within that, the ten days following the fifth day are superior; within those, the five days following the tenth day are superior. Furthermore, according to the *Brahmapurāṇa*, the thirteenth day conjoined with the *Maghā* asterism is preeminent.
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Aśvayuj, the *śrāddha* should be performed day after day."
Or for a fortnight less one-third, or indeed for half a fortnight.
Especially with śyāmāka grains, which are well known as being dear to the ancestors.

[196] Regarding this, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* that "the *śrāddha* is performed during the dark fortnight associated with the month of Prauṣṭhapada," whereas in the *Brahmapurāṇa* it is said to be "associated with the month of Āśvayuj. This discrepancy between the two is resolved as follows: In this matter, the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātyāḥ*) conceive of the lunar month as beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, taking the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) that gives its name to the month as its central point, and ending with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). The Northerners (*auttarāḥ*), however, begin on the first day of the dark fortnight and end with the full moon that gives its name to the month. This being the case, according to Southern usage, when the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada occurs and the preceding dark fortnight (starting from the new moon of Prauṣṭhapada) has concluded, the subsequent fortnight is designated as "Prauṣṭhapadya. According to Northern usage, however, when that same full moon marks the conclusion of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the subsequent fortnight falls within the month of Āśvayuj. Thus, by means of these two distinct usages, a single period receives two different designations.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: During the rainy season, Yama releases the ancestors from his abode back into the world of men, leaving his own city empty.
Afflicted by hunger and proclaiming their own misdeeds committed by themselves,
they long for milk-rice mixed with honey for their sons and grandsons.
Therefore, one should satisfy them there according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice mixed with honey,
clarified butter, and sesame seeds, as well as with cool water.
The man who obtains from another's house food only the size of a mouthful,
or who sustains his own life by means of mere alms;
"Or whoever should maintain their body by selling themselves every day—even such a person must perform the *śrāddha* with well-collected substances including sesame oil. Thus [ends the citation].
This is the speech of Brahmā to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
In the fifth fortnight of Āṣāḍha, when the sun is situated in Virgo,
whatever man performs a śrāddha even on a single day,
his ancestors will certainly remain satisfied for the duration of an entire year.
Śāṭyāyani also said:
"The sixteen lunar days that occur in the latter fortnight of Nabhasya, if they coincide with the sun's passage through Virgo, that time is [prescribed] for the rite of Śrāddha."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, it is said: "The ancestors—
whether divine, terrestrial, or celestial, and whether stationary or moving—
all desire the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo."
The god Nārāyaṇa has declared that those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo are equal to sacrificial rites.
He who desires the fruit that is difficult to obtain through the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices should worship the ancestors with water, vegetables, roots, and grain when the sun is in Virgo.

Although only one month occurs when the sun has entered Virgo, nevertheless, because the latter fortnight alone belongs to the ancestors (paitrya) and in accordance with other scriptural statements, it should be understood that the *śrāddha* is to be performed precisely during that [latter fortnight].
As stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "Those sixteen days while the sun has entered Virgo..."
"These are equal to sacrifices; what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible. Thus [it is said].

In this context, although in many scriptural statements it is said that the fortnight (*pakṣa*) itself constitutes the time for the *śrāddha*, and a fortnight consists of exactly fifteen lunar days (*tithi*), nevertheless, due to the occasional increase of a lunar day (*tithivṛddhi*), it may consist of sixteen days. With the intention that there should be no loss of even a single day in that case, it is stated here that "the sixteen lunar days" (*tithiṣoḍaśaka*). This is either to include the first day (*pratipad*) following the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), or the preceding full moon (*pūrṇamāsī*), for it will be taught that the *śrāddha* for the *nāndīmukha* ancestors is performed on that [full moon]. It should be understood that if the sun enters Virgo (*kanyāsaṃkrama*) on any day whatsoever within this fortnight, all sixteen days beginning with the *pratipad* are to be accepted; they are not to be rejected as being prior to the transit (*saṃkramaṇa*). For this very reason, Bṛhan-Manu says:
Whether in the middle or even at the end, whichever fortnight the sun enters [the sign], that entire fortnight is to be honored; therein the Śrāddha is prescribed.

In this context, the mention of the Sun being in Virgo is for the purpose of establishing its superior merit, and not for the purpose of abandoning the rite when that position is absent. Thus it is said in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"Even on other lunar fortnights, the Śrāddha is praised when the Sun is in Virgo;
however, one should perform it especially so when [the Moon] is in the fifth [lunar mansion] while the Sun is in Virgo."
Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍhā as the limit, whichever month may be the fifth fortnight thereafter,
one should perform the Śrāddha there, whether or not the sun enters Virgo.
Kārṣṇājini says:
By offering a śrāddha on the fifth [lunar day], one obtains sons, long life, health, and incomparable sovereignty, as well as abundant fulfillment of all desires.

Thus, it has been stated that by performing [the rites] during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, one attains distinguished desired results. However, regarding the failure to perform them during that time, Kārṣṇājini speaks of the attainment of undesirable results: "The deceased indeed harm him who would neglect the fifth [day]."
Therefore, a wise man should not transgress the paternal rule regarding the fifth generation.

[199] In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "He who does not perform the *śrāddha* rite during the fifth fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha— even if he is poor and offers only vegetables— shall fall into the state of an outcaste."
One should never share a seat, a bed, food, touch, or conversation with him, nor should one ever offer him sacrificial oblations (havya) or ancestral offerings (kavya).

"Those men who will not perform the śrāddha rite will undoubtedly become most sinful; they shall be deprived of progeny, and never at any time shall there be happiness, wealth, or grain for them. Thus it is said.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "If a householder does not perform the *śrāddha* when the Sun has entered Virgo, how can he have wealth or sons? He is tormented by the sighs of his ancestors."
If a person, thinking in his mind that ancestors do not exist,
does not perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there, they drink his blood.

Now, if by some circumstance the fortnight passes without a *śrāddha* having been performed, the *Yamasmṛti* prescribes that the *śrāddha* occasioned by that [transgression] must be performed on the subsequent days, within a specific limit:
"When the sun is in Virgo (*kanyā*), one dwelling at home should offer a *śrāddha* even with vegetables during the interval between the two fifth [lunar days] of both fortnights."

The *haṃsa* is the Sun. "Between the two fifth days of both fortnights" means the intervening period after the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and before the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina; this is the meaning. By this, the performance of *śrāddha* until the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina is permitted.
As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"And as long as the Sun remains in Virgo and Libra respectively..."
At that time, it would be the proper hour for one who possesses faith; otherwise, the city of the pretas would remain empty.
Likewise: "When the sun has entered Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons;
all the cities of the departed remain empty until the appearance of Scorpio."
Then, having been stung by scorpions and rendered hopeless, the ancestors departed;
yet, after pronouncing a most terrible curse, they returned once more to their abode.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "If a man does not offer the *śrāddha* to his ancestors on the day of the moon's waning,
his ancestors remain in distress, overwhelmed by hunger and thirst."
Filled with the desire for their teacher, they await the fortnight of the hungry ghosts,
just as tireless farmers await the rain-cloud day after day.
Even when the fortnight of the ancestors has passed, as long as the sun remains in Virgo,
the ancestors indeed desire the śrāddha offered by their sons.
Furthermore, O King, some desire that even when the sun has entered Libra,
the Śrāddha offered by those born of their own lineage may reach them, as they are tormented by hunger and thirst.
When that period has also passed and the sun has entered Scorpio,
the ancestors, devoid of hope and dejected, then depart for their own abode.
For two months, the ancestors of men wait at the door of their house, having become like the wind, afflicted by thirst and emaciated by hunger.
[201] "O Lord of the Earth, as long as the sun is situated in Virgo and remains in Libra," Sumantu said,
"as long as the sun of great splendor remains in the zodiac sign of Virgo."
From that time onwards, however, [the tax] should indeed be paid until the arrival of the scorpion.
O King, on this fifteenth day known on earth as Dīpānvitā,
if one does not give [offerings] to the ancestors during the Mahālaya, it is as if nothing has been given at all.
In this context, the *mahālaya* refers to the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) of the month of Bhādrapada.
As for that which was stated by Jātūkarṇya:
"The ancestors, residing in the fifth fortnight, long [for offerings]."
"Therefore, it should be given in that very [place]; given elsewhere, it is fruitless.
This statement is intended to indicate the loss of an excellence of fruit, not to establish the total absence of fruit altogether.
Now, the Śrāddha on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī) is explained here in detail.
In the *Manusmṛti*: "Whatever one may offer mixed with honey on the thirteenth lunar day,
that too becomes truly inexhaustible during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."
Yama says:
Those who know the past recite the verses sung by the ancestors:
"May there be born in our own lineage one who would offer [us] on the thirteenth day."
And one should offer milk-rice with honey and clarified butter during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism.
Now, there are two verses sung by the ancestors:
"Viṣṇu, will there be born in our lineage some supreme among men?"
[202] During the rainy season, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, being composed in mind, one should practice.
Whoever should perform a *śrāddha* with honey and rice-pudding (*pāyasa*) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or even under the shade of a banyan tree or an elephant, [attains great merit].

Paiṭhīnasi also said: "Whether it be a son or a grandson, whoever shall give [a cow] made of all metals with a goat during the rainy season and under the Maghā constellation on the thirteenth lunar day [to us]."
"Would there be born among us some righteous one who would increase the lineage?
[As stated] in the Mahābhārata:
'Might there be born in our own family one who would offer [the pinda] to us on the thirteenth day?'"
Under the Maghā asterism, facing south, one should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
praise the son who has been born, just as birds praise the fig tree."
"With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, or milk-rice,
he will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."
Yājñavalkya says: He who gives while staying at Gayā attains everything infinite;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the rainy season, and especially under the Maghā asterism.
When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, having reached the thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā asterism,
one should indeed perform a śrāddha with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).
[203] And this lunar day is more highly esteemed even than the other lunar days of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. Thus it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Or whoever would increase his body by selling himself every day, he too must perform a *śrāddha* with those various well-accumulated materials."
One should strive diligently on the thirteenth lunar day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā constellation.
There is no time superior to this for performing śrāddha rites;
whatever is given here, the ancestors accept it, and it is remembered as inexhaustible.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"O King, the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana) is superior to the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa);
even within that, the Cāturmāsya period is more excellent when Keśava is asleep."

The dark fortnight following the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada) is especially auspicious; within that, the first five days are superior, and the first ten are even better than those. Furthermore, O King, the thirteenth day conjoined with the Maghā nakṣatra is highly recommended.

In this context, "five ancestors" means starting from the fifth ancestor, and "ten ancestors" means starting from the tenth; such is the meaning. Furthermore, this *śrāddha* is declared to be mandatory in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O best of kings, the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is always a time for *śrāddha*;
likewise, O supreme king, the full moon days of Māgha and Śrāvaṇa."
When the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada has passed, as well as the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight,
and likewise the three Aṣṭakās and Anvaṣṭakās, O best of kings—
Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for the Śrāddha.
"One who performs a *śrāddha* on these [days] falls into hell.

Thus [it is said]. Viṣṇu also, having set forth: "The new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the full moon day of Māgha, the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [the latter]," stated this very verse [beginning with] "These are the times for *śrāddha*. Now, here are the prohibitory statements. Jyotirbṛhaspati says:
"The man who performs a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight..."
One should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A householder, even if he has sons, should not perform a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day,
nor should he observe a fast on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
A householder who has sons should not perform a śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day;
nor is fasting desired by anyone on either of the two solstices (ayana).
Āpastamba says:
"On the thirteenth [lunar day], one has many sons, many friends, and beautiful offspring, but they die young.
And Kātyāyana says:
"Young men die there," as stated in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The man who desires liberation for himself along with his ancestors [should go there]."
For one who is childless, the thirteenth lunar day is prescribed for the ancestral rite;
if one who possesses offspring should perform it on that day, his lineage will come to an end.
Ānarta said:
"O Great Sage, why does the destruction of one's lineage occur when a *śrāddha* is performed on the thirteenth lunar day? Explain all of this to me in detail."
Bhartṛyajña said:
O best of kings, in former times, during the Rathantara Kalpa,
there was a man named Sitāśva from the land of Pañcāla who was devoted to his father.
Indeed, he performs the Śrāddha on the thirteenth day with honey, black pot-herbs, or simply with the meat of a rhinoceros, or even with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Once, while other wonderful things were present, he was asked again by the Brahmins filled with curiosity: "O King, why [is this so]?"
The meat of a non-sweet (or bitter) rhinoceros and the black potherb which you offer—
these, once given by the twice-born as sacrificial oblations in a Śrāddha, are not to be rejected and are not to be abandoned.
"Tell me the reason why that is being eaten by us.
Having heard these words of those brahmins, he spoke these words:
I shall speak even that which is unspeakable; listen with well-composed minds.
Formerly, I was indeed a cruel hunter, yet devoted to my father.
While wandering, I once reached the hermitage of Agniveśa at night;
I heard from afar a brahmin instructing his disciples.
Agniveśa said:
When the moon is in the lunar mansion of Pitṛ (Maghā) and the sun is situated in Hasta on the thirteenth day, that shadow should be known as the one called Kuñjarā.
She is highly praised for ancestral rites and brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
therefore, let the auspicious materials for the morning śrāddha be gathered now.
[206] “The *ṛkṣa* of the ancestors” refers to Maghā; “the swan” refers to the sun; “in the hand” means in the hand. The White-Horse One said:
Having heard these words of that sage, I thought this:
"And I too shall perform the śrāddha rite tomorrow morning."
Then, wandering in the forest at dawn for the sake of materials for the śrāddha,
I obtained rhinoceros meat, kālaśāka greens, and honey.
On the thirteenth day, with a concentrated mind, I fed those of my own caste, dedicating the meal to my ancestors with whatever materials were at hand.
By such a śrāddha offering, the ancestors attained satisfaction for twelve years, and I too became a king who remembered his former births.
Therefore, on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha, recollecting its power, I perform this śrāddha with faith by means of these very same offerings.
Having heard those words of his, they and the other people on earth joyfully performed the Śrāddha ceremony on the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhas.
And they attained supreme perfection, vying with the highest of the gods;
consequently, the gods, including the Vasus and Rudras, became envious of them.
"Without doubt, those who perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day shall be afflicted by hunger from this day forward;
whoever shall perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day [shall suffer]."
"When the thousand-rayed sun is situated in Virgo, there shall be the destruction of his lineage"—
by this curse of the gods, this great lunar day was consumed;
from that time forward, no supreme *śrāddha* is performed on this day.
He who performs it out of negligence shall suffer the destruction of his lineage;
this Śrāddha on the thirteenth day is the cause of the severance of one's family line.
Therefore, on that day, even without performing a Śrāddha, one should offer honey-milk porridge (madhupāyasa),
the meat of a rhinoceros (khaḍgamāṃsa), black potherbs (kālaśāka), and the flesh of a boar’s snout (vārdhrīṇasāsyam).

A *vārdhrīṇasa* is an old goat with the characteristics to be described hereafter. In its absence, O King, the most excellent milk-rice (*kṣīrodana*) should be offered to the Brahmins on that day for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
"Even in his absence, water mixed with sesame seeds must be offered. Thus it is said.

Now, some here say: "The statements prohibiting *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) lack authority altogether, because they contradict Manu’s statement beginning with 'Whatever is mixed with honey' (*yat kiṃcin madhunā miśram*). For the *Manusmṛti*, due to its being well-known through Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), being recited by many through tradition, and the impossibility of corrupt readings, is more authoritative than other minor texts that are known only by name, not recited by anyone, have unstable readings, and are suspected of having origins in error and the like; it is superior even to direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) when there is a contradiction with itself."
For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"The authority of Manu’s Smṛti is recognized because it is based upon the meaning of the Vedas;
however, that Smṛti which contradicts the meaning of Manu is not commended."
Manu also said: "Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by Manu for anyone,
all that is ordained in the Veda, for it consists of all-encompassing knowledge."

It is replied: as for what was stated—that because the *Manusmṛti* is equal to the *Śruti*, its injunctions possess greater authority than other *Smṛtis*—that is merely a provisional view. The statement of Bṛhaspati declares the lack of authority for those *Smṛtis* of Buddha and others that contradict the meaning of Manu.

Now, since the Smṛtis of Kātyāyana and others—which are accepted by the learned members of the three higher castes—are connected with the meaning of the Vedas, there exists no ground for their lack of authority; therefore, by the word "Manu" here, all those such as Kātyāyana who remember the meaning of the Vedas are intended by way of synecdoche (upalakṣaṇa). Alternatively, according to the root-index where the root *man* means "to know," the sage who possesses knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is called Manu.

Others, however, say: since it is impossible to prohibit any *śrāddha* whatsoever, the prohibitory statements lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). For instance, this is not a prohibition of the obligatory (*nitya*) *śrāddha*, because Manu says:
"One should offer the *śrāddha* every day with food and drink, or even with water alone."
"Or even by means of water, roots, and fruits, one brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
Dakṣa also said:
"He who eats without having bathed, or without having offered oblations, or without having given gifts..."
"Having become a debtor to the gods and others, he who is childless goes downward.

[And: "One should perform the daily study of the Veda every day; by doing so, one likewise fulfills the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*). Since these passages prescribe the performance of the obligatory *śrāddha* every day and state that failure to do so leads to falling into a lower state, its performance on the thirteenth day is appropriate. Furthermore, there is no prohibition against its occasional (*naimittika*) performance. At least not for that occasioned by the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and so forth, since Yājñavalkya says:
"However, on the anniversary of death, it should be given every month for a year, and likewise annually; the first [offering] is on the eleventh day."

Kātyāyana also says: "Then, year after year, one should give food to the deceased; on the day the deceased passed away"—the meaning is that one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* according to this established conclusion (*siddhānta*). This applies likewise to other *smṛtis* and *purāṇas*. Since what is prescribed for the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and so forth is required on those very anniversaries, its performance cannot be subject to prohibition. Nor can the performance of rites caused by prosperity (*vṛddhi*) and the like be prohibited, because they are prescribed as mandatory at times such as the birth of a son—by such statements as "The birth-rite (*jātakarman*) must be performed upon the birth of a son, equally by men"—just like the *jātakarman* itself. Nor can the *pārvaṇa* rite occasioned by the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) be prohibited, because...
Others say that for a woman who has sons, performing the Śrāddha on the thirteenth day leads indeed to misfortune;
one should not perform it for her alone, but rather should observe the Pārvaṇa rite.

Thus, because its performance is prescribed as mandatory, the meaning is that one should not perform [the rite] for a single group alone; rather, one should perform it for two groups—namely, the paternal group (*pitṛvarga*) and the maternal grandfather’s group (*mātāmahavarga*)—according to the injunction: "One should practice the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]. Nor is there a prohibition against offering the *śrāddha* to a single group, since there is no possibility of such a *śrāddha* being performed for that purpose alone. As it is said: "Wherever the ancestors (*pitaras*) are honored, there the maternal grandfathers (*mātāmahas*) are certainly [honored] as well."

Thus, because Dhaumya’s statement shows that the rules for the *śrāddha* pertain only to two groups (*varga*), nor does it apply to optional (*kāmya*) rites, since even those are specifically prescribed in connection with the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*). Therefore, it is argued that because such a subject matter is impossible, the prohibitory statements lack authority. However, there can sometimes be a prohibition of the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), and the specific (*vaiśeṣika*) rites. For example, in cases such as ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), a prohibition may apply even to a rite specifically prescribed for the occasion of the *trayodaśī*, by means of a specific statement restricted to that alone. This is like the prohibition of taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice, expressed as "one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* in the *atirātra*. And regarding the *śrāddha* on the *trayodaśī*, when its performance is required as an obligation in some way or another, even though Dhaumya’s *smṛti* exists, a prohibition is possible if one performs a *śrāddha* for only one group out of delusion. Thus, the view is held that because no such subject matter is possible, the prohibitory statements lack authority. Consequently, a systematic settlement (*vyavasthā*) must be stated here. In this regard, Śaṅkhaḍhara [states]: "The injunctions for the *śrāddha* on the *maghā-trayodaśī* refer to a *śrāddha* performed with reference to two groups (*varga*). The prohibitions, however, refer to a *śrāddha* performed with reference to only one group. For this very reason, Kārṣṇājini says: [provides the verse].
"One should never commence a *śrāddha* for a single class of ancestors on the thirteenth lunar day;
those who remain unsatisfied therein will indeed harm his progeny. Thus it is said.

One should not commence the rite for a single group—whether consisting only of one's father and ancestors, or only one's maternal grandfather and ancestors—but rather one should perform it for [the ancestors] together with the maternal grandfather and others. The meaning is that if the *śrāddha* is not performed for six generations, there is the fault of violating the prohibition regarding the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*). Others, however, maintain that "groups" (*vargāḥ*) refers to those deceased who have attained the status of *pitṛ*s, such as the group of paternal uncles, the group of brothers, the group of maternal uncles, and so forth. Alternatively, there are two groups: the group of *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the father’s side and the group of *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the mother’s side. Among these groups, a man who has obtained the entitlement to perform *śrāddha* should not perform it on the *maghā-trayodaśī* after having reflected on some reason, such as whether the *śrāddha* for a certain group was already performed or will be performed on another day. Rather, it must be performed for all groups. This is because, among the lunar days that cause satisfaction for the ancestors, the *maghā-trayodaśī* is the most excellent; therefore, a *śrāddha* offered to all the ancestors with substances such as honey-mixed milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is required. Those for whom it is not offered become angry and destroy the progeny of the performer of the *śrāddha*. Thus, the prohibitory statements refer to the *śrāddha* being performed for only one group. Others, however, say that the subject of the prohibition is the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* performed by a householder who has sons.
Jyotis-Bṛhaspati:
If a man performs a Śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death.
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A householder, even if he has sons, should not perform a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day,
nor should he observe a fast on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
And they remember:
"A householder who has sons should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day;
nor is fasting desired by anyone during the two solstices."
Āpastamba says:
"On the thirteenth day, one obtains many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring, but they die young."

Kātyāyana says: "Young men die there. However, some do not consider the cessation of the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* to be due to the defect consisting of the death of a son. For they say: because this result is mandatory (*naiyogika*), it occurs only when it is desired; it does not happen otherwise. As it has been said: "The desired result is known [to follow from the act]; it will not come to one who does not desire it."

Therefore, even when a *śrāddha* is performed, the desired fruit of the action—namely, the death of one's son—does not occur; thus, the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* should be performed even by a householder who has sons.
This is incorrect, for it is said:
"A householder with sons should indeed not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day."
One should know for certain that the attainment of a specific undesirable result required by such prohibitive statements as "one should not [do this]" will befall his eldest son.

By such statements as these, [the performance of the rite] is enjoined; however, a *trayodaśī-śrāddha* in the form of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is not prescribed for anyone who desires the death of a son. Furthermore, no one desires the fruit of an action that is being prohibited, because it is of the nature of harm (*anartha*). Nor is a single utterance of a sentence capable of making known the death of a son as a benefit to one person and as a harm to another, for that would entail the fallacy of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). As for what has been said by some—that since the practice of performing the *śrāddha* on the *trayodaśī* under the *Maghā* asterism is of the nature of *dharma*, it is incorrect to say that undesirable results such as the death of a son occur upon its performance—and likewise that it is incorrect to say that the ancestors, being satisfied, bestow an undesirable fruit—that should not be asserted. For an object established by scripture cannot be overturned by mere reasoning alone, since an object accessible solely through scripture is not within the domain of logic. As it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*, in the section on the *Dāna-dharma*:
One who performs the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day becomes the most distinguished among his kinsmen;
moreover, young men in his household will certainly not die prematurely.

Thus, the refutation of the defect consisting of the death of a youth, as stated by Āpastamba and others, has been performed. Yet even that is not absolute, because by the statement "not necessarily," the possibility of the defect occurring only occasionally is admitted. As for the interpretation of the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*—that they certainly do not die at all—that is not accepted by Śaṅkadhara, Harihara, and others.
Others, however, say:
"The *śrāddha* on the two solstices (*ayana*), and likewise on the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."
And on all the beginnings of the Yugas, except for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).

Thus, because of the statement of Pulastya and because the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is the beginning of a Yuga (*yugādi*), they say that the prohibitionary texts—stating that "the *śrāddha* should be performed without the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)"—have as their subject matter a *śrāddha* accompanied by the offering of rice-balls.
However, some maintain that the subject matter is rather the performance of a *śrāddha* with substances other than milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and so forth;
but that is incorrect, because the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* states a fault in performing a *śrāddha* with substances other than milk-rice and the like.
But Hari and Hara have stated the reason for this as follows:

That is incorrect, because it results in a sentence-meaning that lacks constituent word-meanings (*apadārthavākyārthāpatti*). For instance, "A householder who has sons should not perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day" constitutes the word-meanings (*padārtha*), whereas "The *śrāddha* should not be performed with substances other than milk-rice (*pāyasa*)" would constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). However, Hariharasvāmin himself stated such a regulation: "On the thirteenth day associated with the *Maghā* asterism within the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the *śrāddha* is obligatory and yields great fruit. It is precisely for this purpose that the extensive prayers for sons by the ancestors are heard in the Puranic verses. Therefore, the prohibitive statements concerning the thirteenth day in general—being of the nature of a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*)—fulfill their purpose by excluding the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and applying to the remaining eleven thirteenth days. This point is clearly demonstrated specifically regarding the prohibition of *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* narrative. Alternatively, the prohibitive texts may be established as referring to optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddhas* that are not highly esteemed; for it is recorded in the Smṛtis that the very connection with desire (*kāma*) is a defect in the performance of *śrāddha*.

For instance, after proclaiming the excellence of one's kinsmen and fruits such as having many sons for the performer of the *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, Vyāsa and Āpastamba have also mentioned therein the defect characterized by the premature death of the youth. Thus, these are the specific domains of the prohibitory statements: the *śrāddha* for a single class of ancestors, the *śrāddha* accompanied by *piṇḍas*, the *śrāddha* performed by a householder who has sons, and the optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha*. It is held that the prescriptive statements have other types of *śrāddhas* as their domain.
This concludes the exposition of the *maghā-trayodaśī-śrāddha*.
Now, regarding the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
Yājñavalkya states:
"On the days beginning with the first (*pratipad*), one should perform [the rites] while excluding the fourteenth day."
But for those who have indeed been slain by a weapon, it is offered there to them.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya and Brahma Purāṇas:
"He whose young ancestors have died or have been killed by weapons should perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day (caturdaśī), desiring their satisfaction."
In the *Brahmavaivarta* and *Vāyu Purāṇas*:
"One should cause [the offering] to be given for those who died while still young at home;
indeed, one should give on the fourteenth day for those who were killed by a weapon."
Vṛddha-Manu:
"Excluding the fourteenth day, those experts in ancestral rites perform the śrāddha;
his ancestors, as well as those who were slain by weapons in battle, are gratified."
And Manu says regarding the commencement of rites for specific desires:
"On the thirteenth day, preeminence among kinsmen [is attained]; on the fourteenth day, one has excellent offspring;
and his ancestors who were slain by weapons in battle are gratified."
The mention of "taking up a weapon" is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Those who have died through fasting, weapons, fire, poison, or hanging..."
It is certain that it should be performed on the fourteenth day for the sake of satisfaction.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"And for those whose death is by weapons, or even an untimely death (apamṛtyu),
or for those who have died from calamities, or those who have met a death by poison..."
And for those burnt by fire, those who met death in water, those killed by snakes or tigers, and those who died by horns or by hanging;
O lord of men, a śrāddha for them should be performed on the fourteenth day; when it is performed for them on that day, their satisfaction for the duration of that fortnight shall ensue.

"Unnatural death" (*apamṛtyu*) means untimely death, that is, the death of those who have not yet reached old age. The death of those afflicted by *yakṣas*, *bhūtas*, *grahas*, and so forth, is "death caused by calamities" (*upasargān maraṇam*). According to that school of thought, because the *śrāddha* is performed on every day of the other fortnight, the satisfaction [of the ancestors] is as much as it can be; such is the meaning.
Marīci also says: "For those who kill with poison, weapons, wild beasts, fire, animals, or Brāhmaṇas..."
The ritual should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, it is censured.

Those who have been killed by poison and the like are referred to as such. By this, it is merely the time—the fourteenth day—that is restricted for those killed by weapons and so forth; it does not mean that the *śrāddha* for those killed by weapons occurs only on the fourteenth day. Rather, their *śrāddha* certainly takes place at other times as well. Pracetās also says:
"For those who have perished by climbing trees, by iron [weapons] and the like, by lightning, flames, poison, and the like, or by claws and fangs, the fourteenth day is prescribed."

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there are included means of death similar to those previously mentioned, such as climbing or falling from uneven places like mountain peaks, injury from being struck by stones and the like, hanging, and other forms of self-inflicted harm. As for the statement of Śākaṭāyana, which appears to contradict what has been said: "One should perform the *śrāddha* for those who have perished in water or fire, or through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), at home, or on the road, avoiding only the fourteenth day."

Thus, this refers to living beings who have died by means of water, fire, and so forth, as prescribed for the purpose of atonement (*prāyaścitta*) and the like. For those who die an "unfortunate death" (*pāpamṛtyu*), the *śrāddha* must be performed here on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), because in the statement of Pracetas beginning with "climbing trees," etc., such [deaths] are listed among the category of unfortunate deaths. For this very reason, the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day is not to be performed even for women who have followed their deceased husbands according to the prescribed rite of entering the fire (*agnipraveśa*). Therefore, it is established that for those who have died by unenjoined means such as fire, and for those who have died in battle or through fasting (*prāyopaveśana*), the *śrāddha* on the dark fourteenth day is to be performed, based on the authority of the statements in the *Manu- and Brahma-purāṇas*. Now, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, this [śrāddha] should be performed as a single-offering (*ekoddiṣṭa*) alone. As Gārgya says:
"But the śrāddha performed on the fourteenth day after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for one killed by a weapon must be performed according to the ekoddiṣṭa procedure. Thus says Manu.

"But for those who have been unified into a single piṇḍa, separation is no longer possible after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, when [the deceased] has died on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. Thus it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
[216] Even for a father who has attained equality [with the ancestors] but was slain by a weapon,
the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya*.

The meaning is as follows: even for one who has attained *sārūpya* (similarity in form) by abandoning the state of a *preta* through the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ* (ancestor) upon performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite together with his grandfather and others who have likewise attained the status of *pitṛ*s by abandoning their *preta* state—even for such a person, when the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha is performed on the fourteenth day during the *mahālaya* for a father killed by weapons, a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must still be performed on another day; for the satisfaction of the grandfather and other ancestors is not accomplished by the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha alone.

[Objection: If this is so, then even on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), when the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha has been performed, a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha would also have to be performed for the sake of accomplishing the satisfaction of the grandfather and other ancestors.

Not so; for on the anniversary of a father’s death, there is no traditional injunction (*smaraṇa*) that the grandfather and others are to be offered libations (*tarpaṇīya*), and therefore the *śrāddha* need not be performed for their satisfaction. However, regarding the *Mahālaya*, [it is said]:
"They desire milk-rice mixed with honey from their sons and grandsons;
therefore, one should satisfy them there with milk-rice according to the prescribed rule."

Since there is a traditional injunction that even the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and others are to be propitiated with an offering mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed on another day for their satisfaction. However, for one whose grandfather was also killed by weapons or similar means, a śrāddha for the grandfather—performed as an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite—must be performed on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) during the *mahālaya* festival. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "The *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure applies to one or to two. This means that when either the father or the grandfather has been killed by weapons or similar means, or when both among the three beginning with the father have been killed by such means, a śrāddha for each must be performed individually on the fourteenth day according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Even though the śrāddha for each has been performed by applying the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure to the two, a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed on another day to ensure the satisfaction of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*). It is understood from this that the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure does not apply when all three, beginning with the father, have been killed by weapons or similar means.

[217] Regarding this, some say that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites must be performed separately. Others, however, say that because of the statement "in one or in two," when three—namely the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are killed by weapons or other such means, the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure does not apply. Therefore, when all three have been killed by weapons or the like, on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), only the *pārvaṇa* procedure is to be performed.

And this is logical: for when the three ancestors who have been made *sapiṇḍa* and were killed by weapons are eligible on the fourteenth day—a time specifically prescribed—there is no application of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, which is based on the impossibility of the prescribed time due to the non-attainment of the [other] time for those not killed by weapons.

With this very intention, Aparārka stated: "In that case, if one [of the three] was killed by a weapon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure applies; but if all three are likewise [killed by weapons], then the *pārvaṇa* alone applies. The meaning of this is that if all three are likewise [killed by weapons], there is no application of the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, but rather the *pārvaṇa* alone applies in that instance.

That is incorrect, because the phrase "in one [day] or in two" is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, since the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* is based on the cause of being slain by weapons and so forth, there is no impossibility regarding the time; for an impossibility of the time being the basis [for the rite] is not heard in scripture. Moreover, if the rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* were based on that [time], it would result in its foundation being nothing more than mere conjecture. For this very reason, Devasvāmin stated: "In all three cases of those slain by weapons and so forth, only three separate *ekoddiṣṭas* should be performed, and not a *pārvaṇa*, because there is no direct scriptural statement [to that effect]. In this context, since the meaning of the sentence is understood to be that the *ekoddiṣṭa* for those slain by weapons and so forth occurs on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), the *pārvaṇa* alone should be performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) and other such occasions. However, regarding those who died specifically on the fourteenth day by means of weapons and so forth, a doubt arises as to whether the *pārvaṇa* or the *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed on their anniversary of death.
