To this it is replied: Although the *śrāddha* occasioned by the fourteenth day and the *śrāddha* occasioned by the anniversary of death are distinct according to the logic to be explained in the section on the coincidence of times, when multiple occasions occur simultaneously, and when the single required time—such as the *kutapa* period—is occupied by one occasional rite (*naimittika*), there is no room for a second. Since there is no distinction to be grasped when place, time, performer, and deity are identical, the occasional rites are performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*). Consequently, for those who have adopted the *ekoddiṣṭa* option on the anniversary of death in accordance with the tradition of their own family elders, even on the anniversary of death, the *ekoddiṣṭa* alone is to be performed on the fourteenth day. On the other hand, for those who have adopted the *pārvaṇa* option, it is adopted for as long as they live—just like the *uditānuditahoma* (the fire-oblation performed either after sunrise or before)—and thus it must not be abandoned by them even on the fourteenth day. As for the prohibition of the *pārvaṇa* nature of the *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day, that refers to the *śrāddha* occasioned by the fourteenth day itself, and not to that occasioned by the anniversary of death.

Now, one might object: "In the statement 'there is no *pārvaṇa* on the fourteenth day,' since 'on the fourteenth day' is a qualification for that which is caused by the fourteenth day, there would result both the necessity of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

This is not so; for the specific meaning is obtained through the context and other factors, and thus it does not provide ground for the faults previously mentioned. Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa* regarding the fruitlessness of a *pārvaṇa* performed on the fourteenth day—that too refers only to a *pārvaṇa* occasioned by the fourteenth day itself, and not to one occasioned by the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*).

Now, regarding the fourteenth day, there arises a doubt as to whether one should perform two *śrāddhas*—the *ekoddiṣṭa* for the sake of the [anniversary of] the fourteenth day and the *pārvaṇa* for the sake of the anniversary of death—or only one. This is because their auxiliary characteristics (*aṅga*) differ; since specific details are being observed, a simultaneous performance (*tantrānuṣṭhāna*) is impossible. In this regard, since the prohibition stating "one should not perform two *śrāddhas* on the same day" does not apply to *śrāddhas* performed for different occasions, one should indeed perform both *śrāddhas*.

Not so. Because the deity is one, when performing the two principal rites together, the *pārvaṇa* rules override the *ekoddiṣṭa* rules in order to favor the greater number of *śrāddha* characteristics. Thus, since the occasional rite is accomplished by means of the *pārvaṇa*, there is no performance of the two *śrāddhas* separately. Now, an objection may be raised: there is also an optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*); and since human activity is inclined toward desire and the impulse for desire is intense, when the *śrāddha* occasioned by the fourteenth day is to be performed, it follows that the *ekoddiṣṭa* rules alone should apply.

This would be so if a distinction were not perceived here in favor of the majority; or rather, let there be two *śrāddhas* on this lunar day due to the difference in occasion. Furthermore, within the *mahālaya* fortnight, if a *śrāddha* cannot be performed on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*) by any means, it must be performed on some other day within that fortnight, because the *śrāddha* to be performed during that fortnight is mandatory even when the most excellent primary time is unavailable. On other days, for those killed by weapons as well, only the *pārvaṇa* rite applies, since the *ekoddiṣṭa* rule is prescribed specifically for the fourteenth day. The reason why only the *ekoddiṣṭa* is to be performed on the fourteenth day for those slain by weapons has been stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
Ānarta said:
Why is the fourteenth day prescribed for the *śrāddha* of those killed by weapons?
From what cause does the *ekoddiṣṭa* *śrāddha* arise? Tell me the reason.
Bhartṛyajña said: O King, in a former Great Kalpa, there was a great Asura named Hiraṇyākṣa,
who was powerful, heroic, and a source of terror to all the gods.
Having performed various austerities when the month of Nabhasya had arrived on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Brahmā was fully propitiated by him.
Brahmā said:
"I am well-pleased with you, my child; ask for whatever you desire.
I shall grant it even if it be ungivable, even that which is difficult for gods and asuras to attain."
Hiraṇyākṣa said: "O Lotus-born One, hungry spirits, ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas are constantly rushing toward me."
When the Śrāddha has been performed for the paternal kin while the sun is situated in Virgo,
on that day there generally occurs satisfaction [for the ancestors] lasting for a year.
"Therefore, O Lord, provide for them on this day a means of satisfaction.
Brahmā said:
"Whosoever among men shall offer a *śrāddha* to his ancestors..."
When the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors has arrived in the month of Nabhasya,
that [offering] shall belong to the pretas, the rākṣasas, and the bhūtas.
When he had spoken thus, O King, Brahmā then vanished from sight;
Hiraṇyākṣa, too, being greatly delighted, went to his own home.
And as for that which is given on that day for those slain by weapons—
an Ekoddiṣṭa rite performed with faith by men— I shall tell you the reason for that.
And those who are slain by weapons in battle with a mind free from conceptual construction,
while fighting, are not born again as mortals among men.
Those men who are slain while turning their backs in flight, intent on escape, become pretas; so said the Grandfather.
Even those who, when being struck, speak with wretchedness in the very presence [of their assailants],
or feel remorse once they have been shattered by blows;
Even they may become hungry ghosts here; so Manu Svāyambhuva has declared, for sometimes even the minds of heroes undergo wavering.
On their day as well, an offering should be given there out of fear of their remaining as pretas,
as it must be for all embodied beings who have met with untimely death.
Since the state of being a preta arises [for them], therefore,
O best of kings, that day is specifically proclaimed as worthy of the śrāddha rite for them.
Therefore, men should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa on that day;
after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, I shall explain the reason for that to you.
O King, if his father should ever have fallen into the state of a preta,
a śrāddha must be performed on that day for the sake of his satisfaction.
On that day, the ancestors beginning with the grandfather do not deserve a śrāddha offering anywhere;
if one should offer it out of delusion, it is seized by the rākṣasas.
O King, by the word of Brahmā and by the bhūtas, pretas, and dānavas,
only the ekoddiṣṭa rite is to be performed here, and not the pārvaṇa.
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors, when the sun is situated in Virgo—
for this reason, the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is not prescribed;
for when that day arrives, the śrāddha would become fruitless.
Thus concludes the exposition on the *śrāddha* of the fourteenth day.
Now, it is stated in the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya-sūtra* that this *śrāddha* of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada should not be performed during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*):
"In whichever month there is no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or where there are two transits..."
That should be known as the intercalary month (malamāsa), occurring in the thirtieth month.
In the *Jyotiṣaśāstra* of Bṛhaspati:
"That month in which there is no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or that in which there are two transits—
these are the *saṃsarpa*, the *āṅgirasa*, and the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), and they are all censured."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "When the sun enters [a new sign] on the new moon day during the day and night, that month shall be pure; for when it has passed, it becomes an intercalary month (*adhika*)."
Bhṛgu said:
"When two new moons occur while the sun remains in a single zodiac sign,
that intercalary month (adhikamāsa) should be known as one that destroys the performance of rites for the gods and the ancestors."
Paiṭhīnasi also says:
"All rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti are declared to be performed in the twelfth month;
however, in the thirteenth month, all of them are designated as fruitless."
"Therefore, one should by no means perform those [rites] in the thirteenth month.
Thus it was stated by Sumantu:
"One who performs rituals should never perform a rite during an intercalary month."
"Those who know time declare that an additional month is the impurity of time. Thus it is said; and also in the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa:
"The intercalary month (malimluca) is indeed defiled, being the source of evil."
Being censured by the ancestors and the gods, one should abandon it in all ritual acts.
Śātātapa says:
A sinful act occurring within the year destroys the fruit of sacrifices;
it is a bringer of ruin, overwhelmed by the Nairṛtas, Yātudhānas, and other malevolent beings.
That month which is devoid of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) is declared to be *malimluca*;
known as *malimluca*, it is censured for all ritual acts.
Satyavrata says:
But that month which is the *malimluca* is designated as sinful.

Nor should it be thought that these statements refer to matters other than the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*), for the ancestral rite itself is prohibited by such texts as "He who destroys the performance of *havya* and *kavya* is censured by the ancestors and the gods," and "He is despised by the ancestors and the gods. As for what was stated by Jyotiḥparāśara: "The commencement of Vedic study (*upākarma*), the conclusion (*utsarga*), journeys abroad, festivals, and the *aṣṭakā*s—when there is an increase in the month, these should be performed on the later [lunar day], with the exception of the ancestral rites."
That [rule] refers exclusively to the paternal rites (paitṛka) performed on the occasion of childbirth. For it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"During an eclipse of the moon or sun, upon death, and at the birth of a son—even during an intercalary month—a śrāddha should be offered; it brings about inexhaustible merit."

However, there is no counter-exception here for the ancestral rite (*paitṛka*) performed on the *aṣṭakā* day, because a direct prohibition of it will be demonstrated later. Now, one might object: since the *śrāddha* of the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) is obligatory, its performance even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is not contradictory. For it is stated in the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"Those who know time call the intercalary month the 'impurity' (*mala*) of time."
"One should not perform a special sacrifice here, except for that which is required by an obligatory injunction. Thus [it is said].
This is not so, because this statement refers exclusively to that which is constant and has no other recourse. And thus says the Smṛti:
"One should perform that which is constant when there is no other recourse, and likewise that which is occasional."

When a primary time (*mukhyakāla*) for an obligatory rite (*nitya*) has passed and no secondary alternative time (*jaghanya-kālāntara*) is permitted, the rite would otherwise suffer absolute loss (*atyantaloṣa*), and a penance (*prāyaścitta*) would be required; such a rite, having no other recourse, should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). However, because the *Śrāddha* of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is seen to have a permitted subsequent time, it does not lack an alternative recourse. Therefore, it should not be performed in the intercalary month. For this very reason, an explicit prohibition of this [specific rite] in the intercalary month is observed. To that end, in the *Kāṭhakagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "Likewise, in the intercalary month, one should perform the obligatory and occasional rites that have no other recourse."
Ritual acts such as the Soma sacrifice, even though they are obligatory, [are not to be performed] during the intercalary month (malimluca).

One should avoid performing the Puṣṭīṣṭi, Āgrayaṇa, Agnyādheya, Cāturmāsya, and other such rites; as well as the Mahālaya, the Aṣṭakā Śrāddhas, and the rites of Upākarma and Utsarga— specifically those clearly prescribed for particular months— during the intercalary month (mala-māsa).
The *mahālaya* is the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. It is also stated in the *Bhṛgusmṛti*:

"One should not perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, the Soma sacrifice, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), the *mahālaya*, the consecration of a king, or rites for specific desires when the sun has transgressed [its proper path]."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) also [states]:
"If a month occurs while the sun has entered Virgo but no saṃkrānti has taken place,
then rites for the gods and the ancestors performed when the sun is in Libra yield inexhaustible merit for the performer."
Devala says:
When the Sun is in Virgo, the fortnight for the Śrāddha is proclaimed;
specifically, when the Sun, having passed beyond Sinīvālī, enters Virgo.
"Then, because of the advanced age of the time, the ancestral rites (*pitṛkriyā*) have already passed.
Therefore, the *śrāddha* should not be performed during the second fortnight of Bhādrapada that falls within the intercalary month (*malamāsa*). As for the statement in the *Jyotiḥsiddhānta*:
"When the sun is in Leo, Virgo, Scorpio, or Sagittarius..."
"An intercalary month is not ordained when [the sun] is in Capricorn or Aquarius.
This should be understood as referring to the occurrence of two intercalary months within a single year;
and so it is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
When no solar transit occurs within two months during the course of a year,
the first of those two months shall be considered ordinary, and the subsequent one an intercalary month.

[225] Here, within the period beginning from the transit of the sun into Leo (siṃhasaṃkrānti) and ending with the entry into Pisces (mīnasaṃkramaṇa), whichever month occurs first is merely natural (prākṛta); the meaning is that the subsequent one becomes an anomalous intercalary month (vaikṛta-malamāsa). This same meaning should be explained for the statement of the Brahma-siddhānta: “There is no intercalary month prior to Caitra, but after that, there may be an extra month. Therefore, it is established that the Śrāddha ceremony must not be performed during the latter fortnight (aparapakṣa) of the Mahālaya occurring within an intercalary month.
Now, is it not the case that [the merit] is then indeed lost, or that a rite performed at another time would become a non-meritorious time?
No, for it is to be performed at the subsequent time. Therefore Parāśara said:
"A lunar month that is overtaken by the sun is known as *malimluca* (the intercalary month)."
In that regard, whatever rite has been prescribed, one should have it performed in the following month.
Likewise:
"When the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) does not occur during either the bright or the dark fortnight,
then that monthly rite should be performed in the following month."
Thus, sixty days constitute a month;
having omitted the intercalary half-month, one should thereafter perform the rites for the ancestors, gods, and others.
Prajāpati said:

The commencement of Vedic study (upākarma), the offerings to the gods (havya), the offerings to the ancestors (kavya), as well as the seasonal festivals—these one should regularly perform during the latter [fortnight]; if performed during the former, they become fruitless.
In the science of astrology as well, it is stated by the followers of Bādarāyaṇa: "A month is said to consist of sixty days;
having discarded the first half, the latter half is recommended."
Where two new moon days (amāvāsyā) occur without the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), that month is to be known as *malimluca*; the subsequent one, however, is designated as *uttama*.
Now, regarding the exceptions for the performance of *śrāddha* rites during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), Yama says: "In the case of a fetus, a usurer, a ritual act, monthly *śrāddha* rites,
the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and obligatory rites, the intercalary month is not prescribed [as a time of prohibition]."
Knowledge of the sacred fords (tīrtha), recitation (japa), burnt offerings (homa) with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth,
the birth-rite (jātakarma), the final rites (antyakarma), and likewise the first funeral rite (navaśrāddha);
The *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha, as well as the sixteen *śrāddhas*,

bathing during lunar and solar eclipses, and rites such as *śrāddha*, giving, and recitation— these should be performed even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), whether they are obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*).
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"One should perform the obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month (malimluca),
as well as bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha), the 'elephant's shadow' (gajacchāyā) rite, and likewise the Śrāddha for the deceased."
Also in the *Kāṭhakapariśiṣṭa*:
"Beginning with the consecration of the deceased, the rites of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and the water libation (*udaka*),
ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, should be performed at their proper times as they arise."
The fire-oblation with barley, rice, and sesame seeds, the rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*),

and the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day under the asterism Maghā performed for a specific imminent cause— these should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malimluca*) when there is no other recourse.
In the Saura Purāṇa:
"The śrāddha performed for a single individual is called occasional (naimittika).
That should be performed even in an intercalary month (malamāsa) and even when the time has exceeded its limit, according to dharma."

Vyāsa says: The śrāddha performed at the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and likewise the new-moon śrāddha (*darśaśrāddha*) should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), according to the word of Vyāsa.
Śātātapa says:
One should not exclude the intercalary month (adhimāsa) from the annual Śrāddha;
that Śrāddha which is performed every year must be performed even during a Malamāsa.

This and similar statements refer to the case of an *asaṃvatsarika* (non-annual) rite. This statement follows the view that after performing the annual *śrāddha* during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), that very same rite must be repeated in the following month; regarding this, there are these scriptural authorities. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"The first annual rite (*ābdika*) must be performed by the twice-born even if no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) has occurred."
In the same way, the monthly śrāddha and likewise the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa [are performed].
Paiṭhīnasi says:
"The annual Śrāddha for those who died during an intercalary month must be performed even in an intercalary month,
but never for others."
Yama says: "The first annual śrāddha that falls during an intercalary month (malimluca) should be performed;
however, when the thirteenth [lunar] month arrives, one should perform the annual śrāddha again."
Laghuhārīta states:
"The twice-born should perform the rite of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍakriyā) every year in the twelfth month;
in some cases, it may also take place in the thirteenth month, except for the first year."
Vasiṣṭha says:
When the anniversary day of the annual rite has arrived, if an intercalary month (adhimāsa) should occur, one should perform two śrāddhas; by acting thus, one does not err.

Thus, it is established that—with the exception of the *preta-śrāddhas* ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the *śrāddha* performed on the occasion of a son’s birth, the *śrāddha* caused by an eclipse, the first annual *śrāddha*, the non-initial annual *śrāddha*, the annual *śrāddha* for one who died in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the *gajacchāyā-śrāddha*, the new-moon *śrāddha*, and the daily obligatory *nitya-śrāddha*—no other *śrāddha* should be performed during an intercalary month. This concludes the exception regarding the performance of *śrāddhas* such as those in the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) during an intercalary month, following the definition of the intercalary month. And the definition of the dark fortnight is now completed.
Now follow the solstices (*ayana*) and other such times for *śrāddha* rites.

Although in the statement of Yājñavalkya the solstices (*ayana*), equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and transits (*saṃkrānti*) are described as being separated by the requirements of materials and worthy Brahmins, they are nevertheless described here without such separation due to their common characteristic of being *saṃkrāntis*.
Regarding this, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states:
During the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on the three Aṣṭakās, and during the two solstices—
even water mixed with sesame seeds [is meritorious] here.
A self-controlled man should offer [this] to the ancestors.
"The Śrāddha has been performed by him together with [his] mother"— the ancestors declare this secret.
Because of the statement, "In this case, even water [is sufficient]," they believe that the necessity of performing two Śrāddhas is expressed.
As for that which was said: "The sun's transit, both solstices, the two equinoxes,
the *vyatīpāta* yoga, one’s own birth asterism, and likewise an eclipse of the moon or the sun."

"Prajāpati has declared these times for the *śrāddha* to be optional (*kāmya*). By this statement of Viṣṇu, it is stated that the time of an eclipse and so forth is a time for optional *śrāddha*. That is not correct; for it is not capable of negating its obligatory nature (*nityatva*), since there is no contradiction between its being both obligatory and optional—just as in the case of the *agnihotra* and other rites—by the force of two [conflicting] statements. Śaṅkha says:

Whatever is given during the "elephant's shadow" (hasticchāyā), whatever is given at the sight of Rāhu (during an eclipse), and likewise at the equinoxes and solstices— all that is said to be infinite in merit.

In this regard, although the two solstices (*ayana*) and the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) are already included by the term *saṃkrānti* itself in this statement of Yājñavalkya—"the two solstices and the equinox at the sun’s transit"—the fact that both are mentioned separately should be understood as intended to demonstrate their superior excellence relative to other transits; namely, that the equinox is more excellent than the other transits, and the solstice is more excellent than the equinox. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Lord of the Earth, a *śrāddha* performed at the sun’s transit is praised; among those, the two equinoxes are recommended, and the two solstices especially so."
The definition of the two equinoxes and the two solstices is given in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"When the sun enters Aries and when it then proceeds to Libra,
that time is called the equinox (*viṣuva*), and it brings about imperishability."
O King, when the sun enters Capricorn and Cancer,
that is designated as the solstice (ayana), and it is distinguished as the equinox (viṣuvat).
And at this time, the Śrāddha should be performed even without the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa). As Pulastya said:
"The Śrāddha during the two solstices, likewise during the two equinoxes, and on all the anniversaries of the Yugas, is [performed] without the offering of rice-balls."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*, it is stated that for all *saṃkrāntis*, the *śrāddha* rite is to be performed without the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*):
"The *śrāddha* at the two solstices (*ayana*), likewise at the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*),
and at all *saṃkrāntis*, is [performed] apart from the offering of rice-balls."

On these occasions, the *śrāddha* should be performed without the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*). This prohibition regarding the offering of rice balls applies specifically to the *śrāddha* occasioned by these particular times; it does not apply by extension to those [occasions] such as the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) that might coincide with the solstices (*ayana*) and so forth. For, by the rule "the *śrāddha* on the two solstices," it is understood that the *śrāddha* is permanently connected (*nityānvita*) with the solstices and other such times. And it is only that which is occasioned by them which is permanently connected with them, and nothing else. Furthermore, permanent connection (*nityānvaya*) is stronger than occasional connection (*anityānvaya*).

Furthermore, in this context, the qualification "except for the offering of rice balls" (*piṇḍanirvapaṇād ṛte*) attached to the *śrāddha* being enjoined cannot reasonably refer to a *śrāddha* performed on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) or similar occasions that fall at that time by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). If such a *śrāddha* were enjoined for these times, then this would be the merit [of the rule]: namely, that it is an injunction regarding the performance of the action itself (*bhāvārthavidhi*). Now, the transit of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), its divisions, and the duration of those times are described in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"The sun’s transition into a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) is called a *saṃkrānti*."
It yields great fruit in [the performance of] bathing, giving, recitation, ancestral rites, fire offerings, and so forth.
In the zodiacal sign known as Aries and so forth, as established in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*),
the *Devīpurāṇa* states: "The year, the solstice, the season, the month, the fortnight, the day, and so on, follow in sequence."
O All-pervading One, the Goddess is omnipresent through the division of the subtle and the gross.
Twelve equal transits (saṃkrānti) have been fully described;
however, each one should be understood as being sevenfold—listen how.
O King, the sevenfold *saṃkrānti* is said to be composed of the *rākṣasī* mixed with the *mandā*, *mandākinī*, *dhvāṅkṣī*, *ghorā*, and *mahodarī*.
In fixed asterisms, the Mandā is to be known, like the slow-moving Mandākinī; in swift asterisms, one should recognize it as Dhvāṅkṣī, while in fierce asterisms, it is proclaimed as Ghorā.
Mahodarī is to be known by her movements, and Rākṣasī by the cruel asterisms; when the transition occurs through mixed asterisms, she is likewise designated as Miśritā.
Three, four, five, seven, eight, nine,
and twelve ghaṭikās respectively— this indeed is the ultimate merit.
The past and future experiences consist of fifteen channels;
this is declared to be the gross division for one who desires liberation.
O best of kings, I shall tell you the calculation according to ultimate truth:
the thirty-second part of the time it takes for the eye of a healthy man sitting at ease to blink is proclaimed as that supreme [unit].
A hundredth part of that is called a *truṭi*;
half of a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is the duration of the sun’s transit (*ravi-saṃkrama*).

[232] “*Samāyanetyādi*. The “Goddess” (*devī*) is the form of the *saṃkrānti* (the sun’s passage into a zodiacal sign); she is “all-pervading” (*sarvagatā*), meaning she extends everywhere through gross and subtle components such as the year (*samā*) and so forth. The year and other units are components of the *saṃkrānti*. To explain how this is so, he says: “*dvādaśaiva*,” etc. There are exactly twelve conceptualizations of *saṃkrāntis*, which constitute a “year” (*samā*). This is the intended meaning: one year consists of twelve *saṃkrāntis*; six *saṃkrāntis* make an *ayana* (solstice); two *saṃkrāntis* make a season (*ṛtu*); the time delimited by a single *saṃkrānti* is a month; half a *saṃkrānti* is a fortnight (*pakṣa*); a thirtieth part of a *saṃkrānti* is a day and night (*ahorātra*). By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the watches (*yāma*), half-watches, and muhūrtas are included. Thus, this flow of the sun in the form of *saṃkrānti* is the Goddess whose nature is Power (*śakti*). Regarding each individual *saṃkrānti*, he states the designations such as “slow” (*manda*) and so on for the purpose of determining the duration of the auspicious time (*puṇyakāla*) when it conjoins with the fixed (*dhruva*) and other lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). He says: “*Mandetyādi*. The “fixed” (*dhruva*) ones are four: Rohiṇī and the three *Uttarās*. The “soft” (*mṛdu*) ones are four: Citrā, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Revatī. The “swift” (*kṣipra*) ones are four: Aśvinī, Puṣya, Hasta, and Abhijit. The “fierce” (*ugra*) ones are five: the three *Pūrvas*, Bharaṇī, and Maghā. The “moving” (*cara*) ones are five: Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Punarvasu, and Svātī. The “harsh” (*dāruṇa*) ones are four: Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, and Āśleṣā. The “mixed” (*miśra*) ones are two: Viśākhā and Kṛttikā. Because of the instruction that each one is sevenfold, the lunar mansions of the days are understood here as the fixed ones and so forth, not the great lunar mansions (*mahānakṣatra*). In those [great mansions], a sevenfold division for each one is not applicable. He now states the measurement of the auspicious time.

"Three, four, five," etc. The meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) consists of three *ghaṭikās* during the *mandā* [transit], four during the *mandākinī*, five during the *dhvāṅkṣā*, seven during the *ghorā*, eight during the *mahodarī*, nine during the *rākṣasī*, and twelve during the *miśrā*. The meaning is that when acts such as giving, sacrifice, austerity, and ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) are performed therein, the merit occasioned by the time of the transit (*saṃkrānti*) is ultimate and preeminent. He states "past and future," etc., to show that there is a meritorious time consisting of fifteen *ghaṭikās* in all transits, which yields a fruit slightly less than this. "Experience" (*bhoga*) means pervasion; "in the past" means prior to the transition; "in the future" means in the subsequent time. The meaning is that fifteen *ghaṭikās* before and after the moment of the transit constitute the meritorious time. This pervasion of past and future time should also be understood to apply to the [specific durations] previously mentioned. Here, the priority and posteriority of the meritorious time are to be followed according to the system to be explained later. Having thus stated the gross meritorious time, he speaks of the subtle time, which yields the most excellent fruit, starting with "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthena*). Although half of a thousandth part of a *truṭi* is difficult to perceive, this is taught for the purpose of grasping the time in close proximity to it. Vasiṣṭha says:
The moment of transition is subtle and difficult to perceive even for those with the eyes of a seer;
yet through its conjunction, thirty channels—both below and above—are purified.

In this context, thirty *nāḍīs* are to be understood as fifteen before and fifteen after, according to this calculation. For it is thus that there is agreement with the *Devīpurāṇa*. In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"The Sun proceeds through the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries in succession due to its transit (*saṃkrama*).
There are exactly twelve of these; O twice-born one, hear their names from me."

According to the movement of the sun through the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, there are twelve transits (saṃkrāntis) named after those very signs. For the purpose of instructing upon their relative excellence, the gradations of their duration, and their chronological sequence, he states the fourfold nomenclature beginning with Viṣṇupada:
"One is called Viṣṇupada, likewise the Ṣaḍaśītimukha, the third is the Equinox (viṣuva), and the two solstices (ayana) are the southern and northern."
They say the Viṣṇupada [saṃkrānti] occurs in the signs of Aquarius, Taurus, and Leo;
the Ṣaḍaśītimukha occurs in Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Gemini. When the Sun is in the abode of the Moon (Cancer), his course is the southern solstice (ayana).
The equinox occurs in Cancer, while the solstice occurs between Aries and Libra.

*Kumbha* is well known [as Aquarius]. *Ali* is Scorpio (*vṛścika*). *Go* is Taurus (*vṛṣa*). *Hari* is Leo (*siṃha*). When the sun’s transit (*ayana*) or passage (*saṃkramaṇa*) occurs in these zodiac signs, it is called "Viṣṇupada" (the Foot of Viṣṇu). *Strī* is Virgo (*kanyā*). *Cāpa* is Sagittarius (*dhanuḥ*). *Mīna* and *mithuna* are well known [as Pisces and Gemini]. In these [signs], there is the "Ṣaḍaśītimukha. In *śaśidhāman* (Karkaṭaka/Cancer), there is the southern transit (*yāmyāyana*). In *jhaṣa* (Makara/Capricorn), there is the northern transit (*saumyāyana*). *Aja* is Aries (*meṣa*). *Taulī* is Libra (*tulādhāra*). In those two, it is designated as the "Equinox" (*viṣuva*). Vasiṣṭha also [says]:
The two solstices, the two equinoxes, the four *ṣaḍaśīti*s,
and the four *viṣṇupadī*s— these are remembered as the twelve *saṃkrānti*s.

The two transits of Libra and Aries are the equinoxes; the transits of Cancer and Capricorn are the northern and southern solstices respectively. The others [the remaining four] are situated between these two.
When the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, or Leo, this is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is greater than that of the equinoxes (viṣuva).
The Sun's transit through Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius is declared to be the "mouth of the sixty-fourth" (ṣaḍaśītimukha); its fruit is endowed with sixty-fourfold merit.
Laukāxi says:
"In whose course [the sun enters] at Viṣṇu’s step—at the beginning, the merit from giving and so forth is infinite; likewise at the equinox, it is in the middle."
Indeed, the great sages of the Sixty-four Faces speak thus regarding the past and the northern solstice.
Baudhāyana says: [It is performed] when the sun's course is about to begin, while the Viṣuvat day is occurring,
when the Ṣaḍaśīti-mukha has passed, and when the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) has elapsed.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "When the Ṣaḍaśītimukha has passed, in the middle of the two equinoxes,
and when the northern solstice is about to occur, merit is found in what has already passed."
Vṛddha-vaśiṣṭha says:
"The two meritorious periods are the past and the future northern and southern solstices;
however, during an eclipse, that time [is meritorious], as is the period after it has passed, and the northern solstice."

In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "A gift given at the equinox in the middle, or during the southern transit of the sun; likewise before the commencement of the six-aśīti period, and when the northern transit has passed."

Regarding all these statements, the authors of the legal digests (*smṛtinibandhakārāḥ*) understand that by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "in the past northern solstice," it is meant "and in the future [northern solstice] as well. Baudhāyana states the measure of the aforementioned auspicious times for the eastward and westward passages (*pūrvottarādi-puṇyakāla*): "Ten *nāḍīs* before and ten after the equinox (*viṣuvat*) are declared to be the auspicious time during the sun's transition (*arkasaṃkrānti*) for bathing, giving, recitation, and other rites."
Vasiṣṭha says: Thirty nāḍīs are prescribed for Cancer, and twenty for Capricorn;
when Libra or Aries is present, there are ten nāḍīs on both sides.
When sixty-eight [nāḍīs] have passed, sixty nāḍīs are said to be meritorious; specifically, sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after the Viṣṇupadī are likewise meritorious.

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "The wise know that there are three meritorious moments: six *muhūrtas* at the equinox (*viṣuvat*), three at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, and likewise three at the *viṣṇupada*."
Thirty nāḍīs in Karkaṭaka, and ten more in Makara;
this southern transit will be meritorious, as will the northern transit that has already passed.
Bṛhaspati says: "Thirty auspicious nāḍīs indeed exist in the southern solstice; they have passed in the northern one—so say those who know the ancient lore."
Gautama says: Sixteen nāḍīs are before [the equinox], and sixteen indeed are after;
those same [nāḍīs] are first in the southern [solstice], and then in the past northern solstice.
Marīci: Sixteen nāḍīs before or after the transit [of the sun] constitute the auspicious time for the mere sight of Rāhu.
Śātātapa says:
"The meritorious time for a saṃkrānti (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign) consists of sixteen kalās on both sides;
however, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, it lasts as long as they remain within the range of vision."

In this regard, in some statements the duration of the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) is said to be greater, while in others it is said to be less. Among these, that which is less is for the purpose of demonstrating a superior fruit; however, that which is greater is for the purpose of establishing the mere status of being a meritorious time. It should not be understood, however, that the lesser [duration] is intended to exclude the greater, or that the greater is intended to exclude the lesser. For this very reason, Śātātapa says: "Whichever *nāḍīs* (moments) are proximate, those are considered most meritorious."

This being so, since there is no contradiction among all the statements regarding the limits of the time for merit (*puṇyakāla*), one should not violate the straightforwardness of the scriptural texts for the sake of avoiding such contradictions. On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"When the transit occurs during the day, the entire day is proclaimed to be meritorious;
when the transit occurs at night, half a day is meritorious for bathing and giving. [237]

By this it is stated that even the time of merit (puṇyakāla) in the form of night, though proximate to the transit [of the sun], does not occur; rather, it is only in the form of midday. Furthermore, only that which is proximate to the transit is to be accepted. Regarding this, Gobhila says:
"When the sun transits at night, one should perform that rite during the day;
whether in the preceding or the following [day], the fruit thereof results from proximity."

By the phrase "due to proximity," this is stated: if the transit occurs in the first watch of the night (*pūrvarātra*), then the latter half of the preceding day is meritorious; if it occurs in the last watch of the night (*apararātra*), then the first half of the following day is meritorious. If it occurs at midnight (*madhyarātra*), then because there is no specific distinction, both the latter half of the preceding day and the first half of the following day are meritorious days. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "If [the transit] is below midnight, the ritual act is performed after midday."
After the sun has risen, for two praharas during its upward movement.
"If the sun enters [a new sign] at the exact moment of midnight,
then both days are meritorious, with the exception of Capricorn and Cancer.
Regarding the cases of Capricorn and Cancer, there is the statement of Yajñapārśva:
[238] When the sun’s transit (*saṃkrama*) occurs during the day, it is meritorious for bathing and giving gifts for half a day.
When the transit of the sun occurs at night, it is on the day of the equinox (*viṣuvat*) or the solstice (*ayana*).

Regarding the phrase "on the day of the solstice" (*ayane dine*): when the transit occurs during the day in either the southern or northern course, the meritorious time is indeed that day. Therefore, when the transit of a solstice occurs at night, the meritorious time is even more excellent during that very night.
Baudhāyana says: When the sun, having set, enters the sign of Pisces—
at either evening or at midnight— then another day becomes meritorious.
When the sun, having abandoned the sign of Sagittarius,
enters Pisces at either evening or midnight, then the transit occurs on the following day.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: When [the sun] has passed through Sagittarius and Pisces and reaches Virgo and Gemini,
if it transits during the night according to the division of the first and second halves, [it is a time for giving].
At the end of the day, five *nāḍīs* are remembered as most meritorious;
likewise, at sunrise, five are so for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
In this context, because of the statement regarding its being the most meritorious, there is a great contradiction with the [prescription for] half a day or a fortnight. The Nigama states:
"When [the sun is] in Viṣṇupadī, or indeed in Sagittarius, Pisces, Aries, or Virgo..."
Whether from behind or from ahead, the transition may occur during the night.
"The five *nāḍīs* of the forenoon are declared by the wise to be auspicious, as are the five [of the afternoon], for rites according to the *śruti* and the *smṛti*. Thus [it is said].
‘Nṛyuk’ refers to the zodiac sign of Gemini. He also states the division of the transition (*saṃkrānti*) into prior and subsequent parts based on the distinction of lunar days (*tithi*):
“One should know it to be meritorious at the beginning, provided the lunar day remains undivided;
but once midnight has passed, it should be understood as occurring on the following day.”

The meaning of the statement is that even if the transit occurs within the middle of the previous lunar day (*tithi*) after midnight, then the previous day alone is meritorious; however, if the transit occurs within the subsequent lunar day, then the latter day alone is so. Now, in order to state an exception (*pratiprasava*) for specific transits regarding bathing and other acts prohibited at night, the prohibition itself is first stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"One should not perform bathing at night, nor especially giving gifts;
yet one may perform occasional (*naimittika*) bathing and giving of gifts even during the nights."
Viṣṇu states: "During marriage, vows, the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), consecrations, the birth of a child,
as well as during eclipses, falls [of meteors], and so forth, night is auspicious for bathing and giving gifts."

‘Ṛtu’ refers to conception. ‘Pāta’ is the moment of conjunction during which the moon and sun are visible. Gobhila states: “At the sight of Rāhu [an eclipse], at the solstices, at marriage, at times of calamity, and on occasions of prosperity...”
One should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other such rites at night during optional vows.

‘*Atyayaḥ’ refers to the death of a kinsman. Here, by the word ‘transit’ (*saṃkrānti*), only Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*) are intended; for Vasiṣṭha, in stating that the day is meritorious when the transit occurs at night, specifies “excepting Capricorn and Cancer. Therefore, it is understood that the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding bathing and other rites at night applies only to Capricorn and Cancer. Regarding the other transits, according to the statements of Gobhila and others, the prohibition of bathing and other rites at night certainly remains in force.

On this point, some maintain the following: The rule "excepting [the transits of] Capricorn and Cancer" is an exception to the requirement of taking both halves of the preceding day; it is not, however, an instruction to take the night as a substitute for the entire day. This is because the statements of Baudhāyana and others declare that when the transit occurs at night, only the subsequent day is meritorious (*puṇyāha*). As for the rules regarding the taking of half a day (*dinārdha*), they are intended to mean that if bathing, giving gifts, and so forth are impossible during the sixteen *nāḍikās* (or similar duration) immediately following the transit at night—due to some circumstance—even a distant half-day may be taken. Thus, they say that there is a general counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) allowing bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at night for all transits whatsoever.

Others, however, say that on the occasion of the sun’s transit (saṃkramaṇa), the day is meritorious, whereas for the transit of other planets, the night alone is meritorious. Jaimini also states the merit of the time of transit for other planets: "At the sun's transit into a lunar mansion or a zodiacal sign, six and thirty nāḍīs [preceding and following] are [meritorious]."
Likewise, three palas of the moon are declared by the sages to be auspicious as a single nāḍī.
The [ascensional] differences (nāḍīs) for Mars are four and six palas; for Mercury, three and fourteen palas;
and for Jupiter, four and a half plus seven palas.
And when Venus is in the fourth house from the Guru, there are four with Palāśa.
The two *nāḍīs* of the elephant, joined with seven *palas*, are declared to be most auspicious for Śanaiścara;
during these, one should perform recitation (*japa*), giving (*dāna*), and fire-offerings (*homa*) at the beginning, end, and middle.
By performing this, one attains the abode of the lord of men.

When there is a transit (*saṃkramaṇa*) of the sun into a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or a zodiacal sign (*rāśi*), the period of merit (*puṇyakāla*) consists of sixteen *ghaṭikās*—that is, sixteen *nāḍīs*—extending both before and after that time. For the moon (*indu*), however, it is one *ghaṭikā* joined with thirteen *palas*, specifically three *dharā-palas* (three *palas*) added to those thirteen. For Mars (*bhauma*), it is four *ghaṭikās* joined with one *pala*. For Mercury (*budha*), it is three *ghaṭikās* joined with fourteen *palas*. For Jupiter (*guru*), the teacher (*bṛhaspati*), it is four *ghaṭikās* joined with thirty-seven *palas*. For Venus (*śukra*), it is four *ghaṭikās* plus one *pala*. For Saturn (*śanaiścara*), it is twice eight *nāḍīs* (sixteen *nāḍīs*) joined with seven *palas*. "Nāgas" means eight; "twice-nāgas" (*dvirnāga*) refers to them repeated twice. Among these various positions regarding the exclusion or inclusion of the night, that which is capable of withstanding scrutiny (*kṣodakṣama*) should be accepted.
Thus concludes the description of the *saṃkrānti*. Now, regarding the *vyatīpāta*:
therein, Yājñavalkya provides the praise and other details.
A gift of a hundredfold at the waning of the moon, but a thousandfold at the end of the day;
a hundred-thousandfold at the equinox, and indeed infinite at the *vyatīpāta* conjunction.

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: A gift given on the new moon day (darśa) yields a hundredfold merit; that same gift on a day of solar eclipse (dinakṣaya) yields a hundred times that; on the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti) it yields a hundred times the latter; and on the equinoxes (viṣuva) it yields a hundred times that again.
Those who know the Vedas understand that at the beginning of a Yuga, a gift is a hundredfold; at the solstice, it is multiplied by a hundred;
during a lunar eclipse, it is multiplied by a hundred; during a solar eclipse, it is inexhaustible;
and during the Vyatīpāta yoga, they know the gift to be infinite.
"Śataghna" means "multiplied by a hundred. *Vyatīpāta* here refers to the seventeenth among the yogas, beginning with *viṣkambha*. Regarding its origin, Gālava says:
"A most fierce person, born from the gaze of the eyes of the Moon and the Sun, resembling the splendor of the fire of time (*kālānala*)."
When a planet is rising, another is setting, and they are observed in conjunction, this is called the *vyatipāta* yoga.

Furthermore, bathing, giving gifts, performing *śrāddha*, and other such rites performed at the times of its emergence, its circling, and its descent, as well as immediately after it has descended, yield great fruit. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"At the time of its emergence, [the merit is] a hundred-thousandfold; at the hour of its circling, it is ten-millionfold;
at the time of its descent, it is multiplied by a hundred million; and when it has descended, recitation, giving, and so forth become inexhaustible."
And regarding the duration of birth and so forth, it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"In the case of birth [of a planet], the duration is twenty-two [nāḍīs]; in its revolution, twenty-one;
in its fall, ten nāḍīs; and when it has fallen, seven nāḍīs."
But Vṛddhamanu has shown another type of *vyatīpāta*:
"If the new moon (*amā*) occurs on a Sunday under the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, or Āśleṣā, that is called *vyatīpāta*."

*Nāgadaivata* is Aśleṣā. The word "head" (*mastaka*) is connected individually with Śravaṇa and the others. Some, however, explain "head" as Mṛgaśiras. *Amā* means the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). If that [new moon] occurs on a Sunday conjoined with these lunar mansions, then that very conjunction is known by the name *vyatīpāta*. According to another treatise:
"If Jupiter and Mars are situated in Leo, and the Sun should be in Aries during the bright fortnight..."
The lunar day (tithi) joined with the Karabha [nakṣatra] and designated as Pāśa is here called the Vyatīpāta yoga.
For by the gift of cows, land, gold, and clothing in this [world], having abandoned all evil,
one attains heroism, the state of Indra, and freedom from disease.
A human being attains sovereignty over mortals.
‘Pañcānana’ is the lion. ‘Guru and Bhūmiputra’ are Jupiter and Mars. ‘Pāśābhidhānā’ is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). ‘Karabha’ is the asterism Hasta. Bhṛgu says:
“The time of the equality of declination (krāntisāmya) has been declared by the lords of sages to be similar to a solar eclipse.”
Regarding this, Bhārgava states that [the merit] is ten million times greater than that of giving, offering oblations, reciting mantras, worshipping, and performing sacrifices.

This is the meaning: when the longitudinal movements (krānti) of the sun and moon are equal, two auspicious times (puṇyakāla) occur. One is called *vyatīpāta*, and the other is called *vaidhṛti*. Among them, the *vyatīpāta*, characterized by the equality of longitudinal movement, occurs sequentially during five and a half yogas starting from the latter half of *gaṇḍa*. The one designated as *vaidhṛti*, however, occurs sequentially during five and a half yogas starting from the *śukla* yoga. Furthermore, the duration of those parvan-times is possible from ten *ghaṭikās* up to one hundred and seventy-one.
And likewise, in the *Jyotiṣa*, an auxiliary of the Vedas:
"The occurrence of the *vyatīpāta* yoga arises from the latter half of Gaṇḍa;
that which occurs at the beginning of the bright fortnight is known as *vaidhṛti*."
It is likewise held that he [the teacher] exists in relation to five other persons;
thus, this dyad is the sole means for accomplishing what is well-done.
Viṣṇu said:
"That which is given during the Vaidhṛti yoga and the Vyatīpāta yoga becomes inexhaustible.
Bharadvāja said:
There is no end to what is given during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛta yogas;
indeed, the Vyatīpāta is especially so, for it is proclaimed to be subtle.
In its broad sense, however, the twenty-seventh yoga is well known as Vaidhṛta. Regarding this, Pitāmaha states that a Śrāddha must be performed during Vyatīpāta:
"On the new moon day, during Vyatīpāta, on the full moon day, and on the Aṣṭakā days, a learned man who does not perform the Śrāddha incurs the need for expiation."
In this context, the statement "one must perform the expiation" indicates the necessity of performing the śrāddha.
Thus concludes the description of Vyatīpāta.
Now, regarding Gajacchāyā (the Elephant’s Shadow): in the Skanda Purāṇa it is said—
“When the Moon is in the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) and the Sun is situated in Hasta...”
The lunar day belonging to Vaiśravaṇa is indeed remembered as Gajacchāyā.

‘Indu’ refers to the moon; ‘pitṛdaivatyam’ refers to the lunar mansion Maghā; ‘haṃsa’ refers to the sun; ‘kara’ refers to the lunar mansion Hasta; and ‘vaiśravaṇī tithi’ refers to the thirteenth day (trayodaśī). As stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
“When the sun is situated in the sign of Leo (Haṃsa) and the thirteenth lunar day is conjoined with Maghā...”
That lunar day is indeed named Vaiśravaṇī; it is the shadow of the elephant.
In the *Brahmāpurāṇa*: "The conjunction of the Maghā constellation and the thirteenth lunar day is known as *kuñjaracchāya*;
it occurs when the moon is situated in Maghā and the sun is positioned in Hasta."

This is the meaning: when the sun is situated in Hasta and there is a conjunction with Maghā presided over by the Moon on the thirteenth lunar day, that is designated as *gajacchāyā* (elephant-shadow). And this occurs during the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada. The word *chāyā* is neuter according to the rule *vibhāṣā senāsurācchāyā*. Baudhāyana said: "That new moon which, while the sun is in Haṃsa (Svāti), is conjoined with Karā (Hasta), should be known as *kuñjaracchāyā*."
"Haṃsa" refers to the Sun; because the constellation Hasta has Haṃsa as its presiding deity, it too is called "haṃsa. "Endowed with rays" means accompanied by the Moon and the [constellation] Haṃsa.
As it is said: "When Rāhu (Saiṃhikeya) swallows the Sun during the junctions of the lunar phases, that is declared to be Gajacchāyā; one should perform the Śrāddha rite at that time."

‘Saiṃhikeya’ is Rāhu. ‘At the junctions of the lunar phases (parvasandhiṣu)’ means at the junctions of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad). ‘Gajacchāyā’ (the shadow of the elephant)—by way of context, this term is also used to denote a specific time or place. Manu says:
“May there be born in our lineage one who would give [to us] on the thirteenth day.”
And milk-rice with honey and ghee, when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east.
A region where the shadow falls toward the east is called a "prākchāya" region; it is in such a region that the elephant is well known.
This is also stated in the Mahābhārata:
"With a goat made entirely of copper, one whose vow is fixed during the rainy season..."
[246] "In the shadows of elephants, one should offer a *śrāddha* according to the rule, fanned by the flapping of ears"—this is the remainder of the sense.

By the phrase "with all iron," meaning with an animal whose entire body is red, and by the mention of being "fanned by the flapping of ears," it is understood that this statement refers specifically to the shadow of a living elephant. (As stated) in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
When the moon has entered a tree, its shadow should face the east;
that is called "Gaja-chāyā" (the elephant's shadow), and one should perform the Śrāddha rite during it.
The meaning is "in the afternoon of the new moon day.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One should feed the Brahmins with ghee and pour ghee upon the ground."
One should also offer a śrāddha in the shadow of an elephant; such a person does not grieve.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the words of the ancestors are as follows:
"At Gayā, during the appearance of Rāhu, one should feed a yogin with the meat of a rhinoceros under the shadow of an elephant within our lineage."
By that, we shall have satisfaction that lasts for an aeon;
the donor shall become one who acts according to his will in all worlds.
If even one of these five were not present, we would still attain great satisfaction; how much more so when all these riches are complete?
In this regard, the fault of one who eats at a *śrāddha* is shown in another *smṛti*:
"One who accepts a black antelope skin, one who sells semen, and one who eats while reclining in the 'elephant's shadow'—such a person shall not become a man again. Thus it is said.
It is also stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Having eaten during a period of impurity following death or birth, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or in the shadow of an elephant, one shall go to hell."

And this is the fault regarding eating in "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā). Some have stated that it refers to the shadow of an actual elephant perceived by the senses, while others say it refers to the technical or conventional definition of "elephant-shadow. In this matter, no clear distinguishing reason is found; thus, the fault applies universally.
This concludes the determination of "elephant-shadow."
Now, regarding the eclipse of the moon and the sun:
concerning the praise and other matters therein, Śātātapa says:
"Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and ancestral rites (śrāddha) yield infinite merit at the sight of Rāhu."
The night belongs to the Asuras; therefore, one should avoid it.
Devala says:
Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed during the daytime on the occasion of a solar eclipse,
so too are bathing and giving gifts ordained at night for a lunar eclipse.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "When Rāhu, the great planet, eclipses either the moon or the sun, the merit is said to be inexhaustible; this is especially so when it occurs at the sun."
‘Dṛṣṭe’ means ‘fit for seeing. Vyāsa says:
“All gifts are equal to land; all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā.”
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, all water is equal to the Gaṅgā;
the merit is a hundred thousandfold when the moon is eclipsed, and ten times that when the sun is eclipsed.
But when the waters of the Gaṅgā are present, the merit is ten millionfold for the moon and one hundred millionfold for the sun.

In the Devīpurāṇa: "An eclipse during the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent; but an eclipse during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā, O great sage, is meritorious."
In Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious; in Māgha, the Sannihatī is auspicious;
in Phālguna, the Varaṇā is meritorious; and in Caitra, the Sarasvatī is meritorious.
In the month of Vaiśākha, the excellent river Candrabhāgā is meritorious;
in Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; and in Āṣāḍha, the Tāpikā river [is meritorious].
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the river named Sindhu is preeminent; in Prauṣṭhapada, the Gaṇḍakī is most excellent;
in Āśvina, the Sarayū is supreme; and furthermore, the Narmadā is exceedingly meritorious.
The Godāvarī is greatly meritorious when the moon is joined with Rāhu,
and when the sun is eclipsed by the moon— that form of darkness, O high-minded one.
Through contact with the waters of the Narmadā, a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
even ordinary men touch and immerse themselves therein.
By remembering [this], one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; by seeing it, the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
by touching it, the merit born of a Gomedha sacrifice; by drinking [the water] there, one attains the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice;
and by bathing there, one undoubtedly acquires the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
During an eclipse of the sun or moon, as well as during the northern solstice, the Gaṅgā should be viewed in this same way; likewise, the goddess Sarasvatī.
In the expression "Gaṅgā-Yamunā," the entire *dvandva* compound optionally takes the singular form; thus, there is a singular collective state (*ekavadbhāva*).

[249] Although here one observes a designation primarily based on an extended application (*atideśa*), as in "But in Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious," nevertheless, in accordance with the introductory statement "In Kārttika, the taking of the vow (*grahaṇa*) is best," it should be understood that in all cases the time of the vow itself is what is primary.
Vyāsa says:
If it falls on a Sunday, it belongs to the Sun; likewise, if it falls on a Monday, it belongs to the Moon.
This is known as the Cūḍāmaṇi [yoga], and in that case, the fruit shall be infinite.
Whatever merit is obtained on other weekdays during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
that merit is said to be multiplied ten millionfold during the Cūḍāmaṇi yoga.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "A Śrāddha offered at the sight of Rāhu remains [efficacious] as long as the moon and stars exist; endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire."
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said:
"Indeed, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony,
by him the entire earth is effectively placed into the hand of the brāhmaṇa."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"The gods are satisfied at the moment of contact, likewise the ancestors;
humans [are satisfied] at the middle time, and the Rākṣasas at the time of release."
The meaning is that when a *śrāddha* is performed at the beginning, middle, and end of an eclipse, the gods and others are satisfied respectively.
Śātātapa states in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"A *śrāddha* must indeed be performed upon the sight of Rāhu, even at the cost of one's entire possessions."
But one who does not perform that śrāddha sinks like a cow in the mud.

[250] This statement indicates the necessity of the *śrāddha*. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, having established the necessity of this *śrāddha* as being occasional (*naimittika*), its optional nature (*kāmyatva*) is also set forth: "The new moon day, the three *aṣṭakās*, the three [days] beginning with the month of Pauṣa, the three auspicious *anvaṣṭakās*, and likewise the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha."
The thirteenth lunar day conjoined with the Maghā constellation, especially during the rainy season—
these are declared to be the daily, obligatory times for performing the ancestral śrāddha rites.
However, a funeral rite for kinsmen must be performed during an eclipse of the moon or sun; otherwise, one would become a denizen of hell.
Voluntary śrāddhas are recommended during eclipses and similar occasions; likewise, at the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the vyatīpāta yoga, they yield infinite merit.

"At the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the Śrāddha is inexhaustible; likewise on birthdays and under all lunar mansions (nakṣatras), the optional (kāmya) rite should especially be performed. Thus it is stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.

O son, [one should perform it] upon meeting a distinguished Brahmin, during solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), during the Vyatīpāta yoga,
upon obtaining materials suitable for a Śrāddha, and likewise upon seeing an evil dream.
"One should perform a Śrāddha at will during afflictions caused by planets at the time of one's birth-star.

Here, the meaning of "at will" (*icchayā*) is that one should perform the Śrāddha at times such as a solar eclipse with the desire for the fruit of heaven; it does not mean, however, that one should perform it only if one wishes to do so, and not otherwise. [251] In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the time of death, or upon the birth of a son—even during an intercalary month—a gift should be given; what is thus given brings about inexhaustible merit.
Śātātapa says:

In times of distress, when there is no sacred fire, at a holy bathing place, and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a twice-born man may perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a rite with raw food); however, a Śūdra may always perform it [in this manner].
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When there is an eclipse of the sun or moon at night, and likewise an eclipse of the moon during the day,
one should not perform a ritual bath, nor should one ever give a gift."
Thus concludes the determination of the lunar days (grahaṇa). Now, the beginnings of the Yugas. In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
The third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika,
the full moon of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya—
these are remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas (Yugādis), which cause what is given to be inexhaustible.
*Nabhasya* is *Bhādrapada*. Here, all days except for the thirteenth are auspicious in the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*). Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The Kṛta Yuga was established on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha;
the Tretā [Yuga] was established on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika."
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Dvāpara Yuga begins;
and likewise, on the full moon day of Māgha, the terrible Kali Yuga begins. These lunar days are traditionally remembered as the "Yugādyas," the beginnings of the Yugas.

The ellipsis is "the Kṛtayuga has commenced. Regarding this, some— considering that the two beginnings of the Yugas are situated in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) based on the statement from the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*, "O Kṛṣṇa, the wise know the two [beginnings] to be likewise in the two hundred [days]"— assert that the new moon of Māgha alone is the beginning of the Yuga (*yugādi*).
And so it is said in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Now listen, O Indra among kings, to the beginnings of the Yugas, which are dear to the ancestors;
by the mere recitation of their names, even the accumulation of sins is destroyed."
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava,
the new moon of Tapas (Māgha), and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa) are,
respectively, the beginnings of the Tretā, Kṛta, Kali, and Dvāpara ages.
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, and especially during the libations for the ancestors,
these [times] render what has been performed inexhaustible and yield great fruit for one's meritorious deeds.
"In Mādhava" means in Vaiśākha; "sitā" means the bright fortnight; "of Tapas" means of Māgha.
[This is stated] in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "That which is the third day of the month of Vaiśākha..."
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika;
the thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya; and [the same] in the month of Māgha.
A self-restrained man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him, a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years.
The ancestors call this a secret.
The connection is as follows: "That which is the third, that which is the ninth," and so forth.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
"The third day of Vaiśākha is equal to the Kṛta Yuga."
That ninth day of the month of Kārttika is indeed equal to the Tretā Yuga.
The thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya is considered equal to the Dvāpara age;
O King, the fifteenth day of Māgha is remembered as equal to the Kali age.
O King of kings, these four auspicious beginnings of the ages are called "the first days of the ages" (yugādis) by the ancient sages for that reason.
Fasting, austerity, charity, ancestral rites, burnt offerings, and likewise the chanting of mantras—
whatever is performed here, all of it becomes ten millionfold in merit.

It is equal to the Kṛta Yuga. The meaning is that the merit which would be obtained by performing rituals every single day throughout the entire Kṛta Yuga is obtained on this very lunar day alone. Here, the word *koṭi* refers to an extreme abundance.
As stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"The third day of Vaiśākha and the ninth day of Kārttika..."
The fifteenth day of Māgha and the thirteenth day of Nabhasya are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas; gifts given on these occasions yield inexhaustible results.
Devala says: The third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha joined with Rohiṇī,
and the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya joined with Maghā.
For these are remembered as the beginnings of the ages (yugādi), which cause what is given to become inexhaustible.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
men should perform the Śrāddha according to the procedure for a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*)."
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada and of Māgha, on the day of the moon's waning,
a Śrāddha should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa), just as in the case of the Dakṣiṇāyana.
The meaning is "without the offering of rice-balls" (piṇḍanirvapaṇa). Thus end the beginnings of the Yugas. Now, the endings of the Yugas.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"At the sun's transit into Leo, there is the end of the Kṛta Yuga;
then, at the transit into Scorpio, there is the end of the Tretā Yuga."
The end of the Dvāpara age is designated by the sun's transit into Taurus (Vṛṣa-saṃkrānti),
and likewise, the end of the Kali age occurs at the transit into Aquarius (Kumbha-saṃkrānti).
It is said that a Śrāddha performed on these beginnings and ends of the ages yields inexhaustible merit.
Thus end the sections on the ends of the Yugas. Now follow the beginnings of the Manvantaras, as described in the Mātsya and Brahma Purāṇas.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh day of Pauṣa,
the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
The tenth day of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the month of Māgha,
the full moon of Kārttika, the full moon of Phālguna, the full moon of Caitra, and likewise the fifteenth of Jyeṣṭha—
these are the beginnings of Manvantaras, which render whatever is given inexhaustible.

[255] One should know that bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors— all these, when performed on the first days of the Manvantaras, become inexhaustible.
Except for the new moon day (amāvāsyā) and the eighth day (aṣṭamī), all [the others] are indeed bright fortnights (śukla).
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa, it is established that the new moon day of Śrāvaṇa and the dark eighth day of Bhādrapada are the beginnings of Manvantaras (manvantarādayaḥ). For example:
"The bright ninth day of Āśvina, and likewise the twelfth day of Kārttika..."
The third day of the month of Caitra and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
Likewise, the new moon of Śrāvaṇa, the eleventh day of Pauṣa,
the tenth day of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya, the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Caitra, as well as the fifteenth day of Jyeṣṭha—
these are indeed the beginnings of Manvantaras, which render whatever is given inexhaustible.

In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*, it is stated that the third day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is also the beginning of a Manvantara: "O child, O lord of men, hear from me those [days] which are the beginnings of Manvantaras;
they are eternally dear to the ancestors and bring about the destruction of all sins."
In those [days], even a mere offering of water mixed with sesame seeds,
given to the ancestors upon the earth with a mind purified by faith, attains imperishability.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth of Kārttika,
the third of Māgha, and likewise that of Bhādrapada.
The new moon day of the month of Tapasya, as well as the eleventh day of Pauṣa;
likewise, the tenth day of Āṣāḍha and the seventh day of the month of Māgha.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
and likewise that of the month of Kārttika and of Phālguna.
O King, these five full-moon days—Caitra, Jyeṣṭha, and Māsa—are declared to be the beginnings of Manvantaras; among them, those which are full for you [are especially significant].
Having bathed even in these [rivers], whoever should offer [water] mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass,
dedicating it to the ancestors, shall attain the supreme goal.
In this world and in the next, by the grace of the ancestors,
what need is there for various kinds of food, flavors, garments, or ritual fees?
In the *Matsya-purāṇa* and the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"That [day] on which, at the beginning of a Manvantara, the Sun ascended his chariot on the seventh day of the month of Māgha— that indeed shall be known as Rathasaptamī."
A self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him, a śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years.
The ancestors declare this to be a secret.
Thus end the beginnings of the Manvantaras. Now, the beginnings of the Kalpas. Regarding this, it is said in the Nāgarakhaṇḍa:
Now, O King, the auspicious lunar days (tithis) marking the beginning of the Kalpas and other such periods are described;
when a Śrāddha is performed on these days, the satisfaction of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
In ancient times, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Śveta Kalpa occurred;
on its thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, Udāna was born.
The Kalpa named Nārasiṃha began on the first lunar day of the dark fortnight;
then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Gaurī-kalpa was also fashioned.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, Nīlalohita [appeared];
but on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, the one named Gāruḍa set forth.
Samāna, however, was born on the second day of the dark fortnight;
Māheśvara met with him on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
O King, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the manifestation of Vāmadeva occurred;
and on the full moon of that same month, the Kūrma incarnation took place.
On the third day of the dark fortnight, he encountered the Āgneya;
on the new moon day of the fortnight of the ancestors, it spread by resorting to that very [fire].
On the pure fourth day of the bright fortnight, the Rathyantara ritual was performed;
on the corresponding fourth day of that same dark fortnight, the Soma ritual took place.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, Raurava appeared;
on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of that same month, Mānava came into being.
Having reached the sixth lunar day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, he became Prāṇādhipa;
but on the sixth day of the dark fortnight, his [aspect] named Tatpuruṣa arose.
O lord of the people, after many kalpas, Vaikuṇṭha entered [the body] during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, and likewise during its dark fortnight.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the Kalpa named Kandarpa arose;
on the dark fortnight, however, the conception of the Lakṣmīkalpa was born.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Saṅghakalpa was undertaken;
on the dark fortnight, however, the Sāvitrīkalpa commenced.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, Īśāna indeed appeared;
on the dark fortnight, the commencement of the Aghora Kalpa took place.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, Vyāna was born;
and on that very same mixed lunar day, O King, Vārāha appeared.
O King, O high-minded one, the Sārasvata sacrifice takes place on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, while the Virāja sacrifice occurs on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight.

Thus, these thirty kalpas are the lunar days (tithis) of Parameṣṭhin; I have declared them to be the most meritorious commencement days. When a śrāddha is performed on those days, its merit extends for the duration of a kalpa.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The third day of Vaiśākha, the dark [third] of Phālguna,
the fifth of the month of Caitra, and likewise its final [fifth]."
The thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the seventh of Kārttika,
and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa— these seven I remember as the beginnings of the Kalpas; indeed, they render whatever is given inexhaustible.

The "final" [day] is the new moon (amāvāsyā). The third of Vaiśākha, the third of Phālguna, the fifth of Caitra, and the new moon of Caitra are the dark [parvan days]. The thirteenth of Māgha, the seventh of Kārttika, and the ninth of Mārgaśīrṣa are the bright [parvan days].
These are the beginnings of the Kalpas.
Now, the time is characterized by the availability of the material requisites for a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"But when the requisite materials for a sacred occasion are available, one need not observe a restriction of time."
And having obtained a worthy Brahmin as a recipient, the Śrāddha rite is ordained to be performed immediately.

A "sacred ford" (*tīrtha*) refers to Gayā and the like; "substance" (*dravya*) refers to food and so forth, as will be described later. Having obtained a Brāhmaṇa distinguished by such qualifications as being a master of the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one should not wait for another time, but rather perform the *śrāddha* at that very moment. Here, from the expression "immediately" (*sadyas*), its obligatory nature is understood. As stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:

"Upon obtaining a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, at the solstices (*ayana*), when there is an abundance of materials suitable for a *śrāddha*, and likewise upon witnessing misfortune..."
"One should perform a śrāddha at will during afflictions caused by planets at the time of one's birth-star. Thus it is said.
In this regard, it has already been explained in the section on "Receiving" (*grahaṇaprakaraṇa*) how the word "desire" (*icchā*) is not contradicted by [the rule of] permanence.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "And when a learned *śrotriya*, a knower of the Vedas who maintains the sacred fires, comes to one's house..."
Even by that single person, an auspicious *śrāddha* should be performed, just as at the equinoxes (*viṣuva*).
When the materials for a Śrāddha are obtained and there is the company of virtuous persons,
the Śrāddha should be performed by the best of the twice-born according to the Pārvaṇa rite.

In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, even the optional (*kāmya*) *śrāddha* is mentioned at a time characterized by the availability of suitable materials and a qualified Brahmin. For instance, immediately following the statement, "Listen to the rites for specific desires," there occurs this passage: "When one recognizes that a desirable material for the *śrāddha* has arrived, or a distinguished twice-born guest, one should perform the *śrāddha*; likewise during the *vyatīpāta* yoga or at the solstices (*ayana*)."
Thus concludes the determination of the time characterized by the perfection of the substance and the Brahmin.
[260] Now follows the miscellaneous times.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: Hereafter I shall proclaim that which was uttered by Viṣṇu—
the Śrāddha known as "Common," which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the double transit of the sun, or at any ordinary solar ingress;
or on the new moon day, or during the Aṣṭakā festivals, especially in the dark fortnight.
During the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; when there is an encounter between a material object and a Brāhmaṇa; during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, Vaidhṛti, and on Sundays.
Likewise,
in the Brahma Purāṇa, regarding the full moon day of Vaiśākha, an eclipse, and the festival of Mahālaya: [it states as follows].
In this world, one should offer the *śrāddha* ceremony every month at the waning of the moon;
likewise, the *śrāddha* should also be performed on the full-moon day when the moon enters a new constellation.
O Lord of Cows, men here should always perform the *śrāddha*;
likewise, the wise should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* on occasions such as birth ceremonies and the like.
When the sun has entered Virgo, for fifteen days,
the Śrāddha is prescribed there according to the Pārvaṇa rite.
Jātūkarṇa said:
"During an eclipse of a planet, upon the birth of a son, during the Maghā constellation for ancestral rites, or during either of the two solstices."
Whatever is given constantly in a conch-shell and likewise in a lotus becomes equal to a thousand gold coins.

In this context, some, interpreting the word *nityam* (constant) as being connected with the verb *dattam* (given), assert that rites such as the *śrāddha* are obligatory on occasions like lunar eclipses. Alternatively, *anityam* may mean "daily" or "throughout one's life.
