Regarding the phrase "in the *maghā* [nakṣatra] for the ancestors," the meaning is: in the *maghā* constellations situated within the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. Śaṅkha himself also states the definition of the two [terms]: "The best of the twice-born call the new moon day, when the moon has waned, 'Śaṅkha';
the *aṣṭakā* days are 'Padma'. What is given on those two occasions is likewise inexhaustible."
But Śaṅkha said:
"When there is a Viṣṭi yoga, a Vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise a Sunday, that is declared to be named Padmaka; and its merit is four times that of an Ayanā."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "He who always performs a *śrāddha* during the dark fortnight of Āśvina and the first [fortnight] of Kārttika shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
At that time, Janārdana, the soul of all, abandons sleep;
a śrāddha performed then is infinite—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise,
O King, one should know that a śrāddha performed during an eclipse of Rāhu is inexhaustible;
it should also be performed at the ripening of rice and at the ripening of barley.
O Great King, those two should never be abandoned except on the occasion of a śrāddha ceremony.
Śātātapa says:
"The ancestors long for food during fresh rains, at the first-fruits, upon the covering of a house, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism."
Therefore, one should always give with diligence to learned Brahmins.
The Grandfather said:
"On the new moon day, during the vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon day, and on the aṣṭakā days,
a learned man who does not perform the śrāddha falls into hell."
Thus end the miscellaneous times.
Now, the times for optional *śrāddha* rites.
Among these, first are the lunar days (*tithis*). On this point, Kātyāyana says:

Now follow the rites for specific desires (*kāmyāni*). On the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), one obtains beautiful women; on the second, the birth of daughters; on the third, horses; on the fourth, small livestock; on the fifth, sons; on the sixth, one becomes a traveler; on the seventh, agriculture; on the eighth, trade; on the ninth, one-hoofed animals; on the tenth, cattle; on the eleventh, servants; on the twelfth, wealth, grain, base metals, and preeminence among one's kin; on the thirteenth, gold; on the fourteenth, young men who have been slain by weapons; and on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), everything. Thus it is said.
Āpastamba.

When performed on any day of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), one gratifies the ancestors; however, due to the restriction of time, there are specific differences in the results for the performer. When performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born. On the second, a female-dominated lineage. On the third, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). On the fourth, small livestock. On the fifth, a male child who has many offspring and does not die childless. On the sixth, one who is habitually traveling and gambling with dice. On the seventh, success in agriculture. On the eighth, prosperity. On the ninth, single-hoofed animals. On the tenth, success in legal affairs. On the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead. On the twelfth, one becomes possessed of cattle. On the thirteenth, one has many friends, handsome offspring, but reaches the age of youth and dies. On the fourteenth, success in weaponry. On the fifteenth, prosperity.
"By constantly performing acts of faith, one attains [the goal]," so states Viṣṇu in the section concerning eligibility.

On the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), one obtains beautiful women in the home; on the second, an excellent maiden; on the third, horses; on the fourth, fame; on the fifth, prosperity; on the sixth, victory at gambling; on the seventh, agriculture; on the eighth, commerce; on the ninth, cattle; on the tenth, swift steeds; on the eleventh, sons endowed with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*); on the twelfth, gold and silver; on the thirteenth, good fortune; on the fifteenth, all desires; and for the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) of those slain by weapons, the fourteenth day is recommended.
Regarding the injunction "one should perform the *śrāddha*," Hārīta states:

one desiring a son [should perform it] on the fifth lunar day; one desiring wealth on the sixth; one desiring cattle on the seventh; one desiring sovereignty on the eighth; one desiring victory on the ninth; one desiring food on the tenth; one desiring prosperity on the eleventh; one desiring a wife on the twelfth; one desiring fame on the thirteenth; one desiring spiritual power (*bhūti*) on the fourteenth; and one desiring well-being (*svasti*) should perform it on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), while one desiring all things may do so on that same day. Paiṭhīnasi says:

On the fifth day, one desiring a son should sacrifice; on the sixth, one desiring cattle; on the seventh, one desiring prosperity; on the eighth, one desiring food; on the ninth, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); on the tenth, one desiring all things; on the eleventh, one desiring wealth; on the twelfth, one desiring land; on the thirteenth, mastery over women; on the fourteenth, [the offering is for] those killed by weapons; and on the new moon day, one desiring all things. Manu says: "Performing a *śrāddha* on the first day of the lunar fortnight, one obtains handsome sons."
On the second day, however, one should give a maiden; on the third day, bards.
On the fourth day, one obtains small animals; on the fifth, beautiful sons;
on the sixth, gambling; and on the seventh, a man also gains agriculture.
On the eighth day as well, the giver of a śrāddha always obtains success in trade;
on the ninth day, he obtains single-hoofed animals, and likewise on the tenth day, double-hoofed animals.
Likewise, on the eleventh day [one obtains] silver and sons endowed with Vedic luster;
on the twelfth day, gold, silver, and even base metals.

On the thirteenth day, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; on the fourteenth day, one gains excellent offspring, and his ancestors, as well as those who were slain by weapons in battle, are gratified.
By performing a śrāddha on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight, one attains all desires— those specified for the first day of the month and others— which are vast and pleasing to the mind.
"Vandinaḥ" refers to panegyrists.
[This is stated] in the *Brahma Purāṇa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, for fifteen days..."
In that case, the Śrāddha is prescribed according to the Pārvaṇa rite.
The first lunar day (pratipad) leads to the acquisition of wealth; the second bestows bipeds;
the third grants desired boons; and the fourth destroys sins.
On the fifth day one attains prosperity; on the sixth, a man becomes worthy of worship;
on the seventh, lordship over the Gaṇas; and on the eighth, supreme intelligence.
On the ninth day one attains prosperity; on the tenth, the fulfillment of all desires;
and on the eleventh, one devoted to ritual action likewise obtains all the Vedas.
On the twelfth day, the worshiper of the ancestors obtains victory and gain,
as well as progeny, intelligence, cattle, prosperity, independence, and supreme nourishment.
A person devoted to faith who performs the Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day attains long life and sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
He whose young ancestors have died or been slain by a weapon must perform the rite on the fourteenth day, if he desires their satisfaction.
A pure man who diligently performs the śrāddha on the new moon day attains all his desires and enjoys residence in heaven.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Beautiful women in the home, the birth of daughters, as well as wealth,
all desired objects, fame, prosperity, victory at dice, and agriculture.
The giver of a śrāddha obtains, in due order, trade, cattle, horses, as well as sons, gold, silver, and good fortune.
O King, this [rite] should be performed starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight up until the thirteenth;
however, on the fourteenth day, it should be performed for those men who were killed by weapons.
A person who always performs the *śrāddha* on the fifteenth days obtains all their desires;
therefore, O lord of men, it should be performed with great effort.
The Śrāddha should always be performed by those who know it on the fifteenth days.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The eighth day that falls in the dark fortnight when the sun has entered Virgo is a merit-bestowing destroyer of sins, which increases the bliss of Śiva."
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these, when performed on that day, O Three-eyed One, truly become sources of great merit.
O Sage, a Śrāddha performed on that day and a Homa conducted according to the rules yield special results;
therefore, a wise person should diligently perform the Śrāddha on that occasion.
The wise know that on the fifth day there shall be a single meal, and on the sixth, a night-meal;
on the seventh day there shall be a fast, and on the eighth day one should worship Śiva.
Having worshipped Śiva with devotion, one should perform the ancestral śrāddha rite;
having performed the śrāddha according to the rules, one should eat that which has been offered to the ancestors.
But he who performs a śrāddha ceremony here, having worshipped the Three-eyed One,
for him his ancestors shall remain satisfied for fifteen years.
Thus end the lunar days for specific desires.
Now, the asterisms. Regarding this, Manu says:
By performing [the rites] on odd lunar days and under odd asterisms, one attains all desires;
and by worshipping the ancestors on even days, one obtains abundant progeny.
‘Yukṣu’ means on even [days]; ‘ayukṣu’ means on odd [days].
Yama says: by performing [the rite] on even days and lunar mansions, one shall obtain all desires.
By worshipping the ancestors during the Gajacchāyā, one obtains abundant progeny.

Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, through [the performance of this rite], one obtains heaven, progeny, vigor, heroism, land, strength, as well as a preeminent son, good fortune, prosperity, leadership, and sacred learning."
The turning of the wheel of sovereignty, as well as success in trade and other such pursuits,
freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal.
He who duly bestows at a śrāddha dharma, knowledge, medical success, base metals, cattle such as goats and the like, horses, and long life;
One who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy shall obtain all desires by [worshipping] the stars beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī.
‘Pravṛttacakratā’ is the state of possessing unimpeded sovereign power;
[it refers to] Viṣṇu.

Heaven is attained under Kṛttikā; offspring under Rohiṇī; spiritual luster under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras); success in rites for Rudra under Raudra (Ārdrā); the earth under Punarvasu; nourishment under Puṣya; prosperity under Sārpa (Āśleṣā); all desires under Paitrya (Maghā); good fortune under Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī); wealth under Āryamaṇa (Uttaraphalgunī); preeminence among kinsmen under Hasta; handsome sons under Tvāṣṭra (Citrā); success in trade under Svāti; gold under Viśākhā; friends under Maitra (Anurādhā); sovereignty under Śākra (Jyeṣṭhā); agriculture under Mūla; success in sea-voyage under Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā); all desires under Vaiśvadeva (Uttarāṣāḍhā); preeminence under Abhijit; all desires under Śravaṇa; strength under Vāsava (Śraviṣṭhā); health under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj); base metals and goods under Āja (Pūrvabhādrapadā); a house under Āhibradhna (Uttarabhādrapadā); cattle under Pauṣṇa (Revatī); horses under Āśvina (Aśvinī); and life under Yāmya (Bharaṇī).

‘Saumya’ is Mṛgaśiras; ‘Raudra’ is Ārdrā; ‘Sārpam’ is Aśleṣā; ‘Paitrya’ is Maghā; ‘Bhāgya’ is Pūrvaphālgunī; ‘Āryamaṇa’ is Uttarāphālgunī; ‘Tvāṣṭra’ is Citrā; ‘Maitra’ is Anurādhā; ‘Śākra’ is Jyeṣṭhā; ‘Apya’ is Pūrvāṣāḍhā; ‘Vaiśvadeva’ is Uttarāṣāḍhā; ‘Vāruṇa’ is Śatabhiṣaj; ‘Vāsava’ is Dhaniṣṭhā; ‘Āja’ is Pūrvā Bhādrapadā; ‘Āhibradhna’ is Uttarā Bhādrapadā; ‘Pauṣṇa’ is Revatī; ‘Āśvina’ is Aśvinī; and ‘Yāmya’ is Bharaṇī.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara: "Indeed, heaven, offspring, as well as spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa),
success in fierce rites, the earth, nourishment, and likewise prosperity [are attained through this]."
All desires, good fortune, righteousness, preeminence among kinsmen, sons endowed with beauty, success in trade, and abundance of wealth.
Gold, the kingdom of friends, a fruitful harvest,
the profits of sea-voyages, and likewise all desired objects.
Supremacy, as well as all desires, strength, and indeed health.
Base metals, houses, cows, horses, and even one's very life.
By performing the śrāddha consecutively for each individual lunar mansion, starting from Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī within the group of stars, a man undoubtedly attains [the desired fruit].
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"By worshipping the ancestors under the asterism Kṛttikā, a human being attains heaven;
one desiring offspring [attains them] under Rohiṇī, and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one obtains splendor."
One obtains valor under Ārdrā, and lands and such under Punarvasu;
by always worshipping Puṣya, one gains nourishment, and under Aśleṣā, excellent sons.
Under Maghā, one attains preeminence among kinsmen; under the two Phalgunīs, good fortune;
and under the Uttarās, one becomes disposed to generosity and possessed of offspring.
The man who offers the *śrāddha* into whose hand it falls attains preeminence;
moreover, under the asterism Citrā, he shall be endowed with beauty and likewise obtain offspring.
Svāti bestows profit from trade; Viśākhā grants the desire for sons.
Those who perform [rites] under Anurādhā attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Under Jyeṣṭhā one gains sovereignty, and under Mūla, supreme health.
Under the Āṣāḍhās one attains fame; under the Uttarās, freedom from sorrow;
under Śravaṇa, auspicious worlds; and under Dhaniṣṭhās, great wealth.
One gains knowledge of the Vedas under Abhijit, success as a physician under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), goats and other livestock under Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise a wife under Uttarabhādrapadā.

By performing a śrāddha under the Revatī asterisms, one likewise obtains base metals; under the Aśvinī asterisms, one obtains horses; and under the Bharaṇī asterisms, one attains an excellent lifespan.
Therefore, one who knows the truth should perform rites for desired objects during these lunar mansions.
As stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Yama, however, declared those *śrāddha* rites to Śaśibindu."
Listen now to those rites for the fulfillment of desires, which are prescribed individually for each of the lunar mansions.
The man who constantly performs the ancestral rite (śrāddha) with devotion and application,
he who is wise and bestows the sacred fire, and he who sacrifices— he is free from all affliction.
One desiring offspring should perform a śrāddha under Rohiṇī; under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), one obtains brilliance;
and by performing a śrāddha under Ārdrā, one attains success in cruel deeds.
One who performs a *śrāddha* under the asterism Punarvasu shall obtain a son who is a sharer of his ancestral fields;
furthermore, a man desiring prosperity should perform a *śrāddha* under the asterism Puṣya.
By worshipping the ancestors under Aśleṣā, one obtains heroic sons;
by performing the Śrāddha rite under Maghā, one becomes the most distinguished among one's kinsmen.
A man who worships the ancestors during the Phālgunī constellations attains good fortune;
he who performs this rite under the Uttarā constellation will certainly become preeminent in character.
He who offers libations to the ancestors while his hand [is joined with the moon] becomes the foremost of all;
and he who performs [the rite] under Citrā shall behold handsome sons.
One who performs [the śrāddha] under Svātī shall obtain profit from trade;
however, a man desiring a son should endeavor to perform the śrāddha under Viśākhā.
A man who undertakes [this] under Anurādhā may set the wheel in motion;
moreover, he who does so constantly under Jyeṣṭhā shall obtain supreme sovereignty.
Under Mūla one desires health; under Āṣāḍhā, Maheśvara [is propitiated];
and under the Uttarā-Āṣāḍhās, a man shall be freed from sorrow.
Upon hearing [this] in the worlds of Manu, one shall attain the supreme goal;
under Dhaniṣṭhā, one shall obtain sovereignty, enjoyments, and abundant wealth.
Performing a śrāddha under the constellation Abhijit, one obtains the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs;
performing it under the constellation Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), one attains success in medicine.
In the former *prauṣṭhapada* [nakṣatra], one who partakes of the offering shall obtain many goats and other livestock;
in the latter [nakṣatra], without transgressing, he shall obtain thousands of cows.
One who performs the Revatī rite obtains wealth consisting of many base metals;
one enjoys horses under Āśvinī, and under Bharaṇī, one attains the highest lifespan.
By performing this rite of faith, Śaśibindu obtained this entire earth;
having acquired it, he ruled over it with excellence.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having performed [the rite] under the asterism Kṛttikā, the best of the twice-born obtains heaven;
under Rohiṇī, offspring; and under Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), spiritual luster."
One attains success in fierce deeds and valor under Ārdrā;
under Punarvasu, success in agriculture; under Puṣya, nourishment;
likewise, all desires under Āśleṣā, and good fortune under Maghā.
One should find wealth under Ārdrā; under Phālgunī, there is the destruction of evil;
likewise, under Hasta, preeminence among kinsmen; and under Citrā, many sons.
Success in trade under Svāti; gold-making under Viśākhā;
many friends under Anurādhā (Maitra); and likewise sovereignty under Jyeṣṭhā (Śakra).
Under Mūla one obtains success in agriculture; under Āpya (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), success from the sea;
under Vaiśvadeva (Uttarāṣāḍhā), all desires; and under Śravaṇa, preeminence once again.
Likewise, under Dhaniṣṭhā one obtains desires; under Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), supreme strength;
under Ajaikapād, base metals; and under Āhibradhna (Pūrvabhādrapadā), an auspicious house.
If one offers a śrāddha under Revatī, there will be many cattle; likewise, under Aśvinī, there will be horses;
and under Yama (Bharaṇī), one who offers the śrāddha shall have a long life.

In this regard, other statements from the *Brahma-purāṇa* and other texts, although differing in expression, do not in any way contain meanings exceeding those previously stated; therefore, they are not recorded here.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Performing śrāddhas under the Maghā nakṣatra, one shall obtain all desires."
By him, the ancestors are always directly honored.
Thus end the asterisms for optional rites. Now, the days of the week. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

One who constantly performs a *śrāddha* on Sunday attains health; on Monday, good fortune; on Tuesday, victory in battle; on Wednesday, all desires; on Thursday, the desired knowledge; on Friday, wealth; and on Saturday, long life. "On Tuesday" (*kauje*) means on the day of Maṅgala; "on Thursday" (*jaive*) means on the day of Bṛhaspati. [Source: *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now, O King, I shall describe to you the optional Śrāddhas,
which grant health, good fortune, and likewise victory in battle.
A man who always performs the śrāddha on the days of the Sun and the other planets in this manner obtains all desires, as well as knowledge, wealth, and even long life;
he attains these in due order— of this there is no doubt.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: On Sunday there is health; on Monday, good fortune;
on Tuesday, victory everywhere; and on Wednesday, all desires are fulfilled.
One shall obtain desired knowledge from Jupiter, wealth from Venus,
and furthermore, long life and very rare health from Saturn.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*,
Brahmā said:
"Those men who perform a *śrāddha* when the day of the Sun has arrived..."
Seven births have arisen for you, existing without contradiction.
O Bull-bannered One, when a lunar mansion consists of five stars and falls on the day of the God of Gods,
that day is remembered as one that bestows sons.
In that case, there should be fasting, and likewise a Śrāddha ceremony should be performed;
furthermore, the consumption of the middle *piṇḍa* is prescribed.
Having fasted, one should indeed worship the Lord of Rays (Gopati) with devotion,
using incense, garlands, and offerings endowed with divine fragrances.
Having thus worshipped Vivasvat, O hero of great intelligence, he sleeps upon the ground at night right before him while reciting the Śveta hymn; then,
rising in the morning and having performed his ablutions, he offers the supreme *arghya*.
One should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas with Karavīra flowers mixed with red sandalwood.
Having worshipped the three-eyed Lord of Planets and Spirits while he is seated,
and having likewise worshipped Vīra, one should then perform the Śrāddha rite.
O God of excellent vows, one should provide for the divine rite there with five Brāhmaṇas known as Magas, both celestial and terrestrial.
O slayer of Andhaka, having designated the Brahmins as paternal ancestors of the earth,
one should then perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha in this manner, which is dear to the Sun.
When the Śrāddha ceremony is completed according to the rules, O observer of noble vows, one should eat the middle pinda while standing before the God of gods, reciting the mantra.
O Lord of Gods, this is that very *piṇḍa* which has always been desired by you; I eat it before you so that there may be progeny for me through your grace,
O God, according to what my mind desires to request.
When the Sun-god is worshipped in this manner, he becomes the bestower of sons;
therefore, this day of the week is proclaimed as the "son-bestowing" (putrada) day of the deity.
Thus, the man who always worships Bhāskara here,
being intent on fasting during the Śrāddha ceremony, obtains a son and wealth.
Wealth, grain, gold, health, and supreme happiness;
having personally attained the world of the Sun, one shall thereafter become a king, O monarch.
In brilliance he resembled a twice-born brahmin, in luster he was like a jackal;
in valor he was equal to the Lord of Rays (the Sun), and in profundity he was like the one born from a jar (Agastya).

‘Non-hostile’ (*avirodhinaḥ*) means free from enemies. The four constellations named Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Hasta each have five stars. A ‘bull’ (*go*) that is excellent is a ‘bull-cow’ (*govṛṣa*); he whose banner is such a one is ‘Govṛṣadhvaja’ (the Bull-bannered One). The words *vṛṣa*, *vyāghra*, *puṅgava*, and *kuñjara* denote excellence when used as the final member of a compound, as seen in examples such as *bharatarṣabha*. ‘Devadeva’ refers to the Sun. Fasting (*upavāsa*) here is on Saturday; the *śrāddha* rite is on Sunday. This will become clear from the passage beginning with “having risen in the morning. The consumption of the middle *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) is understood here to apply to the sacrificer alone, whereas in other *śrāddhas* it is prescribed for the wife, and thus she performs it. However, in this case, since both husband and wife who desire a son have a joint entitlement and no specific distinction is mentioned, it is logical that both consume the *piṇḍa*. Furthermore, in other rites for those desiring a son, the consumption of the remainder by both is observed. For example, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*: “Having cooked rice with milk, they two should eat it mixed with clarified butter,” and so forth. Likewise, in this very context, after the oblation: “Having offered and taken [the portion], he eats; he gives [the remainder] to the other. ‘Gopati’ is the Sun; he is to be worshipped in an image made of gold or other materials according to the method described in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, or in the sky. ‘Śveta’ is the six-syllabled solar mantra known as Mahāśvetā, famous as *khagolkāya namaḥ*. The offering of the *arghya* water should be performed on a sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*) while facing the Sun situated in the sky. Because of the repetition of the word ‘having worshipped’ (*pūjayitvā*), another form of worship is indicated; thus, the five deities—the planets, Bhūteśa, and others—are to be worshipped on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending in the dative case. ‘Divine deer’ (*divyā magāḥ*) refers to those known as Bhojakas, who are well-known in the North as a particular class of Brahmins; others are ‘terrestrial’ (*bhaumāḥ*). Here, having seated the deer in place of the Vaiśvadeva Brahmins, one should seat other Brahmins in place of the Pitṛs. Thus, the mention of ‘always’ (*sadā*) here indicates a repetition for the sake of obtaining a specific fruit. ‘Prabhā’ is brilliance. ‘Dvija’ is the Moon. ‘Kānti’ is luster. ‘Jambuka’ is Varuṇa, according to the saying, “Varuṇa is indeed Jambuka. Varuṇa is a specific form of the Sun, as seen in the statement, “Varuṇa shines in the month of Māgha. ‘Gopati’ means Śambhu (Śiva). ‘Kalaśodbhava’ is Agastya, and he is intended here in his profound aspect.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"When the fourth lunar day occurs conjoined with the planets Venus and Mars,
a Brāhmaṇa who performs a *śrāddha* ceremony with faith shall not be reborn as a *preta* after death."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: If the Moon [be in conjunction] on the new moon day, or the Sun on the seventh,
or if there should be a Tuesday on the fourteenth or the fourth lunar day.
At that time, one who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should perform a śrāddha ceremony for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
The ancestors rejoice in heaven, seated upon celestial chariots in the sky for that very duration; such indeed is the fruit for the performer of the śrāddha.
Thus end the days for optional rites.
Now follow the miscellaneous times for optional rites.

In that regard, the Viṣṇupurāṇa states: "O Lord of Men, one should perform the Aṣṭakā rites on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight month after month; now hear from me the times for optional rites."
Having learned that a distinguished twice-born man worthy of the *śrāddha* has arrived, or that there is a special substance available,
one should perform the *śrāddha* during a *vyatīpāta* yoga or at the solstices (*ayana*).
O protector of the earth, when the equinox occurs, as well as during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
the sun moves through all the zodiacal signs.
One should perform voluntary śrāddhas during afflictions caused by constellations and planets, upon seeing evil dreams, and likewise at the arrival of the new harvest.

In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "The Śrāddha should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) month after month when the moon has waned; likewise, it must certainly be performed during the Aṣṭakās. Now learn from me the times for performing it according to one's desire."

O son, [one should perform it] upon meeting a distinguished Brāhmaṇa, during solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), during the Vyatīpāta yoga,
upon obtaining materials suitable for a Śrāddha, and likewise upon seeing an evil dream.
If one wishes, one may perform a śrāddha during afflictions caused by planets at the time of one's birth-star.
Viṣṇu also said: "The Saṃkrānti, the Viṣuva, especially the two Ayanas,
the Vyatīpāta, one's own birth-star (janmarkṣa), and likewise an eclipse of the moon or sun."
Thus Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha as being for the fulfillment of specific desires;
whatever Śrāddha is offered on these occasions conduces to infinity.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "One who is always pure should diligently perform the *śrāddha* on the new moon day;
he obtains all desires and, at the end, attains heaven."
One should offer clarified butter on the new moon day; this is the great means for nourishing Soma.
Thus nourished, Soma will sustain the three worlds.
Constantly worshipped and praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas,
he is honored with all kinds of beautiful flowers and every kind of desirable provision.
Seated in a celestial chariot, the devotee of the ancestors who is firm in his vows shall sport with thousands of Apsarases through dance, instrumental music,
and song; the gods, Gandharvas, and hosts of Siddhas always praise him.
A devotee of the ancestors, however, shall obtain all desires by worshipping the ancestral deities with devotion on the new moon day,
since the fruit thereof is inexhaustible.
Likewise: "Bestowing nourishment, progeny, memory, intelligence, sons, and even sovereignty,
one who performs [this rite] on the full moon attains everything in its entirety."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The rite for the Nāndīmukhas should be performed every year on the full moon day when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, according to the words of Varāha."

On whichever day during the month of Bhādrapada the sun enters the zodiac sign of Virgo (Kanyā), on the full moon day occurring within that month, a Śrāddha for the Nāndīmukha ancestors must be performed; for there is a scriptural injunction stating that this is obligatory every year. Furthermore, by the term "Nāndīmukha" here, the three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) are intended. For in this very Purāṇa, immediately following this statement, it is said:
"Those who are above the grandfather (pitāmaha), those three shall be the Nāndīmukhas."
"Because they possess the notion of a serene countenance, they are indeed auspicious.
In this context, by the word *pitāmaha* (grandfather), the *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather) is indicated. As it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather..."
"For these three ancestors are proclaimed to be 'tear-faced' (aśrumukha);
those three who precede them are remembered as 'joyful-faced' (nāndīmukha).

Since this statement regarding the *nāndīmukha* is syntactically unified with the injunction for the *śrāddha* occasioned by the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), the term *nāndīmukha* in other types of *śrāddha* should not be understood as referring to the three ancestors beyond the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*).

Now, for what purpose is the designation "Nāndīmukha" applied to these? It might be argued that, just as in passages such as "the Pitṛs are to be known as the Vasus," the words "Vasu" and so forth are intended to enjoin the visualization of identity with the Vasus and others, so too here the term is intended to enjoin the visualization of identity with the group of Pitṛs called Nāndīmukha, as described in the section concerning the non-difference from the group of Pitṛs belonging to the Vārāha Kalpa.

That is not correct; because it has been shown here that the derivation of the word "Nāndīmukha" is intended to mean "those whose faces are joyful" (*prasannamukha*) due to their connection with rejoicing (*nandana*). Therefore, it is not for the purpose of instructing in a visualization of identity.

Now, just as in the case of the Kauṇḍapāyinī sacrifice, where the word "agnihotra" is applied to another rite (the Sāma-homa) and, by conveying a state of similarity to that other, serves to extend the ritual details (*dharma*) of the regular *agnihotra*, so too here the term "Nāndīmukha" serves to extend the well-known ritual details of the Nāndīmukha performed on occasions such as the birth of a son. This is not so, because the answer has already been stated. For this word "para" is not employed with the intention of expressing similarity to another; rather, it is used because [the ancestors] have faces (*mukha*) that cause delight (*nandana*). Therefore, we consider its purpose to be purely commendatory (*praśaṃsā*).

Hārīta says: The Aṣṭakā rites, the Māgha offerings, festivals for prosperity, pilgrimages, and the occasions for the birth of a son— this is remembered as the constant, additional duty toward the ancestors that must be performed every month.
From the Brahmavaivarta and Vāyu Purāṇas:
Now I shall explain Time, which is honored in the rite of Śrāddha by those who perform the occasional,
the occasional-for-a-purpose, and the perpetual Śrāddha rites.
The three *aṣṭakā*s, which grant sons and are rooted in wealth—
these are the optional times for miscellaneous rites. Now follow the specific times for *śrāddha* ceremonies.

In this regard, we have already previously determined the times for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, following the sequence established by the statements of Yājñavalkya. Now, the times for the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) śrāddha are being described. Among these, first is the determination of the day of death (*kṣayāha*). In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The [śrāddha] for one's mother and father must be performed every year on the anniversary of their death."
Indeed, [the inheritance] belongs to the childless paternal uncle and likewise to the elder brother.

By the statement "the *śrāddha* for the mother and others should be performed," it is implied that it must be performed by sons and others; this is intended merely as an illustration of those entitled [to perform the rite]. In the phrase "of the brother," the words "who is sonless" (*aputrasya*) are to be supplied. By the word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭhasya*), it is shown that the annual *śrāddha* is not mandatory for a younger brother. And thus: "The father should not give [the *śrāddha*] for his son, nor likewise the elder brother for his younger brother."

Thus, because the fixed entitlement has been refuted, even for a sonless younger brother, the annual rite must certainly be performed based on an unfixed entitlement such as affection (*sneha*). And so it has been said:
"If one should perform [the rite] out of affection, provided it is without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
This has already been explained in detail previously in the section on entitlement (*adhikāra-prakaraṇa*). In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:

O Varārohā, O Mahādevī, I and Hari do not accept the worship of that man who does not perform the *śrāddha* with devotion on the anniversary of his father’s death, nor likewise on the anniversary of his mother’s death at the end of the year.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O best of birds, among all Śrāddhas, that which is always performed by the wise on the anniversary of death is considered the most excellent."
O tiger among birds, he who does not perform the śrāddha with devotion on the anniversary of his father’s death,
nor on the anniversary of his mother’s death at the end of the year—
O best of birds, neither I, nor Hari,
nor Brahmā, nor Rudra, nor any other hosts of deities accept his worship.
Therefore, O tiger among birds, a man— especially one who maintains a household— should diligently perform [the rites] every year on the anniversary of his death.
O Lord of Birds, that householder who does not perform the śrāddha for his mother and father every year on the anniversary of their death;
He goes to a terrible hell known by the name Tāmisra;
thereafter, he becomes a wicked-souled hog or a bird in a city.

Here, by the term *mṛtāha* (the day of death), what is intended is the lunar date (*tithi*) occurring on the day of death, because the primary *mṛtāha* is impossible at the end of a year. For those very same days do not recur; indeed, individual days have neither specific names nor identifying marks. Therefore, one might argue that the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) would fall on whichever day it happens to be, and not on the final day of the year, because of the rule regarding the "final day of the year. To this we reply: no.

No; for that would result in the inclusion of the day of death being rendered meaningless. Therefore, the lunar day (*tithi*) occurring on the day of death is intended. The mention of "day" (*ahaḥ*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the night; by this, that same lunar day is obtained even for one who dies at night. And thus it is established that the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) should be performed on the lunar day connected to the day of death at the end of the year.
And in this regard: "The lunar day upon reaching which the sun rises..."
That lunar day (tithi) should be known as complete for the performance of acts such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its setting,
that entire tithi is to be understood as valid for acts such as ritual bathing, giving gifts, and recitation of mantras.

Thus, according to the statements of Devala and others, just as at the time of performing a rite one accepts a lunar day (*tithi*) by imagining it to be complete even though it is not actually present, it is not so with the lunar day occurring on the anniversary of death; that day is not accepted merely because of its connection to the death, but rather only as the lunar day existing at the very moment of death. Therefore, in the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*), the lunar day denoted by the term "death-day" should be understood as precisely that which existed at the time of death.
As Vasiṣṭha states in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*:
"In the case of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*) or the death of men, the lunar day is recorded as being that which exists at that specific moment."
In the rite for the ancestors (pitrya), when touched at the time of sunset, it is called "full" (pūrṇā).

The term ‘tātkālikī’ (pertaining to that specific time) means that for both [the breaking of a fast and death], the lunar day (*tithi*) is precisely that which exists at the time when the vow, such as a fast, is concluded, or when death occurs; it is not one that exists at any other time. In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), such as the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) and others, even if the lunar day of the time of death has only three *muhūrtas* remaining during the morning or other periods, or if it merely touches the time of sunset, it is declared to be complete. When the occasion for performing the annual anniversary on the lunar day of death has arrived, if that day still exists at the end of the day even at the time of sunset, then—considering it to exist during the *kutapa* and *aparāhṇa* periods—one should perform the *śrāddha* on that very day characterized by those times, starting from the *kutapa*.
Alternatively, here by the term "day of death" (mṛtāha) is intended a full day and night (ahorātra) characterized by three specific features.
As Vyāsa says:
"On whichever day, in whichever month, fortnight, and lunar date (tithi), a person dies..."
"Each year, that anniversary of his death (kṣayāha) is known to be of such a nature.

Here, "of such a nature" means endowed with the three characteristics [of the lunar month, lunar fortnight, and lunar day]. In this context, the months, fortnights, and days and nights to be taken are exclusively lunar (cāndra), not solar (saura) or civil (sāvana). These are defined in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
"From new moon to new moon is the lunar [month]; the month consisting of thirty days is the civil (sāvana)."
A solar month is defined by those who know it as being distinguished by the sun's transit (saṃkrānti);
likewise,
a lunar month is from the first day of the bright fortnight to the new moon (darśa), and a civil (sāvana) month consists of thirty days.
"As long as the sun remains in a single zodiac sign, that period, together with the sun, is a month.
Regarding these months, Vyāsa states that for ancestral rites such as the annual *sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha*, only the lunar month is to be accepted:
"The solar month is prescribed for marriage and similar occasions; the *sāvana* (lunar-solar) month is prescribed for sacrifices and the like."
"In the annual rite for the ancestors (pitr-kārya), the month is traditionally held to be lunar. Thus says Laghu-Hārīta:
"Since the sun revolves like a wheel by the power of time..."
Therefore, the annual śrāddha should be performed, marked by the specific month.
The mark of the month must indeed be made, beginning with Pauṣa, Māgha, and so forth;
for it is by that procedure that the month is proclaimed.

The designation "Pauṣa" and so forth must be understood as referring exclusively to the lunar month. In that regard, although it is possible for the ritual time (*karmakāla*) to overlap with the following day as well, nevertheless, because there is no reason to bypass the first [day], the *śrāddha* should be performed on the preceding day alone. Sumantu says:
"If the lunar day (*tithi*) of the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) should span two days..."
"One should offer the rice-ball to the east"—this is the statement of the descendant of Aṅgiras.
Vṛddhayājñavalkya states: "The lunar day (tithi) on which the sun sets is to be known as the one for rites dedicated to the gods. This is also found in the Śivarahasya and the Saura Purāṇa.
Generally, those desiring the fruits of divine rites should fast on the latter part of the lunar day;
for the great seers have declared that the root [of the day] is for the sake of ancestral satisfaction and belongs to the ancestors.
"Root" (mūla) means the commencement.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The wise know that the portion at the end of the lunar day, called 'the liquor' (surā), is indeed to be observed as a fast."
The root of the lunar day is declared by those learned in the scriptures and experts in time to be the ancestral [deity].
The traditional teaching is: "Lunar days occurring in the forenoon are fruit-bestowing for rites dedicated to the gods;
likewise, those occurring in the afternoon should be known as auspicious for matters concerning the ancestors."

In this context, "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) refers to a subtle period of time, which should be understood as one of the various afternoons that will be described below. Therefore, for the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*), the lunar day (*tithi*) associated with the previous day should be accepted; and that [lunar day] must be taken only if it lasts for three *muhūrtas* during the afternoon, but not if it is less than three *muhūrtas*. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "When the sun has risen, it is the time for the gods; when the sun has set, it is for the ancestors.
A lunar day that lasts for two *muhūrtas* during the afternoon is [valid] for offerings to both gods and ancestors."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the sun has risen, for the subsequent period of two *muhūrtas* of the day, it is "divine" (*daivata*), pertaining to the gods. And when he has set, the three *muhūrtas* of the day preceding that are "ancestral" (*pitrya*), pertaining to the ancestors. Therefore, whichever lunar day (*tithi*) extends over such a duration of time is to be accepted, respectively, for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*). Thus, it being established that the [lunar day] lasting three *muhūrtas* prior to sunset is to be accepted, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"In the case of vows, fasts, ritual bathing, and so forth, even if it lasts for but a single *ghaṭikā*..."

"That lunar day (tithi) is to be taken at its rising; however, for rites concerning the ancestors (paitṛka), it is the opposite. Here, "the opposite" refers to that which is connected with the time of sunset. And as stated by Vyāsa:
"Even if [a tithi] exists for only a single digit (kalā) at the time of sunset during the day..."
"That very [lunar day] is to be accepted for the annual śrāddha; any other causes the loss of sons.
And as for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"In rites for the ancestors, if touched at the time of sunset, the preceding [lunar day] is declared [to be the one to be used]."

This [time] extends through three muhūrtas of the afternoon of the preceding day; why then is it praised by way of logic? It is not for the purpose of including a duration of merely one ghaṭikā or so, because such a duration is insufficient for the ritual act, and because on the following day, the afternoon sufficient for the ritual act is obtained as its extent. For this very reason, Hārīta says: "That is to say..."

The full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) on which the moon is conjoined with the asterism Puṣya is called *pauṣī*. The month in which that occurs is the *pauṣa* month. The same applies to *māgha* and the others. As Pāṇini stated: "Time conjoined with an asterism" (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*), and "[A word ending in the first case denotes] the name of that [month] in which such a full moon occurs" (*sāsmin paurṇamāsīti saṃjñāyām*). Such a designation does not exist for the solar or civil months, nor is there a fixed rule regarding their conjunction with such a full moon; therefore, at the beginning of the annual cycle and other such occasions, only the lunar month is to be taken. Furthermore, as for the statement: "In whichever zodiac sign the sun has entered when a person meets their end..."
The ancestral rites on the anniversary of death should be performed in that very same zodiac sign.
This refers to the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). If there is a misfortune during an intercalary month, one should rely on the solar measurement;
that very day shall be the [proper] time for his *śrāddha*, funeral cakes, water offerings, and so forth.

The month has been explained. Half of it is a fortnight (*pakṣa*). A lunar day (*tithi*), however, is a solar day and night (*ahorātra*) according to the moon. This is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "A solar day and night is from sunrise to sunrise; but the enjoyment of a lunar day (*tithi*), which is one-thirtieth part of the sun's zodiacal sign, is lunar (*aindava*)."

A *sāvana* day-and-night (*ahorātra*) is the period from one sunrise until the next. The "solar" (*saura*) day-and-night refers to the Sun’s passage through thirty degrees of a zodiacal sign (such as Aries and so forth); this is the meaning of "the degrees of the signs. Regarding "the duration of a lunar day" (*tithi-sambhoga*): the time required for the Moon to traverse twelve-thirtieths (twelve degrees) of a sign is the duration of a lunar day; that is a *cāndra* day-and-night, which is designated by names such as the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so on. Thus, a *sāvana* day-and-night—characterized by a month and accompanied by its specific intercalary or expunged days—is to be understood as what is expressed by the term "the anniversary of death" (*mṛtāha*).
Thus concludes the determination regarding the day of death (kṣayāha). [286] Now follows the determination regarding the duality of the day of death.
In that regard, when there is a conflict regarding the lunar day for the *kṣayāha* śrāddha, the day that pervades the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*) should be accepted. As Vyāsa says:
"Whichever time belongs to a particular rite, the lunar day that pervades that time is the one to be used for performing the rites;
its waning or waxing is no cause [for concern]."

But when there is equality of the lunar day (tithi) such that both lunar days are connected with the afternoon, then in the annual Śrāddha, which follows the procedure of the Pārvaṇa rite, the earlier lunar day alone is to be taken. For it is said: "In the ancestral rites of the forefathers during the afternoon, however, that [lunar day] which continues into the afternoon is to be accepted for the ritual of the ancestors, and not that which continues into the forenoon."
Also in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:

"When even a single ghaṭikā remains for the observance of a vow or fast, that lunar day (tithi) should be known as complete; however, for rites pertaining to the ancestors, it is that which occurs in the afternoon."
Furthermore, words such as "astam" (setting) refer specifically to the afternoon. Thus Vṛddha-Manu says: "The ancestors honor that [day] upon which the sun sets;
for the Self-Existent One himself assigned that lunar day (tithi) to them during the afternoon."
Manu also says:
"The ancestors attend that [day] on which the sun sets;
for it was given by the Self-born to the ancestors during the afternoon."
For this very reason, it is stated in the Śivarahasya, Brahmavaivarta, Saura, and Nāradīya Purāṇas:
"If one performs the annual anniversary of a father's death on the new moon or full moon day when it is overlapped by the preceding tithi, he falls into hell."
As for the scriptural statement beginning with "of the pairs, fire, pairs, and elements," that refers to the subject matter of vows, fasts, and the like. Vyāsa states this:
"The honorability of the pairs [of lunar days] on the second and subsequent days applies to observances such as restrictive rules (niyama);
however, in cases such as the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite or rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), there is an injunction regarding increase or decrease [of the duration]."

The phrase beginning with "ekoddiṣṭa" is indicative of the ancestral śrāddha (paitṛka-śrāddha). Thus, it is established that when the lunar days (tithis) are equal, the earlier one is to be accepted. However, regarding inequality, Baudhāyana says:
"That is the lunar day for which the sun rises during that day and night;
in the waxing fortnight, [it is the day] on which the sun rises, but in the waning [fortnight], it is that on which the sun sets."
Referring specifically to this very case, he himself said:
"When a lunar day (tithi) belonging to the past extends across two afternoons during its waning, the former [day] should be observed; likewise, in the case of its increase, the latter [day]."
As for what was stated by Vyāghra regarding the adoption of the subsequent lunar day even when there is equality of duration:

"Dwindling (kharva), arrogance (darpa), and likewise violence (hiṃsā)—these are the three characteristics of a lunar day. Dwindling and arrogance are to be honored as belonging to the subsequent [day], while violence belongs to the preceding time."

"Kharva" means equality; "darpa" means increase; "hiṃsā" means decrease. Let this doctrine of equality pertain to lunar days other than those associated with the new moon (kṣayāha). And as for the verse: "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken."

Such is the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya; however, because the terms "bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*) and "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) indicate rites for the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*), it must be established as referring merely to the division of time for rites for the gods and the ancestors. Thus, the determination of the connection with the *pārvaṇa* rite depends upon the contact with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). This time has been analyzed as a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rite which follows the procedure of the *pārvaṇa*. Since the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite occurs at midday, the determination of the time for the subsidiary elements of the annual *śrāddha* should be performed by carrying out the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure based on the contact with midday in both the preceding and following days. Regarding this, Manu says:
The *daivika* śrāddha is performed in the forenoon, the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) in the morning.
Hārīta also says:
"The *āmaśrāddha* is in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday,
the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon, and that performed on the occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) in the morning."
Vṛddhagautama says:
That lunar day which extends through the midday (madhyāhna) shall be the one for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite;
that which extends through the afternoon (aparāhṇa) shall be the lunar day for the Pārvaṇa rite.

Whichever lunar day (tithi) extends across midday—whether it be the preceding or the following one—it is upon that day that offerings should be given to the ancestors; neither waning nor waxing [of the moon] is a cause for concern.

Thus concludes the determination regarding the doubling of the anniversary day (*kṣayāha*) when it is omitted. Now, the times for the annual *śrāddha* when the anniversary day is unknown are given in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
Aruṇa said: O Lord of the Immortals, how can that man who does not know even the day or the month [of his parents' passing] perform the rites for his deceased parents, O highly wise one?
Let him perform the *śrāddha* for those two according to the rules for the duration of a year.
In this context, "of the parents" is an elliptical expression.
Āditya said:
"O son of Vinatā, that Mānaka who does not know the anniversary of his parents' death..."
Therefore, O King, the annual śrāddha ceremony should be performed on the new moon day.

If the date [of death] of one who has died—whether he was away from home or not—is unknown, the meaning is that the annual śrāddha should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) of that month. Bṛhaspati says this: "If the day of death is not known when someone has passed away while abroad, but the month is known, then it should be on the new moon day of that month, as if it were the day of death."
The term "when he has gone abroad" (proṣite) is an indicative mark for causes such as ignorance [of the date]. "'On the new moon' (darśe)" means on the new moon day of that month.
"'On the anniversary of death' (mṛtāhani)"—the ellipsis is "that [śrāddha] should be performed there.
Regarding this very subject, Marīci states that the śrāddha should be performed on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen and the day of death is unknown,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

In this context, by the statement that the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is more highly praised, it is understood that the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is also permitted. Consequently, when an option between the bright and dark eleventh days (*ekādaśī*) arises, the following rule is established: when the month and the fortnight are known, but the specific lunar day (*tithi*) alone is not ascertained, the *śrāddha* should be performed on the eleventh day of that fortnight belonging to that month, because there is no reason to abandon a known fortnight. Furthermore, if even the fortnight is unknown, it should be performed on the dark eleventh day; if that is unavailable, then on the bright eleventh day as well.
In the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa: "The man who knows only the day but not the month should perform [the rite] in Mārgaśīrṣa, or Bhādrapada, or Māgha."

However, for one whose day of death is known but whose month is not known, the *śrāddha* should be performed on that same day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"When the month is not known but the day alone is known, then that day shall occur in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha."

But when both the day and the month of one who has died while away from home are unknown, then the annual rite for him should be performed on the day and in the month corresponding to the time of his departure. As Bṛhaspati says: "When, moreover, the day and month of death are not known, then the day and month of departure should be taken, according to the direction previously stated."

This is its meaning: if the date of departure is known but the month is not, one should perform the annual rite on the new moon day occurring within that month; if the date of departure is known but the month is not, one should perform it on that very same date in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. However, if both the date and the month of departure are unknown, one should perform it on the date and in the month corresponding to the time when the news of his death was heard. Thus says Pracetas: "If the [date] is unknown, [one should perform it] on the new moon day or on the day of hearing [the news]. By "day of hearing," he means the lunar day on which the report of the death was heard. This is also stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Upon hearing news of death, those two [rites] should be performed according to the sequence previously stated.

Furthermore, if the lunar day (*tithi*) of death and the month are remembered, it should be performed on that very same lunar day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha. If both the lunar day and the month are forgotten, it should be performed on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) of either Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa. Thus it is said in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"If one does not know the day of death, nor the month in any way whatsoever..."
Therefore, one should perform the Śrāddha on the new moon day in the months of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa.
‘In some way’ (*kathaṃcana*) means by any characteristic whatsoever, such as hearing of the departure for death;
as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
“Even without being on a journey, those two [the husband and wife] may become separated when they have forgotten one another.”
At that time as well, those two should be grasped from the corpse and so forth, just as before.

Regarding one who has gone abroad and for whom there is news of his death, but no news of him being alive, and for whom there is no return for fifteen years— after that period, having fashioned a representation of his body with *pālāśa* wood sticks or *kuśa* grass and having performed the cremation rite according to the prescribed rules, Jātūkarṇa says that the annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsarika*) should be performed on a day corresponding to the lunar fortnight, month, and date of his passing. "When a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor his return,
after fifteen years have passed, one should fashion a representation [of him]."
Then, one should perform his consecration according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should carry out all the remaining rites beginning with that very [consecration].
And this will be shown in detail in the section on the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* for one who has died while away from home.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for the annual anniversary when the day of death is unknown.
This concludes the exposition on the timing of the annual anniversary.

[292] Now, the times for the *śrāddha* rites for the deceased (*preta*). Regarding that, Āśvalāyana—establishing the designation "nine *śrāddhas*" (*nava-śrāddha*) for those performed during the ten-day period—states that they bear the name "nine *śrāddhas*" until the end of the tenth day. Bhartṛyajña states this in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
Listen now to those three things for the purpose of accumulation:
one should perform the śrāddha at the very place where death occurred.
Then there is the ekoddiṣṭa; next, the śrāddha where rest was provided on the way; thereafter, the third śrāddha is prescribed at the place of collection (saṃcayana).
Likewise on the fifth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth,
and eleventh days— these are the nine śrāddhas;
by them, the preta who has not yet reached the Vaitaraṇī river shall obtain satisfaction.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O twice-born ones, on the third day, on the funeral pyre where the deceased was cremated, one should perform the domestic *śrāddha* at the end of the period of impurity; this they declare to be the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
Kātyāyana said: That which is given here for a living being on the fourth, the fifth, as well as the ninth and the eleventh [days], is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Vyāsa says: That which is indeed given to a living being on the first, the seventh, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [days] is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Śaṅkha says:
Even one who is not a Śūdra may perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day;
there is purity for the performer at that moment, but he remains impure thereafter.
"Fresh" means new. Paiṭhīnasi states: "In the case of immediate purification, [the gift] should be given on the eleventh day for the deceased."
That very day [is auspicious] for him when it comes to the funeral feast, the bed, the seat, and so forth.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "On the first day, one should feed the twice-born at the door of the house for the sake of the deceased;
on the second day, the clipping of the nails (or the preparation of the funeral pyre) should be performed by the kinsmen."
On the fourth day, the collection of the bones should be performed by all the kinsmen;
one should employ even-numbered Brahmins who are pure and endowed with faith.
On the fifth, the ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day, one should feed an even number of Brahmins; that, they know, is the *navaśrāddha*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the fourth day for Brāhmaṇas, on the fifth day for kings (Kṣatriyas),
on the ninth day for those of the Vaiśya caste, and after the tenth day for Śūdras."
Atri:
For the sake of the deceased, one should then feed Brāhmaṇas at the end of the birth-impurity period;
here, for the purpose of the śrāddha, however, one [should feed them] on the eleventh day.

This being the case, it is understood that the feeding of Brahmins performed at the conclusion of the period of impurity on the eleventh day is a distinct ritual act separate from the *navaśrāddha*. Bṛhaspati states:
"On the fourth day, food should indeed be given to Brahmins by the relatives."
One should, according to one's ability, give cows, gold, and wealth for the sake of the deceased.
"In the fourth" means on the day of the *saṃcaya* (the gathering of the bones).
"One should diligently give whatever was desired by the living [deceased]"—
the meaning is that one should give whatever was desired by that deceased person while he was alive.
Thus end the times for the nine *śrāddhas*.
Next are the times for the *preta-śrāddhas*, which are well known as the "sixteen *śrāddhas*. Regarding this, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
For the ancestors who have abandoned their bodies, the sixteen śrāddhas should always be performed on the fourth, fifth,
ninth, and eleventh days [of the lunar fortnight].
Then, over the course of twelve months, the Śrāddha rites should be performed twelve times according to the Vedic injunctions; therein, one should satisfy the brāhmaṇas with offerings.
Jātūkarṇa says:
"The twelve monthly rites, the first, the two six-monthly rites,
and the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa— these constitute the sixteen śrāddhas."
In order to define the two *śrāddhas* prescribed for the sixth month, he says:
"When six months are completed by one day less, or even when they are three days less than a year,
then the two *ṣāṇmāsika* [rites] should take place."

The meaning is that when six months or years are less than [the full duration] by one day or three days, then the rite for the six-month anniversary or the annual anniversary should be performed. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The *śrāddha* for the collection of bones, the three-fortnightly rite, and the monthly rites..."
Paiṭhīnasi: The two Śrāddhas for the six-monthly and annual periods should take place on the day preceding [the actual anniversary];
however, the monthly Śrāddhas should be performed on their own respective days or even on the twelfth day.
Likewise: "One should perform the sixteen śrāddhas prior to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa;
one should indeed perform all of them according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the twelfth day, after a month, and after three fortnights,
and thereafter, O twice-born ones, it should be performed month by month for as long as a year."
After that, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should be performed in due order.
Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, it is declared once more that from that point forward,
he is liberated from the state of a *preta* and has attained the status of a *pitṛ*.
Vyāghrapāda says:
On the eleventh day, in the fourth month, every month for a year,
and likewise every year on the anniversary of death, one should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Kātyāyana states the specific rule regarding the *śrāddha* for one who has died with the sacred fires (*agnimat-preta*):
"The *śrāddha* for one who maintained the sacred fires should be performed on the eleventh day after cremation;
however, one should always perform the obligatory (*dhruva*) rites on the anniversary of the day of death."
Those [rites] after three fortnights are fixed. For this very reason, Jātūkarṇa said:
"The śrāddha that occurs after three fortnights should take place on the day of death itself;
however, one should perform the cremation for a twice-born who maintained the sacred fires before that time."
Hārīta, however, has stated the alternative time-periods for the monthly rites in cases where one is incapable:
"The primary śrāddha is performed month after month; if that is not possible, one should perform it every season, or every twelve days, or all twelve on a single day."

In that regard, in the subsequent section, the postponement of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite when old age has arrived will be explained. We shall explain therein also the postponement of the monthly (*māsika*) rites and their non-recurrence based on that same [postponement].
Thus ends the time for the rites commonly known as the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Now, the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

In that regard, when the twelve monthly rites have been performed in due order and the year is complete, the time for the *sāṃvatsarika* [annual] *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—provided it has not been performed with fire—is thereafter. And so it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, after describing the *śrāddhas* ending with the monthly ones:
"Then, when the year is complete, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is properly performed by men; the procedure for that is now declared."

Furthermore, the fact that this time period is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* performed by one who lacks a sacred fire (*anagnimat*) for a deceased person to whom the rite is addressed (*anagnimad-daivatyā*), as well as another occasional (*naimittika*) time, is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"O bull of the Bharatas, the sacrificer who lacks a sacred fire should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a deceased person who did not maintain a sacred fire on the preceding day."

And it was said by Pulastya: "In accordance with dharma, one who maintains no sacred fire (niragni) should perform the rite of offering the funeral cakes (sahapiṇḍatva) for his father and mother when the full year has elapsed, whether there be a rite of prosperity (vṛddhi) or not."

*Vṛddhi* refers to prosperity (*abhyudaya*) in the form of the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the investiture of the sacred thread (*mauñjī*), marriage (*vivāha*), and so forth; this is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative term) for any ritual action that serves as the occasion for a *nāndī-śrāddha*. This becomes clear from Uśanas’s statement, “Upon the arrival of the installation of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and other such events,” and from Śāṭyāyani’s statement, “one should perform the *nāndīmukha*. The meaning is that on the very day when such prosperity occurs, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* beforehand and then perform the rite known as *nāndīmukha*, which is an ancillary part of it. By this, it is also shown that one who has commenced the entitlement [to perform ancestral rites] but has not yet completed the *preta-śrāddha* lacks the entitlement to perform the *caula*, *mauñjī*, marriage, or *ādhāna*, as well as the *nāndī-śrāddha* that is an ancillary part of them. Laghu-Hārīta says:
A brother, or a brother’s son, a sapinda relative, or even a disciple, shall perform the sapindikarana rite;
thereafter, one should perform the auspicious rites (abhyudayika).
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Then, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is established as taking place after one year;
however, if there is to be an occasion for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), one may perform it even before that."
Intending that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* be performed earlier than the *nāndīśrāddha* which constitutes a constituent part of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), Uśanas says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father, which is normally performed on the anniversary of death during the annual rite,
may take place even before the year [of the death] upon the occasion of the fire-consecration and other such rites."

In this case, even when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is being postponed, the preceding monthly rites (*māsika*) must be performed by postponing them as well, according to the principle that "when the final rite is postponed, everything up to that point is postponed. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"One should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* without having offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*;
for if those are omitted, the deceased does not attain the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*)."

This applies only to the case of postponement (*apakarṣa*). For if there is no postponement, that [performance] is established simply by the prescription of the sequence. For this very reason, Śāṭyāyani says:
"A twice-born man, when about to perform the *nāndīmukha* rite, should postpone all the funeral offerings (*preta-śrāddha*) as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and then perform them."
As for the statement of Laugākṣi: "For him whose sapiṇḍīkaraṇa occurs before the completion of a year,
the monthly offerings and the water-pot (udakumbha) must also be given for that year."

However, that [rule] should be explained as referring to the subject of re-performance mentioned by the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*—namely, "one should perform those very [rites] again"—by means of the principle of postponement (*apakarṣanyāya*), even when the monthly rites (*māsika*) have already been performed. Regarding the phrase "having postponed" (*apakṛṣya*), Āhośanā states: "But he who performs the *preta-śrāddhas* while being devoid of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, that performer of *śrāddhas* is cooked in a terrible hell together with his ancestors."

The statement, "He who would postpone the *śrāddhas* for the deceased when an occasion for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) has not arrived," implies by its very meaning that there is no postponement in the absence of such an occasion; this rule pertains to those who are capable [of performing the rites]. However, regarding those who are incapable, Gobhila states the various options for the timing of the postponement even without the arrival of an occasion for prosperity: "When a full year, six months, or three fortnights have passed, or on whatever day an occasion for prosperity may occur."

In this regard, some maintain the following arrangement: that the two options—"at the end of a full year" or "on the day when an auspicious occasion (vṛddhi) occurs"—apply exclusively to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (anagnika), whereas the two options—"after six months" or "after three fortnights"—apply exclusively to those who do maintain the sacred fires (sāgnika). To support this, they cite the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "For one who maintains the sacred fires, the time for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is after three fortnights in the case of rites for prosperity (vṛddhi), sacrifices (iṣṭi), and works of public utility (pūrta);
or else, one may perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa at the completion of the full year."

They cite the statements that will be discussed in the section concerning the time for *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimant*). Here, this must be said: if there are options such as "three fortnights" and so forth for one characterized by the qualification of maintaining the fires, let them be the primary alternatives (*mukhyakalpa*) even for one capable of performing it at the end of the year. However, those [options] prompted by the capacity of one who lacks the fires, having attained syntactic unity with the option of the year mentioned in Gobhila’s statement regarding the present case, let them be secondary alternatives (*anukalpa*). Vyāghra, however, states that even for those without fires, the twelfth day itself is the recommended time for *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, along with the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Because family customs are infinite, because the lifespan of men is subject to decline,
and because the body is unstable, the twelve-day period is recommended.
Thus end the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for those who maintain no sacred fire (*ananika*). Now follows the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for those who maintain a sacred fire (*sāgnika*).
Regarding this, Laghuhārīta says:
But when there is no fire, O hero, the householder should then perform [the rite];
if the deceased possessed the sacred fires, the *sapiṇḍana* should indeed take place after three fortnights.

In this case, if the householder performing the *śrāddha* is devoid of the *āhavanīya* fire while the deceased possesses the *āhavanīya*, then that performer should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for that deceased person once three fortnights have elapsed from the day of death.
Likewise: "O King, if the sacrificer possesses the sacred fires while the deceased is without them..."
The Sapindikarana rite should be performed by the sons on the twelfth day.

In this context, it should be understood that [the rite] is performed on the twelfth day starting from the anniversary of death. Kātyāyana says: "Having completed the eleventh-day rite, a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his mother and father according to the rules, either on the full moon day or before it."

The intention here is as follows: On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) must perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha. And that [śrāddha] has as its deities the father and others together with their wives, provided the mother and father are deceased. However, the status of being a deity in the *darśa-śrāddha* and other rites is not possible for those two until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, because it is traditionally taught (*smaraṇa*) that this rite occurs subsequent to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Therefore, thinking that there should be no omission of either the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* or the śrāddha, the Brahmin who maintains the fires, having completed the funeral rites (*pretakārya*) to be performed on the eleventh day, should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his mother and father on some day prior to the new moon. The mention of the "Brahmin" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), since the same logic applies to Kṣatriyas and others as well.
Hārīta states another alternative: "But that which is the preceding new moon (amāvāsyā), on that [day one should perform it].
For this very reason, Jābāla says:
"A son who maintains the sacred fires (agnimān) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* before the new moon."
But after ten nights have passed, another [rite] is likewise performed.

The meaning is that after the ten-day period beginning from the day of death, on whichever first new moon (*darśa*) occurs thereafter, one who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimān*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his parents. The mention of "ten days" is intended to indicate the period of ritual impurity (*aśauca*). Thus, three times for the performance of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one who maintains the fires have been stated: "the twelfth day; any day prior to the new moon occurring after the ten days; and the new moon itself occurring after the ten days."
Thus are the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for those who maintain the sacred fires;
thus [are they] for members of the three twice-born classes.
Now, regarding the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a *śūdra*:
with the phrase "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed" understood as a recurring injunction, Viṣṇu states:
"For the *mantra*-recitation of *śūdras* is prescribed on the twelfth day."

The elders maintain that this refers to the case of a Śūdra who performs a *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). By the force of the scriptural injunction, the performance of the *śrāddha* occurs even in the midst of impurity (*aśauca*).
Thus end the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a Śūdra.
Thus end the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

[301] Thus, in this section, the times for the following have been set forth: the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; the two types of *pārvaṇa* rites known as *sapiṇḍa-anvāhāryaka* and *sādhāraṇa*; the *vṛddhi-karma* (rites of prosperity); the *kāmya-śrāddha* (optional rites for specific desires); the *sāṃvatsarika-śrāddha* (annual anniversary rites); those well-known as the *nava-śrāddha* (nine funeral rites) and the *ṣoḍaśa-śrāddha* (sixteen funeral rites); and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Now, while other times for *śrāddha* must be stated, the following is said: the *tīrtha-śrāddha* (pilgrimage rite), the *śuddhi-śrāddha* (purification rite)...

Regarding the *daivika-śrāddha*, the *yātrā-śrāddha*, the *jīvacchrāddha*, and the *goṣṭhī-śrāddha*, their times are indeed those prescribed by the specific injunctions of authority; these have been explained in the section on specific authorities (*viśeṣādhikāra-prakaraṇa*). Among them, the time for the *tīrtha-śrāddha* is immediately upon reaching the sacred site, whether at the [usual] time or an improper time, because of the traditional teaching of the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Whether at an improper time or at the proper time, the *śrāddha* at a sacred site should be performed by men. The time for the *śuddhi-śrāddha* is upon the completion of the purificatory vow (*śuddhivratasamāpti*) performed for the sake of destroying sin.

"One should perform the *śrāddha* at the conclusion of the vow, with gifts of cows, gold, food, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)," according to the statement of Jābāla. The time for the *daivika-śrāddha* consists of the lunar day (*tithi*), the day of the week (*vāra*), and so forth, presided over by the respective deities who are to be gratified. One should diligently perform that *śrāddha* on the new moon (*darśa*) and other occasions, just as in the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) *śrāddha*.
Thus, it is from the observation of the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.

The time for the *yātrāśrāddha* (pilgrimage rite) is the day prior to the start of a pilgrimage and the day immediately following the return home after completing a pilgrimage; this is established by the hearing of such texts as the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* ("One should go to another country... and the *Brahmapurāṇa* and *Agnipurāṇa* ("Whoever [performs] a pilgrimage to sacred sites..."). The time for the *jīvacchrāddha* (living-libation rite) is the period subsequent to the death-time inferred from the observation of omens by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), as taught in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* and other texts ("The *jīvacchrāddha* should be performed..."). The time for the *goṣṭhīśrāddha* (social gathering rite) is precisely when a group of Brahmins has assembled, according to the statement in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "That *śrāddha* which is performed in a social gathering (*goṣṭhī*)... The time for the sixteen *śrāddhas* that are constituent parts of renunciation (*saṇnyāsa*) is the day preceding the eight *śrāddhas* beginning with the *daiva*, based on the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating: "But from the *daiva* [śrāddha], [the others follow] due to renunciation... and so forth.
Thus the section on deities has been defined.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

According to the statement of Śaunaka beginning with "On the previous day, the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha," the time for the śrāddha known as the Nārāyaṇabali—for those who died by an untimely death or who possessed specific transgressions—is any eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-ekādaśī*) that occurs when the full year has elapsed from the anniversary of their death.
And likewise, in the *Bhaviṣyottara*, after enumerating those who have died a miserable death and those who have committed specific sins, it is said:
"When a full year has passed, compassionate persons should perform [the rite] for them,
