having reached the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) of the bright fortnight."
And so forth.
Thus end the times for *tīrtha-śrāddha* and other rites.
Thus end the specific times for *śrāddha*.

Now, regarding the times for the transgression of the primary period (*mukhyakāla*): these are of two kinds—secondary (*gauṇa*) and those prescribed as alternative options (*anukalpika*). In this regard, it must first be considered: when the primary time is impossible, should the secondary time be adopted or not? But what is the primary, and what is the secondary? That which is specifically enjoined is the primary; for example, in the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other rites, the morning (*prātaḥ*) and so forth. That which is not specifically enjoined, but occurs in proximity to them and is brought into the status of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) within those very rites, such as the *saṅgava* period and so forth, is the secondary. Thus says Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana:
"A time subsequent to its own [proper] time is secondary for a preceding rite;
or rather, some maintain that even a future action constitutes a secondary time for a previous rite, just like an interval between primary times. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: that which is subsequent to the time of the preceding rite and prior to the time of the succeeding rite—meaning the intermediate period between the two rites—is to be understood as "secondary" (*gauṇa*) with respect to the preceding rite. Alternatively, they consider even the primary time of the future action to be secondary with respect to the preceding rite, just like the aforementioned interval. But how could it be suspected that the time of the succeeding rite might not be grasped for the performance of the preceding rite, such that the preceding rite—having fallen from its own time—is almost as if destroyed, while the succeeding rite, because it has not fallen from its own time, remains in an undestroyed state? In that case, if the preceding rite were performed at the time of the succeeding rite, it would result in destroying what is not yet destroyed for the sake of restoring what is already lost; that would be like attempting to kill a living person in the hope of reviving one who is dead. This is said when there is room for both rites at the time of the succeeding rite, and not when such room does not exist.

[Objection: Is it not the case that for a time occurring in proximity to the primary time (*mukhyakāla*), a figurative (*lākṣika*) usage is more appropriate, since its application is obtained through an inseparable connection with the denoted object?

[Reply: True indeed. Nevertheless, there is no contradiction in describing that [proximate time] as secondary (*gauṇa*), because its application by words such as "morning" (*prātaḥ*) is based on worldly convention, wherein qualities such as the softness of the heat serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the time of the morning sun.
[Objection: But since that [convention] is not explicitly taught, how can its acceptability even be suspected?
We say it is by way of substitution (*pratinidhi*).
But if that is so, then by some kind of similarity, the words "morning" and so forth might occasionally apply even at midday and other times.

What is undesirable here? For indeed, sometimes when there is no availability of [a primary term] such as *saṅga* (meeting), which possesses extreme similarity and is accompanied by frequent figurative usage, [the secondary term is used]. Thus, regarding this doubt—considering that in certain sentences connected with time, such as "the *śrāddha* for the gods in the forenoon," the action is enjoined as subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the time—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that when the prescribed time, which is the primary element, has passed, one should not perform the rite at another time in order to favor the subordinate action. The author established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "For the action is enjoined in relation to the time, not the time in relation to the action. Therefore, actions alone possess primacy, because the action is enjoined by restating the time. Consequently, when the prescribed time—which is subordinate to the action—has passed, one must perform the rite even at a secondary time in order to favor the primary action. For it is improper to abandon the action simply because of the loss of the time; indeed, one does not abandon a meal merely because a single side-dish is spoiled."

That is incorrect. First of all, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here does not hold by treating the action as a subordinate element (*guṇībhāva*), because the action is connected with a fruit. According to the maxim that "that which is without a fruit in proximity to something possessing a fruit is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to it," time itself is the subsidiary. Nor should it be argued that the mention of a fruit is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of meaning, since the action is intended for another purpose—namely, for the sake of time—because there is no understanding that time is intended for the sake of an action that possesses a fruit. Furthermore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) stated by treating the existence of time as a subordinate element is also untenable, because the reason adduced is unproven (*asiddha*). For an action is not enjoined here by way of a restatement of time, since there is an absence of the prior attainment (*prāpti*) of time from any other source.

[Objection: But surely, since time is not established by another sentence, this will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of worldly practice regarding what is known from the calendar as the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth.

[Reply: Not so. If there were an injunction of a ritual action (*karma-vidhi*) based on a restatement of the nature of time already established in the world, that [time] would itself be the result; consequently, because it would lack the status of being an auxiliary to a fruitful action, the injunction would fall into the error of being purposeless (*ānarthakya*). Furthermore, in this ritual, a connection with another ritual action is not possible for the time that is the objective (*uddeśya*), because that [connection] is intended only to follow immediately after the performance of this very ritual.

But if that is so, then even in the case of the injunction "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," since the injunction of the sacrifice is determined by referring back to the one desiring heaven, how is it not the case that the injunction is purposeless?

It is said: although the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is syntactically connected to the sentence as the objective (*uddeśya*), nevertheless, because an efficient force (*bhāvanā*) first requires an object to be brought about (*bhāvya*), and because the person—being of an already established nature—is incapable of being such an object, it is heaven itself, which is the object of the desire like the person desiring heaven, that is established as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The person desiring heaven, however, is merely restated as something already established. Just as in the case of "the priests proceed wearing red turbans" (*lohitoṣṇīṣam ṛtvijaṃ pracaranti*), where the priests—the subjects—are already established and thus the sentence refers only to the previously unestablished attribute, so it is here as well. As stated by Maṇḍana Miśra:
"Because that which is to be brought about (the object) is what is required, words expressing desire are indeed intent upon that [object].
That the qualifier is primary in cases such as 'daṇḍin' (the man with a staff) has been demonstrated. Thus it is said.

[305] Therefore, it has been stated that the rule for ritual action applies there by way of non-delusion regarding time. Thus, since the aforementioned prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*) positions were previously shown to be untenable, those two are now stated here as being correct. First, the prima facie position: when obligatory and occasional rites have become incumbent due to their necessity, and since the injunction "as one may be able" is attached for the sake of accomplishing the essential nature of such acts, it is established that when the requisite materials are unavailable, one must take a suitable substitute. Consequently, when the primary time is not available, one must adopt a secondary (*gauṇa*) time. Regarding this, Trikaṇḍamaṇḍana says:
"When it is impossible to perform the rite at the primary time, it must be performed even during the secondary time; here, the secondary [time] is also of such a nature.
By "of such a nature," it is meant that it resembles the primary time. By this, its fitness as a substitute is demonstrated. The Smṛtis also show the acceptance of the secondary time.
"The wise man must perform his obligatory duty (nitya-karma) somehow or other;
there is no omission of it once it has been undertaken, especially in the case of ancestral rites (paitṛka).
Likewise:

Rites prescribed for the daytime that have been omitted through negligence should indeed be performed until the first watch of the night. However, a wise person must certainly not perform a *śrāddha* during the two twilights or at night.

The aforementioned prohibition of specific times for the *smārta* twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth is only applicable when there is otherwise an occasion to adopt those times in their primary sense. Furthermore, because of the force of the injunction "one should perform [the rite] as [is prescribed]," even those auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) that are enjoined as if they were permanent (*nitya*) become non-permanent (*anitya*). Thus Paiṭhīnasi says: "The auxiliary elements, together with the principal [rite], both exist and do not exist."

Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction in adopting a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) when the primary time has passed, then it would follow that for rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, which are prescribed for times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), they could be performed on the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) and so forth if the prescribed time is unavailable. What kind of consequence is this? For the proponent of accepting secondary time would indeed accept that performance. However, this acceptance of secondary time does not apply to optional (*kāmya*) rites, because in those cases, the qualification (*adhikāra*) is established only for one who is capable of offering all the constituent parts (*aṅga*). A certain distinction regarding the performance of a rite by means of adopting secondary time has been stated by Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana; it is mentioned here incidentally.
During these secondary times, one should perform the rite enjoined;

one should perform the expiation prescribed in the section on penances. Performing a rite enjoined for another time during these aforementioned secondary times, one should perform the expiation—the ritual atonement—prescribed in the section on penances. An alternative view has also been stated by that same author:
"Or, without performing the penance, one may perform it during a secondary time."

In this context, the perception of anteriority (*pūrvakālatā*) in the expression *akṛtvā* is not intended to be significant. Thus, when the inclusion of a secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) might be assumed, it is here prescribed: since in all cases a time specified in the locative case is an unattainable property (*anupādeya*), it possesses only the nature of a subject (*uddeśya*) and is designated as a causal condition (*nimitta*); and because there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) without the prescribed time when that [time] serves as a qualification of the entitled person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), an act performed at another time would be as if not done at all. Therefore, one should not resort to a secondary time. Furthermore, the absence of entitlement in the absence of the prescribed time has been established in the section on the Sāntapanīya sacrifice in the sūtra: "of the cause for the attainment [of the entitlement]" (*prāpaṇāvanimittasya*).
For this very reason, Laugākṣi says:
"Time is known through calculation; the deities abide in time.
A single oblation offered at the proper time is better than hundreds of thousands or tens of millions offered at the wrong time."

As for what is stated in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* regarding the acceptance of secondary (gauṇa) times, that was said while adhering to the Śaiva Siddhānta according to the logic of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and thus it should be disregarded. As for the Smṛti passage beginning with "in whatever way possible" (*yathā kathaṃcit*), it does not establish the acceptance of secondary times therein; rather, it establishes precisely the non-acceptance [of such times]. For its meaning is understood as follows: when a rite has reached its own time, its omission or non-performance should not occur due to the lack of primary materials and the like. Instead, at that very time, it must be performed "in whatever way possible" by employing other materials similar to the primary ones, even if it results in some deficiency. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "rites prescribed for the day" (*dinoditāni karmāṇi*) does not declare that all rites and all secondary times are to be accepted by virtue of their being secondary. Rather, in certain rites, only a specific alternative time—otherwise unestablished by logic just like the primary time—is enjoined as a substitute (*anukalpa*). By the force of those scriptural statements, only those rites specifically ordained for particular times—such as the year, season, month, or lunar day—are deemed fit to be performed at another time when the original time has passed. As for the prohibition of *śrāddha* during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) and night, that too is applicable only to what is obtained through worldly inclination (*rāga*) or through fallacious reasoning, just like the eating [of forbidden food].
Alternatively,
provided there is wealth, the excellence of Brahmins, and a desire for the śrāddha,
a tīrtha-śrāddha should always be performed by men, whether out of season or in season.
It should be performed early in the day.

By these [statements], this prohibition applies to the *śrāddha* performed at times other than the afternoon—specifically during the periods of the twilights (*saṃdhyā*) and so forth. As for the fact that the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites is seen to occur during secondary (*gauṇa*) times when the primary time has passed, that is in some cases for the sake of avoiding reproach or for the satisfaction of the mind; and in other cases, it is because there is an injunction for another time as a substitute (*anukalpa*). Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, since one lacks the qualification (*adhikāra*) once the prescribed time has passed, one should not allow the primary time to pass merely due to the unavailability of the primary substance. This very point was presented with a preliminary doubt and resolved in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana*: "If the primary rite exists at the primary time, the passing of that time must not occur. But if wealth cannot be obtained at all, then which among time and substance is primary, or even secondary?"
Let that wealth be accepted even if it pertains to a secondary time, provided it relies upon the primary time;
for there should be no waiting for a secondary time merely because the primary substance has been obtained.

Thus, this statement regarding established fact (*siddhavacana*) would not require the inclusion of the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*); however, since the statement exists, it means that for a secondary [rite], the impurity applies either from that [time] or even beyond it. Regarding this, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"But when impurity arises during a *śrāddha* to be given to the ancestors..."
But once the period of impurity has passed, the śrāddha rite for them is prescribed.

The meaning is this: when impurity (*aśauca*) arises for those entitled to perform the *śrāddha* prior to the primary time, then the ancestral rite (*paitṛka karma*) must be performed at the time immediately following the cessation of that impurity—provided that the time proximate to the primary period has not been defiled by the impurity.
As for the statement of Atri:
"If the day should be defiled by something such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), [then one should wait]."
"One should perform it either immediately after death, or on that very same day. Thus [it is said].

In this context, the rule regarding the lunar day (*tithi*) and the fortnight (*pakṣa*) should be understood as applying to the primary time when other causes mentioned by the word "etcetera" have obstructed [the performance]; this must be so conceived in order to avoid contradiction with the preceding statement. Furthermore, this refers specifically to the monthly *śrāddha* performed on the anniversary of death (*kṣayāha*) during the waning of the fortnight. For in that case, even if there is no contact with the time touched by the month, the lunar day belonging to the fortnight alone is to be accepted. Therefore, Devala says: "Regarding the phrase 'in the fortnight' (*pakṣe*), if the day of death is defiled by impurity due to birth or death (*mṛtakasūtaka*), the *śrāddha* should be performed after passing over that period once the impurity has ceased. This does not apply if the impurity is known prior to the commencement of cooking or the invitation. Likewise, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
For a sacrificial priest who has accepted the madhuparka offering from the patron,
it is the settled rule that there is no impurity if ten days have elapsed [since the death].
In the same way, for a learned Brahmin who has received initiation at a great sacrifice,
no ritual bath exists until the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) has taken place.
When the difficult fire-oblations and other rites have been completed and the Brahmins and others have been fed,
there shall be no [transgression] for anyone else, even for one who has undertaken a vow.

[309] For one who has reached the final stage, or for another who has set out for the sake of alms, for a forest-dweller, or for any other who still possesses a formal obligation, there is no such thing; however, for one who has desisted from the right to accept gifts, it does not exist at all.
In the case of the *gomaṇḍala* sacrifice and others, even when the time for protection has passed for the Vaiśyas,
once the Brahmins have been invited and the *śrāddha* rite has commenced;
For when a Brahmin has been invited and has ceased his Vedic recitation,
there is no impurity whatsoever as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
Furthermore, there is never any fault in performing śrāddha and other rites when the birth or death impurity of either the giver or the receiver is unknown.
If [the fault] is recognized, the penance and other rites would apply to the eater alone;
however, if half the meal has been consumed by the Brahmins, it falls upon the giver.
When someone has discarded the remnants of that [food] and, being composed,
sips water for purification with another's water, the twice-born become pure.
If a period of impurity (sūtaka) occurs between a wedding and a sacrifice, the remaining food should be provided by others; it shall not touch either the donors or the eaters.
Here,
when the Brahmins had been invited and the śrāddha rite had commenced, [the following occurred].

Thus, because of the presentation of these two cases: when the invitation has been issued prior to the commencement of cooking, there is an absence of impurity (*āśauca*) from the time of the invitation until the completion of the rite; however, when the invitation is made before the cooking, then there is an absence of impurity from the commencement of the cooking until the completion of the rite. This is because the very beginning of the cooking constitutes the first limb of the *śrāddha*, and thus there is no lack of commencement of the *śrāddha* itself. Regarding the statement, "If some [relative] of the giver should perish while the meal is being eaten," the resolution of the contradiction with the previously mentioned rule—"among the invited Brahmins... and so forth—must be understood as follows: this refers either to the impurity arising from a *sapiṇḍa* of the giver who dies at that moment, or to the impurity arising from someone who dies in the house where the *śrāddha* is being performed. As for the rule, "The remaining food should be given away by others," this refers to births or deaths occurring among people other than those in the house of the eaters. In the phrase, "It should not touch the givers or the eaters," the word "fault" (*doṣa*) is to be supplied.
Āha Kratu says: "There is no fault in giving material that was previously intended for the rite.

It has been stated that when the qualified performer is defiled by impurity (*aśauca*), the *śrāddha* must be performed after the lapse of the primary time once the impurity has ceased. Since the householder’s entitlement is shared with his wife, when she is defiled by the impurity resulting from the appearance of menses (*rajas*), and the *śrāddha* is thus required to be performed after the lapse of the primary time upon the cessation of that impurity, Uśanas declares that the husband alone, even while his wife is menstruating, must perform an *ām-śrāddha* (a *śrāddha* with raw food) precisely during the primary time."

"One who is without a wife, one who is traveling abroad, and one whose wife is in her menses—these should not perform [the śrāddha] with cooked food; for them, the use of raw food (āma) is prescribed.
Regarding this rule for the *adravya-śrāddha* (śrāddha without material offerings), there is an exception preceded by a specific restriction in certain cases.
When an obstacle arises for the twice-born during a Śrāddha, an Āma-Śrāddha (a rite with raw food) is prescribed;
this applies to the obligatory rites on the new moon day and so forth, but not to those performed monthly or annually.

Prohibition of the *āma-śrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) regarding monthly and annual observances: When the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) arrives and one's wife happens to be in her menstrual period, one should perform the *śrāddha* on that very day using cooked food (*anna*) alone, and not with raw food (*āma*), nor at another time. As stated in another *Smṛti*:
"When the annual [anniversary] has arrived and one's wife is in her menstrual period..."
One should not perform that śrāddha on the fifth day, nor on the anniversary of his death.
If the childless wife herself is the performer of the annual *śrāddha* for her husband, then:
"But when the year of the husband's death has arrived, if the childless wife happens to be in her menses, she should perform that on the fifth day."

This is because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Gautama. The meaning is as follows: when an obstacle to a *śrāddha* occurs—such as the appearance of the menses in the wife—it is proclaimed that an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food) should be performed; however, this applies only to those [rites] occurring on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth, and not to those occurring on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), such as the monthly (*māsika*) or annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rites. Rather, those must be performed with cooked food (*pakvānna*) alone, and by one who has only a single wife. Furthermore: "But when the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has arrived and an obstacle arises, one should diligently perform that *śrāddha* on another day of that same lunar date."

"In another" means in the immediately following month. "On that lunar day" means on the anniversary of death. "In that" means in that fortnight, whether bright or dark, when he died. The meaning is that one should perform the *śrāddha* which was delayed due to an obstacle. Even regarding the phrase "if there is an obstacle," for the sake of not contradicting the statement of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, a qualification must be understood: namely, that the cause is other than impurity (*aśauca*). When an obstacle arises due to the cause of impurity, even in the case of the monthly rites, the performance of the *śrāddha* immediately after the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is to be followed as stated in the words of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. For this very reason, Devasvāmin has also said:

This statement by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga concerns the period of impurity due to birth (sūtaka); however, regarding the interruption of that day due to other causes, there is the statement from another Smṛti: "But when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived, if an obstacle should arise," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for the statement of Vyāsa:
"When an obstacle to the Śrāddha has arisen due to an intervening death or birth-impurity, one should perform it on the new moon day; some wise authorities say it should be done upon purification."

"In the midst of the impurity of death or birth" means when death or birth occurs during the performance of a *śrāddha* before the commencement of the cooking. "On the new moon day" means on the day of the *amāvāsyā*. "Upon purification" means after the period of impurity has ended. This refers to the annual *śrāddha* for a deceased person whose date of death was previously unknown. The mention of the new moon day is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the eleventh day of both the bright and dark fortnights.
For this very reason, Marīci states: "When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises and the date of death is unknown," [312]
It should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

The syntactical connection is that [the rite] should be performed especially on that Ekādaśī which falls in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), because in ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) the dark fortnight alone is to be accepted. It should be understood that the superiority of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) for ancestral rites over even the dark Ekādaśī is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). As for the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

"When the monthly anniversary (*māsika*) or the annual anniversary (*ābdika*) has arrived during an impurity caused by death (*antarāmṛtasūtaka*), the wise say that it should be performed upon purification, or else on a blade of *darbha* grass."

The statement "one should perform [the rite] again for that same duration" refers to the *anvaṣṭakya* (monthly) *śrāddha* as prescribed; this is because, regarding the monthly *ekoddiṣṭa*-type *śrāddha*, an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) has already been stated previously. In this context, the period immediately following purification is superior, as it is proximate to the primary time (*mukhyakāla*). However, the time of the new moon (*darśakāla*) is inferior to that, as it lacks proximity to the primary time; so it should be understood. And thus says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"Once purified, one should give [the offering] on whichever lunar day (*tithi*) occurs."
"That lunar day (tithi) is to be observed by him, and never any other.

This is the meaning: one who has become pure must perform the rite. Therefore, if purity is not possible at the primary time, then whichever lunar day follows immediately after that purity is obtained—that lunar day is to be performed as a constituent part of the ritual; it should be understood as such. That primary lunar day which was defiled by impurity is never to be practiced. However, the primary lunar day that is undefiled by impurity is always to be practiced.
"One should not arbitrarily interrupt the lunar day except due to impurity."
"The funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and the śrāddha offering must be given; one must never cause their interruption. Thus it is said.

"By chance" (*yadṛcchayā*) means according to one's own will; "the *śrāddha*" refers to the satiation of Brahmins, and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) must also be performed, thus [the two] are to be combined. Here, by the term *śrāddha*, only the satiation of Brahmins is used figuratively, and not in its primary sense, because the primary meaning consists of the triad comprising the *agnaukaraṇa*, the satiation of Brahmins, and the offering of the *piṇḍas*. The meaning of the phrase "one should never cause an interruption" (*vicchittiṃ naiva kārayet*) is as follows: even if it is impossible to perform the entire meaning of the term *śrāddha*, one should perform at least that portion of it according to one's capacity. In no way should one cause an interruption in the ritual. For this very reason, there is a traditional scriptural authority (*nigama*).

"For one who has maintained the sacred fires, the worship of the ancestors is performed with the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) alone, or else he should feed Brāhmaṇas. In this matter, the arrangement depends on one's capacity. Consequently, when there is an inability to follow the second alternative, the understanding of what was stated first arises. It must be accepted in this way precisely so that this [first option] does not become sublated.

Now, one might object: let the division based on the similarity of the illustrative example—rooted in the assumption of a derivative sense—be set aside by the statements regarding the threefold, fourfold, and other divisions that will be shown later.

True. There is indeed a sublation [of the etymological meaning] because a technical (pāribhāṣika) term—whether taught by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) itself or otherwise—is stronger than an etymological (*yaugika*) or conceptual (*kālpnika*) one due to its lack of occasion for application (*anavakāśatva*). However, it is precisely so that the etymological meaning may not be sublated by the technical definition that the meaning established through etymology (*yogasiddha*) is also accepted.
As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "The forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is from sunrise until the turning point (*āvartana*), and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is after that."

"Āvartana" refers to the day; thus, one opinion holds that the second part of the day divided into two is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Another opinion holds that the third part of the day divided into three is the afternoon. Regarding this, the Śruti says: "The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors; therefore, one gives [the offering] in the afternoon. From this, the understanding arises that the Śruti, having conceived three parts—each measuring fifteen *muhūrtas*—of the day consisting of fifteen *muhūrtas* named "forenoon" and so forth, assigns them respectively to the rites for the gods, humans, and ancestors. Here, I shall demonstrate in the section on application (*viniyoga*) the time for performing the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha* prescribed for the afternoon, according to its measure as the third part of the day. That too should be understood as the afternoon being the third part of the day divided into three, as shown elsewhere. Furthermore, because of the prohibition against defiling the wife who is entitled to participate, or because there is no specific rule regarding another wife in the absence of a menstruating wife, the rite must be performed precisely at the time when the obstacle in the form of the appearance of menses has passed. And that time is stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
A woman who has reached her menses becomes pure on the fourth day after bathing;
however, for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day.
In another Smṛti:
"When the day of death has arrived, if his wife is in her menses, the Śrāddha should not be performed then; one should perform it on the fifth day."
However, for one who has taken another wife while still possessing the entitlement [to perform the rite], since that entitlement has not lapsed, the rite must be performed at the primary time itself.
Thus, these are the times regarding the lapse of the primary time.

Now, in this regard, for a certain *śrāddha*, the morning time is prescribed; for another, the forenoon; for another, midday; and for another, the afternoon. Furthermore, the evening time is prohibited. Therefore, for the sake of distinguishing between them, it is said that "the afternoon is superior to the forenoon."

Now, it might be argued that in this context regarding the *śrāddha*, only the superiority of the afternoon over the forenoon is being stated; it is not, however, the case that the day is divided into two parts and the first part is designated as "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*). To this it is replied: when a month is divided into two, its two parts become the "former" and "latter" fortnights (*pakṣa*). These two serve as the illustrative examples here, and by virtue of their similarity, they lead one to understand that when the day is likewise divided into two, its former and latter parts are designated as "forenoon" and "afternoon. This is because the status of an illustrative example is established through similarity based on mere superiority.

True. Because no other such division is adopted and because of the requirement for complete conformity, the cognition of the intended division arises; and so that this may not be sublated, it must be accepted in this way. Thus, one view is that the third part of the day divided into three parts is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
Alternatively, another view is that when divided into four unequal parts, the third part is the afternoon.
And so Gobhila says: "The forenoon consists of one and a half *praharas*, likewise the midday consists of one *prahara*, the afternoon extends up to the third [part], and the evening is beyond that."

The meaning here is as follows: the portion of the day beginning from sunrise and measuring one and a half *praharas* is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). That which follows, measuring one *prahara*, is midday (*madhyāhna*). That which follows thereafter, measuring half a *prahara* up until the end of the third *prahara*, is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). And that which follows thereafter, measuring exactly one *prahara*, they call the evening (*sāyāhna*).
Thus, there is the view that the afternoon is the third part of a day divided into four parts.
Furthermore, there is another view that the afternoon is the fourth part of a day divided into five equal parts.
In this regard, there is the Śatapatha-Śruti:

"The Āditya alone is all the seasons: when he rises, it is spring; when it is the time of the cows gathering (saṅgava), it is summer; when it is midday, it is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, it is autumn; and when he sets, it is winter. Thus, when the day—measured at fifteen *muhūrtas*—is divided fivefold, there arise the five periods beginning with morning (*prātaḥ*), each measured at three *muhūrtas*. In this context, although the injunction regarding the setting up of the fires (*ādhāna*) is immediately connected to the midday period by the scriptural statement, "Therefore, one should set up the fires specifically at midday," the division into five parts is heard as a subordinate element. For, by serving to indicate the specific duration of the times required for the rites prescribed for the morning and other periods, this division attains a connection with all desires (*sarvakāma*). Therefore, this fivefold division, consisting of parts measured at three *muhūrtas*, is seen as being common to all. And so it is said in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:

The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration. Midday consists of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise; the evening consists of three muhūrtas, during which all ritual acts are excluded. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, Parāśara stated that this division is useful solely for the rites prescribed for that specific time:
"From the first streak of light until the sun [is fully risen], there are exactly three muhūrtas;
this is remembered as the morning (prātaḥ), and it is the fifth part of the day."
The period of twilight (saṅgava) consists of three muhūrtas; then midday (madhyāhna) is equal to that;
after that, there are three muhūrtas which constitute the distinguished afternoon (aparāhṇa).

"The fifth part of the day is known as *sāyāhna* (the afternoon). Whatever is prescribed for these [periods], that a wise person should perform. Here, *rekhā* refers to the portion of the rising solar disc that first becomes perceptible, appearing like a mere line. "From the sun" means from the sunrise. Thus, it is stated that those *muhūrta*s which occur there starting from the line [of the rising sun] until the actual sunrise are designated as *prātaḥ* (morning).

For it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "From the appearance of the first streak of light until the sun has risen for three muhūrtas, that time is known as 'morning' (prātaḥ); it constitutes the fifth part of the day."
The meaning is that whatever rite is prescribed for these times, such as morning and so forth, one should perform each of those during these aforementioned periods measured by three muhūrtas.

[317] Now, the periods of time such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth, which are measured by the elaboration of the aforementioned statements, are indeed called *kalpas*. In that regard, when the day is divided into two parts, the forenoon begins from the observation of half the solar disc and extends until the completion of the first half of the eighth *muhūrta*. When divided into three parts, it starts from the appearance of the sun’s crest and lasts until the end of the fifth *muhūrta*. When divided into four parts, it begins from that same point and extends until the completion of the first half of the third quarter of the sixth *muhūrta*. However, when divided into five parts, the forenoon must be stated to consist of a period measuring six *muhūrtas* starting from sunrise; for in that case, the meaning of the word "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) should be explained by assuming an etymological function (*yaugikī vṛtti*). Even though the first six *muhūrtas* of the day are already occupied by the two designations of "morning" (*prātaḥ*) and "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*), nevertheless, because this [fivefold division] serves a different purpose, it does not constitute an obstacle to the application of the name "forenoon."
Thus ends the fourfold distinction regarding the forenoon. Now follow the ritual procedures for midday.

In a twofold division of the day, midday (*madhyāhna*) is that period sufficient for the performance of the duties prescribed for midday, situated on both sides of the central moment of the day. Furthermore, one need not accept the introduction of any contradictory alternative designation here. In a threefold division, midday extends from the sixth *muhūrta* until the conclusion of the tenth *muhūrta*. In a fourfold division, it begins from the latter half of the third quarter of the sixth *muhūrta* and lasts until the completion of the first quarter of the second *muhūrta* of the tenth *muhūrta*. In a fivefold division, however, it begins from the sixth *muhūrta* and lasts until the conclusion of the tenth *muhūrta*.

Thus concludes the fourfold division of the midday. Now follow the alternatives for the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). When divided into two parts, the afternoon begins from the latter half of the eighth *muhūrta* and extends until the commencement of the evening twilight (*paścimasandhyā*). When divided into three parts, it begins from the eleventh *muhūrta* and extends until the end of the evening twilight. When divided into four parts, it begins from the latter half of the second quarter of the tenth *muhūrta* and extends until the conclusion of the first quarter of the twelfth *muhūrta*. When divided into five parts, it begins from the tenth *muhūrta* and extends until the end of the twelfth *muhūrta*.
Thus concludes the fourfold division of the afternoon. Now, regarding the divisions of the evening (*sāyāhna*):

in a twofold or threefold division, the time suitable for the performance of rites prescribed for that period should be reckoned as beginning from before sunset. In a fourfold division, it begins from the second quarter of the twelfth *muhūrta* and extends until the setting of the sun. In a fivefold division, the evening begins from the thirteenth *muhūrta* and lasts until the setting of the sun.

Furthermore, these periods such as the *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon) and so forth should be adopted according to availability, without overstepping the applications that will be described hereafter. Moreover, according to the gradation of excellence, whichever time is more subtle (*sūkṣma*) in relation to another is more commendable than that. When, by means of a statement regarding a "great limit" (*mahāvadhivacana*), the status of being *pūrvāhṇa* is established for a large duration of time, the status of being *pūrvāhṇa* is likewise established for a single part of it. Just as when the status of being the Gaṅgā is established for a specific flow of water beginning from the caves of the Himavat and ending at the boundary of the eastern ocean, the status of being the Gaṅgā is likewise established for a single part of the flow situated within it; otherwise, how could one observe the fulfillment of an injunction—such as "one should bathe in the Gaṅgā" or "one should perform the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) in the afternoon"—when it is performed in a part of that [time]? Some maintain that words are common to both a whole and its parts. As it has been said by the Teachers: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here. Thus, the meaning is that the word is used in a general sense with respect to both the whole and its parts. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the application of the term *pūrvāhṇa* to a portion of the forenoon. This is because the rule is not restricted to the whole alone, as in the case of the statement, "One should perform the *agnihotra* in the morning. For if it were so restricted, the performance of the *agnihotra* in the latter part of the morning would not be valid. Furthermore, since the *pūrvāhṇa* is defined as the first three *muhūrtas*, the period following immediately after the *pūrvāhṇa* is called *madhyāhna*. "Just as the word 'water' (toya) is accepted to refer both to a single drop and to a collection [of water], so too is it well-said that a sentence and a word [are meaningful] because they consist of substances in conjunction.

[319] Therefore, it must be stated that [the intermediate time-period] possesses meaning either by excluding other parts of the forenoon as determined by the statement of an intermediate limit, or by being intent on conveying the excellence of its own denotation. Regarding these two positions, in the first case, there would be the faults of rendering the statement of the major limit purposeless and contradicting it. Consequently, it is concluded that the statement of the intermediate limit is for the sake of indicating a higher degree of excellence.
Now, regarding the time of Kutapa, according to the Skanda and Vāyu Purāṇas:
"At that moment when the Lord of Rays (the Sun) shines fully upon the earth with his rays..."
That time should be known as Kutapa; what is given then yields great fruit.

The word *kuḥ* means the earth; *gopatiḥ* is the sun; with *gobhiḥ*, meaning its own rays; *kārtsnyena*, meaning entirely; at whatever moment he *tapati*, meaning makes hot, that time is to be known as *kutapa*. Thus, by this, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word *kutapa* is established, and this *kutapa* is defined. For indeed, due to the contraction of all shadows, it is only at the very middle of the day that the sun heats the entire earth; therefore, the middle of the day is determined to be the *kutapa*. And although it is measured by a *muhūrta*, it is referred to by the word *kṣaṇa* (moment) through figurative usage (*upacāra-vṛtti*), having considered the brevity [of the period]. For it is said in the Vāyu Purāṇa itself:
"The period after the seventh muhūrta and before the ninth muhūrta is to be known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors during that time becomes inexhaustible.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
The muhūrtas of the day are always known to be fifteen;
among them, that which is the eighth muhūrta is remembered as the time called Kutapa.

However, items such as the sword and the vessel, which are included under the term *kutapa* and are impossible to separate because they remain present at midday, are written here specifically due to the context of midday. As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"Brahmins, blankets, cows, silver, fire, and guests as well..."
Sesame seeds, darbha grass, and midday—all these are traditionally known as kutapa.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "Midday, a vessel of rhinoceros horn, as well as a Nepalese blanket,
silver, darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter's son is remembered as the eighth."
They say that "pāpa" means contemptible; because these eight cause torment for such a person, they are renowned as his "kutapas."
However, the Kauṣītakins read another [time], namely *kālakambala*.
Thus ends the section on the *kutapa*.
Now, the application (*viniyoga*) of these times, beginning with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), for the *śrāddhas* such as the *pārvaṇa* is described. To that effect, Śātātapa says:
The *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) is performed in the forenoon, while that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) is performed in the morning. Manu also says:
"The *mātṛka-śrāddha* is in the forenoon, but the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* is in the afternoon."
"But the *ekoddiṣṭa* [should be performed] at midday, while that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) is in the forenoon. Thus it is said in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"A wise man should perform the *śrāddha* in the forenoon of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*)."
"But during the afternoon of the dark fortnight, one must not let the moon pass beyond Rohiṇī. Thus it is said.

In this regard, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* or *ekoddiṣṭa* *śrāddha* should be commenced precisely during the first half of the *kutapa* period within the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). However, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), it should be commenced precisely during the second half of the *kutapa* period within the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). This statement is intended to establish that for the *pārvaṇa*, the first half of the *kutapa* is prescribed, whereas for the *ekoddiṣṭa*, the latter half is prescribed. For, by the opposite arrangement, the midday (*madhyāhna*) and afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) for the first and second halves respectively are already established by other injunctions. Alternatively, by the phrase "of the bright fortnight," the *daivika* (deity-oriented) *śrāddha* prescribed for that fortnight is indicated, and the forenoon is thereby enjoined; by the phrase "dark fortnight," the *paitṛka* (ancestor-oriented) is indicated, and the afternoon is enjoined. In this way, since there is no conflict with other injunctions, the midday and afternoon periods will not be set aside when they are otherwise applicable. Regarding the application of the afternoon period specifically, Śātātapa states:
"That which is declared as the Darśa-śrāddha is proclaimed as the Pārvaṇa;
therein, an offering in the afternoon is praised for the ancestors. Thus it is said.

Regarding the *darśa-śrāddha* performed by one who has not maintained the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* fire, or performed by women, *śūdras*, and others: in that case, the injunction specifies that it must follow the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* to be performed in the afternoon, as stated by the author of the *Kalpasūtra* in the words, "On the new moon day, they perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the afternoon. In accordance with this, the third part of the day—divided into three parts—should be taken as far as possible before the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). Thus Manu says:
"The *Piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha is recommended when the moon has waned."
"In the third part of the day, not too close to the twilight. Likewise:
"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires [should eat] at the waning of the moon."
"One should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* Śrāddha every month.
Nor should it be said:
"But he who possesses the sacred fire, having performed the *pitṛyajña*, [should perform] that which is called *tarpaṇa*..."
One should always perform the Śrāddha rite consisting of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka at the waning of the moon.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, the *anvāhāryaka* follows immediately after the *pitṛyajña*—known as the *tarpaṇa* and included within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—and not immediately after the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. It is in accordance with this that the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is prescribed. For Laugākṣi says:
"Having performed the rites at the end of the fortnight and the *vaiśvadeva*, the wise man who maintains the sacred fires should then perform the *piṇḍayajña*, and after that, the *anvāhāryaka*."

Therefore, following the conclusion of the Pitṛyajña—which is to be performed after the Piṇḍapitṛyajña—the third part of the day, extending up to but not including the time too close to twilight, should be taken for the Darśa-śrāddha. This is the application of the afternoon time;
now follows the application of the forenoon time.

In this context, since the rule "the *daivika* śrāddha is in the forenoon" (*tatra pūrvāhṇe daivikaṃ śrāddham*) refers to the forenoon that constitutes a limb of the *daivika* śrāddha—and there is nothing further to be said regarding it—it is stated with reference to the *āmāśrāddha* (śrāddha with raw food) which constitutes its own limb. Regarding this, some have determined that the injunction for the forenoon—namely, "but the *āmāśrāddha* is in the forenoon"—applies exclusively to the *āmāśrāddha* performed by the twice-born (*dvija*), and not even to the *āmāśrāddha* performed by a Śūdra. For he [the proponent of this view] thinks that if it applied to the *āmāśrāddha* performed by both [twice-born and Śūdras], then while the afternoon would be absolutely excluded in one case, it would be optionally included in the other; thus, a discrepancy would arise wherein the rule is mandatory in one instance and merely optional in the other.
For instance:

in the case of a *śrāddha* for twice-born (*dvija*) guests, one should set aside the afternoon time prescribed by extension (*atideśika*) by completely overriding it, and establish the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*). This is because the direct injunction (*upadeśa*)—to the effect that "the forenoon shall be observed"—is stronger than the extended rule; thus, rather than setting it aside by partially overriding the afternoon time prescribed by extension, one establishes the forenoon. However, in the case of a *śrāddha* for *śūdra* guests, since [the afternoon] has equal force due to another direct injunction, one should establish it by partially overriding the afternoon time prescribed by direct injunction (*aupadeśika*).

[323] Therefore, there is indeed a discrepancy. How, then, is it that for the *amaśrāddha* of the twice-born (*dvija*), the afternoon time is derived by extension (*ātideśika*), whereas for the *amaśrāddha* of the Śūdra, it is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*)?

It is said: The primary *pārvaṇa* rite, consisting of the feeding of Brahmins, is obligatory (*nitya*). That pertains exclusively to the agent who is a twice-born (*dvija*), and not to one whose agent is a Śūdra, because for the latter, since the *śrāddha* consisting of feeding Brahmins is prohibited, an *āmāśrāddha* (a *śrāddha* with uncooked food) is prescribed as the very obligation. Even if the rule regarding cooked food (*pakvānna*) were to apply there by overriding the prohibition, a disparity would arise: namely, that in the case of a Śūdra, the override of the prohibition would be required, whereas in the case of a twice-born, it would be unnecessary. Thus, that which is the primary *pārvaṇa*—the "Brahmin-nature" (*brāhmaṇya*) consisting of feeding Brahmins—is both obligatory and restricted to the agent who is a twice-born. However, the *āmāśrāddha* prescribed for twice-born agents on account of causes such as the impossibility of cooking is non-obligatory (*anitya*). This being the case, the ritual properties (*dharma*) taught in the archetype (*prakṛti*), beginning with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), must pertain only to the obligatory rite consisting of feeding Brahmins, and not to any other. For even the *āmāśrāddha* performed by a twice-born agent suffers from the contradiction of being both obligatory and non-obligatory. Just as the properties such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation are taught as belonging only to the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it is concluded with the Agniṣṭoma, and not to any other non-obligatory form; or as the purchase of Soma and so forth belong only to the obligatory Jyotiṣṭoma accomplished by the substance Soma, and not to any non-obligatory form accomplished by another substance—though in the latter case they occur only by extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, in the non-obligatory *āmāśrāddha* performed by a twice-born agent, the afternoon occurs only by extension. But for the Śūdra’s *āmāśrāddha*, because it is not occasional and is thus obligatory, the afternoon occurs by direct injunction (*upadeśa*); hence it is "injunctional" (*aupadeśika*). There, the afternoon [of the Śūdra rite] overrides the afternoon [of the twice-born rite] which is optional due to its status as an extended application (*atideśa*) from the twice-born *āmāśrāddha*. Consequently, this rule for the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), being confounded by such a disparity—being obligatory in one case and optional in the other—must resort to a single subject. And that [forenoon], avoiding the Śūdra’s *āmāśrāddha* which is defective due to its optionality, resorts only to the twice-born *āmāśrāddha*. This being so...
That time which is declared as Kutapa after midday— whatever is given to the ancestors at that very time, even with mere uncooked food, becomes inexhaustible.

[324] Thus, this statement merely reiterates the afternoon, because the afternoon is obtained through the general statement itself. Therefore, the *śūdra-amaśrāddha* takes place when the afternoon has commenced from the latter half of the *kutapa* period; however, the *dvija-amaśrāddha* takes place in the forenoon.
This concludes the application of the forenoon.
Now follows the application of the midday.

Regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, although it is taught that "it should be at midday" (*madhyāhne*), whereby five *muhūrtas* beginning with the sixth are prescribed as the time for the *ekoddiṣṭa* by virtue of being "midday," nevertheless, because the *kutapa* period is most highly recommended, one should strive to commence the *śrāddha* during the *kutapa*. As it is said in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Since the sun always becomes weaker at midday, therefore the commencement [of the rite] at that time is distinguished as yielding infinite fruit."
Gautama states that just as the commencement of the *śrāddha* at the *kutapa* time is distinguished, so too is its conclusion at the *rohiṇa* time:
"Having commenced the *śrāddha* at the *kutapa*, the wise man, knowing the rule and adhering to the ritual, should perform it until the *rohiṇa*; he must not overstep the *rohiṇa*."

‘Rohiṇa’ is the ninth muhūrta. The phrase “one should not pass beyond” is intended to praise the completion [of the rite] within Rohiṇa, not to prohibit the transgression of Rohiṇa; for that [period] also, being midday and afternoon, is a constituent part (aṅga) of the śrāddha. For this very reason, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states that the five muhūrtas beginning from Kutapa constitute a constituent part of the śrāddha: “The four muhūrtas that follow the muhūrta of Kutapa—these five muhūrtas are indeed desired as the abode of Svadhā.”

[325] The intended meaning of the phrase "the abode of *svadhā*" is this: this time is for the *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa* rites characterized by the utterance of *svadhā*, but not for the divine (*daivika*) rite or the *nāndī-śrāddha* characterized by the utterance of *svāhā*; for those two are prescribed specifically for the forenoon and the morning. Thus concludes the application of the midday. Now follows the application of the morning time.

In this context, the rule "in the morning" refers to the *vṛddhi*-śrāddha performed on account of prosperity; it concerns those *vṛddhi*-śrāddhas other than that occasioned by the birth of a son, for the latter is prescribed specifically when the occasion of a son's birth has occurred. Furthermore, since the time of birth itself is not fixed, the requirement that the rite be performed immediately thereafter establishes its own fixed timing.

Now, one might ask: why is the *śrāddha* rite, even when prescribed for a specific occasion, not postponed until its own proper time for the *vaiśvānarīya* sacrifice? Know that it is because there is no cause for postponement; indeed, impurity (*āśauca*) is not a cause for postponement. For the *vaiśvānarīya* sacrifice was not instituted for the purpose of removing the defect of impurity.
Now, it may be argued: "Giving, receiving, burnt offerings (*homa*), Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors—"
Except for the offering of funeral cakes to the departed, [this applies] until the cessation of ritual impurity.
The postponement [of the impurity] is due to compliance with such prohibitions as these.

In that regard, because the specific rule stating "one should perform a *śrāddha* when a son is born" overrides the prohibition by virtue of being a contingent injunction (*naimittika-vidhi*), there exists an extensive body of scriptural statements to the effect that at that time there is no impurity. On this point, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
The father, the grandfather,
and likewise the great-grandfather are born once again on that very day and experience it;
therefore, that day is meritorious and increases the satisfaction of the ancestors.
In the Āditya Purāṇa as well:
"When a son is born to the twice-born, both the gods and the ancestors come;
therefore, that day is meritorious and always to be honored."
Therein, one should give gold, land, a cow, a horse, a chariot,
an umbrella, clothing, garlands, a bed, a seat, and a house.
Hārīta also said:
"When a son is born, because of the joy of his parents, that day is meritorious."

"From the joy of the ancestors" means because of the arising of excessive delight; "meritorious" (puṇya) means purifying; that day is [meritorious] precisely because of the giving [of gifts]. The meaning is that this is the time for merit. In this case, since the day of the son's birth is not defiled by impurity (āśauca), the Śrāddha occasioned by the birth must be performed at that very time; it should not be postponed until after the period of impurity has passed. Although in the statements of Śaṅkha and others it appears that "that day is meritorious," nevertheless, it should be understood that it must be done even before the interruption of the study of the Vedas (śuśruṇābhyucchedāt). And so says Hārīta:

"Before the severance of the umbilical cord, they perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and acts for the sake of merit (*puṇya*); once the umbilical cord is severed, [the period of] impurity (*āśauca*) begins.

Here, "purificatory rite" refers to the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*). "Acts for the sake of merit" refers to the giving of gifts such as molasses, sesame seeds, oil, cows, land, gold, clothing, grain, and so forth.
Manu also says:
"The birth-rite (jātakarma) for a male child is prescribed before the cutting of the umbilical cord.
Here, "cutting" (vardhana) means severing.
Jaimini also [states this].
As long as the stalk has not perished, it is not sufficient for the birth-impurity to set in;
only after the stalk is severed is the birth-impurity prescribed.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The *śrāddha* should indeed be performed when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed upon the birth of a son;
or else, it should be performed by those of self-restraint once the period of impurity has ended."

On the day of a son’s birth, until the cutting of the umbilical cord, that day is meritorious. On that occasion, one should perform the *jātakarman* and the *āmaśrāddha*, or give sacrificial vessels together with gold. When the umbilical cord is severed, impurity (*aśauca*) sets in; therefore, the *śrāddha* must be performed strictly before the cutting of the navel-string. And because this is an occasional rite (*naimittika*), it should be performed even at night. As Vyāsa says: "One should not perform a ritual bath at night, nor especially a gift; however, one may perform an occasional bath and gift even during the nights."
Likewise:

"Giving on occasions such as the lunar stations (grahaṇa), weddings, the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), journeys, times of distress, and childbirth is known as occasional (naimittika) giving; it is not considered faulty even at night."

"What is given on the birth of a son, on a journey, or on every anniversary [of a death] is inexhaustible. And this [gift] must be performed even if, at that time, there is a coincidence of impurity caused by another birth-impurity (*sutaka*). Thus Prajāpati says:
"But when the birth of a son occurs while a *sūtaka* has arisen..."
The performer's immediate purification is cleansed by the preceding period of impurity.

"Of the performer" means of the one who performs the birth-rite (*jātakarma*). The meaning is that once the previously ongoing impurity (*janmāśauca*) has ceased, he becomes pure for that rite. However, if this rite was not performed at that time—either because the performer of the *jātakarma* was unavailable or due to the onset of another period of impurity caused by a death (*śāvāśauca*)—then it should be performed on some day after the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) has ended, specifically during the morning.

But surely, why should this rite—which has fallen from its own proper time—be performed at another time? For rituals such as those for an eclipse, or rites bound to specific causal conditions (*nimitta*), are not performed even when their designated time has passed.
True, that is so; however, this [present case] is performed because of a direct scriptural injunction. Thus it is said in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The *śrāddha* must indeed be performed while the umbilical cord is still uncut upon the birth of a son."
"Or else, when the period of impurity has ceased, [the rite] should be performed by those of self-restraint.

In this regard, the cessation of impurity is also a time for this [rite]; however, that [cessation] is not based on the impossibility of performing it prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord. Why is this so? We say: because of the statement of Vaijavāpāyana:
"Immediately after birth, the *jātakarman* should be performed according to the rule."
"If, by fate, the time has passed, it should be performed even when the period of impurity (sūtaka) has elapsed.
Thus ends the application regarding the morning time. Now, the prohibited times:
Regarding this, Vyāghrapāda said:
"The abandonment of Smārta rites occurs during the period of impurity (sūtaka), except in the case of Rāhu [an eclipse];
for Śrauta rites, one attains purity by bathing at that very time."

During any period of impurity (*sūtaka*) other than that caused by Rāhu, one should not perform Smārta rites such as the *śrāddha* and others; however, Śrauta rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *agnihotra* should be performed immediately after bathing, according to Aparārka. He explained this with the intention that the term *sūtaka* applies even during birth-impurity (*jananāśauca*) and when death occurs at a time directly preceding an eclipse of the moon or sun caused by Rāhu. Others, however, explain it differently: during *sūtaka*, which is birth-impurity, the abandonment of all ritual acts must be observed; the phrase "except for Rāhu" means excluding those acts occasioned by the sight of Rāhu. In the first explanation, it is established that *śrāddha* is not to be performed during either birth- or death-impurity; in the second explanation, it is established that *śrāddha* is not to be performed during birth-impurity alone. Furthermore, the word "karma" refers to ritual acts other than the offering of funeral cakes (*pretapiṇḍa*). Thus says Paiṭhīnasi: [Text of Paiṭhīnasi follows]

"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors— these should be suspended during a period of impurity, with the exception of the offering of rice-balls for the deceased. Thus say Manu and Śātātapa.

"One should not perform a *śrāddha* at night, for that time is declared to belong to the *rākṣasas*; nor during either of the two twilights, nor when the sun has only recently risen. It is called *rākṣasī* because powerful *rākṣasas* roam about during it, or because they become strong; for on such a night, the *śrāddha* is plundered by the *rākṣasas*. Furthermore, the *śrāddha* must not be performed during the preceding and following twilights either.
Regarding the duration of the two twilights, Yājñavalkya said:
"The preceding twilight is said to last for two muhūrtas before sunrise;
and that twilight lasts for three ghaṭikās once the sun has risen above the setting mountain."

The statement "when the sun has not yet risen" is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the time proximate to the morning twilight (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*); by this, the time proximate to the evening twilight (*paścimasaṃdhyā*) is also obtained. Thus, by this [text], the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* prescribed for the morning—which might otherwise apply to both the morning twilight and its proximate time—is prohibited. Furthermore, the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] prescribed for the afternoon—which might otherwise apply to both the evening twilight and its proximate time—is prohibited. However, there is no prohibition whatsoever regarding the middle twilight and its proximate time, because that period is characterized as *kutapa*. [In the] *Skanda Purāṇa*:
One should never perform the worship of the ancestors during the twilight;
that time is declared to belong to the Asuras, and one should avoid performing the Śrāddha rite then.

By this prohibition against performing [the Śrāddha] in proximity to the twilight (saṃdhyā), for one who is unable to begin or complete the Śrāddha before the evening time, the evening period excluding the vicinity of the twilight is thereby permitted. As for the statement from the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "The three-muhūrta period of the evening (sāyāhna) is excluded from all ritual acts."
If a man performs a Śrāddha when the fourth watch of the day has arrived,
that Śrāddha becomes demonic (āsura), and the giver shall go to hell.
And there is this statement of Baudhāyana:
"If the sun has become weak during the final portion of the day, that śrāddha becomes āsura; it does not reach the ancestors."
Yājñavalkya says:
For those desiring the fruits of rites for the gods, the lunar day (tithi) should generally be observed as ending at its conclusion;
for the great seers have declared that the root [of the rite] is for the sake of the ancestors, and it is called *paitra* (pertaining to the ancestors).
"Root" means the beginning.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The wise know that the end of the lunar day (tithi), called *sura*, is indeed to be observed as a fast."
The root of the lunar day is said to be the paternal [day] by those learned in the scriptures and experts in time.

The *Nigama* states: "If one performs a *śrāddha* during the forenoon and the donor goes to hell"— this statement of Hārīta applies only to those capable of completing the commencement and conclusion of the *śrāddha* prior to the evening time.
Vyāghrapāt said:
"One who knows the ritual rules, is endowed with faith, and correctly bestows gifts upon a worthy recipient,
attains unsurpassed excellence by performing this at any time other than during the night."
"Night" refers to the twilight (*saṃdhyā*). Viṣṇu states an exception to the prohibition regarding twilight and its proximate times:
"Indeed, the wise should not perform a *śrāddha* during twilight or at night;
however, even during those two times, it should be performed if there is an eclipse of the moon (*rāhudarśana*)."
"Rāhudarśana" refers to a lunar eclipse.
These are the prohibited times.
Now, the prohibited times for rites concerning the deceased (pretakriyā).
Regarding this, Gārgya says:
"If the consecration of the body (saṃskāra) occurs by the force of direct perception, one should not subtract a day at all;
even if the rite of consecration is performed again during the period of impurity (āśauca)."
In that case, however, the day for purification should be determined according to the circumstances;
if the deceased is cremated again after the period of impurity has ceased, [the rites should be performed on the day of that second cremation].
If the rites for the deceased are to be performed more than a year after death, one should select a day after having purified it; among these, the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) is best,
as is the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), yet even then one should avoid a day of lunar loss (dinakṣaya).

In this context, the funeral rite (*pretasaṃskāra*) for a deceased person is of two kinds: one for the actual body, and the other for a substitute image (*pratikṛti*). Regarding the rite for the actual body, there is no opportunity for examining whether the day is auspicious or inauspicious. However, for the rite of the substitute image, there are three periods: during the period of impurity (*āśauca*), within a year, and after a year has passed. Among these, when the rite for the substitute image is performed during the period of impurity, it should be carried out—provided it is possible—at a time avoiding the lunar days (*tithi*), constellations (*nakṣatra*), and so forth that will be mentioned below. When the rite for the substitute image is performed outside the period of impurity but within a year, then the purification of the commencement time must certainly be performed according to the method to be described. Even when it is performed after a year has passed, the time must likewise be purified; however, in that case, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) are particularly meritorious when they coincide. Furthermore, a day of lost lunar time (*dinakṣayadina*) must be avoided in all cases. Thus says Marīci.
On the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight falling on a Friday at the confluence of the Nandā with the Tripuṣkara,
a householder should not perform a Śrāddha ceremony, for fear of the loss of sons and wealth.

The first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days are *nandā*. "The day of Bhārgava" refers to Friday. The asterisms named Kṛttikā, Punarvasu, Uttaraphālgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā are called "tripuṣkaras. By the word *śrāddha* here, funeral rites for the deceased (*pretakriyā*) are intended. He himself states that among these, starting with the *nandā* days, those in the middle are the most inauspicious: "On the eleventh day, on a *nandā*, on a *sinīvālī*, on a Friday, on the fourteenth day of the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), and under the Kṛttikās—these are the tripuṣkaras."

In this context, the phrase "one should not perform a *śrāddha*" is to be supplied as a grammatical connection. The relationship is that [it should not be performed] on the day of Sinīvālī or on the day of Bhṛgu.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "One should not perform [a rite] under the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) under which a man was born."
O Bhārata, one should not perform [the rite] during the two months of Prauṣṭhapada, nor during the month of Āgneya;
one should also avoid all harsh [nakṣatras] and the pratyari [yoga].

[333] Here, the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) belongs to the performer of the *śrāddha*. "Of the two *prauṣṭhapadas*" refers to the two *bhādrapadās*. "The *āgneya*" is Kṛttikā. "The *dāruṇa* [asterisms]" are Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla. The fifth, fourteenth, and twenty-third asterisms from the birth asterism are the "counter-asterisms" (*pratyara*). According to Jyotiḥparāśara: "The funeral rites for humans are in no way recommended during the *sādhāraṇa*, *dhruva*, *ugra*, and *maitra* [asterisms], nor at Puṣkara, nor when the twin stars [Aśvinī and Bharaṇī] preside."

The *sādhāraṇa* [nakṣatras] are Kṛttikā and Viśākhā. The *dhruva* [nakṣatras] are the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī. The *ugra* [nakṣatras] are the three Pūrvas, Bharaṇī, and Maghā. The *maitra* [nakṣatras] are Mṛgaśīrṣa, Citrā, Anurādhā, and Revatī. The *tripuṣkara* nakṣatras have been mentioned. *Yamalādhiṣṭha* is Dhaniṣṭhā, because Mṛgaśīrṣa and Citrā are already included among the *maitra* nakṣatras. In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"One should avoid [performing rites] when the Moon is in its fourth, eighth, or twelfth [house]."
Rites for the deceased should be performed during Vyatīpāta, Vaidhṛti, and likewise during Parigha.
On the day known as Viṣṭi, on Saturdays,
especially on the thirteenth lunar day, and likewise during the three birth-asterisms;
The tenth and the nineteenth lunar mansions from the birth asterism constitute the three *janmatārās*.
Kāśyapa said: "Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Maghā, Śleṣā, and Mūla with its three quarters [are the *janmatārās*]."
The rites for the deceased are extremely inauspicious under the five asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā.
The two Phālgunīs, Rohiṇī, Anurādhā,
Punarvasu, the two Āṣāḍhas, and Viśākhā— these constellations, having two quarters,
should be avoided if they are even slightly afflicted, provided that other options are available.

[334] Thus, when it follows that the performance of rites for the deceased (*pretakṛtya*) is prohibited in these cases, Gobhila states an exception: "On a Nandā day, on a Friday, on the fourteenth lunar day, during the three birth-constellations,
and from the eleventh day onwards, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is not forbidden."
"Three births" refers to the three birth-stars (*janmatārā*). According to Vaijavāpa: "When the eleventh day has arrived for the deceased who has been directly cremated..."
Nothing whatsoever, such as the lunar mansion, the lunar day, or the weekday, need be purified.

If funeral rites for the deceased must be performed by chance on a day of solar transit (saṃkrānti), the anniversary of a yuga or manvantara, or on the new moon (darśa), there is no need to examine the suitability of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or other such factors.
Thus end the prohibited times for the rites for the deceased.
Now follow the prohibited times for the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Regarding this, Pulastya says:

"Likewise, on the two solstices (*ayana*), the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and on all the beginnings of the *yugas*, the *śrāddha* is to be performed without the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*).
Regarding these times, the *śrāddha* is to be performed "without the offering of rice-balls," that is, excluding the giving of the *piṇḍas*.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "On the third day of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of Kārttika, both being bright fortnights, men should perform the Śrāddha according to the procedure for a Saṃkrānti."

In this context, although the solstices (*ayana*) and other such occasions are already included by the phrase "at the transits" (*saṃkrāntiṣu*), their explicit mention again is for the purpose of highlighting that the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) performed at those times is exceedingly censurable. By the phrase "according to the procedure for the transit," the absence of rice-balls is indicated. The passage beginning with "on the third day of Vaiśākha" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all the beginnings of the *yugas* (*yugādi*), because of the statement of Pulastya: "And on all the beginnings of the *yugas*. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The *śrāddha* should be performed during the two solstices, likewise during the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and at the transits, excluding the offering of rice-balls."
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the Śrāddha ceremony should be performed by men according to the rules for a Saṃkrānti.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, on the new moon day of Māgha,
and likewise during the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), a śrāddha should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa).
And when a learned Śrotriya— one who knows the Vedas and understands the sacred fires— comes to one's home,
then with him alone one should perform the most excellent Śrāddha on the occasion of the Viṣuvat.

"Superior to the *viṣuvat* [equinox] is the *viṣuvat-śrāddha*, the most excellent. Even a *śrāddha* performed on account of the arrival of a learned *śrotriya* ought, according to the general rule of recitation, to be without rice-balls (*apiṇḍa*). Bṛhatpārāśara states:
'On the beginnings of the Yugas, on the *Maghā* [nakṣatra], on the *viṣuvat*, and likewise on the solstices (*ayana*')."
And one should certainly not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) under the asterism Bharaṇī.
Regarding the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada conjoined with the Maghā asterism, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"On that occasion, a great worship should be performed for the ancestors;
however, one who has an eldest son should avoid the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) during that asterism."

"In that case as well"—that is, even on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada—if the moon is situated in the *maghā* nakṣatra, which is presided over by the ancestors (*pitṛdaivata*), a "great" worship characterized by the *śrāddha* rite must be performed. However, if the performer of the rite has an eldest son—that is, if his first-born son is living—then while performing the *śrāddha* there, he should avoid the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). The meaning is that he should perform the *śrāddha* without the rice-balls. By the term "having an eldest son," the defect characterized by the destruction of the eldest son is indicated for the offering of rice-balls when it occurs during the *maghā* period, the thirteenth-day period, or when both coincide.
And in that regard, it is stated in the Mahābhārata: "O Bhārata, by fasting on the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), by breaking the fast [on that same day],
and by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) under the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes."
Jyotiḥpārāśara states: "When a marriage has been performed, the sapindas should indeed avoid [officiating at] marriages for twelve months;
however, in the case of the investiture of the sacred thread (mauñjībandha), they should avoid it for six months."
The exception to this rule is as follows:
during the Mahālaya festival, at a Śrāddha for Gayā, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
and likewise at the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for any mortal whatsoever.

"Even one who has performed the wedding ceremony should always perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa)," so says Vṛddha-Śātātapa. "That Śrāddha which is prescribed as being devoid of the offering of the rice-balls..."
In this rite, the recitation of the *svadhā* is omitted, but the scattering of food (*vikira*) is not omitted;
