the offering of imperishable water, the sacrificial fee, and the expressions of well-being and goodwill remain as they were.
Thus end the prohibited times for the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).

In this regard, the following is investigated: Do the *śrāddhas* performed after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—those associated with the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the *aṣṭakās*, the *vyatīpāta*, the solstices (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, the *yugas*, the *anukalpas*, and so forth, as well as those connected to the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) and other such occasions—differ at each respective time, or not? To that end, this is considered: Are the statements specifying these times injunctions for the origination (*utpatti-vidhi*) of the ritual acts, or are they injunctions regarding the time for acts already originated? In this matter, although an injunction regarding the verbal root’s meaning (*bhāvārtha*) and an injunction regarding the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) would result from prescribing a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*), nevertheless, because the injunctive power transfers to the qualifier and because of parsimony (*lāghava*), these are indeed injunctions of subordinate qualities; thus, they do not bring about a difference in the ritual acts. Therefore, due to the unity of the act, even when multiple times occur simultaneously, performance takes place at one optional time rather than at all of them. How much less, then, could there be separate performance for times occurring simultaneously? Thus, when times coincide, a single *śrāddha* should be performed once. For it is not accepted by anyone that there should be a repetition of the primary act (*pradhāna*) merely out of deference to subordinate qualities in the form of specific times. As for the repetition of the *homa* in accordance with times such as evening and morning, that is due to the repetition of the occasion (*nimitta*) consisting of life as delimited by those specific times.

To this it is replied: Where there is an original enunciation (*utpatti*) of the rite in proximity, then in those sentences containing qualifiers (*guṇa*), because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of that same rite, there occurs an injunction of only the qualifier. But here, since there is no original enunciation, and because there is no other way [to proceed], the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) does not apply in the case of an injunction of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). If one were to instead assume an original enunciation, then by abandoning the injunction of a qualified whole everywhere, there would be a distinction [of rites] based on the qualifiers in some cases. Therefore, because it is an injunction of a qualified whole, there is a distinction between the *śrāddhas* according to each specific time. Furthermore, since eclipses and so forth serve as the occasional causes (*nimitta*), when they differ, the distinction [between the rites] is clear. Thus, it is established that upon the arrival of that specific time, that particular *śrāddha* must be performed.

Now, a doubt arises regarding the coincidence of time and the coincidence of causes: among the various *śrāddhas* belonging to those specific times and those specific occasions, should only one be performed, or should all be performed separately, or rather by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*)? Since it is prohibited to perform multiple *śrāddhas* on a single day, the prima facie view is that only one should be performed; to this, it is replied: "When many have passed away at the same time, or even two..."
Having performed the cooking by means of a single vessel, one should perform the śrāddha offerings separately for each.
[338] First for the one who died previously, then for the second, and then for the third; this is the sequence to be followed in cases of simultaneous deaths.

Thus, since Bhṛgu has stated that one may perform many *śrāddhas* for various occasions on the same day, and since [the rule] beginning with "twelve days are recommended" explains the performance of various *preta-śrāddhas* on a single day,
one should not perform two *śrāddhas* anywhere on the same day.

Thus, since it is established that this prohibition applies specifically to the *śrāddha* performed for the sake of prosperity (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*) initiated by those who are dull-witted due to their faith, the position is adopted that all [the various types of *śrāddha*] must be performed separately. As for the statement that there is a single performance (*tantra-anuṣṭhāna*) of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries of the *āgneya* and other sacrifices because of the identity of place, time, and agent—and because no distinction is perceived—that is appropriate only for subsidiaries grasped within a single injunctive rule of performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*), but not for independent primary acts (*pradhāna*). Furthermore, the argument that the *nitya-apūrva* (the transcendental result of the obligatory rite) is included when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* are performed for the sake of a *kāmya-apūrva* (the result of a desire-based rite) is also properly stated only when there is identity of the ritual action (*karmaikya*). For the very same collections of rites such as the *āgneya* and others which serve the purpose of the *kāmya-apūrva* are understood to serve the purpose of the *nitya-apūrva* as well, owing to the identity of their originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*). Any conventional usage of "difference" (*bheda*) in that case is based on a distinction in the temporal determination of cognition caused by the connection with limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as the form of desire (*kāma*) or the form of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), and is not based on a real ontological difference. However, the difference between *apūrvas* is real, arising from the difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, although this [distinction of the *śrāddha*s] is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), it is discussed under the section on the definition of difference (*bhedalakṣaṇa*) on the grounds that it follows upon the difference between *apūrvas*.

[Objection: But surely, even though it is real, a distinction between the productive urges (*bhāvanā*) of sacrifice, giving, and offering has been established, based on the difference in cognition caused by the coloring [of the cognition] by the various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the meanings of their respective verbal roots?

[Reply: True. However, in those cases, the distinction manifested through the coloring by the root-meanings was accepted as real because there was no sublation (*bādhaka*). In the present case, however, it is unreal because there exists a sublation in the form of the unity of the ritual action (*karman*) brought about by the singleness of the originative injunction (*utpatti-śāstra*).

Therefore, in this case, because the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same, the obligatory performance is accomplished by means of the very *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices performed for the sake of a desired transcendental result (*kāmyāpūrva*); thus, a separate performance is not carried out. However, when the ritual action is distinct, since the transcendental result of one cannot be established by another, the other must also be performed for its own sake. Or, let it be granted that there is here some real, albeit subtle, difference in the ritual action; yet that difference is of a different nature from other types of difference. For something accepted as a general rule in one context does not necessarily have to be sought elsewhere.

To this it is replied: even when there is a plurality of ritual acts (*karman*), if there is unity of place, time, agent, and so forth, the accomplishment of all acts occurs through a single performance; indeed, the simultaneous completion of all prior rites arises. For at that time, no distinction is perceived as to "this has been completed" and "this has not. Furthermore, it is accepted that even when there is a difference in sacrifices (*yāga*), if the deity is one, the performance is *tantra* (common/shared). This is established in the section concerning the *sānnāyya*, the crossing of a river in a dream, rain, and the recitation of mantras over impurities (*amedhya*), where it is stated that when multiple causes in the form of the sight of various impurities occur simultaneously, and the repetition of the occasional rite consisting of the mantra "The mind is poor, the eye is poor" would otherwise be required for each individual cause, a single performance of the occasional rite takes place due to the absence of any perceived distinction. Thus it stands in one part [of the tradition].

Therefore, when there is a convergence of occasions for *śrāddha*, a convergence of times, a unity of place, a unity of performer, and a unity of deity, since there is no basis for distinguishing between them, the performance of all *śrāddhas* should be carried out by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*). This being the case, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform these *śrāddhas*—those occasioned by the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), those occasioned by the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), and those occasioned by the *vyatīpāta* yoga—all by way of a single ritual procedure.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the convergence of times.
Thus [ends the section] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, the sovereign of all administrative authorities...

The fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Times for Śrāddha," in the *Śrāddhakalpa* within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the scholar Śrī Hemādri, the sovereign of all auspicious undertakings and an expert in the sciences, is completed.
[340] Now begins the sixth chapter.
Regarding those waves initiated by the intermingling of the Sarasvatī’s cascades:

The collections of the Vedas, Smṛtis, and treatises on ethics are praised for their devoted attention to rivaling the swarms of thick fish and tortoises; now, that very Hemādri, the lord of ministers, composes this work describing the Brahmins who are fit for the Śrāddha and those who are otherwise.
Now, the Brāhmaṇas are described.

Here, following the discussion of place and time, and since the performance of the Śrāddha rite must be determined, the Brāhmaṇas—who correspond to the Āhavanīya fire as the locus for the offering of oblations—are described prior to the sacrificial materials and other elements, because they are the first to be secured. Furthermore, since in Śrāddhas performed by members of all four castes it is ordained that only Brāhmaṇas are to be invited, they alone are the ones to be appointed.
In this regard follows the praise of the Brāhmaṇas.
Regarding this, the Taittirīya Śruti states:

"As many deities as there are, they all dwell in a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda. Therefore, one should pay homage day after day to Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, and one should not utter anything vulgar toward them; for it is these very deities whom one pleases.
Here, "homage" (namaskāra) is intended to signify worship in general.

The *Śatapatha-śruti* also states: "There are indeed two kinds of gods: the gods who are truly gods, and those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in them, who are the human-gods. For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: oblations belong to the gods, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the human-gods, the Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in them. With oblations one gratifies the gods, and with sacrificial fees one gratifies the human-gods, the Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in them. Both these classes of gods, being gratified, place him in the state of immortality. Thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
Brahmins are the deity on earth; Brahmins are the deity in heaven.
There is no being superior to Brahmins in the three worlds.
They could make a non-deity into a deity, and they could make a deity into a non-deity;
for the highly blessed Brāhmaṇas, the twice-born, are constantly worshipped.
According to the sacred tradition, the gods were first born from the Brāhmaṇas;
since the entire world arose from the Brāhmaṇas, the twice-born are therefore most worthy of worship.
The deities, the ancestors, the sages, and likewise the nāgas eat from their mouths; what being could be greater than that?
Yājñavalkya says: Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas,
for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the preservation of dharma.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "There is no god equal to the Brahmin; there is no teacher equal to the Brahmin. There is no enemy greater than the Brahmin; there is no ordinance greater than the Brahmin."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the Lord says:
"When Brāhmaṇas are constantly honored, I am honored; of this there is no doubt.
And when they are reviled, I too am reviled in all my activities."
"O King Yudhiṣṭhira, the Brahmins are my supreme refuge; he who honors them, I behold in my own true form."
In the Skanda Purāṇa, the words of Īśvara addressed to the Goddess:
"O Goddess, foremost among the leaders of Brahmins, these Brahmins are indeed mines of the Vedas, like oceans are of jewels; they should be honored with diligent effort."
“O Goddess with the face of the moon, whose face is the chief of brahmins!”— this is an address to the Goddess.
Where brahmins learned in the Vedas do not consume the supreme oblation,
there the gods, O Queen of Gods, never eat the oblation at any time.
Neither Nārāyaṇa, nor Ananta, nor Brahmā, nor Skanda, nor the fire-crested Agni,
take delight in that action wherein Brahmins are not honored.
A wise person should honor those Brahmins by whose grace long life, righteousness, happiness, wealth, prosperity, fame, and residence in heaven are easily obtained.
Thus ends the praise of the Brāhmaṇa.
Now follows the definition of a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding this, the teachers say:

"A Brāhmaṇa is one who is the substratum of the genus *brāhmaṇatva*. Here, although it is impossible for there to be a grosser cause that manifests the lower universal (*avāntarasāmānya*) of "humanity"—since there is an absence of any distinction based on substance, quality, action, or configuration that could be experienced through the mere contact of the eyes without depending on instruction, as is the case with the exclusion of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others from those intended to be recognized as Brāhmaṇas—nevertheless, there certainly exists a manifestation of *brāhmaṇatva* consisting of subtler qualities such as good character (*sauśīlya*), which is manifested by a specific cognition dependent on the instruction regarding birth from a pure lineage of mother and father, and which is witnessed by both the examiner and the non-examiner. Moreover, everyone accepts that even in the case of gems and the like, there is an appearance that manifests a universal, even though it depends upon instruction.

[Objection: Is not "being born from a lineage of pure parents" simply "being born from parents belonging to the Brāhmaṇa caste"? If so, then in the case of such instruction, there arises a mutual dependence that obstructs comprehension: the knowledge of Brāhmaṇahood depends upon the knowledge of the meaning of the instruction, and the knowledge of the meaning of the instruction depends upon the knowledge of Brāhmaṇahood.

[Reply: Not so. This is the meaning of the instruction here: a Brāhmaṇa is one who possesses the universal *brāhmaṇatva* (Brāhmaṇahood). However, what establishes that *brāhmaṇatva* is the fact of being born from such [parents].

But then, in a case such as the authoritative instruction that "the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is established by the fact of being born from a Brāhmaṇa alone," since there is an absence of knowledge regarding the establishment of *brāhmaṇatva*—which is itself internalized within the establishing property—it is impossible for such [an instruction] to serve as a means for the knowledge of that establishment; consequently, there would follow the fallacies of mutual dependence, self-dependence, and infinite regress.

Not so. Let it be granted that mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and other such faults apply to its being a *jñāpaka* (informative cause); however, they do not apply when it is a *kāraka* (productive cause), because it functions as a cause by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*). And this instruction concerns the productive cause, not the informative cause. Thus, following the instruction regarding the productive cause of the formal distinction, there certainly exists a comprehension of the universal "brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇatva-sāmānya*), brought about by the manifestation of the previously mentioned specific qualities that reveal brahminhood.

But if this were the case, then for a man who has heard such an instruction, upon encountering a Brahmin whose lineage and name have never been seen or known before, yet whose specific conduct and dress are observed, a cognition of "Brahminhood" would arise without doubt merely by the contact of the eyes. Consequently, there would be no need for questioning or investigation. If, on the other hand, it is argued that because the defining condition (*upādhi*)—characterized by being born from a pure lineage of mother and father—is not perceived as residing in that particular individual, the universal (*sāmānya*) inhering therein remains unmanifest, then, since that defining condition must function as a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*), the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) and so forth inevitably follows.
Not so. This indicative nature (*liṅgatva*) of the causal factor (*kāraka*), which transcends the stage of formal instruction, is indeed faultless as a means of cognition (*jñāpaka*).

Now, it might be argued: "In this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), where the god of love (*makaradhvaja*) is difficult to ward off and the family is rooted in passion, what room is there for the conceptualization of caste?"

That is not so. For we observe that families protected by men who pride themselves on their lineage and by women of similar status are indeed seen to be corrupted while they persist. Furthermore, this matter has been elaborated upon in various treatises, so we shall desist here. Moreover, the definition of a Brāhmaṇa is not the perfection of the practices of sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts, nor the possession of non-violence, truthfulness, purity, and so forth. For even if one lacks any one of these—officiating, teaching, or receiving gifts—if there exists merely the practice of studying, sacrificing, and giving, the conventional usage of "Brāhmaṇa" remains uncorrupted among those of the Brāhmaṇa caste; thus, the collection of all these qualities cannot be the defining characteristic. Nor can the lack of such a collection be the definition, since these qualities exist among Kṣatriyas and others. Nor can the combination of officiating, teaching, and receiving gifts be the definition of a Brāhmaṇa; for in that case, one who observes the vow of renouncing the acceptance of gifts would not be a Brāhmaṇa, as he would lack one of the three. Conversely, one regarded as a Kṣatriya who possesses these three would erroneously become a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, it is prescribed that a person who is already a Brāhmaṇa may accept gifts, officiate at sacrifices, or teach for the sake of his livelihood. Therefore, acts such as accepting gifts cannot be the cause for applying the pre-existing designation "Brāhmaṇa" to one who acquires them later. If you argue that they are like the case of a *pūpa* (a cake), we say no; for things established through a principle of necessity (*ananyagatinyāya*) cannot be applied to objects where that necessity does not apply.
As for what is stated in the Vahnipurāṇa—that conduct alone is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa:
"Neither birth, O King, nor lineage, nor Vedic study, nor sacred learning are the causes of being twice-born; conduct alone is indeed the cause."
What will noble birth avail a wicked soul devoid of virtuous conduct? Do worms not breed even within fragrant flowers?
O lord of the people, nothing is exclusively pure;
therefore, O father, let conduct be investigated. Is it not seen that even Rākṣasas possess such conduct?
What is the use of much study for one who is as wicked as an actor? Only he has truly studied and heard the scriptures who puts their teachings into practice.
Just as water in a skull-cup and milk in sandalwood are defiled by the defect of their container, so too is sacred learning defiled when its conduct is lacking.
Even one who has mastered the four Vedas, if he is of evil conduct, is considered inferior to a Śūdra;
therefore, O Great King, know that conduct is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Truthfulness, self-control, austerity, charity, non-violence, and restraint of the senses—
O King of kings, he in whom these are seen is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
And as it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"But he who has been purified by the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*), who is pure,
perfected in the study of the Vedas, and established in the six duties..."
One who speaks the truth, eats only the remains of the meal, is virtuous, and is dear to his teacher;
one who is devoted to the vow of truth and intent upon truth—he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Asceticism, sacred learning, and noble birth—these are the causes of being a Brāhmaṇa.
Truth, charity, austerity, sacrifice, benevolence, and forgiveness [are the marks] of men;
he in whom austerity is seen is traditionally known as a Brāhmaṇa.
"In the six duties" refers to sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
"One who eats vighasa" is one who eats what remains after guests and others who must necessarily be fed have eaten. And thus Vyāsa says:
"To the gods, to the ancestors, to the servants, and together with the guests..."
"But he who eats what remains after giving is called an eater of *vighasa*.
And that which was stated by Yama and Śātātapa:
"Austerity, righteousness, compassion, charity, truth, knowledge, sacred learning, and mercy—"
Knowledge, humility, and non-stealing—this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
And as it was said by Vasiṣṭha: "Yoga, austerity, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity, learning, modesty,
sacred knowledge, and faith— this is the definition of a Brāhmaṇa."
He whom no one knows as either existing or non-existing, as unlearned or deeply learned, as one of good conduct or of bad conduct— he is a Brāhmaṇa.
And as it was said by Yama: "He who is constantly devoted to non-violence, who offers oblations into the sacred fire,
who is devoted to his own wife, and who is a giver— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa."
He whose learning follows wisdom, and whose wisdom follows learning,
who does not transgress the noble boundaries— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
The gods know him as a Brahmin who performs worship for the sake of blessings and wealth only as a matter of circumstance, being free from greed and delusion.

"Blessings" means benedictions. "For the sake of wealth" means for the acquisition of riches. "Veneration" means hospitality or the worship of deities. "Occasions" refers to various introductory topics or attachments to various subjects. Truth, charity, forgiveness, good conduct, kindness, compassion, and mercy—wherever these are seen in this world, the gods know him as a Brāhmaṇa.
The term ‘ghṛṇā’ refers to a dispute regarding what is contemptible.

All of this is not intended to refute the caste of Brāhmaṇahood (*brāhmaṇatvajāti*) by establishing that conduct (*śīla*), behavior (*vṛtta*), and so forth, are the grounds for the application of the word ‘Brāhmaṇa’; rather, it is intended to establish the excellence inherent in a Brāhmaṇa that entitles him to partake of *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors). This is just as the statement, “Other animals are not cattle; cows and horses are cattle,” is intended to establish the excellence of cows and horses.
For this very reason, Baudhāyana said: [text follows].
Knowledge, austerity, and birth—this is the definition of a Brahmin.
He who is devoid of knowledge and austerity is merely a Brahmin by birth.

Thus, the definition of a praiseworthy Brāhmaṇa worthy of *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) consists in being endowed with knowledge (*vidyā*) and other such qualities. However, the "Brāhmaṇahood" found in one devoid of knowledge and the rest means merely the connection with the genus (*jāti*) that is the form of Brāhmaṇahood; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "only a Brāhmaṇa by birth," the analysis of the compound is: "he is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone. For this very reason, in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, the possession of knowledge and other qualities is stated to be the cause for the "worthiness" (*pātratva*) of Brāhmaṇas, not for the application of the word "Brāhmaṇa" itself.
This concludes the definition of a Brāhmaṇa. Now follows the definition of a Brāhmaṇa who has become a worthy recipient (*pātrībhūta*).
Yājñavalkya says: One does not become a worthy recipient through learning alone, nor even through austerity;
rather, that person in whom both conduct and these two [learning and austerity] reside is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient.
The Vedas, together with the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the epics (smṛtis), the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā, constitute knowledge (vidyā).
Devala states the definition of austerity (tapas):

Now we shall explain the rule for austerity (*tapas*). It is as follows: austerity is the heating of the body through vows (*vrata*), fasts (*upavāsa*), and observances (*niyama*). Vows and the others have also been shown by that same authority. Among these, the vows (*vrata*) include celibacy, speaking the truth, abstaining from honey and meat, silence, not begging, approaching one’s wife only during her season, and so forth. Fasting (*upavāsa*) is the non-eating of food. Observances (*niyama*) include the habit of reciting sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), service to mother, father, cows, and Brahmins, visiting holy places of pilgrimage (*puṇyakṣetra*), bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), not seeking relief from cold, heat, rain, sun, or dew; lying on thorns, gravel, *darbha* grass, wooden planks, straw mats, sand, or the bare ground; wearing wet clothes during the winter and cool seasons; sleeping in water during the rains; standing during the day in the midst of five fires during the summer and spring; abstaining from sweet foods such as molasses, salt, milk products, oils, and grains; and eating fruits, roots, vegetables, flowers, or oil-cakes. Austerity is the performance of the duties prescribed for one’s own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
Vṛddhaśātātapa says:
A Brahmin who is devoted to Vedic study, observant of restraints, ascetic, possessed of knowledge, patient, self-controlled, and truthful in speech, is declared here to be a worthy recipient.

"Veda-study" (*svādhāya*) refers to the Veda; one who is engaged in its teaching, comprehension, and exposition is "possessed of Veda-study" (*svādhāyavān*). "Possessed of observances" (*niyamavān*) means one who is endowed with the *yamas* and *niyamas*. And these are as follows: "Celibacy, compassion, patience, meditation, truthfulness, sincerity, non-violence, non-stealing, gentleness, and self-restraint—these are recorded as the *yamas*. (YDh 3.312)
Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, and restraint of the generative organ are the observances (niyamas); likewise, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance.

Thus, that which was spoken by Yājñavalkya is to be understood. In this context: *brahmacarya* (celibacy) is the avoidance of association with forbidden women; *dayā* (compassion) is the desire to counteract the calamities of all living beings; *kṣānti* (forbearance) is the endurance of the suffering caused by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*); *dhyāna* (meditation) is the constant contemplation of one's chosen deity; *satya* (truthfulness) is speaking words that accord with reality for the benefit of beings; *akalkatā* (freedom from guile) is the absence of deceit; *ahiṃsā* (non-violence) is the avoidance of killing not sanctioned by law; *asteya* (non-stealing) is the non-appropriation of another’s property that cannot be taken away; *mādhurya* (gentleness) is possessing a demeanor, speech, and conduct that cause pleasure to others; *dama* (self-restraint) is the removal of the intoxication of the senses through means such as eating measured portions of food, for the purpose of ceasing self-willed behavior; *snāna* (ablution) consists of daily and occasional immersion in water and so forth; *mauna* (silence) is the avoidance of engaging in prohibited speech; *upavāsa* (fasting) is the daily and occasional abstention from food for a day and night; *ijyā* (sacrifice) is the necessary relinquishment of one’s own wealth dedicated to a deity; *svādhyāya* (study) is the study of the Vedas; *upasthanigraha* (control of the generative organ) is the turning away from the act of discharging semen in an unordained manner; *guruśuśrūṣā* (service to the teacher) is acting in accordance with the teacher’s will; *śauca* (purity) is the removal of external and internal impurities; *akrodha* (absence of anger) is the avoidance of specific internal disturbances that serve as the cause for initiating cruel acts such as killing, threatening, or cursing; and *apramādatā* (heedfulness) is vigilance regarding what is prescribed and the non-performance of what is forbidden. One is called a *jñānavit* (knower of knowledge) because of the attainment of knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) through the Veda.

In the Mahābhārata: "O bull among the twice-born, the sages know him to be a worthy recipient who has studied the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and has desisted from the six types of worldly activities."
Vasiṣṭha says: What kind of vessel consisting of the Veda is that which has no regard for "śūdrānna"?
"Śūdrānna" refers to food obtained through the acceptance of wealth from a Śūdra. For if one avoids actual śūdrānna, what indeed would constitute being an "excessive vessel" (atipātra)?
Bṛhaspati says:

One who is a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) is a worthy recipient; one who has mastered the Vedas is a worthy recipient; but the most excellent of all recipients is he in whose stomach no food belonging to a Śūdra resides.
Vyāsa says:
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
however, that vessel which is unmixed [with worldly qualities] is remembered as the supreme vessel.
"Unmixed" means free from contact with those who have fallen into confusion of lineage, confusion of occupation, and so forth.
R̥ṣyaśṛṅga says:
[350] "One vessel consists of the Veda; another vessel consists of austerity."
They know that the guest is the supreme vessel; that is the highest recipient.
The characteristics of a guest will be described in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Patience, lack of desire, self-restraint, truthfulness, generosity, good conduct, austerity, and learning."
This is declared to be the supreme eightfold characteristic of a worthy recipient.
The characteristics of ethical conduct (*śīla*) will be explained below. Devala says:
One who is pure in three respects, of frugal livelihood, compassionate, and with all senses under control.
One who is liberated from the defects of birth is called a brahmin, a worthy recipient.

One who possesses three "white" (pure) lineages, knowledge, and conduct is called "triśukla. "Ghṛṇāluḥ" means compassionate. "Sakalendriyaḥ" means one whose limbs are neither deficient nor redundant. "Vimukto yonidoṣaiḥ" means one who does not commit acts that cause the mixing of castes.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says: [one who is] rich in Vedic study, of noble birth, and tranquil...

They say that a Brahmin who knows the sacrificial rites, who fears sin, who is learned, who is patient toward women, who is righteous, who provides refuge for cows, and who is worn out by his vows, is a worthy recipient.

"Patient toward women" means being forbearing regarding women, that is, free from lust. "One who seeks refuge in cows" means one devoted to the service of cows. "Wearied by vows" means one whose body and senses have been withered through the performance of religious observances.
Yama also said:
"One endowed with knowledge, virtuous in character, and tranquil..."
Patient, self-controlled, truthful, and grateful;
one who is weary of worldly life, devoted to the welfare of cows, a refuge for cows, a giver, a performer of sacrifices— such a Brahmin is a worthy recipient.
‘One whose livelihood is impaired’ (*vṛttiglāna*) means one whose body is emaciated by subsisting on gleaned grains and the like. ‘A sacrificer’ (*yajvā*) means one who performs sacrifices.

This is the definition of a Brāhmaṇa who has become a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Now, in connection with the description of the designations for such recipients, other designations of Brāhmaṇas are also stated, which are based on their possession or lack of possession of lineage, character, conduct, and so forth, and which are useful for knowing the distinctions between superior, middling, and inferior [recipients].
Regarding this, Devala says: "The *mātra*, the *brāhmaṇa*, the *śrotriya*, the one devoted to austerity (*tapas*), the *anūcāna*, as well as the *bhrūṇa*, the *ṛṣikalpa*, the *ṛṣi*, and the *muni*."
Thus these eight types of Brāhmaṇas have been declared in the primary revelation;
among them, the one most devoted to austerity is the best, by virtue of his excellence in knowledge and conduct.
The meaning is: "due to the cause of excellence produced by preeminence in learning and conduct.
He himself states their definitions according to the order of enumeration:
"When one is born into a family of Brāhmaṇas, he is merely one by birth (jātimātra)."
One who is unendowed [with learning] and devoid of ritual action is designated as "Mātra."
"Unendowed" means one who has not undergone the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
Having passed the eleventh year, a twice-born man who possesses proper conduct,
is restrained, truthful, and compassionate, is declared to be a *brāhmaṇa*.

‘Ekādaśātikramaḥ’ refers to the study of the Veda with some portion deficient. ‘Nivṛttaḥ’ means tranquil. Having studied one recensional branch (śākhā) or the entire collection along with its six auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), a Brahmin who is devoted to the six duties and knows the Dharma is called a Śrotriya.
Yama also says:
He who learns the three verses of Sāvitrī preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
and has lived the life of a religious student— he indeed is called a *śrotriya*.
"Preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,"—the remainder being "the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*s).
In the *Brahmavaivarta* as well, the definition of a *śrotriya* is stated:
"One is known as a Brāhmaṇa by birth; he is called a *dvija* (twice-born) through the sacramental rites."
And by means of knowledge as well; one who possesses these three is called a Śrotriya.

Devala says: One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), whose soul is pure, who is free from sin, who is disciplined, and who has attained the status of a learned Vedic scholar— such a person is remembered as an *anūcāna*.
One who is endowed with the qualities of a learned scholar, restrained by sacrifice and Vedic study,
who eats only the remnants of the meal and has conquered his senses, is called a *bhrūṇa* by the wise.
He who, having acquired all knowledge both Vedic and worldly,
constantly dwells as a forest-dweller without being bound to a specific stage of life, is remembered as being equal to a seer (ṛṣi).
"Laukika" refers to knowledge such as the acquisition of wealth and so forth.
One whose semen is drawn upward (a celibate ascetic), fierce in austerity, restrained in diet, and free from doubt;
capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, and true to his word—such a one becomes a *ṛṣi*.
He whose covenant, intention, and purpose are true is "one of true covenant" (*satyasaṃdha*), meaning one whose resolve is true.
A sage (*muni*) is traditionally defined as one who has desisted from worldly activity, knows all principles of reality, is free from desire and anger,
is established in meditation, is inactive, is a giver, and is "threefold pure" (*triśukla*).
‘Nivṛttaḥ’ means one who has desisted from prohibited and desire-driven actions; ‘niḥkriyaḥ’ means one who is devoid of activities such as the acquisition of wealth.
Thus, they are exalted by their lineage, learning, and conduct.
O best of Brahmins, those known as the Triśuklas are honored at the Soma-pressings and other rites. Saṃvarta says:
[353] "The origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their departure and return..."
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance would be one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O best of the Bharatas, that twice-born man who teaches a disciple for whom the initiation ceremony has been performed the entire Veda along with its secret doctrines..."
O mighty-armed one, the wise declare him to be a teacher.
Bṛhaspati said: "He who gathers the scriptures together, establishes them in right conduct,
and practices them himself— he is called an Ācārya."
Manu says:
One should know that person to be a guru in this world who benefits one’s learning, whether it be little or much, by means of such assistance to one’s studies.

"Whether it be the whole, or half, or a quarter, or even a single syllable— whichever one receives from another, one must certainly show respect to that person. Thus it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*.
He who instructs a disciple appropriately through refined (saṃskṛta) or vernacular (prākṛta) speech, and by means of the local dialect and other such methods, is known as a guru.
In the Mahābhārata: "That teacher who, for the sake of his own livelihood, teaches even a single portion of the Veda or the Vedāṅgas is called an Upādhyāya."
Vyāsa says: He who, having been chosen, performs the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), as well as the Agniṣṭoma and other rites,
is indeed called an officiating priest (ṛtvij).
In the Śivadharmottara: "He who knows the Self alone— the creator of the moving and the unmoving, the all-pervading Lord of infinite power— is remembered as a knower of the Self."
Devoted to the dharma of Śiva, tranquil, and dedicated to the knowledge of Śiva,
these Brahmins shall be exponents of the Śivadharma and practitioners of Śiva-yoga.
Manu: One seeking progeny, one about to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions,
one who seeks wealth for the sake of a teacher, for the sake of his father or mother, one seeking to study the Vedas, and one who is afflicted by illness— [these should not be refused alms].
One should know these nine types of Snātakas to be Brāhmaṇas who are mendicants for the sake of dharma.

‘Sāntānikaḥ’ means one for whom the purpose is progeny; that is, one seeking marriage. ‘Adhvagaḥ’ here refers to one who has set out for the sake of dharma. ‘Sārvavedasaḥ’ is one who has performed a sacrifice in which his entire property is given as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ‘Upatāpī’ is one afflicted by disease. In the Āditya Purāṇa:
“Those free from anger, devoted to dharma, peaceful, and delighting in tranquility and self-restraint...”
And those brahmins, O Great King, are remembered as virtuous when they are free from desire.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "The region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa;
those twice-born who are born there are indeed proclaimed as virtuous."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"A girl of eight years who is given away while endowed with learning and good character is called Gaurī; the son born of her is proclaimed to be a Gaura."
Hārīta says: "The section (*kāṇḍa*) of these [scriptures] is called the family-exposition (*kulavyākhyā*), while the chapters (*parvan*) are said to be the ages (*yuga*).
He who measures out and protects that [exposition] is 'one of noble birth' (*kulīna*); such is the sacred tradition (*śruti*)."

Devala says: One who knows the distinction between dharma and adharma, is established in the teachings of the Vedas, possesses ritual action, modesty, and patience, and is wise, is an Ārya; the Mleccha is the opposite of this.
Yama said: That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
A twice-born man who is not fickle with his hands or feet, nor fickle with his eyes, and likewise not fickle with his speech— this is the characteristic of a refined person.
Thus end the designations for praiseworthy Brāhmaṇas. Now, regarding those who are not Brāhmaṇas,
Śātātapa says:
The sage Śātātapa declared that there are six types of non-Brāhmaṇas:
the first among them is the king’s servant, and the second is the buyer and seller.
The third is one who has many patrons; the fourth is a priest for a village;
but the fifth among them is one who receives wages from both a village and a city.
But that twice-born man who does not attend upon the morning twilight before the sun has risen, nor the evening twilight while the sun is still present, is considered the sixth type of non-Brahmin.
Vyāsa says: One born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa, yet devoid of the purificatory rites of mantra and living solely by virtue of his birth, is indeed not a Brāhmaṇa.
Manu says: A Brāhmaṇa does not become [unworthy] by [singing] Ṛg-verses, nor by being a merchant, nor a bard,
nor by assuming the dress of a Śūdra, nor by being a thief, nor a physician.
"Anṛk" means devoid of the Ṛgveda; that is to say, one who is destitute of the Veda. "Kuśīlava" refers to one whose livelihood consists of singing and dancing.
Devala says: A Brahmin living for a year in a village where there is water only from a well [incurs this fault].
Indeed, through the complete failure of purity and conduct, one is released from the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, regarding those who are unworthy Brahmins:
on this point Hārīta says, "Those who kill birds, fish, or deer, and those who slay snakes or tortoises..."
For they are indeed called "bad Brahmins" because they are addicted to the slaughter of various living beings.
Likewise:
"Furthermore, he whose Veda, sacrificial altar, and three ancestral lineages (triyuga) decline is indeed called a 'bad Brahmin' and is censured among those who discourse on Brahman."

‘Veda’ refers to the study of the Vedas; ‘Vedī’ refers to the sacrifices, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which have the Veda as their means. ‘Triyugam’ means as far as the three pairs of ancestors beginning with the great-grandfather and ending with the father; ‘sīdati’ means it perishes or is cut off. Yama says:
"He whose Veda and Vedī are cut off for three generations... [357]
He indeed is called a "bad Brahmin" who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
Now, regarding those beginning with the husband of a *vṛṣalī*:

here, by the term *vṛṣalīpati*, specifically the husband of a *śūdrā* is understood through the force of the etymological connection (*yoga*). His censure has been explained in detail in the section on the thirteen kinds of sons. However, Uśanas defines the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) *vṛṣalīpati* thus:
"A barren woman should be known as a *vṛṣalī*, and so too one whose offspring have died."
Another who should be known as a Vṛṣalī is a maiden who has reached her menses.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, should marry this girl,
one should know him to be untrustworthy, unfit for the company at a meal, and the husband of a Vṛṣalī— [as stated] in the Camatkārakhaṇḍa.
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the Bull;
those who treat him with contempt, the gods know as *vṛṣalas*, excluded from all dharma.

In the same way, a woman is a *vṛṣalī*, and her husband is a *vṛṣalīpati*. He who performs "prevention" (*alam*) [of dharma] is a *vṛṣala*; the meaning is that he is a destroyer of dharma. As stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "A *śūdrī* is called a *vṛṣalī*, and he who is her husband is a *vṛṣalīpati*."
Through contact with one who has food remnants on their mouth, the husband of a Vṛṣalī woman becomes an outcaste.
She who, having abandoned her own husband, takes pleasure with another man, is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; a Śūdra woman does not become a *vṛṣalī*.
The Cāṇḍālī, the unchaste woman, the prostitute, she who has her menses, the maiden, she who has been married into one's own lineage, and the Śūdra woman— these are proclaimed as Vṛṣalīs.
If an unmarried girl sees her menses while in her father's house, her ancestors fall; such a girl becomes a *vṛṣalī*.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, should marry such a girl,
one should know him to be an untrustworthy man, unfit for the company at a meal, and the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
A man who, out of delusion, approaches another's wife is called ignorant;
he alone should be known as fallen who constantly indulges in such acts within his own home.
Yama:
"He who is the husband of a *punarbhu* (a remarried woman) shall be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Manu: [as above].
The wise call the husband of a woman who has had a previous husband a *didhiṣūpati*;
he is the twice-born man whose first wife is the *didhiṣū*, and she alone is his housewife.
Devala, however, says:
"The husband of a woman who has married again while her elder brother is still living is called a *didhiṣūpati*.
A twice-born man is likewise a *didhiṣū* if he marries before his elder brother; she alone is the mistress of his household."
Vṛddha-Manu:
He who, out of lust, becomes attached to the wife of a deceased brother—
even if she has been appointed [to bear a son] according to dharma— is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*.
Devala says:
One who has concealed his marks (*gūḍhaliṅgin*) is an *avakīrṇin*, as is one whose vows have been broken (*bhagnavrata*).

[359] "One who has concealed his marks" means one who is devoid of the staff and other insignia prescribed for the stages of life (*āśrama*), such as that of the student (*brahmacarya*). "One whose vows have been broken" means one whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been violated.
Yama says: "He who, being under a vow, approaches a woman is called an *avakīrṇin*.
'Under a vow' (*vratī*) means a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*)."
Now, those who are equal to Śūdras. Regarding this, Devala says:
"Those who do not regularly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and who always eat without having bathed..."
Having lost their purity, these fall [from their status] and, according to dharma, become equal to Śūdras.
Vasiṣṭha says: Those who cohabit with a menstruating woman, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks a Vedic scholar— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
‘Udakyā’ means a woman in her menses; she is one who stands near [others] at the time of bathing, eating, performing worship to the gods, and so forth.
Baudhāyana says: “Those who tend cattle, those who trade, as well as artisans and actors...”
O King, one should treat even Brahmins who are usurers just as one treats Śūdras.
‘Artisans’ (*kāravaḥ*) are those who subsist on the wages of craftsmen such as carpenters and the like. ‘Moneylenders’ (*vārddhuṣikāḥ*) are those whose characteristics will be described below.
Manu says: “Cattle-herders, traders, as well as artisans and actors... [Manusmṛti 4.216].
O King, one should treat learned Brahmins who are servants with the same manner as one treats Śūdras of low caste.
[360] "Those who are to be sent away by those of low caste" means those such as Śūdras who are to be sent away.
Those who, having turned away from their own duties, subsist on the food of others and desire the status of the twice-born— one should treat them like Śūdras.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"O Lord of the People, he who has neither the Veda, nor recitation, nor sacred knowledge, should be regarded as a Śūdra; so said the blessed Manu."
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and excluded from hospitality—
all such twice-born men, even if they are learned in the Vedas, should be known as Śūdras.
The mention of the *vaiśvadeva* is intended as an illustration for the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*). In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"For the Blessed Dharma is indeed a bull; he who causes it to be obstructed..."
The gods know him as a vṛṣala, one who has been cast out from all dharma.
Devala said:
"A twice-born man who, having eaten the food of a second father, has reached maturity, is to be known as an *avareḍha*; by birth, he follows the dharma of a Śūdra."

"Of the second" refers to the adoptive father (*pratigrahītṛ*) or the purchaser (*kretṛ*). One who has been raised on the food and so forth of his [adoptive] father is an "avareḍha," meaning one such as a *dattaka* (given son), a *krīta* (bought son), and others.
Manu also mentions another kind of *avareḍha*:
"But he who is born by a father through a wife of equal caste by means of a second [man]..."
He should be known as an *avareḍha*, for by birth he possesses the nature of a Śūdra.
Now, regarding those who merely claim to be Brahmins and so forth,
Vyāsa says: "One who is endowed with the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and likewise with the initiation ceremony (upanayana)..."
He who neither performs his duties nor studies is called a "brāhmaṇa in name only."
Saṃvarta says: A Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya who do not observe vows, and a Śūdra— these three non-Brāhmaṇas,
as well as a Brāhmaṇa devoid of Vedic study and vows, are called "mere Brāhmaṇas" (brāhmaṇabruva).
Vasiṣṭha says: An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas— these three are bearers of names only.
One who has undergone the rites beginning with conception and likewise possesses the initiation ceremony,
yet neither performs the prescribed duties nor studies, is called a "brāhmaṇa-in-name" (brāhmaṇabruva).
Hārīta states: "One who is a servant to a Śūdra, one hired by a king, a Vṛṣala who performs sacrifices for a village,
and one who lives by killing and binding— these six are Brahmin outcasts."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"He who cooks food for his own sake and not for the sake of the gods or guests—
even he is unworthy of the *śrāddha* rite, and he is called a *brahmarākṣasa*."
Hārīta says:
Even those endowed with learning and noble lineage, if they are of base conduct and lowest among men,
constantly devoted to honey-based products, are proclaimed to be Yātudhānas.
Viṣṇu:
He who declares his country, lineage, family, or learning for the sake of food is proclaimed, according to the laws of Vaivasvata, as one who eats what has been vomited.
Those men who delight in the conceit "we are all-knowing," who eat what has been vomited,
and who are greedy for funeral rites and gifts, should be shunned.
Now, regarding the *kuṇḍa*, *golaka*, and others. Manu and Śātātapa state:
"Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others."
A Kuṇḍa is one born while the husband is alive; a Golaka is one born after the husband has died.

Those two, having been born in the field of another, indeed destroy the offerings to gods and ancestors for the givers, both after death and in this world, even when they are appointed to those duties.
Bṛhaspati says: Adultery is indeed unrighteousness, and from it are born the Kuṇḍa and Golaka;
they are unworthy of funeral rites (aśrāddheya) and their food is not to be eaten (abhojyānna). Those born of the wife’s field (kṣetraja) and others are even more inauspicious than them.
Yama said:
He who is born by another while his father is still living is called a *kuṇḍa*.
The Brāhmaṇa who eats the food of such a person is declared a *kuṇḍāśin*.
Parāśara says:
A son born to a man while he is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; when the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*.
He who eats the food of these two is called a *kuṇḍāśin*.
Having mentioned the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, Manu says:
"The twice-born man who eats the food of those two is called a *kuṇḍāśin*. [In] the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made of sixty-four pure palas shall contain four prasthas;
he who swallows that falls downward.
He who swallows— that is, eats— at a single meal an amount of food measuring four *prasthas* is a *kuṇḍāśin*.
Now, regarding the *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas*,
Hārīta says as follows:
Those who are sons of Śūdra women, whether they are given away or are known as those purchased—all of them have been declared by Maitriṇa to be Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to the family of another, becomes by that misconduct a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*; of this there is no doubt.
One's own family is called "kāṇḍa"; he who, having placed that behind him, goes to another family is therefore known as a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*.
Yama also said:
"One who receives a gift in times of distress, one who denies what was given, and one who is the son of a Vaiṣṇavī—
these three, as well as the Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas, have been declared by Manu."

A widow who is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu through vows such as fasting for a month is a "Vaiṣṇavī"; a son born from a man of the same caste to her in that state is a "Vaiṣṇavīsuta. After instructing a Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into extensive distress on how to adopt the livelihoods of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, Nārada says: "But a Brāhmaṇa who, out of passion, delights in that very [lower] mode of life is declared to be a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, fallen from the path, and excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*)."
Devala says:
The husband of a Vaiśya woman is a Kṛṣṇapṛṣṭha; he is a Kāṇḍapṛṣṭha and a Bhaṭa.
Now, regarding those who follow the "vow of the cat" and so forth, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"One who makes a banner of righteousness, yet is always greedy, deceitful, and a deceiver of the world..."
One who is violent and deceives everyone should be known as a "cat-vowed" person.
He whose banner of righteousness is always raised high like the banner of the gods,
yet whose sins remain concealed— that is known as the "cat-vow" (baiḍāla-vrata).
Yama says:
He who pursues the practice of vows while setting aside the underlying cause,
concealing his sin under the guise of a vow— that is indeed called the "cat-vow" (baiḍāla-vrata).
Having seized great wealth and abandoned his outward signs, he should return [to worldly life];
that vow which conceals one who has moved from a stage of life is called "the cat-vow" (baiḍāla).

For when someone, having acquired vast wealth by unjust means, fears its confiscation by kings and others, and thus changes his marks from those of a previous stage of life (*āśrama*) to adopt the highly venerable stage of a renunciant (*yati*) in order to protect that property— his vow is known as "cat-like" (*baiḍāla*). However, he who has formally entered a stage of life but does not abide by it,
through such neglect of the *āśrama*, that vow is called "cat-like."
Having offered water and performed the formal acceptance of the girl,
he who has achieved his purpose but possesses no wealth— that is the vow known as "cat-like."

When one who has already given his daughter to a worthy suitor with a water-pouring ceremony (jalapūrva), having thereby fulfilled his duty, nevertheless desires to give her again to another, he is as if not wealthy and not one who has fulfilled his purpose; such conduct of his is the "cat-vow" (*baiḍālavratam*). And when one, having accepted what is sufficient for his fixed obligations, yet considers himself as if not having fulfilled his purpose due to lack of contentment, his conduct likewise is the cat-vow. Furthermore, that which consists in going to the hermitage of ascetics and then returning again, violating the duties of an ascetic—that is called the vow named the "cat-vow."
A twice-born man who looks downward, who is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends,
crafty, and falsely humble, is one who practices the "heron-vow."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"The Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Nirgranthas, those who know the Pañcarātra,
the Kāpālikas, the Pāśupatas, and those who are of such heretical (pāṣaṇḍa) types."
A twice-born man who does not belong to any stage of life, or one who belongs to a stage of life in vain,
as well as those Brahmins who maintain a false stage of life— these should be known as defilers of the śrāddha.
Devala says:
A Brahmin who is intent on the worship of the gods for three years while seeking wealth is called a *devalaka*; he is censured in rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Likewise: "One who subsists on the portions of the deities shall be known by the name Devalaka;
he shall be designated as a Karaṇa and shall engage in legal proceedings within the assemblies."
He should be known as a house-burner, for he has indeed burned many a corpse.
"Burned by a corpse" (pretadagdha) means one who burns corpses;
and he too would be a house-burner who sets fire to a dwelling out of malice.
And those who set forest fires are the burners of fields, crops, and the earth.
A wife is called a *mahiṣī*, and she who is unfaithful is likewise so termed;
the child conceived in her is indeed known as a *māhiṣaka*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"A wife is called *mahiṣī*, and she may indeed be unfaithful;
he who tolerates her fault is known as a *māhiṣaka*."
Devala says: A twice-born man who sells dairy products, a seller of cattle,
and one who sells molasses, salt, or sesame seeds is a seller of forbidden goods.
He who, among the castes— whether low, high, or middling—
is unrestrained and practices the conduct of another caste, is indeed a defiler of the castes.
The wise say that one who is alone and overcome by calamity is truly fortunate;
O Brahmin, know that a usurer is one who lives off the growth of grass.
Viṣṇu:
He who reviles another living being and praises his own qualities is indeed called a usurer, and is censured in all ritual acts.
Vasiṣṭha says:
He who, having taken grain at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda.
He who has married a woman of the same lineage becomes a Brahmin possessing that lineage;
a Brahmin who constantly performs services for the king is known as an *adhikṛta*.
Nārada says: He who teaches children in a village should be known as a *putrācārya* (son-teacher);
or, one from whom knowledge has been acquired by a son is called a *putrācārya*.

That Brahmin who wanders from house to house like a bee for the sake of wealth, out of excessive greed, is called a *bhrāmarī*. But he who performs wicked austerities is known by the designation of a *mūḍha*.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:

"He who, out of laziness, has not worshipped the gods and others with his Vedic study and the sacred fires— he who has cast them aside— should be known as a *nirākṛti*, one who has rejected the immortals."
Gautama:
A Brahmin who has forgotten the Veda after having studied it becomes a Nirākṛti. Devala: [The same].
He who, for the sake of accumulating wealth from profit, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, and his children and wife,
is known as a miser (kadarya).
Uśanas says: "A *ghaṇṭika* is a bell-caster who sounds the bell at the time of a king's awakening. Vṛddhagautama says: [the same].
He who, out of delusion, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, his children, his wife,
and his parents and dependents, is known as a miser.
Hārīta says:
Those lowest of men who cover heaven with many sins are known as *durālānas*, because their bodies are difficult to reach [in the afterlife].
‘Heaven’ means the other world; ‘they conceal’ means they obscure it. ‘Because of the body’s difficult attainment’ means because of its being brought about by wicked karma.
Yama said: Those who seize the property of others are thieves and the lowest of Brahmins;
because they have failed to attain the goal of the body, they are remembered as those who are difficult to restrain.
Those who have strayed from their own duties are proclaimed to be atheists (nāstikas).
Kātyāyana says: One should avoid that person who is corrupt in speech, whether he imitates or utters the sound "huṃ," coughing, or whatever else is censured in the world.
Now, those who have fallen [from their caste]: Uśanas says, "And those who employ priests for whom they do not offer the *samānaya* oblation, and those who sell the revealed scriptures."
And Manu has declared those who have had other husbands previously, those who have not given birth, and those who are outcasts.
‘Those who have had another [husband] before’ refers to women such as *punarbhūs* and others.
Yama says: “By teaching the Veda to a Śūdra, a Brahmin falls; of this there is no doubt.”
Devala says:
Both he who teaches for a fee and he who is taught for a fee—
both these Brahmins fall, because of the buying and selling of the Veda.
And it has been said by Gārgya:
"If a man should take a wife or likewise perform the establishment of the domestic fire while his elder uterine brother remains [unmarried], he becomes fallen."
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "He who cooks food for his own sake and not for the sake of the gods or guests—even he does not deserve to partake in the *śrāddha*; fallen, he becomes a *brahmarākṣasa*."
the eunuchs. Devala says:
The *ṣaṇḍaka*, the wind-born *ṣaṇḍa*, the *ṣaṇḍa*, the impotent (*klība*), the neuter (*napuṃsaka*), and the *kīlaka*— thus is this category of *ṣaṇḍa* explained in its various divisions.
Among them, one who speaks like a woman and possesses the characteristics of a woman is a *ṣaṇḍaka*;
likewise, one who, having been a man, subsequently cuts off his own male organs.

A woman who assumes the form of a man and possesses qualities characteristic of male conduct may be called *vātaja-ṣaṇḍa*, or by the name *strī-ṣaṇḍa*. A *ṣaṇḍa* may also be one who lacks the feminine gender; indeed, a *ṣaṇḍa* is characterized by a withered penis.
He should be known as a "stake" (kīlaka) who, out of impotence, first unites his wife with another man and afterwards enjoys her himself.
Now, regarding those who are naked:
concerning this, Parāśara says, "One may be naked when wearing saffron-colored robes; one is naked when wearing only a loincloth."
One wearing soiled clothes is naked, as is one covered by only half a cloth.

A decoction is an extract of a dyeing substance; cloth dyed with that is *kāṣāya*. One wearing such [cloth] is called "naked. A strip of cloth (*vastracīrikā*) sufficient to cover only the private parts, which is to be worn by means of tying a waist-string at the front and back, is a *kaupīna*. A householder or others who, though not explicitly authorized to wear it, wear only that much are "naked. One whose garment is unwashed, or who possesses garments washed by a dyer and the like, is "clothed in dirty raiment" (*malavadvāsas*). One wearing one half of a single, uncut cloth while covering the other half is said to be "covered by a half-cloth" (*ardhapaṭāvṛta*), or one who wears a tattered cloth (*khaṇḍapaṭavasanā*).
In the *Bhṛgusmṛti* and the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"One is naked if wearing soiled clothes; one is naked if possessing only a loincloth;
likewise, one is naked if lacking the upper garment, if having both arms exposed, or if entirely unclothed."
One who wears saffron-colored robes is considered "naked," while one who wears only half a garment is known as "half-naked."

"Kaupīnakevalaḥ" means wearing only a loincloth (*kaupīna*). A *kaccha* is the hem of a garment used for covering the private parts; one who is "without it" (*vimukta*) is devoid of the three *kacchas*. "Anuttarīyaḥ" means lacking an upper garment (*uttarīya*). A *kakṣā* is a cloth for binding the waist. When a person has worn a garment such that its second half is tied around the waist, or another cloth is joined across it to form a constricted width for securing the waist, that is the second *kakṣā*. One possessing this is called "dvikakṣaḥ. And Yājñavalkya refers to this second *kakṣā* by the term "āsurī."
"For that which is tied outside the waistband after being wrapped around becomes demonic (āsuri)," so it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
"Since the triple Veda (trayī) is the covering for all beings..."
Those who indeed abandon her out of delusion are proclaimed to be naked.
Now, regarding those who marry before their elder brother and so forth,
Devala says:
"Furthermore, he who, while the elder brother remains unmarried, marries by passing over that elder brother..."
Both the one who is superseded and the one who supersedes shall incur [the same guilt].

The meaning of the statement is that when the elder brother (*jyeṣṭha*) is "unmarried" (*aniviṣṭa*), i.e., has not performed his marriage, and the younger brother takes a wife—that is, performs the taking of a spouse—then the elder is called a *parivitti* and the other (the younger) a *parivettṛ*. Manu [3.171]:
"He who enters into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra* while the elder brother remains [unmarried]..."
He is to be known as the *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries before the elder), while the elder brother is the *parivitti*.

Regarding the word ‘sthite’ (while [the elder] remains), the ellipsis is “without having entered into the union of marriage and the *agnihotra*. What is intended here is the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) which is required for subsequent rites such as the *agnihotra*.
And it has been stated by Gārgya:
“While the eldest uterine brother remains, one should not take a wife.”
Likewise, the establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya) and the formal setting up of the sacred fires (adhāna) [are permitted]; otherwise, one becomes fallen.

‘Āvasathya’ refers to the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathyādhāna*), which is to say, the installation of the *aupāsana* fire performed at the time of the partition of the inheritance. This is because the performance of the *aupāsana* installation at the time of marriage has already been precluded by the rule, “one should not take a wife [if one’s elder brother is unmarried]. For this very reason, in the statement of Brahmagarbha, “One should establish the *aupāsana* fire at its own time when marrying,” it is understood that by the term ‘its own time,’ only the time of the partition of the inheritance is meant, and not the time of marriage as well. ‘Installation’ (*ādhāna*) refers to the installation of the *gārhapatya* and other fires. ‘He becomes fallen’ means he becomes guilty of a minor offense (*upapātakin*), since both the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*) and the elder brother so superseded (*parivitti*) are mentioned in the enumeration of minor offenses.
Laukāxi says: "If one establishes the sacred fires while a full brother, the elder, is still present,
then of those two, the elder is the 'one for whom the fire was carried away' (paryāhita), and the younger is the 'carrier' (paryadhātṛ)."

From the mention of "uterine" (sodarya) brothers, it is understood that when a non-uterine elder brother remains, there is no fault of sin (pātitya) for a younger brother even if he takes a wife or performs other such acts. Śātātapa, however, has explicitly stated the absence of fault regarding non-uterine brothers: "And in the case of the sons of a paternal uncle, the son of a co-wife, or the son of another man's wife—even if these elder brothers remain, [there is no fault] for the younger brothers."
There is no fault in superseding a marriage when it involves the union with the sacred fires and the wife.

"Paternal uncles' sons" refers to the sons of one's father's brothers. "Sons of a co-wife" (sāpatnāḥ) refers to those born of different mothers. "Sons of another man's wife" refers to brothers produced in the field of another by their own progenitor, according to the technical definition of *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (sons belonging to two lineages). The meaning is that even when these elder brothers exist, there is no fault known as *parivettṛtva* (the state of being a superseder) for younger brothers who enter into marriage and the sacred fire-ritual (*agnisaṃyoga*) beforehand. The mention of "sons of another man's wife" is intended to include by implication adopted sons (*dattaka*) and others as well. For this very reason, Yama says: "Paternal uncles' sons, sons of a co-wife, and likewise sons of another [man],"...
There is no unrighteousness in superseding [a wife] for the sake of [establishing] the sacred fires and religious duties.

There is no unrighteousness for one who marries past his elder brothers—whether they be sons of others who have attained the status of being his father’s sons through gift, purchase, or other means, or even biological brothers. Śātātapa states that even when a biological elder brother exists, there is no fault for the younger brother in certain cases of superseding: "When [the elder] is impotent, residing in another country, an outcast, a mendicant, or devoted to the practice of Yoga, there is no fault in superseding him."
A "mendicant" (*bhikṣuka*) is one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*). One "devoted to the science of yoga" (*yogaśāstrābhiyukta*) is one who is dispassionate (*virakta*). Kātyāyana also says:

[One should avoid] those residing in another country, eunuchs, those with only one testicle, those not born of the same womb (half-brothers), those addicted to prostitutes, the fallen (*patita*), those equal to Śūdras, and those who are excessively diseased.
Those who are dull-witted, mute, blind, deaf, hunchbacked, dwarfed, or lame; those who are very old, those who are without wives, those devoted to agriculture, and those belonging to the king.
One does not incur blame by marrying those who are addicted to the increase of wealth, those who act out of mere lust,
as well as deceivers and thieves.

[373] ‘One with a single testicle’ refers to one whose testicles are enlarged due to disease. ‘The diseased’ refers to one suffering from an incurable illness. ‘The lame’ refers to one whose two feet are broken. ‘Those without wives’ refers to lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*). ‘Those who do not act out of desire’ refers to those who, by their own will, never perform marriage. ‘Deceivers’ refers to those intent on vain efforts for the purpose of cheating others. In this context, if there are those such as eunuchs (*klība*) and others who are entirely ineligible for marriage, there is no fault in superseding them even without waiting for a specific time. However, if there are those who might become eligible for marriage at another time—such as those living in another country, those detached from home, those excessively attached to prostitutes, those devoted to agriculture, those subservient to a king, those addicted to increasing wealth, those who do not act out of desire, deceivers, and thieves—in the presence of such persons, there is no fault for those who perform supersession after waiting for the aforementioned time.
Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says concerning an elder brother who resides in another country:

"If one does not wait for an elder brother who has not married for eight, ten, or twelve years, he becomes liable to penance. The intention is that once he has returned from another country, he becomes eligible for marriage and other such rites. In this context, one must wait twelve years for an elder brother who has gone to another country for the sake of dharma or for the sake of wealth.
And so says the Smṛti:
"An elder brother who has departed for the sake of dharma or wealth should be waited for for twelve years, even if he is heard of again and again."

The phrase "for the sake of Dharma and Artha" is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for Vidyā (learning) as well. For this very reason, Gautama, having introduced the topic with "when the husband has disappeared," stated regarding the period of waiting for a wife by a Brāhmaṇa: "twelve years on account of learning," and further specified: "and likewise for a younger brother when the elder brother [is away], regarding marriage and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). "When the husband has disappeared" means when he is unknown to have gone where—that is, when he has gone to an extremely distant land. "On account of learning" means when the husband has gone to another country for the purpose of acquiring knowledge; in such a case, the Brāhmaṇa's wife, having waited twelve years, may perform her ritual duties and so forth. Similarly, a younger Brāhmaṇa brother, having waited twelve years while the elder brother is away in another country for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, may proceed with marriage and the establishment of the fires. However, if the elder brother has gone to another country for some other purpose, there are two options: eight or ten years. What is intended here is this: if the elder brother has gone to another country and, after accomplishing his own desired task, does not return despite being capable of doing so, and his life becomes doubtful such that the possibility of his returning for marriage is removed, then if the younger brother subsequently enters into marriage and the *agnihotra*, he incurs no fault of being a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother). In the same way, even in the case of those excessively attached to courtesans or the like, if they remain in that state for some time and their inherent disposition is determined such that the possibility of marriage is removed, then if the younger brother subsequently performs marriage and so forth, there is no fault. With this very intention, Sumantu also said: [374] "If a man, having gone abroad, does not return for twelve years, his wife may marry another man after waiting for him for that long. And: "If a younger brother marries while the elder brother is absent and his life is uncertain, he is not a *parivettṛ*. And: "If a man remains abroad for more than twelve years, his wife may marry another man. One whose mind is attached to vices, or an atheist, or an elder brother who is disinclined toward dharma,
may allow his younger brother who desires dharma to perform the fire-consecration ceremony (ādhāna).

The mention of "establishing the sacred fires" (adhāna) is intended to include marriage as well; however, since eunuchs and others are by their very nature entirely unfit for marriage, they need not be waited for even for a short period of time.
Thus says the Smṛti:
"One who is insane, a criminal, a leper, an outcast, or indeed a eunuch..."
One suffering from pulmonary consumption and one afflicted by chronic illness should not be expected to wait.
There is no fault in superseding one who is lame, dwarfed, humpbacked, stammering, dull-witted, born blind, deaf, or mute.

The meaning is that when such an elder brother exists, there is no fault in the younger brother’s marrying before him. Likewise, even regarding the entitlement to establish the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), if the elder brother—who is eligible for the rite—remains without having established them, there is no fault of being a "marrying-before" (*parivettṛ*) for the younger brother who establishes the fires with his permission.
Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"And when the elder brother is without the sacred fires, how may the younger brother establish them?"
Having obtained the permission of his elder brother, he should perform the Agnihotra according to the prescribed rule.

The meaning is that even when the elder brother is eligible for the *ādhāna*, if he disregards the procedure for *ādhāna* and does not undertake the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), then the younger brother may perform the *ādhāna* after obtaining his permission. This very same point was also stated by Sumantu:
"As long as the elder brother remains [eligible], one should certainly not cause the *ādhāna* to be performed."
But once permitted, he should act according to the word of Śaṅkha.
The mention of the "elder brother" is intended to indicate the father as well;
and thus that same [text] states:
"In the case of one whose father has not performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), how indeed should the son cause it to be performed?"
There is the qualification for the Agnihotra sacrifice, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.
Likewise:
"For one permitted by the father, the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) shall always take place.
The remainder [of the sense] is: "for the son who has been permitted by the father. The mention of the "father" is intended to indicate the grandfather as well.
For this very reason, Uśanas says:
"If one's father or grandfather, or even an elder brother, is without the sacred fire,
there is no fault in superseding him regarding the performance of austerity, the Agnihotra, or the recitation of mantras."
In this case as well, the phrase "of one who has been authorized by his father and others" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The word *mantra* serves to indicate the Veda. Thus says Śātātapa:
"Neither sacrificial fires, nor the Vedas, nor ascetic penances supersede [the elder brother]."
Nor is there faith in one who is younger, nor in a girl who is deformed.

The meaning is this: just as when an elder brother remains without having performed Vedic study, asceticism, or *śrāddha* rites, those [rites] performed by the younger brother—even without the elder’s permission—do not become causes for supersession (*parivedana*), so too the consecration of sacred fires (*agny-ādheya*) performed with the elder brother’s permission does not become a cause for supersession. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "a girl who is deformed" (*virūpikā*), the meaning is as follows: when an elder sister who is eligible for marriage remains unmarried and deformed in appearance, a marriage performed by the younger sister—even without her elder sister’s permission—is not a fault, provided it is done out of fear that the time for marriage has passed. Thus, in cases other than those described, regarding supersession even in the case of girls, everything stated concerning the supersession of a groom (*vara-parivedana*) should be applied. Hārīta states that if a younger brother marries before his elder brother, a fault occurs even if the elder brother has given his permission.
But how can one become a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder brothers) among all his uterine brothers?
They marry by means of wives, but not by means of the *agnihotra* fire or the sacrificial rite.

It is established that those who are permitted [to perform] the *agnihotra* and other such rites do not marry before their elder brothers; however, the meaning of the statement is that even those who are permitted may marry before their elder brothers with respect to their wives. Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya says: "He who proceeds with the *tretā* fires while disregarding the *āvasathya* fire..."
Thus he becomes one who has not maintained the sacred fires, and is likewise called a "supplanter."
