The meaning of this is as follows: "Having disregarded"—that is, having failed to establish—the *āvasathya* fire, which is the *aupāsana* fire, "in the *tretā*"—that is, in the establishment of the triad of fires beginning with the *gārhapatya*—"he who proceeds" becomes precisely "one who has not established the sacred fires" (*anāhitāgni*). Likewise, because he establishes the *gārhapatya* and other fires first without having established the *aupāsana* fire, he is called a *parivitti*. Thus end the cases of the *parivitti* and others;
these are the names for Brahmins of disreputable character.
Thus ends the section on the definitions of Brāhmaṇas.
Now, the Brāhmaṇas who are commended for the *śrāddha* rite are described. Regarding this, Manu and Śātātapa state:

In this regard, I shall describe in their entirety those who are to be fed and those who are to be avoided among the best of the twice-born, as well as how many there are and by whom they are to be served.
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.

He who studies his own entire branch (śākhā), consisting of both Mantra and Brāhmaṇa, is a "Śrotriya. In a Śrāddha rite, the oblations prescribed for the Viśvedevas are called "havya," while those prescribed for the ancestors (pitṛs) are called "kavya. "To the most worthy" means to one who possesses noble lineage, good character, and learning. "Given to him," even apart from the Śrāddha, becomes "of great fruit. Vasiṣṭha says:
"Havya and kavya offerings should always be given only to a Śrotriya."
The deities do not receive satisfaction from that which is given to one who is not learned in the Vedas.
Manu said:
"Where thousands upon thousands of those ignorant of the Ṛgveda eat,
a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully supersedes them all."

[378] "Anṛcām" should be understood as "those who do not know the meaning of the Vedas. Since it has been stated that gifts are to be given only to one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), there is no possibility at all for those who have not studied them. Medhātithi, however, has shown an alternative reading where "anṛcā" ends in the nominative plural; in that view, the construction is "where a thousand *anṛcas* eat. "Mantravit" means one who knows the meaning of the Vedas. "Prītaḥ" means satisfied, that is to say, fed. "Arhati" means he accepts or assimilates "all" those "anṛcas. And since there is non-difference [between the one and the many], the meaning is that the fruit which is obtained when those thousands are fed is attained in the case of a single person.
Offerings for the ancestors and oblations for the gods should be given to those preeminent in knowledge;
for hands smeared with blood are not cleansed by blood alone.

"Superior by knowledge and learning" means those who excel through wisdom; to them alone, and not to others, should offerings to the gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*) be given. Just as hands smeared with blood do not become clean even when washed with blood, so too the ancestors do not obtain the fruit of the ritual when served by the meal of an ignorant Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise, [the scripture] states:
"It makes both the givers and the recipients partakers of the fruit."
A sacrificial fee given to a learned man according to the rules brings reward both in this world and after death.

The *dakṣiṇā* (priestly fee) that is given to a learned man makes both the giver and the recipient partakers of the fruit. This is a praise [of such a gift]: this giving to a learned man is such that it unites even the recipient with invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*), how much more so the giver? "In the afterlife" (*pretya*) heaven is the fruit; "in this world," fame. Regarding the injunction "one should feed [them]," Gautama states: "Some say that the first [gift] should be given to those who are accomplished in Vedic learning, speech, appearance, age, and character, and who are young;
others say it should be like [the offering made] to the ancestors."

"Endowed with speech" means those who speak refined Sanskrit. "Endowed with beauty" means those with pleasing bodies. [379] "Endowed with age" means those whose age is matured; for they generally possess pure intellects due to their tranquility regarding sensual attachments. "Endowed with virtue" means those who act for the welfare of all living beings through mind, speech, and body. He states an exception to being endowed with age: "To the young," that is, to the youths; "first," meaning the first *śrāddhas*, namely the *nava-śrāddhas* (new *śrāddhas*). Or, "first" may mean principal, because the young are capable of fulfilling all the rules and requirements of the *śrāddha*. "Some [say] like the father": some hold that one should feed Brahmins equal to the father—namely, a youth for the sake of the father, an elder for the sake of the grandfather, and an even more elderly man for the sake of the great-grandfather.

Vasiṣṭha: On the day before [the Śrāddha], having assembled Brāhmaṇas— ascetics, householders, virtuous men who are not yet advanced in age, those not engaged in forbidden acts, those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), disciples, and resident pupils— one should give [the offerings] to the ancestors.

"On the previous day," that is, on the day before the day of the *śrāddha*, "having assembled" or invited "the *brāhmaṇas*"; "ascetics" (*yatayaḥ*) refers to those who have renounced the world. In their absence, [one may invite] "householders. The characteristics of a virtuous person (*sādhu*) have been stated: "not of advanced age," meaning not too old; "not engaged in forbidden acts," meaning those who avoid prohibited things; and "those who are neither disciples nor pupils," meaning not servants—so says Kātyāyana.

Some [authorities] say that one should invite *snātakas*, ascetics (*yatīs*), or virtuous householders (*gṛhasthasādhus*) who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyas*), elderly, irreproachable, and established in their own duties; or even students (*śiṣyas*) of good conduct in the absence of those [others]. A *snātaka* is one who has performed the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*) but has not yet married. An "elderly person" (*vṛddha*) is one who is preeminent in learning and austerity. Those who possess no blemish or fault on the mother's or father's side are "irreproachable" (*anavadya*). "Established in their own duties" means devoted to the *śrauta* and *smārta* rites prescribed for their respective stages of life (*āśrama*). In the absence of Brahmins possessing the aforementioned characteristics, one may also invite students of good conduct. Thus says Āpastamba.

Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is superior, as is one who is destitute of wealth. [2.17.10] When there is equality in terms of tranquility (*śama*), austerity (*tapas*), learning (*śruta*), conduct (*śīla*), and so forth, the one advanced in age is the best. Even when there is equality in age, one who is destitute of wealth—that is, one whose means of subsistence are exhausted—is superior. And he should be one who has become destitute of wealth by his own choice, and not because he is unfit or unable to receive gifts. Paiṭhīnasi says:

"To one who is self-restrained and pure, the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) should be given at all times; therefore, it is known that [one must be] pure. "Self-restrained" means disciplined. "Pure" means endowed with both external and internal purity. "At all times" means during birth, death, the feeding of gods, and so forth. This meaning is understood from the Śruti. He cites the opening words of the Śruti: "Therefore, [one must be] pure. — Āpastamba.
One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual performances.

‘Mantravantaḥ’ means those who have studied the Vedas. ‘In all rites’ refers to those Śrauta and Smārta rituals in which the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is prescribed. Here, some—considering the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) to be like a bride based on their common characteristics (*sādharmya*), and thinking that the oblations must be offered to those belonging to one’s own Vedic branch (*svaśākhīya*)—employ only those of their own branch, distinguished by qualities such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), for the Śrāddha. That is incorrect, because nowhere in the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Gṛhyas, or Kalpasūtras is there a rule restricting [the invitees] to one’s own branch; on the contrary, in the Smṛtis and other texts, we see injunctions for those belonging to various branches and students of various Vedas, such as: “one who has mastered the three *Nāciketa* fires, the three *Madhu* sections, the three *Suparṇa* hymns, and the singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*. Nor should it be thought that these rules apply only to Śrāddhas performed by Śūdras, as there is no evidence for such a restriction. Furthermore, it is not logical to establish a restrictive rule merely by observing a similarity to a bride, since such a similarity can be explained otherwise. Moreover, from what source is the rule regarding a single Vedic branch (*ekaśākhādhyāyin*) for the bride known, on the strength of which it could be extended to the sacrificial oblation? If you say it is from custom (*ācāra*), [we reply: we observe that in the giving and receiving of brides, the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) act only with those of their own branch and carefully avoid those of other branches. From this, they conclude that a restrictive rule exists here. Do not say so; for the conduct of the cultured is rooted in the knowledge or ignorance of family lineage and so forth, and these two depend upon proximity or distance. Generally, those who study the same branch desire mutual association for the sake of studying their own recension, performing Vedic vows, domestic rites, and the practice of twilight prayers (*saṃdhyopāsana*). Due to this proximity, they know each other’s families, character, and conduct, and thus respect the rules for matrimonial alliance. Conversely, those of other branches, because they live in different regions, are not trusted because their true nature is unknown. Even among those who study the same branch, matrimonial alliances are not found between those who do not know one another. Therefore, it is the knowledge of family lineage arising from living in the same region and similar circumstances that is the cause for initiating matrimonial relations. As for the fact that some do not enter into such relations despite having similarities, the reason is this: among those whose ancestors lived in very distant lands and followed mutually despised local customs, even if they happened to meet at some later time, they did not engage in matrimonial alliances with one another while maintaining pride in their respective families and guilds (*śreṇi*). Consequently, that non-engagement persists through their lineages for a long time. Thus, it is established that there is no restrictive rule for inviting Brāhmaṇas of one’s own branch either in the giving of a bride or in the offering of oblations. This being the case, the statements to be cited later will have a consistent meaning.
Yama said:
Those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them,
who are devoted to their own duties, patient, performative of rites, and ascetic;
To them, once they have become tranquil, both the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and the *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) are presented.

Those who have returned home after studying one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas are "Veda-snātakas. Those who have returned after completing their study of the meaning of the Vedas (*vedārthavicāra*) are "Vidyā-snātakas. Those who have returned after completing their vows of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*) are "Vrata-snātakas. The term *śrotriya* is used even for those who have mastered the Vedas in order to demonstrate their constant devotion to the study of the Vedas. Those who endure the suffering of the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) are "patient" (*kṣānta*). Those who are free from anger are "tranquil" (*śānta*). Manu says:
"Householders who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who have bathed [after completing] Vedic knowledge, Vedic study, and vows..."
One should honor them with offerings to gods and ancestors, and one should avoid those who act contrary to this.
"Householders" means those living as householders. Likewise:
"One should diligently feed at a śrāddha a Bahvṛca who has mastered the Veda."
Then, the Adhvaryu who has reached the end of his branch and the Chandoga who has not yet completed his [recitation].
If any one of these, being duly honored, should eat at his *śrāddha*,
the satisfaction of his ancestors shall be eternal and extend to seven generations.

The terms *vedapāraga*, *śākhāntaga*, and *āsamāptika*—which have synonymous meanings—are used to denote those who study all the branches (*śākhās*) of the Veda. One who studies the *Ṛgveda* is a *Bahvṛca*. One who goes to the "far shore" (*pāra*), that is, the end, of the Veda is a *Vedapāraga*. This is not a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) such as the *Adhvaryu*; rather, the *Adhvaryu* is a person who studies the *Yajurveda*. One who goes to the end, the far shore, of a branch consisting of Mantra and Brāhmaṇa is a *Śākhāntaga*. A *Chandoga* is one who studies the Sāmaveda. An *Āsamāptika* is one for whom there is no completion [of the study]. If one should eat at the *śrāddha* of even one among these three types, there shall be satisfaction for seven generations of ancestors. Regarding the word "honored" (*arcita*), Medhātithi explains that the phrase "seven generations" (*sāptapauruṣī*) is intended to indicate a great duration of time; it means for as long as seven future generations of sons, grandsons, and so forth have been born or will be born. "Eternal" (*śāśvatī*) means uninterrupted.

But surely, by the very terms *bahvṛca* and so forth, those who study the respective Vedas are each individually enjoined. Therefore, what is the purpose of saying "one of these"? Some say: this is for the purpose of excluding the followers of the Atharvaveda (*ātharvaṇika*). Only one of these—namely the *bahvṛca*, the *adhvaryu*, or the *chandoga*—is to be fed at a *śrāddha*, but no one other than them. For in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated that "the triple knowledge consists of the Ṛks, the Yajus, and the Sāmans," and thus the Atharvāṅgirases are not designated as a form of knowledge.

That is incorrect, because it contradicts many statements by Yama, Śātātapa, and others who prescribe the Atharvaṇikas and declare that there is a fault in bypassing them. Furthermore, this is the meaning of the *Śatapatha-śruti*: the triple knowledge (*trayi vidyā*)—consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—is alone useful for the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) rites, and no other; it does not mean, however, that anything beyond these is not knowledge at all. Indeed, it is heard in the *Brahmayajña* section of the *Śatapatha*: "By the mention of the *svādhyāya* of the Brāhmaṇas, there is praise of the earlier Atharvāṅgirases: 'He who, being learned, studies the *svādhyāya* of the Atharvāṅgirases day after day, satisfies the gods with fat-offerings; they, being satisfied, satisfy him with security of possession (*yogakṣema*), with vital breath, with semen, with his whole self, and with all meritorious accomplishments; streams of clarified butter and streams of honey flow toward the ancestors as *svadhā* offerings. In the *Pāriplava-brāhmaṇa* of the *Aśvamedhika-kāṇḍa*, their status as bearers of the name "Veda" is also seen: "'The Atharvans are the Veda, this is it'—thus he should recite as if explaining one section (*parva*) of the Atharvans. 'The Aṅgirases are the Veda, this is it'—thus he should recite as if explaining one section of the Aṅgirases. Even in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other texts, the intention is to designate the Atharvāṅgirases themselves as the fourth Veda in the statement, "The limbs are the four Vedas. Therefore, this [text] is not intended for the exclusion of the Atharvaṇikas; rather, it means that three persons should be invited for the ancestral rite (*pitṛkṛtya*). By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the Chāndoga and," the three are always to be understood as the Bahvṛca, the Adhvaryu, and the Chāndoga. As for the phrase "one of these," it was stated to remove the doubt that those who study only one of the other Vedas might also be included.
Yama says:
One who knows the *Trisuparṇa* is a *Bahvṛca*; one who sings the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* is a *Chandoga*;
one who maintains the five fires is a *Yajurvedin*; and one who knows the *Atharva* is a *Brahmaśīrṣaka*.
One who knows the self, one who knows the limbs, and likewise the son of a woman married according to the Brahma rite—
all these may be [appointed] in their entirety, or even a single part thereof.
Three are higher and three are lower, and the self is the seventh therein;
all those seven persons together consume that food.

The *Trisuparṇa* is a portion of the *Ṛgveda* and *Yajurveda*; he who possesses the vow (*vrata*) required for its study is called a *Trisuparṇa*. The *Jyeṣṭhasāman* is a specific *Sāman* chant. The *Pañcāgni-vidyā* is a teaching of the *Yajurveda*; because of his connection to the vow required for its study, a person is called a *Pañcāgni*. Alternatively, one for whom the five fires—the *Gārhapatya*, *Āhavanīya*, *Dakṣiṇāgni*, *Sabhya*, and *Āvasathya*—exist is a *Pañcāgni*. The *Brahmaśīrṣa* is a portion of an *Atharva* Upaniṣad; one who knows it is a *Brahmaśīrṣaka*. An *Ātmavit* is one who knows the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). A *Brahmadeyā* is a woman wedded according to the *Brāhma* form of marriage; a son born of her is a *Brahmadeyāsuta*. "All these" refers to those beginning with the *Bahvṛca* (Ṛgvedin). Regarding the phrase "even a single portion," if all those mentioned are unavailable, however many can be obtained, that many should be accepted. "Superior" (*para*) refers to the generations from the fourth onwards; "inferior" (*avara*) refers to the three preceding the fourth: the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. The "Self" (*ātman*) is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). These seven persons consume the food given to a distinguished recipient (*viśiṣṭapātra*). Just as the *Śrāddha* rite benefits the six generations beginning with the father, so too does it produce a distinguished fruit for the sacrificer in the next world.
Bṛhaspati said:
[385] If one should feed but a single person at a śrāddha, one should feed a Chāndoga there;
for the threefold collection—the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas—is present in him.
One might wander the entire earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves,
searching for one who contemplates the syllables of the Sāmans for the sake of the ancestors, were such a person to be found.
The father is satisfied by the *ṛc*, the grandfather by the *yajus*, and the great-grandfather by the *sāman*; the singer of the *chandoga* hymns is even more superior than that.
Yama and Śātātapa state:
"One should feed a Chandoga at a Śrāddha, a Bahvṛca at the Vaiśvadeva rite,
an Adhvaryu for rites of nourishment (puṣṭikarma), and an Atharvaṇa for rites of pacification (śāntikarma)."
Ritual action performed for the sake of nourishment is *puṣṭikarma*. That which is performed for the purpose of pacifying misfortune is *śāntikarma*. Śātātapa says:
"If one should feed even a single person at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors..."
"The fruit for him is indeed infinite and inexhaustible; such is the sacred revelation."

"Infinite" means without end; "inexhaustible" means not diminished. But he who would feed another at a śrāddha while Atharvan priests are present—the deities, together with the ancestors, depart from that [offering] disappointed.

Therefore, with every effort, one should feed an Atharvavedin at the time of a śrāddha ceremony during offerings to the gods and ancestors; for that [offering] becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Yājñavalkya says: One who is foremost among all the Vedas, a śrotriya, a knower of Brahman, young,
a knower of the meaning of the Vedas, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, one who knows the Trimadhu, and one who knows the Trisuparṇa [are qualified].

[386] Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to ritual action, devoted to austerity, those who maintain the five fires, lifelong celibates, and those who are devoted to their fathers and mothers, are the means for the perfection of the śrāddha.

‘Foremost’ (*agryaḥ*) means the chief among students. ‘In all’ (*sarveṣu*) refers to the four Vedas. ‘Vedic scholar’ (*śrotriyaḥ*) is one who studies his own Vedic branch according to the prescribed rules. ‘Knower of Brahman’ (*brahmavit*) is one who knows the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads. ‘Young’ (*yuvā*) means middle-aged. ‘Knower of the meaning of the Vedas’ (*vedārthavit*) is one who understands the meaning of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. One who, having performed the vow known as *trimadhu*, studies that specific portion of the Ṛgveda is called ‘*trimadhu*’. One who studies the section of the Yajurveda bearing that name after performing the *trisuparṇa* vow is a ‘*trisuparṇika*’. ‘Devoted to ritual action’ (*karmaniṣṭhāḥ*) means those intent on the performance of enjoined duties. ‘For the success of the Śrāddha’ (*śrāddhasaṃpade*) means for the prosperity of the Śrāddha rite.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"And those who are knowers of the Bhāṣya, and those who are devoted to grammar,
and those who study the Purāṇas or even the Dharmaśāstra."
And those who have bathed at sacred fords after exerting themselves,
and those who have performed the final purificatory ablutions (avabhṛtha) in all sacrifices;
Those who are always devoted to truthful vows, those who are intent upon their own duty,
those who are free from anger and dedicated to forbearance— one should employ them at the Śrāddha rites.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "One who is a master of the Atharvaveda, a knower of the Vedas, one whose lineage is known, one endowed with noble birth,
a knower of the Purāṇas, devoted to Brahman, and intent upon the study and recitation of the Veda."
One devoted to Śiva, one intent on the ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava; one who honors Brahmins, a knower of Yoga, one who is tranquil, self-conquered, and of virtuous character—
one should always feed these at rites for the gods and the ancestors.
[387] Those Brāhmaṇas who know the Maṇḍala and those who know the Puruṣa-sūkta—
by seeing them, a man is quickly liberated from all sins.
Those best of the twice-born who are devoted to the recitation of the Śatarudrīya rescue their ancestors when they are diligently fed during a śrāddha ceremony.
Likewise:
"One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī should be employed in rites for the gods and ancestors;
no sin remains in him, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf."
"A drop of water" is *abbinduḥ*. "Puṣkara" is a lotus leaf.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One who knows the six limbs, one who performs sacrifice, a yogi, and one who knows the true nature of sacrifice..."
The Brahmin who eats only what is unasked for, and who is indeed conversant with the ritual rules for the Śrāddha ceremony.
One who has mastered even a single one of the eighteen branches of knowledge;
one who knows the *trimadhu* and the *trisauparṇa*; one who maintains the five sacred fires; and one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*.
The four Vedas, the four Upavedas, the six Aṅgas, the Smṛtis, the Purāṇas, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge.
He who has been purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa or Parāka penances and observances,
and who knows the treatise on polity (Nītiśāstra) of Bṛhaspati as well as the science of grammar (Śabdavidyā);
He who is always purified by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is superior to hundreds of other pure persons, even if he should perform an improper act.

What need is there for much speaking here? Those two, who were knowers of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and students of the Atharvaśiras, were formerly requested by their ancestors to perform the ancestral rites after they had completed their ascetic penance.
In the Mahābhārata:
"And those who have exerted themselves in performing ablutions at sacred fords,
and who have bathed in the final purificatory rites (avabhṛtha) at sacrifices accompanied by sessions (sattra)."
Those who are non-oppressive, not fickle, patient, self-controlled, and have conquered their senses,
as well as those who delight in all dharmas— one should employ these among the faithful.
Free from anger, devoted to their duties, and always delighting in self-restraint—such are the virtuous Brahmins; what is given to them yields great fruit.
To those who are free from pride, patient with all, joyful, masters of their senses,
benevolent toward all beings, and friendly— what is given to them yields great fruit.
That which is given to those who are free from greed, pure, learned, modest, truthful,
and devoted to their own duties, yields great fruit.
Exalted by wisdom, learning, virtuous conduct, and noble lineage—
even a single bull among the twice-born in this world can deliver his entire family.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:

One should always feed at śrāddha ceremonies a person whose food is not provided by others, who is weary from compassion, who is of meager means, who does not beg, who is devoted to solitude, and who possesses a sense of shame.

"One whose prepared food does not exist is 'akḷptānnaḥ' (one who has no ready food). 'Ghṛṇā' means compassion; one who possesses that is 'ghṛṇī' (compassionate). 'Klāntaḥ' means exhausted by religious observances (*vrata*); one who is both compassionate and exhausted is 'ghṛṇiklāntaḥ'. Alternatively, 'ghṛṇiklāntaḥ' refers to one exhausted by the rays of the sun due to the habit of wandering on pilgrimages. One whose livelihood (*vṛtti*) or subsistence (*vartana*) is meager because of the restriction on accepting gifts and so forth is 'kṛśavṛttiḥ'. 'Hrīmān' means modest or possessing a sense of shame. Such Brahmins—householders who know the meaning of the Vedas and are free from pride—"
One should engage those accompanied by their wives and sons in the *śrāddha* rite;
for the wife is remembered as half of one's body, and thus [the self] is not complete without her. Nor is there a world for one who has no son—this is the eternal Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "Now we shall describe those brāhmaṇas who are worthy of being invited to a *śrāddha*:
one who is distinguished, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), a yogin, a knower of the Vedas, and a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*."
He who maintains the five fires, is devoted to ritual action, is devoted to austerity, and has conquered his senses.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"One should feed ascetics (yatis) or the Vālakhilyas at the rite of śrāddha;
one should honor and satisfy forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) and students (upakurvāṇas)."
He who feeds a householder has the Viśvedevas honored;
by feeding a forest-dweller, the Ṛṣis; and by feeding a Vālakhilya, Purandara.
By honoring ascetics, one directly honors Brahmā himself. The five stages of life (āśramas) are purifying, yet those who delight in worldly attachments do not abide in them.
The four stages of life are meritorious in both ancestral rites (śrāddha) and rites for the gods (daiva).
Likewise:
"The ancestral offering (śrāddha) should be given to Brahmins who are self-restrained, maintainers of the sacred fires,
pure, learned, and especially those well-versed in the Vedas."
One who knows the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa, one who is proficient in the meaning of the Purāṇas,
one who is free from guile, one who is easily satisfied, and one who avoids accepting gifts—
these Brāhmaṇas should be appointed at the head of the row for the Śrāddha.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "One who has mastered the *Triṇāciketa* and the *Sauparṇī*, one who recites the *Dharmadroṇa*,
one who immediately washes away [impurities], and one who is devoted to assisting others."
One who gives choice food, one who eats choice food, and one who is always devoted to silent recitation—
these indeed are to be known as the distinguished Brāhmaṇas for the successful accomplishment of the Śrāddha.
In the Bārhaspatya-saṃhitā:
"Those who, being full of faith, recite the Smṛtis proclaimed by Aṅgiras, Nārada, Bhṛgu, and Bṛhaspati, should be diligently employed [as witnesses]."
Those firmly established in Vedānta are especially qualified as expounders at śrāddha ceremonies.
Pracetas said: One who has mastered the Triṇāciketa, the Trimadhu, and the Trisuparṇa; one who knows the six Vedāṅgas;
and likewise another who is established in knowledge, established in austerity, and established in ritual action.
One who is self-controlled, devoted to his mother, worships the gods with faith,
and subsists by gleaning ears of grain and the like— such is the son of a *śrotriya*.
These Brahmins are of great merit and are worthy recipients for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
Yama says: That which is eaten by those Brahmins who do not specify the constellations, lunar days, auspicious days, moments, and auspicious omens, becomes indeed inexhaustible.
The learned, desiring infinite fruit, should with great effort establish offerings for the gods and ancestors upon a twice-born man who has become a worthy recipient.
Yājñavalkya: Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth should be given, duly honored, to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man who desires his own welfare.

In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "Indeed, those Brāhmaṇas who have different *pravara*s, as well as those who belong to different *gotra*s and are unrelated, are to be known as suitable for the accomplishment of the *śrāddha*."

In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: "In Śrāddha rites, those Brāhmaṇas who are most proficient in Vedic knowledge should be employed, provided they are free from ties of kinship by birth, lineage, mantra, pupilage, or marriage."

"Those connected by marriage" refers to maternal uncles and others; "those connected by lineage" refers to sapindas and others; "those connected by sacred knowledge" refers to teachers and others; "those connected as pupils" refers to instructors in the arts and sciences. These are the praiseworthy Brahmins.
Now, those who are worthy of the row (pāṅkteyas).

Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Now, those worthy of the row (pāṅkteya) are: one who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅga); one who maintains the five fires; a learned reciter (anūcāna); one who has studied the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Upaniṣads, and Dharmaśāstras; a śrotriya; one who has performed the three Nāciketa fire-altars, the three Madhu rites, and the Trisuparṇa; a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman; one who studies the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Upaniṣads, and Dharmaśāstras; one devoted to the Vedas; one who constantly maintains the sacred fires; and one who is intent on serving his mother and father and delights in the Dharmaśāstras. The "Sāṃkhya scripture" is that of Kapila. The "Yoga scripture" is that of Patañjali. The "Upaniṣad scripture" refers to the Vedāntas. "One who constantly maintains the fires" means one who perpetually performs the Agnihotra sacrifice.
[392] Hārīta states the qualities of family, sacred learning, conduct, behavior, appearance, and virtue for the purpose of defining those worthy of the row (*pāṅkteya*).

Stability, the uninterrupted study of the Vedas, not being born of a mixed marriage, and having a lineage of seers (*ārṣeya*)—these are the qualities of family. The Veda, the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), Dharma, the inner self (*adhyātma*), specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*), and stability—this is the sixfold sacred learning (*śruta*). Reverence for Brahmins, devotion to gods and ancestors, impartiality, gentleness, not causing pain to others, lack of envy, mildness, absence of harshness, friendliness, pleasant speech, gratitude, providing refuge, and tranquility—this is the thirteenfold conduct (*śīla*). Forbearance, self-restraint, compassion, generosity, non-violence, honoring teachers, purity, bathing, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), austerity (*tapas*), Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), truthfulness, contentment, firmness in vows, and observance of minor vows—this is the sixteenfold behavior (*vṛtta*). Therefore, those who are of noble birth, possessed of sacred learning, endowed with good character, established in proper conduct, truthful, free from physical defects, and worthy of the *pāṅkta* (the company at a ritual meal) [are to be honored].

The meaning of this is as follows: the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* states that "stability" (*sthiti*) is persistence for a long period of time in the form of a continuous stream. Harihara, however, says: "Stability is abiding in the duties pertaining to caste, stage of life, and so forth as prescribed by the scriptures, and not deviating from them even in times of adversity.
As they say:
"Not wavering when entreated, and not proceeding upon an improper path."
"Since steadfastness is maintained even in adversity, that quality is called stability."

"Knowledge of the uninterrupted Veda" (*avicchinna-vedavit-tva*) refers to being a knower of the Veda that has remained unbroken through a continuous lineage of fathers, grandfathers, and so forth—just like the status of being a *brāhmaṇa*—by virtue of being the proclaimer of the *caraṇas*, such as the Toraṇāyaṇīyas and others.
As they say:
"The *caraṇa* is remembered in a family through a lineage of *vipras*, just like [the memory of] one's caste (*jāti*)."
The uninterrupted knowledge of that Veda is proclaimed as *vedana*.

Others, however, state that the quality of family (*kulaguṇa*) consists in the uninterruptedness of the study of the Vedas and the performance of sacrifices among one’s ancestors due to the non-interruption of the Veda and its branches; and that the absence of confusion regarding the womb (*ayonisaṃkara*) consists in not producing offspring from women of a different caste and being free from association with other families through the adoption of sons (*dattaka*) and the like; and that *ārṣeya* (the status of belonging to a lineage of seers) consists in knowing the sages belonging to one’s own *pravara* lineage, as seen in the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "He who is known as a learned scholar (*anūcāna*), he is a seer (*ṛṣi*); such is one who belongs to a lineage of seers (*ārṣeya*)."

These, for their part, are the qualities of noble lineage that serve as causes of purity. The Veda is fourfold, distinguished by the divisions of the *Ṛg* and the others. The limbs of the Veda (*vedāṅga*) are those beginning with phonetics (*śikṣā*). Thus it has been said: "Phonetics, ritual procedure, grammar, etymology, the course of the celestial bodies, and prosody—these are declared to be the six limbs of the Veda."

‘Dharma’ refers to the treatises on law (*dharmaśāstra*) such as those of Manu and others. ‘Adhyātma’ refers to the science of the discrimination of the Self. ‘Vijñāna’ refers to the Nyāya philosophy and similar systems, which are the cause for specific knowledge regarding categories such as the means and objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-prameya*). ‘Sthiti’ refers to the sciences of livelihood (*vārtā*) and so forth, which are the causes of stability; or ‘sthiti’ may refer to the non-forgetting of what has been studied; or ‘sthiti’ may refer to that in which the sequence of dharma and the rest is described, such as in the *Itihāsas*. In this way, the fourteen branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*), beginning with the Vedas, are mentioned. Hearing these six is ‘śruta’. ‘Brahmaṇyatā’ is goodness toward Brahmins. ‘Devapitṛbhaktatā’ is the performance of rites for the gods and ancestors without deceit. ‘Pitṛbhaktatā’ is the service of one’s parents while they are living without guile. ‘Samatā’ is the state of being free from attachment and aversion. ‘Saumyatā’ is conduct that is pleasing to all people. ‘Aparopatāpitā’ is the absence of causing pain to others through speech and other means. ‘Anasūyatā’ is not exposing the faults of others. ‘Mṛdutā’ is having a heart that is not harsh. ‘Apāruṣya’ is freedom from quarreling. ‘Maitratā’ is a serene state of mind. ‘Priyavāditā’ is rejoicing in those who do good. ‘Kṛtajñatā’ is the recognition of favors received. Regarding ‘śaraṇyatā’: according to the memory of the lexicon (*abhidhānakośa*), “*śaraṇa*” means a refuge, a shelter, or a protector; thus, a refuge itself is “śaraṇya. Here, the suffix is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, one who is fit (*sādhu*) for providing refuge—meaning for being a shelter or a protector—is “śaraṇya”; the state of being such is ‘śaraṇyatā’. ‘Praśānti’ is the absence of pride regarding learning and so forth. Those [qualities] explained under forbearance (*kṣamā*) and the rest are not explained here again. ‘Dāna’ is the transfer of ownership to another after one’s own possession has ceased, performed according to rule. ‘Japa’ is the repetition of specific mantras. ‘Homa’ is the renunciation of one’s own ownership ending in an offering (*prakṣepānta*) dedicated to a deity. ‘Saṃtoṣa’ is freedom from craving. ‘Dṛḍhavratatva’ is the non-abandonment of the vows one has undertaken. ‘Upavratitva’ is eating only once a day on the tenth lunar day and so forth. Vyāsa has stated the primary vows (*vrata*) and the secondary vows (*upavrata*).
Non-violence, truthful speech, celibacy, freedom from guile,
and non-stealing— these five are both the restraints (yamāḥ) and the observances (vratāni).
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, purity, moderation in food,
and vigilance are the five observances (niyamas) and the minor vows (upavratas).
Yama said: I shall describe those Brāhmaṇas worthy of the row (pāṅkteya), to whom what is given becomes inexhaustible;
upon seeing whom, all beings find peace of mind.
And even a single person who sits among them purifies the entire row;
one may likewise purify a hundred or a hundred thousand people, even while merely looking at them from all sides.
Having paid homage to the twice-born, I shall proclaim [this] before you;
listen as I recite those [lineages] which are untainted by the Vedic revelation.
Those who drink soma, who are free from passion, knowers of dharma, and tranquil in intellect;
who observe vows, abide by their restraints, and approach their wives only during the proper season.
Even one who maintains the five fires, or one who studies the Yajurveda,
or a Bahvṛca (Rigvedin) who knows the Trisuparṇa, or one who knows the Trimadhu;
The *Trimadhu*, a portion of the Ṛgveda and its associated vow;
the *Triṇāciketa*; the *Virajas*; the *Chandoga* who sings the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*;
and one who has studied the *Atharvaśiras*: all these are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
The *Viraja* is a specific mantra; by its study, a person also becomes "free from passion" (*viraja*). The *Atharvaśiras* is a portion of the *Atharvaveda*.

Furthermore, one who is a child yet maintains the sacred fire (*agnihotrī*), one who knows the principles of logic (*nyāyavid*), one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅgavid*), one who knows the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, and one who is a reciter of the Dharma—[these are also qualified].
The Rṣivratin, the Ṛṣīka, as well as the Dvādaśavārṣika,
the son of a Brahmadeya woman, the Garbhaśuddha, and the Sahasrada;
He observed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow, was truthful in speech, and was a knower of the Purāṇas;
he was proficient in all branches of learning, tranquil, and free from all taint.
Devoted to the worship of the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, intent upon knowledge, liberated from all things, steadfast, and sustained by Brahman— he is the best of the twice-born.
One who has no enemies and no friends, who is friendly and a knower of the self;
one who is a *snātaka*, devoted to silent recitation, and always fond of flowers and offerings.
He was upright, gentle, patient, self-controlled, devoted to the vow of truth,
pure, a knower of the Vedas, a knower of all the scriptures, and dedicated to fasting.
The householder and the student who is a knower of the four Vedas—
these are proclaimed as the meritorious twice-born ones worthy of the company at a funeral feast; when engaged in offerings to the gods and ancestors, they certainly deliver [the sacrificer].

"Ṛṣīkaḥ": one whose qualities are slightly less than those of a *ṛṣi*; he is called *ṛṣīka* because he is "slightly deficient in qualities compared to a *ṛṣi*"—so states the traditional teaching of Sumantu. "Dvādaśavārṣikaḥ": one who observes the Vedic vows for twelve years. "Sahasradaḥ": Medhātithi explains this as "one who gives a thousand cows. Regarding the phrase "liberated from all," the word "debts" (*ṛṇāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Anamitraḥ": free from enemies. "Na cāmitraḥ": not an enemy to anyone. "Maitraḥ": devoted to friendship. "Ghṛṇī": compassionate.
Thus [are] those worthy of the company.
Now, those who purify the company.
Āpastamba:

Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row when it has been defiled by those unworthy of the row— those best of the twice-born who are the sanctifiers of the assembly.

A "row" (*paṅkti*) refers to an assembly that has been "defiled" or corrupted by those "unfit for the row" (*apāṅktayaḥ*), whose characteristics will be described below. Listen with full attention to those Brāhmaṇas by whom [the row] "is purified"—that is, rendered free from defect—[those] who are about to be described in their entirety. These words are explanatory (*arthavāda*). For just as one who eats in a single row, if he is corrupt, defiles even those who are not corrupt, so too a purifier of the row (*paṅktipāvanaḥ*), by virtue of his excellence of qualities, dispels even the defects committed by others; such is the meaning. Nor does this authorize the feeding of those unfit for the row. Rather, it means that a purifier of the row must certainly be sought out.
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expositions [of the scriptures],
and who are born into lineages of Vedic scholars, should be known as the purifiers of the assembly.

"Foremost" (*agryāḥ*) means excellent. "In all," that is, even in all four "Vedas," means those who have accepted all the Vedas through tradition by way of dispelling all doubts. "Expositions" (*pravacanāni*) refers to those treatises (*aṅgas*) in which the meaning of the Veda is proclaimed or explained; the sense is that they are those by whom the six-limbed Veda (*ṣaḍaṅga-veda*) has been studied or is being studied. "Born into a lineage of Vedic scholars" (*śrotriyānvayajāḥ*) means those whose fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, were likewise such [scholars].

[Objection: It has been stated that giving is for the learned (*vidvat*), yet learning is not mentioned here; nor is it possible to establish the status of being a "purifier of the assembly" (*paṅktipāvana*) without such learning. For the status of being a purifier of the assembly depends upon specific qualities, and it is not logical [to apply it] when those qualities are absent. [Response: It is said: this is for the purpose of giving to a mere *śrotriya* in the absence of a learned person. When a learned person is not available, giving to a *śrotriya*—though secondary—is indeed declared to be primary. [Such persons are]: one who has thrice kindled the *Nāciketa* fire, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the *Triṣuparṇa*, and one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
One who belongs to a lineage of Brahman-gifts and one who chants the Jyeṣṭha-sāman.

The portion of the Veda known as the *Tṛṇāciketa* belongs to the Adhvaryus and begins with the words "having drunk water, having chewed grass," and so forth; because of his connection to the study of that [text], a person is also called "Tṛṇāciketa" here.

Others, however, maintain that "Triṇāciketa" refers to one who has performed the vow prescribed for those studying the *Triṇāciketa* [section of the Veda]; here too, the person is designated by way of a secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇā*). One should not think, however, that mere [observance of] this constitutes being a sanctifier of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). Rather, this quality is to be seen as an additional attribute when it coexists with qualities such as being a *śrotriya*. Similarly, the *Pañcāgnividyā* is the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*; because of his connection with the knowledge of that, the person is also called "Pañcāgni."

Others, however, say that he who possesses the three *tretā* fires, as well as the two—the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*—is one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*). The *trisuparṇa* is a mantra; it is recited in the *Taittirīyaka* or the *Bāhvṛcya* [Vedas] that "those Brahmins who recite the *trisuparṇa*" and so forth, as well as the vow (*vrata*) known as *trisuparṇa*. One who knows the Veda with its six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is a "knower of the six limbs" (*ṣaḍaṅgavit*). A "successor of a gift to a Brahmin" (*brahmadeyānusantāna*) is one born from a woman who was given in marriage by means of a gift to a Brahmin. The "singer of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*" refers to the *ājyadoha* and other *āraṇyaka-sāmans*, as well as the vow known as *jyeṣṭhasāman*; he who studies that [text] by performing that vow is thus called.
One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, an expounder, a celibate student, one who bestows a thousand gifts,
and one who has lived a hundred years— these Brāhmaṇas should be known as purifiers of the assembly.

Since the knowledge of the six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) has already been mentioned, one who understands the meaning of the Veda by himself alone through his own exceptional intelligence, without those auxiliary limbs, is intended here as an "expounder of the Veda's meaning" (*vedārthavit*). An "expounder" (*pravaktā*) is either a teacher of the Veda or its commentator. A "celibate student" (*brahmacārī*) is one who dwells in the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya-āśrama*). Others maintain that the mention of the "celibate student" is intended to indicate youth. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya stated: "A learned man (*śrotriya*), a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), and a youth (*yuvan*). And it is also stated in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra*: "The gift for youths is first; for those of paternal age," and so forth.

"Of paternal age" means that one should invite Brahmins who are of equal age to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, serving as their respective representatives. Since the word *sahasra* signifies "many," "giver of a thousand" (*sahasrada*) means "one who gives much. "One with a hundred years of life" (*śatāyuḥ*) refers to one of advanced age; for such a person, due to the fullness of his cheeks, attains the status of a worthy recipient. In the word "hundred" (*śata*), by virtue of common usage, "years" are understood as the number to be counted.
Yama says: "Brahmins who have completed their Vedic studies and vows are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*)."
Those who are devoted to the practice of vows, though emaciated and of meager means;
But those twice-born ones who have transcended unrighteousness are purifiers of the assembly— those Brahmins who perform sacrificial sessions, abide by their vows, and are esteemed by the Vedas.

In this context, there is also the reading "mantriṇaḥ" (those who recite mantras). According to that view, the *mantriṇaḥ* are those devoted to the silent recitation (*japa*) of mantras such as the Gāyatrī;
and those twice-born ones who have desisted from harming living beings are the purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvanāḥ*).
They are devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, tranquil, patient, and free from envy.
Those twice-born men who are free from attachment to receiving gifts are purifiers of the assembly.
Those Brahmins who observe the sacrificial sessions, who abide by their vows, who are esteemed for their Vedic learning,
and who are endowed with auspicious conduct— those Brahmins are purifiers of the assembly.
These indeed are the gods upon the surface of the earth, created of old by the gods;
whatever is given to them as an offering to the ancestors or the deities becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise: "The learned, those of good vows, the peaceful, and the Brāhmaṇas who purify the assembly—what they eat goes to the gods; what they eat goes to the ancestors."
Śaṅkha says: A Brāhmaṇa who knows the six Vedāṅgas, who knows the three Suparṇa hymns, who is a student of the Ṛgveda, who sings the Jyeṣṭhasāman,
who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, and who maintains the five sacred fires— such Brāhmaṇas are purifiers of the assembly.
One who maintains the lineage of a Brahmadeya gift, one who bestows a Brahmadeya gift,
and one who is the master of a Brahmadeya gift— such Brahmins are purifiers of the assembly.
Those Brahmins who have mastered the Yajus, those who have thoroughly mastered the Sāmans,
and those who study the Atharvashiras are purifiers of the assembly.
The wise ascetic who is constantly devoted to yoga, for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal,
and who is habituated to meditation— such learned ones, O Brahmins, are purifiers of the assembly.
Devala said: Now I shall further describe other Brāhmaṇas who purify the assembly (paṅktipāvana),
who are capable in the offerings to the gods and ancestors (havyakavya), and who are honored for their own virtues.
Brahmins who are proficient in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, born of pure lineage, and who do not falter in their own duties, indeed sanctify their own row.

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, a singer of the Sāmaveda, and a performer of the Soma sacrifice— these Brāhmaṇas are purifiers of the assembly.
One who is established in the highest stage of life (the forest hermitage), one who lives a hundred years, one who chants the Jyeṣṭha-Sāman,
one who maintains the sacred fires, and those who drink the Soma— these Brāhmaṇas are purifiers of the assembly.
Those who know the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and the Dharma; those who have completed their vows (snātaka); those who maintain the sacred fire (agnihotrī);
and those whose lineage has received the gift of a Brahman—these are to be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).

Hārīta says: "Ten persons on either side [of a row] purify the line: one who has mastered the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one who has performed the *triṇāciketa* rite, one who knows the *trimadhu*, one who knows the *trisauparṇa*, one who knows the *triśīrṣa*, a singer of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who maintains the five fires (*pañcāgni*), one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who recites the *rudra* hymns, a perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*), one who approaches his wife only during her season (*ṛtukālābhigāmī*), and one who knows the ultimate reality (*tattvavit*).
Moreover, they cite this regarding the matter:"
He in whose house there are the five fires— the pacana and the pācana— and in which the three sacrificial fires are kindled every morning and evening, that brahmin is a purifier of the assembly.
They say that a *snātaka* endowed with the aforementioned qualities is equal to a thousand;
one who possesses the qualities of the five fires and so forth is said to be equal to a hundred thousand.
Whether it be a single verse or an entire row extending for a *yojana*,
a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, when appointed to the head of the row, purifies it.

By the phrase "ten on both sides who are learned in the Vedas" (*daśobhayataḥ śrotriyāḥ*), the purity of ten generations on both the mother’s and the father’s side as stated by Yājñavalkya and others is indicated. One who studies the three "heads" (*śīrṣa*)—namely, the *Rudraśiras*, the *Vaiśvānaraśiras*, and the *Atharvaśiras*—is called "three-headed" (*triśīrṣā*). A "reciter of the Rudra" (*rudrajāpī*) is one devoted to the recitation and meditation upon the Rudra-hymns, beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, in your wrath" (*namas te rudra manyave*). One whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) is a perpetual celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*), for in the case of a householder, the state of having upward-drawn semen is generally inappropriate. He is "one who approaches his wife only during her season" (*ṛtukālābhigāmī*), and that refers specifically to his lawful wives, according to the statement of Vyāsa: "He who [approaches] always... He is a "knower of reality" (*tattvavit*), meaning one who knows the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); and he does so even without taking up the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), since the practice of self-knowledge is said to be possible even in the stage of a householder and so forth. One who cooks food for the sake of the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) is a "cooker" (*pacana*), referring to the domestic fire (*āvasathya*). One who causes [others] to cook is a "causer of cooking" (*pācana*), referring to the social fire (*sabhya*). Their status as instigators is figurative, based on their connection to the duty characterized by proximity to the regular cook. The triad of fires—the *Gārhapatya*, *Āhavanīya*, and *Dakṣiṇāgni*—is the "Triad" (*tretā*). He in whose house these five fires blaze is [described]. One who has received the Veda along with its observances (*vrata*) up to the point of understanding its meaning is a "graduate" (*snātaka*); they say such a person, when endowed with qualities like tranquility and self-control, is "equal to a thousand" because he purifies the row of diners consisting of a thousand twice-born men. For it is said: "Those Brahmins who recite the *Trisuparṇa* kill the sin of foeticide; they purify the row of diners up to a thousand. That very person, endowed with qualities such as maintaining the five fires, is "equal to a hundred thousand" (*śatasāhasra*), meaning he purifies a row of diners numbering one hundred thousand. A knower of Brahman who knows the secret of the Veda purifies the row of those "devoid of verses" (*anṛcām*)—those lacking the Veda—extending over a distance of a full *yojana*.
Gautama said:

"Those who purify the assembly (paṅktipāvana) are: one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who maintains the five fires, a Snātaka, one who knows the Mantras, one who knows the Brāhmaṇas, one who knows the Dharma, and one who is the offspring of a lineage where the gift of a daughter in marriage was made to a worthy Brahmin.
Viṣṇu also says thus.
Just as [the following are] purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) in rites for the ancestors, so too are they in rites for the gods.

Vasiṣṭha says: one who has performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice; one who maintains the five fires; one who knows the *trisuparṇa*; one who knows the *caturmedha*; a follower of the *Vājasaneyi* school; one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*); one who is the descendant of a lineage where the gift of the Veda (*brahmadeyā*) was maintained; one who chants the *chandoga* hymns; one who sings the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas; one who studies the Dharma; and one whose maternal and paternal lineages extend ten generations and are known to be learned *śrotriyas*. These learned men and those who have completed their student-life (*snātaka*) are purifiers of the assembly.

"Fourfold-sacrificer" (*caturmedhī*) refers to one who performs the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, for in that rite there are four sacrificial portions (*medhā*). Or, it refers to one who performs the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. The connection is that such a person is a follower of the Vājasaneyi school. The plural "the learned ones" (*vidvāṃsaḥ*) is used to indicate that learning is of many kinds.
Āpastamba states:

"One who knows the *Trimadhu*, one who knows the *Trisuparṇa*, one who knows the *Triṇāciketa*, one who maintains the five fires, a singer of the *Chandoga* verses, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who has studied the Veda, and the son of a learned man—these, when eating at a *śrāddha*, become purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*)."

Baudhāyana says: "One who knows the *trimadhu*, one who knows the *triṇāciketa*, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who knows the *triśīrṣaka*, and one who chants the *jyeṣṭhasāman*—these are the purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*s). Paiṭhīnasi says:

Now, therefore, follow those who purify the company (paṅktipāvanas): one who has mastered the three Nāciketa fire-altars, one who knows the three Madhu verses, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, a Chāndoga who has fulfilled his vows, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāman, one who has studied the Veda, the son of a learned teacher (anūcāna), one who continues the lineage of a daughter given in marriage for the sake of Brahman, one who has offered a thousand oblations, one who recites the Rudrādhyāya, one who knows the four Vedas and the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅgas), one who studies the Atharvaśiras, one who maintains the five sacred fires, and one who chants the Veda—these are the purifiers of the company. Each one of them, when appointed to the head of the row, purifies the company even by the thousands. Regarding the term "Rudrādhyāyin," it refers to one whose habit is the recitation of the Śatarudrīya. Thus says Uśanas.

In this regard, those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) are as follows: a Brāhmaṇa who has completed his studies of the Vedas and the vows of ablution (*vedavidyāvratasnātaka*); one whose conduct and boundaries of character have remained unbroken through five generations; one who knows the *trisuparṇa* hymns; one who is learned in the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga-vij*); one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*; one whose study of the Dharma has not been interrupted for a hundred years; one who has mastered the recitation of mantras and the like, as well as the *jāpya* and *pravacana* texts; one who approaches his wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtukālābhigāmī*); one who is pure in lineage for ten generations according to the Vedic rules; and one who is a *snātaka*. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

Now, those who sanctify the company (*paṅktipāvana*) are: one who has thrice kindled the *Nāciketa* fire, one who maintains the five fires, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who has mastered the Vedas, one who has mastered even a single subsidiary Vedic science (*vedāṅga*), one who has mastered the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Grammar, one who has mastered even a single treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), one purified by sacred fords, one purified by sacrifice, one purified by austerity, one purified by truth, one purified by charity, one purified by mantras, one devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, one whose lineage is descended from a woman wedded according to the *Brāhma* rite, one who knows the *Trisuparṇa* hymn, a son-in-law, and a daughter’s son—these are especially worthy recipients, regardless of their age.
"One whose lineage is descended from a woman wedded according to the *Brāhma* rite" (*brahmadeyānusantāna*) means one whose progeny is from a woman married through the *Brāhma* form of marriage.
Those who maintain the lineage of a religious gift, those who do not withhold such gifts, and those who are the masters of religious gifts— these Brahmins are the sanctifiers of the assembly.

In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "One who knows the six limbs [of the Veda], a knower of the yoga of knowledge, one versed in all systems of thought, and likewise a Yāyāvara— these five should be known as the purifiers of the row."

The *sarvatantraśālīna* is a specific type of householder; the *yāyāvara* is also a specific type of householder. As stated in the Vedic commentary: "Those who are devoted to certain Vedic expositions (*bhāṣya*), those who delight in grammar, and those who study the Purāṇas or the Dharmaśāstras."
One who has mastered even a single one of the fourteen branches of knowledge,
and he who recites the Śrāddhakalpa— all of them are purifiers of the company.
Gārgya said:
Those Brahmins who know how to give and how to eat, who are firm in their vows, endowed with the knowledge of purificatory rites, are the sanctifiers of the assembly.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Whether he be a devotee of Viṣṇu or one devoted solely to Mahādeva, that Brāhmaṇa who is constantly intent on the worship of Mahādeva is a purifier of the assembly."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Moreover, they cite this:
"Now, even if one who knows the mantras is afflicted by bodily defects that defile the assembly..."
Yama said that he who does not find fault [with others] is indeed a purifier of the assembly.

The mention of one who knows the *mantras* is intended as an indicator of the excellence of his qualities. When such a person exists, even if he is joined with defects pertaining to the body, he is not to be defiled; for he is connected to signs of defects that have been almost entirely exhausted through the experience of suffering in previous births. The mention of "Yama" is for the sake of praise, for he is indeed one who knows the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*). He is a sanctifier of the row (*paṅktipāvana*) because he is currently free from fault. Thus end the sanctifiers of the row. Now, the sanctifiers of the sanctifiers of the row:
Vṛddha Manu says: "He who explains [the ritual], he who investigates the sacrifice,
and he who knows the absolute liberation of the Self— these are the purifiers of those who purify the assembly."

He who explains words by analyzing them into roots and suffixes according to the grammatical treatises composed by Pāṇini and others; he who investigates the ritual of sacrifice (*adhvara-yajña-karman*) through the mature deliberation of the Mīmāṃsā system and elucidates it with discrimination; and he who knows and directly realizes the non-dual Brahman which is the absolute liberation of the Self (*ātma-kaivalya*): these are purifiers even of those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). The meaning is that they are exceedingly most meritorious. Therefore, it should be understood that among all those previously mentioned, these must first be sought out with diligence.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"He who explains the sacred word (*vāk*), he who investigates the sacrifice (*adhvara*),
and he who knows the rules for the melodies of the *Sāman*— these are the purifiers of those who purify the assembly."
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "One who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a performer of sacrifices, peaceful, self-controlled, endowed with forbearance,
free from desire, and an ascetic— these are the purifiers of those who purify the assembly."
The wise man, free from greed, tranquil, content with whatever he has,
possessing equal vision, and truthful in speech— such persons purify even those who purify the assembly.
He is equal toward enemy and friend, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same;
he neither feels attachment nor aversion—he is the purifier of those who purify the assembly.
In the *Garuḍapurāṇa*:
"Those who are proficient in the meaning of the Sāṃkhya scriptures, who know the true principles of the meaning of the Yoga scriptures,
and whose intellects are firmly established in Vedānta— these are the purifiers of even those who purify the assembly."
One who speaks kindly, is pure, observes silence, is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
is habituated to solitude, and is meditative— such persons purify even those who purify the assembly.
Purified by the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), devoted to the withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra),
untouched by the pleasant and the unpleasant, he is the purifier even of those who purify the assembly.
The steadfast one devoted to breath-control, who is friendly and compassionate,
whose self is purified by knowledge of the supreme self— such persons are the purifiers even of those who purify the assembly.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "He who neither censures, nor hates, nor grieves, nor desires;
who delights in the Self and whose desires are fulfilled—he is the purifier of those who purify the assembly."
But he who perceives all beings in the Self alone,
and the Self in all beings— he is the purifier of purifiers.
Untouched by hunger and thirst, as well as by cold, heat, and the like,
and by sorrow and delusion— such are those who purify even the purifiers of the assembly.
He who, being pure, incessantly utters the single-syllable Brahman "Om," with his intellect one-pointedly fixed on the Self— he is the purifier of those who purify the assembly.
One who has restrained the senses, is devoted to austerity, free from desire and possession,
whose mind and self are centered on knowledge and realized wisdom— he is the purifier even of those who purify the assembly.
Thus [are described] those who purify even the purifiers of the assembly.
Now, the employment of yogins at a *śrāddha* rite is stated.
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
One should always feed yogins who have perceived reality and are wise;
there is no doubt that what is given to them becomes inexhaustible.

"Yogins" refers to those engaged in the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*). "Principles" (*tattvāni*) refers to Mahat and the rest, characterized by their specific locations, times, instruments, states, existence, and essential natures, which have been perceived by them through scripture and direct perception. Alternatively, "the Principle" (*tattvam*) is the true nature of the Self, seen by one who has removed superimposition, doubt, and non-determination; those by whom this has been made the object of direct realization—produced by a purified internal organ arising from the vision of certainty resulting from the awakening of inquiry into Vedāntic statements—are meant here. For this very reason, they are "wise" (*manīṣiṇaḥ*), meaning those who, having first distinguished between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, are intent upon the means for attaining the acceptable reality of the Self after having abandoned the fivefold objects of the senses. Because the instruction "one should feed" is stated without qualification, it is understood that this applies to rites for the gods, ancestors, and men; or, by virtue of the context, it specifically refers to rites for the ancestors. The word "always" (*nityam*) indicates a rule. Here, feeding yogins every day simply because one is alive is not being enjoined. Rather, when rites consisting of feeding—such as those for the gods and ancestors—have arisen due to other specific occasions, and when yogins fit to be fed are available, then yogins must certainly be fed while others may be fed at will. This is the meaning of "always. Alternatively, the word "always" is used for the sake of emphasis. Emphasis serves to indicate an abundance of fruit. He states this abundance: "But what is given to them becomes inexhaustible"—this is a certainty, not a matter of doubt.
In the *Brahmavaivarta* as well, after first praising the yogi, the greatness of the fruit for his devotee is shown:
"He who knows the *Ṛg-veda* knows the Vedas; he who knows the *Yajur-veda* knows the sacrifices."
He who knows the Sāmans knows Brahman;
for he who knows the Yogas knows all.

"Indeed, he who knows the *Ṛks* knows the Vedas; he alone eats who eats with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This is the Śruti. The same applies to what follows. Furthermore, regarding the *Ṛks* mentioned in the context of the *Śrāddha*, the Śruti states: "He who knows the *Ṛks* becomes one who knows all the Vedas. The term "*Yajūṃṣi*" refers to those [formulas] which take the form of injunctions for sacrifices such as the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*—including both those that provide indirect assistance (*ārādupakāraka*) and those that provide direct assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*)—as well as those in the form of mantras that serve as reminders. "He who knows them knows the sacrifices. The term "*Sāmāni*" refers to the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* and others, which consist of melodies based on the *Ṛks*. He who knows these knows the *Śabdabrahman*, which is the means to the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman (*Parabrahman*). "He who knows the Self (*ātman*) born of the purified mind through direct realization knows everything"; the meaning is that nothing remains for him to be known.
Likewise:
"Indeed, the entire three worlds are pervaded without interval by the lords of yogis,
because they perceive everything whatsoever that exists within the world."
Having brought under control both the manifest and the unmanifest, as well as the principle of *sattva* beyond that,
the Great-Souled One created everything— both being and non-being, and both together— as the totality of *sattva*.
[408] The liberation and other goals of the great-souled ones are created by the knowledge of the Omniscient One;
therefore, one who is always devoted to them attains auspiciousness as easily as the opening of an eye.
The collection of the three worlds is "the triple world" (trailokya); "all that [is known] by the lords of yogins."

By means of unimpeded yoga, they have attained sovereignty and greatness among yogis; [the world] has been "pervaded" by them at all times without interruption, brought into a connection with their own essential nature. He states the mark that indicates such pervasion: "Because they see everything. "Everything" refers to the entire collection of the Vedas; "they see" means they directly perceive it. Thus, there is the Pātañjala Sūtra: "Knowledge of the worlds [arises] from *saṃyama* on the sun. "Manifest" (*vyakta*) means a gross object fit for the perception of all people, that is to say, an effect. "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) means subtle, that is to say, a cause. Alternatively, "manifest" refers to the effects of the *guṇas*, such as the earth and so forth, while "unmanifest" refers to *prakṛti*. The word "having mastered" (*vaśīkṛtya*) is to be understood as being followed by the word "being" (*santaḥ*). "Sattva" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*) or the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is dominated by the quality of *sattva*. Furthermore, they see the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*), who is beyond that [intellect].
The intellect is higher than the mind, but that which is higher than the intellect is He.

Thus, from the words of the Blessed One: "existent" (*sat*) refers to the sphere of correct application; its opposite is "non-existent" (*asat*); and "both-natured" (*sadasat*) refers to that which is both existent and non-existent. By the "Great Self" (*mahātmanā*) means by the Blessed Lord Brahmā. "Omniscient" (*sarvajñaḥ*) refers to the Lord (*īśvara*); knowledge concerning Him is "omniscient knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*). Since for those Great Ones, liberation and so forth are "created" by such omniscient knowledge, they are therefore "refined" (*śiṣṭa*). Consequently, one who is "devoted" (*bhakta*) to them—performing service and the like—"obtains" (*prāpnoti*) manifold "auspicious" (*śubha*) fruits that are "like an unfolding" (*unmeṣavat*), increasing further and further.
Likewise: "Through ritual action and the worship of the guru, yogins establish a connection;
and by that, their ancestors are nourished through the increase of yoga."
The ancestors, adorned with yoga, having been nourished by Soma in turn,
nourish the three worlds through yoga, by which they live.
[409] For the power of the ancestors indeed arises from yoga, and from yoga the moon proceeds;
therefore, śrāddha offerings should always be diligently given to the yogins.

By means of "action" (*kriyayā*)—that is, by rites such as the *agnihotra* prescribed for those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*)—and by "worship of the gurus" (*gurupūjābhiḥ*), meaning through devotion to both the higher and lower gurus, yogis perform the distinguished eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*). And by means of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) produced by that yoga, they cause their own fathers, grandfathers, and so forth, as well as the *agniṣvātta* ancestors and others, to be "satisfied" (*āpyāyayante*), that is, they please them. Being thus satisfied, they in turn satisfy "Soma," the moon. For when the moon is thus satisfied, the three worlds, being nourished by it, "live"—that is, they endure for a long time. The reason for this succession of satisfaction has been stated in the passage beginning with "for the strength of the ancestors... Therefore, because yogis possess the performance of yoga which is beneficial for the livelihood of the entire universe and are thus superior to all others, one should invite them—even with great effort involving the hardship of requests and the like—and honor them, and offer *śrāddha* ceremonies to them.
Likewise: "The food enjoyed by a yogin excels a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices, and a thousand Puṇḍarīka sacrifices."
The sacrifices beginning with the Aśvamedha and ending with the Puṇḍarīka;
the Soma-sacrifice, the Pitṛ-gaṇa, and the Yoga-sacrifice which is the Moon;
and the application of yoga during the Śrāddha—therefore, this should be performed by one who possesses knowledge.
Therefore, this entire universe is delimited by a finite measure;
it is contained within ignorance, for in Yoga, a valid cognition of such finitude is not accepted.
Therefore, the oblation offered to yogis yields infinite fruit;
do not think, out of pride, that "the effect must conform to its cause."
In whosever house a man of knowledge eats or drinks water at any time, that patron becomes one who has accomplished all his purposes; of this there is no doubt.

‘Niyoga’ means an invitation. This entire universe, being within the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*), is conceived as being limited by a certain measure (*iyattā*). In Yoga, however, there is no such "measure of limitation" (*iyattā-pramā*), that is, no conceptualization of finite dimensions. Therefore, the oblation (*havis*) offered to those distinguished by immeasurable Yoga becomes "yielding infinite fruit," meaning it yields truly limitless results. The reason for this is as follows: the effect conforms to its cause. For it is observed that the properties of the effect follow the properties of the cause. Consequently, from an immeasurable cause, it is fitting that the effect itself should be immeasurable. Thus, "do not think otherwise"—the meaning is: do not entertain any other view.
Chāgaleya said:
Hari, the enemy of the Daityas, is known by the knowers of Yoga as the manifest, direct Brahman.
Therefore, those who know Yoga should be fed at Śrāddha ceremonies for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"In whosever house a man of knowledge eats or even drinks water,
by him a meritorious act has been performed here, and three lineages have been delivered."

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A Brahmin who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who is a practitioner of knowledge-yoga (*jñānayogin*), and who indeed knows the true nature of yoga— him one should feed at the rite of ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) while eating only what is unasked for."
Seated upon the stage of yoga consisting of the reflective awareness of the pure Self, which is denoted by the term "samādhi," one is called a "knower of the yoga of knowledge" (jñānayogin).
As stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "In former times, the sacrifice to the ancestors was declared by the great sages to be full of many defects."
And through the preservation of yoga, it becomes free from obstacles and devoid of flaws.

"Unobstructed" (*niṣpratyūha*) means free from harm caused by *yātudhānas* and others. "Without flaw" (*niśchidra*) means devoid of deficiencies in the fruit resulting from defects such as omissions or excesses.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"And at that time, yogins should be fed at the *śrāddha* by the wise man."
For the ancestors are the foundation of yoga; therefore, one should always worship them.
This [occurs] at times such as the new moon, the *aṣṭakā*, the *kutapa*, and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). The word "always" (*sadā*) applies to all ritual performances of the *śrāddha*.
Likewise:
"If a yogi is present, he alone is entitled to the seat of honor among a thousand Brahmins."
He should ferry across both the sacrificer and the eaters, like a boat upon the water.

One who stands at the beginning of the row of a thousand Brahmins is called "one occupying the foremost seat" (*agrāsanī*). He should ferry them across the great ocean of saṃsāra—this is the ellipsis. Likewise:
Likewise, the verses concerning the ancestors are sung here by those who discourse on Brahman—
those very verses which were formerly sung by the ancestors to King Aila.
When will there be born in our lineage a preeminent son who,
on this earth, shall offer funeral cakes made from the remnants of food consumed by yogis?
"Of King Aila Purūravas," [it was said] "formerly" by his ancestors, that he would set aside even a small portion from the food remaining after he had eaten and "give us" (the ancestors) "piṇḍas.
Āpastamba states another verse:
"Even if one born in a [low] family should feed a yogin..."
By that effortful honoring of a Brahmin at the śrāddha, we are satisfied.
Thus is the injunction regarding the *śrāddha* for yogins. Now, the supreme excellence of yogins is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
He who studies the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs is considered one who has accomplished his purpose;
he is born with a purified karma and is deemed fit for the *śrāddha* when he is self-restrained.
One who takes refuge in Yoga is superior to ten thousand such as he.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
"One who knows the mantras, being pleased, rightfully deserves [the merit of] all those thousands of Brahmins whom one might feed according to their arrival."
Even if one were to feed thousands of such men who know the Dharma,
a single gratified Snātaka is worth all of them for one who listens.
What is eaten by a single teacher of yoga protects from great fear a thousand persons who form mental resolves and a hundred *snātaka* students.
A single yogin excels over a thousand householders, even over a hundred forest-dwellers, and over a thousand celibate students.
Whether he be an atheist, one who violates the dharma, one of mixed caste, or even a thief—a yogi will surely deliver him completely; so said Prajāpati.
One might stand on one foot for a hundred years subsisting only on air;
yet the practitioner of meditation is superior to that—such is the instruction of Brahmā.

"‘Yathāgatān’ means as they have arrived; that is to say, those who are devoid of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), study, and knowledge of its meaning. Even if such persons are fed by the thousands, feeding a single Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda and its meaning is equal [in merit]. The meaning is that he is capable of generating the same amount of merit (*sukṛta*) produced by feeding that many Brāhmaṇas. ‘Snātakaḥ prītaḥ’: the word ‘by food’ is to be supplied. ‘Saṃkalpinaḥ’ refers to those habituated to the performance of various vows. And by feeding a single teacher of Yoga (*yogācārya*), one protects—that is, saves—the host from great fear of sin due to his equality with them."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa:
One should feed a peaceful yogin who delights in the knowledge of reality;
