in his absence, one should feed a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) who is self-controlled, or likewise a student (upakurvāṇaka).

Therefore, with diligence, one should feed a lord of yogis who is intent upon the knowledge of the Lord during offerings to gods and ancestors, rather than other twice-born men if they are unavailable.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A single yogin excels over a thousand householders, a hundred forest-dwellers, and a thousand celibate students."
Whether one is an atheist, a practitioner of forbidden acts, of mixed caste, or even a thief—
Prajāpati has declared that there is no other qualification for giving to yogis.
The ancestors of that person are gratified, just as farmers are by a timely rain,
if a son or even a grandson should feed one who is absorbed in meditation.
Āhośanā said:
Whoever, relying upon the dharma of yoga, knows even a little— whether they belong to the various castes or stages of life— they are considered by us to be the supreme recipient.

The meaning is that those who correctly follow the conduct of their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*) are considered "the supreme recipient" (*paramaṃ pātram*), as stated in the first half of the verse. This praise of the yogi is because Śātātapa has specified them as "those who have seen the reality" (*dṛṣṭatattva*).
And in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"But those who are always established in conduct (*vṛtta*), as well as the wise (*jñānin*) and the meditators (*dhyānin*)...

Since this statement declares that only those established in conduct—namely the wise and the meditators—are worthy of being fed, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the thorough establishment in the reality of the Self and so forth, and "meditation" (*dhyāna*) is the contemplation of Brahman in its formed and formless aspects.
(Mahābhārata, Bhagavadgītā).
"The yogi is superior to the ascetics, and he is considered superior to the men of knowledge;
the yogi is also superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. Thus concludes the exposition on the supreme excellence of yogis.
Now, elsewhere Chāgaleya speaks of the fault of transgressing against a yogin:
"If one should worship a householder while bypassing a yogin."
One does not obtain that fruit; rather, one causes the entire lineage to suffer.

"A householder" refers to one who is not a yogi; he does not obtain the fruit of that [offering]. Likewise, "the entire lineage"—meaning all the ancestors born of his own lineage—he would "torment," that is, he would make them suffer through the sin (pratyavāya) produced by the transgression of the rule. Furthermore: "Having bypassed the yogi, they feed one another."
Both the giver and the consumer go to hell together with their kinsmen.

In this case, it should be understood that both the giver and the consumer go to hell, provided that both have the intention of transgressing the rules of propriety. Therefore, it says: "they feed one another. Here, the giver feeds the practitioner with the thought, "Now that he has been fed, he will feed me in his own home; what of it? The consumer likewise eats while maintaining that same mental orientation. Thus, there is the intention of transgressing propriety on the part of both. However, when only the transgression of the giver is intended, then there is no fault for the consumer. When a transgression is committed through negligence in the absence of such an intention, there is merely a deficiency in the *śrāddha* rite; in that case, neither person falls into hell.
Vṛddhaśātātapa also says:
"If one should bypass a yogin and feed a householder instead, he does not obtain the fruit [of that act]; rather, he causes even one who resides in heaven to fall."

"He who remains only in the household and not in yoga is not a true householder here. The phrase "those staying in heaven" refers to one's own ancestors; for it is said: "They pass over the yogi and honor one another instead;
those who consume [the offerings] while always giving [only to others] shall dwell in hell along with their kinsmen."
Thus concludes the examination of the faults incurred by a yogin through transgression. Now, the state of being a yogin for householders and others is described.

In this context, what is called *yoga* is, in its primary sense, the relationship characterized by the unification of the individual self (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Although this [unity] is natural and common to all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), it remains obscured by the appearance of difference produced by beginningless ignorance; thus, it belongs not to transmigrating individual selves, but only to those who are liberated. The means for this is the knowledge of the reality of the Self. And the means for that is the eight-limbed *yoga*, beginning with the restraints (*yama*) and ending with meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Alternatively, based on the etymological derivation from the instrumental case—that "by means of this, the individual self is joined with the Supreme Self"—that [eightfold path] is *yoga* in its primary sense. By virtue of the authority of the scriptures (*śruti*), even householders and others who possess that [yoga] are *yogins*. Nor should it be said: "Since *yoga* is the means to liberation, the connection with *yoga* belongs only to one desiring liberation, not to a householder. Do not say so. For it is possible for a householder whose mind is becoming dispassionate toward the objects of the senses—corrupted by manifold defects—to desire liberation, which surpasses all other human goals. And when that desire exists, it is entirely appropriate for a learned man capable of practicing the means to perform *yoga*, having fulfilled his specific duties. Furthermore, liberation follows from *yoga* properly practiced. Nor should it be argued that there is no opportunity for the practice of *yoga* for a householder, whose time is occupied by the performance of duties pertaining to his own stage of life (*āśrama*), because like a mendicant (*bhikṣu*), he too has the opportunity during the intervals between the performance of fixed-time rituals. Nor is the practice of *yoga* useless for a householder simply because *yoga* accompanied by the fourth stage of life (*turīyāśrama*) alone is the means to liberation; for the traditional authorities (*smṛti*) record: [The text here provides a verse from the Smṛti. ...and so forth. Thus, the practice of *yoga* is indeed beneficial even for a householder.

"One who has acquired wealth by righteous means, is devoted to the knowledge of reality, is fond of guests, performs ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and speaks the truth—even as a householder, he is liberated. Furthermore, it is heard that liberation was attained through the practice of yoga even by householders such as Janaka, Jābāla, Vāmadeva, Prahlāda, and others. In this context, "devoted to the knowledge of reality" should be understood as "devoted to the knowledge of the reality of the Self. By this, it is effectively stated that for the householder as well, the eightfold path—beginning with the restraints (*yama*) and ending with meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which serves as the means to the knowledge of the reality of the Self—is prescribed.
And so it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"Whether they be householders, lifelong celibates, forest-dwellers,
or ascetics, yogis worship the Supreme Self within their own selves."

Therefore, householders and others are also yogins. This being the case, since householders and others may be equal in their possession of qualities such as the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), it follows that among them, those who are yogins are the ones before whom *śrāddhas* should be offered.
Now, if the injunction for *śrāddhas* is stated on account of the ascetic’s (*yati*) absolute distinction, regarding this Manu says:
Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, others likewise to austerity;
some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others likewise to ritual action.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavyas) should be established with effort among those steadfast in knowledge;
offerings to the gods (havyas) and to the ancestors (kavyas) should be given to all four [classes] alike.

"One established in knowledge" (*jñāniṣṭha*) is a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*); for him, there is a culmination—that is, a pre-eminence—in the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). "One established in austerity" (*taponiṣṭha*) is a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); for he is designated as an ascetic (*tāpasa*), since the rule for austerity states that he should practice the "five fires" (*pañcatapas*) in the summer. "Those established in austerity and Vedic study" (*tapaḥsvādhyāyaniṣṭhāḥ*) are the religious students (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*). "Those established in ritual action" (*karmaniṣṭhāḥ*) are the householders (*gṛhasthāḥ*). Regarding these as well, "oblations to the ancestors" (*kavyāni*)—the food offerings presented for the sake of the *pitṛs*—"are to be established in those established in knowledge"; the meaning is that they are to be given to them. Because of the mention of "effort," in their absence, they may be given to others as well. "Oblations to the gods" (*havyāni*) are to be established in all four classes [of the aforementioned]. "According to rule" means by the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
In the Bārhaspatya-saṃhitā:
"For ascetics are established in knowledge; forest-dwellers are established in austerity;
householders are indeed established in ritual action; and the first [stage] is established in the study of the Vedas."

"The 'first' are the students (brahmacārins). Oblations to the ancestors (kavyas) should be diligently presented to those established in knowledge; however, oblations to the gods (havyas) and to the ancestors (kavyas) should be given to all four [classes of Brahmins]. Thus it is said.
In the *Yamasmṛti* and the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"The ascetic who, knowing the true nature of the qualities (*guṇas*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), eats the sacrificial oblation (*havis*),
surpasses by a thousandfold the fruit obtained by those who know the Vedas."
Therefore, a self-controlled ascetic, or a Vedic scholar, or a celibate student, should be fed at the seat of honor by one performing a sacrifice; by that, the sacrifice is not impaired.
Yama speaks of the fault in a mendicant eating before others: "If a mendicant does not eat first at the sacrifice of a patron,
the host of Rākṣasas seizes from him what is undesirable and extraordinary."
"Adbhutam aniṣṭam" means [calamity] in the form of the destruction of sons, wife, and so forth; by connection with that, the host of Rākṣasas "harate," meaning they bring it upon oneself.
As stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Those śrāddhas which the lords of yogis and ascetics established in Brahman [perform]..."
These very things certainly adorn [the offerings] for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors.
The wise declare that ascetics who know the twenty-five principles and are devoted to the fivefold discipline of the stages of life are worthy recipients for the offerings of *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
Those who feed disciplined ascetics who are free from passion and hatred and are self-realized,
obtain an infinite reward for those who provide such offerings.
Offerings to the ancestors (kavya) should be diligently established among those steadfast in knowledge,
and offerings to the gods (havya) should likewise be given according to the rule, but never to those whose souls are possessed by false egoism.
The wise person who properly honors a yogācārya ascetic with devotion attains a fruit that corresponds to the cause.
Hari, the enemy of the Daityas and a knower of yoga, is the manifest, embodied Brahman;
from him [proceed] I, Nārāyaṇa, and Brahmā, who take refuge in the bodies of ascetics.
One who is constantly engaged in meditation and free from all attachments should worship the one whose seed is Dharma during rites for the gods and the ancestors.
Chāgaleya said:
One should honor an ascetic at a *śrāddha* ceremony with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and foods prepared with milk; this brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
A celibate student and an ascetic are indeed always worthy of worship;
whatever merit may be produced by that [worship], one shall obtain a sixth part of it.
Since recitation, yoga, and sacrifice are all established therein,
salutation and worship offered to him become inexhaustible.
A student, as well as an ascetic, may go to the householder’s hermitage;
there he should offer himself for food, drink, fruit, and flowers.
That which is given to ascetics who are constantly engaged in yoga, who are free from passion, who perform austerities,
and who have desisted from all undertakings, is inexhaustible.
Food that is offered with great reverence to a self-controlled ascetic who is free from passion does not diminish,
even after hundreds of millions of eons, due to the power of faith.

In this regard, the ascetic (yati) must be provided with food as the foremost among those entitled to eat, by virtue of his being the refuge of all stages of life (āśrama) and his preeminence in knowledge and meditation.
Thus it is said in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The ascetic, however, shall be the first eater among all Brahmins."
The best of the twice-born who should study the Vedas with the Itihāsas as the fifth;
Immediately after that, this ascetic should be appointed by one who knows;
after him, one learned in the three Vedas, and after him, one learned in two Vedas.
After him, one who knows a single Veda; after that, one who studies daily.

[420] "Of all Brahmins" refers to those in the stages of student (*brahmacārin*), householder (*gṛhastha*), and forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). "Of all" refers to those who have mastered the *trimadhu*, *trisuparṇa*, *triṇāciketa*, and other such texts. "Foremost" means the principal recipient; he is called "the first-eater" (*agrabhuk*) because he is the primary consumer [of the merit], not because he eats at the earliest time. That best of the twice-born who studies the four Vedas along with the *itihāsas* should be appointed immediately after the ascetic (*yati*). Such is the sequence for those who know three Vedas and so forth. "One who studies daily" is one who is constantly engaged in the study of the Veda. [This is stated] in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
First, he should invite ascetics or Snātakas who perform the three duties;
in their absence, householders who are devoted to the knowledge of Brahman.
Those for whom officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and giving are the only three activities are called *atrikarmiṇaḥ*. "Snātakas" here means forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*).
Vasiṣṭha says:
"On the day before [the funeral], having assembled Brāhmaṇas—ascetics (*yatīs*), householders, virtuous men, and those of advanced age—one should give [the offerings] to the ancestors."
"Having assembled" means having brought about a connection with the performance of the *śrāddha* rite by means of an invitation. In the *Nārada-smṛti*:
"He who, disregarding ascetics (*yatis*), should feed other twice-born (*dvija*) men..."
One who dwells in a village while remaining conscious [of his vows] falls as an oblation to the Rākṣasas.

If one, despite knowing that ascetics (yatis) reside in one's own village, should disregard them and feed others such as householders at a *śrāddha*, then all that food intended for the *śrāddha* feast gratifies only the *rākṣasas* and not the ancestors (*pitṛs*). By this, it is stated that an ascetic residing in one's own village is to be invited to a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa* and *Mārkaṇḍeya-purāṇa* that even an ascetic who has not been invited, but has arrived for alms at the time of the *śrāddha*, is to be fed.
Furthermore, when self-controlled ascetics come at the proper time for alms,
he, with a restrained mind, should satisfy them by bowing down and other such acts, and then feed them.

In this context, since it is already established that a monk who has been invited is entitled to eat in the row of invited Brahmins simply by virtue of the invitation, and likewise one who has arrived at the doorway as a guest, this statement is intended for the purpose of permitting a monk who resides in that very village—who, through negligence, was not invited but nevertheless presents himself at the time of the *śrāddha*—to eat at the *śrāddha*. The plural number is used either to include many such monks or to encompass the various types of ascetics (*yati*). A specific place for the seating of the monk is stated in the *Bārhaspatyasaṃhitā*:
At the time of the ancestral rite (śrāddha), one should feed an ascetic who has arrived in the place of the ancestors;
one should serve him first, or else while he stands by the side.

The meaning of "one should feed [him] in the place of the ancestors" is that one should cause the food being offered for the sake of the deceased to be eaten [by him]. The meaning of "one should serve him first" is that one should perform the primary ancestral rite (*paitrya*).
He states another alternative: "or if he is standing at the side," meaning one may feed him like a guest in the row of invited Brahmins.

In this matter, the settled rule is as follows: among Brāhmaṇas, one should feed an ascetic who arrived before the calculation of the paternal and grandpaternal lineages in the place of the ancestors (pitṛ-sthāna). However, one who arrives later should be fed like a guest in the presence of the twice-born invited to the Śrāddha, so as not to contradict the intended sequence of the ritual acts already commenced. Furthermore, even if he arrives prior to the time of the Śrāddha, one should feed him after requesting him properly and having him wait until the time of the Śrāddha has arrived.
Yama states that an ascetic (*yati*) or a student (*brahmacārin*) who has arrived at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony should be fed, whether as a recipient of the *śrāddha* or as a guest:
"A mendicant or a student who has arrived for the purpose of eating—
if he arrives even after [the others] have already sat down, one should certainly feed him as well."
Chāgaleya states the specific fruit and the reason for feeding [such a person] at the time of a śrāddha:
"One should feed an ascetic who is a fellow student of sacred knowledge even during a śrāddha;
he delivers the brāhmaṇas, as well as the hosts of one's fathers and mothers, from sin."
Wherever ascetics and celibate students eat, there the ancestors and gods partake; such a person attains the supreme goal.
They rescue the donor, as well as his sons, his wife, and his ancestors;
therefore, one should honor with every effort a guest who has arrived at one's hermitage.
Both the student of sacred knowledge and the ascetic are the rightful owners of cooked food;
those who cook for themselves eat [their own sin], whereas he who does not cook does not cook [for himself].
He [the same author] states the distinction of the ascetic (yati) from those such as the student (brahmacārin):
"A single ascetic excels even over thousands of students, hundreds of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha),
and thousands of householders."

This being so, when it is possible, ascetics (yatayas) should be fed at a *śrāddha* ceremony; in their absence, celibate students (*brahmacārins*) and others. And thus it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"In the absence of ascetic mendicants, one should also honor a forest-dweller (*vanastha*)."
Even if he does not obtain that, one who is indifferent, steadfast, and has restrained his senses [is successful].
The term ‘udāsīnaḥ’ refers to one who has no connection with the donor. Śātātapa says: “One should feed ascetics (yatis). Regarding that, a specific detail is stated in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.

At the time of a śrāddha rite, one should avoid those who are shaven-headed, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes; instead, one should cause offerings to be given to those with topknots, those whose garments are dyed with mineral pigments, and those who carry the triple staff.
For those great-souled ones, ever established in their vows, possessed of knowledge and likewise absorbed in meditation,
and devoted to the gods, purify others even by the mere sight of them.

‘Muṇḍās’ are those whose heads are shaven along with the top-knot (*śikhā*). ‘Jaṭilās’ are the Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Kālamukhas, and others. ‘Kāṣāyas’ are those wearing garments dyed with the astringent decoctions of the *aśvattha* tree and so forth.

Baudhāyana states: “One should especially avoid these at the time of a *śrāddha*. However, one should diligently give [offerings] to those who possess the top-knot, wear ochre-colored garments, and carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*). By this, it is understood that all the statements of the Yogins refer exclusively to ascetics (*yatis*) endowed with these specific characteristics.
"Surely one who observes the vow should always subsist on alms and not eat the food of a single person;
for it is traditionally taught that the livelihood of those observing vows through alms is equal to fasting."
Since Manu has thus prohibited students (*brahmacārin*) from eating food given by a single person,
[it follows that] a renunciant (*yati*), having collected eight, ten, or twelve alms-foods (*bhikṣā*),
should dry them all completely and then eat them, O best of the twice-born.

Since Saṃvarta has thus prescribed for an ascetic (*yati*) the practice of eating from a collection of alms-food (*bhikṣākadambaka*), how could those two [the *kuṭīcaka* and *bahūdaka*] eat at a *śrāddha*?

To this we reply: because it is observed that an ascetic is permitted to eat food from a single source when he is unable to wander for alms, when it is impossible to obtain food from many sources, and for the sake of favoring others. As Kārṣṇājini says:
"An ascetic may eat from a single source when he is incapable [of wandering] or for the sake of favoring others."
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"He should eat whatever he may obtain in a Brāhmaṇa household.
Yājñavalkya, however, permitted the religious student (brahmacārin) to eat food from a single source.

Established in the life of celibacy (brahmacarya), a Brahmin should not eat food from a single source except in times of distress; however, he may eat at a śrāddha feast at his pleasure, provided he does not violate his vow.

A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) shall not eat the food of a single person except in times of distress. However, if he is a Brahmin who has been invited, he may eat the food of a single person even when there is no distress, provided it is at a *śrāddha* ceremony. In that case, he should eat while avoiding honey, meat, and other items that would violate his vow.
Manu also says: "At a rite for the gods, one should act like a deity; at a rite for the ancestors, one should act like a seer."
If he eats at his pleasure when invited, his vow is not violated.

In a rite dedicated to the gods (*daivika*), when invited, the celibate student (*brahmacārī*) eats. How should he eat? "Like one observing a vow" (*vratavat*); that is to say, in accordance with his vows, excluding honey and meat. In a rite dedicated to the ancestors (*paitrya*), he may also eat; "like a seer" (*ṛṣivat*), meaning likewise excluding honey and meat. "At will" (*kāmaṃ*) means according to his desire. In this way, his vow of celibacy is not violated; otherwise, it would be violated—this is the sense. Therefore, for an ascetic (*yati*) who, being requested by the virtuous and desiring to show them favor, eats at a *śrāddha*, no transgression occurs. Alternatively, he destroys the extremely slight transgression produced by eating food provided by others by means of the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), such as breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth, which exist in the form of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
But even so, since honey and meat are prescribed as the primary items to be eaten at a *śrāddha*, how can the eating of food by an ascetic (*yati*) be justified?

It is said: because there is no restrictive rule regarding honey and meat. For if such a restriction existed, the *śrāddha* would not be accomplished by means of mere "sage-food" (*muni-anna*) and the like in its absence; yet this is not desired. Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule for the ascetic (*yati*) regarding the *śrāddha*. For if such a restriction existed, the *śrāddha* would not be accomplished by householder *śrotriyas* who have mastered the *Triṇāciketa* and other texts in the absence of an ascetic; yet this too is not desired. Therefore, in a performance of the *śrāddha* that excludes honey and meat, the feeding of an ascetic is appropriate, and in a performance that excludes an ascetic, the preparation of honey and meat is appropriate—thus, nothing is untenable. Since the rules for honey and meat and for the ascetic are both mandatory (*nityavat*), their optional status (*pākṣikatva*) is resorted to as a last resort (*agatyā*) in order to provide scope for both. Now, why is it not accepted that even in a *śrāddha* performance containing honey and meat, the ascetic’s meal excludes honey and the rest? We reply: because there is no contradiction in the acts of offering (*nirvāpa*) and cooking being intended for all the ancestors.

Now, why is there no consumption of honey or meat for an ascetic (*yati*) at a *śrāddha*? If it is argued that this is because of the prohibition, "An ascetic shall not eat honey or meat," that is not so; for that prohibition pertains to the person's own welfare (*puruṣārtha*), and thus lacks the capacity to sublate a meal intended for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), just as the prohibition against killing does not sublate killing performed within a sacrifice. But surely, even though the *godohana* vessel serves the person's welfare, it is seen to sublate the *camasa* cup which serves the purpose of the sacrifice.

True. That which accomplishes a task to be achieved through items subservient to the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) is restricted to that [sacrificial context] when it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). However, in this case, the act of eating honey and meat, which is subservient to the sacrifice, is not capable of accomplishing the act of eating for the sake of the person, because there is no connection between it and either the sacrifice or any item belonging to the sacrifice. In contrast, even though the *godohana* vessel serves the purpose of the person, it possesses a connection with the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*)—which is subservient to the sacrifice—in the form of the relationship between the substratum and the supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).
Now, why should this prohibition—"Why should an ascetic not eat honey or meat?"—not apply specifically to the eating at a *śrāddha*, which is for the sake of the sacrifice?

We reply: If it were to result in a prohibition of what is already established by scripture, it would lead to an undesirable dilemma; furthermore, the eating of honey and meat obtained through desire would become unrestricted for the ascetic (*yati*). If you argue that there should be a prohibition of both, then there is indeed a contradiction due to this disparity: in one case [the eating of sacrificial food] it would depend on another injunction, while in the other case it would be independent. Moreover, it is contradictory to claim that this very same act serves both the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) and the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, the prohibition of the eating of honey and meat obtained through desire pertains to the person’s own interest and does not preclude the eating of food that serves as an auxiliary to the ritual and is obtained through an injunction. Consequently, the eating of honey and meat by an ascetic at a *śrāddha* feast is not faulty.

To this it is replied: The injunction "one should feed" prescribes the consumption of honey and meat as an activity of the *prayojaka* (the instigator), namely the performer who is authorized for the *śrāddha*. It does not, however, prescribe such consumption as an activity of the *niyojya* (the person enjoined), namely the ascetic (*yati*). Therefore, how can there not be a prohibition [for the ascetic]? If you argue that because the act is implied by the injunction regarding the *prayojaka*'s activity, it is indeed prescribed [for the ascetic], then the acceptance [of gifts] implied by the injunction "one should give a ewe or one with two faces" would also be prescribed, and thus it would not be a fault [to accept such gifts]. Furthermore, if this eating were prescribed for everyone, including the *śrotriya* and others, then the ritual deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) of the *śrāddha* would occur if even a single individual among them did not eat.

If it is argued that [eating] is prescribed for one who has been invited, then for what reason should the consumption of honey and meat be censured? If you say that one should invite an ascetic (*yati*) to the *śrāddha* rite in order to fulfill the injunction regarding one's own entitlement, just as in the case of accepting gifts (*pratigraha*), then for what purpose would the ascetic accept the invitation? If you say it is for the sake of favoring the inviter, we observe that no one desires even a trace of favoring others while plunging themselves into such a mire of sin. Therefore, it remains that the ascetic’s acceptance of an invitation is based solely on passion (*rāga*). And thus, because it falls under the scope of prohibitions, there is no eating of honey or meat even at a *śrāddha*. Alternatively, if he accepts the invitation because of the prohibition stating, "One who is invited by an irreproachable person should not decline," and because the rule for eating states, "Having accepted the invitation, they too should eat while restrained in speech," and because of the prohibition against rejecting what has been served, then the ascetic’s eating of the honey and meat provided at the *śrāddha* is indeed prescribed following the acceptance of the invitation.

To this we reply: Departure [from the hermitage] would entail merely a transgression (*pratyavāya*), whereas the consumption of honey and meat would result in the very loss of one's stage of life (*āśramabhraṃśa*). Therefore, departure alone is the proper course. Nor is there even a transgression in departing, because it is contrary to the duties of the ascetic stage (*yatyāśramadharma*), and because the injunctions regarding non-departure and so forth pertain to those other than the ascetic. Thus, it is established that the ascetic is enjoined to perform the *śrāddha* rite excluding honey and meat, and that the preparation of honey and meat applies to rites performed excluding the ascetic’s specific injunctions. This concludes the section on the ascetic’s role in the *śrāddha*.
Now, in order to state that a guest is to be fed in the row of those invited to a *śrāddha*, the nature of a guest is first described. In this regard, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:
"One whose family and name are unknown, who has arrived at that very moment, who is hungry, who has come while weary, who is begging, and who possesses nothing..."
They declare a Brahmin to be a guest; he should be honored according to one's ability by the wise.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "One who arrives for the Vaiśvadeva rite unthought of and uninvited—
one should recognize him as a guest, but not one who has arrived previously."
Since he has arrived unexpectedly, for that reason he is called a guest.
Śātātapa also said: "Whether he be a friend or a foe, a fool or even a scholar,
one who arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who leads one to heaven."
Manu also says:
"One who stays for even a single night is considered a guest (*atithi*) of a Brahmin;
because he stays for an indefinite time, he is therefore called a guest."
[428] The mention of the "brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of excluding the kṣatriya and others. Manu himself has also said this:
"A kṣatriya is not called a guest in the house of a brāhmaṇa."
A Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a friend, kinsmen, and even a teacher.
Yama said:
"That high-souled person by whom all [observances of] lunar days, festivals, and celebrations have been abandoned is a guest for all beings; the rest are known as mere visitors."
A practitioner of vows or an ascetic who stays for a single night is called a guest (*atithi*);
because he dwells there only temporarily, they know him as a guest.

‘Tithi’ refers to the lunar days beginning with the first day (pratipad) of the fortnight, such as Dīpālikā; ‘parvan’ refers to the full-moon and new-moon days (amāvāsyā) and so forth; ‘festivals’ (utsavāḥ) refer to marriages and similar occasions. The meaning is that he who has renounced these—being devoted to the duties of an ascetic (yati)—which are causes for obtaining special kinds of food, is a guest (atithi). A ‘vratī’ is a student (brahmacārī), and a ‘yati’ is a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka); only these two, who follow the prescribed dharma, are designated as guests, and not householders or forest-dwellers. Regarding those two, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states that they are designated as “visitors” (abhyāgata): “A Vālakhilya and a yati should always be known as a guest.”

"One who has arrived as a guest should be a cook (*pacāna*); one who has arrived as a guest should be a non-cook (*apācaka*). Here, "Bālakhilya" refers to a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). "Pacānaḥ" means cooking; the meaning is that he may be either a householder or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who acts as a cook. Furthermore, there are two types of guests: those who arrive at midday and those who arrive in the evening.
Regarding the guest who arrives at midday, it is stated in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:

"At the time of midday, even when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been performed, one should diligently honor a guest who has arrived with dust on his feet and is weary from travel; such a guest is always a Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is said.
But one who arrives in the evening is designated by the term *sūryoḍha*. Regarding him, Pracetas said:
"He who arrives in the evening at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, or who comes to the house in the evening—he is to be honored like a god; he is remembered as the *sūryoḍha* guest."

The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice belongs to the evening. One should not think that a guest who arrives only at the time of the midday or evening Vaiśvadeva is acceptable, while one who arrives at any other time is not. For Manu has said:
"A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by the householder;
whether he arrives at the proper time or not, he must not remain in the house without eating."
Yājñavalkya said:

A guest is not to be turned away even in the evening, [even] with mere words, grass, and water. A guest who arrives in the evening must be honored even by the gift of words, grass, and water in the absence of food; he must certainly not be rejected.
Another name for this [guest], who is characterized by such qualities as arriving unexpectedly and appearing at the time of a *śrāddha*, has also been stated by Paiṭhīnasi:
"If a *śrotriya* is seen from anywhere at the time of a *śrāddha*, he purifies the *śrāddha*; therefore, he is designated as a *kutapa*."

One who has come from some unknown place and purifies the faithful is called an *atithi* by the technical term *kutapa*. It is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* that even one who resides in the same village does not possess the status of an *atithi*, even if he arrives unexpectedly. [430] *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
One should not consider a resident of one's own village to be a guest, nor likewise one who is not a Brahmin.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"One should not treat a friend or a resident of one's own village as a guest."
In the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"The wise do not declare one who belongs to the same village to be a guest.
As for that which is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
A guest who is neither fierce nor vulgar, neither ignorant nor lacking in discernment;
one who does not dwell [there], who does not form attachments, and who is not intent on service—such a one is a true guest.
Thus, this should be understood as applying when there is a great number of guests and a lack of capacity.
As Śaṅkha says:

"If one is not able [to feed] many, one should give first to a single person of good character; if a Śrotriya has arrived first, then to him. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa who has come unexpectedly from another village at the time of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, whose lineage and name are unknown, and who is devoid of any connection such as friendship, is an *atithi* (guest).
Thus the definition should be understood as stated.
This concludes the determination of the nature of the guest.
Now follows the praise of the guest.
In the Śivadharmottara: "For the sake of favoring the worlds and for the observation of the śrāddha,
the gods and yogins wander upon the earth in the form of guests."
"Yogas" refers to yogins. In the *Āditya Purāṇa*:
"Therefore, for one established in the householder stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*), no other deity is prescribed."
"Except for a guest, O illustrious lady; reflect upon this truth."
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Lord of Men, Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Śukra, Vahni, the Vasus, and Yama— these indeed enter the guest and consume the food."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The gods wander this earth in the form of brahmins;
therefore, one should diligently honor a guest who has arrived."
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"For householders, there is no friend superior to a guest;
for by coming to their home out of compassion, he delivers the entire family."
The Siddhas wander the earth out of curiosity and at their own will;
they constantly bestow their grace upon householders who are most devoted to dharma.
For they have arrived in the courtyard of the house in the form of guests;
therefore, O King, guests are always to be honored by everyone.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"The dust from whose feet purifies the homes of householders,
and the water used for washing whose feet shakes off all sin."
For those whom honoring and bowing down to excels even sacrifice,
and for whom food and water given in charity deliver the entire family.
What is greater than guests in the three worlds?
O high-minded one, auspicious guests are to be saluted from afar even by the gods; how much more so by householders devoted to their duties!
Kārṣṇājini says: "Sesame seeds protect against the Asuras; sesame protect against the Rākṣasas;
a learned Śrotriya protects against one unworthy of the company; a guest is the protector of all."
Thus ends the praise of the guest.
Now follows the prohibition against testing the guest.
Regarding this, in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
A wise man should not inquire about one's lineage, conduct, or Vedic study;
he should regard that person as Prajāpati, regardless of whether his outward appearance is beautiful or unattractive.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"Without having asked about one's Vedic study, lineage, conduct, or family,
the householder should regard that guest who has arrived as Hiraṇyagarbha himself."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: Whether he is handsome or deformed, dirty or dressed in soiled garments,
one should never fail to honor a guest out of the suspicion that he might be a lord among yogins.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa as well:
"A wise man should never examine an unknown twice-born guest at a śrāddha;
for perfected beings (siddhas) wander this earth in the form of brahmins."
The gods and the lords of yogis wander across the vast earth bounded by the oceans,
assuming various forms as they sport in accordance with the law of the subjects.
In the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa:
[433] One should not examine the conduct, nor the learning, nor the lineage,
nor the character, nor the country and so forth of a guest who has arrived.
Whether one is ugly or beautiful, poorly clothed or well-dressed, learned or unlearned, or possessed of virtues or devoid of them—
One should consider this guest who has arrived to be none other than Viṣṇu himself, Nārāyaṇa, Hari; one should never entertain any doubt regarding him.
(Vāyupurāṇa)

For upon seeing a guest who has arrived— whether he be an enemy or a kinsman, or whoever he may be— one should never entertain doubt [as to how to treat him], regarding him as if he were a beloved relative who had come.
For learning and the like are not recorded as the causes of his venerability;
by the mere fact of being a guest, he becomes a sanctifier of the assembly.
Great-souled ones wander this earth as guests for the sake of favoring the world; therefore, you should not question them.
Through the consideration of merits and demerits, these [ascetics] become disparaged;
such disparagement burns the householder.
Therefore, one should never adopt any conduct whatsoever toward a guest.
Thus ends the prohibition against testing a guest.
Now follows the rule for honoring a guest. Regarding this, Manu says:
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him with due ceremony and in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Hārīta also says:
"One should offer him a welcome, water for the hands, water for the feet, water for sipping, and a seat.
Parāśara also says:
One should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies,
as well as by offering a seat and washing his feet.
With faith, as well as with food, with kind inquiries and attentiveness,
and by following him on his departure, the householder should generate joy [in the guest].
In the *Yama-smṛti*:
"One should offer one's eye, offer one's mind, and offer speech that is pleasant and true;
and upon rising, one should offer a seat—this is the fivefold dharma."
The command "to rise" refers to the case of a learned *śrotriya* guest.

For this very reason, Āpastamba states: "To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Vedas], one should give a seat, food, and water; one need not rise for him. But for one who is worthy of salutation, one should rise and offer salutation."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "One should give one's sight, one should give one's mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
one should follow [the guest] and attend upon him—this is the sacrifice with five sacrificial fees."
One should offer water for the feet, a seat, a lamp, food, and shelter for the sake of honoring the guest; that is a sacrifice with five sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Whatever would always satisfy him, just as one satisfies a guest,
that very thing a wise man should do by giving even of his own self.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:

"Therefore, one should go out to meet a guest who is arriving with palms joined in reverence, honoring him with a welcome, a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), a bath, food, a bed, and so forth. [435]
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
Therefore, one should go out to meet a guest who is arriving with palms joined in reverence;
one should honor him with offerings of water for the hands (arghya) and for washing the feet (pādya), as well as with foot-ointments and food.
To one who is thirsty, weary, exhausted, or hungry,
one who desires the fruit of sacrifice should give with due honor.
O Brahmin, one should never say to a hungry man, "There is nothing.
To him who gives with due respect, it is said that an unprecedented sacrifice has been performed.
Manu describes the manner of honoring when there is an assembly of guests of both low and high status:

"One should provide the highest [hospitality] for the highest, the lowest for the lowest, and the equal for the equal—consisting of a seat, lodging, a bed, escorting them on their departure, and attendance. Thus it is said.
Hārīta refutes any inequality regarding the food of those seated in a single row:
"For those who possess superior learning and austerity, a first seat is prescribed;
however, for those standing together in a row, eating and so forth are declared to be equal."
Vasiṣṭha states the fault in such inequality:
"If, in a single row, one gives unequally out of affection, fear, or for the sake of wealth..."
The sages declare that this is the sin of killing a Brahmin, seen in the Vedas and sung by the seers.
"Uneven" means that for one person it is excellent, while for another it is inferior.
This concludes the procedure for honoring guests.
Now follows the fruit of honoring guests.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should honor a guest who has arrived, whether seen or not, when he is weary."
It is my conviction that by this act, he would have given away a hundred cows along with a bull.
Viṣṇu also says:
"A householder does not attain such worlds through Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, ritual sacrifice, or austerity as he does from honoring a guest."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "The wise say that when a guest is honored, whatever auspicious thing he contemplates in his mind, its fruit is equal even to a hundred sacrifices."
In the Mahābhārata: "By giving food to a Brāhmaṇa guest according to the prescribed rule,
the donor attains happiness and is honored even by the gods."
In the *Śivarahasya*:
"He who daily gives well-prepared food to guests attains the same world as Brahmā; thus said Parāśara."

In this *Mahābhārata*, there is the speech of the pigeon who, out of greed for victory and because food was unavailable, desired to offer hospitality to the hunter that was unsuitable for his own body:
"In the dialogues between the deities and the seers,
I have repeatedly heard of the great dharma regarding the honoring of guests."
When a guest who has come from afar with hope, emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue,
is properly honored, that is itself austerity and sacrifice.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The man here who would constantly perform the honoring of guests with water, grass, and gentle, substantial words..."
He shall always be honored among the assemblies of the gods,
and when born again in the world of men, he becomes prosperous.
Thus ends the fruit of honoring guests.
Now, the fault of one who does not offer hospitality is described. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
He who does not honor with devotion a guest who is weary on the road, unknown, and afflicted by hunger and thirst— him they call a slayer of Brahmins.

And this transgression, equal to the killing of a Brahmin, is to be understood as occurring when one fails to attend to a guest who is an extremely worthy recipient, provided that one has the capacity [to do so].
Likewise, in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
"But he who, having encountered a worthy guest endowed with good character, does not honor him..."
He takes away that person's merit and bestows their sin upon himself.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "When the Vaiśvadeva rite has arrived, one should not insult anyone;
for the guest who departs with his hopes shattered takes away the host's merit."
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs having given that person his own misdeeds and taking away their merit."
[438] "Of that householder, having given his own misdeed and taken his merit, he departs. Devala also says:
"The guest who, having come to the house, turns away..."
And he who is devoid of hope for the unconditioned immediately destroys his noble lineage.
Manu said: No guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of one's ability with a seat, food, a bed, water, or roots and fruits.
Manu, Viṣṇu, and Śātātapa [state]:
"Those among the Brahmins from whose house a guest departs without having eaten have indeed attained the state of a donkey, a camel, or a horse."
And in whosever house a Brahmin stays without being fed,
his ancestors and the gods do not partake of his offerings to the gods (havya) or to the ancestors (kavya).
If a guest who is seeking alms in one's village is indeed turned away with effort, the sin of killing a Brahmin is ordained for that person.
Even for one cooking only vegetables or living by gleaning ears of grain,
no guest should be turned away dejected, whether in one's own country or in a foreign land.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O King, whatever sin is incurred when a guest who is a deity turns away disappointed,
that very same sin is multiplied eightfold for men when the sun has set and he turns away disappointed."
Thus ends the description of the faults incurred by one who fails to offer hospitality.
Now,
it is stated that a guest who has arrived at the time of a *śrāddha* must be fed in the row of those participating in the *śrāddha*.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"A Brāhmaṇa or even a mendicant who has arrived for the purpose of a meal..."
Having been permitted by the Brahmins, he should honor them according to his ability.
One should feed a mendicant or a Brahmin who arrives at that time, with the permission of the Brahmins. Yama also says:
"A mendicant or a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who has arrived for the purpose of a meal..."
When they have sat down, he should arrive and feed him as well, according to his desire.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"At that time, if a guest— a most excellent twice-born man seeking food—
arrives there, he should, with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, feed him as well according to his desire."
Yogins become benefactors through various forms,
wandering this earth with their true nature unrecognized.
Therefore, a wise man should honor a guest who has arrived at the time of a *śrāddha*;
for an unhonored guest destroys the fruit of the performance of the *śrāddha*, even if he is a lord among the twice-born.
Śātātapa states the fault of not feeding him: "A śrāddha in which a guest does not eat is not praised;
nor is that which is eaten by those who lack learning and good conduct, or by those who are not śrotriyas."
It has been stated that such a person who performs a *śrāddha* incurs transgression. In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"But he who disregards a guest who has arrived at a *śrāddha*, whether for the ancestral rite or the divine rite..."
The gods indeed cast him out, just as they did when Parāvasu was slain.
Therefore, a wise person should honor a guest even with all their possessions;
likewise, both forest-dwellers and householders are guests when they arrive among the virtuous.
A wandering ascetic or a student who arrives at the proper time is designated as a "guest."

One must certainly honor him at the *śrāddha* ceremony; for the gods "expel" (*nirasyanti*)—that is, cast out—the performer of the *śrāddha* who fails to honor him. Just as the *hotṛ* priest, when sitting upon his seat, expels the specific Asura named Parāvasu with the mantra, "Parāvasu is expelled," so too do the gods remove the performer from the heavenly world. Regarding the *śrāddha* where the guest is treated with contempt, Chāgaleya and Vṛddha-Śātātapa have declared that there is sin even for those who eat:
"Those ignorant twice-born men who eat at a *śrāddha* devoid of hospitality, they go to the womb of a crow through that food and drink prepared in vain."

This transgression applies to those Brāhmaṇas who, out of greed or negligence, cause a patron who is somehow disregarding a guest to accept [the food] by instructing him in the duties toward a guest. However, this feeding of a guest is to be understood as occurring only when someone possessing the characteristics of a guest has actually arrived; it is not to be performed by somehow imagining someone to be a guest—even though there is a scriptural mention of a fault in performing a *śrāddha* devoid of a guest—when no guest is present. This is because one whom he himself has merely imagined lacks the status of a guest, as he does not possess the actual characteristics thereof.

Manu states that Kṣatriyas and others who are not guests, yet possess qualities similar to those of a guest— such as having arrived from a distant land or at an unusual time— should be fed after the Brāhmaṇas have eaten:
"But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest,
he may, at his pleasure, be fed even after the Brāhmaṇas have finished eating."

In this context, because of the mention of the word *kāma* (desire), it is understood that eating for them is not mandatory. As for the passage in the Viṣṇupurāṇa stating, "But to those of the [other] castes who have arrived with the status of guests, food should be given according to one's ability and in order," which suggests that Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas should be made to sit in a single row according to the sequence of their castes and then fed as guests—that should be understood as referring exclusively to occasions other than the Śrāddha, since non-Brāhmaṇas have no connection to the Śrāddha rite. And as for that which is in the Purāṇa...
The remaining guests he should feed in another house according to his means.

Thus, it appears as if being invited into another house while following the rule for feeding non-Brāhmaṇas is contradictory to the guest’s eating in the row of those at a *śrāddha* feast; however, that [contradiction] should be understood as referring either to a case where no space is available in that house, or to Brāhmaṇas other than the guest who are to eat after the *śrāddha* has concluded. Even then, the former case refers specifically to the position of one who is to be provided with the remnants of the *śrāddha* Brāhmaṇas’ meal. In the alternative case, however, it means "in the house" itself. Regarding one who creates an obstacle to the *śrāddha* by another means—namely, by manifesting the state of a false guest while lacking the characteristics of a true guest and thus begging for food—Hārīta says:
A Brahmin who creates an obstacle destroys the fourfold evil of one who desires food at the meal of the Lord of Food (Viṣṇu) and his row.

The term "of those desiring food" refers to those who are to eat the remaining food, or, in the context of a *śrāddha*, it means the ancestors (*pitṛs*) who are to be satiated by the food prepared for the *śrāddha*.
This concludes the description of the guest’s eligibility to eat in the *śrāddha* row.

Now, in the event that Brahmins possessing the aforementioned characteristics are unavailable, an alternative method (*anukalpa*) is stated for performing the *śrāddha* even with those of inferior qualities. Regarding this, after describing the most excellent twice-born ones—those preeminent in knowledge and so forth—Manu says:
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
however, this secondary rule (*anukalpa*) should be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.
This, which was just mentioned, is the "first," that is, the primary "kalpa," or rule, for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).

However, this "alternative method" (*anukalpa*) which is about to be described—meaning an arrangement (*kalpana*) made subsequently (*anu*) after the primary one—is that which is practiced in the absence of the primary method. Previously, it was stated that the gift should be given to the most excellent person; hereafter, he will state that in the absence of such a person, it should be given to one who is more excellent, in his absence to one who is excellent, and in his absence to one who is slightly superior. Likewise, it was previously stated that the gift should be given to a non-relative; in the absence of that, it should be given to relatives, as he will state hereafter. This alternative method is praised because it is practiced by the virtuous.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"If monks are not available, one should feed auspicious meditators;
if they too are unavailable, one should feed lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins)."
Even in their absence, one should feed a neutral householder as well.

"Bhikṣus" are ascetics who carry the three staffs (*tridaṇḍa*); "forest-dwellers" (*vānaprasthas*) are those devoted to meditation; "indifferent" (*udāsīnaḥ*) means unrelated to the giver or free from the state of being friend or foe. First of all, it has already been established that *bhikṣus* alone are to be accepted as the most excellent. In their absence, forest-dwellers. If even they are unavailable, lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārins*) who have mastered the Vedas. In their absence as well, householders endowed with qualities such as purifying the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Yogis should first be honored in funeral rites (*śrāddha*) by those of self-restrained mind."
In the absence of those, those who know the Vedas by mere recitation are to be employed thereafter;
for this great ritual is considered to be accomplished through the [proper] vessels.

Even among householders, those who are not practitioners of yoga (*ayogin*) but are knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) are the foremost. In their absence, there are "knowers of the Vedas" (*vedavid*), meaning those who understand the meaning of the Vedas. In their absence as well, there are those who perform "mere recitation" (*pāṭhamātra*), meaning those who merely recite the Veda.
The author of the *Nirukta* also speaks in praise of the knowers of the Vedas:
"This man was indeed a mere pillar, a carrier of a burden."
He who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning, gains nothing;
but he who knows the meaning attains all prosperity and, with his sins shaken off by knowledge, goes to the heavenly realm.

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "A Brahmin who merely carries the weight of the scriptures like a pillar, yet does not understand their meaning—how can he be a worthy recipient? How can he deserve an invitation?"
Therefore, one should cause the most learned person alone to offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations;
however, in his absence, one may employ someone who has merely studied the Veda.

The combination of both being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyatva*) and being the son of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriyaputratva*) was previously stated as the cause for preeminence. Now, when there is a doubt as to what is proper in the absence of either one, Manu says: "If one has a father who is not learned in the Vedas but a son who has mastered the Vedas, or if one has a son who is not learned in the Vedas but a father who has mastered the Vedas..."
One should know the elder of these two to be the one whose father is a Vedic scholar;
however, the other deserves honor for the sake of honoring the sacred mantras.

Regarding the doubt as to which of two men is superior—one whose father is unlearned but who himself has studied the Veda with its auxiliary branches (sāṅga), and another whose father has mastered the Veda but who himself is unlearned—the author states the established conclusion. Between these two, he should know that the one whose father is a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) is "superior" (*jyāyāṃsam*) and thus fit for the *śrāddha*. As for the "other"—he who is himself a *śrotriya*—he too deserves "hospitality" (*satkāram*), meaning the status of being fed at the *śrāddha*, for the purpose of honoring the mantras he has studied, provided the former is absent. However, for one who, though born into a family of *śrotriyas*, is devoid of good conduct (*vṛtta*), there is no superiority based on mere lineage due to his failure to perform prescribed duties.
Thus it is said in the Agni Purāṇa:
"Of what use is a vast lineage to an embodied being who is devoid of good conduct? Do worms not also arise within fragrant flowers?"
Jātūkarṇa also says:

One should not honor, even with a mere word, those lowest of the twice-born who, though endowed with learning and noble lineage, are devoid of good conduct and are unworthy of offerings to the gods and ancestors.

However, if in someone’s family no great quality is known and no fault is heard of, and he himself is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, he too should be accepted in the absence of one from a renowned lineage who is most learned. Manu says:
"What do you ask about the Brahmin’s father, or what do you ask about his mother?"
If there is anything to be known that has been heard, it is remembered as being due to one's mother and father.

From the very question itself, it is understood that there is a lack of knowledge regarding the defects of the lineage and family. "Learned" (*śruta*) refers to the scripture; "knowable" (*vedya*) refers to the ritual action to be performed as understood through the scripture. If these two exist, then they alone are the mother and father—what is the use of knowing [the biological] parents? Manu states that between learning and conduct, conduct is superior: "A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better even if he knows only the essence of the *Gāyatrī*, than one who knows the four Vedas but is unrestrained, eating all things and selling all things."
The meaning of the statement is that even one with very little knowledge who is steadfast in his own practice is superior, whereas one with vast knowledge who acts according to his own whims is not.
As stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"O bull of the Bharatas, he who mutters the *Sāvitrī* at the three times of day..."
O King, one who maintains the practice of living on alms is fit for an invitation.
One who is capable and worthy of being invited to a *ketana* (invitation) is called a *ketanatama*. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Brahmins who are constantly devoted to virtuous conduct are [worthy], even if their learning is very slight."
Having eaten, those born of noble lineage also bring satisfaction to their ancestors.
Therefore, O tiger among kings, one should employ at the śrāddha those brāhmaṇas who are endowed with family conduct, even if they possess only limited learning.

In the *Mahābhārata*, it is stated that even for those who have few faults but many virtues, those who are free from worldly knowledge yet habitually perform their own duties, and those who possess faults but whose souls are purified by expiation— when a recipient endowed with all virtues cannot be found, such persons may be accepted as objects of favor. O bull of the Bharatas, listen further to the description of those Brāhmaṇas who are designated for the *śrāddha* ceremony, regarding both the giver and the receiver, in terms of this favor.
O King, those who have fulfilled their vows, who are endowed with virtues,
who are farmers, who know the Sāvitrī, and who are observant of ritual duties— they are worthy of being invited.
One may appoint even a twice-born man of noble birth who follows the dharma of a Kṣatriya as a marker in battle,
but one should never, my dear, designate a merchant for Śrāddha rites.
O King, that brahmin who maintains the sacred fire, who dwells in a village, who is free from theft, and who is exceedingly timid— he is fit to be invited.
O bull of the Bharatas, he who mutters the Sāvitrī twice a day,
subsists on alms, and performs his ritual duties— he, O King, is worthy of being invited to a feast.
O King, one who performs the fire-oblation at sunrise and sunset, who is constantly devoted to his daily duties,
who is non-violent and possesses few faults— he is worthy of being invited to a feast.
O bull of the Bharatas, O King, that Brāhmaṇa who follows the mode of life of a householder, who is modest in conduct and pure in livelihood, is worthy of being invited to a feast.
Even one who is vow-less, a gambler, a thief, a seller of living beings, or a merchant,
if he has subsequently drunk Soma, he too deserves an invitation to the sacrifice.
Having first acquired wealth through harsh agricultural labors, one should later practice austerity; such a person, O King, is worthy of being invited as a guest.

"O King, having first acquired wealth through harsh labors in agriculture, one may afterwards become a host to all guests; such a person is worthy of being invited. Thus, after describing the eligibility for being fed at a *śrāddha* by those who are not related, the *Garuḍa Purāṇa* states:
Indeed, when neutral persons who are not [yet] obtained are available, even relatives may be fed, as well as maternal uncles,
brothers-in-law, officiating priests, sacrificial priests, pupils, teachers, and so forth.

A *mātula* is a mother’s brother. A *śyāla* is a wife’s brother. A *yājya* is one for whom one performs the office of a priest. An *ṛtvij* is a sacrificer. A *śiṣya* is one to be taught. An *ācārya* is a teacher of the Veda. Āpastamba says:

"One should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or being a pupil. However, if others are deficient in qualities, even a uterine brother who excels them should be fed. By this, pupils are also explained."

One should feed "knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*)—those who understand the meaning of the Vedas or are established in the knowledge of the supreme self (*adhyātma*), and who are Brāhmaṇas free from [the restrictions of] kinship through birth and so forth. Regarding "others" (*pareṣām*), those who are free from such kinship: if there is a deficiency in their conduct, learning, or other virtues, then even a uterine brother (*sodarya*) endowed with all virtues (*samudetaḥ*) should be fed. How much more so, then, those with distant connections, such as brothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, sons-in-law, maternal uncles, and so on? By this [rule regarding] the "endowed" uterine brother, those who are "resident pupils" (*antevāsinaḥ*) or "neighbors" (*samīpavāsinaḥ*) are explained. Gautama states that one should feed them, following the same principle.

"And some say that one should feed disciples and those of the same lineage (*sagotra*), provided they possess the [required] qualities, beyond three [guests]. By the word "and" (*ca*), those such as the *yājya* (one for whom one performs sacrifices) are included; by the second "and," those of the same *ārṣeya* (same ancestral seer) are included. The phrase "beyond three" means that first of all, three principal guests who are unrelated should be invited. The meaning is that after those three unrelated guests, one should feed disciples and others who possess the quality of being "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*). Others, however, explain it thus: among those of the same lineage, one who possesses the [required] qualities should be fed beyond three persons.
On this point, Vasiṣṭha says:
"One should feed even one's pupils who possess good qualities.
"Possessing good qualities" means possessing excellence of virtue. By the use of the word "even," it is implied that one should also feed resident students (antevāsins).
In the *Manu* and *Kūrma Purāṇas*:

"One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister's son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter's son, the husband of a daughter, a kinsman, as well as the officiating priest and the one for whom he performs sacrifices."

The *mātāmaha* is the father of one’s mother. The *svastrīya* is the son of one’s sister. The *guru* is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "the husband of a daughter of the people" (*viś*), the *viṭpati* is the son-in-law; or alternatively, the *viṭpati* is the guest (*atithi*). For Medhātithi explains that he, having arrived at the house, is the ultimate representative of all the people (*viś*). It has been stated that a guest should be fed in the presence of the twice-born invited to the *śrāddha*. However, if those eating at the *śrāddha* do not possess excellent qualities, then this [guest] should be fed at the *śrāddha* itself; thus, he serves as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).

One may, at will, honor at a *śrāddha* a maternal relative, a maternal uncle, a brother-in-law, and others who are of a different lineage (*asagotra*) and endowed with good qualities; however, one should not honor a friend, even if he is distinguished, nor an enemy.
For when an oblation is consumed by one who harbors hatred, it becomes fruitless after death.

"Even one who is handsome" means even one who is learned; from the use of the word "at will," it is understood that this is a secondary option (*anukalpa*). While the phrase "provided there is excellence of faith" (*śrāddhasaṃpad*) continues to apply, Yājñavalkya says:
"The sister's son, the officiating priest, the son-in-law, the person for whom one sacrifices, the father-in-law, and the maternal uncle."
The three Nāciketas fires, the daughter's son, the disciple, and one's kinsmen and relatives.
In the Vāyupurāṇa: One who is devoted to his mother and father, a sister’s son, one who knows the Sāmaveda,
as well as the officiating priest (ṛtvij), the family priest (purohita), the teacher (ācārya), and the sub-teacher (upādhyāya)— one should feed these.
A maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a relative, and one who recites the Droṇa—
these Brāhmaṇas, who have mastered the Vedas, should be appointed at a Śrāddha ceremony.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should also diligently feed the daughter's son, the father-in-law, the preceptor,
the husband of the sister, the maternal uncle, the kinsman, the officiating priest, the teacher, and the brother-in-law."
In this context, the "guru" refers to a teacher of arts and other such sciences. As stated in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"The daughter's son, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the son-in-law, the sister's son, and likewise the father-in-law..."
Those devoted to their parents, as well as disciples, relatives, and kinsmen, are worthy of being fed.
Regarding those such as the *triṇāciketa*, it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the sister’s son, the daughter’s son, the son-in-law, the father-in-law,
the maternal uncle, one devoted to austerity, and the husband of one’s father’s or mother’s sister."

O King, one should first employ these previously mentioned persons in the śrāddha for the sake of pleasing the ancestors: disciples, relatives, and those devoted to one's mother and father; and in the case of secondary options (*anukalpa*), those who follow immediately after them.
One should first employ those previously mentioned, such as the Triṇāciketa and others; thereafter, one should employ these [others], beginning with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as substitutes.
Regarding this, it has been stated by Śaṅkhadhara:

These maternal uncles and others, being free from defects such as leprosy or lameness and possessing the merit of merely performing the *saṃdhyopāsana*, may be appointed as substitutes (*anukalpa*). However, if they are learned (*vidvāṃsaḥ*), then they are to be employed as the primary option (*mukhyakalpa*) itself. We do not know what the basis for this interpretation is. We, however, say this: these are indeed substituted when there is an absence of those who possess superior qualities yet remain indifferent [to the duty]. Now, a substitute is first sought as one who is very similar; in the absence of such, one who is dissimilar is accepted. Since maternal uncles and others possess superior qualities, they are the most similar to those who possess superior qualities and are indifferent; thus, they are substituted first. In their absence, those with middling qualities are taken; and in their absence, those with inferior qualities. This being the case, the qualifying attributes such as "being more virtuous" and "having mastered the Vedas" would also be consistent.

Now, if these are indeed substitutes, then they would obtain by themselves through similarity in the absence of the primary; thus, the statements regarding secondary options (anukalpa) would be rendered entirely purposeless.

No; for it is appropriate to regard them as restrictive (niyamārtha), just like the mention of *pūtīka* plants. Just as when there is an absence of *soma*, and many very similar substitutes have become available, a restriction is made by scriptural statement that "only *pūtīkas* are to be pressed," so too here these statements will serve a restrictive purpose. This was stated by Jaimini: "In some cases, an injunction is for the sake of restriction. And the restriction here is as follows: just as in the absence of those with superior qualities who are indifferent (*udāsīna*), those with superior qualities such as maternal uncles (*mātula*) first become available due to their similarity in the excellence of their qualities; likewise, due to their similarity in indifference, those of middling qualities who are indifferent become available. In that context, it is restricted that "only maternal uncles and the like are to be accepted. And this being the case, even the subsequent statements regarding the transgression of relatives will be for the sake of restriction: in the absence of a primary Brāhmaṇa, others are not to be accepted after bypassing maternal uncles and the rest. Regarding the phrase "even [the father-in-law and others]," should it not rather be interpreted as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) according to logical reasoning? However, if the reading is *amūrkhan* ("not fools"), then everything is entirely faultless. Alternatively, the statements regarding the non-transgression of fools may refer to the eating of desired food for the purpose of disposing of the remnants of the *śrāddha* meal used with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, in accordance with the rule: "The remaining food should be eaten together with those one loves."
Gārgya said:
One should not offer the sacrificial oblation to one of the same *gotra*, nor likewise to one with the same *pravara*;
nor should one offer it to one whose lineage is unknown; as is the case with a maiden, so is the sacrificial oblation.
For in the absence of those belonging to other lineages, one should feed those of a single lineage;
and in the absence of those with dissimilar *pravara*s, one may even feed those with identical *pravara*s.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"In the absence of those belonging to other gotras, one may feed even those of the same gotra.
Here, it is understood that by the term *sagotra*, just as non-relatives of the same gotra are permitted, so too are relatives such as *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* permitted.
Regarding this, Atri states a specific distinction:
"But those of the same lineage (gotrin) who are within six generations of the deceased man are not fit for the śrāddha;
however, even those born of the same lineage may be fed at the śrāddha if they are beyond the sixth generation."

Those who do not extend beyond six generations are here understood by the term "avāk" (downward). Consequently, the meaning of that statement is that within a lineage, six generations of men are not to be fed at a *śrāddha*. In the absence of those endowed with virtuous qualities (*guṇavantaḥ*), even those beginning from the seventh generation who are perfected in Vedic learning (*śruta-adhyayana-saṃpanna*) may be fed. Regarding this, after the discussion on those who purify the company (*paṅktipāvana*), Baudhāyana states:

"In their absence, one who knows the secret doctrines (*rahasyavit*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* [Vedas] constitute the greatness of the *śrāddha*; therefore, one should feed such a person, even if he is a *sapiṇḍa*."

A "knower of secrets" (*rahasyavit*) is one who knows the meaning of the Vedānta. Since the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas constitute the "greatness"—that is, the factors that bring about the majesty—of the *śrāddha*, therefore one should feed even a *sapiṇḍa* who possesses such knowledge, namely, one who knows the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas. Furthermore, this term *sapiṇḍa* refers specifically to those within seven generations, because we see that those beyond three generations are eligible to be fed as *sapiṇḍas*. This has been stated by Gautama:
"One should feed a virtuous person beyond the third [generation].
However, those prior to the fourth generation (i.e., the first three) are not at all to be fed.
Regarding this, Sumantu said:
"The father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather [are the primary recipients] in śrāddha rites;
likewise, the father's paternal uncle, the sister's son, and sons and others are not to be fed."

The relationship is that of "the sons and so forth of the father. Here, the eating of the *śrāddha* meal is prohibited because the fathers and grandfathers serve as the presiding entities (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for whom the rite is intended; however, it is not prohibited when they serve as presiding entities for other rites, such as separate *śrāddhas*. Or else, one may cause one's own father to eat at the *śrāddha* like a Brahmin, or his grandfather may eat that *śrāddha* directly, being duly honored.

This is because such passages demonstrate that they are to be fed at the *śrāddha*. However, Atri has stated that those who are more distinguished—such as the father, grandfather, brother, son, or even a *sapiṇḍa*—are to be appointed to the *vaiśvadeva* rite:
"The father, grandfather, brother, son, or a *sapiṇḍa* are not eligible for one another [in the *śrāddha*], nor are officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) so [eligible]."
For these—the officiating priests, sons, and so forth—are recorded as Brāhmaṇas belonging to the same lineage;
they should be employed at the Vaiśvadeva rite if they are more distinguished by their virtues.

Therefore, when Āpastamba states that a brother born of the same womb who has risen together [in status] is to be fed, that too should be understood as applying to the Vaiśvadeva rite. Vasiṣṭha declares the acceptance of those lacking qualities as a secondary option (*anukalpa*) when qualified secondary options are unavailable:
"Compassion is the highest dharma; whatever is given to one who asks, one should invite with every possible means those who do not ask but are in distress."

Compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the highest, most excellent dharma. Therefore, even in the absence of those possessing qualities, that which is given to one who asks—even if they lack qualities—constitutes a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). For what reason should one not provide for those who are suffering and habitually do not ask, even if they lack qualities, when those with qualities are unavailable? [The text says] "by all means," meaning by such means as they would accept the invitation; this shows that one should invite them with great care. It further shows that when those who do not ask are suffering due to a lack of gains, one should give to them when they do ask. He [the author] states that one should not find fault with such Brahmins even when their conduct appears deficient in virtuous practice.
In every age, there are specific duties, and for those duties there are specific twice-born ones;
one must not disparage them, for those twice-born ones take their form according to the age.

"Regarding those duties that exist in each age"—meaning those states of suffering such as speaking untruths and so forth, which are bound by the varying degrees of passion, hatred, and other qualities corresponding to each *yuga*—"among those duties, those who are twice-born": among those twice-born who abide in such evil natures, even among the *vipras* appropriate to a particular age, only those who are truly excellent should be accepted. However, Manu speaks of the fault of one capable of following the primary rule (*prathamakalpa*) who instead practices a secondary rule (*anukalpa*): "He who is capable of the primary rule but abides in the secondary rule—no fruit pertaining to the hereafter exists for that person of wicked mind."

‘Prabhuḥ’ means capable of accomplishing [the task]. ‘Saṃparāyaḥ’ means the future time, since Amarasimha has stated that the word *saṃparāya* denotes that [time]. Alternatively, the meaning is this: in ‘saṃparāye’, i.e., in the future time, there exists no fruit such as heaven and so forth.
