This concludes the exposition of the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). Now follows the non-transgression regarding the Brāhmaṇas present at hand.
In that regard, the *Smṛtis* of Śātātapa and Parāśara state:
"He who bypasses a nearby Brāhmaṇa who is studying,
whether during a meal or the giving of gifts, burns his family unto the seventh generation."

In this context, when among twice-born men of equal qualities residing in the same village, invitations for a *śrāddha* are being accepted according to one's own preference, even if by chance some are bypassed, it does not constitute a fault. The meaning is that one should not bypass a Brahmin who is proximate through intellectual connection; one should not reject him and accept another. For by bypassing such a person, one "burns" one's own family—starting from oneself up to the seventh generation—with the fire of hell, reducing it to ashes. (As stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*).
Whoever bypasses a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby while studying,
whether during a meal or at acts of giving, shall cause his family to be consumed for three generations.

"Extending to three generations" means up to the third generation. Although it is established by implication that the fault mentioned for bypassing a proximate person who has studied the Veda does not apply when bypassing someone else, this has been reinforced by Vyāsa, Vaśiṣṭha, and Śātātapa through the presentation of reasons:
"There is no offense in bypassing a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Veda;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes while setting aside a blazing fire."

When a Brahmin who is "devoid of the Vedas"—that is, one who lacks the study of the Vedas—is bypassed and not chosen, no fault whatsoever arises for him [the donor] consisting of the loss of the intended purpose caused by that bypass, nor any transgression (pratyavāya) and so forth; because such a person is not fit for the offering of the oblation (havis). This is illustrated by the example: just as an oblation is not fit to be cast into ashes once the fire has been left aside.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"There is never any fault in bypassing one who is devoid of qualities."
In this context, "proximate" is of two kinds: one who dwells in a nearby house and one who is related by blood, such as a maternal uncle and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that the transgression of both types of those who are proximate cannot be prohibited. For, in the case of the superior [guest], since he is the primary option (*prathamakalpa*) in relation to one who is not proximate, his non-transgression is established by that very fact; and in the case of the equal [guest], there is no possibility of transgression according to the maxim that "there is no reason to transgress what is present. Nor should it be said that this [non-transgression] is merely a matter of attainment (*prāpti*). For if, on account of the parsimony [of the rule], one were to prohibit the transgression of that inferior [guest] because he has been invited, it would subvert all injunctions and prohibitions regarding the worthy and the unworthy. Therefore, the prohibition of transgression is untenable. Alternatively, let it be that this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the phrase "not from one who has risen," meaning that something other than the transgression must be performed. What is that "other"? Is it the invitation? This is not so, because it has already been refuted by the same arguments used to criticize the alternatives in the case of the prohibition-pakṣa. Thus, even as an exclusion, it is not possible, and furthermore, there is another fault: a contradiction with the injunction for an alternative when there is a prohibition against the related [guest]. Therefore, the distinction of the scope (*viṣayavibhāga*) must be stated in a way that avoids contradiction between the prohibition of transgression, the prohibition of the related [guest], and the injunction for an alternative.

It is said: when a neutral person of the highest quality is not available, then the rule for the secondary alternative applies; and since at that time it would follow that one might accept a neutral person of middling quality, those relatives who possess either the highest or middling qualities must be accepted first. However, among neutrals of inferior quality, only those relatives who possess middling or inferior qualities are to be accepted. This is the scope of the prohibition against bypassing [superior candidates]. It has been stated that one must not bypass a qualified candidate who is present, but one may bypass one who is unqualified.
[455] Now it is stated that one must not bypass even a person who is present but not studying; as it says in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*,
Aruṇa said:
"So it is, O Lord of the World, God of gods, Master of the Universe! However, O Lord, there is a statement which I heard previously from that Great-Souled One."
O leader of the planets, listen here as Nārada speaks;
O best of gods, hear from me as I speak of dharma and artha which bring about happiness.
But he who [approaches] a nearby twice-born man of the Śukla caste who speaks kindly—
whether he be a fool or a scholar, or even one devoid of good conduct—
A wise man should not bypass one who is afflicted by poverty,
for he thereby passes over seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself as well.
O bird, by transgressing against them, a twice-born man would cause himself to fall into a terrible hell;
therefore, a wise man should not overstep his neighboring Brahmins.
Likewise, O bird, one should honor all kinsmen, as well as the daughter's son, the husband of the daughter,
and especially the sister's son and other relatives.
O Lord of Cows, a man must not transgress these [rules], even if they appear to be established for his own benefit;
by transgressing them, he shall go to the most terrible Raurava hell.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "Likewise, all kinsmen, as well as the daughter's son, the husband of a daughter,
the sister's son especially, and even the groups of relatives."
"A man should not transgress these [duties], O fair-faced one, even if they are performed by fools. Thus it is said in the *Mahābhārata*:
"O bird, even a Brahmin whose essence consists solely of the *Gāyatrī* is worthy of honor."
One should especially not live near a house if that person has fallen from their status.

Even that Brāhmaṇa in whom there exists at least the Gāyatrī mantra—which is the essence of all knowledge and the very core of Brāhmaṇahood—attains honor as a secondary option (*anukalpa*) in rites such as the Śrāddha. If, moreover, being of such a nature, he should reside in a house close to one's own, then by virtue of that proximity, he receives honor especially; the use of the word "especially" indicates that this [proximity] must not be disregarded.

However, this non-transgression regarding a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is not present—which is prescribed in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* and other texts—occurs only when a virtuous Brāhmaṇa who is present cannot be found; if one is available, there is indeed transgression.
And so it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"If there should be a superior Brāhmaṇa, endowed with good conduct and other virtues, even though he be far away..."
To him it should be given with effort, even by passing over those who are nearby.

"Superior" means one who possesses excellence in qualities such as Vedic study, conduct, and so forth. From the mention of "superior," it is understood that if [the guest] is equal, then one must not bypass the one standing nearby. As it is said: "Having heard of a Brahmin endowed with virtues and possessed of noble character, one should go to him from afar, honor him, and worship him with great effort."

The meaning is that one should bypass a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby but devoid of qualities such as Vedic study and proper conduct, and instead feed one who possesses those qualities, even if he is far away, when performing rites such as the Śrāddha.
Baudhāyana also says:
"If in a man's house there is a fool, even if a man of great learning resides far away..."
It should be given to one who is learned; there is no transgression in [not giving it] to a fool.
Also in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"But for one who has a fool in his own house and a virtuous man far away, the gift should be given to the virtuous one; there is no transgression in not giving to the fool."

"There is no transgression" means that there is no fault of transgression. By the phrase "in a single house," this is indicated: even extreme proximity in such a case does not constitute a cause for transgression. As for what is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*—that even when a person rich in qualities is far away, one must not bypass a nearby person who lacks qualities—the text says: "That fool who, bypassing a nearby Brāhmaṇa (provided he is not an outcast), feeds a distant one though he be rich in qualities, shall go to hell."
Therefore, one should honor him and not consider his lack of merit;
one should consider only his birth or his extensive virtues, O bird.
For this reason, a wise man should first invite a Brāhmaṇa who is nearby.

This should be explained as being for the purpose of showing the proximity of those not to be bypassed among those already mentioned previously, so as not to contradict the many statements cited above; it is not, however, for the purpose of establishing non-bypassing even when qualities and other factors are absent at a distance. Alternatively, this [rule] should be described as referring to a Brāhmaṇa who is a fool, who is near the house, and who possesses a body that is co-referential with him (i.e., shares his status). Or rather, it should be described as referring to a divine guest (*daiva*), because in that case, a virtuous householder will be mentioned later by way of a prohibition against testing him. Or, such is the systematic arrangement of these statements: the prohibition regarding social connection applies to the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), while the injunction regarding the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) applies to the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Regarding this, Atri says:
"A father, a grandfather, a brother, or a son who is a *sapiṇḍa*—these are not eligible to perform the *śrāddha* for one another; likewise, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are not eligible."

"Even these—officiating priests, sons, and so forth—are *sakulya* Brahmins and twice-born ones who should be appointed at the *vaiśvadeva* rite, provided they are more distinguished by their qualities.

Alternatively, this non-transgression of kinship may refer to some other divine or human feast on occasions such as prosperity-rites (*abhyudaya*) distinct from the *śrāddha*; or else, it refers to the consumption of the remaining food following the performance of the *śrāddha*. Thus, everything is faultless.
Thus ends the section on not bypassing Brahmins who are present. Now, the Brahmins who are to be avoided, according to the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
Now I shall fully declare those lowest of the twice-born who are to be avoided.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"Henceforth, hear from me the examination of the Brahmin regarding his lineage (*visarga*)."

‘Visargaḥ’ means dismissal or abandonment—that is to say, rejection. Although it follows from the very description of the characteristics of the Brāhmaṇas to be accepted that others are excluded by implication, Satyavrata clearly states that the mention of their defects for the purpose of avoidance is intended so that, in the event that those possessing the aforementioned qualities cannot be found, one might occasionally accept those who are free from these specific defects. He says: “In a rite performed without the prescribed rules, there may be some fruit; however, there is no fruit at all when the son of a wicked Brāhmaṇa is present. If it is given to a wicked Brahmin, that gift shall bear no fruit either in this world or in the next.

It is traditionally taught that virtuous Brahmins should be fed by a son using the substances prescribed according to the rules. In this regard, even if performed by one who has no son, a *śrāddha* that is deficient in its ritual procedure or lacks the prescribed substances and so forth still yields some fruit. However, the meaning is that if a wicked Brahmin, corrupted by the faults to be described hereafter, is fed, the *śrāddha* is utterly destroyed.
Yama says: "Just as a seed sown here in barren soil perishes quickly,"
Likewise, an oblation to the gods or an offering to the ancestors given to those unworthy perishes.
"Ūṣara" refers to a region of saline soil. As it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"Just as a seed sown in saline soil does not sprout..."
Or rather, the sower of the seed would not receive a share of the crop;
likewise, a funeral offering (*śrāddha*) consumed by one who is unworthy yields no fruit either in this world or in the next.
Vyāsa and Śātātapa state:
"A seed sown upon a barren rock, milking from a broken vessel,
an oblation poured into ashes— just so is a gift given to the unworthy."
Manu says: He who gives to one unworthy and does not give to one worthy,
through his ignorance of the worthy and the unworthy, falls away from dharma as well.

The purpose of stating the defects [of certain persons] is not only to indicate that by accepting those who possess such defects one incurs sin (*pratyavāya*), but also to show that the specific rite at hand is destroyed; furthermore, this sin is demonstrated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Those censurable ones, the lowest of Brahmins, must not be fed at a *śrāddha*.
By those whose food is eaten, the *śrāddha* is ruined, and it causes the ancestors and the givers to fall."
"Should cause to fall" means he should connect [the person] with transgression.
In the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Where there is the favoring of the wicked and the humiliation of the virtuous..."
In that case, a terrible punishment ordained by the gods falls immediately.
Dakṣa said:
"Likewise, he who gives a gift to an unworthy recipient who is devoid of scriptural injunctions [incurs the same]."
For not only does that [merit] go away, but his remainder also perishes.
Viṣṇu: Just as a man sinks in water with a stone boat,
so do both the giver and the recipient sink.
Thus Vasiṣṭha said:
"Those kingdoms in which ignorant people eat the food that should be eaten by the learned suffer from drought, or a great danger arises."
"They encounter" means they attain [misfortune].
Even those who are somehow deficient in virtues and possessed of faults, if seated in the company of those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), do not bring about calamity—
those best of the twice-born by whom a row defiled by those unworthy of the assembly is purified.

Because it has been stated thus by Manu, for this very reason Sumantu has declared that those who are somehow being accepted despite possessing defects may be mixed with those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*):
"The one-eyed, the *kuṇḍa*, the *maṇḍa*, and even those without skin or hair—
all these should be employed at a *śrāddha* when mixed with those who have mastered the Vedas."

"Kāṇāḥ" means one-eyed. "Kuṇḍāḥ" means those whose feet are unable to walk. "Maṇḍāḥ" means those with crooked shanks. "Acarmāṇaḥ" means those with skin diseases. "Without hair" means bald; this is the meaning. However, Kāśyapa has stated a specific rule regarding the mixing [of categories]:
"One should feed those who are one-eyed and so forth at a *daiva* rite or a *śrāddha*, but one should exclude them from a gift (*dāna*). [461]

One should feed [unfit persons] during the *vaiśvadeva* portion when they are present at a *śrāddha*, but one should avoid them during the actual gift-giving (*dāna*). When those who are "purifiers of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*) have been mixed with those who are defective due to negligence and have been fed, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed according to the circumstances, based on the gravity of the offense; for there is the saying: "In a heavy sin, heavy [expiations]; in a light sin, light ones. This point was elucidated by Medhātithi while explaining the intent of the verse of Manu beginning with "The blind from birth and those who are not the cause... Furthermore, Yama, Manu, and Śātātapa state that even the eater at a *śrāddha* incurs demerit if he is unworthy.
As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows at offerings to the gods and ancestors,
so many flaming spears and iron balls shall he swallow after death.

‘Piṇḍān’ means morsels of food. ‘Amantravit’ means one devoid of the Vedas. ‘Dīptān’ means heated by fire. ‘Ṛṣṭiḥ’ is a specific type of weapon. ‘Ayoguḍāḥ’ means iron balls. Yama is the destroyer of the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors).
A Brahmin who is devoted to unrighteousness and is foolish shall never attain the higher worlds.
Intending all this, Yājñavalkya said:
"Cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth, should be given with honor to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man desiring his own welfare."
It was promised that those to be avoided would be defined. Regarding this, Manu first states concerning friends and others:
"One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; his [friendship] should be cultivated with wealth.
One should feed at a *śrāddha* that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend."

This prohibition applies specifically when one possesses prior qualities such as Vedic learning (*śrotriya*) and so forth, yet acts out of a motive of mere friendliness. A "friend" (*mitra*) is one whose mental, verbal, and physical conduct is consistently favorable.
"Inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) is the act of pleasing the heart. An "enemy" (*ari*) is a foe. One should feed him who is free from hatred toward both passion and aversion;
that is, one for whom *śrāddha* rites and sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are primarily directed toward friends.
For such a person, there is no fruit after death, neither in the ancestral rites (śrāddha) nor in the sacrificial offerings (havis).

This is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) to the preceding prohibition. The word *mitra* (friend) has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning; thus, the sense is "those for whom friendship (*maitrī*) is predominant. "Sacrificial offerings" (*havīṃṣi*) means things to be offered (*havya*). The indeclinable *pretya* denotes the next world (*paraloka*); it cannot be construed with the suffix *-kyap* because that would imply a lack of a common agent (*asamānakartṛkatva*). "That man who, out of delusion, forms friendships for the sake of Śrāddha rites—he, the lowest of the twice-born, who makes friendship his motive for Śrāddha, falls from the heavenly world."

"Saṃgatāni" means friendships. "Out of delusion" (mohāt) means not knowing the meaning of the scriptures. "Falls from heaven" (svargāc cyavate) means he is no longer connected with heaven. Regarding one for whom a faithful friend (*śrāddham mitra*) is the cause of gaining friends: the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) is for the sake of illustration; for Medhātithi has explained at length that even by a Śūdra, Brāhmaṇas who have become friends must not be accepted [for such a feast].
That which is called a *sambhojanī* feast is a demonic (*paiśācī*) sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) given by the twice-born;
it remains only in this world, and its weight is confined to a single household.

A "joint meal" is one where food is eaten together; indeed, it proceeds from a shared meal of friendliness. This is the custom of the *piśācas*: that at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*), friends are gathered. That sacrificial gift remains right here, for its fruit is the acquisition of friends.
The meaning is that it results in nothing more than the acquisition of friends.
He whose *śrāddha* rites and sacrificial offerings are primarily for the sake of making friends does not go to heaven after giving at ancestral rites or sacrifices to the gods.
He who forms attachments through ancestral rites does not travel by the path of the gods,
just as a pipal fruit remains bound when it has not yet been released.
A friend who relies solely on funeral offerings falls from the heavenly world.

The term "devayāna" (the path of the gods) is also an elliptical designation for the "pitṛyāṇa" (the path of the ancestors). The word "vā" has the sense of comparison. "Pippalam" refers to the fruit of the *pippala* tree.
[This is the view of] Hārīta.
He who forms attachments through ancestral rites does not travel by the path of the gods;
he is like a mango fruit fallen from its stalk or released from its bond.
One who considers a funeral offering as a mere friend falls from heaven to this world.
Yama and Āpastamba state:
"The 'communal meal' is called the alms of the Piśācas;
it goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods."
Right here she wanders, her merit exhausted, like a cow that has lost its calf wandering within the stall.
Regarding the *śrāddha*, Gautama states:
"And one should not perform friendly services with that [offering].
In the *Bārhaspatya-saṃhitā*:
For one whose ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) and oblations (*havis*) are primarily for the sake of friends,
there shall be no fruit after death, because of their mutual feeding upon one another.
In the Mahābhārata:
He whose *śrāddha* rites and sacrificial offerings are centered primarily on friends does not gratify the ancestors or the gods, nor does he go to heaven.
But he who forms attachments through ancestral rites does not travel by the path of the gods;
he is like one who has released a *pippala* fruit from its bond.
One who considers a funeral offering as a mere friend falls from the heavenly world.
Therefore, one who performs ancestral rites should not show favoritism toward a friend;
he should bestow wealth upon friends for the sake of winning them over.
As for one whom he considers neither an enemy nor a friend— [he should give to him as well].
One should feed that neutral person at the ritual for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha).

In the absence of one who is indifferent to excellent qualities, one may at times accept a friend who possesses such qualities; however, an enemy should not be accepted even as a secondary alternative. Thus Manu says:
"One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, but not even a learned enemy.
For the sacrificial offering consumed by one who hates it becomes fruitless after death."
‘Abhirūpa’ means suitable.
It is stated in the Bārhaspatya-saṃhitā that even a neutral person, if possible, should certainly not be accepted as a friend.
He who, bypassing a neutral person, invites a friend to a śrāddha feast,
gains no fruit for that act in the afterlife, because of the mutual exchange of gifts.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One should not feed those of the same *gotra* or the same *pravara*;
for the ancestors do not consume the sacrificial offering given to such persons."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One should never feed Brahmins of the same *gotra* at a *śrāddha*;
for when the sacrificial oblation is consumed by those of the same *gotra*, it merely circulates right here in this world."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "At a śrāddha, Brahmins related by birth, those connected by lineage, as well as those related through mantras or discipleship, should never be fed."
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Disciples, officiating priests, those for whom one performs sacrifices, friends, as well as enemies,
fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, maternal uncles, and others— these should not be fed at *śrāddha* ceremonies."
Thus [are defined] friends and the others.
Now, those who do not study and so forth;
regarding them, Manu, Vyāsa, and Yama [state]:
For a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw;
one should not offer sacrificial oblations to him, for an offering is not poured into ashes.

Just as thieves and the like are defilers of the assembly (*paṅktidūṣaka*), so too is one who has not studied [the Veda] a defiler of that same assembly; it is for this purpose that there is a restatement. Just as a grass-fire is unable to cook the sacrificial offerings and is extinguished—its power exhausted—as soon as the offering is poured, so too is the fool who has not studied. As a sower does not obtain fruit after sowing seed in barren soil, even so the giver does not obtain fruit when he offers the oblation to one who knows no Ṛg-verses.
*Īriṇaṃ* means saline soil. *Anṛce* means devoid of the Vedas. Śātātapa says:
"The *havya* (offerings to the gods) or *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) must not be given to those who are ignorant."
In the Mahābhārata (13.90.40):
"Just as an offering poured into an extinguished fire reaches neither the gods nor the ancestors,"
Likewise, what is given thus dances and sings;
and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which he bestows upon one who is unlearned in the Ṛgveda covers [or obstructs] him.
That sacrificial fee which is given to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda destroys both [the giver and the receiver] and does not benefit them;
moreover, as it falls, it sinks into a pit.
He shall cause those preta-spirits to fall from the path of the gods.
"Both" refers to the giver and the enjoyer. "Does not protect" means he does not sustain them. "Ayanī" is a state of sin.
As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "He whose Veda and Vedas are lost for three generations..."
Such a person is indeed a wicked Brāhmaṇa and is never worthy of invitations to Śrāddha and other rites.
Vyāsa says: "To a Brāhmaṇa who has abandoned the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), who has fallen from his vows, and who is devoid of the Vedas..."
While food is being given, she weeps; what evil deed have I committed?
Viṣṇu:
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a brahmin who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas.
Whatever wealth, acquired according to the prescribed rule, is given to these three types of persons,
it leads to misfortune for both the giver and the recipient in the next world.
Yama said:
[467] To those who observe no vows, who possess no sacred mantras, and who subsist merely by their caste—no gift should be given to them; even a stone cannot save a stone.
Likewise:
"As a royal capital that is empty, as a well without water,
and as an oblation poured into what is not fire, so is a gift given to a twice-born man who has not studied the Vedas."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa it is said:
"Both he who recites the Vedas as a bearer of the Vedas and he who subsists by means of the Vedas—
neither of these two is worthy of the śrāddha, nor indeed the husband of a *putrikā* (appointed daughter)."

A "vedabhṛta" is one who has been paid a fee for the acquisition of the Vedas. "Livelihood from the Veda" refers to receiving wealth through such means as teaching for a short duration (ghaṭikā). In the Mahābhārata:
"O Bhārata, both the Brahmin who is the instructor and he who is instructed..."
Even those two are not worthy of the offerings of the faithful, for they are sellers of the Veda.
And those who have taught their own private recitation (svādhyāya) without prior instruction—these are indeed sellers of the Veda; one should not feed them at śrāddha ceremonies.
Those who, having been commanded, "Recite this section, recite this chapter," and so forth, proceed to study, are those to whom the instruction has been given.
Whatever they do, whatever they eat, whatever they offer in sacrifice, and whatever they give— by that [act], even if performed according to rule, they fall into great impurity through their sin.
They are considered unfit to be fed by the virtuous, and likewise they themselves are remembered as unfit to eat;
both the giver and the eater from them shall incur great faults.

Those great-souled ones who are pure by virtue of their own karma and established in truth are not to be engaged in debate within assemblies; they have reached a definitive conclusion regarding women and Śūdras.
Those who teach the unrefined and those who teach for a fee enter into terrible darkness; so said Vaivasvata.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Those who here recite the Vedas out of greed, delusion, or seeking rewards— they are indeed sellers of Brahman and are to be avoided at the performance of a Śrāddha rite."
Yama says:
Twice-born men who teach the Veda to a *vṛṣala* do not deserve to receive gifts;
by teaching a *śūdra*, a Brahmin falls from his status—of this there is no doubt.
Thus [are described] those who do not study and so forth. Now, those with bodily defects. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:

One should feed [the guests] twice, excluding those who are naked, those with white [leprosy], the dejected, those with black teeth, and those with bad nails. Regarding "naked": some say this refers to one with a skin disease or one who is bald. "White" means one with white leprosy (*śvitrin*). "Dejected" means one afflicted by leprosy (*kuṣṭhin*). "Black-teethed" means one whose teeth are naturally black. "Bad-nailed" means one with deformed nails. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should certainly not feed those who are wicked. One should also avoid those with skin diseases, those with deformed nails, lepers, those with vitiligo, those with black teeth, and others who have deficient or redundant limbs.

‘Duścarmā’ means one afflicted with elephantiasis (gajacarma). ‘Kuṣṭhī’ is well known. ‘Śvitrī’ means one who has white leprosy (śvetakuṣṭha). ‘Hīnam’ means deficient in size or number; he whose ‘aṅgam’—that is, a limb—is thus is ‘hīnāṅgaḥ’. Similarly, there is the ‘atiriktāṅgaḥ’ (one with an extra limb). This deficiency of limbs may occur either by nature or through injury such as amputation, and both cases are included here. Kātyāyana, following the word ‘āmantrayet’ (he should invite), states:

“One should exclude those who are naked, white-skinned, distressed, leprous, having black teeth, pierced [by arrows], born of a low-caste woman, diseased, deformed, afflicted with white leprosy, or having deformed nails.”

"One whose generative organ has been pierced" means one whose penis has been perforated. "Afflicted by disease" refers to one suffering from an incurable illness or one possessed of the sinful diseases mentioned by Devala. "Deformed" means one with missing limbs.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Those whose minds are struck down by fate are not worthy to eat at a *śrāddha*."
One who is impotent, mute, has diseased nails, is bald, or suffers from dental disease;
One with black teeth, a putrid nose, a missing limb, or an extra finger;
one suffering from throat disease, a goiter, or cracked limbs, and one afflicted by fever; those who are lame, humpbacked, or eunuchs, and others who are deformed in appearance.

"Ṣaṇḍaḥ" refers to the six types previously described by their characteristics. "Mūkaḥ" is one deprived of speech. "Khalvāṭaḥ" is one devoid of hair. "Pūtināsaḥ" is one with a foul-smelling nose or suffering from diseases of the nose and eyes. "Galarogī" is one afflicted with throat diseases such as goiter (galagaṇḍa) and the like. "Gaḍumān" is one who is hunchbacked. "Khañjaḥ" is one who is lame. "Tūparaḥ" is one who, even in youth, has not grown a beard. [This is stated] in the Skanda Purāṇa.
One-eyed men, those with deformed ears, those with blotchy skin, the bald, those with black teeth,
those with diseased nails, those afflicted with leprosy, the twice-naked, and those with perforated penises.
One-eyed, pot-bellied, and scabby; mute, blind, deaf, and dull-witted;
excessively tall, excessively short, excessively stout, and exceedingly thin.

A wise man should avoid those who are hairless, those with excessive body hair, and those who are exceedingly fair or dark, even if they are learned in the Vedas, when performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
"Insentient" means those whose minds are mute.
Śālaṅkāyana says:
"That which is eaten by those whose ears have not been pierced, and likewise by those with long ears."
And that which is eaten by those with burnt ears indeed goes to the Rākṣasas.
Gobhila states the characteristic of those with long ears:
"Brāhmaṇas whose ears have not been pierced, those who are black, and likewise those with long ears, should be avoided with great effort at the performance of a Śrāddha rite."
Hārīta says: "The two ears hanging down below the region of the jaw are proclaimed to be auspicious when they measure two or three finger-breadths; thus Śātātapa has declared."
Thus [are described] those with physical defects.
Now, those of censurable conduct.
Vyāsa and Śātātapa:
Seed sown in salt soil, that which is offered as an oblation into ashes,
and that which is given to those devoid of ritual action— their destruction is ordained.
"Devoid of action" (*akriyāhīnāḥ*) means those who are empty of the performance of prescribed duties. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"One should not give to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa, nor should one give to a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of action."
Nor should one give wealth to one who merely calls himself a Brahmin, nor to a bad Brahmin.
The characteristics of those who are not Brahmins and others have been stated in the section on designations (*saṃjñāprakaraṇa*). Hārīta says:
"The seller praises the merchandise; the buyer disparages its qualities."
Prajāpati [declared] that one who employs deceitful means and a gambler are not to be trusted.
"Vyāja" means fraud; "kitava" means a rogue. Thus says Yama.
The gods do not eat the food of a slanderer, nor do they eat the food of one who speaks untruth;
they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of him in whose house lives a paramour.

The ancestors do not partake of the sacrificial offering from one who approaches with harsh words, nor from one wearing red inner garments, nor from one whose ears extend more than two finger-breadths beyond the eyes.

A "backbiter" (*piśuna*) is one who reveals the faults of others. One "subjugated by his wife" (*bhāryājita*) is one who is dependent on his wife. An "adulterer" (*upapati*) is a constant paramour. One who wears a red inner garment—that is, a lower cloth—is "one with a red inner garment" (*raktāntaravāsas*). One whose ears have grown more than two finger-breadths due to the insertion of palm leaves or similar objects into the earlobes is "one whose ears exceed two fingers" (*dvyaṅgulātītakarṇa*).
Āpastamba states: "One who dyes indigo and one who wears indigo-dyed clothing [are excluded]."
Nothing at all should be given to him, for he is indeed like a caṇḍāla.
He who sows indigo seeds in a field is called "the one who plows for indigo.
Manu says:
"That which is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those such as a *parivetṛ* (one who marries before his elder brother), and so forth..."
Whatever is eaten by others who are unworthy of the company at a meal, that indeed the Rākṣasas consume.
Hārīta says: Just as milk in an unbaked vessel, or as an oblation poured into ashes,
even so wealth perishes when given to one who is engaged in trivial activities and does not abide in right conduct.
Yama said:
Offerings to the ancestors and oblations to the gods given out of delusion perish,
as do seeds sown in saline soil upon those who have become like ashes.
Just as one offers clarified butter into a fire that has been extinguished,
so too does what is given reach neither the gods nor the ancestors; it is merely danced and sung.
And whatever sacrificial fee one gives to one who is unlearned in the Ṛgveda;
One may certainly employ a Brahmin who possesses proper conduct, but one should not give in such a manner to others;
food given to one who is unlearned in the Vedas cries out.
Whatever is given to him, the Yātudhānas carry it away.
Therefore, one should diligently give gifts to those who are equal or superior; for the twice-born, enriched by learning and austerity, enable one to cross over [saṃsāra].
If a man offers an oblation for one born of an improper marriage,
neither his ancestors nor the gods accept that oblation.
Whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, where a drinker of intoxicants eats,
that offering does not reach the gods or the ancestors of the giver.
One should not give sacrificial oblations (havis) to a drinker of intoxicants at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
what is given to such a person perishes, just like an offering poured into ashes.
The hand of the giver exists, yet the tongue of the eater differs;
he swallows blazing morsels— such a *śrāddha* becomes false where that lowest of the twice-born eats in the company of a drunkard and a Niṣāda.
There the gods do not eat, nor do they drink the sacrificial oblation;
for the *śrāddha* rites and the oblations have been consumed by the husbands of *vṛṣalī*s.
They do not gratify the ancestors or the gods, and the donor does not go to heaven. Hārīta says:
"Śrāddhas and sacrificial offerings consumed by the husbands of Śūdra women [yield no fruit]."
The offerings do not reach the gods, and the donor does not go to heaven.
Yama said: Those who have strayed from their own duties are proclaimed to be thieves;
whatever ancestral offering (kavya) one gives to them, that perishes for him after death.
But those of small intelligence who give [food] to them with prior knowledge [of their status],
O observer of good vows, all eat excrement for a hundred years.
Therefore, by one desiring to give, the *daiva* and *śrāddha* rites should be performed in every respect.
It should be given to those who are tranquil, and never to those who are not tranquil.
What is given to a temple-priest is lost; what is given to a usurer finds no firm footing;
and what is given to a merchant brings no fruit either in this world or the next.
An offering given to a twice-born man who has remarried is like a libation poured upon ashes;

what is given to a seller of Soma is like excrement; to a physician, it is like pus and blood; to one who has fallen from his caste, it is like phlegm; and to an ungrateful person, it is said to be like poison.
But in the case of others who are unworthy— those excluded from the row (apāṅktya) as previously described—
the fat, skin, flesh, marrow, and so forth, become [the result] when they are requested [as alms].
In the *Vāyu Purāṇa*: "A twice-born man who approaches his wife in vain, or officiates at a sacrifice for one who is ineligible, or who is an atheist, does not deserve to partake in a *śrāddha*."
He who cooks food for his own sake and not for the sake of the gods or guests—
even such a man, fallen and become a Brahmarākṣasa, is unworthy of the Śrāddha.
One should not feed at śrāddha ceremonies those who always wear red garments, those who delight in slander, and those who are devoted to wealth and sensual pleasure.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who, while studying, considers himself a scholar and destroys the reputation of others by means of his learning..."
O Brahmin, he commits the murder of a Brahmin;
for his worlds come to an end at this point.
All the Vedas along with the six auxiliary limbs, Sāṃkhya, the Purāṇas, and birth in a noble family—
none of these constitute the ultimate goal.
O King, for a man who is devoid of virtue, [there is no happiness].
Attraction, the destruction of enemies, agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing,
and even the selfless service of one's elders.
This task does not belong to a Brahmin.
These twice-born ones, practicing what is censured,
are to be avoided at rites for the ancestors and the gods;
by accepting those who are censurable through the power of delusion, [one incurs sin].
And by means of a great-souled one, he causes his ancestors to be immersed [in merit].
Thus end those of censurable conduct. Now, those outside the [four] stages of life (āśrama). According to Kārṣṇājini:
The four stages of life (āśramas) are meritorious for both ancestral rites (śrāddha) and rites for the gods (daiva);
however, one should never cause a śrāddha to be offered to those who stand outside the four stages of life.
Pracetas said:
"The Rākṣasas who have gone outside the hermitage in the form of twice-born brahmins—to them no sacrificial offering (havya) should be given; for nothing is poured into ashes."
Devala says:
"That which is given to one who stands outside the four stages of life (āśrama) becomes fruitless.
[In the] Vāyu Purāṇa:
He who stands outside the four stages of life subsisting on air alone, and he who,
being a non-ascetic, propounds the doctrine of liberation— both of these are defilers of the assembly.
One who lacks self-restraint regarding the senses,
even if he be a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) endowed with great erudition and engaged in severe austerity,
should not be invited as a Brahmin if he performs penance outside of a prescribed stage of life (*āśrama*).
The Śākya who denies rebirth, the nihilist, the reviler of the Vedas,
and those who revile meditators— all these are defilers of the assembly.

[476] One should avoid those who propound "rebirth" (*aupapatti*) through dry logic due to their association with the Śākyas; likewise, one should avoid all those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and mendicants in rags, as well as all those who are merciless, of corrupt conduct, and mere beggars.
One should carefully avoid those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "The Buddhists, the Śrāvakas, the Nirgranthas, the knowers of the Pañcarātra, and the Jinas..."
The Kāpaṭikas, the Pāśupatas, the heretics, and those of similar kind.
If these evil-minded ones of a tamasic nature eat the sacrificial offerings,
that śrāddha will not yield fruit for him either in this world or after death.
A twice-born man who belongs to no stage of life, or one who belongs to a stage of life in vain,
as well as those Brahmins whose stages of life are false, should be known as defilers of the assembly.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "A Brahmin who belongs to no stage of life (āśrama), whether he has matted hair or a shaven head,
and who has abandoned his duties in vain— he should be avoided from afar at a Śrāddha."

In the Nandipurāṇa: "Those who, under the pretext of teaching the knowledge of Brahman, perform great evil deeds—they are to be avoided in all activities; they are outcasts (cāṇḍālas) in the form of the twice-born."
Those twice-born individuals who, under the pretext of teaching the knowledge of Brahman, exist in any state whatsoever,
must indeed be banished from the country by a king who practices righteousness.
In the Padma Purāṇa: All those who harbor false intentions, or twice-born men of wicked conduct,
as well as those who profess false doctrines and are hypocrites, are to be avoided in all ritual acts.
Those who, being themselves deluded, give instruction on Brahman to people out of a desire for wealth are indeed rogues and deceivers of the ignorant.
One should not, even out of affection, honor those who sell the Veda, the sinful,
or those who serve actions that are contrary to the duties of their caste and stage of life.
One should avoid those who are shaven-headed, those with matted hair, and those wearing saffron robes at a *śrāddha*.
As stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*:
"A Brahmin who belongs to no stage of life (*āśrama*), whether he has matted hair or is shaven-headed, and one who is [so] in vain..."
One who wears the saffron robe in vain—one should avoid such a person from afar at a funeral feast (śrāddha).
Those evil-minded and base fools who, under the pretext of renunciation,
abandon their duties— they too must be avoided with great effort.
Even those who have not perceived the truth, yet stand outside the path of ritual action, are undoubtedly fallen; they should be excluded from all religious rites.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"The wearing of matted hair by men who are shaven-headed, who consume liquor, and who are devoid of all purity is entirely in vain."
A person goes to hell even by conversing with those who have been excluded from the offering of water and the ancestral funeral cakes (pinda).
Thus [end] those excluded from the hermitages.
Now, those unworthy of an invitation.
Regarding this, in the Mahābhārata:
[478] O King, as many Brahmins as have fallen from their caste, as well as those who are dull-witted or insane, do not deserve an invitation to a rite for the gods or for the ancestors.
"Outcasts" (patitāḥ) are those who possess the mortal sins that cause loss of caste. "Insane" (unmattāḥ) are those suffering from the disease of insanity.
O King, one with vitiligo, one afflicted by leprosy, a eunuch, one whose arm is paralyzed, one suffering from epilepsy, and one who is blind—such a person does not deserve an invitation to a feast.
A "klība" is a eunuch; one whose half of the body is incapacitated for action due to the disease of hemiplegia is "pakṣaghata";
physicians, temple-priests (devalakas), those who maintain vows in vain, and sellers of soma—O King, these do not deserve an invitation.
‘Devalakas’ are those who worship deities for a price. ‘Vṛthāniyamadhāriṇas’ are hypocrites. ‘Somavikrayiṇas’ are sellers of the soma creeper.
O King, singers, dancers, acrobats, musicians, storytellers, and public lecturers likewise do not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast.

"Plavakas" are actors; "bodhakas" are bards. Those who are priests for Śūdras, as well as those who are teachers of Śūdras, and likewise the disciples of Śūdras, do not deserve an invitation to a śrāddha.

Those who teach the science of grammar and other treatises to Śūdras are "teachers of the low-born" (vṛṣalādhyāpakas); likewise are those who have Śūdra disciples. O King, a Brāhmaṇa who has previously, out of desire, accepted another caste [as his wife], does not deserve an invitation to a feast, even if he is learned in all branches of knowledge.
By whom, having not married daughters of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, the acceptance of women from other castes was primarily practiced;
and those Brahmins who maintain no sacred fires, those who carry out the dead, thieves, and those who have fallen from their caste— O King, these do not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast.

Those who maintain no sacred fires (*anagnayaḥ*), meaning those who have not established the consecrated fires; those who carry out the dead for a price, known as *mṛtaniryātaka*s; thieves (*stenāḥ*); and those previously unknown, O Bhārata, as well as those who previously belonged to a religious guild (*gaṇa*), and those who are the sons of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)—these do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*.

Those whose ancestors were not previously known are called "those of unknown ancestry" (*aparijñātapūrvāḥ*). Those who are foremost or leaders in their groups or assemblies are "leaders of the assembly" (*gaṇapūrvāḥ*). "Those preceded by the sons of appointed daughters" (*putrikāputrapūrvāḥ*) refers to those belonging to the lineage of the sons of such appointed daughters.
O King, he who is a debtor, the twice-born man who is a usurer, and he whose livelihood consists of the sale of living beings—these, O King, do not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast.

He who incurs debt for purposes other than necessary expenses is an "incumbent of debt" (*ṛṇakartṛ*). A "moneylender" (*vārddhuṣika*) is one who lives on interest from grain. One whose livelihood consists of the "sale of life" (*prāṇavikrayavṛtti*) is a servant.
O bull among the Bharatas, a *tripūrvaka*, a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, and a Yavana [are also excluded].
And a Brahmin who performs no ritual acts likewise does not deserve an invitation to a śrāddha feast.

‘Tripūrvaḥ’ means one born of three [castes]. ‘Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhaḥ’ is one possessing the characteristics previously described. ‘Yavanaḥ’ is one born in the land of the Yavanas. These are those unworthy of being invited. Now, those excluded from the row (apāṅkteya).
Āhośana says:

Furthermore, there are those who are excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*). These include the mentally dull, the deaf, the blind, those with vitiligo, lepers, those with deformed hands, those with black teeth, usurers, temple-priests (*devalaka*), merchants, eunuchs, members of a guild, physicians, sons of remarried women, the one-eyed, those who live by their craft, the outcaste (*patita*), those who associate with outcasts, gamblers, liars, hypocrites, and those corrupted by others, and so forth.

One who is confused regarding the understanding of injunctions and prohibitions is a "jaḍa" (insentient/dull-witted). One deficient in the sense of hearing is a "badhira" (deaf). One without eyes is an "andha" (blind). One afflicted with white leprosy is a "śvitrī. A "kuṣṭhī" (leper) is well known. One with deformed hands is a "kuṇi. One who is naturally black-toothed is a "śyāvadanta. One who lives on the interest of grain when other means of livelihood exist is a "vārddhuṣika" (usurer). One who worships a deity for a fee or consumes the property of a deity is a "devalaka. One who subsists on the business of buying and selling is a "vaṇik" (merchant). A "ṣaṇḍha" is defined by its specific characteristics in the section on the six types [of eunuchs]. A "gaṇa" is a corporation; those who always live by a single profession are here denoted by the word "gaṇa," and a Brāhmaṇa who possesses fourfold knowledge but belongs to such a group is a "gaṇābhyantara. One who treats diseases for the sake of wealth is a "cikitsaka" (physician); however, Medhātithi maintains that he is praiseworthy if he seeks to treat them for the sake of Dharma. A woman remarried is a "punarbhū," and her offspring is a "paunarbhava. One deficient in one eye is a "kāṇa"; or, one who looks askance is a "kāṇa. One whose livelihood consists in building houses, palaces, and so forth, is a "śilpopajīvī" (artisan). One defiled by association with a perpetrator of a mortal sin is a "patita" (outcaste). A "saṃprayoktā" is a gambler. A "kitava" is a cheat. One whose habit is speaking untruth is an "anṛta" (liar). One who practices Dharma through deception for the sake of worldly favor is a "dāmbhika" (hypocrite). One who has been subjected to humiliation by others due to being accused of a most grievous sin is a "paraparibhāvita."
Manu says:
"Those who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, and those who live as atheists—
Manu has declared that such men are unworthy of being invited as Brahmins for offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya)."
One should not feed at a śrāddha those who officiate for a multitude of people— such as one with matted hair who does not study, one who is weak, or likewise a gambler.
Physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade— these should be avoided at rites for the gods and the ancestors.
A servant of a village or of a king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth,
one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, a younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has been expelled from his caste, a hater of Brahmins, an elder brother whose younger brother has married before him, and one who belongs to a religious guild (gaṇa).
One who is of bad character, one who has broken his vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, the son of a remarried woman, one who is one-eyed, and he in whose house lives a paramour;
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught for a fee,
one whose pupil is a Śūdra, one whose teacher is a Śūdra, one who is corrupt in speech, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka.
Having abandoned his mother, father, and teacher without cause,
and having entered into association with outcasts through Brahmanical or matrimonial connections;
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel made of human skull, a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
One who quarrels with his father, a gambler, a drunkard,
one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids [are unfit to be witnesses].

One who makes bows and arrows, one who is the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried, a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is a teacher to his own son.
One suffering from epilepsy, one with scrofulous swellings, one with leucoderma, as well as a slanderer, a madman, a blind man, and likewise one who reviles the Vedas— these should be avoided.
One who trains elephants, horses, or camels; one who lives by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras);
one who raises birds; and likewise a teacher of warfare.
He who breaks the channels of the streams and delights in obstructing them;
he who constructs houses, acts as a messenger, and likewise plants trees.
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, one who defiles a maiden, one who is violent, one who subsists on the service of Śūdras, and one who performs sacrifices for groups (of people).
One devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, one who constantly begs,
one who lives by agriculture, one suffering from elephantiasis, and one who is censured by the virtuous— these are likewise excluded.
A butcher of sheep, a butcher of buffaloes, the husband of a woman previously married to another, and one who carries out the dead— these must be avoided with great effort.
A learned man, the best among the twice-born, should avoid both of these lowest of the twice-born, who are of censurable conduct and unworthy of the company at a meal.

‘Thieves (*stenāḥ*)’ are those who steal property belonging to anyone other than Brāhmaṇas, since others are designated by the term ‘outcastes (*patitāḥ*)’. ‘Outcastes (*patitāḥ*)’ are those guilty of the great sins (*mahāpātakin*). A ‘eunuch (*klībaḥ*)’ is a neuter; this is seen from the scriptural indication: “Do not yield to weakness, O son of Kuntī. Harihara says: “A *klība* is one devoid of semen. Those whose settled conviction (*sthitaprajñā*) is that “there is no gift, there is no oblation, there is no other world,” their ‘conduct (*vṛttiḥ*)’ or practice—namely, lack of faith—is ‘atheistic conduct (*nāstikavṛttiḥ*)’; those whose conduct is such are ‘those of atheistic conduct (*nāstikavṛttayaḥ*)’. This is a compound with the loss of the middle member (*uttarapadalopa*). Alternatively, they are so called because atheism (*nāstikyam*) is their mode of life (*vṛttiḥ*) or livelihood. The mention of Manu is for the sake of showing respect for the prohibition. Medhātithi says a ‘jaṭila’ is a religious student (*brahmacārī*); here, one who has not studied or has not yet begun his studies is prohibited, for a student who has begun his studies is enjoined [to wear matted hair]. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility at all of connection with study (so how could there be a prohibition?), because connection is possible through rules such as “even a daughter’s son while observing vows,” etc. A ‘*duvālaḥ*’ is one with red hair or a bald man; others read ‘*durvalaḥ*’. ‘*Durvalaḥ*’ means one whose banner is lowered, or one incapable of eating. ‘*Pūgān*’ means groups or associations; they ‘perform sacrifices (*yājayanti*)’ for them. ‘Meat-sellers (*māṃsavikrayiṇaḥ*)’ are well known. ‘By trade (*vipaṇena*)’ means by forbidden merchandise such as salt. A ‘servant (*preṣyaḥ*)’ of a village or a king is one who carries out orders. A ‘bad-nail person (*kunakhī*)’ is one with deformed nails. One who acts in opposition to a teacher in all matters due to his prohibition is ‘one who opposes the teacher (*guroḥ pratiroddhā*)’. An ‘abandoned-fire person (*tyaktāgniḥ*)’ is one who has abandoned either of the two sets of fires: the three sacred fires (*tretā*) or the domestic fire (*vārṣyāgnihotra*). A ‘consumptive (*yakṣmī*)’ is one seized by pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*). A ‘herdsman (*paśupālaḥ*)’ is one who guards cattle for the sake of a livelihood. A ‘negligent (*nirākṛtiḥ*)’ is one who, despite being qualified, neglects the performance of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), or one who has forgotten the Veda; others say it means one of ugly appearance. A ‘hater of the Vedas (*brahmadviṭ*)’ is one who hates Brāhmaṇas or the Veda. The ‘younger brother who marries before the elder (*parivettṛ*)’ and the ‘elder brother so superseded (*parivitti*)’ have characteristics described previously. ‘Actors (*kuśīlavāḥ*)’ include bards, dancers, singers, and so forth. An ‘unchaste student (*avakīrṇī*)’ is one whose vow of celibacy has been violated. A ‘*vṛṣalī*’ is a Śūdra woman; her husband is meant. Or they consider the logic of the word ‘*adūkṣan*’ (having milked) to apply here, meaning the husband of a *vṛṣalī* herself. A ‘paramour (*upapatiḥ*)’ is the lover of a wife. And he is one who, being neglected, lives right in the house. A ‘hired servant (*bhṛtakaḥ*)’ is one who receives wages according to an agreement such as “I will do this for so much money”; a teacher who is such a hired servant is a ‘hired teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpakaḥ*)’. Likewise, one taught by such a person is ‘taught by a hired teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpitaḥ*)’. A ‘Śūdra pupil (*śūdraśiṣyaḥ*)’ is a Śūdra student in grammar and other sciences. A ‘teacher (*guruḥ*)’ of a Śūdra is also meant; here, even though it is a subordinate member of the compound, it is connected [to the list], because the state of being a despised teacher belongs to all [categories], and it is specifically the status of a Śūdra teacher that is condemned, not others. A ‘corrupt in speech (*vāgduṣṭaḥ*)’ is one who speaks harshly or untruthfully, or one who is accused. ‘*Kuṇḍa*’ and ‘*golaka*’ have their characteristics stated previously. Here, ‘teacher (*guruḥ*)’ refers to the preceptor (*ācārya*). One who abandons mother, father, or teacher when there is no cause for abandoning them due to a sin like killing a Brāhmaṇa. Abandonment means failing to perform service and so forth. ‘Abandoning the teacher (*gurutyāgaḥ*)’ means, while the teacher is capable of teaching, one abandons him and studies elsewhere. By ‘Brāhma connections (*brāhmaiḥ*)’ are meant officiating at sacrifices, teaching, etc.; by ‘marital connections (*yaunaiḥ*)’ are meant giving a daughter in marriage, etc. He who has entered into association with outcastes, according to the rule: “By associating with an outcaste for a year, one becomes an outcaste. Although the associate is already included by the term ‘outcaste,’ this is said to prohibit [association] even before a year has passed. An ‘incendiary (*āgāradāhī*)’ is one who burns houses and the like. A ‘poisoner (*garadaḥ*)’ is one who administers artificial or natural poison. One who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka* is a ‘*kuṇḍāśī*’. A ‘*kuṇḍa*’ is a measure of capacity (*āḍhaka*); or a ‘*kuṇḍāśī*’ is one who eats food measured by that amount. A ‘seller of Soma (*somavikrayī*)’ is one who sells a specific plant for sacrifice or medicine, or one who sells a sacrifice for which Soma is the means. A ‘sea-farer (*samudrayāyī*)’ is one who goes to or crosses the ocean by ship and the like. A ‘bard (*bandī*)’ is a reciter of praises. A ‘grinder (*taikaḥ*)’ is one who grinds sesame seeds and the like. A ‘fraudster (*kūṭakārakaḥ*)’ is one who speaks falsely as a witness, or a maker of counterfeit coins and the like. One who disputes with his father regarding shares and so forth, speaking in opposition through the method of prior and subsequent arguments. A ‘gambler (*kitavaḥ*)’ is one who looks at the dice with a sidelong glance; others read ‘*kātaraḥ*’ (timid), meaning one whose pupils are like those of a parrot. A ‘liquor-drinker (*madyapaḥ*)’ is one who drinks *ariṣṭa* (fermented liquor) other than *surā*. A ‘sufferer from a foul disease (*pāparogī*)’ is a leper. An ‘accused (*abhiśastaḥ*)’ is one charged with a major or minor sin. A ‘hypocrite (*dāmbhikaḥ*)’ is well known in the world. Even if there is no certainty that he performed the act, he is still included. A ‘seller of liquids (*rasavikrayī*)’ is a seller of poison, according to Medhātithi. Śaṅkhadhara says it is a seller of substances based on
Having given one-sixth to the king, one-twentieth to the deities,
and one-thirtieth to the Brahmins, one incurs no fault by practicing agriculture.

This and more has been set forth by the authors of the *Smṛtis*. One who, due to a physical defect, stands on one leg is called a *ślīpadī*. One whose fault is not perceived through direct observation but who is seen being censured by the virtuous is "one censured by the good" (*sadbhir ninditaḥ*). One for whom sheep (*urabhrāḥ*) are the merchandise is an "ewer-keeper" (*aurabhrikaḥ*); likewise, a "buffalo-keeper" (*māhiṣikaḥ*). A woman who has another man as her prior [husband] is a "previously married woman" (*parapūrvā*), such as an unchaste woman; her husband is a "husband of a previously married woman" (*parapūrvāpatiḥ*). One who, for a price, escorts or carries out the dead is a "funeral carrier" (*pretaniryāpakaḥ*). Those of "despised conduct" (*vigarhitācārāḥ*) are those whose behavior is blameworthy. "Excluded from the row" (*apāṅkteyāḥ*) means unworthy of the company at a meal. "In both cases" refers to rites for the gods (*daiva*) and for the ancestors (*pitrya*).
On this point, Sumantu said:

Thieves, gamblers, keepers of gambling houses, groups [of such], courtesans, Śūdras, slaves, those who approach women forbidden to them, those who marry before their elder brothers (*parivettṛ*), those whose younger brothers marry first (*parivitti*), those who have superseded their elder brothers in marriage (*paryāhita*), those who have been superseded by their younger brothers (*paryādhātṛ*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the blind, the deaf, professional bards (*cāraṇa*), eunuchs, those who have broken their vows of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*), usurers, poisoners, false witnesses, atheists, husbands of low-caste women (*vṛṣalīpati*), those who eat what has been offered to others, those who have abandoned the sacred fires, sellers of Soma, sellers of forbidden goods, sellers of what is not for sale, those who live by astrology, storytellers, those who eat from the vessels of outcasts, those born of adultery, makers of machines, those who live by the sword, those with diseased skin, the fierce, the pierced, those who serve as temple-priests for hire (*devalaka*), the impotent, those who have fallen from their status, those who have returned after being excommunicated, those with deformed nails, those afflicted with leprosy, those with black teeth, merchants, artisans, those who live by playing musical instruments, dancing, singing, or keeping time, those who live by almanacs, long-distance travelers, stone-crushers, and those with missing or redundant limbs—these, wearing discolored garments, are excluded from the company at meals.

A "thief" (*taskara*) is a robber. One who tends goats for the sake of livelihood is an "ajapāla. A "gaṇa" is a multitude. A "gaṇikā" is a courtesan. A *śūdra* is well known. He is the "servant" (*preṣya*) of these [groups]. From the prohibition against serving a *śūdra*, it is understood that in times of great distress, service to those of other castes is permitted provided they are free from other defects.
As Pracetas said: "A Brāhmaṇa fallen into great distress may resort to service to a Kṣatriya."
One must not serve a Śūdra, even if one’s life-breaths have reached the throat.

One who goes to women who should not be approached is an *agamyāgāmī*. When the elder brother has not yet established the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) but the younger brother has already established them, the younger is called *paryādhātṛ* and the elder is called *paryāhita*; this has been determined in detail previously. A *cāraṇa* here refers to a naked teacher (*nagnācārya*), because he wanders here and there proclaiming his fame; however, a specific type of *cāraṇa*, namely a dancer, will be mentioned later by the term "one who lives by dancing. One who gives false testimony is a *kūṭasākṣī*. One who eats without having performed the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) is an *upahūtādaḥ*. An *utsṛṣṭāgniḥ* is one who has abandoned the sacred fires. One who sells sesame, barley, and other items that should not be sold is an *avikreyavikretā*. One who lives by the profession of copying books is a *paustikaḥ*, or alternatively, a seller of books or a copyist for a fee. A *kathakaḥ* is a narrator of stories such as the *Bṛhatkathā* for the amusement of common people. A *yantrakāraḥ* is a maker of machines for the purpose of hunting in forts and such places, or for the purpose of battle. A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhaḥ* is one who lives by weapons; for the traditional rule of grammar (*nāmānuśāsana*) states, "A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* is one who lives by weapons. Others, however, read the word as *kāṇḍaspaṣṭaḥ*; its definition was stated previously. A *duścarmā* is one afflicted with a skin disease that is difficult to cure. [488] A *caṇḍaḥ* is one whose penis-skin has been cut off; the root *caṇḍi* (meaning "to remove bark") belongs to the *cur-ādi* class, and thus *caṇḍaḥ* is derived from *caṇḍayati*. This condition, known as *viddhaśiśna*, is well-known among the Dravidians; for there, having made an incision in the vein below the penis and testicles, libertines fashion ornaments of pearls and the like set in gold rings. One who has fallen away from the vows after having undertaken them, such as those of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), is an *ārūḍhapatitaḥ*. *Prāyaḥ* refers to fasting unto death preceded by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*); for the *Trikāṇḍa-smaraṇa* states, "The masculine noun *prāyaḥ* refers to renunciation and fasting unto death. One who has risen after abandoning such fasting is a *prāyotthitaḥ*. A *kilāśī* is one suffering from ringworm (*sidhma*). *Vāditram* is a musical instrument to be struck. *Nṛtyam* is dancing. *Gītam* is singing. *Tālaḥ* refers to rhythmic patterns such as *cañcatpuṭa*; one who lives by proficiency in these arts is meant. One who predicts the stars and so forth out of a desire for wealth is a *mūlyasāṃvatsarikaḥ*. And it has been said by Manu:
"One should not announce another's lunar day (tithi), nor should one point out the constellations (nakṣatras).

A "great traveler" (*mahāpathika*) is one who travels by sea or is a constant wanderer. A "stone-pounder" (*aśmakuṭṭaka*) is a stone-cutter for the construction of palaces and other structures. "Those with deficient limbs" (*hīnāṅga*) refers to those such as the lame and so forth. "Those with extra limbs" (*adhikāṅga*) refers to those with six fingers and the like. "Those with discolored garments" (*virāgavāsas*) are those whose clothes are dyed with various colors such as madder (*āñjiṣṭha*) and so forth; or alternatively, they are those whose garments are dyed with red ochre (*gairika*) and the like for the purpose of deceiving the world, even without having taken up the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*). And Yama says:
Hear from me as I declare those other twice-born who are excluded from the company at meals;
to them, a gift given does not perform its function for either the gods or the ancestors.
The one-eyed, the hunchbacked, the eunuchs, the ungrateful, those who violate the teacher’s bed,
the slayers of Brahmins, the drinkers of intoxicants, thieves, the killers of cows, and physicians;
Those who desire sovereignty, as well as the insane, those who sell livestock, village headmen, those who cheat with scales, artisans, and village beggars;
Guilds and royal sacrificers who have been corrupted by low-caste women;
and the king’s servants—those who are blind, deaf, mute, bald, and lame.
Those who live by the arts, those who sell the Veda,
those Brahmins who carry the staff and banner [of office], and those who perform village services;
Those who set fire to houses, those who administer poison, those who burn forests, those who eat from sacrificial bowls, temple-priests for hire, and those who violate the wives of others;
Those with black teeth, those with deformed nails, artisans, those afflicted with leprosy,
merchants, those who kill honey-bees, and those twice-born men who are trainers of elephants and horses;
Those who defile maidens, those who revile Brahmins,
informers, those who raise animals for slaughter, gamblers, and actors;
Those who break their vows, those who obstruct the giving of gifts,
those who live by breeding goats, those who live by breeding buffaloes, those who sell all manner of goods,
those who are devoted to the Vaiṣṇava sects, and those who burn with the fire-brands of the Śalākā; [these are excluded].
A maker of bows, one who lives by deceit, a betrayer of friends, and indeed a rogue.
Likewise, one who makes arrows should be avoided, as well as the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried;
so too those afflicted with jaundice, scrofula, consumption, and epilepsy.
A slanderer, a false witness, one who suffers from a chronic disease, one whose efforts are in vain,
one who has returned from the life of a wandering mendicant, and one who has entered the religious life in vain— these are [excluded].
But he who is born of one who has gone forth, and he who has abandoned the life of one who has gone forth— Yama, the son of Vivasvat, declares both of them to be *brahmacaṇḍālas*.
One who serves as a messenger for a king, one who serves a village or a city,
one who travels by sea, one who subsists on trade, and those who sell their hair;

One who has broken his vow of celibacy, a slayer of heroes, a slayer of a guru, one who reviles his father, a seller of cows, a person of wicked conduct, and one who performs sacrifices for a multitude; [490] these are the ones excluded.
A drunkard, a miser, one who quarrels with his father,
a magistrate, a husband of a female ascetic, one who has abandoned himself, and a defiler of women;

One whose conduct is censured by the virtuous, one who has abandoned his own duties, one who has been superseded in marriage by a younger brother, one who marries before his elder brother, a teacher for hire, and one who has neglected the Vedic study— these are excluded.
One who teaches a Śūdra, one who teaches his own daughter, one who has a Śūdra as a pupil, an atheist, a corrupt teacher of children, one who is arrogant, and likewise an oil-presser;
Thieves, usurers, the wicked, those who destroy the property of others,
those excluded from the four stages of life (āśramas), and others who defile the row (paṅkti)—
one should not appoint those twice-born men who possess such characteristics.

‘Gurutalpagaḥ’ means one who has sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru. One who desires to bring a kingdom under his control for the sake of priesthood or for the sake of performing sacrifices is ‘rāṣṭrakāmaḥ’. One who deceives or cheats a village is a ‘grāmakūṭakaḥ’; the meaning is that he consumes the village’s wealth through many fraudulent transactions. A ‘tulākūṭaḥ’ is a deceiver who uses false weights. One who is repeatedly drunk upon by a *vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman)—that is, repeatedly kissed—is a ‘vṛṣalīprapītaḥ’. ‘Śreṇyaḥ’ refers to guilds such as goldsmiths and others; one who officiates as a priest for them is a ‘śreṇīyājakaḥ’. One who lives by interest on gold is a ‘kalopajīvī’, or one who lives by the sixty-four arts (*kalā*). A ‘brahmavikrayī’ is a seller of the Veda or of a son, or one who teaches the sacred knowledge (*brahmavidyā*) for the sake of a livelihood. One who is a great offender and has been punished by the king with branding on the foot or other parts is called a ‘daṇḍadhvajaḥ’. A ‘madhuhantā’ is one who destroys honey-bees for the purpose of collecting honey. A ‘sūcakaḥ’ is one who employs means to discover the faults of others. One who fosters a fault of another already made public by someone else and confirms it with corroborating speech [is also included]. ‘Samayāḥ’ are the regulations established by kings and others. Those who live by goats and sheep are ‘ājāvikāḥ’; likewise, those who live by buffaloes are ‘māhiṣikāḥ’. Or, they may be the sons of unchaste women. ‘Vaiṣṇavīṣu’ refers to illusions such as sorcery (*indrajāla*); those whose minds are fixed upon these are ‘saktāḥ’. ‘Śalākā’ is a surgical instrument and ‘dāhaḥ’ is cauterization by fire; those who practice medicine by these two means are ‘śalākādāhinaḥ’. One whose nature is to do harm is a ‘śaṭhaḥ’. An ‘iṣukartā’ is a maker of arrows. One who dwells in stages of life (*āśrama*) not prescribed by the scriptures is a ‘vṛthāśramī’. One who resolves, “I shall become a renunciant,” but does not actually undertake renunciation is a ‘pravrajyopanivṛttaḥ’. One who becomes a renunciant without any dispassion or similar motive is a ‘vṛthāpravrajitaḥ’. One begotten by a renunciant is a ‘pravrajitāj jātaḥ’. One who has formally accepted renunciation according to rule and then fallen away from it is a ‘pravrajyāvasitaḥ’. One who lives by the *vārttā*—the Vaiśya occupation consisting of agriculture, trade, and so forth—is a ‘vārttāśī’. Alternatively, one who learns all the news of the world through secret movements and reports it to the king is also known in the world as a ‘vārttāśī’ man because he lives by news. There is also a reading ‘vāntāśī’; its definition is stated in the section on technical terms (*saṃjñāprakaraṇa*). A ‘keśavikrayī’ is a seller of chowries and the like. A ‘vīraghnaḥ’ is a killer of children; this is based on the etymological explanation of the Vedic verse, “He makes me as if I were a childless woman” (*avīrām iva mām ayam*), which is interpreted to mean “He makes me as if I were a woman who is not a child” (*abālām iva mām ayam*). A ‘pūgayājakaḥ’ is an officiating priest for a *pūga*, which is a group of people of the same caste and the same profession. The definition of a miser (*kadarya*) has been stated previously. A ‘dāṇḍikaḥ’ is an official authorized to inflict punishment for offenses. A ‘bandhukībhartā’ is the husband of an unchaste woman. A ‘tyaktātmā’ is one who has attempted suicide. A ‘dāradūṣakaḥ’ is one who corrupts noble women by providing them with facial pleasure or by uniting them with other men. Or, a ‘dāradūṣakaḥ’ is one who falsely accuses his former wives due to being infatuated with another woman. A ‘bhṛtyācāryaḥ’ is one who teaches for wages or one who was taught by a paid teacher. Likewise, a ‘śūdrācāryaḥ’. A ‘dārakācāryaḥ’ is a teacher of letters for children. One who lives by measuring grain, land, and so forth is a ‘mānakṛt’. Among these, some have been explained and some are easily understood.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

A thief who does not recite the Ṛgveda, a royal servant, one who subsists by planting trees, a poisoner, an incendiary, one who lives with dogs, a Śūdra teacher, a bard, a bell-ringer, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, one who subsists by predicting the stars and so forth, a Brahmin’s servant, a drinker of intoxicants, a seller of the Veda, a gambler, a forger, and those who sell human beings as cattle—these are persons excluded from the company at a meal (apāṅkteya).

One who has not studied the Vedas is "anṛk" (one devoid of Ṛg-verses). One who wanders with packs of dogs is a "śvāgaṇika. One who subsists by means of dancing, singing, and the like, preceded by the binding of small bells and such, is a "ghāṇṭika. Alternatively, one who begs from house to house while sounding a large bell is also a "ghāṇṭika"; he is well known as a "Ghaṇṭāla" in the land of Gurjara. One who acquires wealth by deceiving the world while wearing the garb of one liberated in this life is a "brahmapuruṣa. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

Those with deformed nails, those suffering from chronic skin diseases, those with black teeth, one who quarrels with his father, one who is conquered by women, a leper, a eunuch, a gambler, one who is difficult to restrain, one with skin disease, one born of a womb of liquor, one whose generative organ is perforated, an outcast, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, a seller of sacrifices or the Vedas, a merchant, a priest for a village, one falsely accused, one born of a Vṛṣalī woman, one who has married before his elder brother, one who marries while his younger brother is unmarried, the husband of a Didhiṣū, the son of a remarried woman, a Golaka, a Kuṇḍa, a goat-herd, a thief, a professional soldier, and a servant—these are those excluded from the row. One should not feed these at a Śrāddha nor in the performance of a sacrifice.
He in whose house the wife alone primarily manages all affairs, and who, being fearful, conducts himself under her dependence, is "one conquered by a woman" (*strījita*).
And it has been said by Yama:
"The ancestors do not eat at the rite for the gods, nor do they eat when there is one who speaks untruth."

"They do not eat the food of one who is conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house there is a paramour. [493] A "son born of a liquor-drinker's womb" (*surāgarbha*) is either one conceived in the womb of a woman who drinks liquor, or one begotten by a liquor-drinker who has performed penance. A "seller of sacred sites" (*tīrthavikrayī*) is one who sells the merit acquired through pilgrimages and other such acts. Thus says Śātātapa.
The food of those who perform sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with small sacrificial fees must not be eaten; they are proclaimed to be unworthy of the row at a meal.
Devala says: One who lives off the treasury of the gods shall be known by the name Devalaka;
he is to be understood as unfit for the company at the meal (apāṅkteya) in all rites at all times.

Manu says: "Whatever is eaten by twice-born men who have not observed their vows, as well as by those who marry before their elder brothers and the like, and by others excluded from the company at meals— that indeed the Rākṣasas consume."
Yama says:
One who is unworthy of the row quickly burns [the merit] as soon as he looks upon it;
the fruit is lost to those [givers], and the gift itself perishes.

"The fruit of that [desire-based rite] is lost" refers to the failure of a rite performed for a specific wish (*kāmya*). "And even the gift perishes" refers to the failure of an obligatory rite (*nityakarman*). These are those unworthy of the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*).
Now, those who defile the company (*paṅktidūṣaka*):
Śaṅkha says: Those Brahmins who are engaged in improper occupations, those who follow the "vow of the cat," and those who are deceitful;
as well as those with missing limbs or extra limbs—these should be known as defilers of the row.
One with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with a skin disease, the husband of a Śūdra woman,
one afflicted with leprosy, and one suffering from pulmonary consumption— these, O Brāhmaṇas, are defilers of the row.
Those who act in opposition to their gurus, those who destroy the Vedas and the sacred fires,
those who abandon their gurus, and such Brahmins are defilers of the assembly.
Those who study during forbidden times, those devoid of purity and proper conduct,
and those whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of Śūdras— such Brāhmaṇas are defilers of the assembly.

Those who perform actions neither enjoined nor prohibited are "those established in non-action" (*avikarmasthāḥ*). Those who have forgotten the Vedas and abandoned the sacred fires are "those who have extinguished the Veda and the fire" (*vedāgnyutsādinaḥ*). Those who eat food given by a Śūdra are "those whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra's food" (*śūdrānnarasapuṣṭāṅgāḥ*). Hārīta says:
[those who are] physicians, servants of low-caste people, artisans, gamblers, those who play with dogs, those who live by birds, fish-slayers, wrestlers, and those who frequent prostitutes—...
