One should exclude from rites for the gods and the ancestors those who live on usury, snake-charmers, outcasts, hired teachers, those taught by hired teachers, oil-pressers, informers, judges, actors, and the like; as well as atheists, eunuchs, misers, gamblers, liars, those who neglect their prayers, burnt offerings, twilight devotions, and purification; those born of illicit unions, those born of mixed castes, those of impure birth, those who subsist on the livelihood of non-Brahmins, those who live by crossing rivers, those who live by fetters, the husband of a Śūdra woman, Śūdras, village beggars, thieves, arsonists, poisoners, and sellers of Soma.

Singers, dancers, fletchers, those who live by astrology, those who travel across the great ocean, those afflicted with chronic diseases, long-distance travelers, outcasts, and the priests of outcasts— these are the polluters of the row when they do not desist.

A *kāruka* is an artisan. One who lives by means of birds such as hawks and the like is a *śakunijīva*. A *āveṣṭa* is a neck-strap used for the purpose of death. One who is hired at a sacrifice for the sake of slaughtering animals with that *āveṣṭa* is an *āveṣṭika*. One who lives on the dowry (*śulka*) collected from unchaste women is a *pauṃścala*. One who plays with snakes is an *āhituṇḍika*, meaning a snake-charmer. One who has fallen away from his religious order (*āśrama*) is a *pratyavasita*. One who lives by selling oil and such things is a *tailika*. A boatman is a *niyāmaka*, meaning one who leads the way for a caravan. One whose habit is hunting is an *ākrīḍī*. That which belongs to oneself is "one's own" (*sauva*); that which is both this and a mixture (*saṃkara*) is *sauvasaṃkara*, meaning a mixture of livelihoods. A cruel person is a *narāśaṃsa*; one who praises or flatters men is also a *narāśaṃsa*. One who goes to the great ocean is a traveler to other islands. One who has set out because he wishes to die is a *mahāpathika*. Or, one who has come from a distant foreign land via the great road is prohibited because his family and character are unknown. Those who do not turn back are those who do not perform penance (*prāyaścitta*).
Viṣṇu also says:

One should exclude from the Śrāddha those with deficient or extra limbs, those who follow forbidden occupations, those who act like cats (hypocrites), those who wear religious marks in vain, those who live by astrology, temple-priests, physicians, those whose sons are not yet married, those who perform sacrifices for many, those who officiate as priests for a village, those who sacrifice for Śūdras, Vratyas, those who sacrifice for them, those who work on festive occasions (eunuchs?), informers, teachers for a fee, those taught by paid teachers, those nourished by the food of Śūdras, those associated with outcasts, those who do not study the Vedas, those who have fallen away from the twilight prayers, royal servants, Ugras, those quarreling with their fathers, and those who have abandoned their father, guru, sacred fire, or Vedic study. One should avoid these at the Śrāddha.
For these have always been declared to be defilers of the row for a brahmin;
a wise man should avoid them with effort during the performance of a śrāddha rite.
The *vrātyas* are those who have fallen away from the *sāvitrī*. The *parvakāras* are those who work with reeds. An *ugra* is one who is fierce, violent, and exceedingly wrathful.
Āpastamba states: "A *śvitrin* (one afflicted with leucoderma), a *śipiviṣṭa*, one who approaches another's wife, and a *upaputra* (an illicit son) born of a *śūdra* father and a *brāhmaṇī* mother."

[496] He who is born from a Śūdra—who is equal to a Śūdra—as his father, upon a Brāhmaṇa woman of pure lineage; the characteristics of one equal to a Śūdra have been stated in the section on designations (saṃjñāprakaraṇa). Devala says:

The killers of a cow, a master, one who trusts them, an Annada, an ascetic, a kinsman, or a friend; those who abandon their mother, father, son, wife, or the sacred fire; the destroyer of a sacrifice; the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; a seller of Soma; a *vrātya*; and one who neglects his duties—these are the outcasts (*patita*). The paramour of a woman; the husband of a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*; the husband of a *didhiṣū*; one who teaches for a fee; one who hires himself out as a servant; a teacher of the Vedas; a priest for those unworthy of sacrifice; a seller of forbidden goods; a miser; one who causes confusion among the castes; an ignoble man; one fallen from purity; one who worships base deities; a usurer; a divider of a lineage; an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*); a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*); one with black spots on his back; a professional soldier; one who has been expelled from the community; one who has broken his vow of celibacy; a barbarian; a low-caste person; one who performs sacrifices for others; one who sets fire to houses; and the six types of eunuchs—these are the secondary sinners (*upapātakin*). Those who give false testimony due to affection or enmity; those who destroy property; those conquered by women; those who break bridges; actors and dancers; those who live by the sword; those who preach the Dharma for profit; perpetual beggars; those who subsist on penance; rogues; those who practice sorcery; hunters; atheists; slanderers; Śabaras; merchants; bards; the son of a remarried woman; one who nourishes himself alone; a tax-collector; one who travels by sea; one habituated to malevolent magic; an oil-presser; a teacher of the scriptures; a physician; a hired servant; a defiler of virgins; a killer of an embryo; a cruel man; a magician; a betrayer of friends; one who misappropriates gifts; a breaker of agreements; one harsh in speech or punishment; one incapable of work; a craftsman; an elephant-driver; and debtors—these are the ones subject to degradation (*pātanīyaka*). Those afflicted by the eight great diseases, those with impaired senses, those with missing limbs, and those with extra limbs are the polluters of the assembly line (*paṅktidūṣaka*). The eight great diseases are insanity, skin disease, consumption, asthma, diabetes, fistula-in-ano, and urinary stones. Those with impaired senses include the mentally dull, the blind, the one-eyed, the deaf, and the one with a withered arm. Those with foul ulcers where both parts are moistened are the most sinful of all.
These five types of lowest of men have been declared as those to be avoided;
they possess their own specific characteristics, and a distinction among them is observed here.
Likewise:
All these have been described in succession as wicked Brahmins—
despised for their actions, their birth, and the defects of their bodies.
Those lowest of men who have fallen due to the fault of their actions go to terrible hells,
abandoned here even by the virtuous.
Those who are afflicted by defects of the womb, as well as those afflicted by diseases born of the body—
even if they are innocent— should be avoided right here in this world.
The ungrateful, the slanderer, the cruel, the atheist, the deceitful, the rogue,
and the betrayer of friends— all these, by their very nature, have hell as their abode.
Furthermore, all these shall become unfit for food and unworthy of participating in ritual acts;
they are cast out from the state of Brahmanhood, following the power of their sinful faults.

The word "killer" (*ghātaka*) is connected individually with each of the seven [categories] beginning with the cow; the word "renouncer" (*tyāgin*) is connected with the five beginning with the mother. In that context, it should be understood as follows: the parents when aged, the son when an infant, the wife, and virtuous persons.

A "yajñāpahantṛ" is one who obstructs a sacrifice; a "niṣkriya" is one who fails to perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites. A "golabhartṛ" is one who adopts as his own son a child belonging to another lineage (*gotra*), specifically a Vaidheya. One who causes confusion of castes through delusion is an "anyagotrabhid. The definitions of a "kṛṣṇapṛṣṭha," a "mleccha," an "avareṭa," and a "karaṇa" are to be found in the section on terminology (*saṃjñāprakaraṇa*). A "brahmadharmā" is one for whom Brahman alone is dharma; the meaning is that he abandons all duties under the pretext of being a knower of Brahman. An "anārya" is an unrefined person. A "nikṛta" is one intent on the employment of deceit. A "pṛṣṭhaghātaka" is one who strikes from behind; the meaning is one who employs means of injury in secret, or one who cuts off the tail of a *camarī* cow, or one who engages in trade by pulling out the tails of oxen. A "tālāvacaraṇa" is a player of the *tāla* (clapping or cymbals); since the root *car* has the sense of eating, it may also mean one who eats the *tāla* fruit or the resin of the *tāla* tree. A "dharmapāṭhaka" is a reciter of those rules of conduct not ordained by the *Śruti* or *Smṛti*. A "prāyaścittavṛtti" is one whose livelihood is derived from wealth obtained by instructing others in penance, or by acting as a substitute for their penance, or by performing penances on behalf of others. A "dhūrta" is a deceiver. A "sādhanika" is one authorized over horses and other means of transport. A "mṛgayu" is one addicted to the vice of hunting. An "ātmambhari" is one devoted solely to filling his own belly without offering anything to the gods, ancestors, and others. A "bhrūṇaghna" is a destroyer of the embryo. A "kuhaka" is a hypocrite. A "dattāpavyayī" is one who squanders wealth given by others.
Yama said:
As long as one who does not purify the assembly looks upon the row [of diners],
the fruit [of the merit] is lost from that sight by that evil-minded person.
Likewise:
"As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras looks upon while seated in a row, all that gift of the donor is rendered fruitless; of this there is no doubt."
Manu says: As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [gifts] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the meritorious gift.

In this context, physical contact is not intended, because Yama has stated, "he looks upon. "Paurtika" means that which arises from *pūrta*—the fruit produced by gifts made outside the sacrificial altar.
Likewise:
"As many rows of diners as he beholds when [a guest] is among those unworthy of the row (*apāṅktya*)."
The foolish giver does not obtain the fruit of that many [gifts].
A fool is a simpleton.
[499] Having looked [upon him], a blind man destroys the merit of ninety [gifts], a one-eyed man that of sixty, a leper that of a hundred,
but one afflicted with a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the donor.

Because a blind person lacks sight, their proximity is indicated by this [rule]. Therefore, the meaning is that a blind person should not be attended upon from any distance within the range of vision of one who possesses eyes, provided that the space is unobstructed. In this context, "one afflicted with a foul disease" refers to a leper (*kuṣṭhin*).
Yama says: "A one-eyed man sees for sixty [hands], a eunuch for a hundred, and a leper for as far as he can see."
A hundred [become] afflicted with white leprosy, and a thousand likewise fall from their caste.
The word "defiles" (*dūṣayati*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The distinction in number is for the purpose of differentiating the penances according to the degree of the fault.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"O King, listen as I enumerate those who defile the row (*paṅkti-dūṣyas*)."
A gambler, a killer of an embryo, one afflicted by consumption, a younger brother who marries before his elder, and one who has been expelled from the community.
A village servant, a usurer, a singer, a seller of all things,
an arsonist, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* woman, and a seller of Soma.
A palmist, one supported by a king, an oil-presser, a forger,
one who disputes with his father, and he in whose house lives a paramour.
One who is falsely accused, a thief, one who lives by his craft,
a maker of arrows, a spy, a betrayer of friends, and an adulterer.
One who lacks vows, a teacher of such, likewise a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, one who has superseded his younger brother in marriage, one with a skin disease, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
One who is of bad character, a temple-priest, and one who lives by the stars—
one should recognize these here as those who defile the row of Brahmins.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One who betrays a friend, one with deformed nails, a eunuch, one suffering from consumption, one with white leprosy, a merchant by trade, one with black teeth, one who is bald, one who is one-eyed, one who is blind, one who is deaf, and one who is mentally dull."
Mute, lame, with crooked hands, impotent, afflicted with skin disease,
deformed, squint-eyed, leprous, red-eyed, humpbacked, dwarf, misshapen, and indolent.

An enemy, one of low birth, a cattle-herder, an outcaste, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, a younger brother who marries before his elder, and the son of a woman married before her elder sister.
A twice-born man who eats at the first *śrāddha* ceremony,
one who performs the consecration for the son of a *vṛṣalī*, one who is ignorant of the Rigveda (*anṛca*), and the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister remains unmarried (*didhiṣūpati*).
One who teaches for a fee, one who has been taught by a paid teacher,
one who rears bitches or elephants, a hunter, and a seller of Soma;
One who is falsely accused, a thief, an outcast, a usurer, a rogue, a slanderer, one who has abandoned the Vedas, and one who is cruel for having deserted his wife and the sacred fire;
The king’s domestic priest, a servant, one devoid of learning, or one who is envious;
a younger brother married before his elder, a menial, a cruel person, a fool, and likewise a temple-priest (devalaka).
One who indicates the stars for a living, one who calculates the lunar phases, a censurable person,
one who officiates at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, a eunuch, and others who are base—
these should not be appointed at a *śrāddha* feast; for they are defilers of the row, and their presence would make the rite corrupt.

In the Kūrma Purāṇa: one with diseased skin, one with deformed nails, one afflicted by leprosy, one with white leucoderma, one with black teeth, a drinker of intoxicants, one attached to a Śūdra woman, a killer of an embryo, and one who marries the widow of his younger brother; [these are excluded].

[501] A house-burner, one who eats from a sacrificial vessel, twice-born men who sell Soma, a younger brother who marries before his elder, a violent man, an elder brother whose younger brother has married first, and one who neglects the sacred rites;
One who seeks rebirth, a usurer, a fortune-teller by the stars,
one who lives by singing and instrumental music, one who is afflicted by disease, and one who is one-eyed;
One with missing limbs, one with redundant limbs, one who has broken his vow of chastity, a defiler of food, a *kuṇḍa* or *golaka*, one accused of a crime, and a temple-priest (*devala*).
One who betrays friends, a slanderer, one who is constantly subservient to his wife,
one who abandons his mother, father, or teacher, and likewise one who abandons his own wife;
One who betrays his lineage, one who has fallen from purity, a professional soldier, one who is childless, a false witness, a beggar, and one who lives by his own body;
One who travels by sea, one who commits murder, likewise one who breaks an agreement,
and one who delights in reviling the Vedas— these are especially those who defile the row.
Furthermore, all those whose food is not to be eaten and those who are unworthy of ritual acts,
as well as those who have violated their vows of celibacy and those who are accused of crimes, are to be avoided first of all.
O Brahmins, those whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of Śūdras, who have abandoned the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana),
and who are devoid of the great sacrifices (mahāyajña), are defilers of the assembly.

One who causes the destruction of what has been acquired, one who abandons the vow of silence while eating, and those who are characterized by tamas and rajas— such Brāhmaṇas, O Brāhmaṇas, are defilers of the assembly.
Thus end those who defile the assembly. Now, the miscellaneous [offenses].
Regarding this, Gautama says: [502]

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, one who has fallen from his caste, one who lives by such fallen ways, an atheist, a deserter of the army, one who marries before his elder brother, the husband of such a woman, one who sacrifices for a group of women, one who performs sacrifices for a village, one who neglects his sacred fires, a drunkard, a spy, a false witness, a fraudulent person, one who reviles the Vedas, one whose wife has a paramour, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa*, a seller of Soma, an arsonist, a poisoner, one who violates his vow of chastity, a servant of a guild, one who approaches forbidden women, a violent man, one who marries before his younger brother, the younger brother who so marries, one who causes an elder brother to marry again, one who causes a younger brother to marry again, one who abandons himself, one who is weak, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, the son of a remarried woman, a gambler, one born of an illicit union, a servant of a king, a counterfeit maker, the husband of a Śūdra woman, one who has renounced the world, a dandy, a usurer, a merchant, one who lives by a craft, one who lives by the bow, one who lives by music, one who lives by drumming, dancing, or singing, those who have divided their inheritance against the father's will, disciples, and those of the same lineage (*sagotra*).

"Dependent on them" (*tadvṛtti*) means one whose livelihood depends on those [fallen persons]. A "slayer of heroes" (*vīrahā*) is a slayer of kings. A "sacrificer for a village of women" (*strīgrāmayājaka*) is one who performs sacrifices for a group of women. A "magician" (*prātihārika*) is one who is a conjurer or a performer of illusions. "One to whom a paramour belongs" (*upapatiryasya*) means one whose wife is constantly unchaste. "One who has abandoned himself" (*tyaktātmā*) is one who has made an effort to give up his life. "One who does not mutter prayers" (*ajāpaḥ*) is one devoid of the recitation of the *gāyatrī* and other mantras. A "counterfeiter" (*prātirūpika*) is one who makes fraudulent imitations of goods. A "gladiator" (*jyāśīla*) is one devoted to the practice of weapons. And those who have taken a share from their father's house even against his will.
Yājñavalkya: One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is one-eyed, one born of a remarried woman,
one who teaches for a fee, a eunuch, a defiler of virgins, and one who is accused of a crime;

A betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, one who marries before his elder brother, one who abandons his mother, father, or teacher, one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress), the son of a *vṛṣala*, the husband of a woman previously married to another, a thief, and those whose actions are corrupt— these are censured.

Kaśyapa says: One should diligently avoid these Brahmins in all ritual acts: those who have lost their virility, officiating priests, killers of embryos, the deformed, and those who predict the future by means of the stars.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "Listen, I shall tell you who those are who have been designated as unworthy:
those with missing limbs, those with extra limbs, those who eat all things, and those who are outcasts."
Those with black teeth, those who study the Vedas for selfish ends, those who sell the Vedas,
those who corrupt the Vedas, or those who are devoid of the Vedic scriptures;
Those afflicted with skin diseases, the doubly naked, those who harm others,
those beset by public scandal, atheists, and liars as well— [these one should avoid].
Those who live by usury, those who follow forbidden occupations, those devoid of purity and proper conduct,
those who are excessively tall or emaciated, and those who are excessively stout or excessively hairy.
One who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) should exclude from the śrāddha those who are hairless,
as well as those devoted to the wives of others and those who are the husbands of low-caste women (vṛṣalī).
The deceitful, the thief, the greedy, the king’s servant, those who live by empty means,

one born of a woman of the same *gotra*, as well as those born of women with the same *pravara*, the younger brother who has established the sacred fires before his elder, and one who has already performed a marriage— these are excluded from the company at a meal.

Likewise: one who was initiated first but is younger, having abandoned his elder brother with whom he was united; one who abandons his mother and father; and likewise one who violates the bed of his guru.
A farmer who has completed his marriage but abandons a faultless wife,
an artisan who is negligent, a merchant who carries weapons—
these one should avoid at a *śrāddha*, as well as those whose lineage is unknown.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "I shall now declare those who are to be avoided; listen as I speak:
the gambler, the drunkard, the one afflicted with consumption, the cattle-herder, and the outcast."
A village servant, a usurer, a singer, a merchant,
one who burns down houses, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel belonging to a harlot, and a seller of Soma.
One who travels by sea, one with a skin disease, an oil-presser, a forger,
one who quarrels with his father, and he in whose house lives a paramour— these are unworthy of receiving gifts.
Likewise, one who is falsely accused, a thief, one who lives by his craft,
an informer, an evildoer, and he who betrays friends.
One who begs for alms from a group, an atheist, one devoid of the Vedas,
a madman, a heretic, a rogue, a killer of an embryo, and one who violates the teacher’s bed.
One who lives as a physician, one who serves as a messenger, one who goes to another's wife,
and one who sells the Vedas, religious observances, and austerities.
What is given to an atheist is lost; it yields no fruit either in this world or the next.
The same applies to one who misappropriates deposits, a gambler, and a reviler of the Vedas.
Likewise, what is given to a merchant, to an artisan devoid of righteousness,
or to a twice-born man born of a remarried woman, is like an offering poured upon ashes.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "These are to be eaten with effort; now learn from me those who are to be avoided:
the outcaste (patita), the accused (abhiśasta), the eunuch (klība), the kinsman (bandhu), the slanderer (piśuna), the deformed (vyaṅga), and the diseased (rogin)."

Those with deformed nails, those with blackened teeth, those afflicted with leprosy, those born of adultery or incest, those who wear matted hair, the younger brother who marries before his elder, one who has abandoned his soul, and those who act like the intoxicated, the insane, or the crane.
Those who follow the "cat-vow" (hypocrisy), the deceitful, the hypocrites, and the like;
the ungrateful, the nihilists, and likewise those dwelling in barbarian lands—[these are excluded].
One who knows the Dharma should avoid all these— at the times of the Śrāddha ceremony— the Triśaṅkus, Karavīras, Andhras, Cīnas, Draviḍas, and Kuṅkaṇas.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas, as well as the Saurāṣṭras and Gurjaras,
the Ābhīras and Kauṅkaṇas, and the Drāviḍas from the Deccan."
One should avoid the Brāhmaṇas of Āvantya and Māgadha.
Thus end the miscellaneous topics.

Now, for the purpose of fully understanding the faults and virtues that serve as the causes for the rejection or acceptance of Brahmins, the examination [of them] is described. Regarding this, it is said in the Mahābhārata:
"O Great King, at śrāddha ceremonies, a wise man should examine the Brahmins."
By means of lineage, conduct, age, beauty, learning, and discipline.
The mention of "family" (*kula*) and so forth is intended as an illustration for the mere qualification of being worthy to eat at a *śrāddha*. As stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Therefore, [the offering] should be given to a twice-born who has been examined and is a fit recipient (*pātra*)."
This ritual of the śrāddha is always difficult to perform and is full of many pitfalls.

Since this ritual of the *śrāddha* is "fraught with many pitfalls" (*bahucchala*)—such that one might wish to turn away from it due to any one of its various defects—it must be offered to a twice-born who has been examined for his worthiness by virtue of possessing Vedic learning, vows, and virtuous conduct, after first eliminating defects such as being a eunuch, a heretic, a usurer, a temple-priest, or one who observes the "cat-vow. Furthermore, this ritual perishes upon encountering even the slightest defect pertaining to the place, time, action, materials, the performer, or the recipient. Likewise, it possesses numerous subtle loopholes that are difficult to close, serving as gateways for the movement of *rākṣasas* who seize upon these pitfalls and create obstacles to the *śrāddha*. Therefore, it is a difficult undertaking. Consequently, it is rendered free of loopholes by those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*), who possess specific qualifications such as having kindled the *Nāciketa* fire three times, and who are established in yoga.
Thus it has been said:
"The ancestral sacrifice (paitra-yajña) was formerly declared by the great seers to be full of many flaws;
yet, through the skill of a yogi, it becomes free from obstacles and flawless."
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the company (*paṅktipāvana*), one should examine a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding this examination, Manu and Śātātapa provide instruction on the necessary qualities:
"One should examine from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas."
He is considered a worthy recipient for the offering of oblations to the gods and ancestors, and he is remembered as a guest.

"One should examine from afar" means that one should examine at a time much earlier than the actual moment of the *śrāddha* offering; for if the examination were conducted at that very time, it would cause distress to the Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, one should not perform the examination oneself directly, but rather have it done by another person, so that the Brāhmaṇa does not perceive: "He is examining me for this particular purpose. Or else, "from afar" refers to the lineage: one should examine whether ten or three generations on both the maternal and paternal sides have mastered the Vedas. The meaning is that such an examination—namely, that ten or three generations in both the paternal and maternal lineages are renowned for having mastered the Vedas, and that one is oneself a master of the Vedas—is necessarily to be performed at a *śrāddha*. For this very reason, Hārīta and Vyāsa stated: "Ten ancestors on both sides [should be] learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)."
He whose paternal and maternal ancestors for ten generations have been learned in the Vedas,
and who always approaches his wives only during their fertile periods as prescribed by dharma;
Śaṅkha and Likhita also have stated:

"He whose ten ancestors on both the maternal and paternal sides are known to be learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), wise, and *snātaka*s—such persons are purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*). Regarding the inability to ascertain ten generations, Chāgaleya has also prescribed an examination of three generations.
"One should provide everything for the *śrāddha* that is endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of learning and virtuous conduct, and renowned among the three classes of men. Thus it is said.

Medhātithi explains that "Veda" refers to the knowledge of the rites prescribed by the Veda; one who reaches its "pāra," meaning its completion, is a "vedapāraga. Therefore, a *śrotriya*—one who has studied the *mantra-saṃhitā* and the *Brāhmaṇa* alone—is designated as a *vedapāraga*. The mention of the *vedapāraga* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those qualities that purify the company at a meal (*paṅktipāvana*). Regarding the phrase "he is the *tīrtha* for offerings to gods and ancestors": a *tīrtha* is like a sacred ford. Just as those seeking water obtain it by descending through a ford, in the same way, the offerings (*havya-kavya*) made to such a Brāhmaṇa reach the ancestors. This is stated here incidentally regarding the act of giving: such a Brāhmaṇa becomes a guest (*atithi*) for other superior gifts, such as cattle, land, sesame, and gold. The meaning is that just as food given to a guest who has arrived in person yields great fruit due to the absence of hesitation, so too do the offerings to gods and ancestors yield great fruit when given without reservation to such a Brāhmaṇa.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
One should examine from afar those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas—
whether they are liked or disliked— and bring them at that time.

‘Desirable’ refers to friends; ‘undesirable’ refers to enemies. Their summoning—those who were previously examined at a much earlier time—must be carried out at that time, at the time of the ritual action. As stated in the *Yamasmṛti*:
“One should examine from afar those Brahmins who have observed their vows.”
Whether they be elders, ascetics, self-controlled, beloved, or otherwise.
Likewise: "One should first examine the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas,
who are purified of defects arising from the body, and who have fulfilled their vows."

"Previously" means prior even to the day of the *śrāddha*. "Bodily defects" include such things as being one-eyed or having a crooked limb. "Vows" (*vratāni*) refer to celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth.
As Devala says:
"Celibacy, speaking the truth, abstaining from honey and meat, silence, not begging, approaching [one's wife] only during her season—these and others are called vows."
Uśanas said:
In that regard, first of all, an examination of the recipient must be performed; for "recipient" (*pātra*) is a designation for one who is excellent.
Now, are there not also statements seen in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* that are intent on prohibiting the examination of Brāhmaṇas?
The Sun said: "It is exactly so, there is no doubt, just as you say, O sky-traveler.
This is my opinion too, O hero: one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa."
A Brahmin is composed of all the gods and likewise consists of all the worlds;
therefore, one should indeed worship him and not contemplate his faults.
"O son of Vinatā, one should consider only the birth and not the qualities.
Viśvāmitra said:
"A wise man should never examine a Brāhmaṇa."
Having scrutinized the donors, they lead those who have given [such gifts] certainly to hell.
That lowest of the twice-born, a Chandala by his deeds, who consents to an examination out of a desire for gain, is cooked in hell.

If a recipient consents to the examination of himself being conducted by donors—saying, "Examine me; if I am virtuous, then let that which you desire be given"—he is certainly cooked in hell like a *caṇḍāla* of action. Thus, the scriptural hearing of the transgression for both the donor and the recipient who consent to the examiner contradicts the injunction for examination.

This is not a fault, because prohibitive statements concern direct examination. That examination which occurs through questions and answers—such as "In what country were you born? What is your lineage? What are you studying? What have you heard?"—is what is prohibited by these [rules].
Thus Gobhila says: "The twice-born man who asks, 'What are you like? or 'What do you know? must be addressed.
For ten thousand years, he sinks into blinding darkness accompanied by tears.
Gautama said:
"But the donor who asks a twice-born man about his learning, his sacred knowledge, and his lineage,
and he who answers him— both of them go to hell."
Bṛhaspati says: If a wicked-minded person, when told, "I shall give this [reward] once you have studied this," should nevertheless study the scriptures or the Veda, he is born as a dog after death.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"There is no questioning of the Vedas; he who questions them is a doer of evil.
Such a person falls away from the fruit of the Vedas, and likewise, the giver falls away from the fruit of his gift. [510]
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "He who, through persistent urging, gives a gift to a Brāhmaṇa goes first to hell, and the Brāhmaṇa follows after him."
A question concerning the subject matter of study and so forth is "anuyoga. [As it is said:
"However many syllables of the Veda one might employ for the sake of material gain, for that many instances one incurs the sin of killing a fetus and indeed the sale of the Veda."

There is no fault whatsoever in examining [the recipient] by means other than direct personal inspection, because the rule for giving prescribes it for one who possesses merit, and because such merit is difficult to ascertain without examination.
As for that which is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"In the gift of food, not even the slightest consideration of the recipient should be made."
Food should indeed be given everywhere by one who desires the Dharma, O twice-born one.
Yet, even if [the recipient] is full of faults, he is faultless; even if [the giver] possesses qualities, it brings excessive merit. Therefore, food should always be given with every effort;
however, in rites for the ancestors, a wise man should examine [the recipient] with great care.
This, however, refers to the giving of food other than that for a *śrāddha*, because examination is prescribed specifically for the *śrāddha*.
Thus Manu says:
"One who knows the Dharma should not examine a Brāhmaṇa at a rite for the gods."
However, regarding rites for the ancestors, a wise man should examine [the recipient] with great care.
Śaṅkha says: One should not examine Brahmins when performing rites for the gods with diligence;
however, they say that examination is appropriate when a rite for the ancestors has arrived.
Regarding this examination of Brāhmaṇas, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The examination [is required] for the Śrāddha, but not for the rite dedicated to the gods. Viṣṇu states:
"In a rite for the gods, one should not examine the Brāhmaṇa; one should examine him with care in a rite for the ancestors."

Regarding this examination of Brāhmaṇas, Gautama states: "And likewise in the case of *havir* offerings; some say only in the *śrāddha*. Here, "*havirṣu*" refers to rites for the gods (*daivakarma*). The plural number is used for the sake of completeness. In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), which are subordinate to those for the gods, as well as in other divine rites, those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) should be fed, while thieves and others are to be excluded. However, the opinion of some is that those enumerated starting from Durvāla are to be excluded only in the *śrāddha*, not in the divine rite.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"A man should never examine Brāhmaṇas in rites for the gods;
however, it is indeed heard in the tradition that examination is required in rites for the ancestors."

In the Mahābhārata: A Kṣatriya who knows the duty of giving should not examine Brāhmaṇas when it concerns rites for the gods or the ancestors; however, they say that examination is proper [in other contexts].
In this world, the deities worship with divine power alone.

Being protected by divine splendor, the virtuous worship the deities; they do not depend upon those who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) and the like for the sake of warding off obstacles to their respective rites, just as one does not require cow’s ghee for that purpose. Therefore, having invited and prepared [the offerings] for the deities, one should give them to all the Brāhmaṇas. The meaning is that one should not perform an absolute examination of their merits and defects therein. Here it is asked: By what means was the examination obtained such that its prohibition is enjoined regarding the giving of food to the deities? We reply: It is obtained through the injunction of the meritorious and the prohibition of the defective. For, when he is being examined, the Brāhmaṇa is known either by his merit or by his defect. And it is not possible to accept or reject him without knowing him. Thus, the injunction and prohibition regarding merit and defect would serve the purpose of introducing [the rule]. Therefore, by those two alone, the examination is obtained by implication (*arthāt*). How, then, should the futility of the injunction and prohibition regarding merit and defect—rendered redundant by the prohibition of examination—be avoided? Now, it may be held that this is not a prohibition, but a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) of the examination, intended to indicate that the injunction and prohibition regarding the Brāhmaṇa possessing merit or defect apply specifically to the giving of food to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Or, if it is a prohibition, the view is that the injunction and prohibition, which take the form of general rules, are restricted (*upasaṃhāra*) to the giving of food to the ancestors alone.

That is not so, because specifically in the case of giving food to the gods (*daiva*), one observes both injunctions and prohibitions regarding Brahmins that pertain to merits and faults. For instance:
"Offerings for the ancestors (*kavya*) and oblations (*haviṣ*) should be given only to one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
And likewise:
Manu has declared those Brahmins who are thieves, outcasts, eunuchs, or who follow the ways of nihilists to be unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

In this context, the word *havya* refers to that which pertains to the gods (*daiva*). Therefore, the prohibition against testing [the recipient] applies to the giving of food for the sake of the gods, as such testing would be improper.

In this regard, we shall first state the solution approved by Śaṅkhadhara: when Brāhmaṇas belonging to both the primary (mukhya) and secondary (anukalpika) categories have assembled, those who are primary should be appointed for the principal ancestral rite (paitrya); whereas others who are free from defects but not particularly distinguished by qualities should be appointed for the Vaiśvadevika rite. Such is the intended meaning of the statement, "In the divine rite, one should not examine [the invitees]. However, his own preferred view is as follows: since the restriction regarding the possession of qualities—expressed in the passage beginning with "to one learned in the Vedas" (śrotriyāyaiva)—and the prohibition regarding those with defects—expressed in the passage beginning with "those who are thieves"—are established by the context as applying specifically to the *havya* (oblation) connected with the Śrāddha, the scope of the rule "in the divine rite, one should not examine" refers to other divine rites (*daiva-karma*) distinct from the Vaiśvadevika which forms a limb of the Śrāddha; that is, it refers to those divine rites where Brāhmaṇas are to be fed as recipients of the oblation offered to the deities.
As for that which is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa by Sauriṇya—that at a Śrāddha one need not examine the person to be fed—it says:
"The Vedic revelation declares that a Śrāddha should be given only after examination;
and O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, straightforwardness is the highest quality."
But he who, abiding in sincerity, gives a śrāddha without examining [the recipient], his ancestors and the deities are satisfied; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, that too should be resolved by this very same principle; or else, it should be explained as referring to *tīrtha-śrāddha* (funeral rites at sacred sites) and to guests (*atithi*). And so it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"At sacred sites, one should never examine Brahmins in any way whatsoever."
"One should feed a seeker of food who has arrived, according to the teaching of Manu.
Regarding the prohibition of testing a guest, it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One should appoint an unknown twice-born man to the role of a guest at the *śrāddha* ceremonies."
Furthermore, an examination of a Brāhmaṇa other than a guest must be performed.
The method of examination is shown in the *Vṛddha-Manusmṛti* and the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Character is to be known from living together; purity from one's conduct."
Wisdom is to be known through conversation; by these three means, one examines a worthy recipient.

"Living together" (*saṃvasana*) means residing for a long time in a very nearby place. "Conversation" (*saṃkathana*) refers to discussion of the scriptures in a friendly spirit for the purpose of determining the true meaning. "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) means either intelligence or superior knowledge.
Jātūkarṇya states that one should accept those Brāhmaṇas who have been determined to possess the required qualities at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Therefore, one should carefully examine those most proficient in the meaning of the Vedas before engaging them at a *śrāddha*.
Even a very small gift, when given to one who has been well-examined, attains infinity.
However, the abandonment [of those] determined to be possessed of faults is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"One should know that those in whom faults are clearly seen, or those who are avoided by the virtuous,
or even those [whose faults become known] through living together, must be diligently shunned."
Devala said:
Among Brahmins as well, one should exclude all those unworthy of the company at rites performed for specific desires;
having examined the Brahmins in many ways, one should invite those who purify the assembly.
Thus concludes the examination of Brāhmaṇas.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the illustrious Paṇḍita Hemādri, the chief minister of all the illustrious departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the great king of kings.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Brāhmaṇas," in the Śrāddhakalpa is completed.
[514] Now begins the seventh chapter:
The Section on the Determination of Those Who Are to Be Excluded.

It is described by the wise Hemādri, who is a supreme mine of merit, a mountain for the river of compassion, a beautiful ocean for the investigation of reality and unreality, radiant with the light of wisdom,
and a nectar-ocean for the speech of the venerable ones.
Now, the multitude of creatures here must be brought to the vicinity of the funeral feast.
Now, in connection with the Brahmins who are to be avoided, other persons also who must be excluded from the *śrāddha* are mentioned. Regarding this, Devala says:
"One with missing limbs, an outcast, a leper, one with a sore, a *pukkasa*, and an atheist..."
Cocks, pigs, and dogs should be avoided from afar at śrāddha ceremonies.
One should avoid one who is deformed, impure, naked, intoxicated, or afflicted by a disease; a woman in her menses; one dressed in blue or saffron garments; and one whose ear is severed.
One should avoid weapons, iron, lead, and those wearing soiled garments at śrāddha ceremonies; one should also avoid food that has been kept overnight.

A *pukkasa* is a specific type of barbarian (*mleccha*). An *nāstika* is one devoid of fear regarding the next world. A *śūkara* is a village pig. A *bībhatsu* is one who is loathsome. An *aśuci* is one lacking purity. A *nagna* is defined by the characteristics stated in the section on terminology. A *chinnakarṇa* is one whose ear has been sewn back; for the other [defects], such a person is already mentioned as having deficient limbs. "Weapon" refers to a sword, a dagger, and so forth. "Kālāyasa" is iron. "Sosa" is the mineral known as lead (*nāga*). One whose lower and upper garments (*antarīya-uttarīya*) are soiled is "one with soiled garments. Like iron and the other items, food that has stood overnight should also be kept away from the place where the *śrāddha* is performed.
Viṣṇu:
Those with missing or extra limbs, Śūdras, outcasts, and those suffering from chronic diseases must not behold the Śrāddha.
Āpastamba: [The same].
One should guard the Śrāddha against the sight of dogs and those who are "apapātra" (excluded from the company).
"Apapātra" means those whose qualities as worthy recipients have fallen away. "Parirakṣeta" means one should ward them off.
— Uśanas.
A village pig, a cat, a cock, a mongoose, a Śūdra, a menstruating woman, and the husband of a Śūdra woman must be removed to a distance—
from the site of the *śrāddha*, as is understood from the context. By "husband of a Śūdra woman" is meant a Brāhmaṇa or other member of the higher castes who has no wife of his own caste.
Manu says:
A Cāṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, and likewise a dog,
as well as a woman in her menses— these six should not look upon twice-born men while they are eating.
In this context, proximity is indicated by the act of looking. Whatever is looked upon by these [unworthy persons] during an oblation, a gift, or a meal—
whether it be an offering for the gods or for the ancestors— that becomes ineffective.

"In the *homa*": in the *agnihotra* and other rites, or in the *śānti-homa* and similar offerings. "In giving" (*pradāne*): regarding gifts such as cows, land, or gold, for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*). "In feeding" (*bhojye*): in the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). "In the divine oblation" (*daive haviṣi*): in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices. "In the ancestral rite" (*pitrye*): in the *śrāddha*. The meaning is that whatever is looked upon by these—such as Cāṇḍālas and others—becomes "untrue" (*ayathātatha*); that is to say, it accomplishes the very opposite of the purpose for which it was performed. Although this occurs in the context of the *śrāddha*, nevertheless, on account of the specific statement, this prohibition applies elsewhere as well, such as in the *homa* and so forth. Others, however, maintain that this prohibition applies only to the *homa* and other acts connected specifically with the *śrāddha*. They explain it as follows: "In the *homa*": at the place of the *agnaukaraṇa-homa*. "In giving": at the place where the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the distribution of food take place. "In feeding": at the place where food is prepared, such as the kitchen. Because of the word "and" (*ca*), if food or the like is even in another location looked upon by Cāṇḍālas and others, it becomes untrue; therefore, the intention is that these persons must be kept far away from the site of the *śrāddha*.
The pig destroys [the merit] by its smell, the cock by the wind from its wings;
the dog by the casting of its gaze, and one born of a low caste by touch.

"One born of a low caste" refers to a Śūdra. And regarding the prohibition against his touching the implements for the Śrāddha at a Śrāddha for the twice-born, this [prohibition] does not apply to one's own [Śūdra servant].
"If he be lame, or even one-eyed, or even a servant of the giver;
or if he have a deficient or redundant limb—one should remove him from there."
"Preṣyaḥ" means a servant. By the use of the word "api" (also), others as well—such as relatives who happen to be present by chance—are to be removed. Yama says:
"The cock, the village pig, the crow, and also the cat..."
The husband of a low-caste woman, a low-caste man, a eunuch, and a menstruating woman—
these should always be strictly avoided at the time of a śrāddha ceremony.
A cock destroys an unprotected *śrāddha* with the wind from its wings;
a village pig, by its smell; and a crow, by its cry.
A dog kills by the casting of its gaze, a cat by hearing;
the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī) by a gift, and likewise a low-caste man (vṛṣala) by his eyes;
a eunuch (ṣaṇḍha) kills by his shadow, and a menstruating woman by touch.
Lame, one-eyed, with a withered arm, or afflicted with leprosy, he shall become a servant to the donor;
or, having either missing limbs or redundant limbs, he shall quickly lead him [to hell] thereafter.

‘Biḍālaḥ’ means a cat. ‘Vṛṣalaḥ’ refers to what is stated in the section on technical terms, or it means a Śūdra. ‘Asaṃvṛtam’ means an uncovered place. ‘Śravaṇena’ means by the hearing of sound. ‘Dānena’ means having been made a worthy recipient; this is the meaning. Hārīta says:
“Whether in a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, even a woman who drinks liquor may touch the sacrificial ground.”
A woman in her menses and an unchaste woman, when the funeral offering (nivāpa) has arrived.
"Nivāpa" refers to the ancestral rite (pitṛkarma). From the word "samupasthita," it should be understood as starting from the commencement of the cooking. Regarding this, Vyāghrapāt says:
"The drinker of spirits, the wanton woman, and likewise one whose husband has been previously married to another..."
At the ancestral rite (śrāddha), they should not look [at one another] from the beginning of the pouring (āvāpa) onwards, in due order.

"Āvāpaḥ" refers to the placing of rice and other ingredients into a cooking pot for the purpose of preparing a meal, beginning from that point until the completion of the food. The meaning is that during the śrāddha rite, those Brahmins who are eating food items—whether staying in the kitchen, the dining hall, or elsewhere—must be kept at a distance so that those such as liquor-drinkers do not see them. The mention of "liquor-drinkers and others" is intended to include all those who are disreputable. As Gautama says:

If dogs, *caṇḍālas*, or outcasts look upon the food, it becomes defiled; therefore, one should perform the *śrāddha* in a screened or concealed place. Alternatively, if it has not been done so, one should scatter sesame seeds all around. Or, a "purifier of the row" (*paṅktipāvana*) seated at the head of the row shall neutralize that entire defect. Bṛhaspati also says: [519] If dogs and the like look upon the food, it becomes as if defiled. For this reason, one should perform the *śrāddha* in a screened place. If it is not done thus, then one should scatter sesame seeds on all sides. Or, a purifier of the row, having been placed at the head of the row, shall neutralize even all such defects. Bṛhaspati also says:
One should provide protection at a *śrāddha* ceremony from the dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), the eunuch, the outcaste, the dog, the pig, the cock, the menstruating woman, and the *caṇḍāla*.
Or he should give [the food] in an enclosed space, or scatter the earth with sesame seeds;
or, while seated, the purifier of the row (paṅktipāvana) should cause that defect to flow away.

A *śvapāka* is a *niṣāda*. A *ṣaṇḍha* is a eunuch. "He should perform protection" means he should act in such a way that there is no defilement caused by the sight of the *śvapāka* and others. "In enclosed places" means in covered areas. The mention of "the earth" is illustrative; as many items as have been defiled by *śvapākas* and the like, so many should be strewn with black sesame seeds. Or, one who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*) should "remove" the defect, that is, take it away.

Viṣṇu states that the place for the *śrāddha* must be enclosed in such a way that the performer of the *śrāddha* does not see even those who are standing at a distance but have been forbidden from looking on. He says: "One should perform the *śrāddha* in an enclosed space; one should not look upon a menstruating woman, a dog, a village pig, or a village cock. One should diligently show the *śrāddha* to a goat. Here, "*śrāddha*" refers to the articles intended for the *śrāddha*. "*Aja*" means a black he-goat. For it is held that by seeing him, the articles defiled by evil glances become purified; therefore, one should show him [the *śrāddha*] with diligence.
In the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*: "Naked persons and others should never behold this śrāddha;
for if it is seen by them, [the offerings] go neither to the fathers nor to the grandfathers."

The ellipsis to be supplied is "the sacrificial offerings were seen by these [people]. "Naked ones" (*nagna*) refers to those who have abandoned the Vedas. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those of that same class who have abandoned the performance of Vedic rites are included. Thus it is stated in that very same work: "Since the Triple Veda (*trayī*) is the covering for all beings, those who indeed abandon it out of delusion are remembered as 'naked ones'."

The *trayī* is the Veda; *saṃvaraṇam* means a covering or cloak. Just as a cloak protects people from cold, wind, and so forth, so too the *trayī*, by causing one to perform one's own duties (*svadharma*), protects from sufferings; thus it shares the likeness of a garment.
Those who follow the doctrines of the Buddhist disciples (*śrāvaka*), the Nirgranthas (Jainas), the Śāktas, the Jīvakas, and the followers of Kapila—those people are indeed "naked" and the like.

"Bauddhas" refers to the followers of Sugata (Buddhists). "Śrāvakas" refers to the Śvetapaṭas (White-robed ones). "Nirgranthas" refers to the Jains. "Śāktas" refers to the Kaulas. "Jīvakas" refers to the followers of Bṛhaspati, that is to say, the Cārvākas. "Kapila" refers to one belonging to the Lokāyata school; those composed by him are the "Kāpilas. In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"That man who wears matted hair in vain, who shaves his head in vain, and who remains naked in vain..."
And those men who are perpetrators of the great sins (mahāpātakin), such as the naked ones and others.
In the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*, Śambhu said:
"O Blessed One, today I am asking you properly about the naked ascetics and others."
Tell me everything, in every way, in full detail, exactly as it is.
Thus addressed, the highly effulgent Bṛhaspati said to him:
"Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when the asuras had been defeated,
all these [heretics] were created by the Self-born One as the presiding authorities over heresy."
[521] While all the Asuras were performing austerities, O King,
Viṣṇu,
the all-pervading Lord whose nature is yoga, being impelled by the gods, resorted to the great illusion that is so difficult to cross and then deluded them for the sake of creating obstacles.
That high-minded one, appearing in the form of a Buddha, spoke to those deluded ones, saying:
"All the gods can be conquered by you through these means."
Having established themselves in the Buddha-dharma, the Śākyas shone forth.
To them, at the end, the Arhat said: "Having become such as he was, and possessing the Dharma together with knowledge, you are therefore remembered as Arhats."
The disciples of the Buddha, the Nirgranthas, and likewise the Siddhaputras—
all these are to be known as Arhats who act with malice.
To those whom he addressed, saying, "Live, having completely cast off the affliction of the Three Vedas," they were born as those known as Jīvakas, excluded from all the sacred laws.
Having become like a celestial being in the sky, he indeed established those doctrines;
they are called the Kāpilas, for Kapila is the Sun.
"Practice them," he said to them, "this command of mine is exceedingly brilliant.
They too should be known as Carakas, deceitful practitioners of unrighteousness.

"Long" (*dīrgha*) and "for a long time" (*ciram*) are thus declared; or [it refers to] the subtle form of the Dharma. Because they were told, "Practice the Dharma," they became those with "long vision" (*dīrghacakṣuṣaḥ*); and because they wore blue rags (*cīra*), they are therefore called *Cīrakas*.
And when Viṣṇu spoke through his illusory power, saying, "This perfectly awakened one is pure; take refuge in that Dharma," for they (the Vaiṣṇavas) are indeed proclaimed to be pure.
You, the Blessed One, have declared that you exist within all beings;
those who are known as Sātvatas are also called Bhāgavatas.
And whoever are the eaters of excrement, those adorned with skull-ornaments,
the Śaivas, the Pāśupatas, and others such as the Pāñcarātras;
Likewise, all other evil-minded ones who belong to the demonic deities are known by their sound as the protectors of the threefold dharma for the worlds.
Because they cause that [truth] to be castrated, for that reason they are called *pāṣaṇḍas*.
Consequently, bound by their own actions, they are established here in this state.
Furthermore, having been born among the Asuras through that cultivated karma,
they reached hell once again, being cultivated by those very same actions.
The Buddhist laywomen, the Nirgranthas, the Śākyas, the Jīvakas, the Pāśupatas,
the Carakas, the Cīrakas, the pure-washed ones, the Siddhaputras, and the Sātvatas.
Those who propound selflessness, who do not perform sacrifices, and who are nihilists,
though abiding in their own duties, are born again and again.
Those men who wear matted hair in vain, those who are shaven-headed in vain, and those who maintain the sacred fire in vain—
all these and others who stand outside the three Vedas are people such as the naked ones and the like.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Those twice-born who have been duly initiated with Vedic mantras and are perpetually entitled to perform sacrifices— they are undoubtedly [institutes of] the stages of life (āśramas)."
Then Brahmā spoke to those heretics who were not refined by mantras, excluded from sacrifices, and likewise wandering in the lower realms.
Those who are family outcasts, those who are breathless, hunters, boxers, and leapers,
as well as those refined by evil deeds— these are proclaimed to be the wrong paths.
All the Mlecchas and those of evil mind will worship you;
for this reason, these such as the naked ones are considered censurable.
A śrāddha meal touched or even seen by these— by killers of Brahmins, ungrateful persons, atheists, and those who violate the teacher’s bed— goes indeed to the Dānavas.
One should avoid by sight those who are thieves and those who are cruel,
and one should also avoid all others who perform evil deeds.
Those who delight in sinful speech toward the deities and the sages,
as well as those who look upon the asuras and the yātudhānas with such intent, go downward.
A eunuch, a discarded person, a cock, a village pig,
and a dog destroy all *śrāddha* offerings by their mere sight.
It must not be seen under any circumstances by those who have suffered loss, by those afflicted with long-term diseases, nor by those who are fallen or impure.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "That śrāddha which is performed when there is the sound arising from a lizard or a mortar, or especially from a winnowing basket, shall go to futility."

Thus ends the section titled "The Description of Those Who Should Not Be Dismissed" in the Śrāddha-kalpa of the Pariśeṣa-khaṇḍa, within the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi composed by the illustrious Hemādri, the Paṇḍita and Chief Minister of all the illustrious departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the Great King of Kings.
The seventh chapter is completed.
[524] Now begins the eighth chapter:
The Section on the Determination of Substances to be Added.
Beholding whose form the world abandons its darkness along with the surges of grief,
he declares what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
All substances here are like the mountain of gold.

Now, once the substrates for the offering of oblations (*havis*) in the *śrāddha* have been determined, the substances to be offered are described in response to the inquiry regarding what should be cast therein. These substances, which belong to oneself, are to be offered after being relinquished with the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and so forth—in mind. Their ownership is established through means well-known in the world; and those means consist of the rules for wealth acquired by righteous methods.
Accordingly, Āpastamba, having enumerated the praiseworthy substances, says:

By these [means], the ancestors experience an even more intense joy and satisfaction for a much longer duration; likewise, by means of wealth acquired through righteous methods and bestowed upon worthy recipients (*tīrtha*).

"Joy" (*prīti*) is an excess of contentment; "satisfaction" (*tṛpti*) is the cessation of suffering. "Much longer" (*drāghīyāṃsam*) means for a very long time. "Acquired through righteous methods" (*dharmānuhṛtena*) means earned by lawful means. "Bestowed upon worthy recipients" (*tīrthapratipannena*) means given to a virtuous recipient (*satpātra*). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state:
Having acquired wealth through righteous means, one should give it to the ancestors.

Regarding this, Sumantu, referring to the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), says: "A wise man should perform [the rites] with wealth acquired by righteous means. Thus, one should carry out the rituals with wealth obtained through lawful means.

Therefore, grains, vegetables, fruits, roots, milk, and so forth, acquired solely by righteous means, should be offered at a *śrāddha*. Righteous methods for acquiring wealth are shown in the *Smṛtis*; regarding this, Manu says:
"There are seven righteous ways of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, the application of labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous."

‘Means of acquiring wealth’ (*vittāgamāḥ*) are the methods for earning property. ‘Lawful’ (*dharmyāḥ*) means that, in the view that they serve human ends (*puruṣārtha*), they do not produce sin; however, in the view that they serve ritual purposes (*kratvartha*), as will be explained later, they are beneficial to the performance of duty (*dharma*) and are causes for its sixfold excellence (*ṣāḍguṇya*). Among these, ‘inheritance’ (*dāya*) is when another person’s property becomes one’s own through the relationship of ownership; here, the relationship of ownership itself is stated as the means. ‘Gain’ (*lābha*) is the acquisition of water, grass, wood, and so forth, which have not been appropriated by another, or the discovery of hidden treasure (*nidhi*). ‘Purchase’ (*kraya*) is the bartering of goods. ‘Conquest’ (*jaya*) is the defeat of an enemy. ‘Lending’ (*prayoga*) is the handing over of another’s property for the sake of interest. ‘Application of labor’ (*karmayoga*) is a connection established through ritual service—such as officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or priesthood—or through craft or service. ‘Acceptance’ (*pratigraha*) is the taking of property being given. A ‘virtuous acceptance’ (*satpratigraha*) is an acceptable, non-prohibited acceptance. Here, the quality of being ‘virtuous’ (*sat*) should also be understood to apply to inheritance and the other means. Among these, inheritance, gain, and purchase are common to all. Conquest belongs only to the Kṣatriya, and it is an illustration for fines, taxes, and so forth. Lending belongs only to the Vaiśya, and it is an illustration for agriculture, trade, and so forth. The application of labor characterized by officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and priesthood, as well as acceptance, belong only to the Brāhmaṇa. The application of labor characterized by craft belongs only to artisans. However, the application of labor characterized by service belongs only to Śūdras and others.

And so says Gautama: "The owner [is established] in the cases of inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and finding; that which is obtained is the additional share of the Brāhmaṇa, that which is won in battle is that of the Kṣatriya, and that which is earned by service is that of the Vaiśya and the Śūdra."

That acquisition which is made through a connection with the life of the owner is *dāya*, meaning "inheritance"; for example, the paternal wealth of sons and grandsons, and the ancestral wealth [of the latter]. That acquisition which is contingent upon the life of the owner is *saṃvibhāga*, "partition," such as the property of brothers and others belonging to those brothers who have already divided. The appropriation of water, grass, wood, and so forth, which has not been previously taken by another, is *parigraha*. The discovery of a treasure-trove and the like is *adhigama*. When these causes exist, one becomes the "owner. "Additional" (*adhika*) means exclusive or specific. "Acquired" (*labdha*) refers to what is obtained through receiving gifts, teaching, or officiating at sacrifices. "Conquered" (*vijita*) refers to what is obtained through victory or fines; this is the additional property of the Kṣatriya. For the Vaiśya and Śūdra, "earnings" (*nirviṣṭa*) are the additional property. Among these, for the Vaiśya, what is obtained from agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth, is "earnings. For the Śūdra, what is obtained in the form of wages for service to the twice-born and the like is "earnings. Likewise, for those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) and the inverse order (*pratiloma*), whatever is specifically mentioned as their exclusive means of livelihood well-known in the world—such as "the charioteership of horses for Sūtas"—all that is expressed by the word "earnings" (*nirviṣṭa*), because all of it consists of the nature of wages. This is according to the lexicographical rule: "The term *nirveśa* denotes both wages and enjoyment."
In this context, Nārada speaks regarding wealth as that which is to be acquired:
"That [wealth] should be known as threefold—white, variegated, and black;
furthermore, its classification is to be understood as sevenfold."
The meaning is that for each of the seven types of white wealth, there are seven subdivisions.

Wealth acquired through learning, valor, austerity, a daughter, officiating at sacrifices for others, disciples, and inheritance constitutes the sevenfold white wealth; its increase is likewise of seven kinds.

The word *āgata* (obtained) is connected with each of the preceding terms, beginning with *śruta*. That which is obtained through *śruta*—that is, through learning (*vidyā*) as the cause; that which is won through valor (*śaurya*) as the cause, or acquired in the form of wages (*bhṛti*); that which is obtained through a gift (*pratigraha*) caused by asceticism (*tapas*). In this context, regarding the "whiteness" (*śuklatva*) of the gift, the purity of both the giver and the recipient should also be understood as a contributing factor. "Obtained through a daughter" (*kanyāgata*) refers to what is received from the father-in-law and others at the time of accepting a daughter in marriage. "Obtained through a pupil" (*śiṣyāgata*) refers to what is acquired from a pupil being taught, such as a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*), caused by the act of instruction. "Inherited" (*anvayāgata*) means obtained as a legacy. In these cases, the quality of "whiteness" should be understood according to the specific entitlement. "Rise (*udaya*) is also of that same kind" means that even the fruit born of actions performed with that wealth is "white. "White" means not mixed with suffering (*duḥkha*).
That which is acquired through usury, agriculture, trade, crafts, tolls, or service,
as well as what is obtained from one who has rendered assistance, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).

"Lending at interest" (*kusīda*) is the investment of wealth for the purpose of increasing one's capital. "Agriculture" (*kṛṣi*) is the work of the plough. "Trade" (*vāṇijya*) is the increase of wealth through the business of buying and selling. In this context, when lending at interest and the others are practiced by anyone other than a Vaiśya during times of distress, they cause the wealth to become "mottled" (*śabala*). However, when not in distress, they cause it to be merely "black" (*kṛṣṇa*). For a Vaiśya, however, these are always "white" (*śukla*). "Crafts" (*śilpa*) is the work of artisans; even that, when performed by one person for another, is a cause of mottledness. "Toll" (*śulka*) is the tax levied on merchants and the like; and that is "mottled" for those other than the king. "Service" (*anuvṛtti*) is the attendance upon the twice-born; wealth acquired thereby is "mottled" for anyone other than a Śūdra. Whatever is received in the form of a return for a favor rendered is "mottled" for everyone. And "mottledness" consists in being slightly productive of demerit (*pratyavāya*). The fruit of an action performed with such wealth is also "mottled," meaning it is permeated with suffering.
That which is acquired through gambling, theft, distress, forgery, violence,
or by means of fraud— that is called "black" for all.

One who, while in the service of a king or similar authority, somehow obtains a favor from someone that he himself had expected, and in return says to him, "If I cause you to perform this favor for me, then you must give this to me," thereby acquiring wealth, is a *pārśvika*. Likewise, one who acquires wealth by demonstrating the averting of calamities is also a *pārśvika*. Furthermore, one who takes wealth from a person of high caste and, having no desire to return it, does not stand before that person, is also a *pārśvika*. The wealth acquired by such means is "black" (*kṛṣṇa*). "Gambling" (*dyūta*) refers to playing with dice and the like; the wealth acquired by that is black for all except Kṣatriyas. "Theft" (*caurya*) is secret misappropriation. "Oppression" (*ārti*) is the infliction of pain upon others. "Forgery" (*pratirūpaka*) is the making of counterfeit gems, gold, and so forth, for the purpose of deceiving others. "Violence" (*sāhasa*) is seizing property in the presence of the owner while accepting the risk of losing one's own life. "Fraud" (*vyāja*) is hypocrisy, such as performing asceticism for show. Wealth acquired by these means is "black" for everyone, resulting primarily in suffering.
By means of that, buying and selling, giving and receiving,
as well as various activities and even the enjoyment of wealth, proceed.
Whatever a person performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit for that, both in this world and after death.

"By whatever kind [of substance]"—whether white, variegated, or black—"whatever" one performs for the sake of the next world, such as giving and so forth, or for this world, such as rites for peace (*śāntika*) or prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), "the fruit thereof becomes of that same kind. By a white [substance], the fruit is white, meaning free from suffering. By a variegated [substance], it is variegated, meaning a mixture of pleasure and pain. By a black [substance], it is black, meaning much cause of suffering and little pleasure.
As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Merit performed with white wealth shall yield abundant fruit."
Variegated wealth yields middling fruit; black wealth yields inferior fruit.
In the Brahma-world: he who, endowed with faith, performs a righteous act with white wealth,
having found a worthy recipient for that purpose, attains divinity thereby.
With a passionate disposition and with wealth that is mixed, one should give gifts to those who ask; such a person experiences the fruit of that in human existence.
But that lowest of men who, being of a dark disposition, gives black wealth,
enjoys the fruit of that action after death in the state of an animal.
Nārada says:
That [gift], moreover, is recorded as being of twelve kinds according to its dependence on the respective castes.
Thus, wealth is threefold according to the distinction of white and so forth; by relying on each of the four castes, it becomes twelvefold through the distinction of its bases.
He states another twelvefold classification of that very same [wealth]:
"The common [wealth] shall be of three kinds."

However, regarding the specific [wealth] among the three castes, it is ninefold because there are three types for each caste; thus, both taken together, they constitute twelve types, since the specific categories of wealth belonging to a Śūdra will be explained separately. "Inherited property, a gift of affection, and what is obtained together with a wife—these are the three types of wealth common to all castes without distinction."
"Gift of affection" means that which is obtained through a gift of affection.
The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa should be known as having three characteristics:
that which is obtained through receiving gifts, from a patron for whom one sacrifices, and likewise from a pupil.
They say that for a Kṣatriya as well, there are three specific kinds of wealth:
that acquired in battle, from imprisonment, and from fines and legal proceedings.
"From labor" means from the taking of taxes; "from legal proceedings" means by means of justice.

The specific wealth of a Vaiśya should be known as having three characteristics: agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. That of a Śūdra, however, consists of service to these [higher castes] and through their favor.

[530] Furthermore, for a Śūdra, that which is obtained "from these" twice-born castes "by way of favor"—that is, through the mental satisfaction arising from service—is his exclusive means of acquisition. Such is the lawful acquisition of wealth for all castes;
it would be unlawful by way of the opposite, unless there is a most urgent distress.

Thus, the lawful means of acquiring property have been described without distinction for both women and men; now, those pertaining specifically to women are stated: that which is received before the fire, that which is received at the wedding procession, and that which is given as a token of affection;
Woman's property is declared by tradition to be of six kinds: that obtained from brothers, mother, and father.
The nature of the property consisting of the *adhyagni* and other types has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"Whatever is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is declared by the virtuous to be the *strīdhana* known as *adhyagni*."
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being given away from her father's house is declared to be the woman’s property known as *adhyāvāhanika*.
Whatever is given out of affection by a mother-in-law or a father-in-law,
as well as that which is given for the purpose of worshipping their feet, is called "prītidatta" (a gift of affection).
Whether by a married woman or by an unmarried maiden, what is obtained from the husband’s father’s house,
or from a brother, or from the parents, is declared to be *saudāyika* (a woman’s separate property).
Furthermore:
"Bandhudatta," as well as "śulka" and "anvādheyaka.

That which is given by the maternal relatives and the paternal relatives of the maiden is "bandhudatta. That which is given so that she may be married is "śulka. That which is given after the marriage is "anvādheyaka."
And it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"Whatever is obtained by a woman from her brother's family after marriage,
as well as what is obtained from her husband's family, is known as *anvādheya* property."
Yājñavalkya: That which is given by the father, mother, husband, or brothers; that which is received in the presence of the sacred fire;
and that which is given upon supersession—this is declared to be the woman's property (*strīdhana*).

That which was given by the father and others, and that which was given by the maternal uncle and others in the presence of the fire at the time of marriage; "ādhivedanika" means on account of supersession. This refers to what is to be given to a superseded wife, as will be stated later in the verse beginning with "He should give an equal amount as ādhivedanika," and which is already established by the rule beginning with "The wife and the daughters."
"And the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares... [Manu 9.118];
"The sister's fee belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death" [Yājñavalkya 2.125];
and "The mother shall obtain the inheritance of a son who dies without offspring" [Yājñavalkya 2.135].
"And when the mother has also passed away, the father's mother shall take the wealth. Thus it is said:
"But when the mother has died, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother's inheritance equally."
"Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth according to their merit and with affection. And:
"That which is the mother's separate property (yautaka) belongs exclusively to the unmarried daughter."

"The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established [in life]"; and "for the wife is the desired [heir] of the nuptial wealth"—by such statements, the property of women acquired through lawful means is established as being rightfully theirs. Thus, the rule for the use of wealth acquired by lawful means in rites such as the *śrāddha* has been shown. This concludes the rule regarding wealth acquired by lawful means. Now, the prohibition of wealth acquired by unlawful means is demonstrated.
The elder Śātātapa said:
"He who performs funeral rites for the deceased with wealth acquired by unjust means..."
He does not obtain that fruit, because of his improper acquisition of that object.
‘Post-mortem rites’ refers to the *śrāddha* and other such ceremonies.
Devala also said:
"Even if one were to give away the entire earth acquired through unjust means..."
Except for faith, one shall not obtain any prosperity from an unworthy recipient.
"Bhūti" means the fruit. In the Vahnipurāṇa:
"For that unwise man who, having taken wealth acquired through unjust means..."
One who desires the Dharma performs sacrifice, yet does not enjoy the fruit of that Dharma.
But that sinful man who is a mere caviler regarding the Dharma gives gifts to the Brahmins solely for the sake of gaining the world's confidence.
A Brahmin who, though greedy for dharma, acts with sinful deeds and is devoid of his rightful portion,
being possessed by passion and delusion despite appearing tranquil, shall attain a defiled womb.
Thus, having acquired wealth through greed, he who performs sacrifices and gives gifts does not achieve success because of that evil deed resulting from his wicked acquisition.
Whatever rites are undertaken with these and many other riches acquired through unjust means, the *piśācas* are the presiding deities therein.
Śātātapa said:
Wealth obtained from the sale of the Vedas, that which is earned by a woman,
and that which is acquired from a eunuch— these are not desired [for ritual use] and must not be given to the ancestors or the gods.
"Born from the sale of the Veda" means obtained through the sale of the Veda. And the sale of the Veda is of six kinds, as stated in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"Proclaiming it, explaining it, receiving gifts preceded by questions, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and debating—this is the sixfold sale of the Veda. Thus it is said.

"Proclaiming" (*prakhyāpanam*) is the public display of one's studies here and there for the sake of wealth, thinking, "I am such a person who has studied the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. "Exegesis" (*vyākhyānam*) is the exposition of the meaning of the Vedas out of a desire for gain. "Disputation" (*vādaḥ*) is a debate concerning the Vedas and their meanings that results in the defeat of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), undertaken for the sake of fame, profit, and honor. "Earned from women" refers to wealth acquired by living off the activities of women, or earned among women, or obtained through the sale of women. A "eunuch" (*klībaḥ*) is a hermaphrodite. Vyāsa says:
"Wealth born from the sale of the Vedas, that which is earned from a woman, and [wealth from] a eunuch is not desired [as a gift]."
That which has been acquired from a eunuch should not be given to the ancestors or to the gods.
