Whatever is acquired by a woman through her own independence, by means such as usury and the like, that must not be taken by the husband.
As stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "And whatever is obtained through bribes and the like, or whatever is earned from an outcast."
And wealth arising from the improper bride-price of a maiden is also censured in this context.
Having said, "Give this for the sake of my ancestors," whatever has been acquired must always be avoided by the virtuous in the performance of the śrāddha rite.

That which is given to royal officials for the purpose of removing obstacles to a task or for remedying a calamity is called "bribery" (*utkoca*); whatever is obtained in that form [is forbidden]. That which arises from the price for a bride in excess of a pair of cattle is "improperly obtained bride-price" (*anyāyakanyāśulkottham*). Likewise, one should avoid in the performance of a *śrāddha* rite every kind of wealth that has been solicited under the pretext that it is for the purpose of performing the *śrāddha*. As stated in the *Revākhaṇḍa*:
"The property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍeśvara..."
Three kinds of falling are observed: from giving, from leaping over, and from eating.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who steals an elephant, a horse, a cow, a draft-ox, a gem, a pearl, or gold in secret, yet later offers them as a gift..."
Those who are joined with such actions do not go to heaven where the enjoyers dwell;
being base, they are cooked in hell.
But that donor who bestows a gift by taking away the wealth of another goes to hell; the fruit of that gift belongs to the one whose wealth it was.
Likewise:
that which is already consumed, unknown, insufficient, or unrefined—
whatever one gives to Brahmins, that remains in the ashes.
"Paribhuktam" refers to items such as clothing that have been accepted and used; "aparyāptam" refers to things incapable of fulfilling their intended purpose, such as an old ox.
This concludes the prohibition against wealth acquired through unrighteous means.
Thus, rites such as *śrāddha* must be performed with wealth earned by righteous means, and not with whatever may be acquired by any means whatsoever.

Yet, by these statements shown by the person (*puruṣa*), that [purposefulness] is set aside. It was not stated by those statements that the rules regarding acquisition have man as their purpose; rather, it is stated that wealth acquired according to the rules has the sacrifice (*kratu*) as its purpose. That is not so; for there is no contradiction in wealth acquired through observances (niyamas) intended for human ends being used for the sake of the sacrifice.
[Objection: But how can observances be for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) unless they first bring about the status of being for the person’s end in the very wealth being acquired?

To this we reply: Observances become for the sake of the person even while producing an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa*) that assists the person. [Objection: But when the visible ownership of wealth—which is useful to the person—is already possible, why postulate an unseen benefit?

It is said in reply: Since the ownership of wealth that benefits a person is established by the mere means [of acquisition] even without a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the restrictive rule has as its sole fruit the production of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit). Therefore, wealth being acquired through restrictive rules such as acceptance of gifts—which, according to you, serve a human purpose through a visible medium—attains a connection with the person either in a neutral form that serves both the sacrifice and the person, or in the form of serving merely those worldly and Vedic actions required by the person. In that case, when the wealth has attained a connection with the person in a neutral form, the statement declares its fitness for use in the sacrifice. But when it is in the form of serving merely the action, then, since the fitness for use in the sacrifice would apply even to what is acquired by unrestricted means, the statement declares the absence of fitness for use in the sacrifice for that which is acquired by unrestricted means; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Or, let it be granted that wealth (*artha*) has the singular nature of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*); nevertheless, since it is already a human goal, let it serve as an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*kratu*). In its capacity as an auxiliary, only its general fitness (*yogyatā*) is expressed by the scriptural statements; it is not said that it is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), so there is no contradiction. As for the lack of fitness regarding wealth acquired through improper acceptance of gifts and the like, this is due to the prohibitory statements. Alternatively, in the *Lipsā-sūtra*, the fact that [wealth] is a human goal—brought forward by the force of the context in the restrictive injunctions concerning acceptance of gifts and so forth—is stated; however, the fact that it is for the sake of the sacrifice, which would have to be inferred from other statements, is not refuted.

Now, if this were the case, sacrifices would have to be performed only with wealth acquired through restricted means (*niyama*), and one’s own purpose (*svārtha*) would likewise have to be accomplished by such means alone. Consequently, for what purpose is there the demonstration—through an extensive treatise—that the rules of acquisition (*arjana-niyama*) serve the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)?

We reply: it is for the sake of establishing the principles of logic (*nyāyavyutpatti*). Alternatively, it is for the sake of ensuring that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is incurred in the event of violating those rules. Or else, it is for the sake of demonstrating that even when other forms of wealth are unavailable, the accomplishment of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) sacrifices is possible even with wealth acquired through the violation of the rules; thus, the position is faultless.
Thus concludes the resolution of contradictions regarding the section on the acquisition of wealth. Now follows the production of substances such as rice and other grains.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*, after establishing that in ancient times this earth was devoid of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhī*), it is stated:
When those [crops] were again devoured,
those creatures, wandering about and afflicted by hunger, went for refuge to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
And having understood in truth that the earth was being swallowed up,
the Lord, the all-pervading one, made Sumeru his calf and milked her.
Then, because this cow was milked by him, crops were produced upon the surface of the earth;
those seeds were formerly both cultivated and wild.
Plants that end with the ripening of their fruit are recorded as seventeen groups:
rice, barley, wheat, beans, and sesame;
For there are indeed priyaṅgu grains, noble koradūṣa, and cīnaka;
as well as mung beans, green gram, lentils, flat beans, and horse gram.
Āḍhakīs and Caṇakas—these are recorded as the seventeen groups;
thus these were born as domestic species, and likewise those that are wild arose.
[537] There are fourteen sacrificial plants, both cultivated and wild:
Indeed, these seven months consist of priyaṅgu and kulattha;
furthermore, there are śyāmāka, nīvāra, wild sesame, and gavedhuka.
Kuruvindas, markaṭakas, and likewise those which are veṇuyavas—
these are indeed recorded as the fourteen medicinal plants, both domestic and wild.

Those whose end comes with the ripening of their fruit are called *phalapākāntāḥ*. "Grains" (*vrīhayaḥ*) refers to the sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭika*). These include the white, pale, and large-grained rice; black rice; *jatūmukha*, *kurkuṇḍaka*, *lācaka*, *parāpataka*, *sūkara*, *koddālaka*, *ojāla*, *cīna*, *śāra*, *vardura*, *gandhana*, *kuruvinda*, *pāṭala*, and so forth. "Small grains" (*aṇavaḥ*) refers to *varayikā*. "Priyaṅgu" is *kaṅgu*, also known as *udāracīna*. "Kuruvindas" are a specific variety of rice. "Koradūṣaka" is *kodrava* (paspalum scrobiculatum). "Nīvāras" are wild grains. "Jarttilas" are black sesame seeds. "Gavedhukas" resemble the seeds of the safflower (*kusumbha*). "Markaṭaka" is a specific type of grass grain. "Veṇuyavas" are bamboo seeds, which are "fit for sacrifice" (*yajñiyāḥ*), meaning worthy of ritual use.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: While being restrained by the high-souled Tvaṣṭṛ, who was performing the sacrifice, the Lord of Śacī drank the Soma; drops of it fell upon the earth.
From that, śyāmāka grains were born, which are honored even for the sake of the ancestors;
likewise wheat, barley, mung beans, and red rice—
all these arose from Soma, and from them comes the nectar for the ancestors.
Therefore, these should be diligently offered in the śrāddha rites by those born of the lineage.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Formerly, as the high-souled Śakra, the lord of Śacī, was drinking Soma while being restrained by Tvaṣṭṛ, the Soma fell upon the earth."
From that, śyāmāka grains were produced and offered for the sake of the ancestors;
some drops of it fell upon the earth in ancient times.
Sugarcane is desirable, cooling, pleasing to the heart,
and sweet; therefore, one who performs the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice for the ancestors with *śyāmāka* grain and sugarcane— providing everything they desire— shall quickly attain success.
Know that those named Śyāmākas and Hastins are resolved upon for sacrifice;
because they were created by the gods, they are remembered as fit for sacrifice.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The drops of nectar that fell from the mouth of the Sun as he was drinking the nectar are known as rice, mung beans, sugarcane, and so forth."
From that [sugar] comes sugar-cane juice, which possesses the nature of nectar;
therefore, sugar is beloved by the Sun and is meritorious for use in offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

‘Śālayaḥ’ (rice varieties) include red śāli, mahāśāli, kalama, tūrṇaka, śakunāhva, sārasa, sukha, dīrghaśūka, rodhra, śūka, sugandha, pataṅga, tapanīya, and so forth. ‘Mudgāḥ’ (mung beans) are a specific type of leguminous grain. ‘Ikṣavaḥ’ (sugarcane varieties) include pauṇḍraka, vāṃśika, karmāra, nepāla, śāta, śatapavarka, and so forth. ‘Śarkarā’ (sugar) is a specific derivative of sugarcane; its varieties include matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa, sitā, and others. As stated in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
“In the beginning, while creating the world, the Creator first created the animals.”
First the rhinoceroses, then the leopards, and after that the tigers were created.
Whatever was created in whatever manner attained purity accordingly;
just as these animals were first created here, O lord of men.
In that same manner, while creating the crops, sesame seeds were fashioned first;
after them, barley and rice, and then indeed the millet.
Wheat, lentils, beans, mung beans, as well as small grains,
wild rice, and śyāmāka— these were created in due order.
When the flowering creepers were created, first the *śatapatrikā* was created by him;
therefore, it is always meritorious for the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
When the Self-Existent One first created vegetables, the kālaśāka was created by him;
therefore, it should be used at a śrāddha, for it makes [the merit] inexhaustible.

O best of the twice-born, when the Self-existent One first created the elements, silver was created by him; therefore, it was ordained for the purpose of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at a śrāddha ceremony.
Then, for the pleasure of the ancestors, silver vessels were made;
and by the Self-born One, while creating the flavors, honey was created first.
Therefore, that śrāddha which is devoid of honey is praised as bestowing satisfaction upon the ancestors,
even if it contains all other flavors.
Even when combined with sweet foods, [an offering] does not lead to the satisfaction of the ancestors at all in a Śrāddha ceremony,
if there is not even a particle of honey present.
Therefore, even the mere mention of their names leads to the satisfaction of the ancestors.
O King, in ancient times, when he was creating plants, he created the darbha grass;
by that act, they attained purity, especially in the performance of śrāddha rites.
O best of kings, by that method, he created the vessels.
The yogins were created first; therefore, they are remembered as worthy of the funeral offerings (śrāddha). By him, while creating the animals, cows were fashioned first.
Therefore, their milk is recommended for the *śrāddha*, especially ghee.
Indeed, when he was creating progeny, those best of the twice-born were created by him first;
thus, when they are gratified at the *śrāddha*, the satisfaction of the ancestors is produced.
By him who created the gods, the Viśvedevas were fashioned in the beginning;
therefore, they are to be worshipped first when the rite of Śrāddha has commenced.
In ancient times, the Śrāddha was first established by these most eminent beings;
thereafter, the Pitāmaha himself created the gods.
Therefore, O King, they have attained supreme renown throughout the worlds of the past;
this entire essence of the śrāddha has been proclaimed by me to you.
O best of kings, this is the supreme secret of the ancestors, which makes what is given inexhaustible. Whoever recites this while a śrāddha is being performed,
that śrāddha becomes inexhaustible for the Brahmins who desire to eat.
O King, whoever hears this endowed with perfect faith shall obtain the merit of a performed śrāddha.
Thus ends the production of substances beginning with *brahma*.
Now, the grains to be taken up are described. Manu says:
I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rules, serves for a long duration and even for eternity.

The word *cirarātra* signifies a long period of time. When a certain oblation produces satisfaction for a long duration, and another produces satisfaction that is indeed infinite, I declare both of these; this is stated for the purpose of making a formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*). The words "are considered to be for the sake of gratification" (*prītayaḥ kalpyante*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis.
"With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, and fruits, the ancestors of men are gratified for a month according to the prescribed rule."

The mention of sesame and other such items is not for the purpose of enumerating other grains; rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the specific fruits resulting from the various vessels used.
Kālaśāka, mahāśalka fish, the meat of the rhinoceros or red deer, honey, and all types of food fit for sages (munyanna) lead to infinite results at the end of the kalpa.

*Kālaśāka* is *kālikāśāka*. *Mahāśalkāḥ* refers to porcupines; others, however, say they are fish scales. *Khaḍga* is the rhinoceros. *Loha* is a black goat or one that is entirely red; for it is recorded in tradition: "A black goat as well as a red one are prescribed specifically for [the attainment of] infinity. Here, the word *loha*, by way of indicating color, applies to the goat endowed with that quality.

The term "iron" (loha) is applied to both black iron and copper, according to the definition. Although this color is possible even in sheep and other animals, nevertheless, based on what is well-known from another Smṛti, only the goat is understood here. Others, however, say that "iron" refers to a bird named Lohapṛṣṭha, just as one might say Devadatta or Datta [is so named despite having other names]. "Honey" (madhu) means honey produced by bees. "Sages" (munayaḥ) are forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas); their "foods" (annāni) are wild rice (nīvāra) and the like. Likewise:
The food of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned,
and salt that is not alkaline— these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis).

‘Milk’ (*payaḥ*) means cow’s milk; here, its derivatives such as curd and so forth are also included, in accordance with the *smṛtis* and established custom. ‘Soma’ is a specific type of herb. ‘Unadulterated’ (*anupaskṛtam*) means unmodified—devoid of objectionable modifications and not prohibited. ‘Free from alkaline salt’ (*akṣāralavaṇam*) refers to salt other than that made from alkaline earth. For if this were a *nañ*-compound containing a *dvandva* (i.e., “not [that which is] both alkaline and salt”), two levels of grammatical function would have to be assumed, and the negative particle would have to be connected to each member individually; this would result in unnecessary complexity. The phrase ‘food by nature’ (*prakṛtyā haviḥ*) applies to those general injunctions where no specific substance has been mentioned, such as “he eats his morning meal with sacrificial food” (*haviṣā prātarāśaṃ bhuṅkte*). It should be understood thus.
Pracetas said:
Black beans, sesame seeds, and fresh rice are excellent,
as are large barley, common barley, and likewise madhūlikā.
Black, white, and red [grains] should be accepted in the rite of Śrāddha.

‘Śvetāḥ’ refers to white-headed barley; ‘mahāyavāḥ’ and ‘vrīhiyavāḥ’ are specific varieties of barley. ‘Madhūlikāḥ’ is a specific variety of *yāvanāla* (millet); its further qualification is that they may be black, white, or red (*lohāḥ*). ‘Lohāḥ’ means reddish. Alternatively, ‘madhūlikāḥ’ may refer to a specific variety of *śāli* rice. Atri also says: “A *śrāddha* performed without wheat is as if it were not performed at all.”
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should satisfy the ancestors with barley, rice, sesame, mung beans, wheat, chickpeas, as well as green gram, millet, and mustard oils."
And likewise, one should worship with wild rice (nīvāra), mung beans (māṣa), and millet (priyaṅgu).
*Caṇaka* is *harimanthaka*, well known in the Mahārāṣṭra country as a food for horses. *Sarṣapa* refers to white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*).
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Rājaśyāmāka, śyāmāka, and likewise praśāntikā..."
Wild rice and lotus roots likewise satisfy the ancestors for six months.
Barley, black gram, wheat, sesame, mung beans, mustard seeds,
millet, kovidāra, and flat beans are auspicious here.
*Praśāntikā* is a specific type of grain well-known in the Middle Country (*madhyadeśa*). *Pauṣkarāḥ* are lotus seeds. *Niṣpāvāḥ* are *vallā* (cowpeas). In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"In the rite of *śrāddha*, *praśāntikā* and *priyaṅgu* should be taken."
These are also similar to śyāmāka grains in their qualities.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "With rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits; with *śyāmāka* grain, chickpeas, vegetables, wild millet, or *priyaṅgu*."
With wheat, sesame seeds, and mung beans, one gratifies the ancestors for a month.

Vyāsa said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, hear from me those sacrificial offerings which those who know the Śrāddha rites prescribe for the time of the Śrāddha; they are intended for specific desires, as well as their respective fruits.
Manu declared that a śrāddha offering containing increasing quantities of sesame seeds becomes inexhaustible;
indeed, among all foods to be consumed, sesame seeds are traditionally held to be the most important.
‘Vardhamānatila’ means abundant with sesame seeds.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: “With wheat, rice, mung beans, satīna beans, and even chickpeas...”
The grandfathers are gratified for one month by what is given at the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
‘Satīnāḥ’ refers to *kalāya* beans, for according to the lexicon, *kalāya* is called *satīnaka*. These are the grains that should be accepted. Now, the grains that should be avoided:
In that regard, the Vāyu Purāṇa states: "One should avoid grains that have not been offered in the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, as well as *paripāṭala* [beans], *rājamāṣa*, *aṇu*, and *mastūra*."

Upon the production of new grain, there is a specific sacrifice for one who has maintained the sacred fires called the *Āgrayaṇa*; however, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, there is the *Āgrayaṇa* with new grain alone.
This is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"With *śyāmāka* millet and with sugarcane, [an offering] is provided for the ancestors that fulfills all desires."

"Whoever performs the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice shall quickly attain success. Thus [it is said]. "Grains of every kind" (*dhānyajātam*) refers to all prescribed types of grain. "Reddish-pink" (*paripāṭalāḥ*) means measuring one *prādeśa* in length. "Kidney-beans" (*rājamāṣāḥ*) are those belonging to the *śimbī* class, also known by the name *nīlasāndra*. "Small grains" (*aṇavaḥ*) have already been explained. "Lentils" (*masūraḥ*) is a specific type of leguminous grain (*śimbidhānya*) shaped like a flat disk, also called *maṅgalyaka*. [This is stated] in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
One should avoid all black grains in the performance of a śrāddha rite;
however, one should not avoid sesame seeds, nor likewise mung beans and māṣa beans.

Regarding the prohibition of sesame (*tila*), mung beans (*mudga*), and black gram (*māṣa*) mentioned here, it does not apply to these by their mere genus; rather, it applies specifically to those that are black in color. For a prohibition must be stated only when there is a possibility of consumption. And the possibility of consumption pertains only to the black varieties. Furthermore, because this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) forms a single syntactical unit with the prohibition of black grains, its scope is restricted solely to the black ones. As for the other varieties of sesame, mung beans, and black gram, there is neither a mandatory injunction nor a prohibition. As for the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, who pointed out a general prohibition of mung beans and black gram in the statement of Bharadvāja—"One should give split pulses (*vidala*) excluding mung beans, pigeon peas (*āḍhakī*), and black gram"—that is based on a confusion regarding the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*). Otherwise, it would follow that even horse gram (*kulattha*), lentils (*masūra*), and so forth—which are prohibited in all *smṛtis* and *purāṇas*—would become permissible. Indeed, the reading including the negative particle is seen in the *Mahārṇava* and other works: "One should not give split pulses, excluding mung beans, pigeon peas, and black gram."

*Āḍhakī* is a specific type of leguminous grain (*śimbidhānya*) denoted by the word *tūvarī*. *Mudga* and *māṣa* are well known. Those grains which are mostly split into two within the interior of a rotating stone mill are called *vidala*, such as *masūra* and others. In this section concerning grains to be accepted or rejected, the rule observed regarding chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *āḍhakī*, flat beans (*niṣpāva*), and so forth, should be established as pertaining to non-black varieties, while the prohibition pertains to black varieties, based on the previously cited statement regarding the avoidance of black grains. Alternatively, an option (*vikalpa*) may be stated according to the principle of what is both enjoined and prohibited.
Sumantu said: "One should not offer the citron (*bījapūraka*) or the black gram (*māṣa*) at a *śrāddha* ceremony. Here, "citron" refers to the *mātuluṅga*.
In the Mahārṇava, the reading of the text is as follows:
"One should not offer at a *śrāddha* the following: *pālakyā*, *nālikā*, *potīka*, *śigru*, *sṛsuka*, *vārttāka*, *bhūstṛṇa*, black gram (*māṣa*), *masūraka*, and artificial salt (*kṛtalavaṇa*).
In the *Śaṅkhadhara*, there is an alternative reading.

"One should not offer pālaṅkyā, apotaka, ālikā, sṛsuka, niṣpāva, masūra, caṇaka, and so forth at a śrāddha. An explanation of pālaṅkyā and the others will be provided in the section on vegetables. "Kṛtāvaṇa" refers to salt produced from alkaline earth. Here, "māṣas" refers to those other than black beans (kṛṣṇamāṣa), namely those denoted by the term rājamāṣa. For it is said: "Monkeys, as well as rājamāṣas, are to be avoided at a śrāddha."
They are prohibited by such statements as these.

[546] But surely, how can those things denoted by the word *rājamāṣa* (king-bean) be understood by the word *māṣa* alone? For that which is denoted by the word *dvijarāja* (king of the twice-born) cannot be made known by the word *dvija* (twice-born) alone. Since the universal exists within its particulars, the cognition of it through the word for the universal is not contradictory; just as the word *śāli* (rice) brings about the cognition of *lohitaśāli* (red rice) and *mahāśāli* (great rice). However, where there is an absence of the capacity to denote a universal that is delimited by such particulars, there is no cognition by way of that path. Moreover, even parts of a denotative word are seen to be denotative themselves, as in the case of *mātuluṅga* and *ulūṅga*.
In the Caturviṃśatimata: "Kodrava, rājamāṣa, kulattha, varaka,
and especially niṣpāva— one should avoid these five."
The wise likewise avoid even bamboo seeds.

‘Kulatthas’ are well-known as a specific type of leguminous grain (śimbidhānya), such as those that serve as various auxiliaries for soups, *vyūṣa*, and so forth, similar to mung beans (*mudga*). Both the white and black varieties are to be avoided, as there is no counter-exception (pratiprasava) for them, just as there is none for black mung beans and the like. ‘Varakas’ are wild mung beans (*vanamudga*). ‘Yāvanālas’ are *jonthalas*. These are to be avoided only when they are distinct from the variety of *jonthala* called *madhūlikā*; alternatively, they describe the word *madhūlikā* as referring to a specific kind of rice. According to that view, all *yāvanālas* whatsoever are to be avoided. Thus says the *Nigama*:
The wise likewise avoid even bamboo seeds;
yet learned sacrificers may offer even oil in times of distress.

The logical connection is that even oil is to be avoided by the wise. However, he says, "In times of distress, the learned performers of sacrifice permit both," in order to authorize the use of both in such circumstances. Therefore, the intended meaning here is that in the absence of other substances, the *śrāddha* must indeed be performed with these two as well; for there is no discarding of what has been obtained, especially in matters pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*). Thus, it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Monkeys and likewise *rājamāṣa* beans are to be avoided at a *śrāddha*."
Drops of water, and lentils, are forbidden in the performance of śrāddha rites.
‘Markaṭakas’ are *laṅkā* beans; ‘vipruṣīkas’ are varieties of *śāli* rice. Kātyāyana states: “In a *śrāddha*, pālaṅkyās, niṣpāvas, and kodravas should not be given.”
Masūra, kṣāra, vārtāka, kulattha, śaṇa, and śigru;

‘Alkali’ (*kṣāra*) refers to barley-alkali and the like. ‘Brinjal’ (*vārtāka*) is the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant known as *kṣudravārtākī*, which is slightly larger than the fruit of the *kaṇṭakārikā* and has a similar shape. ‘Hemp’ (*śaṇa*) is a specific type of grain. Although there is no possibility of its inclusion here because hemp that grows spontaneously is always prohibited, it is possible for hemp produced through cultivation and the like to be included. Furthermore, although red-flowered *śigru* is always forbidden and thus cannot be included here, white-flowered *śigru* may be included as a leaf-vegetable; therefore, the prohibition is meaningful. Alternatively, even though the prohibition was already established for the sake of human conduct (*puruṣārtha*), it is stated again here to prevent defects in the *śrāddha* rite.
Marīci said:
"In a śrāddha, horse-gram (kulattha), chickpeas (caṇaka), and kodrava grain should not be given,
nor should any pungent or tasteless things."
"Pungent substances" refers to long pepper (*pippalī*) and the like.
In the continuation of the phrase "one should avoid," the *Viṣṇusmṛti* states:
"Kidney beans (*rājamāṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), stale food, and prepared salts."
"Stale food" refers to items such as sweetmeats (*modaka*) and the like; this is according to Śaṅkha. [He also forbids] *rājamāṣa* beans, lentils (*masūra*), *kodrava*, and *koradūṣaka* grains.
One should avoid red exudations from trees in the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha).
In this context, "koradūṣaka" refers to wild *kodrava*.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"Grains that are unfit for ancestral offerings (*aśrāddheya*) include *kodrava* as well as *pulaka*."

‘Kodravas’ are *koradūṣakas*. ‘Pulakas’ are grains that are finer than kodrava and the like; for there is an authoritative teaching (*anuśāsana*) stating, “*Pulāka* is a fine grain. The absence of lengthening of the middle vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*) in the Purāṇa. In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
“And I shall declare those who are to be avoided by givers at a *śrāddha* ceremony at all times.”
Masūra, śaṇa, niṣpāva, rājamāṣa, and kulattha;

Kodrava, uddāla, varaka, kusumbha, madhuka, and atasī—these should not be offered by one who desires what is pleasing to the ancestors. *Madhuka* refers to jyeṣṭīmadhu; its inclusion as a vegetable or as a seasoning ingredient for vegetables is hereby prohibited. *Atasī* is the plant known as umā, which produces the very smooth, flattened-shaped seeds that serve as the source material for oil; it is prohibited whether used as a vegetable or as a source of oil.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"I shall now fully declare those things which are detestable and those which are to be avoided at a Śrāddha:
lentils, hemp, sprouted grains, black gram, and safflower."
Kodrava, uddālaka, varaka, kapittha, madhuka, and atasī.
*Kapittha* is the fruit of the *dadhittha*.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Pumpkins, as well as *niṣpāva* and *kodrava* grains, should not be offered at a *śrāddha*."
Masūra, kṣāra, vārtāka, kulattha, śaṇa, and śigru;
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"In all śrāddhas, [one should avoid] collyrium, flowers, safflower, black mustard,
*tovarī*, kidney beans, *kodrava*, and *koradūṣaka*."
And all that is harmful or improper should be avoided, as well as water that has been drawn at night.

"Añjana-puṣpa" means the flower of the *añjana* tree. "Tovarī" refers to *tūvarī*. "Apakriyaṃ" means that which has lost its proper function; that is to say, food that has become spoiled—devoid of its excellent taste, fragrance, and color—due to the absence of its appropriate preparation.
This is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
And *abhiṣavas* (fermented liquors), *śatapuṣpa*, and *gavedhuka* should always be avoided.
"Abhiṣavas" refers to fermented mixtures; "śatapuṣpa" is *niśi*.
[Thus it is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
One should avoid black gram, small grains, lentils, koradūṣaka,
vipruṣa, markaṭa, urā, and kodrava as well.
‘Cora’ means *coraka*.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Markaṭakas, rājamāṣas, and likewise *aṇus* are to be avoided at a *śrāddha*."
Drops of saliva and lentils are also forbidden at the performance of a śrāddha rite.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "At the time of a *śrāddha*, the best of the twice-born should avoid with every effort the *āḍhakī* bean, the *kovidāra* tree, the *pālaṅkyā* plant, and likewise black pepper."

The *kovidāra* is the golden-flowered tree (*kāñcanapuṣpa*). Fresh black peppers, being obtained as independent vegetables, are prohibited; however, dried ones used as an ingredient for seasoning vegetables are not. In the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"King beans (*rājamāṣa*) and likewise others should be avoided with effort by the virtuous."
Masūra, śatapuṣpā, kusumbha, and śrīniketana should be avoided; likewise, atiyava and durālabhā-yava must always be excluded.
‘Atiyavāḥ’ are varieties of *śāli* rice. ‘Śrīniketana’ is the red *bilva*.
Devala says: A wise man should not consume seeds except in the event of illness.
For one would destroy the infinite fruits of these seeds.

"Except in the event of illness" means, without the occurrence of disease or other calamities, one "should not employ [them]," that is, one should not use them. For by using them, one would destroy the abundant prosperity of the crops produced thereby.
These are the grains to be avoided.
Now, the fruits and roots to be accepted:
Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"One should cause mangoes, *pālevata* fruits, sugarcane, grapes, *bhavya* fruits, pomegranates, *vidārī* roots, and *bharuṇḍa* fruits to be offered at the time of the *śrāddha*."
One should diligently offer śṛṅgāṭa, visa, and sebeku at the śrāddha ceremony.

‘Āmrāḥ’ are mango fruits. ‘Pālevatam’ is a fruit shaped like a citron (jambīra), well-known in Kashmir. ‘Mṛdvīkā’ is grape. ‘Bhavyam’ is the karmaraṅga fruit. ‘Vidāryān’ refers to the tubers of the bhūkuśmāṇḍī; or it may refer to the fruits of the black kūṣmāṇḍī. ‘Bharuṇḍāḥ’ are well-known in the region of Kashmir. ‘Śṛṅgāṭakam’ is a water-born three-pointed plant.
Regarding the śṛṅgāṭa: “The śṛṅgāṭa is a water-tuber; it is triangular, three-pointed, and three-forked.”

Thus ends the *Madananighaṇṭu*. "Bisa" refers to the root of the lotus. "Kebuka" is a bulbous root resembling ginger, well-known in the Mahārāṣṭra region. Regarding the prohibition of kebuka, it should be understood as referring to the wild (*āraṇyaka*) variety.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The mango, the hog-plum, the wood-apple, the pomegranate, and the citron..."
Cīṇāka, lakuca, jambu, bhavya, bhūta, and likewise āruka.
Prācīnāmalaka, milk, coconut, parūṣaka,
orange, dates, grapes, and the blue wood-apple (nīlakapittha).
Patola, priyāla, karkandhu, badara,
vaikaṅkata, vatsaka, ervāru, and vāruka—
these varieties of fruit should be offered with diligence at a śrāddha ceremony.

*Āmrātaka* is the fruit of the *kapīta*. *Bilva* is the young *śrīphala*. *Cīṇāka* is shaped very long and resembles the *ervāruka*. *Lakuca* is the fruit of the *likuca*, well-known in the Elā forests. *Jambu* is the fruit of the royal *jambū*. *Bhūta* is the fruit known in the Karṇāṭa country, which is covered with external filaments (*bahiḥkesara*). *Āruka* is the wild cucumber (*vāruka*). *Prācīnāmalaka* is the water-citron (*pānīyāmalaka*). *Kṣīra* is the fruit of the *rājādana*. *Nārikela* is well-known. *Parūṣaka* is well-known in Kuṅkaṇa. *Nāraṅga* and others are well-known. *Nīlakapitthaka* is the green-colored fruit of the *dadhittha*. *Paṭola* is the sweet *paṭola* fruit. *Priyāla*...

The fruit of the *cāra* tree; *karkandhu* is the fruit of the wild jujube (*āraṇyabadarī*); *vaikaṅkata* is the fruit of the *sruvadruma* tree; *vatsaka* is the fruit of the *kuṭaja*; *ervāru* is the sweet cucumber; *vārukāni* are the fruits of the *vārukī*. "Various kinds of fruits" means those possessing the nature of being fruits. The use of the word "carefully" indicates that these are superior to others, but not for the purpose of excluding others. Therefore, even in their absence, for the sake of variety in the food offering, it is permitted to give other fruits as well—provided they are not prohibited by the rules of constant prohibition—in the *śrāddha* ceremony.
Likewise: one should give black pot-herb (kālaśāka), rice-potherb (tandulīya), Vāstuka, radish (mūlaka), as well as wild potherbs, and these flowers.

*Tandulīya* is *alpamāriṣa*. *Vāstuka* is *kaṇṭavāstuka*. By the word *mūlaka*, the long radish (*dīrghamūlaka*) is to be understood, because the globular radish (*piṇḍamūlaka*) is prohibited. *Āraṇyaka-śākāni* refers to wild vegetables such as *phañjī*, *cuñcu*, and so forth; this is said with the intention of what will be mentioned by the word "these" (*amūni*). Likewise:
pomegranate, *māgadhī*, ginger, fresh ginger, and *tintiḍī*.
One should employ āmrātaka, jīraka, and kumbara.

‘Māgadhī’ is long pepper (*pippalī*). ‘Nāgara’ is dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*). ‘Ārdraka’ is fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*). ‘Tintiḍī’ is tamarind (*ciñcā*). ‘Jīraka’ is white cumin (*gaurajīraka*). ‘Kumbara’ is coriander (*kustumburu*). In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
“Bilva, āmalaka, grapes, jackfruit, mango, and pomegranate...”
And the fruits of the bhavya, the pigeon-eye (pārāvata), the walnut (akṣoṭa), the date palm (kharjūra), and the mango (āmra) are auspicious.
Kaseru, kovidāra, tālakanda, as well as bisa,
tamāla, śatakanda, madhvālu, and śītakandalī.
Kāleya, kālaśāka, suniṣaṇṇaka, suvarcalā, meat, vegetables, curd, milk, cuñcu, and likewise vetrāṅkura.
Kaṭaphala, kauṅkaṇī, grapes, lakucha, and mocā; uṣṭragrīva, kacora, tinduka, and that which is called madhu.
The wood-apple, the coconut, the water-chestnut, the parūṣaka fruit,
long pepper, black pepper, the bitter gourd, and the fruit of the bṛhatī plant.
One should offer everything that is fragrant, including *kalāya* beans,
as well as other such items that are savory and sweet;
furthermore, ginger and long radish (*dīrghamūlaka*) should certainly be provided here.

*Āmalaka* is the fruit of the *dhātrī*. *Panasa* is the fruit of the *kaṇṭakiphala*. *Pārāvata* is the *pālevata*. *Ākhoṭa* is the fruit of a *pīlu* tree from another island, commonly known as *ākharoṭa*. *Kaseru* is a hairy tuber found in small ponds, well-known by the name *seru*. *Kovidāra* refers to the tender fruit or flower of the *kāñcanāra* or a similar species of tree. Since the prohibition of *kovidāra* will also be stated later, this is an option. *Tālakanda* is a root found in regions such as Pāṇḍya, shaped like a young palm fruit, produced from the interior of a palm fruit buried underground; or alternatively, the tuber of the *tālamūlī* plant is called *tālakanda*. *Tamāla* is the *tāpiñja*. *Śatakanda* is *śatāvarī*. *Madhvālu* is a specific type of tuber with long hairs and a single sweet flavor, commonly known as *mohālur*. *Śītakandalī* is the cold tuber, meaning *śālūka*. According to Govindarāja, *kāleya* is the vegetable known as *karāla*. *Suniṣaṇṇa* is a water-born variety of vegetable resembling *cāṅgerī*, commonly known as *suṇasuṇa*. *Suvarcalā* is *ādityabhaktā*. *Cūñcu* is commonly known as *cūcur*. *Kaṭphala* is the fruit of the tree named *kaṭphala*. *Kauṅkaṇī drākṣā* is grape produced in the Kuṅkaṇa country; this is also an illustration for any grape that has a sweet taste. *Moca* is the fruit of the banana (*kadalī*). *Uṣṭragrīva* is a fruit shaped like a camel’s neck, well-known in the northern regions. *Tinduka* is the fruit of the *sītisāraka*. *Madhusāhvaya* is *jyeṣṭhīmadhu*. *Bṛhatīphala* is the fruit of the *kaṇṭakārikā*. *Sugandhagandhi* is *karpūra* and *coraka*; it resembles a *piṇḍālu* tuber, has serrated leaves, and is well-known in the Lāṭa country as *sodhī*; others say it is a specific type of tuber. *Siñcantī* is *rudantī*. *Dīrghamūlaka* is a radish other than the *piṇḍamūlaka*.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*, after reciting a passage similar to that in the *Kūrmapurāṇa* beginning with "bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīka," etc., this much distinction is shown:
"The tufts of Agastya are copper-colored; all astringent substances;
fragrant fish and meat; and all types of peas."

‘Agastya’ refers to the sage-tree; its ‘crests’ are its young shoots. ‘Tāmra’ means reddish; ‘kaṣāya’ means having an astringent taste. There are also other crests belonging to trees such as the mango. As stated in the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa:
“The bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, drākṣā, āmrātaka, and pomegranate...”
The bhavya fruit, the pārevata, as well as dates and mangoes.
Kaseruka, vadarī, tālakanda, as well as bisa,
tamāla, śatakanda, madhvālu, and śītakandalī.
Kāleya, black potherb (kālaśāka), mung-bean rice, and suvarcala;
likewise meat, vegetables, curd, milk, curd-milk, and bamboo shoots.
Kaṭphala, kataka, grapes, lakuca, and mocaka; priyāla, āmalaka, cukrīkā, tinduka, and that which is called madhūka.
Vikaṅkata, coconut, śṛṅgāṭaka, parūṣaka,
long pepper, black pepper, paṭola, and the fruit of bṛhatī.
The boundaries of a grove, as well as all varieties of peas (kalāya),
and other such items are commended for the rite of Śrāddha.
*Kataka* is a water-clearing agent. *Cukrikā* is either *cāṅgerī* or *ciñcā*. The "partings" (*sīmantāḥ*) of the "grove" (*ārāmasya*), that is, the garden, are the fresh sprouts.
These are the fruits, roots, and so forth that are to be taken.
Now, regarding fruits, roots, and other items that are to be avoided:
the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"I shall declare those things that must always be avoided in the performance of the Śrāddha rite."
Garlic, leeks, onions, and bulbous radishes.
Kalambā and whatever other plants are deficient in taste and fragrance should be avoided in the rite of Śrāddha; the reason for this shall now be explained.
Long ago, during the war between the gods and the asuras, when Bali was defeated by the deities,
sparkling drops of water fell from him into the hands of the brahmins.
Therefore, these which have grown [wild] are to be avoided in the rite of Śrāddha:
long pepper, black pepper, the patola gourd, and the fruit of the brhati.
Bamboo, the shoot of the *karīra* tree, *surasā*, *arjaka*, and *bhūtṛṇa* grass;
as well as resins not mentioned in the Vedas, salts, and saline soils.

In the performance of *śrāddha* rites, one must avoid garlic (*laśuna*), *gṛñjana*, and *palāṇḍu*—the latter being varieties of onion. These three varieties are mentioned as representative examples of all types of onions. Those specific varieties are shown in the *Suśruta-saṃhitā*:
"Garlic, long-leaved garlic, *picchagandhā*, and *mahauṣadha*."
Karaṇya, palāṇḍu, latārka, parārikā,
gṛñjana, and yavaneṣṭa— these are the ten species of palāṇḍu.

The word *palāṇḍu* (onion) refers to the general category that pervades these ten specific types; it is used for both the general and for one specific type. Among them, the turmeric-colored variety is *gṛñjana*; the white bulb is *palāṇḍu*. The distinguishing characteristics of garlic (*laśuna*) and the others should be sought in medical treatises (*vaidyaka*) and similar works. *Piṇḍamūlakam* is a root with a globular shape. *Kalambā* is a water-born variety of vegetable with leaves shaped like bamboo leaves, or it may be the bitter gourd (*tumbī*). Fresh *pippalī* (long pepper) is prohibited because it is forbidden as an independent vegetable; however, dried ones are permitted as they are intended to serve as flavoring agents. *Paṭola* refers to the fruit of the wild *paṭola*, not the creeper itself; for the creeper is called *paṭola-tihlaka*, which is pungent, and the word *paṭola* is used in the masculine gender according to the *Liṅgānuśāsana*. *Bṛhatīphalam* is the fruit of the small eggplant (*kṣudravārttākī*). *Vāṃśaḥ karīraḥ* means the sprout of bamboo. *Surasaṃ* is the leaf of *nirguṇḍī*. *Arjakam* is the leaf of white *kuṭheraka*. *Bhūtṛṇaḥ* is a specific vegetable known by the name *bhūtīka*. Some say it is well-known in Kashmir; others say it is *kalambīkā*. However, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā* has characterized it thus: "That whose stalk has circular nodes at the joints is *bhūtṛṇa*. Furthermore, while the lexicon states its names are *mālātṛṇaka* and *bhūstṛṇa*, and while the usage with the augment *suṭ* (*sūdbhūtṛṇaḥ*) is seen in other Smṛtis, its usage here without that augment is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

"And tree-exudations not mentioned in the Veda. This means that those tree-exudations other than those permitted as food in the Veda—namely, those that are red in color and produced from incisions—are what is intended by "exudations."

Furthermore, according to the *Taittirīya Śruti*: "Now, indeed, that which is red, or that which flows from a cutting (*vraścana*), must not be eaten; however, anything else may be eaten at will. Here, "cutting" refers to the *veda* (sacrificial grass). Therefore, even the juice of trees and other plants that is not red in color may be consumed. Moreover, not even a single portion of that juice which flows out red in color without a cutting is to be eaten. But anything else may be eaten as one desires. Salts produced from alkaline earth, those that are black and known as *viṭa*, and those that are visible [as such] are prohibited here, because they are likewise forbidden in other *Smṛtis*. Regarding the prohibition of those that are visible, Viṣṇu says:

"One should not give salt that is not directly perceived. Thus, while the prohibition applies to black salt and artificial salts, as will be shown later, it does not prohibit sea salt and other such varieties that are not "unperceived" (i.e., adulterated). Accordingly, following the word "should be given" (*deyam*), the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Cow's milk, curd, ghee, and oil produced from sesame."
“Saindhava salt and likewise that which originates from Lake Mānasa—these two are indeed supremely pure, even though they are perceptible at all times.
Here, “saindhava” means that which arises from the ocean. Regarding both the *saindhava* and the *mānasasaṃbhava*, there is no prohibition even though they are perceptible.
And likewise in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:

"In this cooking, substances with pungent tastes—excluding vegetables prepared with black pepper and long pepper, and excluding *śuṇṭhī*—as well as salts, specifically those salts made from saline earth (*ūṣaramṛttikā*). Regarding the term "women in their menses" (*rajasvalāḥ*), it refers to those whose menstrual flow has not ceased even after the initial three nights and so forth.
Viṣṇu said:
"One should avoid bhūtṛṇa, śigru, mustard, kūṣmāṇḍa, alābu, vārtāka, pālaṅkyā, tandulīyaka, kusumbha, and the milk of a buffalo."

*Śigru* is the *sobhāñjanaka*. Since its red-flowered variety is always prohibited, it cannot be obtained here; however, because the white-flowered variety is available as a leaf vegetable (*patra-śāka*), the prohibition is meaningful. Furthermore, by "mustard" (*sarṣapa*), the black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*) is intended, and not mustard in general, because another Smṛti text specifies a particular prohibition: "the *kusumbha* and the black mustard. And since that [specification] is for the purpose of permitting the remainder, the general statement must be restricted to this particular type of mustard. For general terms are expectant of particulars and conform to them; a particular does not follow a general term by acting as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is because the particular is stronger than the general. Otherwise, within a single sentence, a general word would destroy the linguistic usage of a specific term by making the particular its mere indicator. For what difference is there between a specific term occurring in one sentence or in another? If there were such a difference, then the division into four parts (*caturdhākaraṇa*) would have to be restricted to the *āgneya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). Therefore, "mustard" here refers specifically to the black mustard, and thus the white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*) is indeed to be accepted. *Kūṣmāṇḍa* is the *karkāru*. *Alābu* is the fruit of the *tumbinī*; and that is to be avoided only if it is round, because another text shows a specific distinction: "the *alābu* if it is round. *Vārtāka* is the fruit of the small eggplant (*kṣudravārtīkī*). *Pālaṅkyā* is a specific fragrant substance known as *mukunda*. *Kusuma* is well-known. Regarding the *kusumbha*, since the thornless variety is permanently prohibited, the prohibition serves to exclude even the thorny variety when it is in its tender state and could potentially be used as a vegetable.
In the *Viṣṇu-vacana*, there is an alternative reading:

"One should avoid *pippalī*, *sṛsuka*, *bhūtṛṇa*, *āsurī*, mustard (*sarṣapa*), *surasa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *alābu*, *vārtāka*, *pālaṅkyā*, *tandulīyaka*, *kusumbha*, the root of *piṇḍa*, and the milk of a buffalo.

Here, *sṛsuka* refers to the vegetable of the *khadira* tree. *Āsurī* refers to black mustard (*rājasarṣapa*). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound may be "that which is both *āsurī* and *sarṣapa*"; thus, white mustard (*gaurasarṣapa*) is not to be avoided.
Hārīta also says:

"One should not offer at a *śrāddha* the following: *pālaṅkya*, *nālikā*, *pautīka*, *śigru*, *sṛsuka*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *bhūstṛṇa*, *kaphella*, black gram (*māṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), and artificial salt."

*Mālikā* is a plant with long stalks and small leaves at the top, growing in bodies of water; it is a creeper consisting of stalks and leaves well-known as a vegetable. *Pautīka* (also called *pautika* or *āpādaka*) is a type of herb. Regarding *kaphella*, the commentator on the Hārīta-smṛti states that it is a specific forest species well-known in Kashmir. *Kṛtalavaṇāni* refers to artificial salts. Śaṅkha says:
"Bhūstṛṇa, surasa, śigru, pālaṅkyā, and likewise sṛsuka."
One should avoid the kūṣmāṇḍa, the alābu, the vārtāka, and the kovidāra.
One should avoid the pippala fruit, black pepper, as well as the piṇḍamūlaka root, all prepared salt, and the tip of a bamboo shoot.
"Vaṃśāgra" refers to the sprout of a bamboo, not merely its tip. Śāṭyāyana also says:
"The māriṣa, the nālikā, and that which is red and a kalambikā."
All this food of the Asuras does not reach the ancestors.

*Māriṣa* is a specific type of leafy vegetable known as *jīvaśāka*, resembling *taṇḍulīyaka* but thicker than it. *Kalambikā* is an aquatic plant with sprouts shaped like bamboo leaves; because of the qualification "red," white varieties are not excluded.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"And those that ferment must always be avoided, as well as *śatapuṣpā* and *gavedhukā*."
One should always avoid the fruit of the Jambīra tree, with the exception of its pulp, as well as the Kovidāra flower.

It is also stated that when substances such as water, buttermilk, or sour gruel are mixed with mustard, salt, and so forth, and left for a period of three, five, or seven days, they undergo a change in taste into acidity, alkalinity, and the like. Therefore, one must explain either that the option [of eating] refers to excellent jambu fruits, or that the prohibition applies to them. When someone sneezes upon the fruit or root of a mango tree or the like, it is called *avakṣuta* (sneezed upon); when someone weeps upon it, it is called *avarudita* (wept upon). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for instances involving spitting and other actions that cause contact with impure phlegm and the like. Uśanas also says:
One should avoid the nālikā, hemp, mushrooms, safflower, bottle-gourd, and products of the *viḍ* plant, as well as the *kumbhī*, the *kambu*, the eggplant, and the *kovidāra*.
One should avoid *gṛñjana*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and *piṇḍamūlaka* at a *śrāddha* ceremony,
as well as *karañja* and whatever other things have an excessively strong flavor or odor.
*Chatrāka* is *śatapuṣpā*; others say it is a "parasol" (a mushroom) that appears on the ground or on trees during the rainy season.
Those who eat *chatrāka*, whether it grows from the earth or from a tree, one should know them as slayers of Brahmins, despised among those who discourse on the Veda.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Yama: "Viḍbhavān" refers to those produced from ground-areas defiled by contact with excrement; this is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative term) for those originating from impure ground-areas. "Kumbhī" is the *śrīparṇī* plant. "Kambuka" is a round-shaped gourd fruit (*alābuphala*). Let the word *alābu*, however, serve to prohibit [the consumption of] its leaves and other parts as vegetables. Regarding "kambuka," there is an alternative reading, *ambuka*. "Vṛntāka" is the white eggplant (*śvetavṛntāka*). "Gṛñjana" is well known as the carrot (*gājara*). "Kāñjika" is well known [as fermented gruel]. "Karañja" is the fruit of the *naktamāla* tree. Likewise, others also which are "intense in taste and smell"—that is, those possessing an excessively pungent taste and odor—should also be avoided.
Bhāradvāja said:
Water drawn at night, as well as water from a pond,
and very small amounts of kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, vajrakanda, and long pepper [should be avoided].
The *tandulīyaka* herb, buffalo milk and curd,
*śaimbika*, *karīra*, *kovidāra*, and *gavedhuka*.
Kulattha beans, hemp, cumin, and likewise groats;
any red flower other than the lotus, drumstick tree, and likewise alkaline substances.
"Furthermore, all foodstuffs and edibles that are tasteless—these must never be given at any śrāddha rite. Thus it is said.

‘*Naktoddhṛtam*’ means water drawn from a reservoir at night and set aside separately. ‘*Palvalāmbu*’ is water collected in a very small depression, pit, or basin, whether in a village or a forest; it is qualified as ‘small’ (*svalpam*) because it is insufficient even for the thirst of a single cow. ‘*Vajrakanda*’ is the wild *sūraṇa* (wild ginger). Regarding ‘*māhiṣam*’ (bovine), since it qualifies milk and curd, it is understood that only bovine milk and curd are prohibited. ‘*Masūra*, *kṛṣṇāḍhaka*, black *niṣpāva* (cowpea), black *caṇaka* (chickpea), and other pulses such as various types of *māṣa* and *mudga* are called *śaimbikāni* (leguminous grains). ‘*Karīra*’ is a specific tree growing in arid regions (*jāṅgala*), leafless and bearing fruit shaped like a *badara*. ‘*Jīraka*’ refers to black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīraka*), as specified in another Smṛti text. ‘*Karambhāṇi*’ are parched barley flour mixed with curd. The word ‘*añja*’ denotes a specific species of water-born flower. ‘*Kṣāra*’ refers to alkalis such as *sarjikā* and *yavakṣāra*. ‘*Nīrasāni*’ means those lacking juice, or having a poor taste. ‘*Bhakṣyāṇi*’ are things to be chewed with the teeth and swallowed; ‘*bhojyāni*’ are those fit for consumption without the need for chewing. ‘In all [cases]’ (*sarvasmin*) means in all instances other than the daily Śrāddha, because it is impossible to prepare food every day while excluding items such as *kuṣmāṇḍa*. For this very reason, it is stated in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts with reference to the daily Śrāddha.
"Rāma gratifies the ancestors with *iṅguda*, *badara*, and *bilva* fruits;
whatever food a man eats, his deities eat that same food. Thus said Sumantu.
[562] One should not offer citron or black gram at a *śrāddha*.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The palmyra fruit, the *karuṇa*, the *kākola*, and the fruit of the *bahuputrā* and *arjunī*."
One should avoid the jambīra, the red bilva, and also the fruit of the śāla tree.
The bottle-gourd, the bitter-leafed plant, the pumpkin, and the pungent-leafed variety;
eggplant, the various types of legumes, and those that are hairy or fibrous.
Kāliṅga, red carā, cīṇāka, dhṛtacāraka,
and likewise the fragrant cirbhaṭikā should be avoided at the time of the śrāddha rite.
The skull-cup, kākamācī, karambha, piṇḍamūlaka, gṛñjana, cukrikā, cukra, gājara, and likewise potikā.
One should avoid jīvaka, śatapuṣpā, nālikā, the village pig,
the plough, dancing, mustard seeds, onion, and garlic.
One should avoid *māṇakanda*, *tandulīya*, *viṣakanda*, *gatāsthi*, *puruṣāla*, and *sapiṇḍālu* in the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*).
O best of sages, one should also offer substances with a pungent odor, such as the *kovidāra* and *śigru*,
as well as those that are extremely sour, slimy, or dry, and others besides.

One should certainly not give food that has lost its flavor or that smells of liquor; one should avoid asafoetida, pungent-smelling substances, breadfruit, bhūnimba, nimba, rājika, cumin, products from Kaliṅga, and amlavetasa.
Likewise: safflower, potherbs, citron, drumstick tree,
kovidāra, oil-cake, śigruṣā, lentils, gṛñjana, and hemp.
Kodrava, kokilākṣa, cukra, kambu, and padmaka; the flesh of the cakora and the hawk, and the round gourd and the lotus-stalk.
Having eaten the fruit of palm trees, a man goes to hell;
having offered it to his ancestors, he shall go with them to the river that carries pus.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should not take those things which were themselves prohibited by Varāha out of reverence for the sake of the ancestors.

‘Karuṇa’ refers to the fruit of the *karuṇa* tree, well-known in the Gūrjara country. ‘Kākola’ refers to the fruit of the *kākolī* plant, well-known in the northern regions (*uttarāpatha*). ‘Bahuputrā’ is *śatāvarī*; its root and tender shoots are used. ‘Arjunīphala’ is the fruit of the *kakubha* creeper. ‘Śāla’ is the *sarja* tree. ‘Tikaparṇī’ is *kaṭukarohiṇī*. ‘Kaṭupatrikā’ is *rājikā* (black mustard). ‘Śimbijāti’ refers to various pulse crops such as *kulattha*, *masūra*, and others. ‘Romaśāni’ are the fruits of the *kapijambu*. ‘Rakracāra’ is the fruit of the red *cāra* plant. ‘Dhṛtacāraka’ is *cāra* seed that has been stored for a long time. ‘Kapāla’ is the coconut. ‘Cakra’ refers to substances such as molasses, *madhuka*, sour gruel (*āñjika*), or whey, which have been kept for three days, seven days, or longer in the heat of grain and so forth until they reach a state of extreme whiteness. ‘Gājara’ is what is commonly known in the world as *gājara* (carrot). ‘Jīvaka’ is well-known in the northern regions by that very name among the group of life-promoting herbs (*jīvanīya*) beginning with *kākolī*. ‘Hala’ is *lāṅgalī*. ‘Nṛtya’ is *naṭī*. ‘Ugragandhā’ is *vacā*. ‘Bhūnimba’ is *kirātatiktaka*. ‘Piṇyāka’ is the paste of sesame seeds from which the oil has been extracted by a press. ‘Kokilākṣa’ is *īkṣura*, well-known in the world as *kolisā*. ‘Padmaka’ is well-known by its own name. ‘Cakora’ and ‘śyena’ are specific types of birds.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Garlic, leeks, onions, radishes,
karambha, and whatever other things are deficient in taste and color."
One should avoid garlic, bottle-gourds, salts from saline soil,
and whatever is not praised by word of mouth at a śrāddha ceremony.

"Gandhārikā" means a storehouse; [the word] "saṅgīti" has the sense of "recitation. And as for what is said regarding speech: the meaning is that if, at the time of giving, the donor does not praise [the gift] with words for the sake of showing respect, that too does not contribute to the merit of the *śrāddha*.
Likewise: "That which is putrid, stale, and likewise [food] pressed by a *vārtīka*..."
Indeed, these things should be avoided at a śrāddha, as well as wealth and blood.

"Pūti" means foul-smelling; "lohita" refers to the vegetable known as *vasuka*. Alternatively, it refers to a red-colored substance such as the *karavīra* flower and the like. Others, however, read the text as "likewise a red garment. In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Pippalī, rucaka, and likewise masūraka..."
The *kuṣmāṇḍa*, the *alābu*, the *vārtāka*, the *bhūstṛṇa*, and likewise the *surala*.
One should avoid safflower, the root of the piṇḍa plant, and tandulīyaka;
likewise, one should avoid black gram and the milk of the buffalo.
At the time of a śrāddha ceremony, the best of the twice-born should avoid with every effort the āḍhakī, the kovidāra, the pālaṅkī, and likewise black pepper.
‘Rucaka’ refers to sauvarcala salt.
[This is stated] in the Padma and Matsya Purāṇas:
"Padma, bilvaka, dhattūra, pāribhadra, and aḍharūṣaka..."
Milk, as well as the milk of goats and sheep, should not be offered in rites for the ancestors.
‘Pāribhadra’ is the *nimba* tree; ‘āḍharūṣaka’ is the *siṃhāsya*. In the *Mahābhārata*:
“Among substances containing asafoetida, among vegetables, as well as *mālāna* and garlic...”
Onions, saubhāñjanaka, as well as gṛñjanaka and others [are likewise forbidden].
Gourd-vessels from Kiṣkindhā, black salt,
village pig meat, and whatever has not been offered [to the gods].
Black cumin, vit (vit-salt), and likewise śītapākī;
as well as sprouts and the like, and house-grown śṛṅgāṭakas, are to be avoided.
One should avoid all types of salt as well as rose-apple fruits;
likewise, one should avoid food that has been sneezed upon or over which someone has wept during śrāddha ceremonies.

Regarding the phrase *kiṣkindhajāny alābūni*, some read it as *kukuṇḍakāny alābūni*. They explain that "kukuṇḍakas" are substances similar in nature to mushrooms (*chatrāka*), shaped like balls. "Black salt" (*kṛṣṇaṃ lavaṇam*) refers to *sauvarcala*. Among the ingredients for seasoning vegetables and the like, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is to be avoided. As for the fact that the acceptability of asafoetida is mentioned in the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "Madhuka, rāmaṭha (asafoetida), camphor, black pepper, jaggery, rock salt (*saindhava*), and likewise *tripusa*—these are praised in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite."

Because it is both prescribed and prohibited, this should be understood as being optional (*vikalpa*). Others, however, explain that it refers specifically to asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), because another *smṛti* states: "One should avoid red exudations from trees. Still others say that asafoetida is to be taken as a secondary option (*anukalpa*) when other ingredients for seasoning vegetables are unavailable. Yet others claim it refers to asafoetida used in the form of vegetable preparations and the like, because there is a prohibition against the direct perception of asafoetida, salt, and black pepper when they are unmixed. But this [latter view] is incorrect, because asafoetida is not fit for consumption when separated [from other substances], and because the prohibition applies only to salt when it is directly perceived.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Sugandha, pañcaśimba, all varieties of kalāya,
vāṃśa, karīra, surasa, arjaka, and bhūstṛṇa."
And that which is forbidden as food should not be given in the performance of a śrāddha rite.

"Sugandha" refers to the leaves and so forth of the *gandhanākulyā* plant. "Pañcaśimba" refers to the five types of leguminous grains known as *niṣpāva*, *masūra*, *rājamāṣa*, *maṭha*, and *kulattha*. Furthermore, whatever is prohibited as food in the *Dharmaśāstras* must also not be given.
In response to the question of what that is, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Brinjal, *nālikā*, *pautīka*, safflower, and *aśmantaka*—these vegetables are not to be eaten."
‘Vṛntāka’ refers to the white vṛntāka. And so says Devala:
“One should avoid kaṇḍūra, white vṛntāka, and kumbhāṇḍa.”

*Kaṇḍūra* is the fruit of the *kaṇḍūrā*, also known by the name *prāvṛṣī*; it is covered with many hairs that produce extreme itching. *Kumbhāṇḍa* is a fruit that is round like a jar (*kumbha*), resembling a large gourd. *Kusumbha* is thornless; Devasvāmin states this because it is specified in another Smṛti.
Uśanas declares the fault in eating *kusumbha* and the others:
"The *kusumbha*, the *nālikā* vegetable, the eggplant (*vṛntāka*), and likewise the *pautika*."
Even a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedanta would become fallen if he were to eat it.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: [567] One should avoid garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms, eggplant, and long gourds, as well as anything corrupted by its very nature.
This [practice] is corrupted by its very nature; one should "know" (aveyāt) this. Hārīta says:
One should not eat the fruits of the *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *dadhittha*, *nīpa*, and *mātuluṅga* trees.
‘Dadhittha’ is the fruit of the wood-apple (*kapittha*). ‘Nīpa’ is the leaf of the *kadamba*.
Manu says:
“Red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by cutting [the tree],” and so forth.
One should carefully avoid the milk of a mountain goat and the colostrum of a cow.
*Śailu* is the *śleṣmātaka* tree. "Pīyūṣa" is the milk [of a cow] for ten days after it has given birth.
These are the fruits, roots, and so forth that are to be avoided.
Now follow the milks and other substances that are to be accepted and those that are to be avoided.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: Milk, milk-products, milk-rice (pāyasa), sugar, and honey—
these should always be diligently offered at śrāddha ceremonies for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Food accompanied by curds and milk, cow's ghee mixed with sugar,
and meat— these indeed satisfy all the ancestors," so said Aja.
Regarding the continuation [of the ritual] with the words "the ancestors are satisfied," Manu, Devala, and Kātyāyana state:
"For one year, however, [one should offer] cow's milk and milk-rice (pāyasa). Thus says Manu.
The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, that of a camel, that of one-hoofed animals, as well as the milk of sheep, the milk of a cow in heat, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died; [568]
And among all wild animals, with the exception of the buffalo,
the milk of females and all white-colored substances are indeed to be avoided.

In this context, regarding the reading "the milk of a cow within ten days" (*anirdaśāhaṃ ca goḥ kṣīram*), if the term *anirdaśāha* were to carry over [to the subsequent rules], one might suspect that the prohibition of the ten-day period would apply to camels and other animals as well. To prevent that prohibition from being absolute, one must rely on established custom (*samācāra*). However, if the reading is in the feminine gender, *anirdaśāyāḥ*, there is no such suspicion at all; for terms ending in secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), such as *auṣṭram* and so forth, cannot grammatically connect with *anirdaśāyāḥ*. A cow whose ten days since calving have not yet passed is called *anirdaśā*. "Camel's milk" (*auṣṭram*) refers to that of a female camel (*uṣṭrī*); "single-hoofed milk" (*aikaśapham*) refers to that of mares and others; "sheep's milk" (*āvikam*) refers to that of ewes. Furthermore, because the word "milk" (*kṣīra*) is not repeated in the subsequent rule, and by virtue of custom, the milk of camels, single-hoofed animals, sheep, and cows within ten days of calving—along with their products—is prohibited. The milk of a cow that is both "sāṃdhinī" and "avatsā" is also forbidden. A *sāṃdhinī* is a cow impregnated by a bull. Medhātithi, however, says: a *sāṃdhinī* is one who is normally milked at two times but is somehow milked only once—at night if she was not milked in the morning, or in the morning if she was not milked at night. Others, however, say that because she yields very little milk and is always milked at only one time, the term *sāṃdhinī* applies here due to the connection (*saṃdhāna*) or proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) of the milking; the suffix *-ini* is added to the words *saṃdhā* or *saṃdhi* because they belong to the *vrīhy-ādi* group. Some say that a *sāṃdhinī* is one who has lost her calf and is milked after being joined with another calf; since the word *sāṃdhinī* denotes a specific state, only the milk of that particular state is to be avoided, not the milk of a cow that subsequently loses her calf. The milk of a cow whose calf has died is to be avoided until the grief caused by the loss of the calf has subsided. Even if a cow has a living calf, if she is milked without the calf using husks, sour gruel, oil-cakes, and so forth, her milk is still to be avoided as she is effectively "without a calf" (*vivatsā*). The mention of the word "milk" (*payaḥ*) is because the word *kṣīra* contained within the compound connects with the subsequent rule. Regarding the phrase "of wild animals" (*āraṇyānāṃ mṛgāṇām*), since the masculine gender cannot grammatically connect with the base form *payaḥ*, the intention is simply to denote the genus; thus, by implication, the milk of the yak (*camarī*) and similar animals is understood to be forbidden.

"Except for that of the buffalo" means excluding the milk of the wild buffalo. "Woman's milk" refers to human milk; that too must be avoided at all times. All fermented acids (śukta) are also to be avoided.
Yama says:
"The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, as well as that of goats and buffaloes..."

One should avoid the milk of sheep, of a cow in heat, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals; likewise, one should avoid the milk of a cow that has not yet had a calf, as well as that of a cow whose calf is another's.
But among all forest-dwelling animals, with the exception of the buffalo,
Svāyambhuva has declared that the wool of sheep and other such products should always be avoided.

Yājñavalkya: One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or one that is nursing; as well as the milk of camels, of single-hoofed animals, of antelopes, of wild animals, and of sheep.
Vasiṣṭha:
[The milk of] cows, buffaloes, and goats that have not passed ten days since calving, as well as the milk of a cow in heat, is forbidden for consumption in villages and border regions.
Gautama: [The same].

The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, and that of goats and buffaloes during their period of impurity after birth, is unfit for drinking; as is the milk of sheep, of camels, and of one-hoofed animals; and the milk of cows that are "dripping" (*syandinī*), those that have recently given birth (*yamasū*), those in heat (*saṃdhinī*), and those whose calves are absent.
A "dripping" cow is one whose milk flows out by itself, or whose udder is leaking. A "yamasū" is one that has recently brought forth twins. — Baudhāyana.

The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving, the milk of a cow in heat, and the milk of one whose calf is dead, as well as the milk of a camel, the milk of a one-hoofed animal, and the milk of a ewe, are not to be drunk.
Āpastamba says:

Likewise, the milk of a black antelope, the milk of a female camel, the milk of a doe, the milk of a cow in heat, the milk of a cow that has recently given birth, and the milk of a cow within ten days of calving are not to be drunk.

Hārīta says: One should not drink the milk of a cow that is dripping [with milk] while in heat; nor that of one in her season; nor that of one whose calf has been killed, because she is overcome by grief; nor that of one whose milk has been milked out [before the calf drinks], for that would be as if one were to take food away from someone eating and eat it oneself. Nor [should one drink] the milk of one that has recently calved, because she still has menses. Some say [this applies] after seven nights, others after ten nights, but those who know the Dharma say that even after a month it becomes pus-like.
For thus they say:
For two months one should let the calf suckle; in the third month, one should milk it from two teats;
and in the fourth month, from three teats, according to the rule and according to its strength.

The term *avṛṣasyantī* refers to one who desires intercourse with a bull; "her milk becomes *ṛtumad*" means it belongs to one who is in her fertile period (*ṛtumatī*). By this, it is understood that the milk of one who has ceased her menstrual cycle is not prohibited. "A cow whose calf is killed" means one whose calf has died; the reason given is "because she is overcome by grief. Therefore, there is no prohibition against the milk of one who has forgotten the grief for her calf. The fact that this is a *hetuvannigada-arthavāda* (an explanatory statement appearing as a reason) has been refuted by the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, so it shall not be elaborated upon here. "Apart from the calf" means out of greed for milk. One should not drink the milk of a cow that has been milked after setting aside the living calf elsewhere. He strengthens the prohibition by means of an illustration: just as if one were to forcibly seize "food" from "one eating" and eat it "by oneself," so too is that [the milk]. The connection is: "one should not drink the milk of a cow that has recently calved. "Because of her being in her menses" is the reason. Some say that after seven nights it becomes pus; others say after ten nights; the experts in Dharma (*dharmavidaḥ*) consider it to be after fifteen days—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. In these various views regarding the seven-night period and so forth, the determination of when the cessation of the flow occurs should be observed. The mention of "experts in Dharma" is for the purpose of making known that even at the end of a month there is no doubt regarding the cessation of the flow; therefore, when the cessation of the flow is certain even after seven nights or more, there is no loss of merit (*dharma*) even in drinking the milk.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The milk of buffaloes, cows, and goats is fit for consumption, provided it is ten days old.
Śaṅkha states: [the same].
"The milk of all animals with two teats is unfit for consumption, with the exception of the goat.
Āpastamba, however, states that milk from a tawny cow (*kāpila*) must not be drunk by anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa:
"Whether he be a Kṣatriya established in his duty, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra..."
There is no doer of evil greater than he who drinks the milk of a tawny cow.

The meaning is that one should carefully avoid the milk of a Kapila cow—other than that belonging to a Brāhmaṇa—even if it is the remainder of what was used for rites such as the *śrāddha*. Regarding the fault incurred by a Brāhmaṇa drinking the milk of a Kapila cow when it is other than the remnant of an oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), it is shown in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "The Śūdra who drinks the milk of a Kapila cow is cooked in hell;
a Brāhmaṇa may drink the remnant of an oblation, otherwise he becomes a beast."
When the remnants of the oblation have been drunk by a Brahmin, he attains the status of a Brahmin even in another birth. Likewise:

The meaning is that if a Brahmin drinks the milk of a Kapila cow that has not been offered as a *huta* remnant, he becomes an animal in another birth. Precisely because of the injunction to avoid milk, it is established that its derivatives, such as curd-whey (*kūrcikā*) and the like, must also be avoided; for even in these derivatives, the essence of milk remains present. For this very reason, it is established in the *Mīmāṃsā* that when milk is to be avoided, one must also avoid preparations containing its flavor, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Therefore, Śaṅkha prescribes an expiation for consuming forbidden milk-derivatives, since the transgression of a prohibition has been committed.
"A wise man, being composed and diligent, should perform the seven-night vow when consuming products of those milks that are forbidden.
Although buffalo milk is prohibited in the context of *śrāddha* rites, buffalo ghee must certainly be accepted, because another scriptural statement establishes its excellence.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"At śrāddha rites, one should avoid the milk of buffaloes and the milk of goats;
one should also discard the milk of cows within ten days of calving and that of *saṃdhinī* cows."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Milk other than that of cows is not recommended for śrāddhas;
only the milk of cows, along with its derivatives, serves for the satisfaction of the ancestors."
Sumantu says: Milk, curd, and ghee from cows are indeed purifying in Śrāddha rites;
they say that the ghee of buffaloes is superior, but their milk is never so.
Devala says:
One should avoid the milk of goats, sheep, and buffaloes at śrāddha rites;
however, products derived from [cow's] milk are permitted, as is buffalo ghee.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"The meat of deer, sheep, and camels, all that which has a single hoof,
as well as that of buffaloes and yaks, and also the milk of a cow or a milch-cow within ten days of calving."
Having said, "Give this for the sake of my ancestors," whatever has been brought forth must always be avoided by the virtuous in the rite of the śrāddha; such is that milk.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: One should avoid buffalo, yak, deer, sheep, and milk or ghee produced from one-hoofed animals; likewise, that of the black antelope, camel, and curd or milk obtained by begging.
The scum of clarified butter, the cream of clarified butter, the milk of a cow while she is still wet with birth-fluids,
curd mixed with jaggery and sprinkled with black pepper,
stale curd, thin buttermilk that has become undrinkable, and that which has lost its flavor or is frothy— these are forbidden.

This is the meaning: "The froth from clarified butter" (*ghṛtāt phenaṃ*) refers to the scum removed from clarified butter, which is unfit to be drunk. "The cream from clarified butter" (*ghṛtān maṇḍaṃ*) refers to the thin layer (*santānikā*) skimmed off from clarified butter. Likewise, "the colostrum of a wet cow" (*ārdragoḥ pīyūṣaṃ*) means that milk is unfit to be drunk as long as the cow has not yet ceased to flow and her birth-canal remains moist. Similarly, anything mixed with milk, curd, molasses, or black pepper that has become stale is also unfit to be drunk. Likewise, buttermilk (*takra*) that is "burst" (*dīrṇa*)—meaning it has spontaneously split due to being heated over a fire without stirring with a ladle, or by other means—or that which has lost its flavor and turned white (*naṣṭāsvādaṃ*), or that which has developed froth after standing for many days, is also unfit to be drunk.

Thus end the items regarding milk and other substances that are to be accepted or avoided. Now, regarding meats to be accepted: first, the general rule for the offering of meat at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Manu says:
"The food of sages, milk, soma, meat that is unseasoned,
and salt-free food— these are by their very nature called sacrificial oblations (havis)."
The verse has been explained previously:
"The wise know the monthly ancestral rite (śrāddha) for the ancestors as the *anvāhārya*;
that should be performed with effort using commendable meat."

[574] This *śrāddha* prescribed for every month on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is considered by the sages to be the *anvāhārya* for the ancestors. This should be performed with meat (*āmiṣa*), that is, with flesh—either with what is recommended and not prohibited, or with specific items prescribed for two months such as fish-meat, and so forth. And this is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). In its absence, curds, clarified butter, soup, and the like will be prescribed. Furthermore, meat is a condiment (*vyañjana*) for the food to be eaten, such as rice and other grains; it is not, however, the sole item to be consumed, since he will later state: "And the qualities of soups, vegetables, and so forth," as well as: "As many as there are, and by whomsoever, the foods."
In another Smṛti:
"A Śrāddha performed even if meat is lacking is as good as not performed at all;
for the ancestors are flesh-eaters, though in their absence [substitutes] such as milk-rice (pāyasa) may be used."
In the Purāṇa: "Meat, vegetables, curd, milk, honey, and likewise other [substances]"—
thus is the general rule for the offering of meat at a śrāddha.
Now, the rule regarding the consumption of meat is stated. Manu says:
"That meat which has been consecrated by sprinkling (prokṣita) may be eaten at the desire of Brāhmaṇas."
And when one is enjoined according to the rule, even at the risk of one's life.

The term "prokṣita" refers to meat derived from an animal such as the Agniṣomīya, which has been endowed with purificatory rites (saṃskāra) like sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), as prescribed in injunctions such as "he sprinkles the animal. The word "brāhmaṇakāmyayā" means "by the desire of a Brāhmaṇa"; the word *kāmya* is used here in accordance with Vedic usage.

When Brahmins request it, one may eat meat even if it is of a nature that would otherwise require sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), or even if one has previously made a resolve not to eat it. "According to rule" means according to the scriptures; when "appointed"—that is, made to accept the duty—at the *madhuparka*, a sacrifice, or a *śrāddha*, one should eat the meat. Therefore, having accepted the invitation by saying, "I will eat at the *śrāddha*," one ought not to say, "I will not eat this. However, it was established previously that ascetics (*yati*) and students (*brahmacārin*), even when appointed, must not eat meat. "In the event of the loss of life"—meaning when there is no other food available and the departure of life is certain—one may eat meat, even if forbidden and even repeatedly, and even while observing celibacy, provided it is other than what remains from offerings to the gods or ancestors. This is because of the scriptural injunction, "One should protect oneself from all things," and because avoiding the sin of self-destruction is a mandatory duty.
Yama also says:
"One may eat consecrated meat once, out of a desire to please a Brāhmaṇa, when appointed to a rite for the gods or at a Śrāddha; however, one should avoid it under a vow."
