Yama declares that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh.
Oils, condiments, and salts that have been given with the hand do not reach the giver; having eaten them, one consumes sin.
That which is given with one hand, or that which may be given by a Śūdra—
namely, clarified butter, oil, salt, water, and likewise milk-rice.

The word "to be avoided" (*varjyam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. That which is given directly by hand, without using a ladle or other utensil, is called "given by hand. Likewise, that which is served by Śūdras—even if one asks, "What should be brought?"—is "Śaudra," meaning it is served by Śūdras. Alternatively, *śaudra* means "fit for a Śūdra," that is to say, unfit for a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, even if rice and other food are brought after being asked, "What is that? Bring it for that purpose," it is also considered *śaudra*. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
[616] That which is mixed with liquor or garlic, or even combined with nectar and the like, becomes defiled through such contact; indeed, one should treat it as if it were the leavings of a Śūdra.
Thus end the foods to be avoided. Now, regarding these foods specified as things to be avoided, an exception is made for some of them.
On this point, Manu says:
Curd is edible among sour substances, as is everything produced from curd;
and likewise those [liquors] which are distilled from pure flowers, roots, and fruits.
Likewise: "Whatever food, whether hard or soft, that is mixed with oil and is not forbidden— even if it has stood overnight— it may be eaten, as may all remnants of sacrificial oblations."

Even if it has been stored for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be consumed by the twice-born even if they have not been sprinkled with clarified butter.

‘Dadhisaṃbhavam’ refers to *udaśvit*, honey-syrup (*madhukilāṭa*), *kūrcaka*, and so forth; these are called *śuktas*. Those things which, though sweet in taste, become extremely sour due to the lapse of time or through contact with other substances—such as mangoes, grapes, and the like—are *śuktas*. However, those that are sour by nature, such as pomegranates, *āmalakas*, and citrons, are not *śuktas*, nor are mangoes and such fruits that have not yet reached full ripeness. For this word *śukta* is not a synonym for mere acidity. Among those [sour items], having prohibited those that are sour solely by virtue of time, those mixed with other substances such as roots and so on are permitted. And thus it has been stated by Gautama: "Sour [food] that is not [mixed with] curds."

"Mixing with water" refers to the *parivāsana* (fermentation), that is, those substances which are fermented together with flowers and other ingredients. "Edible food" (*bhakṣya*) consists of parched grains (*dhānā*) and cakes (*śaṣkulī*). "Solid food" (*bhojya*) refers to boiled rice and the like, which is coarse and substantial. If it is not censurable—that is, if its fragrance, color, and taste have not deteriorated—and if it is mixed with fat, then it may be eaten even if it has stood overnight. [617] The separate mention of the remains of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥśeṣa*), even though it is already included among foods mixed with fat for sprinkling, is for the sake of showing special respect for it. "Long-standing" means having been kept for two or three nights. "Produced from barley and wheat" refers to bread, flour-meal, and so forth; these may be eaten even if they are not mixed with fat. "Of milk": "transformations" (*vikriyāḥ*) or derivatives, such as curd, churned milk, and the like.
Yājñavalkya says: Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat, even if it has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even without such fats.

Bṛhaspati says: Curd is fit for consumption, as is anything sour that has originated from curd; likewise, food cooked with rice-alkali and mixed with clarified butter is fit for consumption—so says the Śruti.
Likewise:
all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as those from milk,
and foods such as *rāga*, *khāḍava*, and *cukra*, become stale after a night has passed.
Cakes, parched grain flour, roasted grains, fried cakes, barley meal,
vegetables, meat, sweetmeats, soup, and kṛśara;
Barley gruel, milk-rice, and whatever else is mixed with fats—
all of this may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, but one should avoid anything that has turned sour.

Vasiṣṭha says: One should avoid cakes, fried grains, *karambha*, parched barley flour, fried balls, oil, milk-rice, and vegetables, except when they are fermented (*śukta*); as well as other products made from milk, barley, and flour. Paiṭhīnasi says:

One may eat stale food that has been sprinkled with curds and ghee; for those exceptions (*pratiprasava*) regarding sour or stale food and the like, since they serve solely the purpose of human life (*puruṣārtha*), they do not fall within the scope of the *śrāddha* rite. One should not give food that is hot, nor steamed, nor twice-cooked. Since the rule "one should begin cooking in the morning" prescribes the commencement of cooking on the very day of the *śrāddha*, and because there is thus no possibility of pure stale food occurring, Yama has stated an exception to the rule: "One should not eat food that is not from the market."

"Cakes, flour-meal, parched grains, buttermilk, curd, ghee, and honey— these may be eaten at auspicious occasions, provided there is no smearing of the vessel. This rule applies to buttermilk and the other items mentioned, in cases where they might otherwise be subject to the possibility of being smeared, excluding cakes, flour-meal, and parched grains.
Thus end the exceptions regarding food to be avoided.
Now, concerning waters that may be accepted,
Manu says:
Water that has reached the ground is pure and free from thirst-inducing impurities where a cow would drink it,
provided it is not pervaded by filth and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste.
Viṣṇu: Water situated on the ground is pure if it is such that a cow would not feel thirsty;
likewise, water resting on a stone is pure provided it is not contaminated by impurities.
Water situated on the ground is pure; water resting upon a stone is clean, provided it is free from foul odors, colors, and tastes.
Uśanas says:
Water that has reached the ground is pure when it quenches the thirst of a cow,
provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural fragrance, color, and taste.
Devala says:
Waters found on the earth that are free from odor, endowed with flavor, pure,
and not diminished by being drawn up by cows, are traditionally held to be purifying.
Water that has been drawn out with pure vessels according to the prescribed rule is praised;
however, one should discard water that has been drawn out and has stood for even a single night.
For waters that are not turbid and are abundant, there is no defilement;
however, for those that are meager and have been drawn out, defilement occurs through impurities.
In that regard, one should avoid small ponds, rivers, or lakes that are defiled by impurities, starting from the bathing places (tīrthas).
Yājñavalkya states:
"Water that is pure, which satisfies the throat, and which is in its natural state when situated on the earth [is fit for use].
Having thus described what is not defiled, Vasiṣṭha says:
Prajāpati has declared that all waters situated on the earth, as well as those that provide nourishment for cows, are pure, having enumerated them all.
In continuation of the phrase "pure by means of water," Vasiṣṭha states:

"Those waters which, even if coming from a fissure in the earth, are sufficient for the satiation of cows, and which are not corrupted by color or taste, and which do not originate from an impure source [are pure]."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Water possessing color, taste, and fragrance, which is pure, not drawn up by living creatures or leather bags, and situated on the ground where a cow would not feel thirst—such water is ritually pure. Paiṭhīnasi states: [620]
Water that has reached the ground, which is pure in odor and color, should be used where a cow would not feel thirst; even a great body of water should be avoided if it is turbid.
Yama says: [one should avoid] a water-station in the forest and a jar at a well.
Water in a trough, water contained in a leather bag, and likewise water from a well— these they say are undrinkable even when provided by a Śūdra; however,
one may drink water that has reached the ground after flowing from a river.
Hārīta says:

The waters on earth are pure, with the exception of those that are impure. Furthermore, O Brāhmaṇa, this speech of the gods was: "The fish entered the waters; those gods sought speech from the waters. The waters said to them, 'Purify for us whatever is impure among our offspring and among others; then we shall give back the speech. The gods replied, 'So be it. They entered Agni; they became purified by Agni. Therefore, wherever these [waters] stand, they burn. They entered Vāyu; they became purified by Vāyu. Therefore, wherever these go, they cause a splitting. They entered Soma; they became purified by Soma. Therefore, these are glossy, cool, and flavorful. Yonder sun is Brahmā, the sacrifice, and all the deities; they caused these [waters] to drink day after day through the rays, beginning with the divine rays. Therefore, these are pure and purified during the day and are fit for purification. Therefore, whatever may need to be examined, one should touch it with water; purity is attained. At night, these waters entered Varuṇa; therefore, one should not take them at night. Saying, 'From every station,' one should take them while holding a fire above."

Kātyāyana says: One should not take water at night, nor should one ever do so even if taking it; having placed fire upon them with a supporting vessel, he should recite the mantra, "From every abode... and so forth.

When the sun has set, one should take water; in an emergency, if he should take it at night, he should hold it above the fire while muttering the *yajus* formula: "From every station, O King... [621]. Baudhāyana says:

"One should take water after the sun has set, or one should not"—thus they deliberate. Regarding this, some proponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say that one should take it; others say that one should take it for as long as one takes the water, restraining the breath, for it is Agni who indeed takes the water.
Uśanas:
Rivers, wells, tanks, lakes, and likewise streams—
Svāyambhuva Manu declared that these are not defective when they are uncovered.
Parāśara says:
Even for defects caused by others in wells, embankments, and paths,
as well as for the water in those currents and on the proper field-paths...
Manu declared that both what is to be accepted and what is to be drunk are not defiled by [the giver] being wicked.
Thus are the waters to be accepted. Now, the waters to be avoided,
according to the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Water that is foul-smelling, frothy, or from a stagnant pool should be avoided; likewise, one should not take water at night, nor that which does not satisfy a cow.
That water which has been released for all, and that which comes from a watering-trough and is unfit to be consumed— O dear one, such water must always be avoided in rites for the ancestors.

That water from wells and the like which has not been "abandoned"—meaning not relinquished—by their makers for the sake of the subsistence of all living beings, that water is to be used in the ancestral rites (*pitṛ-karman*). A "watering place" (*nipāna*) is a reservoir intended for holding water to be drunk by cattle and other animals; even water produced there—that is, standing within it—is to be avoided. Yājñavalkya says:
"However, the first waters of a river flowing with its initial current are not to be taken."
And those which have been disturbed by someone, or likewise extracted from their sacred source.

The term "first" (*agrimāḥ*) refers to those produced by the first rainfall; such waters, which remain turbid for one, two, three, or more days due to the force of the current, are not to be taken. However, once the initial force has subsided, waters that have become clear are to be taken. Furthermore, in the case of the second and subsequent surges, they may be taken even if the force has not yet fully subsided. Waters collected in reservoirs other than rivers, however, are considered "first" and are unfit for use for ten nights.
Thus says the traditional text: "Goats, cows, buffaloes, and Brahmin women who have recently given birth..."
They become pure after ten nights, as do new water in the earth.
Furthermore, those waters which have been agitated and rendered turbid by someone, as well as those drawn up from the descent paths at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), are not to be accepted.
Vyāsa says:
"That which has fallen away from a river, and that which has been left behind by a river..."
And one should avoid that water which has flowed away and returned.

That which has become separated from the river current whose waters have dried up by the heat of summer and so forth, and has become stagnant in a pool, is "fallen away from the river" (*nadyāḥ paribhraṣṭam*). That which, having become separate in the form of a small stream, does not again attain union with the great current, is "devoid of the river" (*nadyā vivarjitam*). That which flows upstream, either once or repeatedly, whether by itself or due to some other cause, is "receded and returned" (*gatapratyāgatam*); one should avoid that. Marīci says: "Between the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada, all rivers are in their menses."
One should not perform bathing, nor the libations for gods, sages, and ancestors, during those [periods].

The term *tarpaṇa* (libation) is intended to include *śrāddha* (ancestral rites) and other such ceremonies. *Nabhas* and *nabhasya* refer to the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada; "between those two" means during that interval of time. By using the word *rajasvalā* (menstruating woman) figuratively to express the absence of purity, it precludes the suitability of that water for ritual acts.
Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"Gaṅgā is the daughter of the Sun, and Sarasvatī is born from the Plakṣa tree."
Nor are those others known as the Nadas overcome by passion.
The Yamunā is the "daughter of the Sun" (Ādityaduhitā). The Gaṅgā is the Bhāgīrathī. The Sarasvatī is the one "born from the Plakṣa tree," who, while situated in Kurukṣetra, [is so named].
In another Smṛti: "The Kālindī, the Narmadā, the Gaṅgā, the Plakṣajātā, and the Sarasvatī."
But these sacred rivers,
because they avoid agitation and possess the quality of purity, are not overcome by passion.
The Gaṅgā, the Dharmadrava, the Puṇyā, the Yamunā,
and the Sarasvatī remain stainless even amidst all turbidities due to their internal connection with the dustless realm.
A marketplace, a flow against the current, a place where dust meets the flow of a carriage road—
these do not defile the Ganges, for it is itself a stream of dharma.
Thus end the waters that are to be avoided. Now follows the procedure for bringing water for sprinkling. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani says:
Then, having worshipped the sun and properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) himself,
he should take the sprinkling-water and, with his self fully controlled, go home.
In the phrase "having sipped water" (*ācamya*), the word "twice" (*dvis*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"One who has perfected the austerity, having sipped water twice, should then bring [water] for the purpose of sprinkling."
One who knows the ritual rules should never perform any action without first sprinkling water.
Śāṭyāyani states the procedure for fetching [the water]:
"The fetcher shall wear shoes, hold *darbha* grass, and have an upper garment with its fringe intact.

"Wearing shoes" means having ascended a pair of sandals. "Holding *darbha*" means having hands joined with *darbha* purifiers (*pavitra*). "With an upper garment with its fringe intact" means covered by an upper cloth possessing its fringes. The meaning is that the "fetcher" shall bring water contained in a vessel for the purpose of sprinkling.
Pracetas says: Having taken water that is well-protected, one should go home for the purpose of its use;
being always pure, one should perform sprinkling during the ritual sessions with that which has been taken.

‘Anuguptāḥ’ means not seen by others. ‘Apaḥ’ means water. ‘Gṛhya’ means having taken. ‘Pracārārtham’ means for the purpose of performing the tasks to be accomplished in the house. ‘Savane’ means at the time of the morning libation and so forth. He should go to the house. Having gone there, he should perform sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) after becoming pure with that water for the sake of purifying the materials and the places used for the ritual acts. Uśanas says: “Having sipped water (ācamya) in rivers and the like, even while wearing shoes, provided he does not touch [the water]... ”
Having arrived with a water-pot, he was indeed pure through his diligent effort.
Having sprinkled the ritual materials with that water and performed the ceremonial sipping (ācamana), one should then perform whatever daily rites there may be within the house.
Śātātapa says:

A man who has sipped water (performed *ācamana*) outside near rivers and other such places remains pure even if he touches someone while carrying water; indeed, even when on a public road, a person is truly pure through his own effort.
Garga, however, states another rule regarding the fetching of water:
"At the three junctions of the day, one should fetch water while remaining silent and purify it;
having fetched the materials and the water, one should purify them by sprinkling the site."
"Restrained in speech" means observing silence.
Gobhila says:
Before the time for the lighting of the fires in the evening and morning, one should fetch water that has been protected.
"Or they are to be attended upon.
Thus, "the carrying forth of the fire" means its manifestation; "its time" refers to the specific occasion; "before" means at a prior time.
In this context, there are primary and secondary vessels for fetching water.
Yogiyājñavalkya said:
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is declared to be the primary [vessel].
In its absence, it is traditionally taught that any vessel which does not leak may be used.
Śāṭyāyani says:
A vessel made of gold, silver, wood, clay,
or solid copper, or even a meritorious leaf-cup, is indeed suitable for the sprinkling [of water].
"Patrapuṭa" means a vessel made from excellent leaves, suitable for fetching water; this is to be understood as applicable when other vessels are unavailable.
Thus says Āpastamba:
"But in the absence of [other] vessels, a leaf-vessel is prescribed."
That vessel also should be known as leaking which is not held [properly].
Āpastamba states regarding vessels to be avoided:
"One should not accept water for sprinkling from moss, sand, dūrvā grass, ordinary grass, leaves, or iron vessels; so said the sage Āpastamba."

The prohibition of leaves here should be understood as referring to cases where other vessels are available, or specifically to those that have not been fashioned into the shape of a cup. Indeed, a twice-born man should not perform ritual sprinkling with a vessel that has a spout, nor with one made of bell-metal, nor even with one made from the fruit of an animal part.

‘With a tube’ means made of bamboo or similar materials; ‘with a broken [vessel]’ means one that has cracked; ‘with a bronze vessel’ (kāṃsyapātreṇa) refers to a bell-metal vessel, for *ghoṣa* is a name for bronze according to the Nighaṇṭu. ‘With a part of a living being’ refers to forms such as conch shells or mother-of-pearl. ‘Made from fruit’ means made from coconut, bilva, or similar sources. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: “With seaweed, grass, leaves, and the like, [one should not use] vessels for water that have not been consecrated.”
A wise person should not perform sprinkling with sand, cloth, or ointments.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), items such as reeds and animal parts are included.

"Water-vessels" (*ambubhājana*) refers to water-containers that have not undergone the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as sweeping mentioned in the section on the purification of substances. "Covered with sand or cloth" (*sikatāvastralepa*) means those held together by sand or cloth. Yama also says:
One should not perform sprinkling with water drawn up by the right hand alone, nor with water that is devoid of a vessel and the like, nor with water squeezed from a cloth.

"Devoid of a vessel" means water fetched from moss and the like. "With the left hand" means with the left hand. By this, it is authorized that water collected with the right hand is fit for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Water situated in a vessel, even if fetched with the left hand, is also authorized. Śātātapa says:
"Water held in the left hand without a vessel..."
One should not sprinkle the substance with that [water], nor with water used for wringing out a cloth.
One should not fetch water for the purpose of purification with a portion of one's lower garment;
rather, once it has been fetched, one should sprinkle it with the left hand while holding it with the right.
Śāṭyāyani says:
One who belongs to a single caste (ekajāti), one who is not veiled, and one who is a chatterer should not fetch [water].
Nor indeed should one sprinkle water with the hand or with a cloth.
The Śūdra is "once-born," while the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya—these three castes—are "twice-born. The fourth is the once-born Śūdra; there is no fifth.
Thus it is from the *Manusmṛti*. "A chatterer" means one who is not observing silence.
Pracetās states the duty to be performed immediately after bringing the sprinkling water:
"Having taken up the sprinkling water, he should go toward his home while wearing his sandals."
Therefore, one who is free from pride, having reached home, should perform all prescribed duties.
The vessel for sprinkling water should not be placed anywhere until the sipping of water has been offered and the small water-pot has been consecrated by sprinkling.

By this it is meant that, having performed the sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*) with this [water]—having sipped water (*ācamya*) with some other water provided by someone else without having set [the vessel] down anywhere—one should sprinkle [oneself] and then set down the vessel used for sprinkling. Śāṭyāyani also says:
"Having taken the vessel for sprinkling, one who has gone home should not set it down."
Without performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one becomes pure by sipping water while standing on the ground.
The meaning is that by performing the ritual sipping (ācamana) and sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) while placing [the vessel] on the ground, one becomes purified after having sipped water.
Following the ritual sipping, Pulastya says:
"Having sprinkled all the substances with that [water], and having sipped water again, [one may enter] the house."
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, one should perform ritual acts and hospitable ceremonies.
In this context, the syntactical connection is: "having again performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) in this house, one should sprinkle the materials with that [water].
Garga states which materials are to be sprinkled:
"Restraining one's speech at the three junctions of the day, having fetched protected water, one should purify it."
In the enjoyment of the oblation of the fire-sacrifice, one should [offer] substances, the self, and attendants.
Yama also says:
One should diligently sprinkle a house where [the deity] is habitually present;
one should not perform sacrifice in it at midday or during the twilight hours unless it has been sprinkled.
Garga says:
A drop of water the size of a cow-hide, when poured down,
purifies the ground where no smear of impurities is found, even if it has been covered over.
"A drop of water" (*apāṃ binduḥ*) refers to a single drop. "The earth" (*gām*) means the ground; "cleansed" (*samūḍhām*) means having been swept clean, that is to say, having its refuse removed.
Śāṭyāyani states this for one who is unable to perform the aforementioned sprinkling:
"Having properly sipped water in a river or similar place, being self-controlled, he returns home."
Having drawn water from the water-jar, one should likewise perform the ritual sprinkling.
Or, having sipped water at home after preparing gold, kuśa grass, and water,
and having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), one who has thus rinsed should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) once again.

One view is that, having sipped water twice correctly and being self-restrained, one should personally perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) from a river or similar source, or have it brought by disciples and others. Another view is that, having likewise performed the ritual sipping (*samupaspṛśya*), one should bring water for sprinkling from a *maṇika* (water-jar) kept in the house. Yet another view is that, having performed the sipping as before, one should take water situated anywhere within the house itself, place gold and *kuśa* grass into it, sip water again, and then prepare it for the purpose of sprinkling. Likewise:
"The first [sprinkling] is said to be *āgneya* (related to fire), and the second is from the hand of a Brahmin."
The third is from the water reservoir, and the fourth is traditionally taught to be from the water jar.

The first [type of water] is that which one has fetched oneself from a river or similar source; the second is that brought from that very same place by another pure Brāhmaṇa; the third is that taken from a water-source such as a well situated within the house; and the fourth is that drawn from a *maṇika* (water-jar). A *maṇika* is a vessel containing a large quantity of water. [Thus says] Pracetas.
Whatever sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) a twice-born man performs with fire, [that is also purified].
Those who discourse on Brahman declare that everything is equal to the water of the Gaṅgā.
‘Vaiśvānaram’ [is for] the Āgneya [rite].
Thus is the fetching of the sprinkling water.
Thus [ends the section] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīya, the sovereign of all the Śrīkaraṇas—

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by the scholar Śrī Hemādri, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, in the section on the ritual of *Śrāddha*, this is the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Substances to be Added."
[630] Now begins the ninth chapter:
The requisites for the *śrāddha* rite.

Making the mountains appear as Mount Kailāsa upon the earth, leaving only the serpent Śeṣa in the abode of Bali, and bringing the sun in the sky to a state of equality with the cool-rayed moon through its whiteness—
this man of manifest merit is he whose fame wanders through the three worlds out of curiosity.
Śrī Hemādri states at the outset the collection of requisites associated with the śrāddha rite.
Now, other ancillary sections concerning the *śrāddha* are also stated.

Among them, first regarding the *kuśa* grasses: concerning their origin and the greatness thereof, there is the *Śatapatha-śruti*: "The waters, indeed, being repelled by Vṛtra, rose up and settled on the desert; they became the *darbha* [grass]. Because they rose up and settled (*dṛbh*), therefore they are called *darbha*. These very *darbha* grasses are pure and sacrificially fit waters that have flowed forth from Vṛtra."

"Terrified by Vṛtra"—meaning fearing the son of Tvaṣṭṛ—"the waters," that is, the waters, "flowing toward the desert," meaning the arid wasteland, "emerged," rising upward, "pure," being free from defect; "sacrificial," fit for sacrifice; "not defiled by Vṛtra," meaning not brought to turbidity by Vṛtra. Gobhila says:
"Brahmā stands at the root of the *kuśa* grass, while Keśava is in the middle of the *kuśa*."
One should know Śaṅkara to be on the tip of the blade of kuśa grass, and all the gods to be all around it.
Regarding *darbha* grass, the *Śatapatha-śruti* states:
"The tip is indeed like that of the gods, the middle like that of humans,
and the root like that of the ancestors."
Hārīta also says:
Whatever recitation is performed with kusha grass in hand, whatever gift is given along with kusha grass,
and whatever one eats while having kusha grass in hand— for that, no measure can be found.
A bath with *kuśa* grass becomes purifying; a twice-born man should sip water using *kuśa*;
water drawn up with *kuśa* is equal to the drinking of Soma.
But he who always wears a garland of kuśa grass around his neck is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He who wears the sacred thread on his hand, his neck, his crest-lock, and on both his ears,
is not tainted by sin.
Kauśika said:
A seat of *kuśa* grass is always pure, especially for ascetics;
for one seated upon a *kuśa* seat, the highest yoga is perfected.
Just as no stain of water is seen upon lotus leaves, so for one who holds the purifier in hand, no defilement occurs anywhere.
Hārīta says:
For these Asuras of unmanifest form, who steal away the merit of recitation and burnt offerings,
flee in the ten directions from one whose hands have been purified by the *pavitra*.
Gobhila says: "Just as the thunderbolt belongs to the Lord of the Gods, the trident to Hara,
and the discus-weapon to Viṣṇu, so too do the *kuśa* grasses belong in the hand of a Brahmin."
Now follows the procedure for *kuśa* grass.
Kauśika said:
Having become pure, one should stand in a clean place facing the northeast.
The kusha grass should be touched by the best of the twice-born with the mantra consisting of the syllable *oṃ* alone.
The mantra for uprooting is found in that very same place:
"Born together with Virañci, you are the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), born of creation;
dispel all my sins and be the bringer of well-being."
In another *Smṛti* as well, having stated that very same mantra:
"Having thus recited the mantra, then facing either east or north,
one should extract [the tooth] by cutting it once with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*."
Kārṣṇījini says:
Having loosened the earth with a spade, the wise one should take [the soil] with the *pitṛtīrtha* [finger-position], reciting "huṃ phaṭ huṃ phaṭ" once each time.
Regarding this, Hārīta states the rule for the time:
"In the month of Nabhasya, on the new moon day, the gathering of darbha grass is prescribed. Those darbha blades, being of undiminished potency (ayātayāma), may be employed again and again."
One should not cut [grass] when it is wet, nor should one cut it at night or during the two twilights.

‘Nabhaḥ’ refers to the month of Śrāvaṇa. ‘Yātayāma’ means unfit for use in multiple instances. ‘Ayātayāmāḥ’ means that although they have been used, they are still fit for use in various other rites; this is the sense. Therefore, these [darbhas], having been used, may be employed again and again in other rites after setting aside the occasion for which they were originally prescribed. However, those gathered at another time are unfit for other rites even if they have been used only once, according to the opinion of Śālaṅkāyana. On the new moon day of the month of Nabhas, one who is pure should gather darbhas.
Those Darbha grasses, being fresh and not stale, may be employed again and again.
[633] Furthermore, there is this statement of the Sāṅkhyas:
"The sacrificial grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, and especially the Brāhmaṇas—these are not exhausted;
they may be employed again and again."
And as it is stated in the Gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa:
"Darbha grass, the black antelope skin, the mantras, the Brāhmaṇas, the sacrificial oblation, and the fires—
these are not exhausted by use and may be employed again and again."
That too, according to the previous statement, should be understood as referring specifically to darbha grass taken on the new moon day in the sky.
Mārkaṇḍeya also declares that these [darbhas] are not stale (*ayātayāma*), provided there is an exception:
"One should perform the act of sipping water (*ācamana*) with the hand holding the *pavitra*."
That which is not leavings is pure; however, one should avoid the leavings of those who have eaten.

That *pavitra* with which the sipping of water (*ācamana*) is performed does not become "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*); however, that with which eating is performed must be discarded as being "leftover. And this refers to a *pavitra* without a knot, because of the traditional teaching of Hārīta: "One should not perform the sipping of water with a *pavitra* that has a knot. This also refers specifically to a *pavitra* possessing the *brahmagranthi* (Brahman-knot).
"One should not sip water using the *brahmagranthi* nor with *kāśa* grass and the like at any time," because of this recollection of Āditya. Hārīta says:
The best of the twice-born, being constantly pure, should always perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with a purifier;
that [water] shall not become impure by contact with food, yet one should avoid what remains after eating.

"With *pavitreṇa*" means with hands joined by a *pavitra* (purifier). "That" refers to the *pavitra*; it does not become "impure" (*ucchiṣṭa*), meaning it does not become unfit for ritual action. One should "avoid" or abandon what is "leftover from a meal" (*bhuktaśeṣa*), that which has been brought to the state of being a part of the act of eating. This should be understood to apply to one who is pure and performing the *ācamana* rite, because of the statement "[one who is] restrained" (*prayataḥ*). Others, however, say this refers to the context of the *ācamana* required as a limb of ritual action. And so says Kātyāyana: "With a *pavitra*, or with *darbha* grass, during a ritual limb or in a rite for the ancestors..."
Having made the hand non-empty [of water], one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) at all times;
it should not be done with an empty hand, nor with darbha grass, and one should avoid that which has been left over as residue.
In this context, some maintain that the word *pavitra* refers to a ringed *pavitra*.
Śātātapa says: "In recitation, in fire-offerings, likewise in giving, in Vedic study, and in rites for the ancestors..."
One should, however, make the hand non-empty with gold, silver, and *kuśa* grass.
In recitation, fire-offerings, giving gifts, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors,
a wise man should perform the rites with both hands holding the sacred grass (pavitra), using the left and right hands respectively.
Kaśyapa says:

During bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, giving, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors, one should keep both hands provided with *pavitra* grass and *darbha* blades; otherwise, it is not so.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
A Brāhmaṇa who always stands with Kuśa grass in hand and is free from hypocrisy constantly destroys his sins, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton.
In the Purāṇa as well:
"One should always wear a silken thread (*kauśeya*) as a purifier on the right hand; especially while eating, one should not wash it once it has been taken up."
[635] "Kauśeya-pavitra" means a *darbha* grass purifier.
Atri also says:
"The twice-born should hold the *darbha* purifiers with both hands."
One should apply effort in the retention [of the breath] while it is conjoined with the Brahma-knot.
In the Brahmayajña and in silent recitation (japa), the Brahma-knot is prescribed;
at the time of eating, it is said to be circular; thus, dharma is not lost.

When a loop is formed by doubling the tips of *darbha* grass blades and making a half-twist to the right, and it is then passed through from behind, a circular knot (*vartulagranthi*) is formed. When that same loop is made with a full twist to the right and passed through from the front, it becomes a *brahmagranthi*.
Regarding the rule for which fingers to use when holding the *darbha*, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states:
"The *darbha* should be held with the ring finger, or with both the middle and ring fingers."
The two darbha strainers should be held with both ring fingers.
In another *Smṛti*: "One should wear these two strainers, joined with knots, using the two ring fingers alone; or one may hold the *kuśa* grass with the right hand."

The ring finger is the *anāmikā*. Kātyāyana states the characteristics of the sacrificial grass (*pavitra*): it should not have a hollow interior, it should have a tip, it should be made of *kuśa* grass, and it should consist of two blades.
It should be known as being the size of a span, a purifier wherever it may be found.
Yogayājñavalkya describes the method for preparing the *pavitra* (sacrificial strainers):
"With the mantra 'pavitre stha' (you two are purifiers), one should prepare two *pavitra*s made of *kuśa* grass,
which are not cut from the interior of a clump, are of *kauśa* origin, and are measured at the span of a *prādeśa*."

‘Not within the womb’ means not inside the womb and devoid of a tuft. ‘Cut by *kuśa*’ means cut after having been encircled with *kuśa*. ‘Made of *kuśa*’ means consisting of *kuśa*. “*Pavitrestho vaiṣṇavyo*” is the mantra for cutting.
A specific detail regarding this is stated in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
“With the mantra ‘*pavitrestha*’, two *kuśa* blades are cut at their base.”
With three blades of kuśa grass, those two purifiers (pavitrakas) should be made one span in length.

Āpastamba also says: "He makes two strainers (*pavitre*) from two blades of *darbha* grass that are equal, with their tips intact, and a span (*prādeśa*) in length. [He does so] with the mantra: 'You two are strainers, belonging to Viṣṇu; may he purify you again by means of the mind. He cuts them while placing either a blade of grass or a piece of wood between his fingers, but not with his fingernails. Yajñapārśva also says:
Having performed the rite with the *oṣadhi* mantra upon the joint of the thumb and finger,
one should cut a sacrificial blade (*pavitra*) measuring a span (*prādeśa*), which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
Not with the fingernail, nor with wood, nor with iron, nor with earthen objects [should one scratch].
For by scratching with the fingernail, disease arises; and with wood, wealth is not attained.
Death may result from an iron [sacrificial post], while with those made of clay, quarrel is certain.
The characteristics of the *pavitra* (purifying ring) having rounded knots have been described in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having circumambulated the sacrificial fire three times clockwise, one should insert the cord through the topknot."
The sacred thread (pavitraka) should have its knots formed according to the Vaiṣṇava method.
The "Vaiṣṇava path" refers to the posterior part.
The characteristics of the sacred thread (*pavitra*) featuring the Brahma-knot (*brahmagranthi*) are also stated in that very same place:
"Having abandoned the Vaiṣṇava path, [one should follow] that which issues from the Brahma-path."
Having performed a single circumambulation, it is called a *pavitra*;
that *pavitra* with the *brahmagranthi* knot is proclaimed by the exponents of the Vedas.
[637] The area facing the performer of the *pavitraka* rite is called the "Path of Brahman" (*brahmamārga*).
The number of blades of *darbha* grass for the *pavitra* is also stated therein:
"One should fashion the *brāhma* *pavitra*-wheel with seven tufts of *darbha* grass."
Five [sins] are prescribed for a Kṣatriya, four for a Vaiśya,
two for a Śūdra, and likewise for those born in between.
Mārkaṇḍeya, however, states:
"The purifier for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four blades of *darbha* grass;
for each subsequent caste, it is prescribed to be reduced by one, respectively."
Or it may be for all [the deities]; it should be purified by two [mantras], either knotted or not.
For rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be made with three; likewise for rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika) with five;
and when performing what is called the rite of sorcery (abhicāra), one should make the *pavitraka* with four.
Kauśika states the characteristics of *darbha* grass:
"The auspicious *darbha* grasses that grow in sesame fields have seven leaves;
they are recommended for the twice-born in rites pertaining to the gods (*daiva*) and the ancestors (*pitrya*)."

Darbha grasses that have not yet produced shoots are known as *darbha*, while those that have produced shoots are known as *kuśa*. Those with roots are called *kutapa*, and those with severed tips are designated as *tṛṇa*.
‘Unproduced’ (*aprasūtāḥ*) means those that have not yet borne fruit, i.e., those that have not flowered.
Hārīta also says:
“The tip of a blade of *darbha* grass is said to belong to the gods; however, [the blade] with both root and tip belongs to the ancestors.”
In that regard, those kuśa grasses which are without roots are remembered as kutapas.

A twice-born man should gather auspicious kuśa grass that is uncut at the tips, possessed of leaves, along with their roots, and tender, for the sake of rites for the ancestors, the gods, and the recitation of prayers.
[638] This refers to objects other than the sacrificial grass (prastara) and so forth.
And thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The blades should indeed be green, with their roots intact, glossy, robust, and complete."
They were consecrated by means of the *pitṛtīrtha* at a measurement of one *ratni*.
The finest *kuśa* grasses, with their roots cut off, are to be taken for the purpose of the sacrificial strew;
however, in the fire-ritual and in sacrifice, one should avoid those that have their roots intact.

‘Sapiñjūlāḥ’ means those whose blades are not separated. A *ratni* is the measure of a closed fist; those [blades] prepared with that [measure], having produced an excellence through the taking [of the grass] at the *pitṛtīrtha*, are [called] *sumantu*. Sumantu says: "For rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), auspicious *darbha* grasses with uncut tips are required; indeed, green ones are auspicious."
Rootless kuśa grasses are to be employed in rites for the gods and in recitations such as japa;
those with seven leaves are recommended for rituals pertaining to both the gods and the ancestors.
Kātyāyana said:
Green Darbha grass is for sacrifices; yellow is for the five daily sacrifices;
with their roots, it belongs to the ancestors; and variegated is for the Viśvedevas.
The *kuśa* grasses used for walking upon should be short, while those used as sacrificial seats (*barhis*) should be long.
‘Pañcayajñiyāḥ’ means those worthy of the five sacrifices. ‘Pracaraṇam’ means performance; those worthy of that are ‘pracaraṇīyāḥ’. ‘Pitṛdevatyāḥ’ means dedicated to the ancestors. And so says Yama:
“In the ancestral *śrāddha* rite, the *darbha* grass should be with its roots.”
In all ancestral rites, the hair should be shorn externally and shorn only once.
"Bahirlūnāḥ" means cut near the roots.
And thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Kuśa grasses that are likewise cut near their roots are prescribed for the purpose of Śrāddha."

"Likewise, śyāmāka, nīvāra, and dūrvā grass are prescribed. Furthermore, as for Gobhila’s statement that "in rites for the ancestors [the grass] is cut near the roots," it should be understood that this refers to śrāddhas other than the *ekoddiṣṭa*. On this point, the Purāṇa says:
Until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is performed, all ritual actions must be carried out with straight kuśa grass that has roots and tips, by those who are pure and composed.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the ritual should be performed according to the rules with double the number [of items],
using *darbha* grass grown in sesame fields and carefully doubled.
The libation for the ancestors should be performed according to one's inclination, while that for the deities is done with the root [of the blade];
the ancestral rite is performed with the middle [part], and the gift for humans with effort; one who desires prosperity should perform the rite for the gods with the tip of the kuśa grass.
‘By chance’ (yadṛcchayā) means without any fixed rule.
As stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa: “Whatever rites for the ancestors there may be, such as libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth...”
They should consist of double-stranded darbha grass, especially those with seven leaves.

Regarding this, Hārīta states those [kusha grasses] that are to be avoided: "One should avoid six types of *kuśa* grass: those on a funeral pyre, those on a path, those on sacrificial grounds, and those used for the *prastara*, the *āsana*, and the *piṇḍa*."
Those darbha grasses used in the Brahmayajña and those used in the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa),
once they have been held during the voiding of urine or feces, their disposal is prescribed.
One should carefully avoid *darbha* grass that is impure, that has borne fruit, or that has been torn by fingernails; likewise, one should avoid *kuśa* grass that has been boiled or scorched by fire.

‘Garbhitāḥ’ means those containing an embryo; ‘kvathitāḥ’ means those that have become putrid. Also in the Purāṇa: "Those blades of darbha grass which were made for the sake of a ritual ball (piṇḍa), and by whom the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) was performed..."
And for those who have been held by one who has discharged urine or food remnants, their abandonment is prescribed.
Śāṭyāyana says:
One should discard those [hair-tufts] that were worn during the offering of rice-balls, the Śrāddha rite, or the libation to the ancestors;
likewise, those worn during eating or the voiding of excrement.
Kātyāyana says: Those darbha grasses which are prescribed for the purpose of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and likewise for the purpose of libations (tarpaṇa),
their disposal is ordained once they have been worn during the voiding of feces or urine.
Hārīta states an exception regarding the relinquishment [of the *pavitra*]:

"One should know that those blades of *darbha* which are placed within the waist-knot (*nīvī*) and those which are made part of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) are *pavitra*s; they remain so as long as the body [remains so]."
Gautama also said:
"Those [deities] who reside in the middle of the waist-knot and likewise those who reside in the sacred thread—
there shall be no offense against them when one discharges excrement, urine, or other such waste."
One should not drink with the right hand while the *darbha* grass remains in the left;
however, there is no fault for one drinking while holding [the vessel] with a cloth or similar object.
Hārīta says: A *śrotriya* should personally fetch the sacrificial fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and other such items.
A Brahmin who performs a ritual with *kuśa* grass fetched by a *śūdra* goes to a low state.
A twice-born man may take kuśa grass, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and especially medicinal herbs, even on a day when they are otherwise prohibited, such as the new moon day.
Regarding the substitution for *kuśa* grass when it is unavailable, Śaṅkha says:
"O best of the twice-born, in the absence of *kuśa*, one should diligently perform rites such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) with *kāśa* grass; *kāśa* is traditionally held to be equal to *kuśa*."

Now, the Śatapatha-Śruti: "The sacrifice indeed fled from the gods; having become a horse, it turned away. The gods, pursuing it, seized its tail-hairs and plucked them out. Having plucked them out, they placed them together with the sacrificial fee (sani), and from that these plants came into being: the *pada* and the *bāla*.
[This is found] in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Brahmavaivarta-purāṇa*.
Formerly, this Prajāpati was the most eminent among the renowned;
his hairs, having fallen upon the earth, attained the state of kāśa grass.
Therefore, the *kāśa* grasses are always pure and honored in the performance of *śrāddha* rites;
one who desires prosperity should offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) upon them.
[Those who do so] become endowed with progeny, nourishment, luster, wisdom, fame, and beauty.
They are always radiant, free from sin, and devoid of faults.
Regarding the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) among *kāśa* grasses according to the prescribed rule,
Viṣṇu states:
"In the absence of *kuśa* grass, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* grass in place of *kuśa*."
Yajñapārśva says:
"In the absence of *kuśa* grass, however, *kāśa* grass should be used; *kāśa* is remembered as equal to *kuśa*.
In the absence of *kāśa*, other *darbha* grasses should be taken in their proper order."
"Other *dabhas*": those which perform the functions of *darbha*. These are mentioned by Atri among the ten types of *darbha*:
"Kuśa, kāśa, barley, dūrvā, uśīra, along with kunda, wheat, rice, muñja, and balvaja—these are the ten *darbhas*."

‘Uśīra’ is the *bālaka* grass. ‘Kunduru’ is a specific type of grass well-known by the name *kunda*. ‘Balvaja’ is a specific type of grass resembling *kāśa*, with whose ropes bedsteads are woven by commoners. Regarding *barhis* (sacrificial grass), Yama says: “*Kuśa*, *kāśa*, as well as *dūrvā*, barley, and even rice.”
Balvajas and puṇḍarīkas are said to be the sevenfold sacrificial grass (barhis).
Uśanas says: Piṇḍabarhis, kuśa, kāśa, dūrvā, muñja, and balvaja grasses;
muñja, sugarcane, rice, wheat, barley, kundu, and bālaka.

One who desires prosperity should not perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna) on the eleventh or thirteenth lunar days, nor during the asterisms of Maghā or Kṛttikā, as these are inauspicious.
Regarding the sacrificial grass for the funeral cakes, Gobhila states a prohibition against using *balbaja* grass.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) for the ancestors is cut close to the roots; in their absence, any grass may be used except for awned grass (*śūkatṛṇa*), *śara* reeds, and *balbaja* grass.
"Awned grass" refers to grass possessing awns.
On this point, there is the *Āpastamba Sūtra*.

They bring the sacrificial grass (barhis) cut once together with its roots; or rather, they bring the grasses cut once, severed near their bases. "Upamūlam" means near the root, and "ditāni" means cut.

[643] Prohibited grasses are mentioned in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "At a *śrāddha*, one should always avoid *kṣupa* grasses, as well as *balvaja* grasses, trees, *vīraṇa* grass, *lava* grass, and *varṣā* grass."
One should likewise avoid other such grasses as these.
Thus concludes the description of *kuśa* grass. Now, regarding sesame seeds (*tila*):
first, their origin is described in the *Vārāha Purāṇa*.
Dharaṇī said:
O Lord, how were sesame seeds produced, and by whom were they created? Why are they so dear to the ancestors? You ought to tell me this.
Śrī Varāha said:
In the field of Brahmā at Kurukṣetra, the gods led by Brahmā were present—
the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Bhāskaras, Maruts, and the two Aśvins.
The Viśvedevas, the Rudras, Indra, and Bṛhaspati,
having undertaken their vows, commenced the great sacrifice known as Gosava.
O woman of excellent complexion, the gods were summoned there from all sides,
as well as the self-controlled sages dwelling in various lands.
There, the preeminent Brahmins— the Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ priests—
performed that sacrifice with the utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*.
With foremost oblations of clarified butter purified by mantras,
as the fires were kindled by the *sāmidhenī* verses,
and with the offering of various kinds of food in an unrestrained manner.
While the eaters were being satisfied with whatever they desired,
and cows, land, gold, and garments were being given away at will;
While all the gods of the sorrowless realm were being led away,
and while the officiating priests were indeed gratified by infinite sacrificial fees.
When all the gods had assembled there,
the ancestors then arrived together with King Soma alone.
They had not been invited previously by the gods who were preoccupied with the preparations for the sacrifice;
then those ancestors heard that the Gosava was being performed.
Accompanied by King Sāma, they arrived with great haste;
seeing them at the site of the sacrifice, [the demons] were embarrassed and their minds were filled with fear.
With palms joined in reverence, they all said, "Go! Go!
Then the Pitṛs, together with Soma, their eyes bloodshot with anger, [departed].
With their limbs trembling, they replied: "What is the use of our having come here?
Having previously disregarded us, the sacrifice was commenced by you."
"O gods, have we not indeed been honored by you even with mere words?
Therefore, we shall curse all the sacrificers along with their officiating priests."
Then those gods, being afraid, said to the Grandfather, "Protect us!
Thereupon Viriñca spoke to Kaśyapa, who was certainly accompanied by them at that time.
"O great sage, you must console the hosts of ancestors along with Soma;
so too shall the highly fortunate Kaśyapa act, by the command of the Supreme Lord."
Having bowed with devotion to King Soma and also to the hosts of ancestors,
he praised them with various hymns derived from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
All the ancestors, being pleased, said to him: "O great sage, you must not now create an obstacle to the pronouncing of the curse."
O Sage, if you do not inflict punishment upon these arrogant ones, our minds will find no peace; therefore, do not restrain us.
Then Kaśyapa said to them, "Forgive me, O best among the knowers of yoga;
I give you food that is even superior to the sacrificial portion."
Having spoken thus, the sage then produced from his own limbs black sesame seeds that were exceedingly smooth and more refined even than nectar.
Then the lord of sages created white sesame seeds from his body hairs;
he appointed Soma as their sovereign king.
Having fashioned heaps of sesame seeds, Kaśyapa spoke to the ancestors:
"O ancestors, please accept this food given by me."
"May [this] be for your satisfaction until the end of the kalpa; let the agitation caused by the curse be abandoned.
Then, all the Pitṛs, led by Soma, being pleased, attained supreme satisfaction merely by the sight of the sesame seeds.
With delighted minds, they said: "O bull among sages, we have been saved! What further need is there for a share of the sacrifice? Let sesame seeds alone be our portion."
We have desisted from our curse; may the gods be free from fear.
From this time forward, sesame seeds alone should be offered to us by those endowed with faith.
We have no need even for nectar if we obtain sesame seeds;
for he who shall perform the libation and the śrāddha rite purified with sesame seeds [shall attain our favor].
Out of devotion, he will offer us food made of sesame seeds,
and others will present various articles for giving along with sesame-water offerings.
"We shall gladly grant him offspring, wealth, and heaven," having said this, those ancestors, who were divine yogis, indeed vanished.
The gods, headed by Hiraṇyagarbha, departed as they had come.
Thus were the black and white sesame seeds created by the gods for the Gosava sacrifice dedicated to Soma. What else do you wish to hear?
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The gods have declared that kuśa grass and black sesame seeds, produced from the body of Viṣṇu, are sufficient for the protection of Dharma."
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*,
it is said: "The great sages declare that sesame seeds were born from the sweat of Viṣṇu and the *kuśa* grasses from his very hairs, for the purpose of protecting the *śrāddha*."

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Sesame seeds originated from Viṣṇu; therefore, they are the supreme oblation. Through sesame seeds, O Bhārgava, there arises the gratification of the entire world by means of *śrāddha* and *homa*."
Now, the procedure for the greatness of sesame seeds is described.
In the *Ādityapurāṇa*, Durvāsas said:
How were the sesame seeds produced, and how indeed were they brought down?
O Lord, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely.
Bhānu said:
Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall tell you everything without omission.
Long ago, in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a constant drought that caused the destruction of all living beings.
All the ancestors have arrived, their throats parched with hunger and thirsty;
they performed extensive austerities for the sake of sesame seeds—of this there is no doubt.
For a thousand divine years, those ascetics remained without food,
surrounded by all their hosts and especially by all the gods.
By the Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas;
by Prajāpati, the Lord of the Pitṛs, and the Grandfather of the Gods himself.
"I am well-pleased with you; I shall grant it—tell me what you desire.
The ancestors said:
"O highly fortunate one, give us sesame seeds, for they are what we long for; of this there is no doubt."
We do not live without sesame seeds, nor does sesame remain within the heart.
Brahmā said:
"Go indeed, O best of the twice-born; sesame seeds have been given to all of you, and the ancestors, being fully satisfied, departed taking the sesame seeds with them."
Thereupon, the food of the ancestors became entirely composed of sesame;
satisfied by the nectar of sesame, the ancestors attained liberation.
The man who offers sesame seeds with the desire for the satisfaction of the ancestors obtains the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
He who offers sesame seeds mixed with honey to the foremost of the twice-born on the full moon day of Vaiśākha is liberated from all sins.
He who, full of faith during the śrāddha rites, offers sesame seeds, sweetmeats, and molasses, will be born wealthy and a sharer in the fruits of agriculture; of this there is no doubt.
If one offers it with devotion, even with white sugar or jaggery,
the hosts of ancestors are satisfied and attain the supreme goal;
they bestow upon him long life, heaven, and health as well.
Having prepared krisara with sesame seeds, one should also give sesame cakes.
For one who indeed gives to the ancestors, an imperishable world is considered his;
so too for one who bestows vessels of sesame seeds on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day.
And during the northern solstice as well, the merit of that man who with faith gives sesame seeds to the King of Dharma is infinite.
O Lord, sesame seeds issued forth from the very limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa;
therefore, sesame seeds attained a divine state in matters of giving.
In the Mahābhārata:
"They praise the gift of sesame seeds at a śrāddha as unsurpassed;
O bull among the twice-born, sesame seeds should always be given according to one's ability."
Regarding this, Satyavrata says:
"Jarttilas are said to be black sesame seeds grown in the wild;
they are to be known as jarttilas which have been produced without being tilled."
Āpastamba also says: "Those sesame seeds that grow wild in the forest, ripening without being ploughed—they alone are pure for the śrāddha; those [other] sesame seeds are not truly sesame seeds."

Those sesame seeds (*tila*) that grow in the wilderness on unploughed ground are called *jartila*; they are most highly praised for rites performed with faith (*śrāddhakarma*). However, those cultivated village sesame seeds grown in ploughed fields are merely "well-known" sesame seeds and are not [the true] sesame seeds [required for the rite]. This is not a prohibition against their having the form of sesame seeds, because that would be impossible. Nor is it a prohibition against their performing the function of sesame seeds, because a prohibition against their performing that worldly function would be contradicted by direct perception and other means of knowledge. Nor is it a prohibition against their performing Vedic functions, because that would contradict scriptural injunctions. Thus, it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
The ascetic, the triple staff, the silver vessel as the instrument,
the daughter's son, the kutapa blanket, the time, the goat, and likewise the black antelope skin.
"White, black, and likewise wild, as well as various kinds of sesame seeds—these ten were created by Brahmā himself for the satisfaction of the ancestors. Thus it is said.

In this context, "tridaṇḍī" (the triple-staff bearer) is an adjective qualifying the ascetic (*yati*); "rājatam" (made of silver) qualifies the vessel; and "kutapa" qualifies the time. As for the sesame seeds, there are three distinct substances based on their different qualifiers: white sesame, black sesame, and wild sesame. In this way, the number ten is accounted for. Furthermore, since this statement declares that all types of sesame seeds are fit for Vedic rites, it is not possible for it to be a prohibition of the common sesame seeds from performing those functions. Therefore, the phrase "not sesame seeds, [but] sesame seeds" is merely a form of censure intended to praise the *jartila* (wild sesame) being enjoined, similar to the statement "all other animals are indeed no-animals except for cows and horses."
Thus ends the description of sesame seeds. Now, regarding barley: its origin is found in the Śatapatha-Śruti.

In the beginning, the gods seized a man as their sacrificial victim. When he had been seized, his vital essence (medhas) departed; it entered a horse. They seized the horse; when it had been seized, its vital essence departed; it entered a cow. They seized the cow; when it had been seized, its vital essence departed; it entered a sheep. They seized the sheep; when it had been seized, its vital essence departed; it entered a goat. They seized the goat; when it had been seized, its vital essence departed. It entered this earth. They searched for it as if digging, and they found it: these two, rice and barley. Therefore, even today, people find them as if by digging. Indeed, as much vigor as would have belonged to all those animals had they been sacrificed, so much vigor does the oblation of one who knows this possess.

The meaning of the statement is that by sacrificing all these animals, whatever fruit belongs to the sacrificer, that same fruit would belong to the sacrificer through rice or barley. In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"In ancient times, Tvaṣṭṛ, desiring offspring, praised the Supreme Lord."
Then Gotrabhid begot a son, Vṛtra, who was his enemy.
As soon as he was born, that great-bodied and mighty being, eager to swallow the worlds, struck terror into all beings.
Indeed, for him of immeasurable power, his body visibly increases by the measure of an arrow’s length— downward, upward, and across— in every direction.
That hero pervaded the entire universe with his tiny, yet inexhaustible body;
for he had been restrained by his father while he was desiring to devour the whole world at once.
The mighty one ate the sacrificial offering presented by the gods in the forenoon,
by human beings at midday, and by the hosts of ancestors in the afternoon.
Thus, he alone then devoured all the food;
he alone drank the Soma, and he alone carried away the sacrificial oblation.
Then Bṛhaspati, having been prepared by the gods with the powers of sacrifice,
slowly hurled a blazing thunderbolt at him for the purpose of hurling it.
Struck by that unbearable blow of the mace, Dambha fell to the surface of the earth like Vṛtra, rending asunder the caverns of the netherworld.
Then the Earth, the support of the world, bore all that essence of food which had overflowed and fallen down in streams.
Then, from that [mixture], great medicinal herbs were born as the means for performing sacrifice;
because they were produced from a combination of various food essences, they came to be known by the name *yava*.
Then, after the slaying of the asura Vṛtra, the inhabitants of heaven were thoroughly satisfied;
beholding the barley, they attained supreme contentment.
All the nectar-eaters, being greatly delighted, said to one another:
"This is the taste of both wild and cultivated herbs!"
This essence of King Soma has manifested in the form of barley;
it has been further strengthened by the supreme heroic power of the Asura Vṛtra.
May these, who are our very purification and our supreme oblation,
who are as sweet as nectar, always delight us.
Let the *havis*-sacrifices proceed for those who partake of the nectar of immortality;
let them be employed in these rites, both for pacification and for prosperity.
Whatever is offered to the gods by those possessed of faith,
let that be presented with water mixed [with sesame seeds].
Whatever rites dedicated to the Vaiśvadevas occur during the Śrāddha ceremonies,
let those be performed by these very preeminent masters of the Vedas.
With barley there is wealth, with barley there is charity, with barley there are dice, and barley is the oblation;
wherever there may be a Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, may there be eternal satisfaction.
Having spoken thus, the delighted gods returned to their own abodes;
and the worlds remained as before under the governance of Indra, the subduer of Pāka.
Now, the greatness of barley;
regarding this, there is the Śatapatha-Śruti:

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then all the plants went over to the gods; only the barley did not go over to them. The gods desired to win them back. With these [barley grains], they drew away all the plants from their rivals. Because they drew them away (*ayuvata*), therefore they are called *yava*. They said, "Come, let us place that which is the essence of all plants into the barley. They placed that which was the essence of all plants into the barley. Therefore, wherever other plants wither, these [barley] grow on, rejoicing; for thus they placed the essence into them. And so too does this [sacrificer] now draw away all the plants from his rivals by means of these [barley grains].

Formerly, during the conflict between the gods and the asuras, all the medicinal herbs were seized and carried away by the powerful asuras from the gods. Only the barley (*yava*), because the asuras were afraid of its special power that destroys demons (*rakṣoghna-śakti-viśeṣa*), could not be taken away by them. Then the gods, having routed all the asuras through the very majesty of the gods themselves, took all the medicinal herbs for themselves; therefore, the meaning of the statement is that "barley exists everywhere. Now, regarding the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*):
on this point there is the *Śatapatha-śruti*.
"Immediately that sacrifice is that black antelope skin.
Likewise:
"He indeed mounts one who is superior who mounts the sacrifice; for the sacrifice is the black antelope skin."

The praise of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) by way of its being the essence of the three worlds is also found in that very same passage: "If it is one [skin], that is the form of these worlds; thus he consecrates him (*dīkṣayati*) upon these worlds. Those parts which are white are the form of heaven; those which are black are [the form] of this [earth]. If it were otherwise—those which are black are the form of heaven, and those which are white are [the form] of this [earth]—and those which are brownish-yellow are the form of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); thus he consecrates him upon these worlds."

In the passages beginning with "white" (*śuklāni*), the word "hairs" (*romāṇi*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "'Asyai' means of this earth. "'Babhruṇi' means tawny; 'harīṇi' means yellowish-green in color. [This is] in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
Bhartṛyajña said:
Then, in ancient times, Dakṣa by name, the lord of progeny, was created by the Creator who desired to bring forth creation; he was skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites.
That great ascetic begot one hundred and one daughters,
and he bestowed them upon the gods according to the righteous rite.
With a delighted soul, he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
and twenty-seven to the Moon, the nectar-rayed one.
The wise one gave those other daughters to others;
his daughter named Dākṣāyaṇī was the youngest of them all.
He gave it to the Lord of the Three Worlds, who is clothed in an elephant hide;
once, that man devoted to righteous deeds began to perform a sacrifice.
Having accumulated all the necessary provisions, he summoned the gods, led by Indra, to that great festival.
But having honored the son-in-law Kṛttivāsas,
all the sons-in-law were summoned by him, who is praised by the hosts of gods.
The great sages, Marīci and the others, served as the officiating priests there;
then, that sacrifice was extended with abundant sacrificial fees.
Dwelling in her father’s palace, she beheld all the Yakṣas, the Suparṇas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Ṛṣis, as they all sported without exception.
When Dakṣāyaṇī, her lotus-like face withered from not seeing her beloved,
began scratching the earth in an instant, then—
Approaching her father, the virtuous woman, her eyes agitated with trepidation and overcome with bashfulness,
spoke in faltering words.
"Father, there will be no festival greater than this;
why then has our Lord been forgotten even on this occasion?"
"Even now, let my husband, the creator of the worlds, be summoned here;
without that Lord of Sacrifice, what kind of sacrifice is this of yours?"
Thus addressed by the girl, Dakṣa, his lips quivering with anger, said:
"O child, that formless one is loathsome to behold."
"How can a Kāpālika be admitted into sacrificial grounds?
O daughter, because of such a son-in-law, we are put to shame here."
While these devoted wives are looking on, how can this naked man, who practices such inauspicious conduct, be brought forward?
While Dakṣa was thus speaking many harsh words in his rage,
the slender-limbed woman covered her ears and, remembering the Enemy of Smara (Śiva),
gave up her life then and there; filled with grief, she uttered no further word.
Then, throughout the entire world, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Upon hearing that news concerning Aparṇā, the Destroyer of Tripura, though tormented by grief, fell under the sway of anger alone.
Then, in an instant, placing at his head the enraged army of Gaṇapas,
which was fully armored, the Destroyer of Cities set forth, making the world distressed.
Then a battle commenced with the hosts of the gods,
joined by Nārāyaṇa and others who had arrived out of partiality for Dakṣa’s side.
Then, the hosts of Rudra, having hemmed in the celestial army in battle,
rained down a continuous, thick torrent of arrows without any interval.
Striking at the army with terrible discharges of weapons and missiles,
Śiva, who is without beginning or end, recalled his own power of yoga.
Then, in an instant, the celestial warriors were utterly defeated;
overwhelmed on all sides, they fled in every direction—this way and that.
The gods could not endure the Pināka-wielder, yet they did not slay him;
because of that, those led by Govinda did not find any firmness of mind.
Then the Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, beheld the lord of the sacrifice fleeing, terrified and assuming the form of a black antelope.
Tripuravyādha pierced him with a three-jointed arrow and severed his head in the sky; that [head] is this very Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Even today, the world beholds the source of the Lord of the World’s glory:
that headless trunk of the deer-sacrifice fell upon the earth.
Those expert in the science of architecture call him the Vāstupuruṣa;
from his body, Gaṅgādhara cut away the skin entirely.
Dhūrjaṭi cast off his holy and unsurpassed black antelope skin,
and Virūpākṣa declared it to be the supreme means for accomplishing initiation.
Let this be superior even to all other gifts:
that a man provides a black antelope skin at a śrāddha ceremony.
"His ancestors shall obtain satisfaction lasting until the end of the kalpa.
Having spoken thus, Vāmadeva departed for the Devadāru forest.
Thus, this black antelope skin, which has arisen in this manner and is pure,
should be diligently placed nearby by wise men during a śrāddha ceremony.
By the presence of this [skin], the destination of the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
Having spread it out with the neck pointing southward and the hair facing upward,
one should place all the ritual requisites for the *śrāddha* upon it.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"The proximity to, the sight of, and the gift of a black antelope skin destroy demons,
bestow Vedic luster, and rescue one's cattle and sons."
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "By the touch of a black antelope skin, all objects become pure."
Therefore, those who know the scriptures should strive to establish this in the locations for ancestral rites (śrāddha).
Thus concludes the description of the Kṛṣṇajina.
Now, regarding silver:
first, its origin is described in the Nandipurāṇa.
Then the god Virūpākṣa, assuming the pratyālīḍha stance and taking up an arrow composed of all the gods, stood ready.
Having drawn his bow, with Mount Mandara as the bow and Vāsuki as the string bent into place,
he gazed with unblinking eyes for the sake of slaying Tripura.
Then, a single tear fell from one of his eyes;
from it there arose silver, radiant with its branches and its trunk.
From the second eye, a drop of tear fell from the left;
from that, silver was produced, which is praised for rites concerning the ancestors.

Here, because of the specific qualification "in rites for the ancestors" (*pitṛkarmasu*), the prohibition of silver is understood to apply to rites for the gods (*daivakarmasu*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* concerning silver:
"Since it was produced from the eye of Śiva, it is therefore beloved by the ancestors;
yet it is inauspicious and is to be avoided in sacrifices and rites for the gods."
"Silver is said to be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in all rites for the ancestors," so it is stated in the Taittirīya Śākhā.

The gods and the asuras were engaged in conflict. As the gods were about to achieve victory, they deposited their desirable wealth in Agni, thinking, "It shall be ours if they defeat us. Agni coveted that wealth; he departed with it. The gods, having won the battle, pursued him seeking to recover it. He tried to snatch it away by force; he wept. Because he wept (*arodīt*), that is the origin of Rudra's name, *rudra*. Because those tears became silver (*rajata*) gold, therefore silver gold is not to be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Whoever gives silver gold upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) will have weeping in his house before the end of the year. Therefore, it must not be given upon the sacrificial grass. Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: "In ancient times, the gods and the Asuras were rivals; they were 'unrestrained,' meaning they were prepared for battle. Among them, the gods, desiring victory, as they were setting out toward the battlefield, placed their own most beautiful wealth (*vāma vasu*) into the hand of Agni for protection, thinking: 'If we should be defeated by the Asuras, this wealth will serve as our refuge. Agni, however, out of excessive greed, intensely desired it for himself, thinking, 'Let this be mine alone. Having devised a stratagem there, he moved away from that place—he fled. Then, having conquered the Asuras, the gods, 'desiring to recover' (*avarurūtsamānāḥ*)—that is, wishing to seize—that wealth, went after Agni. They wished to take it back from him 'by force' (*sahasā*), by means of power. Thereupon, Agni wept; from that, he became known by the name Rudra. That 'tear' (*aśru*) which fell from his weeping eye onto the earth became silver. Therefore, in a ritual dedicated to the gods, silver should not be given upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."
Now, the greatness of silver.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "Whatever [item] whatsoever is accompanied by silver in śrāddha rites..."
"That and that is said to be imperishable; this is the secret taught by the ancestors themselves."
Now, in the absence of silver here,
one who makes use of a vessel containing silver during śrāddha rites gratifies the ancestors for sixteen years.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who bestows exceedingly pure silver upon a brāhmaṇa,
having shaken off his sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
He is born in this world handsome, fortunate, and glorious.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Even a story concerning silver, or its sight, or its gift— indeed,
the gift of silver— is infinite, inexhaustible, and leads to heaven."
By this gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"While creating the elements in the beginning, the Self-born One created silver;
therefore, that which is prescribed as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in a *śrāddha* leads to the satisfaction of the ancestors."
In the absence of silver, one should recite its names;
for the ancestors are satisfied, O King, by the recitation of the names of silver.
For there is nothing dearer to the ancestors than silver;
upon seeing silver alone, the ancestors attain unsurpassed joy.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
"O best of the twice-born, he who desires the supreme satisfaction of his ancestors and their inexhaustible state should diligently offer silver at the śrāddha ceremonies."
Whatever is offered to the ancestors and the deities should be given with the hand;
by that, the ancestors shall remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
The man who gives silver as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the rite of śrāddha—
by that, his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers shall be satisfied.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"Whatever is given to the ancestors while holding silver with the forefinger—
there may be an end to atoms, but there is no end to that [merit]."
For the ancestral rites, one should have silver vessels made for the arghya offering;
likewise, one should make the eating vessels out of silver.
A man devoted to his ancestors should indeed have the serving vessels and the alms-bowls made of silver alone.
Indeed, whatever śrāddha is performed in this manner, regardless of where one may be situated, that shall be equivalent to a śrāddha at Gayā; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
A man who, being self-restrained, gives silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at śrāddha rites,
leads both himself and his ancestors to the eternal Brahman.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"That [place] is exceedingly dear to the ancestors; by giving it away, a person attains the state of being beloved."
He obtains a place in the world of Soma for as long as the sages remain fixed upon the Dhruva.

"The sages are fixed in the *dhruva* [pole star]" refers to the sages known as the Seven Sages (*saptarṣi*). Here, the gift of silver is to be understood as being given to the Brahmins at the *śrāddha* ceremony in the form of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth. The praise of silver vessels, however, will be discussed in the section on vessels.
This concludes the description of silver.
Here, [the topic of] gold...
In this regard, there is the Śatapatha Śruti:
"When the horse was sacrificed, its semen issued forth; that became golden gold.
Likewise: [661]

Agni indeed meditated upon the waters, thinking, "May I become united with them. He had sexual union with them and poured his seed into them; that became gold. Therefore, this [gold] resembles fire, for it is the seed of Agni. Therefore, people wash [gold] in water, for he poured it into the water. For this reason, one should not clean it by scrubbing, nor should one do anything else [to it], for it is the seed of the gods. Indeed, this bestows glory upon him and makes him prosper. In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*, the Blessed One said:
That which was the seed of Maheśvara— pure, bright, and most excellent—
was formerly drawn forth by Gaurī from her invincible husband.
In the past, for the benefit of the deities, he cast that [semen] into the fire;
