he drank with his own mouth the seed and the virile essence of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then the fire blazed up like wood placed upon it;
enveloped by its heat, he cast it back again into the Gaṅgā.
And having boiled the Gaṅgā together with the hosts of oceans and rivers,
he then buried it in the earth and caused it to fall upon the mountains.
The earth, along with its continents and great mountain ranges, became like a mass of glowing iron; then that seed of the Lord, together with fire, flowed forth by its own inherent essence.
Having burnt the entire world, he went toward the Śara forest;
from that water which came into contact with Skanda, Skanda was born.
That which was pure became gold; the drops that arose fell as sweat upon Mount Meru, and thus it came to possess both beginning and end.
Meru, composed of trees, shrubs, and creepers and made of supreme gold, had a wood-apple tree at its edge,
and in some places on the mountain, there was a ripe rose-apple tree.
Joined with its root, that great tree grew;
its fruits, as large as mountains, were the sustenance for Laghujīvana.
Exceedingly delicious fruits fell without distinction throughout all seasons;
from their great abundance of juices, there arose a river flowing to the ocean.
It is renowned in the Purāṇas as Jāmbūnadī, possessing the brilliance of the shimmering sun;
it is perpetually ablaze with a heat equal to the flames of fire.
Extending for ten yojanas, it cannot be seen by anyone;
having reached its shore, the earth, through contact with its essence, attains the state of gold.
In this world, even clay that is attached to what is attached to it, or which is merely touched by its essence, is sought after; people desire the most excellent gold.
Whatever other gold is celebrated as being mixed with that,
this [gold] became the pure, supreme, and righteous gold of old.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"The daughter of Himavat was formerly renowned by the name Umā;
in her previous birth, she was Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa."
And due to Dakṣa’s anger, Satī abandoned her own body;
she was born as the daughter of Himavat, renowned in the world as Gaurī.
Having prostrated before the wielder of the Pināka bow, he too gave her to him;
he then performed the marriage of his daughter according to the prescribed rites.
The Grandfather offered oblations into the fire according to the marriage rite;
and as he was performing the sacrifice, a transformation born of love arose within him.
Then, upon seeing that form, the seed of the high-souled one was spilled by the goddess;
it was rubbed with her feet and thereby became manifold.
There, the high-souled Bālakhilyas, who subsist on the rays of the sun, were born;
and the remainder fell into the fire, and that became radiant with the brilliance of flames.
And seeing the son of Vibhāvasu possessed of such blazing radiance as if he had entered into fire itself, the gods then proclaimed it.
Filled with joy because of its auspiciousness, they received it upon their heads;
and the gods made it an ornament for him of supreme splendor.
Now, the greatness of gold. Regarding this, there is a Śatapatha Śruti:
"Gold is the immortal form of the gods."
In the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa: "It was born from the heart of the Lord, a wealth dear to enjoyers,
[as vast as] the ocean, Mount Meru, and the banks of the Jambū river."
Therefore, gold is declared to be the purifier of gods and men, the most beloved and supreme; it is that which is called the purifier among all purifiers.
It is borne on the head by the gods and even by Īśvara—what need is there for others?
[This occurs] through bearing it, touching it, giving it, seeing it, or even chanting its name.
Since merit equal to that of worshipping a *liṅga* is also earned by me [through these acts], therefore,
this [merit] arises from seizing, destroying, hating, or insulting it.
The great [egg] was produced as gold; indeed, the abundant [matter] had vanished. From that very [matter], the first egg of the primordial creation arose.
Therefore, one should make a golden object known as a ring;
for this is indeed the supreme purifier, designated for the ring finger.
And other purifiers consisting of *kuśa* and *dūrvā* grass do not equal even a single sixteenth part of the purifier made of gold.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"That [light] of the gods is like gold;
that of the ancestors resembles the glow-worm; and that of the Daityas is like a variegated [cloud]."
For *nāgas* it is like the color of a parrot, while for women it is said to be yellow.
Regarding gold, Rāmā spoke in the *Vahni Purāṇa*:
"This peerless, purifying substance has arisen here and is renowned."
For this is indeed the supreme seed of Śambhu and the offspring of Jātavedas.
The innate semen of Rudra, produced from Kārttikeya,
is worn by all the gods in their crowns and other ornaments because of its purity.
Agni is indeed all the deities, and gold has that as its essence;
therefore, all the deities become pleased with those who give gold.
"Those who bestow gold rescue ten ancestors and ten descendants from hell; so spoke Bṛhaspati."
Those who bestow gold grant all desires;
so the venerable Marīci, the son of the Grandfather (Brahmā), declared in former times.
The man who constantly bestows gold upon Brahmins rejoices for a long time in heaven like a god— purified and wise.
The fruit of all other gifts follows one for only a single birth;
however, the gift of gold to Gaurīs has a fruit that follows for seven births.
Even after committing a very great sin, he who gives gold is immediately liberated from that sin; there is no doubt about this.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
it is the most purifying of all purifiers among gifts—of this there is no doubt.
There is no object whatsoever in this world, whether as a gift, an ornament, or anything else, that is as supremely purifying as gold.
Bṛhaspati says:
"In the case of houses and other such gifts, the fruit of merit arises in accordance with the value;
therefore, among all forms of giving, gold is remembered as the most excellent."
Just as the work of gold, such as that of making necklaces and the like, is accomplished [from it],
so too is there no gift of gold greater than the gift of a house.
Vedavyāsa: "Those who bestow gold grant all desires;
for thus did the venerable Atri, the son of the Grandfather, declare."
Furthermore, gold is declared by Manu, the lord of men, to be a purifier, auspicious, and inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Manu says: "The giver of land obtains everything; the giver of gold obtains long life.
Saṃvarta says:
The giver of gold attains great prosperity and long life. Viṣṇu says:
through the gift of gold, one attains the same world as Agni.
[666] Viśvāmitra said: O King, wherever in one's house there exists a written record of the gift of gold, even Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas cannot see that place.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Having ascertained the weight of gold and other materials, one should bestow them upon worthy recipients;
endowed with faith in the prescribed rite, one attains one's desired objects."
Vasiṣṭha said: Therefore we have heard that all the deities have Agni as their mouth;
for Agni was produced from Brahmā, and gold was produced from Agni.

Therefore, they bestow gold as an offering to all the deities; for him who goes to the supreme goal, there are indeed worlds belonging to the Creator (Vidhātṛ). And in the heavenly world, O Bhārgava, he shall be consecrated with sovereignty.
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, following the word "gold":
"This is pure, supremely meritorious, and always employed in the rites of the gods; for all wear it, free from impurity, for the sake of stainlessness."
Therefore, all sins are purified when given to worthy recipients according to the prescribed rules, at the proper time and place, and in the presence of Hara.
In the Mahābhārata, these are the words of the father addressed to Bhīma:
"According to the Vedas and the Upaniṣads, gold is indeed the most excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for all rites;
and among all sacrifices, land, cows, and gold are prescribed."
Furthermore, the supreme Vedic injunction is that gold is indeed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O bull among the Bharatas, this has been properly undertaken by you today.
"But rather, let gold be given for the sake of the earth and the cows;
thus we, who know the Dharma, and all our ancestors have been saved and will indeed be saved, for that is the supreme purifier."
"Those who bestow gold deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants; thus spoke their ancestors to Rāma," said Vasiṣṭha in these words addressed to Rāma.
O best of Brahmins, having extracted all jewels, gold— which is endowed with a mass of splendor— is the supreme and most excellent jewel among them.
For this reason, the gods, gandharvas, uragas, rākṣasas,
humans, and piśācas preserve it with great effort.
O best of the Raghus, they shine here with crowns, armlets, and various kinds of ornaments fashioned from gold.
Therefore, it is remembered as the supreme purifier among all purifiers;
for even after giving land, a cow, or anything else here in this world, [this remains superior].
O Lord, the gift of gold is distinguished as supreme;
indeed, gold is said here to be inexhaustible and purifying.
One should bestow this most excellent purifier upon the foremost of the twice-born;
for gold alone is prescribed in all sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Those who give gold indeed become givers forever.
In the Nandipurāṇa: Five *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* are traditionally held to be one *suvarṇa*; by the giving of which one attains the heavenly world.
Gold is the supreme gift; gold is the highest sacrificial fee.
This is the most excellent purifier; this is the great means of securing well-being.
O lord of the people, by giving [this] to Brahmins, one may deliver ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself— even after having committed a hundred sins.
Those men who bestow gold with a pure mind—there is no doubt that they become all the gods; so we have heard.
For Agni is all the deities, and gold is the consumer of oblations;
therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities are given.
And in the absence of fire, they place gold in the positions of the sacrificial fires.
They possess knowledge of the authority of all the Vedas, based on the indications of the revealed scriptures and the treatises.
But those who, having washed it, offer it toward the rising sun while observing the vow, shall indeed attain all their desires.
‘With reference to a vow’ means having undertaken a vow.
The giver of gold enjoys his desired objects in the heavenly world;
clothed in stainless garments, he wanders here and there.
Resplendent in a celestial chariot,
brilliant as the sun and shining with its own radiant luster, crowded with throngs of Apsarases,
drawn by swans and peacocks, and moving according to his will— that best of men shone forth.
Carrying divine fragrances, it moves here and there throughout heaven.
Bṛhaspati said: Gold is the first offspring of Agni;
the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
The three worlds are bestowed by him who gives gold, a cow, and land.
In the *Skānda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*: "Gold is the supreme substance upon the earth;
the gods rejoice if it is given."
The Sun also grants him a celestial mansion for a very long time, so that he wanders therein for as long as [it lasts].
Thus ends the description of gold.
Now, regarding the vessels:
Hārīta [describes] the vessels for the *argha* offering and other purposes therein.

Vessels made of bell-metal, wood, silver, or copper, which are short and used for holding the water of the *arghya* offering, should be prepared. "Short" (*kharvāṇi*) means small. [Thus says] Baijavāpa.
"In the rite of *śrāddha*, the vessels for the *arghya* offering may be made of *khadira* or *udumbara* wood;

they may also be made of stone or clay, or likewise of leaf-cups. Here, "made of *khadira*" means made from the wood of the *bālapattra* tree, and "*audumbara*" means fashioned from the wood of the *jantuphala* tree.
Or it may be made of copper. "Leaf-cups" (*parṇapuṭāḥ*) are specific types of vessels shaped like chalices, fashioned from the leaves of sacrificial trees. Kātyāyana states:

"[The offering is made] in any one of the vessels made of gold, silver, udumbara wood, rhinoceros horn, or precious stones—excluding those made of clay—or in whatever [vessels] are available, or in leaf-cups made of *palāśa* leaves."

"Made of rhinoceros horn" (*khaḍgamaya*) means fashioned from the horn of a rhinoceros. Here, the avoidance of earthenware is [intended] when it is possible [to obtain other materials]. However, if it is not possible, even that [earthenware] may be accepted, according to the statement of Āśvalāyana: "Among those made of metal, stone, and clay... Furthermore, according to the statement of Baijavāpa, "Now, they may be made of stone or clay," the avoidance of or the acceptance of earthenware is to be understood as being determined by the specific Vedic school (*śākhā*). Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: "The daughter's son [should wear] a rhinoceros horn which is seen upon his forehead."
The vessel belonging to that horn is celebrated as the "daughter's son" (dauhitra).
In the Matsya Purāṇa: One should likewise make a vessel from wood, or again from leaves,
or even one born of water, or likewise one originating from the ocean.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is the most excellent for the ancestors.

Those that bear fruit without flowers are *vanaspati*s; that which is made of wood is "made of *vanaspati*. In the case of "made of leaves" (*parṇamaya*), the leaves likewise must belong to *vanaspati*s. "Born in water" refers to a lotus leaf. "Made of ocean" refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like.
Even a story about silver, a sight of it, or even a gift [of silver]—or even that which is to be given with silver vessels or accompanied by silver—is [prohibited].
Even water given with faith is ordained to be inexhaustible;
and silver is considered appropriate for the ancestors even in the matter of the arghya-offering, the funeral rice-ball, and the food.
Since it originated from the eye of Śiva, it is therefore beloved by the ancestors;
yet it is inauspicious for sacrifices and must be avoided in rites for the gods.
Having thus prepared the vessels according to what is available, one should be free from envy.
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: "From the Palāśa tree comes spiritual luster; from the Aśvattha, the attainment of kingship;
and from the Plakṣa, sovereignty over all beings is always proclaimed."
The *plakṣa* tree is the matted-haired one (*jaṭī*).
Nourishment and progeny reside in the *nyagrodha*; it is intellect, wisdom, fortitude, and memory.
The *nyagrodha* is the banyan tree (*vaṭa*).
A vessel that is protective against demons and conducive to fame should be prepared; this is what is called a "pātra. *Kāśmarī* is *śrīparṇī*.
The highest good fortune in the world is said to reside in *madhūka*.
*Madhūka* is the *guḍapuṣpa* (honey-tree).
One who performs [the rite] with a vessel made of *phalgu* shall obtain all desires;
*phalgu* is the *kākodumbarikā*.
Furthermore, in the *arka* (Calotropis gigantea) one attains supreme luster and especially the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*).
"Arka" refers to the *rūpikā*.
In the *bilva* (Aegle marmelos), there is Lakṣmī, austerity, intelligence, and constant longevity.
Indeed, in fields, groves, and ponds, as well as in all crops;
There, Parjanya rains incessantly from a bamboo vessel;
one obtains merit by giving to these [vessels], whether they be made of gold or silver.
Palāśa, phalguna, nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, as well as bilva, sandalwood, and those trees fit for sacrifice; sarala, devadāru, śāla, and likewise khadira.
For these indeed are, without exception, the sources of the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings;
he who gives with them shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.

‘Vikaṅkata’ is the wood used for the *sruva* ladle; ‘sarala’ is *pītadru*; ‘śāla’ is *sarjaka*. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “arghyādi,” vessels for the water-offering (*avanejana*) and other such items, as well as vessels intended for holding the implements of the *śrāddha* ceremony such as sesame and *kuśa* grass, are included.
In that same Purāṇa it is stated:
“A vessel made of silver, or one coated with silver, is prescribed for the ancestors.”
Even a conversation about silver, the sight of it, or its gift [is forbidden].
The gift of silver indeed leads to infinite, inexhaustible heaven;
by this gift, virtuous sons truly deliver their ancestors.
For in ancient times, O dear one, the earth shone after having milked nectar into this vessel;
therefore, what was given therein became inexhaustible for those seeking the end of their hunger for nectar.
Now, regarding the vessels for food.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"One should indeed provide a pleasing metallic vessel for the meal at a *śrāddha*."
One becomes a vessel for desires, for sacred knowledges, and for wealth.
"Taijasa" refers to that which consists of gold, silver, bronze,
and copper. That man who gives vessels made of silver and gold in śrāddha ceremonies obtains, as a donor, the power of irresistible will (prākāmya) as well as wealth.
Even water given with faith in silver vessels, or in those adorned with silver,
is rendered inexhaustible.

In that regard, although silver and golden vessels are prescribed for the *śrāddha* ceremony without distinction, Atri nevertheless established a specific rule for the sake of excellence in quality: "For the Vaiśvadeva rite, golden ones; for the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), silver ones. Viṣṇu states: "For eating, golden and silver [vessels] are used respectively for the gods and the ancestors."
One should offer vessels made of metal, especially those of silver.
Regarding the absence of golden vessels here, Hārīta states:

"Vessels of silver, bell-metal, wood, or copper, intended for the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, should be large. The mere quality of being "large" here should be understood as sufficient to hold all the food prepared for the meal. As for the bell-metal vessel, it must be made of fifty-two *pala*s of bell-metal; in its absence, any available [vessel] may be used.
And so says Atri:
"A bell-metal vessel weighing fifty palas, indeed larger for the purpose of eating,
must always be used by householders in the absence of gold and silver."

The term "by householders" (*gṛhasthaiḥ*) means by those belonging to the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśramibhiḥ*). Furthermore, in this context, the vessel made of *parṇa* leaves must be understood as being specifically made of *palāśa* leaves. This is because the use of any leaf-vessel other than that is prohibited by Atri. As it is said: "Other leaves than those of the *palāśa* tree should not be used for eating."

Because it is specified in this manner, there is no prohibition regarding vessels made of wood and the like. Even in the case of a vessel made of *parṇa* leaves, for the purpose of holding substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), metallic vessels should be procured whenever possible, according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "For the offering of clarified butter and other substances, metallic vessels are to be used. In the absence of these, leaf-cups fashioned from *palāśa* leaves should be employed for holding substances such as clarified butter.
As stated in the Vārāha Purāṇa:
"In this world, one should diligently procure vessels made of gold."
In the absence of those, however, silver [vessels] should be used; and in the absence of those, bronze ones.
In śrāddha ceremonies, when feeding the twice-born, vessels made of palāśa leaves should be used;
indeed, the wise man may also use other vessels, even those made of wood.
One should perform the rites using materials made of clay as they are available, but never with those made of iron,
nor indeed with those of bell-metal;
furthermore, vessels made of lead or even those produced from tin are not recommended here.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one feeds the ancestors at a śrāddha in an earthen vessel,
then the donor, the officiating priest, and the eater shall go to hell."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "He who feeds the ancestors at a *śrāddha* in an earthen vessel goes to a terrible hell, as do the one who eats [the offering] and the officiating priest."
Aṅgiras states: "One should not offer jasmine flowers, nor the leaf of the plantain tree.
Now, regarding the vessels for serving food:
Hārīta says:
"That which is given in a vessel of gold, or one of silver or udumbara wood,
or indeed in a vessel of rhinoceros horn, attains imperishability."
Viṣṇu:
For the offering of clarified butter and other substances, vessels made of metal, vessels of rhinoceros horn, or vessels of *phalgu* wood are recommended.
In this regard, there is a verse:
A gift given with a sword made of gold or silver, or one made of udumbara wood,
or even with a vessel made of phalgu wood, attains imperishability.

Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi states a specific distinction: "For offerings to the gods, golden vessels are best; for those to the ancestors, however, silver ones are best for serving food. So says Manu.
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to inexhaustible results for them.
Furthermore, this serving must necessarily be performed with a vessel such as a ladle, for there is a scriptural prohibition against serving directly with the hand.
As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "One should not give salt directly with an empty hand."
Nor with an iron bowl, nor indeed while possessed by a lack of faith.
That which is given in a vessel made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood becomes inexhaustible; this is especially true when given in a vessel of steel.

Viṣṇu states: "One should not give salt directly with the hand, nor should one give ghee, vegetables, and so forth with the hand. In the absence of a vessel or similar utensil, one should give by interposing a blade of grass or a leaf between the hand [and the food]; thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa."
Oils, salt, and condiments that are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes only sin.
Therefore, an offering should be given from a distance, using either a leaf or a blade of grass;
one should never give with the hand, nor ever with an iron vessel.
Vṛddhaśātātapa, Laghuhārīta, and Vasiṣṭha state:
"If food is served in an iron vessel,
the eater consumes excrement and the giver goes to hell."
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Vessels made of lead and tin, as well as vessels made of the residue of bell-metal (rīti), are unfit for sacrifice.
This is also stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
One should not serve food at a śrāddha with an impure hand, nor with only one hand, nor without kuśa grass; furthermore, one should not serve with a vessel made of iron, nor from an iron vessel.

"By an impure [utensil]" means by one that is unpurified due to contact with foul smears and the like. "By an iron [utensil]" means by a ladle or similar implement made of iron. One should not serve food even in an "iron vessel," meaning a vessel made of iron.
Now, regarding cooking vessels, [the following is said] in the *Carmakāra-khaṇḍa*.
One should prepare the most excellent food for the ancestors in golden vessels;
by that, one obtains fortune, long life, and imperishable prosperity.
But by performing the ancestral rites (paitṛka) using vessels made of silver,
one provides satisfaction for the ancestors that lasts until the dissolution of all beings.
But he who cooks in vessels made of copper with devotion indeed delivers his ancestors from the terrible great ocean of suffering.
In the absence of metallic vessels,
however, one should diligently perform the cooking for the sake of the ancestors in a new, clean earthen pot;
the ancestors are satisfied by that and, being pleased, grant what is desired.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "For the purpose of cooking the food for the ancestors, one should prepare clean pots made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal."
Even if they are made of clay, new, and sturdy,
one should never cook ancestral food in iron vessels.
For at the mere sight of iron, the ancestors flee;
the wise declare that iron is unfit for sacrifice and inauspicious.
Iron is censured among all rites for the gods and the ancestors;
indeed, black iron is especially condemned in ancestral ceremonies.
Furthermore, whatever tools there may be for cutting fruits and vegetables,
their storage must likewise be kept in the kitchen.
In this context, the sight of weapons alone is not intended;
rather, by a wise person desiring the satisfaction of the ancestors in the place of the *śrāddha* rite,
even those items used in the kitchen should be presented as examples.
A seat made of iron spikes should be offered; one must not sit upon it.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
"Having bathed well, the wise man himself should cook the foods in pure vessels made of gold and other metals, or even in those made of clay."
In cases where the coatings are flawless, likewise unimpaired, not made of iron, not cracked,
and never defiled;
However, earthen vessels that have previously been used for other purposes are never [recommended];
for the purpose of storing cooked food, even those made of wood are praised.
[678] Even the ladles and other implements must be made from wood fit for sacrifice. This concludes the description of the vessels. Now, the fragrances.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa: O King, he who, being delighted, offers fragrances to the ancestors,
attains the worlds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases and rejoices in heaven.
Just as fragrances are exceedingly dear to the ancestors when offered in their rites, nothing else is found to be so; therefore, they should be offered with great effort.
Since fragrances are the cause of extreme delight for all the gods as well,
one should therefore worship them with fragrances with great effort.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "To him who indeed offers most enchanting perfumes during the śrāddha rites,
the celestial damsels embrace him in heaven as he applies fragrant unguents to his limbs."
The gods and the ancestors are always pleased with that person who, acting with faith, anoints the limbs of the twice-born.
In the Bhagavatīpurāṇa: "He who indeed anoints brahmins with pure, very smooth, and fragrant sandalwood paste never suffers."
By that very same [ointment] mixed with *aguru*, one attains supreme good fortune;
by anointing oneself with *aguru*, however, one enjoys superhuman pleasures.
The high-minded person who offers sandalwood paste mixed with camphor to the ancestors attains vast renown upon this earth.
He who gives sandalwood from Malaya accompanied by saffron,
or even saffron alone, is born endowed with beauty.
He who offers divine sandalwood paste mixed with musk,
or even musk alone, attains great prosperity.
He who, endowed with faith, offers yakṣakardama incense during funeral rites (śrāddha),
attains the status of a sovereign and rejoices like Mahendra.
But he who offers perfumes scented with various flowers at a śrāddha shall be endowed with all desires and become a dweller in celestial chariots in heaven.
The characteristics of *yakṣakardama*:
camphor, agallochum, *kakkola*, *darpa*, saffron, and sandalwood— this fragrance is called *yakṣakardama*, and it is difficult to find even in heaven.
Thus, that which is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* should be kept in mind. Viṣṇu says: "Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka [wood] are for the purpose of anointment."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should cause sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron to be offered;
by anointing the ancestors with these, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Marīci:
The offering of fragrant white sandalwood, combined with camphor and saffron,
is recommended for both rites dedicated to the gods (daivika) and those dedicated to the ancestors (pitrya).
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One should offer white sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and other auspicious substances for the purpose of anointing, as well as whatever else is dear to the ancestors."
Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, bālaka, tvak, kuṣṭhī, jātipatraka,
nālika, uśīra, musta, granthiparṇa, dūbara, and murā— these and other such substances are suitable as fragrances for the ancestral rites (paitṛka).
Now, the fragrances to be avoided.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"In a *śrāddha* ceremony, the *pālaṅkyā* plant, as well as those produced from *niṣpāvaka*, should not be offered."
"Pālaṅkyā" refers to the fragrant substance known as *mukunda*, for the *Trikāṇḍī* lexicon records: "Pālaṅkyā, *mukunda*, *kunda*, and *kunduru* [are synonyms]."
In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"In *śrāddha* rites, fragrances produced from old wood should not be employed;
nor should they ever be used once they have turned white or become stale."
Nor should those that are foul-smelling be given, especially those that are the leftovers of what has been eaten.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
One should not employ stale or foul-smelling incense in a śrāddha; in rites for the ancestors, that which is known [to be appropriate] should be offered, and never that which is base.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should also avoid *pūtīka*, musk, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), red sandalwood, *kālīyaka*, *joṅgaka*, and *turuṣka*."

‘Pūtīka’ is a specific kind of fragrant grass; for Amarasimha states in his lexicon: “*pūtika* is *karañja* wood, or *prakīrya*, *pūtikaraja*, *pūtika*, and *kalikāraka*. ‘Mṛganābhi’ is musk; because it is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option regarding its use. ‘Rocanā’ is *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone). ‘Raktacandana’ is well known. ‘Kālīyaka’ and ‘joṅgaka’ are two specific types of aromatic substances. *Kālīyaka* is synonymous with *kālānusārya*; for Amarasimha states in the section on fragrant substances: “*vaṃśaka*, *aguru*, *rājārha*, *loha*, *kṛmija*, and *joṅgaka* [are synonyms]. ‘Turuṣka’ is *sihlaka* (bdellium).
Thus ends the determination of perfumes. Now, regarding flowers,
[it is said] in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
He who, being devoted to that [practice], always offers fragrant flowers and excellent soma-juice to the twice-born for the sake of his ancestors, he too goes to the Sun.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He who causes fragrant garlands to be offered to the ancestors,
being ever endowed with prosperity, shall also go to the Sun."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"He who offers fragrant and pleasing flowers to the foremost of the twice-born during a śrāddha shall obtain inexhaustible merit."
The ancestors attain joy through the fragrance of fragrant flowers;
being pleased, they grant the donor his desired wishes.
Therefore, those who desire their own welfare should always worship the ancestors with flowers, leaves, or even flower-clusters, as well as with tender sprouts, barley, or blades of dūrvā grass.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The ancestors, who are the deities of the śrāddha, are always fond of perfumes and garlands;
therefore, one should worship them with fragrant scents and flowers."
Among all enjoyments, flowers are the most excellent both in this world and the next;
therefore, one should indeed offer flowers to the ancestors with devotion.
In this world, that which is given disrespectfully yields a contrary fruit;
therefore, the wise desire that a gift be given with honor and after due worship.
A worship performed without flowers does not become most meritorious;
therefore, a wise man devoted to the śrāddha should gratify the ancestors with the śrāddha offering.
One should always worship first with flowers that are the very best,
which are not stale in appearance, nor damaged,
nor pierced by worms, insects, and the like, but are pure and have been sprinkled with water.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "Barley, wild rice, mung beans, white flowers, and likewise valla beans are always beloved and highly praised by the ancestors here."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"When the species of flowers were created, the hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapatrikā*) was created first;
therefore, it is always the foremost for the performance of *śrāddha* rites."
In the Vāyu and Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇas:
"White flowers are the best, as are lotuses and water-lilies,
and whatever other flowers there are that are endowed with fragrance and color in their entirety."
In this case, lotuses and water-lilies should be offered even if they are not white;
here,
one may also offer red aquatic flowers.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* and the *Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa*, it is stated:
"All varieties of jasmine, the *mallikā*, and the white *yūthikā* should be given; likewise, all water-born flowers and the *campaka*. [683]
‘Jātyaḥ’ are *mālatī* flowers; ‘mallikā’ refers to flowers known as *mudgara*; ‘śvetayūthikā’ refers to golden-colored flowers (*hemakusuma*).
Having thus described grains, fruits, and vegetables, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
“One should give these very flowers, as well as forest-grown vegetables.”
Jāti, campaka, and rodhra flowers, as well as mallikā, bāṇa, and barbarī.
The mango, the aśoka, the āṭarūṣa, as well as the tulasī and the tilaka;
the pārantī, the śatapatra, and also the gandhanepālikā.
Kuñjaka, tagara, mṛgamāra, ketakī, yūthikā, and atimuktā— these, O twice-born ones, are suitable for śrāddha rites.
One should diligently employ the *kamala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka*, as well as the *indīvara*, *kokanada*, and *kalhāra*.

‘Campaka’ is *cāmpeya*; ‘rotra’ is *gālava*; ‘bāṇa’ is *ārttagala*; ‘barbarī’ is *karvarī*; ‘cūta’ is *āmra* (mango); ‘aśoka’ is *vañjula*; ‘āṭarūṣa’ is *siṃhāsya*; ‘tulasī’ is *surasā*. Regarding this [tulasī], its exclusion from *śrāddha* rites has been stated by the author of the *Smṛtyarthasāra*; however, we consider that to be baseless (*nirmūla*), as it is not seen in many *smṛtis*, *itihāsas*, or *purāṇas*. ‘Tilaka’ is *kṣuraka*; ‘pārantī’ is a flower resembling the *śephālikā*; ‘śatapatra’ is well known; ‘nepālikā’ is *navamālikā*; ‘kujaka’ is *kubjaka*; ‘tagara’ is *gandhatagara*; ‘mṛgamāra’ is the *śrāvaṇikā* flower; ‘atimuktaka’ is the flower of the *mādhavī* creeper. The *kamala* and others are well known as varieties of lotuses (*paṅkaja*).
Now, the flowers to be avoided.
Regarding this, there are the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
The *japā*, *sumanā*, *bhaṇḍī*, *rūpikā*,
and *kuraṇṭaka* flowers should always be avoided in the performance of *śrāddha* rites.
Those flowers which are devoid of fragrance, those which have a pungent odor, and those that are otherwise to be avoided should always be excluded from rites performed with faith.
Those flowers which are devoid of fragrance, those which have a pungent odor, and all others that should be avoided must always be shunned by one seeking the ground.

*Japā* is the flower of Rudra (*rudrapuṣpa*). The word *ādi* (and so forth) denotes a class; by it, flowers similar to the *japā* blossom, such as *karavīra* and others, are to be excluded. *Sumanā* is the *jāti* jasmine, according to the traditional authority (*smaraṇa*) which states: "The *sumanā* is the *mālatī* variety. *Bhaṇḍī* is *mañjiṣṭhā*. *Rūpikā* is the *arka*. *Kuraṇṭaka* is the yellow-flowered *mahāsahā*. Here, the prohibition of *jātī* blossoms is not absolute; for if it were an absolute prohibition, the previously cited statement—"all varieties of *jāti* should be offered"—would be rendered devoid of scope. [This is stated] in the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*.
That śrāddha, when combined with jasmine flowers (jātīpuṣpa), shall go to futility.
Aṅgiras said:
"One should not offer jasmine flowers, nor a plantain leaf.
Here, the plantain leaf—which might otherwise be understood as a vessel for food—is prohibited.
Kratu said:
"Born into the lineage of the Asuras, Jātī was previously taken [as a wife].
By the mere sight of her, the ancestors became despondent."

Regarding the phrase "in the previous possession" (*pūrvaparigrahe*), this refers to the occasion of possessing a body in a previous birth. Although in the statement—"For there are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice; here they insert, and from here they take out"—which is in the form of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) using a present-tense description, a prohibitive injunction is inferred for the sake of establishing that explanatory passage—just as an injunction regarding insertion (*āvāpa*) and removal (*udvāpa*) is inferred in the case of the *gāyatrī* and other meters—nevertheless, even this prohibition is merely partial (*pākṣika*). Thus, the statement of Mārkaṇḍeya is not rendered purposeless; rather, it concerns cases where other flowers not prohibited are available. However, it should be understood that the two-fold prohibition applies to cases where such [permissible] flowers are not obtained.
Śaṅkha said:
Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are scentless, those growing from trees at a caitya,
and those that are red in color should be avoided.
Those originating from trees should be given, especially those that are red.
‘Ugragandhāni’ means having unpleasant odors. ‘Caityavṛkṣaḥ’ means a tree in a cremation ground. In the Saura Purāṇa:
"Any lotus other than [the white one], the red flower, and likewise the śiśumāra [flower]," [are prohibited].
All foodstuffs and edibles that are tasteless—
none of these should ever be offered during any śrāddha rite.
Viṣṇu states, following the phrase "one should avoid":
flowers with pungent odors, those produced from thorny plants, and red flowers; likewise:
White and fragrant flowers, even those grown on thorny plants, [are recommended].
From the *Padma-purāṇa* and *Matsya-purāṇa*:
"The lotus, bilva, arka, dhustūra, pāribhadra, and aṭarūṣaka..."
Milk, as well as the products of goats and sheep, should not be given for the purpose of making curds.

The lotus leaf growing on land is prohibited, because that which grows in water is prescribed. "Bilva" is the *śrīphala*. "Dhustūra" is the *unmatta*. "Pāribhadra" is the *mandāra* endowed with red clusters. "Āḍharūṣa" is the *siṃhāsya*.
Thus ends the description of flowers. Now, the incenses (*dhūpa*).
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "One who is devoted to the ancestors and offers incense endowed with the quality of fragrance obtains wives and offspring both in this world and in future births."
He who offers incense such as guggulu and other fragrances to the ancestors,
having mixed them with honey and clarified butter, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the *Agnipurāṇa*:
Having adorned the Brahmins with perfumes and flowers during the Śrāddha rite,
the ancestors, satisfied by that fragrance, partake of the sacrificial oblation.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Then one should gratify the ancestors with delightful and divine incenses;
for when they are pleased, they in turn gratify the giver with all his desires."
Upon smelling the fragrance of incense, which brings supreme delight to the mind, an inexhaustible satisfaction arises for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
There is nothing that causes as much pleasure to the ancestors as incense;
therefore, incense should be offered during the śrāddha by those desiring merit.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Then, one should fumigate the twice-born with fragrant incense;
by that, all the ancestors attain imperishable satisfaction."
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Both sandalwood and agallochum, tamāla,
uśīra, and patrakam, as well as the finest guggulu incense and turuṣka incense."
And here, incenses mixed with ghee and honey should be offered, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "One should offer guggulu combined with honey and ghee.
Śaṅkha also says:
"For the purpose of incense, one should offer guggulu joined with ghee and abundant with honey."
And likewise, one should offer sandalwood, as well as auspicious camphor and saffron.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"He who offers incense such as *guggulu* and the like to the ancestors,
combined with honey and clarified butter, shall obtain the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should burn both sandalwood and agallochum, as well as uśīra and padmaka, turuṣka and guggulu, and ghṛtāka, all together."
Likewise: "Guggulu, sandalwood, śrīvāsa, and likewise aguru—these, O Sage, are the incenses suitable for the ancestors; indeed, guggulu alone [is especially so]."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Incense made from guggulu should be offered, as well as that produced from the essence of sandalwood;
likewise agarwood with camphor, and similarly turuṣka."
The various types of incense, however, should be understood as those mentioned in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
For example:
Agallochum, sandalwood, nut-grass, storax, and likewise vṛṣaṇa.
These should be made in equal proportions; this incense is called "Amṛta."
One should burn here sandalwood with knots, agallochum, and likewise storax, as well as nut-grass, camphor, borax, and sugar.
Thus, O best of gods, this incense called Anantadhūpa has been described;
it consists of black agallochum, sihlaka, bālaka, and likewise vṛṣaṇa.
Sandalwood, tagara, musta, and prabodha mixed with sugar;
likewise camphor, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, uśīra, and sihlaka.
Granthika, vṛṣaṇa, bhīma, kuṅkuma, gṛñjana,
as well as harītakī and uśīra, are declared to be yakṣadhūpa.
O Brahmin, [use] tṛṣaṇa, sihlaka, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise aguru;
O twice-born one, as well as karpūra, mustā, sugar, and cinnamon bark.
Thus, this is the subject of incense, created by the Lord himself:
camphor, sandalwood, spikenard, cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves.
Aloe-wood, *sihlaka*, and incense are declared to be the *prājāpatya* offering;
likewise, *śrīkhaṇḍa*, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, camphor, and *sihlaka*.
Vyañjana, sugar, kṛṣṇa, mahāṅga, and likewise sihlaka—
this incense known as mahāṅga is always dear to the Lord.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Incense made from bālā, rāla, kunduru, śrīveṣṭa, and guggulu is considered the five-flavored incense (pañcarasa)."
In the *Kālottara*: "Incense made from camphor, *dāru* wood, and *aguru*, combined with red sandalwood, is called *samudgaka*; it is beloved by all the deities."

These incenses, beginning with *amṛta*, should be prepared by excluding substances derived from the limbs of living beings and employed in the *śrāddha* ceremony; for Viṣṇu records: "One should not offer anything except *śrī* (turmeric) for the purpose of incense, nor should one give [incense] using oil or ghee.
Devala also says:
"For those incenses produced from the limbs of living beings, and those struck by the breath of the hand..."
Those who possess a pungent odor should not be employed at a śrāddha;
nor should one offer ghee alone, or even if it is spoiled, nor guggulu mixed with grass.
Thus ends the description of incense. Now, the lamps.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
He who, being self-restrained, always offers a lamp to the ancestors,
obtains from that act an incomparable goal and auspicious vision.
Through splendor, fame, longevity, and strength,
he becomes renowned upon the earth and shines in the triple heaven;
surrounded by Apsarases, he rejoices at the forefront of his celestial chariot.
In the Brahma Purāṇa: By the offering of a lamp at a śrāddha, a man becomes radiant;
he becomes handsome, wealthy, and an enjoyer of pleasures, and he experiences happiness and sovereignty.
Therefore, a lamp should always be offered by the sacrificer to the ancestors;
one who performs a śrāddha ceremony without a lamp sinks into blinding darkness.
[690] Lamps should be placed with great care before each of the invited twice-born guests;
for that light shines upon the paths leading to the ancestors.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By offering lamps with faith at sacred sites of pilgrimage (*śrādadeśa*), one obtains excellent vision;
of this there is no doubt, and one is born possessed of splendor."
The lamp is light, the supreme light, the highest knowledge;
therefore, one who gives a lamp at a śrāddha is born possessed of wisdom.
Whoever desires stainless knowledge that utterly eradicates darkness,
let him offer a lamp with devotion to the ancestors and the gods.
May he who, by his own splendor, is the giver of the universe and by whom all things are entirely pervaded—
may he indeed be the one who offers the lamp at the śrāddha.
Just as a lamp, when ignited, destroys darkness on all sides,
even so does that which is given at a śrāddha ceremony destroy all sins.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Lamps with wicks made from white thread should be established for each twice-born person,
their vessels filled with clarified butter derived from either cows or buffaloes."
Alternatively, lamps filled with sesame oil and possessing pure flames should be offered individually according to the prescribed rite, dedicated to the ancestors.
By that light, the ancestors shine everywhere in heaven;
possessing the power to fulfill desires, they grant the donor his wished-for objects.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
He who offers a lamp kindled with ghee to the ancestors moves through the radiant worlds and is not obstructed.
Furthermore, he who lights a lamp there with the ghee of cows rejoices in the worlds of cows together with the lords of the worlds.
If, in the absence of ghee, one offers a lamp fueled by sesame oil to the ancestors, he indeed attains the same world as the Sun.
In the absence of sesame oil, he who offers a lamp at a śrāddha using oils other than those derived from animal parts also crosses over the darkness that is difficult to traverse.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"Lamps made with white wicks and filled with cow's ghee,
as well as oil-lamps made from metal or even from the wood of heartwood trees."
If [such a vessel] is not available, one may give even one made of clay that is pleasing to the mind and properly prepared;
hear now the fruit of the merit for that person who gives it to the ancestors.
Resplendent with splendor, fame, beauty, supreme wisdom, and glory,
he indeed dwells in heaven, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
That man who, having duly honored the ancestors, performs the *ārātrika* ceremony in the divine world filled with the light of jewels, finds delight there.
For he is indeed illuminated in the celestial vault by divine throngs of apsarases with beautiful lamps fashioned from minerals and other materials during the rite of śrāddha.
He who,

intent on his purpose, should offer a vessel for incense and a vessel for the *ārātrika* ceremony dedicated to the ancestors, shall become a recipient of prosperity; for him, there is an imperishable state in heaven.
Viṣṇu [692]:
[Substances] consisting of oily materials should be prepared for the purpose of lamps. Marīci:

"The lamp [should be made] from ghee or sesame oil, but not from any other substance. Here, "other substance" is intended to mean substances consisting of fat or marrow; it does not, however, refer to oily substances derived from seeds such as linseed or safflower. For Śaṅkha says:
A lamp should be offered with ghee, or else with the juice of medicinal herbs;
one should carefully avoid a lamp produced from fat or marrow.

*Vasā* is the fatty substance of the flesh extracted through cooking. *Medas*, however, is a specific type of flesh that covers the heart-lotus; the fat extracted from it through cooking is indicated by the term *medas*. There is also a form of the word *medas* ending in *-a*, as seen in such terms as *medinī*. Now, regarding "covering," [it is stated] in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then give a garment that is unwashed,
new, with its fringes intact, without holes, and free from stains.
In its absence, however, that which has been washed by persons of the same caste should be given;
it should be offered in rites for the ancestors, but never that which has been washed by artisans.
In the Bhagavatī Purāṇa: "For the sake of an undergarment and an upper garment, a wise person should respectfully offer a pair of garments for each [deity] during the ancestral rites."
Or, in the absence of clothing, a ransom should be given according to one's ability.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who offers costly garments to the ancestors is born wealthy in riches and grain, and well-attired.
He becomes handsome, fortunate, illustrious, and beloved by women;
endowed with long life and health, he attains stainless fame.
He who bestows linen garments as white as a mass of moonlight,
having reached the lunar world, sports like a god.
By giving red silken garments, one attains the world of the Sun;
by giving those that are yellow, one indeed goes to the world of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu);
and by giving variegated ones, one is eternally honored in the world of Mahendra.
Having given two garments made of silk thread,
one devoted to his ancestors shall become a king of kings in this world, endowed with beauty and good fortune.
He who offers saffron-colored garments to the ancestors rejoices on the back of the celestial vault for a hundred years with divine enjoyments.
He who gives to the ancestors a garment made of very fine and most beautiful cotton thread shall indeed attain infinite happiness.
By offering something dyed with auspicious colors such as madder and the like, or something beautiful,
to the ancestors and the gods, one attains supreme prosperity.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The high-minded one who bestows garments of great value, such as those made of linen and the like,
at a *śrāddha*, Viṣṇu is pleased with him."
Whoever offers a cloak as well as a turban to the ancestors never beholds the sufferings born of duality.
He who, with a serene mind, gives cloths and garments to be bound together,
being liberated from the bonds of evil, attains the highest prosperity.
At the Śrāddha rites, they should give vermilion and fine garments to the invited women;
those who do so shall be endowed with good fortune.
"Caṇḍātakas" are fine silken garments suitable for women's undergarments. He who gives clothing-cases together with the clothes themselves is filled with all forms of prosperity by his ancestors.
He [gave] new, very thick, spacious, and extremely firm cloaks capable of warding off the suffering arising from cold winds.
One should give to the ancestors here very large, great cloths woven from woolen hair; for such a person, no suffering from dualities exists in this world.
He who offers to the ancestors various garments of diverse colors, suitable for protection against the wind, shall always enjoy good health.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He who gives white garments— silk, linen, cotton, or likewise unwashed fine cloth— at a Śrāddha, obtains abundant fulfillment of his desires."
Likewise:
"For clothing belongs to all the deities and is praised by all the gods;
in the absence of clothing, rituals such as sacrifices and acts of giving would never take place anywhere."
Therefore, garments should be given especially at the time of a śrāddha;
by giving these, one obtains the merit of sacrifice, charity, and austerity.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"And he who gives a new garment during the performance of a *śrāddha* rite obtains long life, sovereignty, and beauty at his pleasure."
Pracetas stated the definition of *ahata* (unbeaten) cloth:
"That which is slightly washed, new, and has never been worn— even if it has been worn [once]—
one should know that as *ahata*, which is purifying for all ritual acts."
‘Slightly washed’ means not washed by a professional washerman.
For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"A wise person should perform religious rites with clothing washed by himself."
But not with one washed by a washerman, nor with one that has been used anywhere.

‘Nejakaḥ’ means a washerman. Although the washerman is already excluded by the mention of “himself” (*svayam*), the explicit prohibition of the washerman is intended to make known that cloth washed even by another person of the same caste (*savarṇa*) is fit for use.
Regarding the *śrāddha*, it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
“Likewise, silk, *kauśeya* silk, cotton cloths, as well as upper garments (*prāvaraka*) and woolen blankets (*bala*).”
The deer-skin should be that of the ruru deer, or it may be made of wool or the fur of a jackal.
For by giving these to Brahmins and feeding them according to the rule,
one who possesses faith obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Extraneous women become beautiful, sons become servants,
all beings remain under one's control, and one attains a body free from disease.
It swiftly destroys prosperity, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun;
yet it shines at the front of a celestial chariot like the moon among the stars.
He who, devoted to his ancestors, gives clothing during the daily ancestral rites (nitya-śrāddha),
attains all desires, as well as sovereignty and heaven itself.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "A garment made of cotton that is black in color should not be given to the ancestors; nor should one that is soiled, nor one that has ever been worn."
It should not be torn, nor frayed at the edges, nor washed, nor even by a weaver.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"One must never give black cotton cloth to the ancestors;
or rather, something other than that which is produced from cotton may be given."
One must not even take the name of clothing dyed with indigo;
from seeing or mentioning indigo, the ancestors depart in despair.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "The wise man should give a sacred thread (yajñopavīta) in the absence of clothing;
by that, he enjoys the entire fruit of giving garments to the ancestors."
Śātātapa says: "One should give a garment with the verse 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'; in its absence, a sacred thread."

Now, this question is deliberated: should the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) be given by a Śūdra to his ancestors, or not? On this point, it is first stated that it *should* be given, because it is generally declared as something to be given at a *śrāddha*. Nor should it be argued that it cannot be given due to the Śūdra’s lack of capacity, since he lacks a *yajñopavīta*; for it is possible to give one that has been acquired through purchase. Nor should it be argued that—just as there is no status of *āhavanīya* fire for what is purchased—there is likewise no status of *yajñopavīta* for a sacred thread produced by purchase with respect to its buyer. This is because the status of *āhavanīya* is understood from the force of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the injunction *ādadhīta* ("one should establish"), which indicates that the fruit of the action accrues to the agent, thereby establishing a singular relationship between the performer and the fire; thus, the status of *āhavanīya* arises in accordance with that requirement. However, the absence of *āhavanīya* status in the case of a purchased fire is merely described. But is there not a middle voice in the injunction regarding the *yajñopavīta*? Even if present, it may be disregarded (*avivakṣita*), since we observe an injunction for the giving of the *yajñopavīta*. Furthermore, no exception (*apavāda*) is seen stating that the *yajñopavīta* should not be given at a Śūdra’s *śrāddha*. Now, it might be argued: "Whatever pleases the ancestors should be given to them, because the purpose of giving at a *śrāddha* is to gratify the ancestors. But the *yajñopavīta* does not please the Śūdra ancestors. This is not so. It is not a source of pleasure in the sense of being an ornament like a necklace or bracelet, because it is not recognized as such by the cognition of those who avoid ornaments. As for the notion of its being an ornament arising from a specific familiarity and resulting in a latent impression (*vāsanā*), that applies only to the three higher castes and thus cannot effect the satisfaction of Śūdra ancestors. Do not say so. Whatever is prescribed or even unprohibited, when given at a *śrāddha*, pleases the Brāhmaṇas who act as the medium; it pleases the ancestors who are the intended recipients by virtue of being the substratum. There is no rule that whatever pleases a person while they are alive must necessarily please them once they have attained the state of an ancestor. Who knows what womb that person has entered in another birth? For this very reason, female ornaments are not given at a *śrāddha* for women, yet *yajñopavītas* are given. Nor is the *yajñopavīta* withheld at a *śrāddha* for a wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*), nor are things like bottle-gourd leaves given instead. Nor is honey or meat withheld at a *śrāddha* for ascetics or students (*brahmacārin*), simply because such items were forbidden to them while living, and thus are not given at their *śrāddha*. If it is argued that these too should not be given due to impropriety or uselessness, we reply: such is not observed in the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Moreover, the *yajñopavīta* is prescribed here in place of clothing. And clothing is certainly useful even for Śūdras. Therefore, the *yajñopavīta* may be given at a Śūdra’s *śrāddha* at will. Apart from its function as a substitute for clothing, whatever is prescribed in the manner to be described—such as perfumes and the like—should also be given, since there is no exception to that rule.
Thus concludes the description of the upper garment. Now, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Having honored the ancestors with garments, one should give a sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Indeed, a Śrāddha performed without the gift of a sacred thread is fruitless."
Therefore, the gift of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is traditionally held to be mandatory.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "One who is faithful and righteous should always give sacred threads for the pleasure of the ancestors; by that, he becomes endowed with the splendor of Brahman."
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The wise man who, being pure, offers to the ancestors a sacred thread (brahmasūtra) fashioned by a Brāhmaṇa shall become one who has mastered the Vedas."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The knower of dharma who gives a sacred thread during the performance of a śrāddha rite obtains the fruit of a gift of the Veda, which is a purifier for all brāhmaṇas."
In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"One who gives a sacred thread (*upavīta*) fashioned with a fine white thread and preceded by the recitation of mantras during a *śrāddha* ceremony becomes wise."
Having given a divine sacred thread made of gold to the ancestors,
one sports in heaven in celestial chariots made of gold.
For one who always gives silver sacred threads to the ancestors,
their lifespan, progeny, vigor, and fame increase.

Previously, when clothing was not obtained, the offering of a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) as its substitute was prescribed. However, here it is understood that even when clothing is available, the sacred thread is enjoined as a primary object of offering, just like perfumes, flowers, and so forth; for this is seen in such passages as "having honored the ancestors with garments," where they are mentioned together. Accordingly, Vaijavāpa says: "Having placed the vessel face down and having spread *kuśa* grass upon it, one should offer—beginning with the gods—perfumes, flowers, incense, a lamp, garments, and a sacred thread."

Thus, because the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is enjoined here as something to be given, it is understood that the *yajñopavīta* is prescribed as a primary object of donation, just like perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
This concludes the description of the *yajñopavīta*.
Now, [follows] the staff and the meditation-band (*yogapaṭṭa*).
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The high-souled one who gives staffs at the *śrāddha* rites for the pleasure of the ancestors is never afflicted by calamities arising from wild beasts."
For those who bestow staffs and meditation-bands upon yogis,
their ancestors— being the most excellent knowers of yoga— are enriched by all objects of desire.
He who gives staffs made of *pālāśa* or *vaiṇava* wood as is appropriate to those observing vows,
to householders, and to ascetics for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
He who gives meditation belts made of silk thread and the like,
having been born into the family of yogins, becomes a king among yogins.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: By giving very firm bamboo staffs that are pleasing and have well-knotted joints for the sake of pleasing one's ancestors, one never encounters fear.
They were fashioned with iron spades at their base,
made of clay and kuśa grass, and were highly effective for digging at the appropriate times.
If one should offer either only water or only staffs at a *śrāddha*,
the ancestors bestow upon him faith, intelligence, purity, and even devotion to the sacred law, both in this life and in other births.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who is devoted to his ancestors and bestows soft and beautiful yogapaṭṭas upon the Brahmins certainly attains Yoga."
By giving other objects useful to yogins, one pleases the ancestors and immediately crosses over evil deeds.
But he who, endowed with faith, gives objects such as staffs and other requisites useful to yogins, shall be happy both in this world and in the next.
Jātūkarṇya said:

Having bestowed a staff upon the foremost of the twice-born during the ancestral rite (pitr̥-karma), one who is devoted [to this duty] becomes exempt from punishment even by Yama; of this there is no doubt.
Śālaṅkāyana said: Having given a new, very firm,
soft, smooth, and unknotted bamboo staff to a twice-born man who has eaten at a śrāddha feast.
Victory arises constantly and one does not see defeat;
if she becomes dappled in color, one overcomes all defilement.
Thus ends [the section on] the staff and the yogapaṭṭī. Now, regarding water-vessels such as the *kamaṇḍalu* and others, [it is said] in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
At the ancestral rites (śrāddha), one endowed with devotion should give to the twice-born a new and beautiful water-pot filled with water for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
By that [act], the ancestors are fully satisfied for twelve years;
and the donor, bringing happiness to all, obtains everything from every quarter.
In the Agni Purāṇa: "Among all the ancestors and gods, there are indeed two that are primary;
namely, food and water, for both are the supreme providers of satisfaction."
Water is surely better than even food; of this there is no doubt. Hunger does not afflict one as much as thirst causes suffering.
Living beings may indeed be able to survive for a time even without food;
however, embodied beings afflicted by thirst do not live for even half a moment.
Those who have fallen into a swoon, when sprinkled with cold waters, immediately regain consciousness; therefore, it is indeed a life-restoring remedy.
For this reason, water should especially be offered for those who have passed away;
through the refreshing of that water, they attain supreme peace.
In the other world, living beings are dependent and tormented by thirst;
they long for waters being offered by their descendants.
For this reason, the libation for the ancestors should be performed with auspicious waters;
moreover, vessels filled with water should be offered on the sacred festival days.
In the village, water-pots of dharma should be given to Brahmins every day;
likewise, on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day, one should cause full jars to be bestowed.
One should perform the watering of the *aśvattha* tree every day for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
during the *śrāddha*, one should give water-pots filled with snow-water.
Thus, he who offers water to the ancestors in these various ways,
being satisfied with all his desires, rejoices for a long time in heaven.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*:
"Having given a water-pot filled with water at a *śrāddha* while being composed in mind,
one attains an imperishable state, with all desires entirely fulfilled."
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"Whoever gives a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
a cow that flows with honey and milk follows after the donor."

He who gives a water-pot with a wheel-fastening at the time of a śrāddha ceremony rejoices for a long time on the summit of Mount Meru, well-satisfied, in a golden celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He who gives a divine water-pot made of gold obtains a divine cow that yields a jarful [of milk] with a mere handful."
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"He who offers a full water-pot to the ancestors with water follows after a stream of honey situated in the midst of a stream of ghee."
He who offers a water-pot fashioned from gold or other precious metals to the ancestors rejoices for a long time in enjoyments upon the Golden Mountain.
He who indeed gives a silver water-pot to the ancestors shall become a righteous king, endowed with all his limbs complete.
He who gives a copper water-pot at śrāddha ceremonies is endowed with great prosperity and is born into a noble family.
He who gives a water-pot made of wood or even of coconut at a śrāddha is born prosperous.
Whoever, with faith, presents various water-vessels made of leather, shall be born happy for a long time.
He of great intelligence who offers new water-pots fashioned from clay during śrāddha ceremonies never encounters suffering.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who constructs tanks, as well as large oblong ponds, wells,
and water-stations for the sake of satisfying the ancestors, goes to the world of Brahmā.
One should provide water-jars filled with water, or a water-dripper;
one may also provide water-pitchers or even small hand-spoons.
He who, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, bestows according to his ability, attains imperishable happiness.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
By giving a water-strainer that wards off living beings from the water to yogis during a Śrāddha ceremony,
a person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand niṣkas.
Thus [are described] water-vessels such as the *kamaṇḍalu* and others. Now, the umbrella (*chatra*). In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
Whoever should give an excellent parasol adorned with flower garlands and the like,
that supreme palace follows after him as he goes.
In the *Bṛhadviṣṇupurāṇa*: "He who, endowed with the welfare of his ancestors, gives a variegated umbrella, shall find no distress anywhere; of this there is no doubt."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "He who indeed bestows an umbrella, saying, 'May this belong to such-and-such a person,' shall be delivered from suffering by that act until the end of his life."
In the *Bhagavatīpurāṇa*:
"By one who offers an umbrella suitable for protection against the rain and the sun,
the ancestors shall be rescued from the difficult-to-cross ocean of suffering."
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "He who gives an umbrella to the ancestors, which wards off rain and heat,
does not experience any suffering arising from the great elements."
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]: Having provided a parasol suitable for the king, endowed with various beauties,
and having assigned an appropriate livelihood for the parasol-bearer;
The man who offers [this] to an eminent Brahmin, intending it for his own ancestors,
shall rule the entire surface of the earth under a single umbrella.
He who, being self-restrained, offers to the ancestors an umbrella with a hundred ribs adorned with white cloth, shall become a king in this world.
He who gives a parasol of beautiful form, constructed from many peacock feathers, shall have his dwelling in the Nandana grove.
The man who gives a beautiful small umbrella as protection from the heat at the time of a śrāddha ceremony never suffers anywhere;
likewise, he who provides an umbrella to ward off the gaze during the rainy season.
For the sake of the welfare of his ancestors, he is not overcome by sufferings. Thus concludes the description of the parasol. Now, regarding the sandals and wooden shoes.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"One should especially give sandals to the Brahmins at śrāddha rites;
thus one obtains divine vision as well as chariots yoked with horses."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The knower of dharma who, at the time of the Śrāddha rite, presents a pair of sandals to each individual foremost of the twice-born for the sake of the ancestors,"
In the world beyond, that celestial chariot awaits the ancestors;
the donor, moreover, attains heaven by means of well-yoked mares-drawn chariots.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Those who, with concentrated minds, bestow sandals upon their ancestors have effectively made a gift of horses; there is no need for further deliberation on this point."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Some [hells] have scorching sands; some are filled with glowing coals;
some are strewn with iron thorns; and some are infested with predatory beasts."
The paths to the realm of Yama for those who have passed away are very difficult to traverse;
the gift of sandals alone is capable of enabling them to cross.
Having personally given sandals to the twice-born according to the prescribed rite,
or to those by whose ancestors they were given, their descendants cross that path.
For this reason, those who know the Purāṇas always praise the gift of sandals at a śrāddha; no other gift is equal to it.
In the Saura Purāṇa:
Having fashioned [the sandals] from very firm leather that is free from foul odor, one should give them—
neither too small nor too large, comfortable for the feet, and soft.
By giving sandals to Brahmins for the sake of the happiness of the ancestors, the ancestors are pleased; being pleased, they grant whatever is desired.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "He who gives straight and complete sandals during the performance of a Śrāddha rite obtains a splendid vehicle as well as comfort for his feet."
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"He who respectfully offers a pair of sandals for the sake of satisfying the ancestors shall have unimpeded passage to the meritorious worlds."
In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"One should offer a pair of sandals made of metal or other materials to the ancestors;
he who does so shall attain travel by celestial chariot (*vaimānikī gati*) in the worlds of the gods."
He who bestows sandals made from elephant tusks indeed obtains variegated vehicles both in this world and after death.
Moreover, that wise person who offers auspicious sandals made of heartwood to the ancestors also enjoys ultimate happiness.
Thus concludes the description of sandals and shoes.
Now, the seats.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "He who offers beautiful seats to the ancestors dwells for a very long time, honored by the gods."
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"To him who bestows most beautiful seats upon the ancestors,
the Mistress of the Seat (Pīṭheśvarī) eternally grants their desired boons."
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "He who provides very smooth and spacious seats at śrāddha ceremonies— for him, the Lotus-born Goddess (Lakṣmī) always dwells in his home."
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "The highly intelligent man who offers a seat to the ancestors dwells for a long time in heaven, free from enmity and at his own will."
In the Camatkārakhaṇḍa:
He who causes a golden seat to be given at the Śrāddha ceremonies,
his seat shall be upon the summit of Mount Meru, in the presence of the Supreme Lord.
He who offers a well-crafted silver seat for the ancestors dwells happily in heaven and sports there for an inexhaustible time.
He who has given a copper seat for the ancestral rites indeed ascends a divine seat and does not fall from it for a long time.
He who gives a seat fashioned from heartwood shall have a noble seat prepared for him when he has gone on high to the celestial realm.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who presents a beautiful auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*) to the ancestors will indeed sit upon a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) and shall not fall from it even after a long time."
But those kings who provide a seat made of cloth and well-strewn with swan feathers attend upon that man as he sits.
Or he who should offer a seat or a garment filled with cotton;
Through their reverence for the ancestors, prosperity approaches them.
He who gives silk cushions and beautiful seats at a *śrāddha* ceremony is indeed provided with a divine throne in heaven; likewise,
by offering mats made of *kuśa* grass to yogis in honor of the ancestors, one gains great merit.
He is born with a purified self, completely liberated from all attachments.
One should present variegated seats made of *caitra* wood to the ancestors;
such a person becomes free from disease, fortunate, and prosperous.
But for that man who would give new woolen blankets for the purpose of using as seats,
the perfection of the eightfold yoga arises for him.
He who, having fashioned a beautiful seat from soft and smooth blades of grass, |||
One should give these at the *śrāddha* rites; for him, prosperity shall quickly become firm in every respect.
This concludes the description of the seats.
Now, [the description of] the bed-covers, sheets, and pillows.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "He who, with the ancestors in mind, gives a bed provided with a mattress, covered with a canopy, and furnished with a pillow..."
His ancestors rejoice, happy for eternal years;
and the donor, having attained heaven and mounted a divine celestial chariot,
is served by the women of the gods while being sung of by the kinnaras.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: "He who indeed gives a couch provided with a beautiful mattress,
along with a pure covering cloth and a lovely pillow..."
Endowed with faith, when the time for the śrāddha has arrived,
he reaches the third heaven, which is possessed of divine enjoyments.
Surrounded by thousands of celestial women, he enjoys himself;
when his time is exhausted, he returns here and becomes beloved by mortal women.
In the Kūrma Purāṇa: "The man who gives a bed with a cotton mattress during the rites for the ancestors is delighted in heaven by deer-eyed women who are devoted to him."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"One who is self-restrained, having with devotion provided for the ancestors a couch fitted with a mattress and constructed from auspicious wood, to the Brahmins during the ancestral rites..."
He is ceaselessly attended by the most excellent throngs of apsarases.
A beautiful swing, provided with a cushion, a pillow,
and adorned with very lovely chains made of precious metals.
He who, devoted to faith, offers in the rites for the ancestors a seat richly adorned with the splendor of an elephant in rut and woven from soft cloths, [attains great merit].
Constantly being sung of in the world of the Gandharvas and Apsarases,
he enjoys various pleasures difficult even for the gods to obtain.
And whoever gives wooden palanquins suitable for beds,
provided with fine coverlets and marked with the image of an elephant in rut,
shall indeed delight in the world of Viśvakarman for ten thousand years.
In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*: "He who gives a bed constructed of wood and adorned with golden plates dwells in the abode of Śakra."
He who provides a bed at a śrāddha ceremony, adorned as is appropriate with leaf-cuttings made of brass, shines in the world of the Sun.
Having given a divine couch made of ivory at a śrāddha ceremony,
one shall go to the lunar world and dwell there for ten thousand autumns.
The wise person who offers to the ancestors a bed woven with silken threads goes to the world of the goddesses.
He who offers a very firm cloth made from cotton threads shall enjoy his desires in the abode of the Moon, just as he wishes.
Having given [a gift] bound with strips of cloth made of hemp, or with threads, or even with wool,
one who is born in a future life obtains beautiful women.
He who offers a pillow made of swan-down to the ancestors rejoices at his pleasure in the world of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
By giving a soft and beautiful cotton mattress,
provided with a pillow, a man becomes possessed of prosperity.
He who gives a beautiful pillow made of swan-feathers becomes eternally possessed of fame and a vessel for all forms of happiness.
Whoever offers a covering of linen or silk thread will be endowed with beauty and become beloved by the people.
To him who offers an upper cloth made of fine cotton thread,
the ancestors grant a long life in this world.
That man who gives a soft leather saddle-cloth shall also be endowed with prosperity and be born on earth free from disease.
By providing a covering made of various skins and lined with soft grass at a śrāddha ceremony, one does not experience suffering anywhere.
He who offers a covering made of soft grass to the yogins at the time of the śrāddha is not overcome by sufferings.
Thus [are described] the bed, the coverlet, the sheet, and the pillow;
and then the fly-whisk, the fan, the mirror, and the hair-ornaments.
[This is from] the Bṛhad-Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Whoever offers a yak-tail fan with devotion is indeed honored for a long time in the world of the Lord of Heaven.
For this is a requisite of kings and is likewise dear to the ancestors;
therefore, a wise man, being diligent, should bestow it upon them with great effort.
By giving a mirror to them, one is born with clear vision;
likewise, by giving a comb for smoothing the hair and a brush for grooming the beard.
In another birth, he obtains a perfectly well-nourished collection of physical forms.
As stated in the *Saurapurāṇa*: "A fly-whisk, a palm-leaf fan, a white parasol, and a mirror..."
Having given these to the ancestors, the protector of the earth shall prosper in this world.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "He who gives a beautiful hair-comb, a fine comb,
and a stainless mirror with the appearance of the full moon,"
One who is pure in heart at the time of the ancestral rite attains an imperishable state in heaven.
A *kaṅkatikā* is a comb made of ivory used for grooming the hair.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*:
"It is produced from the white hair of the tail of a *cāmara* cow."
It was likewise fashioned with a handle variegated with gold.
Having given a fly-whisk to the ancestors, one is fanned by women in heaven;
however, having given that very same object when it is black in color, one becomes a lord of the earth.
By offering a chowrie with a golden handle fashioned from peacock feathers to the ancestors, one is reborn as a king of kings.
By giving a fly-whisk made of long, very white horse-tails at a śrāddha ceremony, one becomes a regional ruler (māṇḍalika).
Whoever offers a fly-whisk fashioned from the hair of a black horse,
by that merit he becomes wealthy and a partaker of the Dharma in this world.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"One should give a fly-whisk to the twice-born and establish it in a temple of Śiva;
for him who does so with the ancestors in mind, his ancestors shall grant all desires."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
[713] Having given a fan and a palm-leaf fan that have been consecrated to a Brahmin,
one shall obtain things that are pleasant to the touch, fragrant, and soft.
A *tālavṛnta* is a cloth fan. In the section on wonders:
it is made from soft leather washed with various astringent decoctions.
Adorned with many variegated colors and beautified by a golden handle.
Those who offer a fan beautifully adorned even with a handle made of ivory,
having gone to Amarāvatī,
are fanned constantly by women with hands graced with excellent bracelets.
Whoever offers a fan fashioned from peacock feathers to the ancestors is also honored in the world of Skanda at the end of his body’s life.
If one offers a fan made by a child or fashioned from bamboo at a śrāddha ceremony, one does not experience any remorse of mind.
He who offers a palm-leaf fan fashioned from a cane-strip or even from other cloths shall become a king; of this there is no doubt.
By offering a fan made of palm leaves or fashioned from birch bark at a śrāddha ceremony, one attains great health.
Having offered a fan to the ancestors, fashioned from split bamboo and finely woven, one enjoys infinite happiness.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
