Having devotedly offered a mirror during the ancestral rites for the ancestors,
one becomes illustrious upon the earth, honored by fame.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "By offering a mirror well-crafted from pure silver to the ancestors, one shall indeed go to the lunar world."
By giving a mirror fashioned from fifty palas of stainless bell-metal, one certainly becomes radiant.
By giving a circular mirror made of thirty palas of bell-metal,
or even one made of twenty-five, one will indeed become radiant with beauty.
Whoever presents a mirror fashioned from ten palas of bell-metal also obtains excellent vision.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: By giving a hair-comb fashioned from ivory for the sake of ancestral rites,
that righteous soul enjoys the world of the Aśvins.
By arranging hair ornaments fashioned from sticks of palm, coconut, bamboo, or cane,
a man certainly becomes fortunate and well-attired.
Having given a comb made of wood as a means for grooming the hair,
one obtains beautiful hair and attains a long life.
By offering a brush made of boar bristles, which makes the beard clean,
to the ancestors, one shall become handsome and fortunate.
Thus concludes the description of the yak-tail fan, the fan, the mirror, and the arrangement of the hair.
Now follow the food, honey, vessels for fruit, the vessel-stand, the *patadgraha*, betel, and its containers.
Regarding the *śrāddha* ceremony, [it is stated] in the *Brahmavaivarta*:
The giver of food obtains a celestial chariot that resembles the rising sun and fulfills all desires, as well as thirty million maidens.
There exists no gift in this world superior to the gift of food;
from food all beings are born and by it they live, of this there is no doubt.
There is no gift in this world superior to the gift of life;
since the three worlds live by means of food, that [gift of food] must therefore be supreme.
Upon food all worlds are established; that is the fruit of the gift of food.
Food is Prajāpati himself; by it all this is pervaded. Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of food.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Various kinds of foods, both savory and soft,
as well as sweet fruits produced according to their seasons."
He who, having prepared it himself with devotion, offers it to the ancestors,
attains union with Brahman through the grace of the ancestors.
In the Nāradīya Purāṇa: "Food is indeed of five kinds— eatable, chewable, lickable, drinkable, and likewise suckable— and it is endowed with substance, fragrance, and flavor."

One should also diligently offer fruits such as grapes, plantains, oranges, and mangoes— endowed with excellence of color, fragrance, taste, and touch— at the time of the śrāddha ceremony to those whose tongue is the mantra.
By that, the ancestors together with the grandfathers attain supreme satisfaction;
they grant him desires difficult to obtain through any other rite.
But that man who offers vessels for the ancestors—
whether made of gold, silver, and so forth, or even of bell-metal—
attains the state of being a worthy recipient for all forms of prosperity.
Having set aside the three-legged stands made of metal and other materials that served as bases for eating vessels,
one should have them conveyed to the house of a Brāhmaṇa for the gratification of one’s ancestors;
such a person attains the status of a support for all his kinsmen without exception.
Having offered a spittoon made of metal for use in spitting, rinsing the mouth, and so forth,
during the time of a Śrāddha ceremony,
and having placed it in the house of a twice-born man, one attains abundant prosperity.
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "Food has been declared by all those who have mastered the Vedas to be Brahman;
and that which is endowed with manifold qualities is difficult to obtain even in the world of the gods."
He who bestows [this] abundantly out of great affection for his ancestors,
being liberated from all suffering, goes to the eternal Brahman.
He who gives betel leaf here, combined with pure camphor,
attains exceedingly vast sovereignty both in this world and in the next.
And he who should give, in their entirety, betel-boxes for the purpose of holding lime, leaves, betel nuts, and so forth, filled with betel nuts and the like;
Likewise, one who possesses a vessel of camphor filled with camphor enjoys divine pleasures while remaining on earth for a thousand years.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Food indeed is the life-breath of living beings; food alone is the nectar in heaven.
The giver of food is declared to be the giver of life, and likewise the giver of food is the giver of immortality."
Therefore, a son must provide a grand feast for the sake of his father;
indeed, a man who gives abundant food should not be considered merely human.
Having his sins utterly consumed by this act, his residence shall be in the city of Viṣṇu.
He who, filled with affection, offers to the ancestors fruits that are fragrant, ripe, and sweet— such as grapes and the like—
shall partake of the nectar of the fruits in the Nandana grove of heaven.
Having offered to the ancestors betel prepared with excellent betel nuts, betel leaves, and fragrant substances such as camphor, one obtains infinite prosperity.
There is nothing dearer to living beings than food;
and there is nothing superior to betel among the objects of enjoyment, for it is the most excellent of them all.
Therefore, one who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors should give both of these;
the giver of food attains health, and the giver of betel-leaf becomes a possessor of enjoyments.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"The giver of food obtains an imperishable, divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, resembling the sun and crowded with divine apsarases."
In the Bhagavatī Purāṇa:
"Food is indeed the life-force of living beings; this statement is well known. Therefore, he who bestows food truly bestows life itself."
Therefore, food should be given abundantly even to the ancestors;
the giver of food attains health and gains a long life.
In the section on the Sahya mountain:
"Indeed, honey is the supreme essence of all medicinal herbs;
it is renowned as the quintessence of all foods, known by the name 'madhu'."
This [honey] is exceedingly dear to both the gods and the ancestors;
therefore, no śrāddha should be performed with anything whatsoever that is devoid of honey.
In a Śrāddha ceremony devoid of honey, the ancestors depart disappointed;
but when both the gods and the ancestors are satisfied with honey, they certainly attain fulfillment.
They remain satisfied by the essence of nectar until the dissolution of all beings.
If honey has somehow been offered to the Brahmins in the meal,
the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) must never be given without honey.
Those by whom rice-balls (piṇḍas) were offered to the ancestors with honey, clarified butter,
and milk-rice (pāyasa) through the pluta-rite, have indeed been delivered from the ocean of debt to their forefathers.
Or those men by whom the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) was performed with honey and milk-rice on the thirteenth day of the Maghā constellation have indeed accomplished their purpose.
By those high-souled men who have offered rice-balls at Gayāśīrṣa with foods mixed with honey, or with parched grain flour soaked in honey;
For more than a hundred million eons, endowed with various enjoyments,
they dwell in the Brahma-world together with their own ancestors.
In the Śrāddha rite, the word "Honey! Honey! is indeed uttered three times;
by these [utterances] addressed to those named Madhu, the ancestors become well-satisfied.
For this reason, those who know the Dharma praise honey at the śrāddha rite,
whether it be contained in a vessel made of gold, silver, or even fashioned from bell-metal.
According to one's capacity, there should be a large and extremely clean food vessel,
accompanied by small vessels for ghee and other items made of gold or similar precious materials.
It is situated within a support-mechanism made of metals such as gold,
and is provided with a waste-receptacle known as a *patadgraha*.
He who gives to the foremost of the twice-born with the thought, "May this be for my ancestors," dwells for a very long time in heaven and becomes a sovereign on the earth.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
One should indeed give a beautiful vessel made of metal to those who eat at the śrāddha;
such a vessel becomes a source of all desires, as well as of knowledge and wealth.
The man who gives silver and gold in śrāddha rites obtains,
through that gift, the fulfillment of his desires as well as wealth.
A vessel made of silver or mixed with silver is said to belong to the ancestors;
by this gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
One should cause vessels filled with salt to be given at a śrāddha;
thus the savory juices, edible foods, and good fortune itself are attained.
He who gives vessels filled with sesame seeds here to the twice-born gives a hundred niṣkas for every single sesame seed; of this there is no doubt.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "Having filled the vessels with fragrant substances, oils, and likewise with scented materials, one should offer them with respect during the *śrāddha*."
Fragrant breezes, great rivers, various pleasures,
and devoted young women attend upon the giver.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "For one who is devoted to his ancestors and offers fruits such as plantains and others to them,
his life in this world is fruitful."
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Those who offer gardens filled with trees bearing delightful fruits and entwined with creepers to their ancestors, preceded by the offering of water;
Having become universal monarchs, they rule over the earth.
Those who offer even a flower garden, or one endowed with just a few trees, to the ancestors, become protectors of the earth; of this there is no doubt.
Those who, out of affection for their ancestors, give even a single fruit-bearing tree or a vine-covered bower to high-souled Brahmins,
are seen upon the surface of the earth as having many sons and great wealth.
But those who, having prepared or obtained fruits,
offer them with devotion to the ancestors, they too will certainly become wealthy.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Those who give excellent betel-nut trees and even pavilions of betel vines to the ancestors dwell together with Apsarases.
The nut-vending tray was full with rows of areca nuts,
provided with black iron devices for splitting the betel nuts.
Having collected in their entirety a vessel for placing leaves filled with radiant leaves,
as well as a vessel of camphor and other such items,
one should present them to the foremost of the twice-born during the śrāddha rites.
And for the purpose of taking betel, one should provide the materials suitable for a year;
when the year is complete, one should cause all of it to be given once again.
Thus, for one who performs this, the ancestors, with delighted minds,
bestow upon him long life, progeny, wealth, and happiness.
Thus concludes the description of the vessel for food, honey, and fruit; the supporting tray; the spittoon; and the betel-leaf and its container.
Now, regarding gold, ornaments, and vehicles, it is said in the Nandipurāṇa:
Among all forms of giving, gold is traditionally held to be the most excellent;
for indeed, all things derive their utility from gold.
Therefore, gold should especially be given to the ancestors;
having honored them with perfumes and the like, and having worshipped them with garments and the like.
"Gold should be presented with the formula, 'This is for him; may it be savory!
However, silver is recommended at the beginning of the rite for the ancestors."
Ornaments made of gold should be given according to one's ability,
such as armlets, necklaces, bracelets, rings, earrings, and so forth.
In Śrāddha rites for women, ornaments should be given to the ladies,
such as anklets, waist-bands, strings of beads, earrings, bracelets, and so forth.
Beautiful ornaments fashioned from clear gems such as necklaces, rubies, lapis lazuli, pearls, emeralds,
and the like, should be offered to the ancestors in accordance with one's own wealth.
Wise persons should diligently provide vehicles— such as palanquins, carts, and horses— at a *śrāddha*, according to their own capacity.
Various kinds of foods and delicious drinks should always be given according to one's desire, gladdening the ancestors.
Thus, for that best of the righteous who performs the *śrāddha* with faith,
whose every sin has been exhausted, whose mind is completely purified,
and whose web of afflictions is severed— liberation alone is the stainless fruit.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Gold is indeed nectar, the very form of the gods; such is the Vedic revelation. The giver of gold at a Śrāddha ceremony becomes a bestower of nectar upon the ancestors."
Therefore, gold should always be given for the pleasure of the ancestors,
or silver according to one's ability, for that is exceedingly dear to them.
He who, having fully honored and clothed the ancestors, bestows gold, obtains merit equal to that of the Tulā-dāna; of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of silver, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
For the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), gold or even silver should be given separately;
by that, his prosperity increases and he attains a long life.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Even a story concerning silver, or its sight, or indeed its gift— specifically,
the gift of silver is said to lead to imperishable heaven."
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "He who, as a worshiper of the ancestors, gives gold or silver,
his residence shall be for ten thousand divine years on the Mountain of Gold."
The high-minded person who offers silver to the ancestors likewise finds that his lineage prospers through the grace of the ancestors.
Furthermore, that fortunate one who, out of devotion, gives priceless ornaments to the ancestors becomes a great favorite of the celestial women.
That man of pure intellect who, having fashioned ornaments from pure Jāmbūnada gold, bestows them upon the foremost of the twice-born at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony,
becomes exceedingly fortunate, possessing great wealth and a share of glory.
He who gives away crafted ornaments made of precious gems shall become a ruler of the earth, honored by all his vassals;
thereafter, after a very long time, he shall attain the same world as Viṣṇu.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "O best of beings, by whom can the merit of that meritorious person be calculated who offers a highly valuable ornament to his ancestors?"
But he who gives beautiful vehicles as means of transport for the sake of comfort to the ancestors shall possess the wonderful sovereignty of celestial chariots.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
By giving a head-ornament at a Śrāddha that is worthy of great wealth, one becomes anointed on the head (a consecrated king) upon the earth; of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of ear ornaments, one will certainly become highly learned;
by giving a neck ornament, however, one will become eloquent and possess a sweet voice.
By giving ornaments for the heart, one is born wise and learned;
by giving ornaments for the arms that have been bestowed, one is born possessed of great strength.
By giving an ornament for the hand, a donor becomes renowned;
he who gives an ornament for the foot becomes worthy of universal veneration.
The wise have declared these to be the fruits for those who have fallen from heaven;
yet, for the gift of ornaments to one's ancestors, heaven is the most excellent fruit.
When ornaments made of silver are given, even liberation is not difficult to attain.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Whatever has been specifically prescribed as excellent should be given to the ancestors;
likewise, food, water, clothing, and especially ornaments."
Vehicles should also be given as gifts for the complete satisfaction of the ancestors.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "At a śrāddha, garments, beds, and seats should be given;
moreover, vehicles especially should be bestowed here by the wise."
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"The paths leading to the next world for those who have passed away are extremely difficult to traverse;
indeed, without the gift of vehicles, they cannot be crossed."
Therefore, vehicles should be given to the ancestors by those born into the lineage.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who provides a palanquin equipped with all necessary implements,
as well as an annual livelihood for the work of carrying it on a swing, [attains great merit]."
For a twice-born man, food sufficient for a year may be given for the sake of his family;
likewise, even the gift of an umbrella should be made during rites for the ancestors.
Furthermore, everything should be given again at the end of the year for the satisfaction of the ancestors;
whether one does this every year or even once, for that man who acts in this way,
there is no returning once he has attained the state of a celestial being in a divine mansion.
But he who gives a horse endowed with auspicious marks for use in ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall have an imperishable residence in the world of the Sun at the end of his body's life.
In the *Camatkārakhaṇḍa*:
"He who gives a young elephant endowed with beautiful characteristics shall dwell for ten thousand years in each of the worlds of the world-protectors."
He who gives to the ancestors a horse that is radiant, of graceful gait, and endowed with auspicious marks, shall possess unimpeded victory upon the earth.
He who gives a beautiful chariot yoked with pairs of horses,
or with large-bodied, young bulls endowed with all auspicious marks,
shall never suffer defeat in any great battle.
By giving a carriage or even a cart with iron wheels, axles,
and a pole to the ancestors, one obtains exceedingly great abundance of wealth.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "At a *śrāddha*, one rejoices with the comfortable chariots offered;
one is honored by kings or increases in wealth and grain."
Thus ends the description of golden ornaments and vehicles.
Now, regarding cows, buffaloes, bulls, camels, and so forth,
according to the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
At a *śrāddha*, cows, female buffaloes, and likewise bulls,
as well as great camels and whatever other auspicious object there may be, should be given as gifts.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Cows, buffaloes, and other such items are to be given as offerings during the rite of Śrāddha;
satisfaction that fulfills all desires for the ancestors should be brought about in the Śrāddhas."
He who satisfies the ancestors at a śrāddha with various kinds of offerings—
all those offerings shall always attend to his home.
In the *Bṛhad-Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "One who gives to the Brahmins a young, milch cow that is easy to milk and has a living calf, with the intent of pleasing the ancestors."
Or for him who has gone to heaven, there shall be a cow that milks all desires.
Having given to the ancestors a well-behaved, auspiciously marked, tawny cow that has a calf, yields much milk, and is adorned with a bell and a chowrie;
Just as the reed fiber becomes pure and separate from the Muñja grass and its husk,
so he becomes pure and separate from all evils.

He who gives a noble buffalo— possessing flawless limbs, free from anger, yielding abundant milk, endowed with excellent qualities, accompanied by her offspring, and rich in ghee— is honored in the world of Brahmā for more than a full hundred thousand years.
In the heavens, lakes filled with milk, clarified butter,
and curds stand ready for the ancestors until the dissolution of all beings;
the donor as well attains heaven for sixty thousand years.
But he who gives draft oxen capable of bearing burdens on their backs—
oxen whose noses have not been pierced and whose testicles are unimpaired— [727]...
Dharma himself, in the form of a bull, becomes manifestly pleased with him;
when this Blessed One is pleased, what indeed is there that cannot be obtained?
Those kings who, having adorned them, give away camels capable of carrying loads and traveling many yojanas, have no doubt [of attaining great merit].
Goats, sheep, and even buffaloes capable of bearing burdens should be offered to the ancestors by one who desires the destruction of all sins;
thus it is stated in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
By giving a white cow to the ancestors, one is glorified in Śvetadvīpa;
by bestowing a black-limbed milch-cow, one does not behold the world of Yama.
By giving a cow of yellow hue, one does not grieve over what has been done or left undone;
by bestowing a red Rohiṇī cow, one overcomes all evil deeds;
and by giving a dark-blue Surabhī cow, one does not suffer the extinction of one's lineage.
Having given a cow characterized by any color whatsoever to the ancestors, one conquers unsurpassed happiness in heaven.
The man who gives strong oxen capable of bearing the yoke obtains the entire fruit of a gift of land.
By gifting oxen capable of bearing loads that carry burdens on their backs,
one becomes exceedingly wealthy among the ancestors.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "For him who bestows upon the ancestors a buffalo with abundant milk and auspicious characteristics, a stream of nectar flows in heaven."
The Blessed One, the slayer of Mahiṣa, is pleased with that man who offers a buffalo capable of bearing heavy burdens to the ancestors.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who gives camels that carry with speed, or even male camels,
his path is never obstructed when he has gone to heaven."
He who offers animals such as goats, sheep, and the like at a śrāddha ceremony,
his household becomes completely filled with progeny and cattle.
Thus ends the description of cows, buffaloes, bulls, camels, and so forth. Now, [the description of] the earth-house, the book, and the gesture of fearlessness, according to the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
A wise man should bestow land upon the Śrāddha according to his ability;
for that indeed brings about the prosperity of the ancestors and fulfills all desires.
For people say that a man who bestows land bestows everything;
he who bestows everything enjoys all desires in the world beyond.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"There exists no other gift equal to the gift of land;
therefore, one who desires prosperity for his ancestors should give land."
By the gift of land, the ancestors, having indeed attained all their desires,
rejoice together with Brahmā until the dissolution of all beings.
In the Bhagavatī Purāṇa:
[729] From the earth come grains, and indeed from the earth come garments;
from the earth come cows, buffaloes, excellent horses, and noble elephants.
Delightful gardens, rivers, wells, and lakes;
parasols, vehicles, beds, and seats.
Indeed, there were heart-pleasing foods and drinks, as well as perfumes and garlands,
and silver, gold, and various kinds of jewels.
Delightful ornaments and whatever else is a means of happiness—
the earth alone is the source of all that, without a doubt.
For this reason, one who is devoted to his ancestors and who desires for them an inexhaustible satisfaction that fulfills all desires should diligently offer land.
The ancestors of one who gives land dwell in the world of Brahmā and roam about in the finest celestial chariots that travel wherever they desire.
The man who gives land, having destroyed all his impurities,
goes to the world of Brahmā, from which, once gone, he does not return.
In the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: "The wise man who desires to satisfy his ancestors with all their shares should, with that intent, bestow land upon them."
By the gift of land, a man sports in heaven for eternal years;
returning here upon the exhaustion of that time, he shall become a powerful sovereign.
And he who bestows upon his ancestors various wonderful houses—
divine, made of gold, auspicious, moving at will,
and endowed with every prosperity— he ascends a celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
He who also presents books to the ancestors during a *śrāddha* ceremony likewise obtains honor in the assembly of the Supreme Lord.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Having worshipped the ancestors with devotion, one should, with a concentrated mind, give land.
Satisfied by the gift of land, they never experience distress anywhere.
He who offers a village or even a small town to the ancestors goes to the abode of Śakra and rejoices there as long as Indra reigns.
He who gives a field at a *śrāddha* ceremony, measuring ten furrows,
or even five furrows, or even just the size of a cow-hide;
If these are not obtained, one may cultivate even two furrows, or even a single furrow,
using plows together with oxen, yokes, goads, and other necessary implements.
A man who provides it with other implements such as ropes, ploughs, and so forth,
obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
when he eventually falls from heaven in due time, he becomes a righteous king on earth.

Furthermore, by giving to the ancestors a field that serves as the source of production for grapes, sugarcane, barley, wheat, mung beans, kidney beans, and sesame seeds, a man shall attain union with Viṣṇu.
Having returned again to the human state, he is endowed with wealth and grain;
possessed of splendor and fame, he is born wise and eloquent.
A house built of baked bricks, whitened with lime,
adorned with the beauty of *mattavāraṇa* panels, and provided with windows, doors, and walls.
Whether it be connected with many stages or indeed belonging to a single stage,
he who gives here to his ancestors goes to the realm of Brahmā.
There, in palaces made of gold and adorned with various jewels,
he constantly delights in dancing, instrumental music, and singing;
he remains in that very place for a hundred thousand divine years.
By giving a house to the ancestors, whether it be even one thatched with grass,
one obtains excellent dwellings, complete with women and wealth.
Having constructed most beautiful palaces for Keśava and others,
he who offers the merit thereof to his parents, grandfathers, and so forth, attains the highest good.
In worlds such as Vaikuṇṭha, that fortunate one rejoices together with his ancestors for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
He who gives well-edited books of the true scriptures is born into a family of Brahmins as a performer of sacrifices and one of great learning.
In the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: When virtuous Brahmins have assembled at the time of a Śrāddha, one should give them righteous scriptures; thus one obtains memory and intelligence.
In the Camatkāra-khaṇḍa:
He who offers books to Brahmins for the sake of his ancestors becomes a learned man, eloquent, intelligent, and deeply versed in sacred knowledge.
He who gives books on the Vedānta to his ancestors,
having been born into a lineage of Vedic scholars, becomes the most excellent knower of the Vedas.
By giving the exposition of the Vyākaraṇa, one shall eternally become the best among the knowers of Brahman;
by the gift of Mīmāṃsā, a man becomes a performer of Soma sacrifices.
By bestowing the treatises on logic, a person becomes most learned;
by giving the Purāṇas, one becomes a devotee of Hari, the Ancient Person.
By the gift of the Dharmaśāstras of Manu and others, one becomes righteous;
by the gift of the arts and sciences, one becomes skilled in the arts.
The wise person who grants fearlessness to living beings on the day of a śrāddha ceremony shall experience no fear whatsoever, both in this world and in the next.
In the Saura Purāṇa: Whatever fear has arisen for anyone, whether from oneself or from another,
a wise person should dispel that when the time for the Śrāddha rite has arrived.
One should remove, according to one's ability, the fear arising from a king, a thief, a serpent, or even a predatory beast during the performance of ancestral rites.
On one side are all sacrifices accompanied by the gift of one's entire possessions as the sacrificial fee;
on the other side is the protection of the life of a living being who is terrified by fear.
Therefore, one should grant the gift of fearlessness at all times,
especially at the time of a funeral rite (śrāddha), for that is considered the supreme dharma.
For just as the great-grandfathers are satisfied by the gift of fearlessness,
they are not so satisfied by garments, food, drink, jewels, ornaments, or gold.
Therefore, one who understands should grant fearlessness at the time of a śrāddha;
those who bestow fearlessness never encounter fear anywhere.
Because of the absence of fear regarding birth and death, liberation is called "fearlessness";
indeed, a man who grants fearlessness to living beings attains that very liberation.
Regarding the *śrāddha* ceremony, the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* states:
"Indeed, no gift excels the gift of life;
therefore, with every effort, one should provide protection for living beings."
Non-violence is sacred to all the gods, a purifier that sanctifies everything;
indeed, the wise declare that among all gifts, the gift of life to living beings is the supreme.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*: "He who indeed grants safety to living beings who desire life at a *śrāddha* ceremony [obtains the merit] of a thousand gifts of horses and a hundred gifts of chariots."
And even with a thousand elephants, the granting of fearlessness is indeed superior.
Whatever jewels, vehicles, and women exist upon the earth—
all that he quickly obtains by bestowing fearlessness at the time of the śrāddha.
But for that man who, at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, should perform the binding and releasing [of the thread],
it is impossible to describe the merit of that doer of virtuous deeds.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
"Whatever men have been made captives— whether by themselves or by others—
that man who liberates them by whatever means possible [attains great merit]."
His ancestors go to the eternal, imperishable state.
Therefore, that man who causes a bard to recite during the ancestral rites attains union with Viṣṇu, liberated from the bonds of karma.
Thus concludes the examination of the underground chamber, the book, and the protection from fear.
[734] Now follow the sūtras concerning collyrium and ointment.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "One should offer collyrium and ointment to the ancestors,
and one should place a new, fine thread upon the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*)."
In that regard, collyrium from Mount Trikakuda is recommended for rites for the ancestors;
likewise, soot taken from a lamp fed with sesame oil is also suitable.
'Trikakuṭa' is the Nīla mountain; that which originates there is 'traikakuda', meaning produced from the powder of stones on the Nīla mountain known as Srotāñjana.
Anointing with sesame oil should likewise be performed by the wise.
Linen or silk thread is also prescribed for the ancestors.
One should cause the ointment and other items to be given, saying, "O so-and-so, anoint yourself; likewise, rub [oil] on yourself.
One should also present the thread, saying, "O so-and-so, this is for you."
By giving collyrium in this manner, a man becomes possessed of sight;
by the gift of ointment, he obtains supreme beauty;
and by the gift of thread for sewing, he shall obtain infinite garments.
In the Vāyupurāṇa:
"The anointing with collyrium and the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas),
when performed according to the sacred mantras, are equal in merit to the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
One should perform all the prescribed rites with diligent effort.
In the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* and the *Vāyupurāṇa*,
they say that *añjana* from Trikakuda is always the best;
and that which is worn [as collyrium] produced from the oil extracted from black sesame seeds from the island [of Dvīpa].
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: One should offer excellent collyrium to the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya),
pronouncing the names of all of them, as well as a thread for the sake of their clothing.
Having properly ground the collyrium, the wise man, standing to the north of the altar,
should take it with three blades of *darbha* grass and perform the rite according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise: there should be a single strainer in the hand; for the ancestors, [the oil] should be offered once each time.
Oil should be given with a vessel, for that serves as an ointment for the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Likewise:
One should provide new linen thread, as well as that made from chickpea-cotton;
one should avoid silk-woven thread, silk cloth thread, and silk (kauśeya).
‘Patrorṇa’ refers to washed silk (*dhautakauśeya*).
However, a wise person should avoid fringes if they are made from the cloth of one’s own hands;
for such [fringed items] do not please [the ancestors], and thus it would be fruitless for the donor as well.

In the Āpastamba-sūtra, however, it is stated that even the fringes of the cloth (vastradaśā) should be given. Having cut off the fringe of the garment with the mantra, "O Pitṛs, these are your garments; O Pitṛs, may we not lack anything other than this," he sets it down, or [he gives] a woolen fringe (*ūrṇāsukā*) in the earlier stage of life, and his own hair in the later stage of life. "Woolen fringe" (*ūrṇāsukāḥ*) means the fringes made of sheep’s wool. "In the later stage of life" (*uttare vayasi*) refers to after fifty years. "His own hair" (*svaṃ loma*)—the remainder is "produced on the chest"—because of the statement of Śāṭyāyani: "After fifty years, the hair of the chest belongs to the sacrificer."

In the *Kātyāyanasūtra*: "He discards this with the words 'etad vaḥ'—either woolen threads for each lump, or a fringe of wool, or he weaves them while adding the hair of the sacrificer on top. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
One should give garments or fringes made of white cloth in the proper order;
or, when one has reached old age, one's own body hairs.
One should provide a new thread made of linen, hemp, or cotton;
one must avoid those made of silk, blue-dyed wool, or red-dyed silk.
In the *Nāgarakhaṇḍa*: "One should offer a thread for each individual piṇḍa separately;
however, one should always apply another [thread] across all the piṇḍas."
Just as a thread does not break, so should he lay them down slowly;
he should cause opposition among them so that they might tear one another apart.
And that [offering] should be given as red, either with [red flowers] or with saffron;
for that which is devoid of a red thread, your śrāddha would be such [ineffective].
Thus was the boon granted by Brahmā to the Rākṣasa who consumes the offerings to the ancestors:
"Whoever gives this thread shall obtain imperishable prosperity."

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "By applying collyrium and ointment, as well as by offering incense and performing the ritual drawing of the sacred thread with *kuśa* grasses grown from seeds, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice."
Thus concludes the examination of the Sūtra on Anjana and Abhyañjana. Now, the miscellaneous [section] from the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa.
[737] Whatever is most excellent in the world and always dear to oneself—
that very thing should be given to the ancestors by one who desires that it be inexhaustible.
(From the Vāyu Purāṇa and the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.)
Having performed worship for the ancestors with perfumes, flowers, incense, and likewise with oblations, as well as with fruits, roots, and prostrations— being self-controlled and pure—
one should afterwards satisfy the twice-born with an abundance of food.
At the times of ancestral rites, the ancestors, having become like the wind, invariably enter the most excellent twice-born; therefore, I tell this to you.
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*: "One should offer perfumes, garlands, and so forth, as well as incense and other items, according to one's capacity.
In that very Purāṇa, there is the speech of the Pitṛs addressed to the Viśvedevas:
"He will honor you first with flowers, perfumes, and likewise with food;
having given to you first, he will then give to us.
When this is done, everything will be perfectly accomplished."
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "One should honor the best of the twice-born with garments, gifts of food, as well as various edibles and drinks, and likewise with cows, horses, and villages."
The ancestors become pleased when the twice-born are honored;
therefore, one should always honor the twice-born according to this rule.
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: [738] Fragrances, flowers, betel, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as sweet food, water, and ice, are recommended for rites performed for the ancestors.
O Vasundharā, he who, endowed with faith, offers these to the ancestors,
is truly virtuous and does what is pleasing to me.
Likewise:
Having seated him upon a seat, one should place a bright umbrella there;
and for the sake of protection, one should cause that umbrella to be presented to the Brāhmaṇa.
Then [he gave] all the beautiful garments and ornaments.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, the words of the ancestors are as follows:
"He who, while possessing wealth, shall give to the Brahmins— dedicating it to us— jewels, garments, great vehicles, and all manner of enjoyments and riches."
Having enjoyed all pleasures, he will go to heaven at the end.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"Sandals, an umbrella, garments, a vessel for food, and a water-pot..."
Beds, seats, vehicles, mirrors, and fans.
He who, full of faith and free from envy, offers well-prepared food, fragrant scents, betel, lamps, and whisks to the ancestors,
crosses over both grief and delusion upon attaining unsurpassed knowledge.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "Food, water, incense, lamps, clothing, garlands,
ointments, as well as cows, buffaloes, female camels, bulls, and so forth."
Mirrors, fans, parasols, couches, seats, and sandals;
palanquins, chariots, and carriages, as well as beautiful mouth-perfumes.
Pleasantly scented garments, fragrant handfuls of powder,
charcoal-burners for the cold, meditation bands, and staffs.
Waist-bands, carrying-slings, girdles, and woolen blankets;
sacred threads, seats, loincloths, and likewise water-pots.
Furthermore, these and other objects should be given by the wise to Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule and as is appropriate, for the pleasure of the ancestors.
The person who gives in this manner with devotion, according to their gains and according to their wealth,
obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Various kinds of ornaments fashioned from gold,
as well as those set with gems, and silken garments such as kṣauma and others."
Whatever fragrant substances there may be— camphor, agallochum, musk, saffron, and the like— as well as pleasing pieces of sandalwood;
Containers for camphor and other substances, as well as a betel-box;
a lamp-stand, an incense-burner, and likewise a food vessel;
utensil-holders, and similarly a spittoon.
Swings and couches with soft cushions of swan-down,
cauldrons made of copper ore, and likewise water-jars made of copper.
There were sacrificial ladles, large spoons, iron vessels,
and various other containers made from metals such as copper, as well as water-pots and jars.
There were auspicious seats, couches, bolsters, and thrones;
chests filled with garments, and beautiful swing-cots.
And new manuscripts of the Mīmāṃsā and other treatises,
as well as beautiful palatial buildings, ponds, wells, and the like.
Villages, fields, rice-paddies, gardens, and groves;
trees, canopies of creepers, and plantations of betel-nut and other such trees.
Carts with their equipment, numerous plows,
pestles and mortars, sickles, stones, churning-sticks, and bowls.
Likewise, collyrium sticks and the dressing of hair—
these and other such items desired by those in the four stages of life.
One should offer what is dear to oneself to the ancestors with a focused mind,
according to one's means and in accordance with the place and time.
Whoever properly gives these articles that serve as means for enjoyment,
for him nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain, both in this world and in the next.
In the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "When ten days had passed, having performed his purification according to the prescribed rule,
he performed the twelfth *śrāddha* as well as the thirteenth."
Then, in honor of his father, he gave wealth to the brahmins,
as well as precious gems, cows, and even vehicles.
In this context, "Bharata" is to be understood as the subject. From the *Brahmavaivarta*:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the gifts along with their fruits."
These are indeed the means for the deliverance of the ancestors, leading them to heaven and bringing happiness to oneself as well.
Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—
all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires their blessing.
By giving a pleasure-pool for recreation, one obtains the fruit of a great sacrifice;
by giving a forest endowed with flowers and fruits, one enjoys the merit of a Gomedha sacrifice.
Likewise:
"He who diligently provides a fire with abundant fuel during the cold season attains the brilliance and clarity of the body's internal fire, as well as beauty and good fortune."
He who gives fuel to the twice-born at the onset of the cold season always conquers in battle, is endowed with prosperity, and shines with splendor.
Likewise:
"By giving a shelter fully equipped with bedding, seats,
and food to ascetics at a *śrāddha* ceremony, one is glorified in the vault of heaven."
"Refuge" means an abode;
pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, various jewels,
and divine vehicles arise for him by the tens of millions.
Gandharvas and Apsarases sing and play instruments for him,
who resembles a great blazing fire and is endowed with all objects of desire.
He obtains an inexhaustible, divine, and radiant splendor like that of the sun and moon;
surrounded by apsarases, he travels at will with the speed of thought.
He dwells at the pinnacle of his celestial palace, being praised from all sides;
they sprinkle him with divine flowers and handfuls of fragrant powder.
Those who always awaken to the delightful sounds of the laughter and ornaments of maidens and young women are truly happy;
[they are not surpassed] even by the gift of a thousand horses or the gift of a hundred chariots.
And better than a thousand gifts of elephants is the state of being established among yogis.
Even with a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūyas,
and a thousand Puṇḍarīka sacrifices, the state of abiding among yogis is superior.
Likewise:
Having offered the first portion of food to guests with palms joined in reverence,
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of all sacrifices and rituals.
Promptly, very hot, unblemished, delicious, and served with side dishes— always moist and given with care and respect to one who is hungry.
One should always offer shelter to guests with palms joined in reverence;
thus they dwell in the abode of the gods along with thousands of divine guests.
One who might give all of these would become a sole ruler over the earth;
yet one becomes happy through three, two, or even a single gift.
Giving is the supreme dharma, honored with reverence by the virtuous;
for sovereignty over the three worlds and its certain stability arise from giving alone.
A king who has lost his kingdom shall regain it; a man without wealth shall obtain the most excellent wealth;
and a man who is always devoted to his ancestors shall regain his exhausted lifespan.
Whatever desires he may wish for in his mind, his ancestors grant them to him;
whatever jewels are upon the earth, as well as vehicles and women—
a man who partakes of the ancestors quickly attains all of that.
In the Mahābhārata: Food, drink, horses, cows, clothing, umbrellas, beds, and seats—
these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the departed spirits (preta).
By giving female and male servants, ornaments, and articles of enjoyment to the ancestors, one attains universal sovereignty; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to the wise Vāsudeva, to his aged maternal uncle, and likewise to Rāma and the others, Dharmarāja—
Then, with reference to all of them, he performed the ancestral rites according to the prescribed rules.
He gave jewels, garments, villages, horses, and even chariots,
as well as women by the hundreds of thousands, to the foremost of the twice-born.
That best of kings, repeatedly directing his attention, gave to the brahmins ornaments, horses, cows, and desirable, excellent women.
Droṇa, Sātyaki, Bhīṣma, Somadatta,
Vāhnika, King Duryodhana, and his sons— each one individually.
Having assigned them one by one to the brahmins, that best of kings gave away his friends and all those led by Jayadratha.
Likewise, the one of great splendor performed the funeral rites for his sons and grandsons, for his ancestors, for himself, and for Gāndhāra.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, while introducing the *śrāddha* rite, there are verses concerning the ancestors:
"May there be some most excellent man in our lineage who would offer us a black antelope skin with golden horns according to the prescribed ritual."
"Could there perhaps be some most excellent man in our family who, when this cow is being presented, would give her to a preeminent Brahmin? [744]
"Could there perhaps be some most excellent man in our family who is a builder of wells, groves, ponds, and large reservoirs?"
Baudhāyana said:
"Reservoirs, wells, and ponds; trees and groves as well;
fields of rice and sugarcane, irrigated plots, and flourishing flower gardens."
By giving at ancestral rites (śrāddha) with a disciplined mind, one delivers both the ancestors and oneself from sin and suffering until the dissolution of all beings (ābhūtasaṃplava).

Thus, when these items to be given have been mentioned, those things which are to be given as part of the worship that constitutes a limb of the *śrāddha* ritual procedure must be offered to the ancestors themselves, preceded by the recitation of their respective names and lineages (*gotra*). On the other hand, other items such as cows, land, gold, black antelope skins (*kṛṣṇājina*), and so forth, which are to be given to Brahmins at the time of the *śrāddha* for the sake of achieving the welfare of one’s own ancestors according to the method described in the *Dānakhaṇḍa*, should not require any other occasion; for they are prescribed specifically with reference to the *śrāddha* itself. And when given in this manner, they serve to secure for the ancestors and for oneself the attainment of distinguished fruits such as heaven.
Thus ends the miscellaneous section. Now, regarding the materials for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to him in his home—
that should be given as a sacrificial fee by one who desires that [gift] be inexhaustible for him.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability, accompanied by sesame seeds, while pronouncing the name and lineage;
as well as cows, land, gold, garments, vehicles, and beds."
Free from stinginess regarding his wealth, he should give whatever is desired by the Brahmins— whether for himself or for his father— thereby showing affection toward the ancestors.

"By name and lineage" means by pronouncing the name and lineage of both the recipient and oneself; having pronounced the name and lineage of the recipient and of oneself, they bestow the gift to be given. However, in the case of giving a daughter in marriage, three males [must be mentioned].

Thus, from the Smṛti of Vyāsa: "According to one's capacity" means in accordance with one's own ability; "bestowing satisfaction upon the ancestors" means pleasing the ancestors through ancestral rites (paitra-karman). Jamadagni says: "One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity, accompanied by sesame seeds, while pronouncing the name and lineage."
Gold, wealth, garments, and righteous beds;
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "Furthermore, out of devotion, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's capacity during the performance of a Śrāddha rite;
[this may consist of] villages, fields, groves, or various flower gardens."
Many-storied and delightful beds and houses,
gold, jewels, garments, silver, and ornaments.
Oxen and buffalo, various kinds of seats, sandals,
male and female slaves, as well as parasols, fans, and chowries.
Plows, carts, carriages, and household utensils.
Whatever is useful for the Brahmins as well as for oneself,
that very thing should be given in the śrāddha rites as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) by one who desires their welfare.
For in whatever measure a substance rich in qualities is abundant,
in that same measure there arises an abundance of fruit for the performer of the *śrāddha*.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"He who gives a cow that has calved for the first time and yields a large quantity of milk during the Śrāddha rites,
the cows attend upon him and the prosperity of his cattle increases."
Whoever gives beds, seats, grounds, and vehicles at Śrāddha ceremonies shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should respectfully cause vessels filled with clarified butter to be given at a Śrāddha;
one enjoys the fruit of many cows, such as those yielding milk-pots and others.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's desire, and one shall obtain the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
The *Puṇḍarīka* is a specific type of sacrifice.
By providing a beautiful dwelling, one obtains the fruit of the *Rājasūya*. [One also gains merit by giving] wells, groves, tanks, fields, cow-pens, and houses.
Having given a cow, one rejoices in heaven eternally as long as the moon and stars endure.
By giving a well-spread bed adorned with jewels at a Śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors are satisfied, and he enjoys infinity in heaven.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Golden and silver vessels, beautiful and auspicious;
elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and prosperous houses."
Shoes, sandals, umbrellas, chowries, and antelope skins;
One should then reflect that the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in sacrifices is meritorious;
even a poor person should give a fee to the Brahmins according to his ability.
The meaning is that the cognition "this is that very same [person]" is the effect [of the practice].
In the *Saura Purāṇa*:
"He who gratifies the twice-born at a *śrāddha* with many sacrificial fees..."
By the grace of the ancestors, he goes to the eternal heaven.
However, one who is unable should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the śrāddha according to his capacity;
for a śrāddha performed without a sacrificial fee is indeed carried off by the Rākṣasas.
Or if one is oppressed by extreme poverty, one may indeed give the sacred thread as a sacrificial fee; by that, the ritual act becomes endowed with excellent merit.
Thus concludes the determination of the materials for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Thus [ends the section] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Hemādri, the Paṇḍita and sovereign over all the departments of the illustrious Mahādevīya, the supreme king of great kings.
In the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, within the *Śrāddhakalpa*, the ninth chapter, titled "The Requisites for the Śrāddha," is concluded.
[748] Now begins the tenth chapter:
That which cannot be accomplished even by thousands of hosts of astrologers—
Then that Hemādri Sūri— who has attained the abundance of well-performed merit and who is a lofty mass of virtues capable of encompassing all—
now expounds the entire technical terminology regarding the rites for the ancestors.
Now, the technical definitions (paribhāṣā).

In this regard, there is a summary of all the scriptures; for that purpose, the following is considered: Should one perform only as much of the *śrāddha* as is prescribed in one’s own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), Kalpa-sūtra, and Gṛhya-sūtra, or should one perform it by incorporating all the duties (*dharma*) ordained in the *smṛtis* of Manu and others? If only that much of the duty is performed, then the instruction found in one’s own branch, Kalpa-sūtra, and Gṛhya-sūtra is meaningful; otherwise, it would be purposeless. Now, if the incorporation of duties ordained in the *smṛtis* is performed, then the *smṛtis* themselves become meaningful, whereas otherwise they would be purposeless. By the same logic, the incorporation of the entire collection of *smārta* duties is also faultless. Nor should it be said that the *smṛtis* will be meaningful for those individuals who lack their own specific branch, Kalpa-sūtra, and Gṛhya-sūtra; for there are no members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who are devoid of their own respective branches and so forth. Nor should it be said that they will be meaningful for *śūdras*; for since the *smṛtis* primarily provide instructions on rites such as initiation (*upanayana*), Vedic study, and the *agnihotra*—which require eligibility belonging to the three higher castes—they must be meaningful with respect to the *traivarṇikas* as well. This is not so. One might instead assume that the *smṛtis* have meaning specifically for *śūdras* regarding certain particular rites. Alternatively, even for the *traivarṇikas*, their utility may be described through the instruction of other *śrāddhas* consisting of many duties. Therefore, the performance of the *śrāddha* as stated in one’s own branch, Kalpa-sūtra, and Gṛhya-sūtra should be carried out exactly as such; it should not be augmented by the inclusion of items from the *smṛtis*. For if it were augmented, it would abandon the sequence and time intended by the injunction for performance and introduce something else. For this very reason, the *śrāddha* performance stated in one’s own branch, Kalpa-sūtra, and Gṛhya-sūtra should not be expanded by the inclusion of items mentioned in other branches and so forth.

Furthermore, because the *kalpasūtras* and *gṛhyasūtras* are restricted to being connected with specific reciters (*adhyetṛ*), and because the indicator (*liṅga*) and the indicated (*liṅgin*) must share a single substratum, the *śruti*—which is the indicated—is inferred as residing in that very same [reciter] based on the *kalpasūtra*, which is the indicator residing in that specific agent. Therefore, the *śrāddha* rites prescribed in one's own respective *kalpasūtra* and *gṛhya* are indeed restricted [to that specific group].

Furthermore, since it is impossible to avoid defects such as redundancy when [the same rite] is enjoined in other recensions (*śākhā*) or other *Gṛhya* texts, if [the rites] were distinct actions (*karmāntara*), then—given that the collection of ritual properties (*dharmajāta*) associated with them could not be connected to the rites of other recensions without the principle of extension (*atideśa*)—the comprehensive inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) of all properties would lack any basis of authority. Nor can it be argued that the restriction [of properties to specific recensions] is untenable due to the impossibility of qualifying adjuncts (*upapada*). This is because such qualifying adjuncts, which specify the agent by way of being a student of a particular *Śākhā* or *Gṛhya*, or by way of the pride of belonging to a particular *Śākhā*, are indeed possible. Nor should it be said that assuming such adjuncts for every injunctive sentence involves an overly complex assumption; for one may assume that all injunctions are simultaneously connected to the adjuncts by referring to them collectively through some pronoun, such as "this" (*idam*) or similar terms.

Not so. For even one who studies a different *śākhā* by abandoning his own ancestral *śākhā* performs only those duties prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of his own family lineage. Likewise, one who has studied two or three Vedas, though he may study another branch (*śākhā*) contained within a different Veda, still practices only the duties prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of his own original *śākhā*. Even one who has not studied the Veda, when performing rites such as the *śrāddha*, follows precisely the procedure taught in the specific *Gṛhya-sūtra* of that particular *śākhā*. Therefore, the qualifying designation characterized by being a student of a specific *śākhā*-Gṛhya does not persist as long as the practice itself; rather, the conceit of belonging to that *śākhā* must be understood as merely a delusion of being its student. Furthermore, this [conceit] cannot exist for one who has studied his own *śākhā* nor for one who has not. In the first case, the knowledge of being its student is true; in the second case, such knowledge is simply impossible. Consequently, the adherence to the specific practices of the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of those two [cases] would be untenable. Moreover, it would follow that even a student of another *śākhā*—who has developed a delusion of being a student of that other *śākhā* due to defects such as wind (*vāta*)—would have to follow the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of that [other] *śākhā*. If it is argued that this rule applies only to a delusion arisen without a [physical] defect, we say no, because a delusion cannot arise without a cause. If it is claimed that a delusion in the form of a superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) can occur even without a defect, then since such a thing could occur everywhere, total confusion would result. Furthermore, if the designation of belonging to another *śākhā* were taken figuratively, then because that [designation] exists [in some sense], there would be the undesirable consequence of adopting the injunctions prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of other *śākhās*. Thus, since a qualifying designation attached to the agent is impossible, the *śrāddha* rites—obtained from all *śākhās*, Kalpa-sūtras, Gṛhya-sūtras, Smṛtis, and established practice—are common to everyone and do not admit of a restrictive distribution (*vyavasthā*). This is not so. Since the status of being born from a specific *śākhā* is never lost, one truly belongs to that *śākhā*. Therefore, it is settled that the *śrāddha* must be performed exactly according to the duties prescribed in the Kalpa-sūtra and Gṛhya-sūtra of one’s own *śākhā*; it should not be expanded by the inclusion of elements from the Smṛtis or elements prescribed in the Kalpa-sūtras and Gṛhya-sūtras of other *śākhās*. Thus it stands.

To this it is replied: By the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that cannot be established otherwise, it has been established in the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*) that the Agnihotra and other rites are one and the same across all recensions, according to the sūtra: "Or rather, they are one, because there is no difference in connection, form, injunction, and name" (*ekaṃ vā saṃyogarūpacodanākhyāviśeṣāt*). In all recensions, because there is no difference in the connection, form, injunction, and name of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, their oneness is determined through recognition. Here, "connection" (*saṃyoga*) is intended to mean the relation to the fruit, as it is the primary factor. "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the substance and deity, because they are internal and define the essential nature of the action. "Injunction" (*codanā*) is the mandate whose object is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) together with the meaning of the verbal root. "Name" (*ākhyā*) is the designation such as "Jyotiṣṭoma. While explaining this very sūtra, the Teachers have said:
"Because of recognition everywhere by means of name, form, qualities, and so forth,
the cognition of a single action does not cease across the various recensional branches."

Furthermore, there is no cause for differentiation here, because it cannot be determined that what is stated in another recension (*śākhā*) serves as a factor for differentiation. If it is argued that mutual non-proximity, as in the case of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), is the differentiator, we say no; for since a single student does not study multiple recensions, the rite of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth, which is being propounded in those other recensions, is not perceived by him, and thus the appearance of difference is impossible. But why is it that a single person does not study another recension? It is because just as a universal form (*ākṛti*) is fully contained within a single individual instance, so too the status of being one's own Veda (*svādhyāyatva*) resides in each individual recension. Consequently, when it is said, "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied," and it is further stated that "one should effect the comprehension of ritual action (*karma-avabodha*) by means of the studied Veda," the Veda is employed for the purpose of comprehending the ritual; therefore, it is understood that only a single recension, characterized by the intended singular number, is to be studied. If one asks, "From where then [is the authority] for studying other Vedas? we reply: from such scriptural injunctions as, "Having studied the Vedas" (*vedān adhītya*), or "having studied two Vedas" (*vedau adhītya*), and so forth.

Furthermore, because ritual action remains expectant (sākāṅkṣa) across different Vedic branches, when there is a combination (samuccaya) of the Vedas for the sake of understanding ritual action, one does not study only a single Veda. However, even within a different recensional branch (śākhā) belonging to the same Veda, a ritual such as the Jyotiṣṭoma is understood in its entirety, independent of other branches. Therefore, since they serve the same purpose, there is an option (vikalpa) among the branches regarding the rule of studying one specific branch within a single Veda.
As the teachers have said:
"In the undertaking of one's own Vedic study (svādhyāya), indeed, only one branch is adopted."
"And there will be an option (*vikalpa*) regarding actions that have the same purpose, provided the action is one and the same.

Now, if—because one does not study a single recension (*śākhā*) contained within a single Veda—one has no cognition of the ritual acts belonging to other recensions, then how could even recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) occur? If it is argued that recognition is possible because, although one does not study it oneself, one hears of it being taught in another recension studied by others, and thus a cognition of the act propounded therein arises, then in that very same way, a cognition of difference (*bhedāvagati*) will also arise.

It is said in reply: Since there is no distinction inherent in the essential nature of the action (*karma*), and since no difference is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), when an immediate recognition arises based on the non-distinction of name, form, and so forth, it prevents the arising of a cognition of difference produced by inference, which is conditioned by mutual non-proximity. Alternatively, let the cognition of the essential nature itself—conjoined with the absence of a cognition of difference—be what effects the result of recognition consisting of valid knowledge of non-difference; thus, while being actually non-recognition, it is called "recognition" in a figurative sense (*gauṇī*). In that case, let some other quality (*guṇa*) be the differentiator.

No, because it is possible for that [action] to be connected with [the two qualities] as alternatives within a single action. But surely, when a quality is already enjoined by the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no room for another quality; thus, just as in the case of the *vājina* (curd-mixture), there must be a difference of actions regarding the other quality. Not so; for when two qualities are enjoined by the originative injunction and possess equal force, an alternative (*vikalpa*) is possible within a single action.

Objection: If indeed the same single ritual action (*karman*) is taught in all recensional branches (*śākhā*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy (*punaruktatā*). Therefore, to avoid this, one must assert a difference in the ritual actions across different branches according to the principle of repetition (*abhyāsa-nyāya*). Reply: Not so. Repetition brings about a distinction [in the ritual] only where a second mention would otherwise be purposeless by virtue of conveying merely that same [action]. However, in another branch, since the repetition serves a purpose—either for the sake of additional qualities (*guṇa*) or for the sake of praise—it does not effect a distinction. Furthermore, this is not a case of redundant repetition; as they say: [The verse: "Wherever a second mention of a known object occurs, it is either for the sake of a quality, or for the sake of praise, or because of a connection with a different person. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.8) Thus, because of the connection with a different person, there is no fault of redundancy. Nor is there a difference in the ritual action, because the ritual is established as one and the same through its constituent parts. For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "The ritual is one and the same, established by its constituent parts; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the sacrifice is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.9) Therefore, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same result. For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same result, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.10) Thus, because of the connection with the same result, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it possesses the same name. For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the identity of the name, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.11) Thus, because of the identity of the name, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same procedure (*kalpa*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same procedure, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.12) Thus, because of the connection with the same procedure, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same deity. For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same deity, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.13) Thus, because of the connection with the same deity, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same material (*dravya*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same material, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.14) Thus, because of the connection with the same material, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same time (*kāla*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same time, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.15) Thus, because of the connection with the same time, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same location (*deśa*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same location, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.16) Thus, because of the connection with the same location, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same fruit (*phala*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same fruit, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.17) Thus, because of the connection with the same fruit, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same agent (*kartṛ*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same agent, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.18) Thus, because of the connection with the same agent, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same purpose (*prayojana*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same purpose, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.19) Thus, because of the connection with the same purpose, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same injunction (*codanā*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same injunction, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.20) Thus, because of the connection with the same injunction, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same sequence (*krama*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same sequence, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.21) Thus, because of the connection with the same sequence, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same order (*pāṭhakrama*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same order, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.22) Thus, because of the connection with the same order, there is no difference in the ritual action. Moreover, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same number (*saṃkhyā*). For this reason, it is said: [The verse: "Because of the connection with the same number, the ritual is one and the same; it is not divided by the division of the branches, just as the *Agnihotra* is not divided by the sacrificers. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.4.23) Thus, because of the connection with the same number, there is no difference in the ritual action. Furthermore, the ritual is established as one and the same because it is connected with the same measure (*māna*). For this reason,
For those [mantras] bound to a single branch, the recitation is indeed known to occur repeatedly;
however, for those beginning with the Kaṇṭha-mantra and ending with the Cāraṇa-mantra, the recitation occurs only once for each branch.

In this regard, due to the rule of studying only one’s own branch (*śākhā*), one who has heard of the *Agnihotra* and other rites contained in that single branch does not hear of them as they appear in another branch. Even if he should occasionally hear of what is being recited by others from another branch, he concludes, "This is merely for the sake of others' understanding. Therefore, because another branch exists for the purpose of conveying knowledge to other persons, it does not constitute a "repetition" (*punar-śruti*). Furthermore, since the various branches exist simultaneously, there is no assumption of repetition; rather, in that case, the state of study proceeds sequentially, just as with a single branch. For when study proceeds sequentially, a certain [textual unit], falling into the status of a repetition, creates a difference in the ritual action (*karma-bheda*). But here, since the hearing occurs simultaneously, what could possibly be a repetition? Thus, just as a rite contained in one branch is not redundant—even though it is heard again in different places or among different persons—because the objects to be conveyed differ, so it is with respect to different branches. As for the objection that "everyone should understand through a single branch alone, making other branches useless," that is not a valid criticism because the various branches are not artificial (*akṛtrima*) and the restriction of students to each branch is beginningless (*anādi*). For this very reason, it should not be said: "Just as it is impossible to perform what has already been done, so too it is impossible to enjoin what has already been enjoined. Consequently, while it is impossible to enjoin in another branch what has already been enjoined in one, and because the branches are present simultaneously, it is also impossible for it to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); therefore, there is indeed a distinction. However, since the injunctions are directed toward different persons—the students of those respective branches—as distinct agents of activity and recipients of instruction, the enjoining of what is already enjoined is not contradictory. Thus, the unity of the ritual action (*karman*) being established, the *Agnihotra* and other rites, when connected with the properties (*dharma*) prescribed in any particular place, are to be performed even by the students of other branches. According to the principle that "one is not instructed solely for oneself," the rite must be performed endowed with those properties. This being the case regarding the integration of all branches (*sarva-śākhā-upasaṃhāra*), it is settled that the *Śrāddha* must be performed by everyone, endowed with all the properties known from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, *Kalpa-sūtras*, *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, *Itihāsas*, and traditional practice (*ācāra*) found in all branches.

For this very reason, we observe that the sages who composed the *Kalpasūtras*, while honoring a particular branch (*śākhā*), were not satisfied with merely recording the duties prescribed in their own branch; they proceeded to incorporate the duties found in other branches as well.

Now, one might object: even though the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same across all branches, it is logical that there should be a distinction in the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) prescribed by the injunctions of each respective branch, based on the specific arrangement for the individuals studying those particular branch *Gṛhyasūtras* and so forth; therefore, there is no need to synthesize all the branches together.

Not so; for in such an arrangement, there is an absence of any means of knowledge such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth. Nor has any other branch of the Veda ever been accepted by anyone as a valid authority for establishing such an arrangement, in the same manner as *śruti* and the other means of proof.

Now, there certainly exists a fixed arrangement regarding the study of specific Vedic branches by specific individuals who have come down through a tradition of practice, based on the injunction: "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied. Therefore, the object of knowledge (prameya), which is presented by such a fixed authority, ought likewise to be restricted accordingly. For instance, since it is held that the injunction to study one's own Veda has a visible purpose—namely, the comprehension of ritual action—it is not logical to assume an invisible purpose when a visible one is possible. In exactly the same way, for the sake of providing a visible purpose for the restriction to the study of specific Vedic branches, it must be accepted that its purpose is the comprehension of rituals as established for specific performers.

It is said in reply: Since for those endowed with exceptional wisdom, the study of other Vedas is permitted just as it is the study of one's own Veda, and since there is no fixed restriction regarding the specific recension (*śākhā*) contained within another Veda, one must study a single recension without such restriction. Furthermore, that study is for the sake of understanding the ritual acts (*karman*), and that understanding is for the sake of performance; thus, when performing rituals belonging to another recension, what restriction could there be? Indeed, the study of a second Veda is not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), for that would result in an inconsistency in the injunctions governing Vedic study.

The study of other recensions (*śākhā*) for the purpose of teaching those specific doctrines to others may indeed have a visible purpose; however, this is not so. For the meaning of the injunction has been determined as "one should produce the understanding of ritual action through the Veda that has been studied," and not "one should cause [others] to produce the understanding of ritual action.

As for the study of those portions of the Veda contained in one's own recension which enjoin rituals to be performed by other qualified agents, that occurs as an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyakatvena*) once the study of the entire recension has been enjoined for the sake of understanding ritual action; thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that there is no inconsistency because the study of a second Veda for the purpose of teaching others is prompted by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*) and not by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), and thus it does not have an invisible spiritual result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), that is not so. For in one case study would be prompted by the injunction for study, while in the other it would be prompted by the injunction for teaching; this would entail an undesirable inconsistency (*vairūpya*). Nor can it be said that in all cases study is prompted by the injunction for study, because that would lead to the contingency of the injunction for study being rendered purposeless (*ānarthakya*).

Furthermore, if the study of the other Vedas were prompted solely by the injunction for Vedic study, then Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas endowed with exceptional intelligence would not obtain the right to study those other Vedas, because they are not authorized as teachers [of those specific branches]. Therefore, there is no restriction of ritual acts based on the arrangement of Vedic schools (śākhā) or domestic manuals (gṛhya).

As for what was said—that if all the branches [of the Veda] were to be combined, the sequence and the time would be contradicted—that is not so. For the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) prescribes the performance after having taken up all the constituent elements (*padārtha*) as established by the means of knowledge such as direct revelation (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and custom (*ācāra*). It does not, however, settle for merely those elements mentioned in its own immediate proximity and thus proceed abruptly.
