For this very reason, in the discussion regarding the inclusion of elements from other sources—such as the Smṛti rules for bathing and sipping water (*ācamana*)—it was explained that even an element entering between the Vedic altar (*vedi*) and the fire (*agni*) must be understood as being included within the scope of the injunction of performance, provided there is no perceived reason to the contrary. Furthermore, sequence is a property of the constituent elements; it is not capable of subverting an element even if that element is established by a weaker means of knowledge.

Moreover, in a certain recensional branch (*śākhā*), only the general rule (*sāmānya*) is taught, not the specific detail (*viśeṣa*). At the time of performance, one must necessarily determine some specific detail through one's own intellect and adopt it. When such a detail is adopted, it may sometimes be one prescribed in another recensional branch. In that case, if that very same [detail] is adopted in accordance with another recensional branch, what indeed would be rendered inconsistent? Even a ritual element belonging to another recensional branch—which is not included within that general rule, which enters into a single performance by way of conjunction due to having a different door [of application], and which does not conflict with the elements stated in one's own recension—would not cause any defect when it is adopted, because the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is of an unlimited magnitude and its entry is not barred by any contradictory means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for a ritual element belonging to another recensional branch that contradicts what is stated in one's own recension, since the means of knowledge are impartial, and since they possess equal force when there is a single door [of application], its adoption according to the logic of option (*vikalpa*) is not considered at all improper by those who follow the principles of logic (*naiyāyika*).

Therefore, it is established that the performance of the ritual must be carried out by synthesizing the constituent elements understood from all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*), Kalpa-sūtras, Gṛhya-sūtras, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and established custom (*ācāra*).
Regarding this point, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"The Brahmins were fed by Rāma according to the rule with food prepared by sages."
Every rite performed according to the Veda, as well as those rites recorded in the Smṛti of Manu,
and the procedure described in the Purāṇas beginning with the Vaiśvadeva offering— [all these are to be performed].

"By one urged by the sages" means impelled by the Munis. "Vedic" refers to that which pertains to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña enjoined by the Vedas; it was brought into the Śrāddha by the extended application (*atideśa*) stating that "the ritual procedure for the ancestors is like that of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. "Mānavī" means prescribed by the scripture composed by Manu. "Smṛtā" means taught by other authors of Dharmaśāstras as well, such as Hārīta, Gautama, and others, after they had recollected the meaning of the Vedas. "Purāṇas" refers to those beginning with the Brāhma-purāṇa, which possess the five characteristics such as primary creation (*sarga*) and secondary dissolution (*pratisarga*). "Uktaḥ" means set forth or explained therein. "Vidhiḥ" refers to the method of performance. Thus, the meaning is that Rāma performed the Śrāddha after synthesizing all the scriptures.
Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini says:
"In self-contained systems, one should not perform what is prescribed in dependent systems;
for the specific rules taught by the exponents of the Vedas are indeed more general than those [of other traditions]."

"In one's own system" (*ātmatantre*) means in one's own scripture consisting of the *śākhā* and *gṛhya* [sūtras]. Whatever essential nature of the items to be performed is not stated therein, that one should perform even according to the sequence of another's system. For it has been determined by the proponents of the Veda that all particulars mentioned in the Veda are common and universal to all performers.
As for the statement of Vaijavāpāyana which contradicts this—namely, "Whether much or little, whatever rite is enjoined in one's own *gṛhya*..."—[it is refuted as follows:]...
When he has accomplished that much of the meaning of the scripture, he becomes one who has accomplished everything.

Thus, some explain it as follows: regarding those rites such as conception (*garbhādhāna*), tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), and marriage, which are correctly described in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* but not correctly described in the legal codes (*smṛti*) of Manu and others—in those cases, there should be no reliance on the *smṛtis*. However, regarding rites such as the ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) and the eight-day festivals (*aṣṭakā*), which are correctly described in the *smṛtis* but not correctly described in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*—in those cases, reliance on the *smṛtis* must indeed be maintained. Therefore, reliance on the *smṛtis* is precluded only for that which is prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*.
However, there is no requirement for the houses of others and so forth; thus, there is a determination of the scope for the principle of universal application, the scriptural injunction, and the vow.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "improper statement" (*asamyaguktatva*) means the mention of only a few constituent elements (*dharma*), and since even in that case one might mention only a small portion of them, the dependence upon *smṛti* (traditional authority) is already precluded? Why, then, is such dependence on it stated in regard to that [type of statement]? [Response: This is not so. Here, "impropriety" (*asamyaktva*) consists in mentioning [the rite] without those constituent elements (*dharma*) that are directly perceptible (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and which, when combined, bring about the actual accomplishment of the ritual's own nature (*svarūpa*). "Propriety" (*samyaktva*), on the other hand, consists in completeness through the mention of those constituent elements that bring about the ritual's own nature. Furthermore, "incompleteness" (*alpatva*) consists in the failure to mention other constituent elements—those whose purpose is solely unseen (*adṛṣṭa*)—even when the mention of the former has been completed. Therefore, in the case of an improper statement, dependence upon *smṛti* is indeed appropriate.

This explanation is untenable; for if the prohibition regarding what is stated in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* refers merely to the requirement of other *Smṛtis*, then the explicit use of the word "one's own" (*sva*) would be rendered meaningless.

Let it be so, then: that which is correctly stated in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* requires no dependence on the *Smṛtis* or *Gṛhya-sūtras* of others, whereas dependence must be exercised regarding that which is not correctly stated therein. For this very reason, an option (*vikalpa*) is accepted for the comprehension of rituals among the various *Śākhās* belonging to a single Veda, while a combination (*samuccaya*) is maintained for the Vedas themselves.

That too is not tenable. If the principle of incorporating (*upasaṃhāra*) duties mentioned in other recensions (*śākhā*) were restricted to rituals that have been incorrectly described, then—just as with the case of different Vedas—a recension that contains incorrect statements would never even be cited in the section concerning "other recensions" (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, since there is no such recension existing within a single Veda, the entire section would become purposeless. Therefore, it must be explained in this way: regarding a rite characterized by few duties as prescribed in one's own recension’s *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the performance should be carried out only after incorporating the additional duties mentioned in other recensions. However, if by some stroke of fate or human incapacity one is unable to incorporate the additional duties mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* of other recensions, then one should perform at least that which is prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of one's own recension, even if it is incomplete. And when that much has been performed, that act becomes equivalent to the complete form of the scriptural meaning achieved through the incorporation of all recensions’ *Gṛhya-sūtras*; thus, this is an alternative procedure (*anukalpa*).

Others, however, explain this statement as being intended to prohibit the performance of rites prescribed in other *gṛhya* texts that contradict the rites prescribed in one's own *gṛhya* text. That is not correct; for it is directly perceived from the statement that its scope concerns rites that are either deficient or excessive. Since contradictory rites are optional (*vaikalpika*), the adoption of one necessitates the abandonment of the other. Furthermore, when the extent of the ritual procedure is equal, it is useless to ask whether it is "more or less," as the phrase "whether much or little" would be irrelevant. Moreover, this statement by Laugākṣi prohibits the incorporation of contradictory rites from other branches (*śākhā*):
"Whether a rule prescribed in one's own branch is deficient or even excessive..."
Therefore, one should not perform a dependent rite for the sake of obtaining progeny.

Thus, even that [statement] is intended solely as a rule for a secondary option (*anukalpa*) regarding the performance of what is prescribed in one's own *śākhā* alone; it is to be explained as restating the fact that the adoption of elements from other *śākhās* follows by implication, and thereby establishing that very secondary option, rather than being intended to prohibit the incorporation of dharmas from other *śākhās*.
As for another statement of Laugākṣi:
"He who, having abandoned his own *śākhā*, should practice the *śākhā* of another..."
Having treated the immeasurable Sage with contempt, he sinks into blind darkness.
Thus, let that [text] be a prohibition against studying other Vedic branches.

Now, if—upon a thorough consideration of the context and other factors—the word *śākhā* refers to the ritual acts prescribed in that [specific] branch (*śākhā*), then it should be explained as follows: this fault applies to the abandonment of what is prescribed in one’s own branch (*sva-śākhā*) in favor of adopting what is found in another branch; it does not apply, however, to the adoption of what is prescribed in another branch in conjunction with what is prescribed in one’s own branch, because of the expression "having abandoned" (*parityajya*). Alternatively, since there is no possibility of abandoning those dharmas prescribed in one’s own branch that are not in conflict with them even when adopting what is prescribed in another branch, this statement is determined to have the purpose of prohibiting the adoption of what is prescribed in another branch if it contradicts what is prescribed in one’s own branch. In this context, the term "seer" (*ṛṣi*) refers to the Veda which is the root of one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, or to the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, or to the established practice (*vyavasthita ācāraḥ*), because these are observed [to be authoritative]. "Having made him unauthoritative" (*apramāṇaṃ kṛtvā*) means having conceived of him as lacking authority. "Sinks into blind darkness" (*andhe tamasi nimajjati*) means that one sinks into ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a particular state of the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*) consisting of the wombs of worms, insects, moths, ants, plants, and so forth, or into a specific hell characterized by sin. However, all auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) recited in another branch that are not in conflict [with one's own] should be combined and the ritual performed.
This has been stated in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
"Whatever is not prescribed in one's own *śākhā*, provided it is not contradictory [to it],
that should be performed by the learned, just like the *agnihotra* and other such rites."
Thus concludes the determination regarding the synthesis of all the treatises.
Now follows the determination regarding the sequential performance (anusamaya).

This [performance] is of two kinds: *padārthānusamaya* (the sequential performance of individual items) and *kāṇḍānusamaya* (the sequential performance of groups of items). Ritualists employ both of these methods in the performance of rites. For instance, regarding the *puroḍāśa* cakes for Agni and Agni-Soma, they desire the sequential performance (*anusamaya*) of the individual items such as placing the potsherds, heating on the fire, and removing from the fire. Even in the *Aśvapratigraheṣṭi*, when there are only a few *puroḍāśa* cakes, they follow this same method; however, when there are hundreds or thousands of them, they accept *kāṇḍānusamaya*. Likewise, in a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), they adopt *padārthānusamaya* for the animal-rites such as the dedication (*upākaraṇa*). And in a group of sacrificial posts (*yūpagaṇa*), they adopt *kāṇḍānusamaya* for the post-rites such as anointing. Therefore, a doubt arises: where is *padārthānusamaya* and where is *kāṇḍānusamaya*? Furthermore, even when *padārthānusamaya* is intended, they sometimes have doubts regarding the measurement of an "item" (*padārtha*), wondering how much constitutes a single item. This is seen, for example, in the case of a handful, potsherds, portions, anointing, sowing, and purification; or in the case of threshing, which includes the spreading of the black antelope skin, placing the mortar, and so on, up to the husking. Moreover, one observes that while something may be an action in itself, it is also seen to be a part of an item in one context but an independent item in another. For example, in the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and *sānnāyya* offerings, the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) is a part of the act of offering; yet in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *sānnāyya*—that very fourfold portion becomes an independent, single item. Similarly, in a group of animals where the deity is the same (*sampratipannadevatāka*), which is a modification of the *agnīṣomīya*, it remains an independent item. But in a group where the deities differ (*vipratipannadevatāka*), it becomes merely a part of the item consisting of the fourfold portion ending with the offering. Therefore, in this *śrāddha* rite as well, one must deliberate and determine where *padārthānusamaya* applies and where *kāṇḍānusamaya* applies among the following: the acts connected to the invited twice-born guests from the invitation until the dismissal; those connected to the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) from the washing (*avanejana*) until the disposal; those connected to the seats from the laying down until the turning face-down; those connected to the *arghya* vessels such as the washing, setting down, and covering; those connected to the eating vessels such as the scattering of *kuśa* grass, barley, sesame, perfumes, and flowers; and those connected to the ritual diagrams (*maṇḍala*). It must be decided whether these are performed sequentially as individual items or as groups of items.

In this regard, first of all, there is this general rule: that the performance is carried out by following the sequence of individual constituent elements (*padārtha*). Therefore, among the Brāhmaṇas and others, having repeated each directly contributing element (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), one should repeat the next according to that same principle, and not repeat the entire section of constituent elements for each individual.

Now, one might object: in such injunctions as "one desiring to satisfy the ancestors" (*pitṛtṛptikāma*) or "one desiring sons and so forth" (*putrādikāma*) should feed Brāhmaṇas or offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), although the Brāhmaṇas and the rice-balls are indicated by the accusative case (the *karma-vibhakti*), they are not intended to be produced (*cikīrṣyeta*) by the act of feeding or offering—just as flour or a cow are not intended to be produced by the acts of *homa* or giving—because they lack any other utility for the past or the future. Therefore, according to the principle that "those things which are not intended to be produced are primary actions" (*pradhāna-karma*), these two are primary actions. Furthermore, like those actions mentioned in proximity to a result that possess a fruit, other primary actions are also taken up as instruments (*karaṇa*) within the statement of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*). Consequently, the syntactical interpretation arises as follows: "One should bring about the satisfaction of the ancestors, or sons, cattle, and heaven, by means of feeding the Brāhmaṇas or offering the rice-balls. In this regard, since no instrument can exist devoid of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the word expressing the procedure is connected with the word denoting the instrument, in the form "thus" (*iti*). Thus, the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*) makes known the simultaneity of the result, the instrument, and the procedure. Such is the operation of the words; the actual state of affairs (*vastu*) is likewise the same. For instance, if the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) were in the past while the instrument and the procedure were in the future, then they would not truly be an instrument and a procedure; for that which exists later cannot be the instrument or the procedure. Similarly, if the object to be produced were in the future while the instrument and procedure were in the past, the same fault would apply; for what has perished cannot function as an instrument or a procedure. Even if the instrument and the procedure were at different times from each other, this same fault remains; for what is either perished or yet to come cannot be either the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) or the beneficiary (*anugrāhya*). Thus, it is established by the performance-injunction that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) share the same time as the primary action.

[Objection: But in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of teaching an impossible matter. For it is not possible for a single agent to perform multiple performances simultaneously. [Reply: True. However, in this case, we accept only that degree of temporal distance (*viprakarṣa*) beyond which performance would be impossible. [Question: Where, then, does the simultaneity (*ekakālatva*) taught by the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) reside? [Reply: Do not say so. Because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) prescribes as much time as is necessarily pervaded by all the constituent elements (*padārtha*) it causes to be performed; thus, there is indeed a single time for all of them. What is enjoined is their *sāhitya* (concomitance), but not within a single moment, for that would lead to the injunction of an impossible matter. Therefore, their *sāhitya* consists in proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And that proximity, as measured by direct statement (*śruti*), meaning (*artha*), and so forth, is established to whatever extent it is determined for each respective element. Consequently, there is neither instability nor futility in the direct statement, meaning, and so on. Thus, the great injunction of performance (*mahāprayogavacana*), while making known the concomitance of all subsidiaries (*aṅga*) with their respective primaries (*pradhāna*), either postulates intermediate injunctions of performance (*avāntaraprayogavacana*) for each primary, or, having manifested its own state as such, declares the concomitance of each primary with its own respective subsidiaries. In this way, having accepted the status of intermediate and further intermediate injunctions of performance, it establishes the concomitance of even the subsidiaries with their own respective groups of subsidiaries. And so, when it is established that a single *brāhmaṇa*, a *piṇḍa* (funeral cake), or a vessel (*pātra*) must be performed together with its group of subsidiaries without being interrupted by the performance of another’s duties, then the method of "section-by-section" performance (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) alone is logical, not the method of "item-by-item" performance (*padārthānusamaya*). To this, it is replied: In cases such as "one should feed the *brāhmaṇas*," "one should offer the *piṇḍas*," or "one should set out the vessels," due to the force of the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) resulting from a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the performance of the *brāhmaṇas* and the others is understood precisely as being mutually concomitant, just as in the case of "they perform with the *prājāpatya* offerings. And that concomitance occurs only through the performance of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) belonging to those [entities], not in their own essential form (*svarūpataḥ*). In that regard, if one were to perform the entire section of subsidiaries (*aṅgakāṇḍa*) for one *brāhmaṇa* and then perform it for another, then because the performance of the first would have already concluded (*apavṛkta*) before the second began, the concomitance would not be established. On the other hand, if one were to perform a single element (*padārtha*) for one [entity] and immediately in the next moment perform that very same element for the other, then the mutual concomitance of the *brāhmaṇas* and the rest is achieved.

[Objection: Surely, for the sake of conforming to the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), the statement regarding mutual concomitance (*sāhitya*) should apply only to those remote auxiliary elements (*ārādupakāraka-aṅga*) which are performed once (*tantra*) for the sake of all [the primary acts].

[Response: Not so. For the concomitance based on the injunction of performance is merely conceptual; it is not right to subvert or restrict the directly perceived (*śruta-pratyakṣa*) concomitance by the force of that [conceptual one].
Therefore, it is established that the rule of sequential performance (*padārthānusamaya*) is the general principle (*autsargika*).

Furthermore, another defect is that if one were to perform the ritual items (*kāṇḍa*) sequentially for each individual guest (the *kāṇḍānusamaya* method), there would be much contradiction. To explain: if, after inviting one guest on the previous day, one were to complete the entire sequence of ritual items for him—from the preparation of the food up to the final disposal—and then proceed to invite the next guest and so forth in the same manner, then several established rules would be violated. These include: the understanding that "one should invite the Brahmins on the previous day" implies a connection with that specific preceding day; the requirement that the performers remain at the place of performance throughout the duration of the rite; the necessity of purity; the prescribed time such as the afternoon of the *kutapa* period; the fact that the food must be warm; the principle of *tantratā* (single performance) whereby instructions and the like need only be uttered once for all those connected to the rite; the brevity of the performance which avoids the contingency of repeated actions; and established tradition (*samācāra*). All of these would be contradicted. In this regard, since approaching the invited person—which is implied by the act of invitation—is not a separate ritual item (*pṛthak-padārtha*), its repetition would be purposeless, leading to an infinite regress and thus failing to establish the invitation itself. Therefore, the sequence must end with the invitation. Even if one were to perform the invitation alone, ending with the proclamation of the restrictive rule (*niyama-śrāvaṇa*), the guests to be invited would be situated far apart from one another; consequently, when approaching them twice, there would arise the contingency of breaking the "brevity of performance" required by the injunction governing the ritual procedure.
Furthermore:
Having touched his right knee and thus invited you here by me,
the wise man should announce the ancestral observances (*niyama*).

In this passage, having stated that each individual invitation conveyed by the singular number possesses a prior temporal sequence (*pūrvakālatā*) through the direct mention of the suffix *-ktvā*, the occurrence of the subsequent moment immediately following the proclamation of the restrictive rule (*niyama-śrāvaṇa*) would also be sublated.
And this should not be asserted [as a valid objection], for [the text continues]:
"By those who are free from anger, ever devoted to purity, and perpetual celibates..."
Both you and I must be present for the performance of the ancestral rites.

Thus, since the injunction for the proclamation of the rules (*niyama-śrāvaṇa*) taught by Devala contains the plural number, it is understood that the connection is with all [the Brahmins] gathered together simultaneously through the simultaneous proclamation of the rules. Therefore, it is not appropriate to perform the invitation alone, or the invitation ending with the proclamation of the rules, in a sequential manner (*anusamaya*). This is because the use of the plural number can be justified as being for the sake of honor. On the morning of the *śrāddha* day, in accordance with the procedural order (*prāvṛttika-krama*), one should first give a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to the Brahmins according to the order of their invitation. Then, following the principle of "sequential performance of individual items" (*padārthānusamaya*), one should provide the oil, unguents, water, and other bathing materials to each Brahmin individually, treating them as a collective set (*kāṇḍānusamaya*) within each person. For instance, the rites beginning with the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and ending with the husking of grain are subordinate parts of a single "substance" (*padārtha*), as they are subsumed under the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) of threshing which results in the production of rice. Thus, in a sacrifice involving multiple seeds (*nānābījeṣṭi*), such as the *Santāna* sacrifice, these acts are performed collectively for each seed, following the principle of "sequential performance of groups" (*kāṇḍānusamaya*). Similarly, the provision of oil and other items for bathing is also a single "substance" because it is subsumed under the productive operation of bathing; therefore, these items should be provided collectively to each Brahmin.

Even in the absence of a formal invitation, Mārkaṇḍeya teaches the performance according to the sequence of individual items (*padārthānusamaya*) in order to dispel the misconception that the inquiry of welcome (*svāgatapraśna*) is merely a part of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
He states: "Having bathed, one should honor each of those invited who have also bathed individually with a welcome."

However, the offerings of materials such as barley-grain and incense should be performed collectively (*tantra*) for each individual mandala out of parsimony. Even in the view that they are to be performed separately, because there is no single ritual act (*ekapadārtha*)—since the act is subsumed under the mental visualization of worship—the rites must be performed as complete units for each mandala, similar to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* method. The acts of washing the feet, offering water for sipping (*ācamana*), providing a seat, and sitting down are to be performed according to the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance of individual acts). Having completed the entire section of acts—including the seat, the moment [of arrival], the invocation (*āvāhana*), the [offering of] water, incense, flowers, lamps, and garments—for the twice-born invited to the *vaiśvadeva* rite, one should then begin the section for those invited to the *paitṛka* rite; for so it is stated in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti* and the *Matsyapurāṇa*.

However, regarding the statement "from the anointing until the encircling," Jaimini also described *kāṇḍānusamaya* (the performance of all rites for one item before moving to the next) based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vacana*) concerning a multitude or group; that same principle should apply here as well due to such an injunction.
And thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Having given water for washing the hands, [he should also give] *kuśa* grass for the purpose of the seats."
Being authorized, one should invoke [the Viśvedevas] with the verse beginning "viśvedevāsaḥ."
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should also pour the *arghya* offering into the hand;
having given water, fragrance, garlands, and the offering of incense along with a lamp.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (aprasavya) and circumambulating to the left for the ancestors,
he should offer double-folded kuśa grass while reciting the verse "uśantas tvā."
"Having invited them, he should, with their permission, recite the mantra *āyantu naḥ*.
The purpose of the barley should be served by sesame seeds; he should perform the *arghya* offering and so forth as before.

Thus, having stated the completion of the section of ritual items beginning with the seat and ending with the covering for the twice-born at the Vaiśvadeva rite, the commencement of that same section for the rites dedicated to the ancestors (*paitṛka*) is established here.
Also in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, beginning with the offering of a seat,
one should fill two vessels after placing upon them *darbha* grass purifiers."
One should offer water with the mantra "śaṃ no devī," barley with "yavo 'si," and likewise worship with perfumes and flowers, then place [the offerings] toward the Vaiśvadeva.
Having invoked [the deities] with these two verses beginning "viśvedevāsaḥ," he should scatter barley grains;
having adorned them with perfumes and flowers, he should offer the *arghya* water with the verse beginning "yā divyāḥ.
Having worshipped them and being permitted by them, he should commence the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*). Thus it is said.

Thus, the ritual items beginning with the seating and ending with the covering of the offerings are performed according to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* (sequential performance by groups) for both the Vaiśvadeva and the Paitṛka rites, as prescribed by the texts. However, regarding the Brahmins belonging to each individual group, these items must be performed according to the *padārthānusamaya* (sequential performance by individual items). Thus, the preparation of the sacrificial enclosure (*parisarpaṇa*), the placing of the vessels, the scattering of sesame seeds, the spreading of the base-ghee (*upastaraṇa*), and the serving of food (*pariveṣaṇa*) are to be done for all the twice-born guests by means of *padārthānusamaya*. The sprinkling of the served food, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), the insertion of the thumb, the dedication to the deities, and the relinquishment of the oblation—all up to the final offering (*pradāna*)—constitute a single ritual unit (*ekapadārtha*) when combined; therefore, they should be performed for each individual Brahmin according to the *kāṇḍānusamaya* principle. Other acts, however, are performed one by one for each vessel, following the rule that the primary act is repeated (*pradhānāvṛtti*) like the Soma sacrifice, whereas those acts suitable for a single performance are performed once (*tantra*) for all Brahmins. Acts such as the washing (*avanejana*) are performed individually. Eye-salve, ointment, and garments are given three times to each person. Regarding the rice-offerings (*piṇḍas*), the application of eye-salve, and so forth, because they are prescribed with specific numerical qualifications—just as in the case of the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), the handfuls of grain, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), the potsherds (*kapāla*), the portions for Agni and others, the consecration (*dīkṣā*), and the ointment for the initiated—the same applies to the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). Thus, these are to be performed with their specific numbers attached.

Now, regarding the view that the performance of the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) is repeated for each [deity], one should perform everything from the setting aside of the food (*annoddharaṇa*) up until the cutting of the portions (*avadāna*) according to the method of sequential performance (*padārthānusamaya*), and then proceed with the four-fold portioning (*caturavatta*) ending precisely with the offering (*pradāna*). Just as in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, where the rule that the four-fold portioning ends with the offering—though it has been extended [from elsewhere] by analogy—is set aside by a specific scriptural injunction when one cuts the portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, so too here, since there is no such exception, the same applies to the *agnaukaraṇa*. Then, regarding the vessels: "everything [is offered] one by one."
Thus concludes the determination regarding the sequence [of the rules].

Now, those whose food may or may not be eaten will be discussed in the section on invitations (*nimantryaṇa-prakaraṇa*). Regarding the rule "one invited by one who is not censurable (*anindya*) should not refuse," therein "those not censurable" are those whose food may be eaten, and "those censurable" are those whose food must not be eaten. Therefore, their distinction is now made. On this point, Gautama says:
"A Brāhmaṇa should eat the food of twice-born men (*dvijāti*) who are praiseworthy in their own duties."
Yama says: One may always eat at the homes of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*); no fault is found in them.
However, one should not eat at the homes of those afflicted by doubt, nor should one cause food to be given to them.

Regarding matters concerning the next world and the doctrines of the scriptures, their mental dispositions are perpetually unsettled by the conceptual constructions of "is" and "is not," and they are thus overcome by such discursive thought.
Yama, Hārīta, Jamadagni, and Paiṭhīnasi [state]:
"One may always eat the food of a Brāhmaṇa, and that of a Kṣatriya on the festival days."
And for a Vaiśya among those [occupations] mentioned, but never for a Śūdra.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is nectar; that of a Kṣatriya is traditionally held to be milk;
the food of a Vaiśya is indeed food; and the food of a Śūdra is traditionally held to be blood.
A Brahmin who, upon death, has eaten the food of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, shall go to the womb corresponding to each of those [castes].

‘Always’ means without restriction of time. ‘On festival days’ (parvasu) means on auspicious days; invited for the sake of a *śrāddha* or similar rites, he may eat in the house of a Kṣatriya. ‘In [their] affairs’ (*prakṛteṣu*) means, that is to say, during occasions such as weddings and other festivities. The passage beginning with ‘[it is] nectar,’ etc., is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the preceding rule. By the statement ‘he would go to various wombs,’ it is understood that one should not eat the food of even the blameless Kṣatriya and Vaiśya more than once. — Paiṭhīnasi:

"One who dies with the food of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya remaining in his stomach enters that very womb," so says Āpastamba. Regarding the three classes beginning with the Kṣatriya, one may eat [their food] by custom; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, it should be eaten [only] by custom, whereas it is unfit to be eaten due to a specific cause when it involves an act for which no penance is prescribed. When an act requiring penance has been performed and the penance completed, the food may be eaten. One may eat the food of all castes provided they abide in their own respective duties, excluding the Śūdra, according to some.

"By nature" means generally. "From a cause" means from a specific motive. "An act not requiring expiation" refers to a committed great sin (*mahāpātaka*) or the like that is unworthy of penance. "Is attached to" means it is connected to. However, regarding "an act requiring expiation," which is fit for penance, for one who has "completed the penance"—that is, one who has performed the required expiation—Vasiṣṭha says:
"[768] One should eat the food of even a thief, provided he is particularly full of faith."
But this is certainly not the case for one who performs many sacrifices, nor for one who initiates many pupils.
The phrase "even of a thief" is for the purpose of praising faith;
and so Manu says:
"Of a learned Śrotriya who is miserly, and of a usurer who is generous..."
Having deliberated upon both, the gods ordained food to be equal.
Prajāpati said to them: "Do not treat the unequal as equal.
The gift of a liberal man, purified by faith, is [efficacious]; the other, given without faith, is destroyed."

He who, despite possessing wealth, fails to nourish himself, his religious duties, and his dependents due to excessive greed, is a "miser" (*kadarya*). A "generous man" (*vadānya*) is one whose nature is to give much. A "usurer" (*vārddhuṣika*) is one who lives off prohibited interest. "Having deliberated" means having reflected. One is a miser even though he is a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), while the other is generous even though he is a usurer. Prajāpati, by setting aside the food of these two as being equal, established that the generosity of the latter alone is superior because it is purified by faith (*śraddhā*). Thus says Baudhāyana.
Having deliberated upon both— the impure person who lacks faith and the pure person who possesses faith— the gods ordained that their food be equal.
Regarding them, Prajāpati said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
that which is slain by one lacking faith is surpassed by that which is purified by faith."
Yama said: He who eats the food of one who is arrogant, foolish, ill-behaved, evil-minded, and lacking in faith, is indeed a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
He who eats the food of his father-in-law eats the impurity of the earth;
they say that food is the impurity of men, and everything is established upon food.
For a man's misdeed rests upon his food;
whoever eats another's food eats that person's guilt as well.

‘Avaliptaḥ’ means proud. ‘Mūrkhaḥ’ means one who has not studied the Vedas. ‘Duṣṭavṛttaḥ’ means one of evil conduct. ‘Durmatiḥ’ means one of cruel disposition. Regarding the phrase “śvaśurānnam,” this is a prohibition against always eating food at the house of one’s father-in-law. Yājñavalkya further states that one should never eat food in the house of others, even if it is otherwise fit to be eaten: "One should not have a taste for another's cooking, except when invited by those who are beyond reproach."
‘Parapākaruciḥ’ means one who desires the food cooked by others. Manu also said: “Those householders who, being impure, subsist upon the food cooked by others...”
Therefore, after death, those who give food and drink go to the state of being cattle.
In this context, the phrase "except in times of distress" is to be understood as a supplement.
To that effect, Yama says:
"He who, while his own cooking is underway, partakes of another's cooking..."
He goes to the state of a horse, the state of a pig, and the state of a donkey.

For a twice-born householder who is nourished by the food of others, whatever sacrifice he performs, whatever gift he gives, whatever austerity he practices, and whatever study he undertakes— all that belongs to the one whose food he has consumed.
But when one approaches his wife after having eaten another's food, those sons belong to the owner of that food;
from food, semen is produced.
Hārīta and Jamadagni say:
Through the food of a Brāhmaṇa one incurs poverty; through the food of a Kṣatriya, servitude; through the food of a Vaiśya, the status of a Śūdra; and through the food of Śūdras, one goes to hell.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "The householder should not desire the food of another; so they declare. Those twice-born householders who consume the cooked food of others [are at fault].
Those of wicked intellect go to the womb of dogs, jackals, and donkeys.
"Having gone near" (upa) means having approached; "those who eat" refers to those who eat by themselves after requesting [food], even without being invited.
Regarding both the food and the eater—namely, the Brāhmaṇa and the Śūdra—Yama, Śātātapa, and Chāgaleya sometimes declare that the food is unfit to be eaten:
"The food of a Brāhmaṇa is unfit to be eaten when it has been invited by a Vṛṣala."
In the same way, food from a *vṛṣala* that has been invited by a Brāhmaṇa [is forbidden].

A Śūdra giving food to Brāhmaṇas, and a Brāhmaṇa giving food to Śūdras—both of these are persons whose food should not be eaten; having eaten [the food of] either, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"Invited" means one for whom an invitation has been received; the remainder of the sense is "having eaten that food.
Manu also mentions others whose food should not be eaten:
"Nor at a sacrifice performed by one who is not a *śrotriya*, nor likewise at a sacrifice offered by a village-priest (*grāmayājī*)."
A Brāhmaṇa should never eat at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch.

‘Aśrotriya’ means one who has not studied [the Veda]; when a sacrifice has been ‘commenced’ (tate) by such a person, a Brāhmaṇa should not eat at that sacrifice. Nor should he eat at a sacrifice performed by ‘grāmayāja’, meaning one who officiates for many; nor where it is offered by a woman or a eunuch. Regarding this, Medhātithi says: "Where the husband is overcome by poverty, and the wife—proud of her dowry wealth or the influence of her kinsmen—becomes the principal figure, that is called a sacrifice offered by a woman.
One should never eat at the sacrifices of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease.
The food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan are both loathed by the wise.

As long as these [conditions] such as intoxication persist, their food is not to be eaten. Others, however, consider "in abundance" (bāhulya) to be the key factor: the food of one who is predominantly impotent (klība) should not be eaten; likewise for one whose nature is dominated by anger. An "afflicted person" (ātura) is one suffering from a chronic disease; a "group" (gaṇa) is a collective, and the food of such a group is "group-food" (gaṇānna). However, there is no designation of "group" for brothers who are undivided, because of the statement: "For brothers who are undivided, a single religious duty prevails."

And for them, the single duty is the very performance of hospitality and other such rites; this is described in that [same] treatise on dharma: "A *gaṇikā* is a courtesan. That which, though edible, is 'loathsome'—that is, censured—by the wise:
the food of a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer, one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, one who is bound, and one in fetters."

‘Gāyana’ here refers to one who subsists by singing; for others, however, singing such as that of the *uparāntaka* and so forth is already prescribed. ‘Takṣā’ means a carpenter. ‘Dīkṣita’ is one who possesses the consecration known as *dīkṣā*, produced by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and other rites. This possession of the consecration known as *dīkṣā* lasts only until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding) sacrifice, because that consecration ceases with the *avabhṛtha*. Thus, although it may appear from this Smṛti that the food of a consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) is unfit to be eaten from the performance of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice until the performance of the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, nevertheless—because of Vedic texts such as "When the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] is completed, one should eat in the house of the sacrificer," which indicate that the food is fit to be eaten precisely before the completion of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice even while the consecration known as *dīkṣā* still exists—it must be understood that the unfitness of the food is stated by this Smṛti and others to last only until that point, in order to avoid contradiction with those [Vedic texts].

Āpastamba, however, has stated that even prior to the offering of the *vapā* (omentum) of the Agniṣomīya animal, once the substance intended for the sacrifice has been set aside, whatever remains of it may be eaten by the initiated (*dīkṣita*). He says: "One should not put on the garment of the initiated; one should not proclaim his evil; one should not eat his food. Or, when the portion for the sacrifice has been assigned, they may eat from the remainder; or when the Agniṣomīya rite is concluded, or when the *vapā* has been offered. In the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, however, the prohibition against eating the food of the initiated before the release of his fingers, and the permission to eat thereafter, are stated along with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Therefore they do not eat of him, for he becomes human; therefore they take his name here, for he becomes human. Now, as to why they do not eat before [that]: just as one would not eat of a sacrificial oblation (*havis*) once it has been offered, so it is in this case. Therefore, one should not eat of the initiated until he releases his fingers here. *Nigaḍaḥ* means "shackled. There is this much distinction between one who is bound and one who is shackled: the former is restrained merely by words, while the latter is constrained by ropes and the like.
The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman,
of a hypocrite, of a physician, of a hunter, of a cruel person, and of one who eats the leavings of others;

the food of a fierce person, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and food from which another has already sipped water— these must not be eaten for ten days after the death of a relative.

‘Abhiśasta’ means one who is accused of having committed an act that causes loss of caste (*patanīya*). ‘Ṣaṇḍa’ means a eunuch. ‘Puṃścalī’ means an unchaste woman. ‘Dāmbhika’ is one who practices dharma solely with the intention of gaining fame, profit, and the like. ‘Cikitsaka’ is one whose livelihood is medicine; this includes both an improper physician and others. ‘Mṛgayu’ is a hunter, one who generally kills deer for the sake of sport or for the sale of meat. ‘Krūra’ means one of a crooked nature, that is to say, one who is difficult to appease. ‘Ucchiṣṭabhojī’ is one whose habit is to eat food left over after being eaten by another. ‘Ugra’ is a specific caste, according to Amarasimha’s definition: “*Ugra* is [the offspring] of a Śūdra and a Kṣatriya”; or it refers to one whose presence is unbearable due to harsh speech and so forth. ‘Sūtikānna’ is food prepared for a woman who has recently given birth; even those belonging to her family must not eat it. ‘Anirdaśa’ means that for ten days the food of those in a state of ritual impurity (*aśauca*) must not be eaten. Therefore, although for Kṣatriyas and others the period of impurity may last longer than ten days, food must still not be eaten for exactly ten days. In the alternative reading *sūtakānna*, the word *sūtaka* refers to persons possessing that impurity, and they are ones whose food is not to be eaten for ten days. The mention of ‘anirdaśa’ is intended to indicate the non-cessation of impurity; thus, whoever has a certain duration of impurity, their food is not to be eaten for that long. Regarding the first reading, there is another interpretation: the food of a *sūtikā*—meaning a cow or other animal that has recently calved—is not to be eaten for ten days, provided that the ten-day period has not elapsed. ‘Paryācānta’ means that which has been interrupted by an *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water); the meaning is that when one sips water while in the middle of eating for some reason, the food already consumed becomes *ucchiṣṭa* (leftover), and it must not be eaten again.

Meat not honored by a ritual, meat from an animal killed for no sacred purpose, food from a woman who has no male relatives, the food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of an outcast, and food that has been sneezed upon.

That which is given with contempt to those worthy of worship is "undignified" (anarcita), but not that given to friends and the like. "Vain meat" (vṛthāmāṃsa) is meat that is neither the remnant of a sacrifice to the gods nor prepared for one's own sake. An "unheroic woman" (avīrā) is one who has neither a husband nor a son. A "hater" (dviṣan) is an enemy. A "citizen" (nagarī) is a master of a city other than the king. "Spat upon" (avakṣuta) refers to that over which a sneeze has been made. And [one should avoid] the food of the slanderer and the liar, and the food of one who sells the merit of sacrifices. Also the food of an actor, a weaver, and indeed the food of an ungrateful person.

A "slanderer" (*piśuna*) is one who breaks apart a matter told in confidence, or one who speaks of another's faults behind their back. An "untruthful person" (*anṛtī*) is one who gives false testimony. A "seller of sacrifices" (*kratuvikrayika*) is one who, having performed a sacrifice (*kratu*), sells it—giving away its fruit for a price by saying, "Let my fruit of the sacrifice be yours. Although in the ultimate sense there is no selling of a sacrifice, nevertheless, the food of one who acts out of such a delusion or through deception is forbidden. A "stage-player" (*śailūṣa*) is the wife of an actor; a "weaver" (*tantuvāya*) is one who subsists on the craft of the needle. An "ungrateful person" (*kṛtaghna*) is one who destroys a benefit received and engages in harm against the benefactor, or one who does not reciprocate a favor.
Of the blacksmith, the Niṣāda, the stage-player, the goldsmith, Vena, and likewise the seller of weapons; [774]

A "blacksmith" (*karmāra*) is one who lives by the profession of working in iron. A "Niṣāda" is one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother. A "stage-player" (*raṅgāvataraka*) is one other than actors or singers, such as a wrestler and the like, or anyone who attends the stage out of curiosity. A "Vena" is one whose sound is that of musical instruments. A "seller of weapons" (*śastravikrayī*) is a seller of swords and the like, whether finished or raw iron. [One should avoid the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers (*śauṇḍika*), and of a washerman; of a dyer (*rajaka*), of a cruel man, and of him in whose house a paramour resides.

Those who keep dogs for the purpose of hunting and the like are "possessors of horses" (*aśvavantaḥ*). "Liquor-sellers" (*śauṇḍikāḥ*) are those addicted to intoxicants, or those who live by the trade of selling them. A "clothes-washer" (*cailanirṇejakaḥ*) is one who cleanses cloth; the meaning is a laundryman. A "dyer" (*rajakaḥ*) is one who applies colors such as blue to garments. A "cruel person" (*nṛśaṃsaḥ*) is one who praises or flatters men—known in the world as a bard—or alternatively, one whose disposition is merciless. An "adulterer" (*upapatiḥ*) is a paramour, specifically one who lives in the house of a woman who has a lover.
Those who support a paramour, those who are entirely conquered by women, and those who consume the food offered for ten days for the deceased— which brings no satisfaction at all.

In the preceding verse, it was stated that one who lives in the house as the wife's paramour is unknown to her husband; here, however, the prohibition concerns food from one who, even though he knows the wife’s paramour is living elsewhere than in the house, tolerates him and neither restrains the wife nor the paramour. Therefore, those whose wives’ paramours live elsewhere and remain unknown are those whose food may be eaten. "Those conquered by women" (*strījitāḥ*) are those in whose houses the wife alone is the mistress and the manager, while the husband himself has no power over his dependents or wealth. The author prohibits the *daśāhika* (food offered during the ten-day period of impurity); that is precisely the *pretānna* (food for the deceased), which is prepared specifically for the sake of the dead. One must also not eat the food of one who lacks the ritual impurity (*āśauca*) of friends or relatives but nevertheless proceeds with the fourth-day *śrāddha* and other rites out of compassion. This is described in the *Rāmāyaṇa* in passages such as, "the *daśāhika*, the *navamika*, and the fourth-day *śrāddha*," and is likewise described by other authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras*. "Displeasing" (*atuṣṭhikaraṃ*) refers to that food upon being eaten of which no satisfaction of the mind arises.
Yājñavalkya said:
One should not eat the food of one who has not given it, of one who maintains no sacred fires, or in times of non-distress; nor the food of a miser, a prisoner, a thief, a eunuch, or a stage-player.
[One should not eat the food] of a lute-player, one accused of a crime, a usurer, a prostitute, one initiated into a group-sacrifice,
a physician, a sick person, an angry person, an unchaste woman, one intoxicated, or an enemy.

[The food] of those who are cruel, fierce, fallen, or outcaste (vrātya); of those who are hypocritical or eat the remnants of others; of women without a protector, of goldsmiths, of those conquered by their wives, and of those who perform sacrifices for an entire village.
[One should avoid] those who sell weapons, liquor-sellers, weavers, those who live by dogs,
the cruel, kings, dyers, the ungrateful, and those who subsist by slaughter.
The food of laundrymen, dyers, those who live by royal service, those who reside in the same house as their teacher, backbiters, liars, as well as wheelwrights,
bards, and sellers of Soma, must not be eaten.

The term "not given" (*adattāni*) is a component of the preceding sentence; its meaning is that one should not eat, except in times of distress, the food of a *śūdra*, of one born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), or of one who has abandoned the sacred fires (*utsṛṣṭāgni*)—even though they may possess the entitlement to the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires—provided they have failed to maintain them. By implication, it is stated that in times of distress one may eat the food of one who lacks the sacred fires. A "thief" (*caura*) is one who seizes the property of others, excluding the property of a Brahmin. A "lute-player" (*vaiṇa*) is one who lives by playing the lute. "Usury" (*vārdhaṣya*) is living on prohibited interest; by this term, the usurer is indicated. An "initiate" (*dīkṣī*) is one consecrated for a sacrifice. An "enemy" (*vidviṭ*) is a foe. An "outcaste" (*patita*) is a perpetrator of a great sin such as the killing of a Brahmin. A "Vrātya" is one who has lost his right to the *Sāvitrī* initiation. One of "dog-like conduct" (*śvavṛttī*) is a servant; or alternatively, one in whose household dogs have their sustenance is a "dog-keeper. A "king" (*rājā*) is the protector of the realm and the city. One who lives by the slaughter of living beings is a "livelihood-by-killing" (*vadhajīvī*). A "washerman" (*cailadhāvaḥ*) is a launderer of clothes. A "liquor-seller" (*surājīvī*) is a seller of intoxicants. "Together with the house of a paramour" (*sahopapativeśma*) refers to a household containing the wife of one's own brother-in-law. A "seller of Soma" (*somavikrayī*) is a seller of the *Soma* creeper. A "wheelman" (*cākrikaḥ*) is an oil-miller. A "panegyrist" (*vandī*) is a reciter of praises for others. The meaning is that the food of these members of the three higher castes, who are tainted by defects such as miserliness, must not be eaten because it is indirectly tainted through its connection to a master defiled by such faults. Although the food of an initiate does not become tainted due to the absence of a defect in its source, it is nonetheless unfit to be eaten solely by the force of the scriptural injunction.
Yama says: Actors, dancers, carpenters, leather-workers, goldsmiths,
village officials, eunuchs, and prostitutes are proclaimed to be those whose food should not be eaten.
A musician, a blacksmith, a potter, a weaver,
one who lives by making wheels, a washerman, a gambler, and likewise a thief.
One who carries a banner for a living, one who subsists on pride, those who live by teaching Śūdras,
a potter, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather;

A ‘naṭa’ is one who performs dance himself; a ‘nartaka’ is an instructor of the art of dancing. ‘Sthāyukas’ are village officials, for Amarasimha states: “*Sthāyuka* refers to an official in charge of a village. A ‘gāndharva’ is a singer. A ‘saucīka’ is one who subsists by the craft of the needle. A ‘tantuvāya’ is a weaver. A ‘cakropajīvī’ is a cartwright. A ‘kitava’ is a gambler. [777] A ‘dhvajī’ is a seller of liquor. A ‘mānopajīvī’ is one who lives by the work of measuring grain and other goods. In some readings, the term ‘dāropajīvī’ appears; in that case, it refers to one who lives on wealth acquired through his wife.
Sumantu says:

The food of those accused of crimes, outcasts, sons of remarried women, killers of embryos, unchaste women, the impure, weapon-makers, oil-pressers, wheelwrights, standard-bearers, goldsmiths, scribes, eunuchs, female slaves, members of a *gaṇa*, and prostitutes, is not to be eaten. Pig-butchers, hunters, distillers, dyers, basket-makers, and leather-workers are those whose food is not to be eaten and from whom gifts are not to be accepted.

‘Cākrika’ refers to a bard (*vaitālika*), according to Amarasimha’s lexicon: “*Vaitālikas*, *bodhakaras*, *cākrikas*, and *ghāṇṭikas* are synonymous. ‘Lekhaka’ means a painter. ‘Paṇḍaka’ means a eunuch (*paṇḍa*). ‘Bandhakī’ means an unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*). ‘Saukarika’ is one who lives by means of pigs. ‘Vyādha’ is one who lives by killing deer. ‘Vuruḍa’ is one who makes his living by crafting bamboo vessels such as winnowing baskets and sieves.

The food of a physician, a hunter, an unchaste woman, a magistrate, a thief, one accused of a crime, a rogue, and an outcast is not to be eaten; likewise the food of a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, a prisoner, a sick person, a seller of Soma, a carpenter, a washerman, a liquor-seller, a butcher, a usurer, and a leather-worker. Also, the food of a Śūdra who has not become a servant, of a paramour, of one who considers himself a paramour, of one who burns down houses, and of one who kills those deserving of death; as well as food proclaimed with "Who will eat this?", food belonging to a group, and food belonging to a courtesan.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps dogs, nor do they eat the food of the husband of a low-caste woman."
They do not eat the food of one who is conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house there is a paramour.

A *dāṇḍika* is one who, taking a staff, moves about in front of kings and others to clear away people; he is a "staff-bearer. A *śaṭha* is one whose heart is crooked. A *takṣaka* is a carpenter. "Of one who is not his own" (*asvabhūtasya*) refers to one toward whom there is no relationship of master and servant. One who "considers" or approves of someone as the paramour of his own wife. A *śvavān* is one for whom dogs exist; [the term refers to] such a person. Gautama.

One should not eat the food of those who have abandoned their kin, of prostitutes, of those accused of crimes, of those whose lineage is unknown, of jailers, carpenters, misers, prison guards, physicians, hunters, poisoners, those who eat the remnants of others' meals, and those who hate social groups—all these being excluded from the company at a meal—before one has reached the age of sixteen. One should also avoid food that is served without a reason, or where the rules for sipping water (*ācamana*) or rising have been neglected; and one should not eat when the host is of a different status than oneself, nor when the seating is uneven or the honors are unequal, nor when the guests themselves are not honored.

"Outcast" (*utsṛṣṭa*) means one who has been excluded from his own caste. "Unfit for mention" (*anapadeśya*) means one whose lineage, character, country, and so forth, are unknown. "A trapper" (*bandhanika*) is one who kills living beings with snares and other such devices. "One who deals in poison" (*viṣacārī*) is one who lives by the science of poisons. "An enemy" (*vidviṣāṇa*) is a foe. One should not eat the food of any of those mentioned previously in this section on those unworthy of the company (*apaṅktya*). "Accompanied by sipping water" (*ācamanavyapeta*) means given by one who has not performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). "Accompanied by rising" (*utthānavyapeta*) means devoid of hospitality such as rising to greet the guest. Likewise, one should not eat what is offered unequally to an equal, or equally to one who is unequal, nor that which is unhonored by one worthy of honor.
Āpastamba.

The food of the *saṅgha* is unfit for consumption, as is that which has been publicly proclaimed [for all]. Also [unfit is the food] of all those who live by their craft, those who live by weapons, those who live by fire, physicians, usurers, and one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) but has not yet purchased the King Soma. Once the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is completed—specifically when the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered—the food of the consecrated may be eaten. Or, if it has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; such is the Brāhmaṇa text. A eunuch, a royal messenger, one who sacrifices with *havis* oblations, one who has renounced the world (*pravrajita*) contrary to the rules, one who would abandon the sacred fires, and one who avoids all [food]—these are excluded. Regarding one who eats everything, a *śrotriya* who has rejected [his duties], the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, one intoxicated, one insane, one bound, a merchant, one who is "sitting in wait" (*pratyupaviṣṭa*), and one who causes another to sit in wait—for as long as that time lasts, [their food is forbidden]. Kāṇva says: "Who is this whose food one might desire? Kautsa says: "One who is meritorious. Vārṣyāyaṇi says: "Whomever might give. For if even dust, being stationary, is to be consumed by a person, then by the giving of food one becomes faultless. Pure alms are to be eaten. Ekata, Kuṇika, Kaṇṭha, Kutsa, and likewise Pauṣkarasādi [hold this view]. Vārṣyāyaṇi says: "Food may be taken from anyone. One should eat from a meritorious person who desires to give; one should not eat from a meritorious person who does not desire to give. He who avoids everyone and does not eat in anyone's house [is one who rejects all].
‘Sarvānnīnaḥ’ means one who eats all kinds of food; for Amarasimha states: “*Sarvānnīna* is one who eats all food, while *gṛdhnu* is one who is greedy. Ślokāpastamba says:
“Only two types of persons belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are fit to be fed: the student (*brahmacārī*) and likewise the householder (*gṛhī*).”
The food of a sage would be unfit to be eaten, as would that of all those who bear external marks.

A "muni" refers to both a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and an ascetic (yati). Regarding "those bearing external marks" (liṅginām), this refers to those who wear insignia outside of what is prescribed by the Vedas. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should avoid the food of those who are frightened, weeping, crying out, reviling, sneezing, eating in a distracted manner, or struck with wonder, as well as the food of madmen, outcasts, and the king's domestic priest.
Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should not eat the food of one who bears malice, nor that of one who harms the knowledge of Brahman, nor the food of those born of a Śūdra woman at a Śrāddha, nor foods that have been treated with contempt.
Devala says:

One should avoid from afar the food of the outcaste, the food of those whose food is unfit to be eaten, the food of those excluded from the ritual row, the food of a Śūdra, and food that is contemptible.
Vasiṣṭha says:
A twice-born man who, by appointment, eats at a birth-rite before ten days have passed,
becomes a worm after the end of his body and feeds upon that very excrement.
Yama said:
But that twice-born man who, having eaten at a *śrāddha* with fresh meat, should give up his life-breaths,
is cooked in most terrible animal wombs from which there is no escape.
But the child who is conceived after a twice-born man has eaten a fresh *śrāddha* meal does not attain knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan.
Likewise: "The food of a king’s servant, the food of a thief,
and likewise food during the period of birth-impurity or death-impurity— these cause even one who dwells in heaven to fall."
Śaṅkha says: A man who eats during the period of impurity caused by a death is born in the womb of a worm;
he in whose house one dies after having eaten his food is born into that person's own lineage.

Āpastamba: One should not eat in a family where someone has died, as long as the ten-day period of impurity (*anirdaśa*) has not passed; likewise when a woman who has recently given birth has not yet emerged from confinement, or while a corpse remains inside the house.

Aṅgiras: From the time of birth until the performance of the purificatory rites, and during the feeding of the child with solid food, those who are not sapinda relatives must not eat; this is especially true at the edge of the cremation ground.
Śātātapa says:
That food for which the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the guest do not eat is to be known as "vain cooking" (vṛthā-pāka); one should never eat from it under any circumstances.
Āpastamba:

One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who hates [others], nor of one who is suspected of a fault or who has been found guilty of one; for it is known from scripture that by doing so, one consumes the evil of that person.
Manu and Vasiṣṭha.
The killer of an embryo wipes away his sin by means of food and other such things; an unfaithful wife, her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer, their teacher; and a thief, the king.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who provides food and so forth; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king."
Aṅgiras: One should never eat in the house of women who have no offspring;
but he who, out of delusion, should eat there, shall go to the Pūyanaraka hell.
"Of women" means of daughters. And so says Chāgaleya:
"One should never eat in the house of a daughter who has no offspring."
And a member of the royal caste may indeed engage in coming and going with a woman by the Gāndharva rite.
One should never eat after giving away a maiden as a *brahmadeya* gift;
if a person of deluded soul should eat first, he will go to hell.
A woman wedded according to one of the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma is an "Agnidattā" (given by the fire).
Yama says: Having especially studied the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs...
Having eaten in the house of a king, one is born in the womb of a worm.
The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
and the food of a Vaiśya or the food of a woman who has recently given birth cuts one off from the higher worlds.
Hārīta says:

The food of a king takes away one's splendor (*tejas*); the food of a Śūdra takes away one's Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*). The food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut off even the worlds [of the afterlife].
He who desires to know his own self as pure and to attain the desired worlds should avoid from afar the food of a group and the food of a courtesan.

And this should be understood as a prohibition against eating the food of a king who has fallen away from his own duty—that is, kings who fail to protect their subjects and act contrary to the scriptures:
"One must never eat the food [of such a king]; by eating it, one goes to the Raurava hell."
Thus it is from the Smṛti of Chāgaleya.
Manu says:
"The food of a king takes away one's splendor (*tejas*); the food of a Śūdra [takes away] one's Vedic luster (*brahmavarcasa*)."
Longevity comes from a goldsmith's food, and fame from the food of a leather-cutter.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength; the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
But as for those others who have been declared in due order to be those whose food must not be eaten,
the wise say that their skin, bones, and hair constitute their food.

"Pūya" means equal to pus; it refers to the food of a physician when consumed. The food of those others who have been mentioned in this section as "those whose food should not be eaten"—specifically those enumerated individually—is equal to skin, bone, and hair. Whatever fault there is in consuming their skin, that same fault applies to their food as well.
Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:

The food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, and that of a usurer are "badly made" (*duṣkṛta*). The food of an astrologer, a village watchman, and a village spy is "poison. The semen of unchaste women, the pus of physicians and surgeons, and the blood of those who have superseded their elder brothers, those who have been superseded, those whose organs are pierced, the husbands of *vṛṣalī* women, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, the husband of an elder sister whose younger sister is married first, the sons of remarried women, and outcasts—these are called "badly made" because they are the causes of evil deeds.

A *sāṃvatsara* is one who lives by teaching auspicious moments (*muhūrta*). A *grāmakauṭa* is a carpenter (*takṣā*) in a village who is not dependent on others; for Amarasimha states, "A *kauṭa-takṣa* is one who is independent. However, according to the reading *grāmakūṭa*, a *grāmakūṭa* is one who sustains himself through various afflictions of the village dwellers.
Yama says: "The food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a slayer of a Brahmin is blood."
The food of a physician is pus; the food of a harlot is semen.
For the food of a washerman is impurity, and that of a leather-worker is sin; likewise, the food of a drunkard and a bell-ringer brings consumption.
One should avoid the food of those others who are unworthy of whose food one may eat;
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.
‘Yakṣmā’ is a disease. ‘Śauṇḍaḥ’ is a seller of liquor. Hārīta says: “The food of a usurer is excrement, and that of physicians is blood.”
The seed of unchaste women is food, but the food of a multitude is a misdeed in this world.

They say that the food of one who has committed a heinous crime, the food of an outcast, the food of a thief, pus and blood, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, menstrual discharge, and the excrement of a dog are all found in the food of one who officiates at sacrifices for Śūdras.
‘Rajas’ refers to the menstrual flow. Paiṭhīnasi states: “A householder should not eat the food of a Śūdra; otherwise, his spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa), strength, and splendor depart.”
Hārīta:
But he who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach indeed attains the state of a donkey, the state of a camel, and the state of a Śūdra.
Vasiṣṭha says: Any twice-born man who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach shall become a village pig or be born into that Śūdra’s family.
For one whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, even if he constantly studies the Vedas, performs fire-sacrifices,
or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher state.
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra,
those sons belong to the one whose food was eaten, and he shall not be a partaker of heaven.
Yama says: A Brāhmaṇa who, while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach, casts off his body—
even if he has maintained the sacred fires and performed sacrifices— shall attain the destiny of a Śūdra.
But for that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires yet does not refrain from the food of a Śūdra, five things perish: his self, the Veda, and the three sacrificial fires.
Aṅgiras:
That twice-born man who for six months eats the censurable food of a Śūdra becomes a Śūdra while alive and, after death, is reborn as a dog.

Since it is established by such statements as "never for a Śūdra" that the food of a Śūdra is unfit to be eaten even once, the mention of "six months" is intended to demonstrate the greater severity of the fault. Vasiṣṭha says:
"He who has eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during his birth-impurity..."
He would go to a terrible hell and be born among the animals.
Even the mention of impurity (*āśauca*) and so forth is solely for the purpose of indicating an excess of fault.
Manu states the specific scope of the prohibition against the food of a *śūdra*, which was previously stated without qualification:
"A learned twice-born man who does not perform *śrāddha* rites shall not eat the cooked food of a *śūdra*."
If he has no other means of subsistence, he may take raw grain from him for one night's supply.

The term *aśrāddhinaḥ* indicates by the word *śrāddha* the ritual acts such as the *pākayajña* prescribed for a Śūdra. Therefore, one should not eat cooked food belonging to anyone other than a "good Śūdra" (*sacchūdra*) who performs the virtuous rites mentioned therein. Alternatively, the reading is *aśraddhinaḥ*, meaning "one who lacks faith. *Āmam* means uncooked grain, rice, and so forth; and that should be *aikarātrikam*, sufficient for one day and not in large quantities. This applies when there is "no other means of subsistence" (*avṛttau*), that is, in the absence of any other way of maintaining oneself.
It has been stated that "one should not eat the food of a Śūdra"; regarding this, Manu and Viṣṇu state an exception for the following purposes:
"A landlord, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]."

An "ardhika" is one who receives half the share of the grain through activities such as plowing the land. A "family friend" (kulamitra) is one whose friendship has descended through the lineage of fathers and grandfathers. A "cowherd" (gopāla) is one who lives by the tending of cattle. "Slaves" (dāsāḥ) include those born in the house and others. The terms "slave" and "cowherd" are relative terms; whoever is someone's slave, and whoever tends someone's cattle, his food is to be eaten by that person. A "barber" (nāpita) is one whose work is shaving. I—

"He who offers himself through the actions of speech, mind, and body, saying, 'I shall dwell taking refuge in you, bound to you'—among Śūdras, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). By this, it is meant that among Śūdras, those such as the *ardhika* and others whose food may be eaten are intended, and not other Śūdras. Manu also clarifies this self-offering:
'Whatever his state of being may be, and whatever he intends to do...'"
And in whatever manner one should serve him, in that same manner one should present oneself—
disclosing one's lineage, one's dress, one's craft, and what one intends to do.

By this statement, one has declared oneself when everything has been reported—whether one has approached you for this specific task, or for some other duty such as protecting the royal household, or how one would serve you with this craft, whether by massaging your feet or by performing domestic chores. However, others, taking the word *ātman* in the phrase "the self (*ātman*), O son (*putra*), is indeed [your name]" to mean offspring, say that this refers to a Śūdra whose daughter is married according to his own desire, and that such a person's food is fit to be eaten. That is incorrect; first of all, this word *ātman* is not clearly used here to refer to a daughter, and the word *putra* is more commonly established as denoting a male. Furthermore, there is no purpose in teaching through an indirect term; if that were the case, it would have been proper simply to say, "and he who gives away his daughter."

Others, however, explain that the mention of "the half-share" (*ardhika*) and so forth is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for Śūdras who are related [by marriage]; by this, the fact that even a *pāraśava* Śūdra’s food is fit to be eaten is established. Yājñavalkya says:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, and the half-sharecropper..."
One whose food may be eaten is the barber, as well as he who offers himself [as a servant].
An *ardhasīrī* is one who receives a share of the fruits of agriculture by means of a ploughshare jointly undertaken with others.
Yama says: "A family friend, a ploughshare partner (*ardhasīrī*), a cowherd, a slave, and a barber [are those who may eat at a funeral]."
These among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Paiṭhīnasi states: "Slaves, barbers, cowherds, family friends, and those who plow half the field with him—
among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]."
Devala says:
One's own slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a farmer—
these five born of the Śūdra caste may have their food eaten by Brāhmaṇas.
Chāgaleya says: The families of cowherds, barbers, potters, and close friends, as well as those who offer themselves [as servants], may have their food eaten.
Regarding the section on Śūdras, Gautama says:
Cattle-herders, farmers, barbers, and servants are those whose food may be eaten.
A "cattle-herder" is a cowherd. A "farmer" is one who plows half the field [with the owner]. A "barber" is a hair-cutter. A "servant" is a slave.
Thus says Sumantu.
Those who have made themselves known as a farmer, a cowherd, a field-guardian, an attendant, or a barber, are permitted to eat his food.
Śāṭyāyani says: a family friend, a son of a noble family, one who provides food, a pupil, and a close companion [are also permitted].
He who provides happiness upon one's gain and who becomes a protector in times of fear—
such Śūdras may have their food eaten, provided they are found to be pleasing to the mind.
A "son of good family" (*kulaputra*) is a slave. Others, however, say that a son of a family head or farmer is a "son of good family. "Is purified" (*vibhāvyate*) means it becomes clear.
This concludes the determination of edible food.
Now, the means for the purification of substances.

In this context, "impurity" (*aśuddhi*) refers to a specific defect that renders a substance or other object unfit for contact and so forth. "Purification" (*śuddhi*), however, is the removal of that defect produced by a specific consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*). It is precisely because of this purification that there arises fitness for application to all ritual acts (*sakalakarmopayogayogyatva*).
As it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"The Vedic and Smārta rites must be performed by one who possesses the requisite qualification."
"With pure means of accomplishment, by one who is clean and endowed with perfect faith. Thus it is said.

Therefore, one who is pure should proceed according to the scriptures using only pure substances. Now, what is the need for scripture here, since purity and impurity are well-established through worldly convention? For the world indeed treats a substance touched by loathsome urine, feces, and so forth as "impure," and as "pure" once its odor and smear have been removed by washing and other means.
