Having recited the Dharmaśāstra that issued forth from the mouth of the Sage,
the readers of the Dharma sing the laws that have fallen from the mouths of the Munis.
The dharma that has been declared by these [authorities] is indeed to be practiced, and not any other;
for the purification of one who exceeds a *droṇa* [in weight] is recited in the treatises on dharma (*dharmaśāstra*).
One should not discard a whole *droṇa* measure of food if it has been licked by dogs or crows;
rather, one should remove only that portion which has been touched by saliva.
Having sprinkled it with water containing gold, one should heat it over a fire.
Touched by the flames of the sacrificial fire and by the water of gold,
and purified by the chanting of mantras by the Brahmins, that food shall become fit for consumption.

He [the author] himself states that food which is less than a *droṇa* in quantity, and which has been defiled by the great contamination of being licked by dogs and other animals, must simply be discarded: "When food has been eaten by dogs, crows, cows, and the like,
or when there is oil or even cow's milk [so contaminated], how can purification occur in that case?"
In that case, one should discard the food;
however, for oily substances, purification is achieved by straining them, while for dairy products, purification is prescribed by means of an ashvattha branch.
Devala also says:
One should not consume food that has been licked by dogs, cats, crows, cocks, or mice, for it is entirely impure in every respect.
He (the same author) states that even if more than one *droṇa* has been touched by a *caṇḍāla*, it must indeed be discarded:
"Food seen by a *caṇḍāla* or even by a dog is unfit for sacrifice;
one should avoid food further still if it has been touched by the remnants of a *caṇḍāla* or others."
Yama says:
At the sacrificial pits of the gods, at weddings, at sacrifices, and at births,
one should not avoid that food which has been touched by crows or dogs.
Having set aside a mere portion of the food, the remainder deserves purification.
Solid objects are purified by sprinkling, and liquid substances by heating;
water, fire, and clarified butter become pure through contact with them.
One should declare that which has been touched by the mouth of a goat to be pure.
Vasiṣṭha:
[832] In a temple grove, at weddings, and during sacrifices that have been commenced,
one should avoid food that has been touched by crows or dogs.
Having set aside just a mouthful of food, the remainder deserves purification:
for liquids by pouring water over them, and for ghee by sprinkling it.
For that which has been touched by the mouth of a goat becomes pure.
Bṛhaspati says: At a sacred ford, during a wedding, on a journey, in battle, during a national upheaval,
in a city, or during a village fire, contact with the impure does not cause defilement.
In Gokula, at the threshing floor, the oil-press, and the sugarcane mill,
the purifications practiced by women are not to be questioned.
Śātātapa says:
Purity need not be scrutinized in a cow-pen, in a kitchen for parching grain, in oil-presses and sugarcane mills, nor among women and children.
Hārīta says: "Manu has declared that roasted grains, oils cooked in a closed vessel, milk-rice, curd, and parched barley flour— these may be eaten by one who eats the food of a Śūdra."

This aforementioned purification, however, must be performed only in times of distress (*āpad*) characterized by the inability to procure other food. In non-distress, one should simply abandon the defiled food and procure another kind of food.
Furthermore, regarding those such as the naked ascetics (*nagna*), it is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*:
"If these [persons] should see the food intended for offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*..."
One should relinquish [the secondary] for the sake of the primary; however, the performance of consecratory rites is prescribed only in times of distress.

Food seen by a naked person (*nagna*) or others must be "discarded" (*utsraṣṭavya*), that is, abandoned. For the sake of the primary rite (*pradhānārtha*)—meaning for the successful completion of the principal acts consisting of the *agnaukaraṇa*, the feeding of Brahmins, and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*)—other food should be prepared. However, in times of distress (*āpad*), food seen by a naked person or others need not be discarded; rather, its purification must be performed. This has been stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"For sacrificial offerings (*havis*) that have already been prepared, the discarding [of those seen by such persons] should be done beforehand;
however, for the sake of purification, there should be sprinkling with water mixed with clay."
One should also perform the scattering of *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seeds) and black sesame seeds,
and one should diligently seek the sight of a twice-born man, the sun, fire, and a cow.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding "offerings" (*haviṣām*), that is, *havya* and *kavya* foods prepared by cooking, if one sees a naked person or others [of such types], "abandonment alone" (*apavarjanam eva*), that is, their total renunciation, is to be performed; this is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*). However, in times of distress (*āpadi*), for the sake of accomplishing the purification (*saṃskāra*) which serves as the cause for removing the defect, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with water mixed with excellent clay is to be prescribed. Likewise, scattering (*avakīraṇa*)—that is, throwing over—the defiled *havya* and *kavya* with white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) and black sesame seeds (*kṛṣṇatila*) should be done. Furthermore, the sight of a twice-born man, the sun, fire, and a goat should be sought. Thus, one should strive so that the *havya* and *kavya* become pure. Alternatively, one may perform the purification of food (*anna-śuddhi*) as declared by Jamadagni.
One may remove the defects of food by means of pure water and *darbha* grass, reciting the *Śuddhavatī*, *Kūṣmāṇḍa*, *Pāvamānī*, and *Taratsamandī* verses.

The meaning is that one should take water consecrated with the *śuddhavatī* and other mantras using *darbha* grass and perform a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for the purpose of removing defects arising from such things as looking at a naked person. The three verses beginning with "eto nv indraṃ stavāma" are the *śuddhavatīs*. The three *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses beginning with "yad devā devahelanaṃ," which are well-known in the Yajurveda, [are also used]. The *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "yad anti yac ca dūrake" [are used]. The *taratsamā* verses beginning with "taratsamandī dhāvati" [are used]. These are the means for purifying cooked food. Now follow the means for purifying water.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "That which is impure, soiled, moist, or smeared with excrement—all that is purified by water; how, then, can there be purification of water itself?"
By the falling of the rays of the sun and moon, by contact with the wind, and by the urine and dung of cows, waters are purified; such is the established rule.

Viṣṇu: From a well containing a dead five-toed animal, or one that is otherwise utterly defiled, one should draw out all the water; the remainder one should purify according to the scriptural injunctions.
Having performed the kindling of the fire, one should subsequently place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a well constructed with baked bricks and filled with fresh water.
In small, stagnant bodies of water on the earth's surface, purification is said to be like that of a well; however, in large ones, there is no defilement.
Parāśara says: Water may be taken from all sources such as ponds, wells, and tanks;
however, if one later sees that it has become impure, it is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If that water is defiled by dogs, cats, or mice having smeared it with bone or skin, it must be purified from the bottom in the same manner.
One should draw out all the water from a place where bones and hides have fallen, or which is frequented by donkeys, monkeys, and pigs; purification is achieved through thorough scrubbing.
If a step-well, a well, or a pond becomes somehow defiled,
it is purified by drawing out a hundred jars [of water] and treating it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
[835] In the case of wells, pits, and ponds, especially when they are doubtful,
one who has taken water from them is purified by drinking a hundred jars of *pañcagavya*.
If sandals, shoes, feces, or urine fall into a well,
one becomes pure by drawing out sixty jars of water and then using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
That which is defiled by impurities, moistened, or smeared with excrement—all that is purified by water; how then could there be any purification of water itself?
By means of the urine and dung of cows, by the rays of the moon, sun, and fire,
and by the force of the wind, the waters attain purity.
Thus end the means for purification by water. Now follow the exceptions regarding impurity. Regarding this, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Śātātapa, and Baudhāyana state:
"A calf is pure when it causes milk to flow; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual intercourse; and a dog is pure when catching deer."

Uśanas says: "The mouth of a woman is pure in secret; birds are pure in causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure in letting milk flow; and a dog is pure in the catching of deer. This continues in the tradition of Paiṭhīnasi.
A calf at the flow of milk, a dog in the catching of game, birds in the falling of fruit, and the face of a woman in sexual union. Śaṅkha says:
"The faces of women, calves, birds, and dogs [are auspicious]."
One is pure after sexual intercourse, from a fountain, from a tree, and likewise after hunting.
All mines are pure; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
a calf is pure at the flow of milk; and a dog is pure when engaged in the catching of wild animals.
Hārīta says:
A calf is pure at the flow of milk; a dog is pure among a herd of deer;
all mines are pure; and a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall.
Manu and Viṣṇu: "The flesh of one killed by dogs, as well as by other carnivorous beasts, by Caṇḍālas and the like, or by robbers— Manu has declared that to be pure."
Yājñavalkya, continuing from the word "pure," states:
"Likewise, meat dropped by dogs, Caṇḍālas, carnivorous animals, and the like. Vasiṣṭha [states]:
Fortunate are the deer slain tomorrow, the fruit fallen by birds,
that which is trodden upon by children, and that which has been used by women.
Merchandise that has been displayed, as well as the defects found on the faces of women,
are not considered blemished even if covered by gnats or flies.
Yama says: "Indeed, whatever water may be on the ground, and whatever meat has been killed by dogs—
the faults that exist in the mouths of women, Manu declared these to be no faults."
Likewise: That which has been stepped over by children, that which has been trodden upon by women, and that in which mosquitoes and flies have settled— none of these are considered defiled.
And those waters which reside upon the earth, and those which provide satisfaction to cows;
Yājñavalkya says: A ray of light, fire, a goat, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and the wind;
droplets, flies, a calf at the time of suckling, and [the calf] during the flow of milk—these are pure to the touch.
Likewise:
"The hand of an artisan, merchandise, alms-food, and the mouth of a woman are pure. Thus says Yama.

One's own bed, seat, clothing, or private parts, even when defiled by impurity, as well as almsfood received from a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), are always pure; such is the settled rule.
Likewise: "The wise do not find fault with a seat, a bed, a vehicle, the mouth of a woman, a kutapa blanket, a razor, or likewise a sacrificial ladle (camasa) during sacrifices."
A cow, a horse, droplets, a shadow, flies, locusts, parrots, a goat, an elephant, weapons in battle, and the rays of the moon and sun— [these are pure].
Earth, fire, water, wind, space, curds, ghee, and roads—
all these are always pure and fit for contact.
Likewise: "Fire is pure; the wind is pure; those who move about in the open air are pure;
water is eternally pure; and a path is pure from being trodden."
Likewise:
Water on the ground is pure; a woman devoted to her husband is pure;
a king intent on dharma is pure; and a contented Brāhmaṇa is pure.
Manu and Baudhāyana state:
"The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise spread out for sale;
almsfood received by a religious student is always pure—this is the settled rule."
Manu and Śātātapa state:
"Flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, the earth, wind, and fire are always pure to the touch."
Viṣṇu states: "The hand of an artisan is always pure; so too are goods that have been displayed for sale, almsfood offered through a Brāhmaṇa, and all mines."
Flies, droplets, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, the earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure— thus says Sumantu.

Women, children, mosquitoes, flies, shadows, seats, beds, vehicles, and droplets of water are always pure. There is no fault regarding drops of clarified butter or grass mats that have not been discarded. Hārīta says: Flies, droplets, women, the earth, water, and fire [are pure].
The cat, the ladle, and the wind are always pure.
Śaṅkha says: Water from a river is pure; likewise, all mines [of precious stones] are pure;
merchandise that has been displayed is pure; and the mouths of horses and goats are pure.
A cow is pure except for its mouth, and a cat is pure when it is walking.
Bṛhaspati and Parāśara state:
"A continuous stream [of water] that is not defiled, dust raised by the wind,
women, the elderly, and children— these are never considered impure."
A fly, droplets of water, a woman, the earth, water, fire, a cat, and a ladle,
as well as the wind, are always pure.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Objects occupied by children or women within houses do not cause impurity; smoke, fire, dust driven by the wind, droplets, shadows, and flies are pure to the touch.
Uśanas says:
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise that has been displayed for sale;
so too are mines, the drinking of Soma, and whatever is praised by word of mouth.
Baudhāyana says: Continuous streams that are not defiled, dust raised by the wind,
and all mines are pure, with the exception of a liquor mine.
Paiṭhīnasi:
All mines are pure, as is merchandise that has been displayed for sale;
a woman is purified by her menstrual flow, and a river by its current.
Furthermore, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"A cow, a goat, a horse, a dog, a fly, or a wind—these are pure in competition. Śātātapa says:
All the pure particles of dust, stirred up by the wind,
settle everywhere except upon asses, goats, dogs, and heaps of refuse.
Uśanas:
The dust raised by elephants, horses, and chariots is always auspicious; however, dust from heaps of other things, or that raised by dogs, donkeys, and camels, is inauspicious.

Baudhāyana says: "One who dwells in a city with his body covered in dust and his eyes and face completely filled with it, being self-restrained, shall attain perfection"—this is not so. The dust of chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious.
The killing of a dog, a goat, a sheep, a donkey, or a garment is commended by the Samūhanī rite.
Śātātapa says: There is no fault of being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) regarding water, nor regarding honey, nor clarified butter;
nor regarding fruits, nor sugarcane, nor minerals, nor women.
That which has been walked over by children, that which has been trodden upon by women, and that in which mosquitoes and flies have settled— none of these things cause defilement.
Paiṭhīnasi:
Honey, clarified butter, fruits, vegetables, and women are not considered leavings.
Devala: [The same].
Manu has declared that there are four kinds of pure things in the world for living beings: the clean, the self-purified, the sacred, and the exclusively pure.
Likewise: "A substance that is new or even stainless is called 'pure' (śuci);
but when it has been cleansed by another means, it is designated as 'purified' (pūta)."
For whatever substance has attained auspiciousness by itself alone—
whether stationary or moving— is remembered as being inherently pure.
That substance which cannot be defiled by others and which itself purifies other things,
and which is worthy of worship in offerings to the gods and ancestors— that is remembered as *pavitra*.
Then all grains, substances, and ornaments,
as well as pure foods— both those that are not to be avoided and those that are to be eaten— these alone [should be offered].
O knower of Dharma, when all substances have been discarded, the perception of impurity arises; yet in that very same [state], purity would not occur again here.
Therefore, the twice-born say that what is pure, functional, and clean is "śuci";
a substance that is stainless, refined, and fit for ritual action is called "pūta."
A dwelling, a water-vessel, a vehicle, a mount,
implements, a razor, a boat, and a seat— these are traditionally held to be pure by their very nature.
Children are pure by their very nature, as are women during a period other than their menses;
for the sin of killing a Brahmin affects women only when they have sexual intercourse during their fertile season.
For it is a settled rule that mines are pure by their very nature regarding the substances they yield;
likewise, merchandise purchased from traders is declared pure according to the Smṛti.
The Blessed Manu has declared that these three are pure: speech that is not defiled, speech that is praiseworthy, and speech that is itself pure and absolute.
Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; cows are pure in their backs;
flowering trees are pure; and Brahmins are pure at all times.
Ashes, honey, gold, *darbha* grass, woolen cloth, sesame seeds,
*apāmārga*, *śirīṣa*, *arka*, lotus, *āmalaka*, and a gem;
Garlands, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, sadābhadrā, priyaṅgu, unbroken rice, gorocanā, parched grain, turmeric, sandalwood, and barley— these are always auspicious.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, tulasī, dhātakī,
and vaṭa— O Brāhmaṇa, these they say are pure for offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
For embodied beings, substances that are nourishing, purgative of impurities, and cleansing are beneficial;
likewise, water, fire, cow dung,
and earth are especially purifying for the sake of cleansing all types of impurity for everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
Likewise: A fire kindled by impurities and not defiled by wicked men is capable of purifying all forms of impurity.
The purity of objects consumed by fire is prescribed;
for vessels touched by flames, purification is certain.
There is no receiving of fire that has been released by a *vṛṣala* except in times of distress;
for the *śvapāka* is the *vṛṣala*, the *brāhmaṇa* is the eater, and the fire is one not consecrated.

The learned never consider it proper to take fire from a Caṇḍāla, from a fire containing impurities, from the fire of a woman who has recently given birth, from the fire of an outcaste, or from a funeral pyre.
A jackal that dwells in a place purified by cow dung, yet frequents cremation grounds and the like, is not considered rustic;
its earth is pure, fine-textured, and free from feces and urine.
Manu and Viṣṇu:
"Those apertures that are above the navel are entirely pure;
those below are impure, as are the impurities that have exuded from the body."

Baudhāyana says: One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. For there is a Vedic revelation: "The part of a person above the navel is pure; that which is downward is impure. Viṣṇu and Yājñavalkya [state the same].
The goat is pure from its mouth, the horse from its front, the cow is not [pure] from its back, and human-born impurities [are not pure] from their front.
Uśanas says:
A man is pure above the navel; the cow is pure on its back; goats are pure from the front; but for women, the heart is the only part that is impure from all sides.
Yama says: A woman who has gone into seclusion is pure; among the mouths of women, wine is pure;
and in matters of touch, women do not cause defilement, just as wind does not defile scents or flavors.
The mouth-fluid of women, as well as their scent and their breath, is impure;
a cow is considered impure from her mouth, whereas a goat is traditionally held to be pure from its mouth.
A cow behind, an elephant on the shoulder, and likewise a pure horse on all sides;
but regarding the urine and feces of men, as well as impure substances and filth, [one must avoid them].
The dung and urine of a cow are always pure; such is the established rule.
Bṛhaspati says:
The feet of Brahmins are pure; the mouth of a goat and a horse is pure;
the backs of cows are pure; and all the limbs of women are pure.
The Moon enjoys her during the first appearance of body hair; the Gandharva, upon the sight of her breasts; and Fire, during the flow of menses. Women are thus pure, and not otherwise.
Whether she has been enjoyed by force, or has fallen into the hands of thieves, or has herself committed misconduct, or has been neglected; [844]
Even a woman who has been utterly corrupted does not deserve abandonment;
for an expiation is prescribed for all, and especially for women.
Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled. Month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharvas gave them beautiful speech;
Pāvaka gave them the capacity to consume all things, for they are indeed pure in every respect.
Yama says: Brāhmaṇas are pure in their feet; cows are pure in their backs;
goats and horses are pure in their mouths; and women are pure in every part.
Those who know all things declare that there are three sins for these women:
the murder of a husband, the killing of a fetus, and the causing of an abortion of one's own womb.
Whatever other things women on earth may do, all those are their own inherent duties; these women have been granted boons by the gods.
In former times, these women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, the Gandharvas, and Agni;
for they have been granted boons by them, and thus they are never at fault.
Soma gave them purity; Gandharva, eloquent speech;
and Hutāśa, the capacity to consume all things. Therefore, women are equal to gold coins.
Yamātrī said:
[845] A woman is not defiled by a paramour; nor is fire by its act of burning;
nor are waters by urine and excrement; nor is a twice-born man by his performance of Vedic rites.
Cows do not become defiled while carrying nectar; women do not become defiled by having been enjoyed by another;
and waters do not become defiled while remaining upon the surface of the earth.
Brahmins are not defiled by the acceptance of gifts.
Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana state:
"A woman is not defiled by a paramour, nor is a Brahmin by the performance of Vedic rites—
whether she has herself acted improperly or has been led astray by a Brahmin."
Whether she has been enjoyed by force or has fallen into the hands of thieves, one should not abandon a defiled woman; her abandonment is not ordained.
A woman who waits for her fertile season becomes pure through the period of her menses;
women are an incomparable means of purification, for they are never defiled.
Indeed, month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
In former times these women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
for they have been granted boons by them, and thus they are never at fault.
Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Agni granted them the power to consume all things; therefore, women are equal to gold.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for women in this world:
the killing of her husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus.
Atri says:
A woman who has been enjoyed by force, or even one who has fallen into the hands of thieves,
is purified by her menses, just as a swift-flowing river is purified by its current.
Whether she has herself committed an offense, or has been led astray by another,
or is utterly corrupted, the abandonment of such a woman is not ordained.
Women are an unsurpassed means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni.
Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Pāvaka bestowed upon them total sanctity; therefore, women are equal to gold.
Yājñavalkya says: Soma bestowed purity upon women, and Gandharva bestowed auspicious speech;
Pāvaka bestowed the state of being entirely pure; therefore, women are indeed pure.
Purification is prescribed after her menses in the case of infidelity;
however, abandonment is ordained if she becomes pregnant, or if she kills her husband or an embryo, or commits some other great sin.
Regarding women, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"There are three sins: killing one's husband, killing a Brahmin, and causing an abortion. He further says: "Month after month they are purified;
month after month their menstrual flow washes away their misdeeds."
Having waited for the time of flowering, she becomes pure through the period of the season.
Soma gave them purity; Gandharva, eloquent speech;
and Agni, the capacity to consume all things; therefore, women are equal to gold.
Yama says:
"Whether she has been enjoyed by force or has fallen into the hands of a thief,"
